name: AX_restricted_difference_3_ap_free_density
title: Problem 8
statement_text: Improve the range of $|S|$ in the following theorem: for each odd prime power $q$ there is $\varepsilon_q>0$ such that if $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q$ with $0\in S$ and $|S|>(q+1)/2$, and $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ satisfies $|A|>q^{(1-\varepsilon_q)n}$, then $A$ contains a nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression whose common difference is in $S^n$.
context_text: For a prime power $q$ and $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q$ with $0\in S$, a three-term arithmetic progression $x,x+d,x+2d$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ has common difference in $S^n$ if every coordinate of $d$ lies in $S$; it is nontrivial if $d\neq0$. The Ellenberg–Gijswijt theorem (the cap set bound) says that a subset of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ without nontrivial three-term progressions has size at most $q^{(1-\varepsilon_q)n}$. The authors adapt Tao's slice rank method to prove: for each odd prime power $q$ there is $\varepsilon_q>0$ such that if $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q$, $0\in S$, $|S|>(q+1)/2$, and $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ contains no nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression with common difference in $S^n$, then $|A|\le q^{(1-\varepsilon_q)n}$. For $S=\{0,1\}$, Bhangale, Khot, Liu and Minzer obtained only a density bound $O_q((\log\log\log n)^{-c_q})$ (improving density Hales–Jewett), and Green suggested that a power-saving bound might hold there. The authors say the problem already seems interesting for $|S|=\lfloor(q+1)/2\rfloor$ and, as suggested by Green, the power-saving bound may hold all the way down to $|S|=2$. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: A note on arithmetic progressions with restricted differences

name: AX_restricted_difference_triangle_removal_lemma
title: Problem 9
statement_text: Is there an arithmetic triangle removal lemma with restricted differences (in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, with the differences restricted to $S^n$ for a fixed $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q$ containing $0$)?
context_text: For a prime power $q$ and $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q$ with $0\in S$, a three-term arithmetic progression $x,x+d,x+2d$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ has common difference in $S^n$ if every coordinate of $d$ lies in $S$; it is nontrivial if $d\neq0$. The Ellenberg–Gijswijt theorem (the cap set bound) says that a subset of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ without nontrivial three-term progressions has size at most $q^{(1-\varepsilon_q)n}$. The authors adapt Tao's slice rank method to prove: for each odd prime power $q$ there is $\varepsilon_q>0$ such that if $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q$, $0\in S$, $|S|>(q+1)/2$, and $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ contains no nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression with common difference in $S^n$, then $|A|\le q^{(1-\varepsilon_q)n}$. The proof goes through a multicolour sum-free theorem: if $(a_{1j},\dots,a_{dj})$, $1\le j\le N$, are $d$-tuples of elements of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ such that $a_{1j_1}+\dots+a_{dj_d}=0$ only when $j_1=\dots=j_d$, then $N\le dM(n,(q-1)n/d,q-1)$, where $M(n,D,a)$ is the number of integer solutions of $x_1+\dots+x_n\le D$ with $0\le x_i\le a$; they also prove a version with an extra polynomial constraint that handles restricted differences. The (unrestricted) multicolour sum-free result was used by Fox and Lovász, and by Fox, Lovász and Sauermann, to prove an arithmetic triangle removal lemma in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ with polynomial bounds (Green's arithmetic triangle removal lemma states that if $X,Y,Z\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ have few solutions to $x+y+z=0$, namely $o(q^{2n})$, then all solutions can be destroyed by removing $o(q^n)$ elements). The authors ask whether a restricted-differences version extending their multicolour result exists; the precise formulation is left open by the paper. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: A note on arithmetic progressions with restricted differences

name: AX_flow_reconfiguration_5_flow_connected
title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: Is it true that for every 2-edge-connected graph $G$, the reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,5)$ is connected?
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops. Given an abelian group $A$, an $A$-flow of $G$ is an orientation of the edges together with values $f:E(G)\to A$ such that at every vertex the sum of incoming values equals the sum of outgoing values; for an integer $k\ge 2$, a $k$-flow is a $\mathbb{Z}$-flow whose values are all less than $k$ in absolute value; a flow is nowhere-zero if no edge gets value $0$. The reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ (resp. $\mathcal{F}(G,A)$) has the nowhere-zero $k$-flows (resp. $A$-flows) of $G$ as vertices, two flows being adjacent if and only if the support of their difference is a cycle (a connected 2-regular subgraph), i.e. one is obtained from the other by adding some value along a cycle; the empty graph counts as connected. This is the natural reconfiguration version of Tutte's 5-flow conjecture; it is incomparable with it, since connectedness of $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ does not imply non-emptiness. The group-flow analogue (with $\mathbb{Z}_5$) is posed separately. Note that the same paper answers this problem negatively: it constructs a graph $G$ with a nowhere-zero $\mathbb{Z}_5$-flow that is an isolated vertex of $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_5)$, so that both $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_5)$ and $\mathcal{F}(G,5)$ are disconnected (the abstract states that the reconfiguration variant of Tutte's 5-flow conjecture is false in the group and integer cases). The weaker question whether some integer $k\ge5$ makes $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ connected for every 2-edge-connected $G$ is also raised.
paper_title: Nowhere-zero flow reconfiguration

name: AX_flow_reconfiguration_group_implies_integer
title: Problem 2.6
statement_text: Let $G$ be a graph and $k$ be an integer. Prove that if $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_{k})$ is connected, then $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ is also connected.
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops. Given an abelian group $A$, an $A$-flow of $G$ is an orientation of the edges together with values $f:E(G)\to A$ such that at every vertex the sum of incoming values equals the sum of outgoing values; for an integer $k\ge 2$, a $k$-flow is a $\mathbb{Z}$-flow whose values are all less than $k$ in absolute value; a flow is nowhere-zero if no edge gets value $0$. The reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ (resp. $\mathcal{F}(G,A)$) has the nowhere-zero $k$-flows (resp. $A$-flows) of $G$ as vertices, two flows being adjacent if and only if the support of their difference is a cycle (a connected 2-regular subgraph); the empty graph counts as connected. $\mathbb{Z}_k$ is the cyclic group of order $k$. The paper observes the easy direction: if $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ is connected then $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_k)$ is connected. Unlike for the existence of nowhere-zero flows (which by Tutte depends only on $|A|$), the group structure matters for reconfiguration: $\mathcal{F}(K_4,\mathbb{Z}_4)$ is disconnected while $\mathcal{F}(K_4,\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2)$ is connected. The authors believe the converse of the observation holds, but cannot prove it even for $k=4$.
paper_title: Nowhere-zero flow reconfiguration

name: AX_regular_digraph_directed_treewidth_ratio_limit
title: Problem 2
statement_text: Let $c_r$ be the minimum of $c(D)$ over all $r$-regular digraphs $D$, where $c(D)$ is the maximum number of openly disjoint directed cycles through a vertex of $D$. Determine $\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{c_{r}}{r}$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops and no parallel arcs, but may contain both arcs $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$; a digraph is $r$-regular if every vertex has out-degree and in-degree exactly $r$. A collection of directed cycles $C_1,\dots,C_k$ is openly disjoint through a vertex if all contain a common vertex $v$ and $V(C_1)\setminus\{v\},\dots,V(C_k)\setminus\{v\}$ are pairwise disjoint; $c(D)$ is the maximum size of such a collection, and trivially $c(D)\le r$ for $r$-regular $D$. Motivated by the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture and its regular variant by Behzad, Chartrand and Wall, Seymour asked whether $c_r=r$ for all $r$; Mader showed this holds for $r=3$ but that $c_r\le r-1$ for $r\ge 8$ (open for $4\le r\le 7$), and conjectured $c_r\to\infty$. The authors prove $c_r\ge\lceil\frac{3}{22}r\rceil$ for every $r$, and, using blow-ups ($c_{rb}\le b\,c_r$) together with $c_8\le 7$, that $c_r\le 7\lceil\frac{r}{8}\rceil$, improving Mader's bound $c_r\le r-\Theta(\sqrt r)$. Using that $(c_r)$ is non-decreasing, they show that $c_r/r$ converges, to $\inf_r c_r/r$, and that the limit lies in $[\frac{3}{22},\frac{7}{8}]$; the problem asks for its exact value.
paper_title: Openly disjoint cycles and directed tree-width of regular digraphs

name: AX_regular_digraph_directed_treewidth_best_constant
title: Informal Question on optimal directed tree-width constant for regular digraphs
statement_text: What is the best-possible constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that every $r$-regular digraph $D$ has directed tree-width at least $\varepsilon r$?
context_text: Digraphs have no loops and no parallel arcs, but may contain both arcs $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$; a digraph is $r$-regular if every vertex has out-degree and in-degree exactly $r$. Directed tree-width $\mathrm{dtw}(D)$ is the parameter of Johnson, Robertson, Seymour and Thomas (defined via arboreal decompositions), measuring how close $D$ is to being acyclic: it is $0$ exactly for acyclic digraphs, it equals the maximum over the strongly connected components, and the symmetric orientation of an undirected graph has directed tree-width equal to its tree-width. For undirected graphs, minimum degree $r$ forces tree-width at least about $r$, but the analogue fails for digraphs: for every $r$ there are digraphs with minimum out- and in-degree at least $r$ and directed tree-width $1$. The authors prove that regularity restores a linear bound: every $r$-regular digraph has directed tree-width at least $\lfloor r/20\rfloor$. This is optimal up to the constant factor, since the complete digraph on $r+1$ vertices (all $r(r+1)$ arcs) is $r$-regular with directed tree-width $r$; hence the best constant $\varepsilon$ lies between about $1/20$ and $1$. As a corollary, regular digraphs of large enough degree contain a subdivision of any given cylindrical wall. The question is posed right after the analogous problem of determining $\lim_{r\to\infty}c_r/r$ for openly disjoint cycles through a vertex.
notes: Posed in the text as 'it would be interesting to determine' following Problem 2, without a formal labelled environment.
paper_title: Openly disjoint cycles and directed tree-width of regular digraphs

name: AX_polynomial_nikiforov_all_graphs_viral
title: Conjecture 1.8
statement_text: For every graph $H$, there exists $d>0$ such that for every $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ and every graph $G$ with $\mathrm{ind}_{H}(G)\leq(\varepsilon^{d}\lvert G\rvert)^{\lvert H\rvert}$, there is an $\varepsilon$-restricted subset of $V(G)$ with size at least $\varepsilon^{d}\lvert G\rvert$.
context_text: Here $|G|$ is the number of vertices, a copy of $H$ in $G$ is an isomorphism from $H$ to an induced subgraph of $G$, $\mathrm{ind}_H(G)$ is the number of copies of $H$ in $G$, and $G$ is $H$-free if $\mathrm{ind}_H(G)=0$. For $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac12)$, a graph is $\varepsilon$-restricted if it or its complement has maximum degree at most $\varepsilon$ times its number of vertices, and a set $S\subseteq V(G)$ is $\varepsilon$-restricted if $G[S]$ is. Rödl's theorem says that for every $H$ and $\varepsilon$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every $H$-free graph has an $\varepsilon$-restricted subset of size at least $\delta|G|$; Nikiforov extended this to graphs with $\mathrm{ind}_H(G)\le(\delta|G|)^{|H|}$. Fox and Sudakov obtained $\delta=2^{-d(\log\frac1\varepsilon)^2}$ and conjectured the polynomial Rödl version $\delta=\varepsilon^d$ for $H$-free graphs, which implies the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (every $H$-free graph has a clique or stable set of size $|G|^{c}$ for some $c=c(H)>0$). This polynomial Nikiforov statement unifies both. A graph $H$ satisfying it is called viral, so the conjecture asserts that every graph is viral. Bucić, Fox and Pham proved that a graph has the Erdős–Hajnal property iff it is viral, so the conjecture is equivalent to the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture. The authors prove that every graph $H$ in which every prime induced subgraph $G'$ with $|G'|\ge3$ (prime meaning not obtainable from smaller graphs by vertex-substitution) has a vertex of degree one and a vertex of degree $|G'|-2$ is viral, giving infinitely many new prime graphs with the Erdős–Hajnal property.
paper_title: Induced subgraph density. IV. New graphs with the Erdős-Hajnal property

name: AX_color_balanced_bipartite_matching_sqrt_k
title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: For all positive integers $k$ and $t$, every colour-balanced $k$-edge-coloured $K_{kt,kt}$ admits a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $f_c(M)=O(\sqrt{k})$.
context_text: A $k$-edge-colouring $c:E(G)\to[k]$ is colour-balanced if all colour classes have the same size. For a colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ or of $K_{kt,kt}$ (where a perfect matching has $kt$ edges), $f_c(M)=\sum_{i=1}^k\big||c^{-1}(i)\cap M|-t\big|$ measures how far a perfect matching $M$ is from being colour-balanced. More generally, for $h:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}^k$ and a subgraph $G'$, write $h(G')=\sum_{e\in E(G')}h(e)$ and $f_h(G')=\left\|h(G')-\frac{e(G')}{e(G)}h(G)\right\|_1$, which measures how far $G'$ is from being representative ($h(G')/e(G')=h(G)/e(G)$); colourings are the case where $h(e)$ is the $c(e)$-th standard basis vector, and then $f_h=f_c$ for colour-balanced $G$. All results assume $\|h(e)\|_1\le1$ for every edge. The authors prove, via a linear relaxation and a necklace-splitting argument, that $K_{n,n}$ always has a perfect matching $M$ with $f_h(M)=O(k^2)$, and deduce $O(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of $K_{2n}$ (resolving a conjecture of Pardey and Rautenbach), $O(\Delta^2k^2\sqrt{\log2\Delta})$ for copies of any $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ in $K_n$, $O(\Delta k^2)$ for spanning forests, and $O_r(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of complete $r$-uniform hypergraphs. Conversely, for infinitely many pairs $(k,t)$ there are colour-balanced $k$-edge-colourings of $K_{kt,kt}$ in which every perfect matching has $f_c(M)\ge\sqrt{k/2}$, and the authors conjecture that this lower bound is the right order for colour-balanced matchings. Any improvement of the $k^2$ bound for $K_{n,n}$ would improve all their other results by the same factor. For $k=n$ a colour-balanced perfect matching is a rainbow one, related to Latin square transversals.
paper_title: Colour-balanced subgraphs

name: AX_color_balanced_complete_matching_constant_bound
title: Conjecture 6.2
statement_text: There exists some absolute constant $C$ such that for all positive integers $k$ and $t$, every colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ admits a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $f_{c}(M)<C$.
context_text: A $k$-edge-colouring $c:E(G)\to[k]$ is colour-balanced if all colour classes have the same size. For a colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ or of $K_{kt,kt}$ (where a perfect matching has $kt$ edges), $f_c(M)=\sum_{i=1}^k\big||c^{-1}(i)\cap M|-t\big|$ measures how far a perfect matching $M$ is from being colour-balanced. The authors prove, via a linear relaxation and a necklace-splitting argument, that $K_{n,n}$ always has a perfect matching $M$ with $f_h(M)=O(k^2)$, and deduce $O(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of $K_{2n}$ (resolving a conjecture of Pardey and Rautenbach), $O(\Delta^2k^2\sqrt{\log2\Delta})$ for copies of any $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ in $K_n$, $O(\Delta k^2)$ for spanning forests, and $O_r(k^2)$ for perfect matchings of complete $r$-uniform hypergraphs. For every $k\ge3$ and $t\ge1$ the authors construct a colour-balanced $k$-edge-colouring of $K_{2kt}$ with no colour-balanced perfect matching (previously only one $3$-coloured $K_6$ example, by Pardey and Rautenbach, was known), which gives a constant lower bound; they conjecture that a constant upper bound holds. Since for $K_{kt,kt}$ there are colourings forcing $f_c(M)\ge\sqrt{k/2}$, the approach through complete bipartite graphs cannot prove this, and new ideas would be needed.
paper_title: Colour-balanced subgraphs

name: AX_color_balanced_spanning_forest_bounds
title: Problem 6.3
statement_text: Improve the bounds on $f_{h}(F)$ for bounded-degree spanning forests $F$ in complete graphs when $k\geq 3$.
context_text: More generally, for $h:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}^k$ and a subgraph $G'$, write $h(G')=\sum_{e\in E(G')}h(e)$ and $f_h(G')=\left\|h(G')-\frac{e(G')}{e(G)}h(G)\right\|_1$, which measures how far $G'$ is from being representative ($h(G')/e(G')=h(G)/e(G)$); colourings are the case where $h(e)$ is the $c(e)$-th standard basis vector, and then $f_h=f_c$ for colour-balanced $G$. All results assume $\|h(e)\|_1\le1$ for every edge. The authors prove that for every $n$-vertex forest $F$ of maximum degree $\Delta$ and every such $h$, $K_n$ contains a copy $F'$ of $F$ with $f_h(F')=O(\Delta k^2)$, showing that the error stays linear in $\Delta$ for $k\ge3$ (the first bound for forests with more than $2$ colours), but they made no effort to optimise the coefficient. For $k=2$ colours, Hollom, Mond and Portier obtained the bound $\frac{\Delta}{2}+18$, tight up to the additive constant.
paper_title: Colour-balanced subgraphs

name: AX_color_balanced_hamilton_cycle_bounds
title: Problem 6.4
statement_text: Improve the bounds on $f_{h}(H)$ for a Hamilton cycle $H$ in complete or complete bipartite graphs.
context_text: More generally, for $h:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}^k$ and a subgraph $G'$, write $h(G')=\sum_{e\in E(G')}h(e)$ and $f_h(G')=\left\|h(G')-\frac{e(G')}{e(G)}h(G)\right\|_1$, which measures how far $G'$ is from being representative ($h(G')/e(G')=h(G)/e(G)$); colourings are the case where $h(e)$ is the $c(e)$-th standard basis vector, and then $f_h=f_c$ for colour-balanced $G$. All results assume $\|h(e)\|_1\le1$ for every edge. Since a Hamilton cycle has maximum degree $2$, the authors' general bound for bounded-degree spanning subgraphs gives a Hamilton cycle $H'$ in $K_n$ with $f_h(H')=O(k^2)$, and their methods give the same bound in complete bipartite graphs. Given an almost representative Hamilton cycle with error $\varepsilon$, a necklace-splitting argument (Alon's necklace theorem) yields an almost representative perfect matching with error $\varepsilon+O(k)$; hence any improvement of the $k^2$ bound for Hamilton cycles improves the bound for perfect matchings, for which the best lower bound in $K_{kt,kt}$ is $\sqrt{k/2}$ and only a constant in $K_{2kt}$.
paper_title: Colour-balanced subgraphs

name: AX_spanning_trees_pivot_gray_code
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Does every graph $G$ admit a pivot Gray code on its spanning trees?
context_text: A Gray code on the spanning trees of a graph $G$ is a listing of all its spanning trees in which consecutive trees differ by an edge exchange (removing one edge and adding another): the revolving door property. Cummins showed that such listings always exist; in fact the flip graph (spanning trees, adjacent when they differ by one edge exchange) is edge-Hamiltonian, and this extends to bases of matroids. A pivot Gray code is one with the strong revolving door property: at each step the removed and added edges share a common endpoint; equivalently, it is a Hamiltonian path in the reconfiguration graph of spanning trees under such pivot exchanges. That reconfiguration graph is easily shown to be connected for every $G$, but it is open whether it always has a Hamiltonian path: the usual induction via $G/e$ and $G-e$ fails because uncontracting $e$ does not preserve the strong revolving door property. Pivot Gray codes are known for fan graphs and, more generally, outerplanar graphs. As Knuth noted, a positive answer would follow from his (harder) question whether every directed graph has a Gray code on its arborescences rooted at a given vertex (spanning trees directed away from the root, consecutive ones differing in one arc), by replacing each edge by two opposite arcs. The authors answer Knuth's question positively for tournaments and show that flip graphs of arborescences may have no Hamiltonian cycle.
paper_title: A Gray code for arborescences of tournaments

name: AX_spanning_tree_anticoncentration_min_degree
title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: Let $d$ be sufficiently large, and let $n$ be sufficiently large relative to $d$. Suppose that $G$ is a connected graph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, and let $\mathcal{T}$ be a uniformly random spanning tree of $G$. Then, for every tree $T$ it holds that $$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\leq n^{-(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}.$$
context_text: A uniformly random spanning tree $\mathcal{T}$ of $G$ is chosen uniformly among all spanning trees, and $\mathcal{T}\cong T$ means isomorphic as unlabeled trees; two spanning trees are non-isomorphic if they are not isomorphic as abstract trees. Lee showed that almost regular graphs of large degree $d$ have $e^{\Omega(n)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees, via the anticoncentration bound $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le e^{-\Omega(n)}$, and conjectured that minimum degree $d$ (large) gives at least $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(1)}$; exponential bounds are impossible since $K_{d,n-d}$ has only $n^{O(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees. The authors prove Lee's conjecture in a strong form: for $d$ large, $n$ large relative to $d$, and $G$ connected with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(d)}$ for every tree $T$, hence $G$ has at least $n^{\Omega(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees; this is optimal up to the constant in the exponent. The conjecture asks for the optimal constant $1/2$, which would match $K_{d,n-d}$: up to isomorphism, a spanning tree of $K_{d,n-d}$ is determined by a minimal subtree connecting the $d$ vertices of the small class (boundedly many configurations) and the numbers of leaves attached to these $d$ vertices, which in a uniformly random spanning tree follow a multinomial distribution with $n-O(d)$ trials and probabilities $1/d$; hence some isomorphism class has probability $\Omega(n^{-(d-1)/2})$.
notes: The full inequality in the statement was not explicitly reproduced in the extracted theorem block; the bound $n^{-(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}$ is inferred from the context text which states the optimal constant should be $1/2$ and that this would match $K_{d,n-d}$.
paper_title: Anticoncentration of random spanning trees in graphs with large minimum degree

name: AX_spanning_tree_nonisomorphic_count_min_degree
title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: Let $d$ be sufficiently large, and let $n$ be sufficiently large relative to $d$. Suppose that $G$ is a connected graph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$. Then, the number of non-isomorphic spanning trees of $G$ is at least $\Omega(n^{d-1})$.
context_text: A uniformly random spanning tree $\mathcal{T}$ of $G$ is chosen uniformly among all spanning trees, and $\mathcal{T}\cong T$ means isomorphic as unlabeled trees; two spanning trees are non-isomorphic if they are not isomorphic as abstract trees. Lee showed that almost regular graphs of large degree $d$ have $e^{\Omega(n)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees, via the anticoncentration bound $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le e^{-\Omega(n)}$, and conjectured that minimum degree $d$ (large) gives at least $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(1)}$; exponential bounds are impossible since $K_{d,n-d}$ has only $n^{O(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees. The authors prove Lee's conjecture in a strong form: for $d$ large, $n$ large relative to $d$, and $G$ connected with $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $d$, $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-\Omega(d)}$ for every tree $T$, hence $G$ has at least $n^{\Omega(d)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees; this is optimal up to the constant in the exponent. The optimal anticoncentration bound $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T}\cong T)\le n^{-(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}$, conjectured by the authors, would only give $n^{(1/2-o_n(1))(d-1)}$ non-isomorphic spanning trees, whereas $K_{d,n-d}$ has $\Omega(n^{d-1})$ of them; the authors conjecture that this larger quantity is an essentially optimal lower bound for all such $G$.
paper_title: Anticoncentration of random spanning trees in graphs with large minimum degree

name: AX_borodin_kostochka_list_dp_equality_threshold
title: Question 5
statement_text: What is the smallest number $\Delta_{0}$ such that every graph $G$ with $\Delta(G)\geq\Delta_{0}$ and $\omega(G)=\Delta(G)-1$ satisfies $\chi(G)=\chi_{\ell}(G)=\chi_{DP}(G)$?
context_text: $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the list chromatic number (the least $k$ such that $G$ can be properly coloured from any lists of size $k$). $\chi_{DP}(G)$ is the correspondence (DP) chromatic number: a $k$-correspondence assignment gives each vertex $v$ a list $L(v)$ of at least $k$ colours and each edge $uv$ a (not necessarily perfect) matching $\Pi(uv)$ between $\{u\}\times L(u)$ and $\{v\}\times L(v)$; an $(L,\Pi)$-colouring picks $\varphi(v)\in L(v)$ for every $v$ such that $\{(u,\varphi(u)),(v,\varphi(v))\}\notin\Pi(uv)$ for every edge; and $\chi_{DP}(G)$ is the least $k$ such that every $k$-correspondence assignment admits such a colouring. Always $\chi(G)\le\chi_\ell(G)\le\chi_{DP}(G)\le\Delta(G)+1$. The Borodin–Kostochka conjecture asserts that $\Delta(G)\ge9$ and $\omega(G)\le\Delta(G)-1$ imply $\chi(G)\le\Delta(G)-1$; Reed proved this for $\Delta(G)\ge10^{14}$, and Choi, Kierstead and Rabern proved the list version for $\Delta(G)\ge10^{20}$. The authors prove the correspondence version: for $\Delta\ge3\cdot10^9$, every graph with maximum degree at most $\Delta$ and clique number at most $\Delta-1$ has $\chi_{DP}(G)\le\Delta-1$, so that graphs with $\Delta(G)\ge 3\cdot10^9$ and $\omega(G)=\Delta(G)-1$ satisfy $\chi=\chi_\ell=\chi_{DP}=\Delta(G)-1$; this gives $\Delta_0\le3\cdot10^9$. The three parameters trivially coincide when $\omega(G)=\Delta(G)+1$, and also when $\omega(G)=\Delta(G)\ge3$ by the correspondence analogue of Brooks' theorem.
paper_title: On Borodin-Kostochka conjecture for correspondence coloring

name: AX_sun_free_graphs_chi_bounded
title: Informal conjecture on sun-free $\chi$-boundedness without net exclusion
statement_text: It could be true that the class of all sun-free graphs is already $\chi$-bounded.
context_text: For $t\ge4$, a $t$-sun is obtained from a $t$-vertex cycle by adding a degree-one neighbour to each vertex of the cycle; a graph is sun-free if it has no induced $t$-sun for any $t\ge4$. A net is the analogous graph built on a triangle (a $3$-vertex cycle with a pendant vertex at each vertex), and net-free means no induced net. A class is $\chi$-bounded if $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for some function $f$ and all its members. Trotignon asked whether triangle-free sun-free graphs have bounded chromatic number, and whether the class of net-free sun-free graphs (called sun-free graphs in his terminology, where the net is a $3$-sun) is $\chi$-bounded. The authors remark that they are not sure why the net needs to be excluded in the second problem, so the class of all sun-free graphs might already be $\chi$-bounded. As partial results, they prove that triangle-free graphs that are $4$-sunspot-free (no induced $4$-sun minus one pendant vertex) and $t$-sun-free for all $t\ge5$ have chromatic number at most $47$, and that bull-free graphs with the same exclusions satisfy $\chi(G)\le\omega(G)^{37}$, where the bull is the net minus one pendant vertex. Shift graphs show that $4$-suns must be excluded for a positive answer even in the triangle-free case.
notes: Expressed as a tentative remark ("it could be true that") following Problem 1.4, not as a labelled conjecture environment.
paper_title: Suns in triangle-free graphs of large chromatic number

name: AX_arithmetic_progression_packing_constant_4_3
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: $m(n)\sim\frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-diameter setting, $A_d=D_d\cap[n]$, and for $D\subseteq[n]$, $m_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{A_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $m_k(n)=m_{[k]}(n)$ for $k\le n$ and $m(n)=m_n(n)$. The authors prove $\left(\frac43-o(1)\right)\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}\le m(n)\le\left(\frac53+o(1)\right)\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$, and suspect that the lower constant $4/3$ is closer to the truth. The lower bound already holds when only prime differences up to $\sqrt n$ are used. In favour of $4/3$, they note that $m_k(n)\le(1.52+o(1))n^{3/2}/\ln n$ for $k\le\sqrt n$ and $m_k(n)=(1+o(1))kn/\ln k$ for $k\ll\sqrt n$. Pinning down the exact constant seems to require additional ideas. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Packing arithmetic progressions

name: AX_arithmetic_progression_packing_primes_asymptotic
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: $M_{\mathbb{P}(n)}(n)\sim\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{n^{3}}{\ln n}$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-size setting, $B_d=\{d,2d,\dots,nd\}$ (the first $n$ multiples of $d$), and for a set $D$ of positive integers, $M_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{B_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $M_k(n)=M_{[k]}(n)$ (defined for every $k$) and $M(n)=M_n(n)$. Here $\mathbb{P}(x)$ denotes the set of primes not exceeding $x$, so the conjecture concerns packing the progressions $\{p,2p,\dots,np\}$ for all primes $p\le n$. The authors prove $\left(\frac16-o(1)\right)\frac{n^3}{\ln n}\le M(n)\le(0.526+o(1))\frac{n^3}{\ln n}$ and conjecture $M(n)\sim\frac16\frac{n^3}{\ln n}$. They view the prime-only versions, this one and the analogous $m_{\mathbb{P}(\sqrt n)}(n)\sim\frac43\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$ (where $m_D(n)$ packs the sets $D_d\cap[n]$, $d\in D$), as apparently much weaker but key to understanding the general setting, and as closely related to each other. The lower bound in this conjecture follows from the proof of their lower bound for $M_k(n)$; the upper bound is open. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Packing arithmetic progressions

name: AX_arithmetic_progression_packing_near_sqrt_n
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: For every $k$ satisfying $\Omega(\sqrt{n})=k<\sqrt{n}$, we have $m_{k}(n)\sim\left(1-\frac{k^{2}}{3n}\right)\frac{k}{\ln k}\cdot n$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-diameter setting, $A_d=D_d\cap[n]$, and for $D\subseteq[n]$, $m_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{A_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $m_k(n)=m_{[k]}(n)$ for $k\le n$ and $m(n)=m_n(n)$. The authors prove that $m(n)=\Theta(n^{3/2}/\ln n)$ (with constants between $4/3$ and $5/3$) and conjecture $m(n)\sim\frac43\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$. For $k\le\sqrt n$ they show $m_k(n)=(1+o(1))kn/\ln k$ when $k\ll\sqrt n$, and $\left(1-\frac{k^2}{3n}-o(1)\right)\frac{kn}{\ln k}\le m_k(n)\le\left(1-\frac{k^2}{3n}+\frac{k^2}{48n}+o(1)\right)\frac{kn}{\ln k}$ when $k\le\sqrt{n/2}$, with a weaker upper bound for $\sqrt{n/2}\le k\le\sqrt n$. If $m(n)\sim\frac43\frac{n^{3/2}}{\ln n}$ holds, this also settles $m_k(n)$ asymptotically for $k\ge\sqrt n$, so the only remaining case is $k<\sqrt n$ with $k$ not $o(\sqrt n)$, which this conjecture addresses (the conjectured value is the lower bound). This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Packing arithmetic progressions

name: AX_arithmetic_progression_packing_two_regimes
title: Conjecture 6
statement_text: If $k\ll n$, then $M_{k}(n)\sim\frac{k^{2}}{2\ln k}\cdot n$, while otherwise, $M_{k}(n)\sim\frac{k^{2}}{2\ln k}\cdot n-\frac{k^{3}}{3\ln k}$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-size setting, $B_d=\{d,2d,\dots,nd\}$ (the first $n$ multiples of $d$), and for a set $D$ of positive integers, $M_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{B_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $M_k(n)=M_{[k]}(n)$ (defined for every $k$) and $M(n)=M_n(n)$. For $k\le n$ the authors prove that $\left(\frac12-o(1)\right)\frac{k^2n}{\ln k}\le M_k(n)\le\left(\frac{\zeta(2)}{2}+o(1)\right)\frac{k^2n}{\ln k}$ when $k\ll n$, and $\left(\frac12-\frac{k}{3n}-o(1)\right)\frac{k^2n}{\ln k}\le M_k(n)$ in general, with corresponding upper bounds involving $\zeta(2)$ and $\zeta(3)$. The conjecture asserts that the lower bounds are asymptotically tight in both regimes, $k\ll n$ and $k$ of order $n$ (with $k<n$). In particular for $k=n$ it gives $M(n)\sim\frac16\frac{n^3}{\ln n}$, also conjectured separately. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Packing arithmetic progressions

name: AX_arithmetic_progression_packing_fixed_n
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: For every fixed $n$ and $k$ tending to infinity, we have $M_{k}(n)=(1+o(1))nk$.
context_text: A family $\{A_1,\dots,A_k\}$ of finite sets of positive integers can be packed into $[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}$ if there are integer shifts $s_i$ such that the shifted copies $s_i+A_i$ lie in $[m]$ and are pairwise disjoint; $m(\mathcal{F})$ is the least such $m$. Let $D_d=\{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$, and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. In the bounded-size setting, $B_d=\{d,2d,\dots,nd\}$ (the first $n$ multiples of $d$), and for a set $D$ of positive integers, $M_D(n)$ is the least $m$ such that $\{B_d:d\in D\}$ can be packed into $[m]$; $M_k(n)=M_{[k]}(n)$ (defined for every $k$) and $M(n)=M_n(n)$. Since the $k$ progressions have $n$ elements each, $M_k(n)\ge nk$ trivially. The authors prove that for every $n$ there is $k_0(n)$ with $M_k(n)\le3nk$ for all $k\ge k_0$, using a hypergraph matching argument: for every $\epsilon>0$ and $k$ large, at least $(1-\epsilon)k$ of the progressions $B_1,\dots,B_k$ can be packed into the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_{nk}$. They suspect that the trivial lower bound is asymptotically correct. Such a bound may fail for general families of $n$-element sets: $k$ copies of $\{1,\dots,r,2r,3r,\dots,(r+1)r\}$ (with $n=2r$) need an interval of length $\Omega(kn^2)$. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Packing arithmetic progressions

name: AX_tverberg_number_s_convex_sets
title: Problem 1.4
statement_text: Determine or estimate the least integer $f=f_{r}(d,s_{1},\ldots,s_{r})$ such that for any set $P$ of $f$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ there is a partition into $r$ pairwise disjoint sets $P=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}P_{i}$ such that for any family of sets $C_{1},\ldots,C_{r}$ with $P_{i}\subset C_{i}$ where $C_{i}$ is an $s_{i}$-convex set for every $i\in[r]$ we have that $\bigcap_{i=1}^{r}C_{i}\neq\emptyset$.
context_text: For an integer $s\geq 1$, a set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ is $s$-convex if it is the union of $s$ convex sets. The two-part case is a problem of Kalai from the 1970s (problem 6.6 in the survey of Bárány and Kalai): determine the least $f(d,s,t)$ such that any $f$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ can be partitioned as $A\cup B$ so that any $s$-convex set containing $A$ intersects any $t$-convex set containing $B$; Bárány and Kalai showed finiteness via hypergraph Ramsey theory with a horrible bound. The present problem is its Tverberg-type generalization to $r$ parts. Radon's theorem is equivalent to $f(d,1,1)=d+2$ and Tverberg's theorem to $f_{r}(d,1,\ldots,1)=(r-1)(d+1)+1$. Using an extended (multi-part) VC-dimension argument, the paper proves $f(d,s,t)=O(dst\log(st+1))$ and $f_{r}(d,s_{1},\ldots,s_{r})=O\left(dr^{2}\log r\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}\cdot\ln(1+\prod_{i=1}^{r}s_{i})\right)$, and the proofs work in abstract separable convexity spaces with bounded Radon number. Following the paper, Chen et al. obtained the nearly matching lower bound $f_r(d,s,\ldots,s)\geq(d-2r+4)s^r$ for $d\geq 2r-2$; the exact determination remains open.
notes: The paper proves the upper bound $f_{r}(d,s_{1},\ldots,s_{r})=O\left(dr^{2}\cdot\log r\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{r}s_{i}\cdot\ln(1+\prod_{i=1}^{r}s_{i})\right)$ via Theorem 1.6, partially addressing this problem. A 2025 paper by Chen et al. (reference [9]) is titled 'A Tverberg-type problem of Kalai: Two negative answers to questions of Alon and Smorodinsky', suggesting specific sub-questions of this problem are attributed to the paper authors.
paper_title: Extended VC-dimension, and Radon and Tverberg type theorems for unions of convex sets

name: AX_large_treewidth_unavoidable_induced_subgraphs
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: What are the unavoidable induced subgraphs of graphs with large treewidth?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. The question asks for a list of graph families such that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains a large member of one of them as an induced subgraph, analogous to the grid theorem. For subgraphs and minors the answer is Robertson and Seymour's theorem: every graph of large treewidth contains a subdivision of a large $r\times r$ wall $W_{r\times r}$ (the $r$-by-$r$ hexagonal grid) as a subgraph. For induced subgraphs the answer must include the basic obstructions: complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs $K_{t,t}$, subdivisions of walls, and line graphs of subdivisions of walls. These are not enough, as shown by non-basic obstructions such as the Pohoata–Davies graphs, occultations and layered wheels. In all of them large treewidth comes with a large complete minor, and the first two even have large complete bipartite induced minors. Here $G$ has an induced minor isomorphic to $H$ if there are pairwise disjoint connected induced subgraphs (branch sets) $G_v$, $v\in V(H)$, such that $G_u$ and $G_v$ are joined by an edge exactly when $uv\in E(H)$. This question is the central goal of the authors' series of papers on induced subgraphs and tree decompositions. In this paper they characterize the unavoidable induced subgraphs of graphs with a large complete bipartite induced minor. Such a graph either has a large wall as an induced minor or contains a large constellation: a graph with a stable set $S$ such that every component of the rest is a path and every vertex of $S$ has a neighbour in each of these paths. They also show that large constellations contain basic obstructions or one of two highly structured types of constellations (generalizing occultations and Pohoata–Davies graphs), and that both types are necessary.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions XVI. Complete bipartite induced minors

name: AX_vertex_transitive_digraph_linear_perimeter_gap
title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: There exists an $\varepsilon>0$ and infinitely many values of $n$ for which there exists a connected vertex transitive digraph of order $n$, whose perimeter gap is at least $\varepsilon n$.
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Trotter and Erdős gave infinitely many connected vertex transitive digraphs with no Hamilton cycle, and Alspach asked in 1981 whether the perimeter gap of such digraphs can be arbitrarily large. The authors answer this: for infinitely many $n$ there is a connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices (a Cartesian product of two directed cycles, a Cayley digraph of an abelian group) with perimeter gap at least $(1-o(1))\ln n$; and they prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n\ge2$ vertices has a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ (and a directed path of length $\Omega(\sqrt n)$), a directed analogue of Babai's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ bound for vertex transitive graphs, the best undirected bound now being $\Omega(n^{9/14})$ (Norin, Steiner, Thomassé, Wollan). Determining the best possible bounds seems far out of reach, since even the undirected case is not understood; the authors propose this conjecture as a more attainable intermediate target, and say that even improving their logarithmic lower bound on the perimeter gap to a polynomial one would be interesting.
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

name: AX_vertex_transitive_digraph_circumference_vs_undirected
title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: Let $c(n)$ denote the minimum circumference of a connected vertex transitive graph on $n$ vertices. Let $d(n)$ denote the minimum circumference of a connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices. Then $d(n)=\Theta(c(n))$.
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Trotter and Erdős gave infinitely many connected vertex transitive digraphs with no Hamilton cycle, and Alspach asked in 1981 whether the perimeter gap of such digraphs can be arbitrarily large. The authors answer this: for infinitely many $n$ there is a connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices (a Cartesian product of two directed cycles, a Cayley digraph of an abelian group) with perimeter gap at least $(1-o(1))\ln n$; and they prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n\ge2$ vertices has a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ (and a directed path of length $\Omega(\sqrt n)$), a directed analogue of Babai's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ bound for vertex transitive graphs, the best undirected bound now being $\Omega(n^{9/14})$ (Norin, Steiner, Thomassé, Wollan). Since an undirected graph is a special digraph, $d(n)\le c(n)$. The authors' $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ bound for digraphs is weaker than the best undirected bound, and they suggest at least matching it asymptotically, or even proving this conjecture that the directed and undirected answers are asymptotically the same. The undirected proofs do not extend because they rely on the fact that any two longest cycles of a 2-connected graph intersect, which fails badly for strongly 2-connected digraphs.
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

name: AX_vertex_transitive_digraph_longest_cycles_intersect
title: Question 4.3
statement_text: Is it true that in any connected vertex transitive digraph, any two longest directed cycles intersect?
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Two cycles intersect if they share a vertex. In a 2-connected undirected graph any two longest cycles intersect, a fact used crucially in all proofs of long cycles in vertex transitive graphs (Babai's $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ bound and its improvements). This fails for strongly 2-connected digraphs: the authors give strongly 2-connected digraphs with all in- and out-degrees equal to 2 whose longest directed cycles have length four and which contain arbitrarily many vertex-disjoint longest cycles (while directed paths are arbitrarily long). They nevertheless prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices has a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$, and ask whether vertex transitivity is a condition that guarantees that longest cycles pairwise intersect, which would help translate undirected results to digraphs.
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

name: AX_vertex_transitive_digraph_path_vs_cycle
title: Question 4.4
statement_text: Does there exist $C>0$ such that in any vertex transitive digraph, the length of a longest path is by at most a factor of $C$ larger than the length of a longest directed cycle?
context_text: All digraphs are finite; a digraph is vertex transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertices, and connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected (for vertex transitive digraphs this coincides with strong connectivity). Pairs of opposite arcs are allowed, so an undirected graph can be viewed as the digraph with both orientations of every edge, and vertex transitive graphs are a special case. The circumference is the length of a longest directed cycle, and the perimeter gap of a digraph is its number of vertices minus its circumference, measuring how far it is from Hamiltonian. Paths and cycles are directed. In connected vertex transitive undirected graphs, the lengths of a longest path and of a longest cycle are within a constant factor of each other by a classical result. The authors prove that every connected vertex transitive digraph on $n$ vertices has a directed path of length $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ but only a directed cycle of length $\Omega(n^{1/3})$; in general digraphs, even strongly 2-connected ones, long directed paths do not force long directed cycles. Their construction of connected vertex transitive digraphs with perimeter gap at least $(1-o(1))\ln n$ shows that the two lengths can differ by at least an additive logarithmic term, since it is a Cayley digraph of an abelian group and such digraphs always have a directed Hamiltonian path (Holsztyński and Strube).
paper_title: Long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs

name: AX_cop_number_sublinear_treedepth
title: Problem 9
statement_text: Is it true that for connected graphs $G$, $\operatorname{cop}(G)=o(\mathrm{td}(G))$?
context_text: In the cops and robber game, cops first choose vertices of $G$ (several may share a vertex), then the robber chooses a vertex; in each subsequent round every cop stays or moves to an adjacent vertex, then the robber does the same, and the cops win if some cop eventually occupies the robber's vertex. The cop number $\operatorname{cop}(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that can guarantee a win. The treedepth $\mathrm{td}(G)$ of a connected graph is the minimum number of vertices on a root-to-leaf path of a rooted tree whose closure (each vertex made adjacent to all its descendants) contains $G$ as a subgraph; it satisfies $\operatorname{tw}(G)+1\le\mathrm{td}(G)\le\operatorname{vc}(G)+1$, where $\operatorname{vc}(G)$ is the vertex cover number (minimum size of a set meeting every edge), so it lies between treewidth and vertex cover number. Meyniel's conjecture asks for $\operatorname{cop}(G)=O(\sqrt n)$ on $n$-vertex connected graphs, and the best bound is $n/2^{(1-o(1))\sqrt{\log n}}$ (Lu–Peng, Scott–Sudakov). Graphs of treewidth $k$ have cop number at most $k/2+1$, and it is unknown whether this is asymptotically tight. The authors prove the first sublinear bound in terms of the vertex cover number, $\operatorname{cop}(G)\le k/2^{(1-o(1))\sqrt{\log k}}$ for connected graphs with $\operatorname{vc}(G)=k$, and ask whether this extends to treedepth. They note that $\operatorname{cop}(G)\le\frac12(\mathrm{td}(G)+1)$ follows easily from the treewidth bound, but do not see how to improve on it significantly.
paper_title: Cops and robber in graphs with bounded vertex cover number

name: AX_tournament_ordering_clique_approximation_algorithm
title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: There is a function $f$ such that for every integer $k$, there is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a tournament $T$, correctly concludes that $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\geq k$, or finds an order $\prec$ of $V(T)$ such that $\omega(T^{\prec})\leq f(k)$
context_text: A feedback arc set (FAS) of a tournament $T$ is a set $F$ of arcs such that $T\setminus F$ is acyclic. Given a total order $\prec$ of $V(T)$, the backedge graph $T^\prec$ is the undirected graph on $V(T)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc; the FASs of $T$ are exactly the edge sets of the graphs $T^\prec$. For a class $\mathcal{C}$ of undirected graphs, a $\mathcal{C}$-FAS is a FAS whose underlying undirected graph belongs to $\mathcal{C}$, and the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem asks whether a given tournament has one. The dichromatic number of $T$ (minimum number of transitive subtournaments partitioning $V(T)$) equals $\min_\prec\chi(T^\prec)$, and by analogy the clique number of a tournament is defined as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)=\min_\prec\omega(T^\prec)$, the minimum over all total orders of $V(T)$; so $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\le k$ if and only if $T$ has a FAS inducing a graph of clique number at most $k$. Deciding whether $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\le k$ was recently proved NP-complete for larger $k$, while deciding whether $T$ has a triangle-free FAS is open (the paper's introduction and conclusion give slightly inconsistent thresholds). Aboulker, Aubian, Charbit and Thomassé proved an approximation version for $k=3$: there are a constant $c$ and a polynomial-time algorithm that, given $T$, correctly concludes that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\ge3$ or finds an order $\prec$ with $\omega(T^\prec)\le c$. The conjecture asks for such an approximation for every $k$.
paper_title: Finding forest-orderings of tournaments is NP-complete

name: AX_tournament_c_fas_paths_matchings_complexity
title: Problem 4.4
statement_text: What is the complexity of the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem when $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of all paths? when $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of graphs with maximum degree $1$?
context_text: A feedback arc set (FAS) of a tournament $T$ is a set $F$ of arcs such that $T\setminus F$ is acyclic. Given a total order $\prec$ of $V(T)$, the backedge graph $T^\prec$ is the undirected graph on $V(T)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc; the FASs of $T$ are exactly the edge sets of the graphs $T^\prec$. For a class $\mathcal{C}$ of undirected graphs, a $\mathcal{C}$-FAS is a FAS whose underlying undirected graph belongs to $\mathcal{C}$, and the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem asks whether a given tournament has one. The authors prove that the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem is NP-complete when $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of forests (by reduction from 3-SAT), and hence also for trees, since a tournament has a forest-ordering if and only if it has a tree-ordering. Deciding whether a tournament is $k$-dicolourable is the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem for $k$-colourable graphs, NP-complete for every $k\ge2$, and Chen et al. showed it is NP-complete to decide whether a tournament has a bipartite backedge graph. It is natural to ask for which classes $\mathcal{C}$ the problem is in P; paths and matchings (graphs of maximum degree at most 1) are two natural candidates. Related motivation: Chudnovsky et al. conjectured that a tournament has the strong Erdős–Hajnal property if and only if it has a FAS inducing a forest.
paper_title: Finding forest-orderings of tournaments is NP-complete

name: AX_domination_packing_ratio_bounded_2_independence
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Which graph classes have bounded domination-to-2-independence ratio?
context_text: The domination number $\gamma(G)$ is the minimum size of a set $D\subseteq V(G)$ such that every vertex is in $D$ or has a neighbor in $D$; the $2$-independence number $\alpha_2(G)$ is the maximum size of a set of vertices pairwise at distance greater than two (equivalently, of a packing of pairwise disjoint closed neighborhoods). Clearly $\alpha_2(G)\le\gamma(G)$, and the fractional relaxations of the two parameters are dual linear programs with equal value, computable in polynomial time; so when $\gamma/\alpha_2$ is bounded both parameters are approximated by their common fractional relaxation, whereas both are hard to approximate in general. The domination-to-2-independence ratio of a class $\mathcal{G}$ is $\sup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\gamma(G)/\alpha_2(G)$, and $\mathcal{G}$ has domination tied to 2-independence if $\gamma(G)\le h(\alpha_2(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{G}$ and some function $h$. The ratio is known to be bounded for trees, strongly chordal and dually chordal graphs (ratio 1), outerplanar graphs, 2-degenerate graphs, unit disk graphs, graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$, all proper minor-closed classes, graphs of bounded twin-width and graphs of bounded weak 2-coloring number (hence all classes of bounded expansion); on the other hand, Cartesian products of cliques, bipartite 3-degenerate graphs and split graphs are not even tied. The paper answers the question for monotone classes (closed under subgraphs) of bounded average degree: such a class has bounded ratio if and only if the slopes of the cascades it contains are bounded, where a cascade is a graph $H$ properly colored with colors v, e, d such that every e-vertex has exactly two v-neighbors and one d-neighbor and there are no other edges, its foundation $F$ is the graph on the v-vertices in which two are adjacent when they have a common e-neighbor, and its slope is $|\mathrm{v}|/\max(\alpha(F),|\mathrm{d}|)$. The question remains open for hereditary (not monotone) classes and for dense classes.
paper_title: Characterization of sparse monotone graph classes with bounded domination-to-2-independence ratio

name: AX_domination_2_independence_tied_classes
title: Problem 2
statement_text: Which graph classes have domination tied to 2-independence?
context_text: The domination number $\gamma(G)$ is the minimum size of a set $D\subseteq V(G)$ such that every vertex is in $D$ or has a neighbor in $D$; the $2$-independence number $\alpha_2(G)$ is the maximum size of a set of vertices pairwise at distance greater than two (equivalently, of a packing of pairwise disjoint closed neighborhoods). Clearly $\alpha_2(G)\le\gamma(G)$, and the fractional relaxations of the two parameters are dual linear programs with equal value, computable in polynomial time; so when $\gamma/\alpha_2$ is bounded both parameters are approximated by their common fractional relaxation, whereas both are hard to approximate in general. The domination-to-2-independence ratio of a class $\mathcal{G}$ is $\sup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\gamma(G)/\alpha_2(G)$, and $\mathcal{G}$ has domination tied to 2-independence if $\gamma(G)\le h(\alpha_2(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{G}$ and some function $h$. Bounded ratio is exactly the case where $h$ can be taken linear, so this is a relaxation of the question which classes have bounded domination-to-2-independence ratio; the authors remark that it seems non-trivial even for sparse monotone classes. Cartesian products of cliques, bipartite 3-degenerate graphs and split graphs do not have domination tied to 2-independence, nor does the class of graphs of maximum average degree at most $d$ for any $d\ge 6$ (for $d<6$ this class has bounded ratio, as the authors show). The paper characterizes bounded ratio for monotone classes of bounded average degree, but this does not settle the tied version: for $k\ge 3$ and $d>0$, the class of graphs of maximum average degree at most $d$ containing no $1$-subdivision of $K_k$ as a subgraph has domination tied to 2-independence, yet for $k\ge5$, $d\ge6$ it has unbounded ratio.
paper_title: Characterization of sparse monotone graph classes with bounded domination-to-2-independence ratio

name: AX_tournament_color_avoiding_path_non_transitive
title: Problem 5.1
statement_text: For some integers $q\geqslant 4$ and $N$, does there exist a non-transitive $q$-edge-colored $N$-vertex tournament whose longest color-avoiding path has strictly fewer than $f_{q,q-1}(N)$ vertices?
context_text: A $q$-edge-colored tournament has each arc coloured with one of $q$ colours (not necessarily properly); a directed path is color-avoiding if its arcs use at most $q-1$ of the $q$ colours. For integers $q\ge r\ge1$, $f_{q,r}(N)$ is the minimum, over all $q$-edge-colourings of the transitive $N$-vertex tournament, of the number of vertices of the longest directed path using at most $r$ colours, and $g_{q,r}(N)$ is the same minimum over all $N$-vertex tournaments, so $g_{q,r}(N)\le f_{q,r}(N)$; the question asks whether $g_{q,q-1}(N)<f_{q,q-1}(N)$ for some $q\ge4$ and $N$. For $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^q$, $x<_ry$ means $x_i<y_i$ in at least $r$ coordinates; an $r$-increasing sequence $x_1,\dots,x_N$ satisfies $x_a<_rx_b$ for all $a<b$, an $r$-comparable set has $x_a<_rx_b$ or $x_b<_rx_a$ for every pair, and $F_{q,r}(n)$ (resp. $G_{q,r}(n)$) is the maximum size of an $r$-increasing sequence (resp. $r$-comparable set) in $[n]^q$. One has $f_{q,q-1}(N)\le n$ iff $F_{q,q-1}(n)\ge N$, and $G_{q,q-1}(n)\ge N$ implies $g_{q,q-1}(N)\le n$, so comparable sets give tournament constructions. For $q=3$ the answer is yes: Hamaker and Stein's tripod-packing construction gives a 2-comparable set in $[7]^3$ larger than any 2-increasing sequence ($G_{3,2}(7)\ge19>F_{3,2}(7)=17$), and the Gowers–Long construction gives $g_{3,2}(N)\le N^{0.649}$ while $f_{3,2}(N)\le(1+o(1))N^{2/3}$ is the best known and conjectured tight. For $q\ge4$ the authors prove $F_{q,r}(n)=G_{q,r}(n)$ whenever $r>2q/3$, in particular for $r=q-1$, so no such vector construction exists; they also prove that every $q$-edge-coloured $N$-vertex tournament has a color-avoiding path on $c_qN^{1-O(1/\sqrt{\log q})}$ vertices and that near-extremal tournaments must be close to transitive. They nevertheless do not expect the extremal tournaments to be exactly transitive.
paper_title: Color-avoiding directed paths in tournaments

name: AX_degenerate_kr_free_fractional_chromatic_max
title: Problem 4.1
statement_text: What is the maximum fractional chromatic number of a $d$-degenerate, $K_{r}$-free graph?
context_text: A graph is $d$-degenerate if its vertices can be ordered $v_1,\dots,v_n$ so that each $v_i$ has at most $d$ neighbours among $v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}$; greedy colouring gives $\chi(G)\le d+1$, and the constructions of Zykov and Tutte show that triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs can have chromatic number $d+1$, but with a huge number of vertices. The fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is $1/p$ for the largest $p\in(0,1]$ such that some probability distribution on independent sets of $G$ puts every vertex in a random independent set with probability at least $p$. Harris conjectured, and Martinsson proved, that triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs have $\chi_f(G)=O(d/\log d)$. $\log^{(b)}$ denotes the $b$-fold iterated logarithm. Johansson's bound for graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ is $O(\Delta/\log\Delta)$ in the triangle-free case and $O_r(\Delta\log\log\Delta/\log\Delta)$ in the $K_r$-free case, so one might guess the answer $O_r(d\log\log d/\log d)$ for $K_r$-free $d$-degenerate graphs. The authors show this is false: for each $r\ge3$ and large $d$ there is a $d$-degenerate $K_r$-free graph with $\chi_f(G)\ge\Omega_r(d/\log^{(r-2)}d)$, so Harris' conjecture does not generalise in the expected way to $K_r$-free graphs for $r\ge4$. The trivial upper bound is $d+1$.
paper_title: Coloring small locally sparse degenerate graphs and related problems

name: AX_degenerate_triangle_free_subexponential_order_coloring
title: Problem 6.1
statement_text: There are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that every triangle-free $d$-degenerate graph $G$ on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices satisfies $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\log(d/\log n)}$, and more generally every graph on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices with an ordering in which every left-neighbourhood spans at most $d$ vertices and at most $d^2/f$ edges satisfies $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\min\{\log f,\log(d/\log n)\}}$. Can the upper bound $2^{cd}$ on the number of vertices assumed in these two results be weakened to $e^{\omega(d)}$ (with a corresponding improvement of the upper bound on $\chi$ when $n=e^{\omega(d)}$)? What if we additionally assume that the graph has large (constant) girth?
context_text: A graph is $d$-degenerate if its vertices can be ordered $v_1,\dots,v_n$ so that each $v_i$ has at most $d$ neighbours among $v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}$; greedy colouring gives $\chi(G)\le d+1$, and the constructions of Zykov and Tutte show that triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs can have chromatic number $d+1$, but with a huge number of vertices. The authors prove: (main theorem) there are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that every triangle-free $d$-degenerate graph on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices has $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\log(d/\log n)}$; (local sparsity version) the same with $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\min\{\log f,\log(d/\log n)\}}$ for every graph on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices with a vertex ordering in which each left-neighbourhood (set of earlier neighbours) has at most $d$ vertices and spans at most $d^2/f$ edges ($2<f<d^2$). Consequently the minimum order $f(d)$ of a triangle-free $d$-degenerate $(d+1)$-chromatic graph satisfies $e^{\Omega(d)}\le f(d)\le e^{O(d^2\log d)}$. The authors consider this the most important open problem left by the paper. Even improving the constant $c$ to a moderately large value, with an appropriate bound on $\chi$, would solve Erdős's problem on graph Ramsey numbers for all triangle-free graphs (via the trivial bound $r(G)\ge|V(G)|$ for graphs with exponentially many vertices), and perhaps for all $H$-free graphs with $H$ almost bipartite.
paper_title: Coloring small locally sparse degenerate graphs and related problems

name: AX_degenerate_triangle_free_max_degree_coloring
title: Problem 6.2
statement_text: Is the following statement true for all $\varepsilon>0$? If $G$ is a $d$-degenerate triangle-free graph with maximum degree $\Delta(G)\leq e^{d^{1-\varepsilon}}$, then we have $\chi(G)=O\left(\frac{d}{\log d}\right)$.
context_text: A graph is $d$-degenerate if its vertices can be ordered $v_1,\dots,v_n$ so that each $v_i$ has at most $d$ neighbours among $v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}$; greedy colouring gives $\chi(G)\le d+1$, and the constructions of Zykov and Tutte show that triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs can have chromatic number $d+1$, but with a huge number of vertices. The authors prove: (main theorem) there are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that every triangle-free $d$-degenerate graph on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices has $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\log(d/\log n)}$; (local sparsity version) the same with $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\min\{\log f,\log(d/\log n)\}}$ for every graph on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices with a vertex ordering in which each left-neighbourhood (set of earlier neighbours) has at most $d$ vertices and spans at most $d^2/f$ edges ($2<f<d^2$). Consequently the minimum order $f(d)$ of a triangle-free $d$-degenerate $(d+1)$-chromatic graph satisfies $e^{\Omega(d)}\le f(d)\le e^{O(d^2\log d)}$. The question asks whether the global assumption on the number of vertices can be replaced by a local one, bounding the maximum degree. Resolving it would likely require localising the random colouring process used in the paper, so that the union bound is replaced by the Lovász Local Lemma. An $H$-immersion is a graph obtained from $H$ by replacing its edges by edge-disjoint (not necessarily vertex-disjoint) paths; Lescure and Meyniel conjectured in 1988 that graphs with no $K_t$-immersion are $(t-1)$-colourable. Since by van den Heuvel and Wood every $K_t$-immersion-free graph splits into two parts inducing subgraphs of maximum degree $O(t^3)$ (and such graphs have degeneracy $O(t)$), an affirmative answer would give $\chi=O(t/\log t)$ for triangle-free graphs with no $K_t$-immersion, which would be optimal up to constants.
paper_title: Coloring small locally sparse degenerate graphs and related problems

name: AX_degenerate_kr_free_extremal_order_exponential
title: Problem 6.3
statement_text: Is it true that if the chromatic number of a $K_{r}$-free $d$-degenerate graph is $d+1$, then the graph has $e^{\Omega_{r}(d)}$ vertices?
context_text: A graph is $d$-degenerate if its vertices can be ordered $v_1,\dots,v_n$ so that each $v_i$ has at most $d$ neighbours among $v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}$; greedy colouring gives $\chi(G)\le d+1$, and the constructions of Zykov and Tutte show that triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs can have chromatic number $d+1$, but with a huge number of vertices. The authors prove: (main theorem) there are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that every triangle-free $d$-degenerate graph on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices has $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\log(d/\log n)}$; (local sparsity version) the same with $\chi(G)\le\frac{Cd}{\min\{\log f,\log(d/\log n)\}}$ for every graph on $n\le2^{cd}$ vertices with a vertex ordering in which each left-neighbourhood (set of earlier neighbours) has at most $d$ vertices and spans at most $d^2/f$ edges ($2<f<d^2$). Consequently the minimum order $f(d)$ of a triangle-free $d$-degenerate $(d+1)$-chromatic graph satisfies $e^{\Omega(d)}\le f(d)\le e^{O(d^2\log d)}$. Let $f_r(d)$ be the minimum order of a $K_r$-free $d$-degenerate $(d+1)$-chromatic graph. Via a connection with on-line colouring (the on-line chromatic number $g_r(n)$ of $n$-vertex $K_r$-free graphs satisfies $g_r(n)=\Omega(n^{(r-2)/(r-1)})$), the authors get $f_r(d)\le e^{O(d^{(r-1)/(r-2)}\log d)}$ for fixed $r$. The question asks whether the exponential lower bound proved for $r=3$ also holds for every $r\ge4$; extending it would need a $K_r$-free analogue of the main colouring theorem, which seems hard with the paper's method, in particular because the fractional chromatic number bound of Martinsson (used for $r=3$) fails for $r\ge4$.
paper_title: Coloring small locally sparse degenerate graphs and related problems

name: AX_degenerate_kr_free_fractional_chromatic_sublinear
title: Problem 6.4
statement_text: Let $r\geq 4$. Is it true that the maximum fractional chromatic number of $K_{r}$-free $d$-degenerate graphs is $o_{r}(d)$?
context_text: A graph is $d$-degenerate if its vertices can be ordered $v_1,\dots,v_n$ so that each $v_i$ has at most $d$ neighbours among $v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}$; greedy colouring gives $\chi(G)\le d+1$, and the constructions of Zykov and Tutte show that triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs can have chromatic number $d+1$, but with a huge number of vertices. The fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is $1/p$ for the largest $p\in(0,1]$ such that some probability distribution on independent sets of $G$ puts every vertex in a random independent set with probability at least $p$. Harris conjectured, and Martinsson proved, that triangle-free $d$-degenerate graphs have $\chi_f(G)=O(d/\log d)$. $\log^{(b)}$ denotes the $b$-fold iterated logarithm. The trivial upper bound for $d$-degenerate graphs is $\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G)\le d+1$. The authors prove that for each $r\ge3$ and large $d$ there is a $d$-degenerate $K_r$-free graph with $\chi_f(G)\ge\Omega_r(d/\log^{(r-2)}d)$, which gets closer to linear in $d$ as $r$ grows, so the question is whether any asymptotic improvement over $d+1$ holds for each fixed $r\ge4$. It is closely related to the question whether $K_r$-free $d$-degenerate $(d+1)$-chromatic graphs must have $e^{\Omega_r(d)}$ vertices.
paper_title: Coloring small locally sparse degenerate graphs and related problems

name: AX_3_coloring_diameter_2_quasipolynomial
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Can 3-colouring be solved on diameter-2 graphs in quasi-polynomial time?
context_text: 3-colouring is the decision problem asking whether the input graph $G$ (on $n$ vertices) has a proper colouring with 3 colours; the diameter of a connected graph is the maximum distance between two vertices. A quasi-polynomial-time algorithm runs in time $2^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}$. Restricting the diameter does not give a hereditary class, which makes the usual branching approaches harder. Adding a universal vertex shows that $k$-colouring is NP-hard on diameter-2 graphs for every $k\ge4$ (and, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis, not solvable in time $2^{o(n)}$), and under ETH 3-colouring diameter-4 graphs cannot be done in time $2^{o(n)}$; this leaves 3-colouring on diameter-2 and diameter-3 graphs as the two notorious open cases identified by Paulusma. For diameter 2, Mertzios and Spirakis gave a subexponential algorithm of running time $2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}$ for list-3-colouring, and the authors note that the problem might even be solvable in polynomial time, which they call the most intriguing open problem in the area. The paper itself improves 3-colouring on diameter-3 graphs to time $2^{O(n^{2/3-\varepsilon})}$ for any $\varepsilon<1/33$ (previously $2^{O((n\log n)^{2/3})}$, with an ETH lower bound of $2^{\Omega(\sqrt n)}$), and explicitly highlights the quasi-polynomial question for diameter 2 as an intermediate target.
paper_title: Faster 3-colouring algorithm for graphs of diameter 3

name: AX_circular_drawing_digraph_forbidden_characterization
title: Open Question on Circular Drawing Characterisation
statement_text: Is there a theorem that says ``every appropriately connected digraph $G$ contains no thing of type $X$ if and only if $G$ admits a circular drawing''?
context_text: Digraphs are finite and may have loops or parallel edges. A circular drawing of a digraph $G$ is a drawing in the plane without crossings, with the origin in one of the regions, such that every edge subtends a positive angle at the origin (in the clockwise sense); then every directed cycle winds around the origin exactly once. Thomassen proved that if $G$ has no loops or parallel edges, every vertex has in- and out-degree at least two, and there are vertices $a,b$ such that every directed cycle contains $a$ or $b$, then $G$ admits a circular drawing if and only if no directed cycle contains both $a$ and $b$; the question asks for a general theorem of this excluded-structure type. A weighting of $G$ is a function $w:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}$ with total weight $1$ on every directed cycle, and $G$ is weightable if it has one; circular drawings give weightings (take the fraction of a full turn subtended by each edge), so digraphs with circular drawings are weightable. The authors hoped for a converse for sufficiently well-connected digraphs (e.g. strongly 2-connected and weakly 3-connected weightable digraphs), but this is false: they exhibit such a weightable digraph with no circular drawing. Weightable digraphs are known to be exactly those with no subdivided double-cycle, and the authors give a construction of all weightable digraphs (planar ones from circular ones, general ones from planar ones) and a polynomial-time recognition algorithm, but they have still not found the hoped-for characterization of digraphs with circular drawings.
notes: No labelled theorem environment; stated as a motivating open question in the introduction and explicitly left unresolved at the end of the introductory discussion.
paper_title: When all directed cycles have the same weight

name: AX_geometric_graph_monotone_path_cover_superlinear
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: For some (possibly, for every) dense $n$-element point set $A$ in general position in the plane, covering the edge set of $K_{n}[A]$ requires a superlinear number of monotone paths.
context_text: A point set in the plane is in general position if no 3 points are collinear. For a set $A$ of $n$ points in general position, the complete geometric graph $K_n[A]$ has vertex set $A$ and all $\binom{n}{2}$ straight-line segments between them as edges. A polygonal path $(v_1,\dots,v_t)$ is monotone in direction $\mathbf{u}\neq\mathbf{0}$ if $\langle \overrightarrow{v_iv_{i+1}},\mathbf{u}\rangle>0$ for every $i$, and it is monotone if it is monotone in some direction; every monotone path is crossing-free. For a constant $\alpha>0$, a set of $n$ points is $\alpha$-dense if the ratio between the longest and the shortest distance between two of its points is at most $\alpha\sqrt{n}$; 'dense' means $\alpha$-dense for some constant $\alpha$. The authors prove that for any $\alpha$-dense point set $A$ in general position, the edge set of $K_n[A]$ can be covered by $O(n^{3/2})$ monotone paths (hence decomposed into $O(n^{3/2})$ monotone matchings), and for $n$ random points in $[0,1]^2$ by $O(n\log n)$ monotone paths with high probability. They suspect the $O(n^{3/2})$ bound for dense sets is not tight but that a superlinear lower bound holds. In contrast, arbitrary point sets may require a quadratic number of monotone paths: $n^2/6+O(n)$ always suffice and some $n$-point sets require at least $n^2/15$.
paper_title: Covering Complete Geometric Graphs by Monotone Paths

name: AX_geometric_graph_plane_path_cover_bound
title: Problem 5.1
statement_text: Does there exist a constant $c>1/2$ with the property that, for infinitely many values of $n$, there are $n$-element point sets $A$ in the plane such that every covering of the edge set of $K_{n}[A]$ by crossing-free paths requires at least $cn$ paths?
context_text: A point set in the plane is in general position if no 3 points are collinear (the paper assumes this for all point sets). For a set $A$ of $n$ points, the complete geometric graph $K_n[A]$ has vertex set $A$ and all straight-line segments between them as edges; a path (or graph) drawn this way is crossing-free (plane) if no two of its edges cross. Araujo, Dumitrescu, Hurtado, Noy and Urrutia asked whether there is a constant $c>0$ such that every complete geometric graph on $n$ vertices can be partitioned into at most $cn$ plane matchings; the best known upper bound for general point sets is $O(n^{3/2})$. Obenaus and Orthaber showed that complete geometric graphs on $n$ vertices ($n$ even) cannot always be partitioned into $n/2$ plane subgraphs, but it is possible that $n/2+o(n)$ plane subgraphs always suffice. Pach, Saghafian and Schnider proved that a complete convex geometric graph on $n$ vertices cannot be decomposed into fewer than $n-1$ plane star-forests. The authors suggest that answering this problem may be a first step towards the question of Araujo et al.
paper_title: Covering Complete Geometric Graphs by Monotone Paths

name: AX_geometric_graph_zigzag_path_cover_number
title: Problem 5.2
statement_text: What is the smallest number $z=z(n)$ such that the edge set of every complete geometric graph on $n$ vertices can be covered by $z$ plane zig-zag paths?
context_text: A point set in the plane is in general position if no 3 points are collinear; a complete geometric graph on $n$ vertices is $K_n[A]$ for a set $A$ of $n$ points in general position, i.e. the points with all straight-line segments between them as edges. A path is plane if no two of its edges cross. A 3-edge path is zig-zag if its two endpoints lie in opposite open halfplanes determined by the line of its middle edge (such a path is always monotone), and a path is zig-zag if any three consecutive edges form a 3-edge zig-zag path; this does not ensure that the path is monotone or even plane. The authors show that for any finite point set $A$ in general position, the edge set of $K_n[A]$ can be covered by plane Hamiltonian zig-zag paths (every segment $ab$ lies on such a path), but the minimum number of (not necessarily Hamiltonian) plane zig-zag paths needed in the worst case is left open.
paper_title: Covering Complete Geometric Graphs by Monotone Paths

name: AX_mis_planar_induced_minor_free_quasipolynomial
title: Question 2
statement_text: Is it true that for every planar graph $H$, Max Independent Set can be solved in quasipolynomial time in the class of graphs excluding $H$ as an induced minor?
context_text: A graph $H$ is an induced minor of $G$ if $H$ can be obtained from $G$ by vertex deletions and edge contractions; $G$ is $H$-induced-minor-free otherwise. Max Independent Set asks for a maximum-size independent set; quasipolynomial time means time $n^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}$. $G_1\uplus G_2$ is the disjoint union, $tG$ the disjoint union of $t$ copies of $G$, $C_t$ the cycle on $t$ vertices. For non-planar $H$ the problem is NP-complete on $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, since they include all planar graphs; no planar $H$ is known for which it is NP-complete. Dallard, Milanič and Štorgel asked whether for every planar $H$ the problem is solvable in polynomial time on $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, which is open even for $H=P_7$; the present question is its quasipolynomial relaxation, for which more is known: quasipolynomial algorithms exist for $H=C_t$ (Gartland et al.) and $H=tC_3$ (Bonamy et al.), and Korhonen gave a $2^{O(n/\log^c n)}$-time algorithm for every planar $H$ (impossible in general graphs under ETH). The paper adds a polynomial $n^{O(t^5)}$ algorithm for the friendship graph $K_1+tK_2$ and a quasipolynomial $n^{O(t^2\log n)+f(t)}$ algorithm ($f$ single-exponential) for $tC_3\uplus C_4$; the case $H=C_4\uplus C_4$ is listed as open.
notes: No parenthetical attribution appears in the theorem header; treated as the paper authors' own question. It is the natural quasipolynomial companion to Question 1.
paper_title: Maximum Independent Set when excluding an induced minor: $K_1 + tK_2$ and $tC_3 \uplus C_4$

name: AX_genus_distribution_unimodal
title: Conjecture 10
statement_text: The genus distribution of every graph $G$ is unimodal.
context_text: Graphs are connected and simple, and surfaces are closed orientable surfaces. The genus distribution (or genus sequence) of $G$ is the sequence $(a_g(G))_{g\ge0}$, where $a_g(G)$ is the number of 2-cell embeddings of $G$ in the orientable surface of genus $g$ (up to ambient homeomorphism). A sequence of non-negative numbers is log-concave if $a_k^2\ge a_{k-1}a_{k+1}$ for every $k\ge1$, and unimodal if it is non-decreasing up to some index and non-increasing afterwards (log-concave sequences without internal zeros are unimodal). Gross, Robbins and Tucker conjectured in 1989 (the LCGD Conjecture) that the genus distribution of every graph is log-concave; the author disproves it, showing that for every $g\ge0$ and $k\ge1$ there is a 4-connected graph of genus $g$ whose genus sequence has $k$ consecutive strictly log-convex terms.
