These counterexamples are still unimodal, and the author suggests that the unimodal weakening of the LCGD Conjecture could, and actually should, still be true. The author compares the LCGD Conjecture with the Heron–Rota–Welsh log-concavity conjecture for matroids, whose weaker unimodal form (Read's conjecture) was proved first by Huh, before the full conjecture was proved by Adiprasito, Huh and Katz.
paper_title: Strong log-convexity of genus sequences

name: AX_genus_distribution_log_concave_triangulations
title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: Every graph that triangulates some surface has log-concave genus distribution.
context_text: Graphs are connected and simple, and surfaces are closed orientable surfaces. The genus distribution (or genus sequence) of $G$ is the sequence $(a_g(G))_{g\ge0}$, where $a_g(G)$ is the number of 2-cell embeddings of $G$ in the orientable surface of genus $g$ (up to ambient homeomorphism). A sequence of non-negative numbers is log-concave if $a_k^2\ge a_{k-1}a_{k+1}$ for every $k\ge1$, and unimodal if it is non-decreasing up to some index and non-increasing afterwards (log-concave sequences without internal zeros are unimodal). Gross, Robbins and Tucker conjectured in 1989 (the LCGD Conjecture) that the genus distribution of every graph is log-concave; the author disproves it, showing that for every $g\ge0$ and $k\ge1$ there is a 4-connected graph of genus $g$ whose genus sequence has $k$ consecutive strictly log-convex terms. A graph triangulates a surface if it has a 2-cell embedding in that surface in which every face is a triangle. After proposing that every genus distribution is unimodal, the author notes that this restricted form of log-concavity also looks plausible.
paper_title: Strong log-convexity of genus sequences

name: AX_anticomplete_xy_paths_erdos_posa_optimal
title: Conjecture 6
statement_text: For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, every graph $G$ and $X,Y\subseteq V(G)$ satisfies one of the following: $G$ contains $k$ pairwise anti-complete $(X,Y)$-paths; or there exists a set $Z\subseteq V(G)$ with $|Z|\leqslant k$ such that $G-N_{G}[Z]$ has no $(X,Y)$-path.
context_text: An $(X,Y)$-path is a path with one end in $X$ and the other in $Y$. For $A\subseteq V(G)$, an $A$-path is a path with at least one edge whose two ends lie in $A$. Two vertex sets are anti-complete if they are disjoint and no edge joins them, and paths are pairwise anti-complete if their vertex sets are. $N_G[Z]$ is the closed neighbourhood of $Z$, i.e. the vertices at distance at most 1 from $Z$. Gallai's theorem states that $G$ contains $k$ disjoint $A$-paths or a set of at most $2k-2$ vertices meeting all $A$-paths. The authors prove an induced analogue: $G$ contains $k$ pairwise anti-complete $A$-paths, or a set $Z$ with $|Z|\le54(k-1)$ (in the current arXiv version; earlier versions state a larger constant) such that $G-N_G[Z]$ has no $A$-path. This resolves the $d=2$ case of Geelen's coarse Gallai conjecture. The conjecture here is the Induced Menger Conjecture, the $d=2$ case of the Coarse Menger Conjecture of Albrechtsen–Huynh–Jacobs–Knappe–Wollan and Georgakopoulos–Papasoglu. That conjecture (for $(X,Y)$-paths at mutual distance at least $d$, with $k-1$ balls of radius $cd$) was shown false for all $d\ge3$ by Nguyen, Scott and Seymour. The bound $|Z|\le k$ would be best possible for radius-1 balls: Albrechtsen et al. constructed a graph with sets $X,Y$ having no two anti-complete $(X,Y)$-paths although $G-N_G[v]$ contains an $(X,Y)$-path for every vertex $v$. If true, the conjecture would imply an Induced Grid Minor Theorem for $K_{1,t}$-induced-subgraph-free graphs conjectured by Dallard et al.
paper_title: An Induced $A$-Path Theorem

name: AX_spectrally_symmetric_graph_edge_density
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Find the minimal constant $\widehat{\rho}\in[0,1]$ such that each spectrally symmetric graph satisfies $\frac{2|E(G)|}{|V(G)|^{2}}\leq\widehat{\rho}$.
context_text: For a digraph $D$ with $a(i,j)$ arcs from $i$ to $j$, the Hermitian adjacency matrix of the second kind is $H(D)=H_{\pi/3}(D)$ with entries $H_{i,j}=e^{i\pi/3}a(i,j)+e^{-i\pi/3}a(j,i)$. A digraph is spectrally symmetric if the spectrum of $H(D)$ is symmetric about $0$, and an undirected graph is spectrally symmetric if it has at least one spectrally symmetric orientation (an assignment of a direction to each edge). Bipartite graphs are spectrally symmetric, but the converse fails (e.g. an orientation of $K_5-E(K_3)$). For undirected adjacency spectra, symmetry forces bipartiteness and hence at most $n^2/4$ edges (Mantel), i.e. density $2|E|/|V|^2\le\frac12$; the problem asks for the analogous density threshold for spectrally symmetric orientations. The authors prove the upper bound $\widehat{\rho}\le\frac{10}{11}$ (a spectral analogue of Mantel's theorem for digraphs; blow-ups of a spectrally symmetric digraph remain spectrally symmetric with the same limit density). An earlier arXiv version had the lower bound $\frac{13}{18}$ from a $6$-vertex example; in the final version, after Seamons found a spectrally symmetric orientation of $K_{11}-3K_2$ (giving $\frac{104}{121}$), the authors give one of $K_{12}-4K_2$, so that $\frac{31}{36}\le\widehat{\rho}\le\frac{10}{11}$. The exact value remains open.
paper_title: Spectrally symmetric orientations of graphs

name: AX_modular_chromatic_index_0k_graphs
title: Conjecture 13
statement_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer. For every $0_{k}$-graph $G$ we have $\chi^{\prime}_{k}(G)\leq k+o(k)$.
context_text: All graphs are simple. For integers $0\le\ell<k$, an $\ell_k$-graph is a graph in which every vertex has degree congruent to $\ell$ modulo $k$; in particular a $0_k$-graph (also called $k$-divisible) has all degrees divisible by $k$. A $\chi'_k$-colouring of $G$ is an edge-colouring in which each colour class (the subgraph formed by the edges of that colour) is a $1_k$-graph, i.e. all its non-zero degrees are congruent to $1$ modulo $k$, and the mod $k$ chromatic index $\chi'_k(G)$ is the minimum number of colours of such a colouring. Pyber proved $\chi'_2(G)\le4$, Scott proved $\chi'_k(G)\le5k^2\log k$, Botler, Colucci and Kohayakawa proved $\chi'_k(G)\le198k-101$ and conjectured $\chi'_k(G)\le k+C$ for an absolute constant $C$ (which must be at least $2$), and Nweit and Yang improved the bound to $177k-93$. The authors prove $\chi'_k(G)\le7k+o(k)$ for odd $k$ and $\le9k+o(k)$ for even $k$, by removing a maximal $1_k$-subgraph and colouring the remaining graph, which has bounded degeneracy, using $\chi'_k(G)\le k+O(d)$ for $d$-degenerate graphs. They propose this conjecture as a route to a better constant: if it holds, removing a maximal $0_k$-subgraph $H$ of $G$ leaves a graph with no non-empty $k$-divisible subgraph, which for odd $k$ is $(2q(k)-2)$-degenerate, where $q(k)$ is the smallest prime at least $k$; colouring $H$ by the conjecture and the rest by their degenerate-graph lemma would give $\chi'_k(G)\le6k+o(k)$ for odd $k$ and $8k+o(k)$ for even $k$.
paper_title: On Modular Edge Colourings of Graphs

name: AX_dom_enum_incomparability_st_free_posets
title: Conjecture 7.1
statement_text: For every $t$, there is an output-polynomial time algorithm for Dom-Enum in incomparability graphs of $S_{t}$-free posets.
context_text: Dom-Enum is the problem of listing all (inclusion-wise) minimal dominating sets of a graph $G$; since there may be exponentially many, an algorithm is output-polynomial if its running time is polynomial in the size of the input plus the number of minimal dominating sets output. Whether Dom-Enum (equivalently, enumeration of the minimal transversals of a hypergraph) admits an output-polynomial algorithm is a long-standing open question, and it is as hard in co-bipartite graphs (complements of bipartite graphs) as in general. The comparability graph of a poset $P$ has an edge between any two comparable elements, its incomparability graph an edge between any two incomparable elements; co-bipartite graphs are incomparability graphs, so Dom-Enum in incomparability graphs is as hard as in general. The dimension of $P$ is the least $d$ such that $P$ is the intersection of $d$ linear orders, and the standard example $S_t$ is the poset on $a_1,\dots,a_t,b_1,\dots,b_t$ with $a_i<b_j$ exactly when $i\ne j$; $S_t$ has dimension $t$, so posets of dimension less than $t$ are $S_t$-free (contain no $S_t$ as an induced suborder), but some $S_t$-free posets have unbounded dimension. The authors give a polynomial-delay algorithm for Dom-Enum in incomparability graphs of posets of bounded dimension (given with the $d$ linear orders) and an incremental-polynomial algorithm in comparability graphs of posets of bounded dimension, the latter actually covering comparability graphs of all $S_t$-free posets. The conjecture asks for the counterpart in incomparability graphs; the authors' proof does not extend naturally since it relies on the bounded-dimension geometric representation, but they believe an extension is possible with different tools. An easier conjecture is the case of $2K_p$-free incomparability graphs ($2K_p$ being two disjoint $p$-cliques), since an $S_{2p}$ suborder yields a $2K_p$ in the incomparability graph; it holds for $p\le2$.
paper_title: Enumerating minimal dominating sets in the (in)comparability graphs of bounded dimension posets

name: AX_dom_enum_incomparability_cobipartite_free
title: Conjecture 7.3
statement_text: For any co-bipartite $H$, there is an output-polynomial time algorithm for Dom-Enum in $H$-free incomparability graphs.
context_text: Dom-Enum is the problem of listing all (inclusion-wise) minimal dominating sets of a graph $G$; since there may be exponentially many, an algorithm is output-polynomial if its running time is polynomial in the size of the input plus the number of minimal dominating sets output. The dimension of $P$ is the least $d$ such that $P$ is the intersection of $d$ linear orders, and the standard example $S_t$ is the poset on $a_1,\dots,a_t,b_1,\dots,b_t$ with $a_i<b_j$ exactly when $i\ne j$; $S_t$ has dimension $t$, so posets of dimension less than $t$ are $S_t$-free (contain no $S_t$ as an induced suborder), but some $S_t$-free posets have unbounded dimension. Since co-bipartite graphs are incomparability graphs and Dom-Enum is hard on them, the question for $H$-free incomparability graphs is only interesting for co-bipartite $H$. Known cases: $H=K_p$ (bounded clique number, i.e. posets of bounded width) is covered by earlier work of Bonamy, Defrain, Heinrich, Pilipczuk and Raymond; $2K_p$-free incomparability graphs are solved for $p\le2$ and conjectured for all $p$, the case $p=3$ being widely open in general graphs; $C_4$-free incomparability graphs are interval graphs, where linear delay is known, while $C_4$ is the smallest open case for general graphs. Rather than debating natural generalizations (two cliques joined by a matching, a clique minus a matching), the authors state this bold conjecture, and remark that there is no blatant reason why the incomparability condition would be necessary.
paper_title: Enumerating minimal dominating sets in the (in)comparability graphs of bounded dimension posets

name: AX_schnyder_wood_uihpt_weak_limit
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: The unique maximal Schnyder wood of the UIHPT is the weak limit of the maximal Schnyder wood of a uniformly random triangulation from $T^m_n$ as $n \to \infty$ and then $m \to \infty$.
context_text: $T^m_n$ is the set of simple $2$-connected triangulations of an $(m+2)$-gon with $n$ interior vertices, rooted at a boundary edge. The UIPT with boundary length $m$ is the local (weak, for balls around the root) limit as $n\to\infty$ of a uniform element of $T^m_n$, and the UIHPT (uniform infinite half-planar triangulation) is the local limit of the UIPT of the $(m+2)$-gon as $m\to\infty$. A Schnyder wood of a triangulation rooted at a boundary edge $(v_r,v_y)$ is an orientation of the edges together with a colouring in red, yellow and blue such that: every interior vertex has exactly three outgoing edges, coloured blue, red, yellow in anticlockwise order, and every incoming edge enters between the outgoing edges of the two other colours; $v_y$ has no outgoing edge and only incoming yellow edges, $v_r$ has one outgoing edge and only incoming red edges; every other boundary vertex has exactly two outgoing edges, red and yellow, and, anticlockwise from the boundary, its incident edges are incoming yellow, outgoing red, incoming blue, outgoing yellow, incoming red. A Schnyder wood is maximal if it has no anticlockwise directed cycle and, for infinite triangulations, no right-directed two-ended infinite path (one leaving the boundary on its right, an 'infinite anticlockwise cycle'). Every finite triangulation has a unique maximal Schnyder wood. The authors prove that every infinite triangulation with finite boundary has a unique maximal Schnyder wood, that the maximal Schnyder wood of the UIPT with boundary length $m$ is the weak limit of the maximal Schnyder wood of a uniform element of $T^m_n$ as $n\to\infty$, and that the UIHPT almost surely has a unique maximal Schnyder wood, which they construct by repeated peeling processes and whose monochromatic subgraphs they describe. The natural peeling process started from a fixed root edge almost surely never explores most of the UIHPT, and this non-locality prevented them from proving the corresponding convergence when $m\to\infty$ after $n\to\infty$. They discuss potential consequences for geodesic paths and for the winding of monochromatic trees in large finite triangulations.
paper_title: Infinite Schnyder Woods

name: AX_schnyder_wood_half_plane_triangulations_existence
title: Open question on Schnyder woods for general half-plane triangulations
statement_text: It would be interesting to know whether Schnyder woods exist on all half-plane triangulations, and if not, to characterise the ones for which they do exist.
context_text: $T^m_n$ is the set of simple $2$-connected triangulations of an $(m+2)$-gon with $n$ interior vertices, rooted at a boundary edge. The UIPT with boundary length $m$ is the local (weak, for balls around the root) limit as $n\to\infty$ of a uniform element of $T^m_n$, and the UIHPT (uniform infinite half-planar triangulation) is the local limit of the UIPT of the $(m+2)$-gon as $m\to\infty$. A Schnyder wood of a triangulation rooted at a boundary edge $(v_r,v_y)$ is an orientation of the edges together with a colouring in red, yellow and blue such that: every interior vertex has exactly three outgoing edges, coloured blue, red, yellow in anticlockwise order, and every incoming edge enters between the outgoing edges of the two other colours; $v_y$ has no outgoing edge and only incoming yellow edges, $v_r$ has one outgoing edge and only incoming red edges; every other boundary vertex has exactly two outgoing edges, red and yellow, and, anticlockwise from the boundary, its incident edges are incoming yellow, outgoing red, incoming blue, outgoing yellow, incoming red. A Schnyder wood is maximal if it has no anticlockwise directed cycle and, for infinite triangulations, no right-directed two-ended infinite path (one leaving the boundary on its right, an 'infinite anticlockwise cycle'). Every finite triangulation has a unique maximal Schnyder wood. A half-plane triangulation is an infinite (one-ended) triangulation with infinite boundary. The authors prove existence and uniqueness of the maximal Schnyder wood for every infinite triangulation with finite boundary and almost surely for the UIHPT; their construction also gives Schnyder woods on other half-plane triangulations with similar properties, and whenever a maximal Schnyder wood of a half-plane triangulation exists it is unique. Existence in general is left open.
paper_title: Infinite Schnyder Woods

name: AX_schnyder_wood_random_wooded_triangulations_limit
title: Open question on local limit of uniformly random wooded triangulations
statement_text: It would be interesting to understand the local limit of uniformly random wooded triangulations as the boundary length tends to infinity, and whether such wooded triangulations have a local limit, which would be a random wooded triangulation of the half-plane different from the one constructed in this work.
context_text: $T^m_n$ is the set of simple $2$-connected triangulations of an $(m+2)$-gon with $n$ interior vertices, rooted at a boundary edge. The UIPT with boundary length $m$ is the local (weak, for balls around the root) limit as $n\to\infty$ of a uniform element of $T^m_n$, and the UIHPT (uniform infinite half-planar triangulation) is the local limit of the UIPT of the $(m+2)$-gon as $m\to\infty$. A wooded triangulation is a triangulation together with a Schnyder wood; a uniformly random wooded triangulation is uniform over such pairs, which differs from taking the maximal Schnyder wood of a uniform triangulation. By results of Bernardi and Bonichon, the heights of the trees in a uniform wooded triangulation with $n$ faces are $\Theta(\sqrt n)$ in probability and in expectation, while in the maximal Schnyder wood of a uniform triangulation the height of a uniformly random vertex has expectation of order $n^{3/4}$ (Chapuy). The authors construct the maximal Schnyder wood of the UIHPT; a local limit of uniformly random wooded triangulations as the boundary length tends to infinity, if it exists, would be a different random wooded triangulation of the half-plane.
paper_title: Infinite Schnyder Woods

name: AX_generic_norm_distinct_distances_lower_bound
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: For every fixed $d$ the following holds for all $d$-norms $\|\cdot\|$ but a meagre set. For all $n>n_{0}(d)$, any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ that do not all lie in an affine hyperplane determine at least $(d-o(1))n$ distinct distances with respect to $\|\cdot\|$, where the $o(1)$-term tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity.
context_text: A $d$-norm is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^d$; identifying a norm with its unit ball, the Hausdorff distance between unit balls (the largest distance from a point of one ball to the other ball) makes the space of $d$-norms a metric space, and it is a Baire space. A set of norms is nowhere dense if every non-empty open set contains a non-empty open set disjoint from it, and meagre if it is a countable union of nowhere dense sets; "all $d$-norms but a meagre set" thus means typical (generic) norms. Alon, Bucić and Sauermann proved that in all $d$-norms but a meagre set, any $n>n_0(d)$ points determine at least $(1-o(1))n$ distinct distances, which is tight because $n$ points in arithmetic progression on a line determine $n-1$ distances in every norm. Since that extremal example is one-dimensional, the conjecture concerns $d$-dimensional sets, i.e. sets not contained in an affine hyperplane. It is trivial for $d=1$ but open already for $d=2$. The authors prove that any $d$-dimensional set of $n$ points determines at least $bdn$ lines with pairwise distinct directions for an absolute constant $b\ge1/48$, and deduce the weaker bound of $(bd-o(1))n$ distinct distances for typical $d$-norms; they also note that $n-d+1$ points in arithmetic progression on a line plus $d-1$ further points in general position show the minimum is $\Theta(nd)$, and that a $(d-1)n-O(d^2)$ conjecture on distinct directions would give $(d-1-o(1))n$ distances. This is discrete geometry rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Distinct Directions and Distinct Distances in $\mathbb{R}^d$

name: AX_tree_independence_polynomial_biclique_free
title: Question 5.2
statement_text: Is is true that for every positive integer $\mu$ there exists a polynomial $\mathsf{p}_{\mu}$ such that every $K_{t,t}$-free graph $G$ with $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)\leqslant\mu$ satisfies $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)\leqslant\mathsf{p}_{\mu}(t)$?
context_text: $H$-free means having no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; in particular $K_{t,t}$-free excludes the biclique $K_{t,t}$ as an induced subgraph. For a tree decomposition $\mathcal{T}$ of $G$, its independence number is the maximum of $\alpha(G[B])$ over its bags $B$, and its induced matching number is the maximum size of an induced matching $M$ of $G$ such that some bag contains at least one endpoint of every edge of $M$. The tree-independence number $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)$ and the induced matching treewidth $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)$ (introduced by Yolov) are the minimum of these measures over all tree decompositions of $G$. Always $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)\le\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)$, but complete bipartite graphs have induced matching treewidth $1$ and unbounded tree-independence number. Abrishami et al. proved that every $K_{t,t}$-free graph with $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)\le\mu$ has tree-independence number bounded by a function of $\mu$ and $t$ (exponential in $\mu$ even for fixed $t$); the authors improve this to $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)=O_t(\mu^{3t^2+1})$, polynomial in $\mu$ for fixed $t$. A bound polynomial in both $\mu$ and $t$ is impossible: for every $t$ there is a graph that is $K_{t,t}$-free and $tK_2$-free (so of induced matching treewidth less than $t$) with tree-independence number $2^{\Omega(t)}$. This does not rule out a bound polynomial in $t$ for each fixed $\mu$, which is what the question asks.
paper_title: Induced matching treewidth and tree-independence number, revisited

name: AX_tree_independence_polynomial_induced_biclique_number
title: Question 5.3
statement_text: Is it true that for classes of graphs with bounded induced matching treewidth, tree-independence number is bounded from above by a polynomial function of the induced biclique number?
context_text: $H$-free means having no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; in particular $K_{t,t}$-free excludes the biclique $K_{t,t}$ as an induced subgraph. For a tree decomposition $\mathcal{T}$ of $G$, its independence number is the maximum of $\alpha(G[B])$ over its bags $B$, and its induced matching number is the maximum size of an induced matching $M$ of $G$ such that some bag contains at least one endpoint of every edge of $M$. The tree-independence number $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)$ and the induced matching treewidth $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)$ (introduced by Yolov) are the minimum of these measures over all tree decompositions of $G$. Always $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)\le\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)$, but complete bipartite graphs have induced matching treewidth $1$ and unbounded tree-independence number. Abrishami et al. proved that every $K_{t,t}$-free graph with $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)\le\mu$ has tree-independence number bounded by a function of $\mu$ and $t$ (exponential in $\mu$ even for fixed $t$); the authors improve this to $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)=O_t(\mu^{3t^2+1})$, polynomial in $\mu$ for fixed $t$. A bound polynomial in both $\mu$ and $t$ is impossible: for every $t$ there is a graph that is $K_{t,t}$-free and $tK_2$-free (so of induced matching treewidth less than $t$) with tree-independence number $2^{\Omega(t)}$. The induced biclique number of $G$ is the largest nonnegative integer $t$ such that $G$ contains an induced subgraph isomorphic to $K_{t,t}$; it is a lower bound on tree-independence number (up to a constant) and has been studied in several recent contexts. The authors note that this question is an equivalent restatement of asking whether, for every $\mu$, there is a polynomial $p_\mu$ such that every $K_{t,t}$-free graph $G$ with $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\mu}(G)\le\mu$ satisfies $\operatorname{tree\textnormal{-}\alpha}(G)\le p_\mu(t)$.
notes: Explicitly stated by the authors to be equivalent to Question 5.2.
paper_title: Induced matching treewidth and tree-independence number, revisited

name: AX_ordered_complete_graph_monochromatic_nonnested_matching
title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: Determine the smallest $m$ such that in every $2$-coloring of the edges of the ordered complete graph $K_{m}$, there is a monochromatic non-nested matching of size $n$.
context_text: This is a problem from the open problem session of the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025), presented by János Barát. The vertices of the complete graph $K_m$ are identified with $\{1,\dots,m\}$ in this order. Two independent edges $ij$ and $st$ (with $i<j$, $s<t$) are nested if $i<s<t<j$ or $s<i<j<t$; a non-nested matching is a matching in which no two edges are nested. In the unordered setting, $3n-1$ vertices always force a monochromatic matching with $n$ edges, and this is tight. Here the answer is trivially between $3n-1$ and $4n-2$, and Barát, Gyárfás and Tóth conjectured that the lower bound $3n-1$ is optimal. The upper bound was improved by a small additive constant (with small cases checked up to $n=5$ or $6$), and a more substantial improvement relies on a Turán-type conjecture that Barát, Freschi and Tóth can prove only with a small error term: once this error term is erased, $m>(2+\sqrt3)n$ would suffice.
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_random_4_regular_graph_polynomial_coefficient
title: Problem 2.1
statement_text: Let $G$ be a random 4-regular graph. Is it true that the coefficient of $P_{G}$ at $\prod_{v\in V(G)}v^{2}$ is a.a.s. non-zero?
context_text: Problem presented by Zdeněk Dvořák at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A random 4-regular graph is here the union of two independent uniformly random Hamiltonian cycles on the same vertex set (a multigraph, simple with constant probability; a uniformly random 4-regular graph a.a.s. contains two disjoint Hamiltonian cycles, and the union of four random perfect matchings is another a.a.s. equivalent model); a.a.s. means with probability tending to $1$. Such a graph is a.a.s. 3-colourable, but it is open whether it is a.a.s. 3-choosable. The graph polynomial is $P_G=\prod_{uv\in E(G)}(u-v)$, whose variables correspond to the vertices of $G$. By the Alon–Tarsi theorem, if the coefficient of $\prod_{v}v^{f(v)}$ in $P_G$ is non-zero for some $f:V(G)\to\{0,\dots,k-1\}$, then $G$ is $k$-choosable. All monomials of $P_G$ have total degree $|E(G)|$, so for a 4-regular graph the only relevant monomial with exponents at most $2$ is $\prod_v v^2$, and a positive answer would show that random 4-regular graphs are a.a.s. 3-choosable. In the two Hamiltonian cycles model the expected value of the coefficient is zero, so a proof would need an anti-concentration inequality, and a disproof a concentration result.
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_cycles_union_k4_copies_4_colorable
title: Problem 3.1
statement_text: Let $G$ be a disjoint union of cycles. Let $H$ be a disjoint union of $K_{4}$'s. Is $G\cup H$ 4-colourable?
context_text: Problem presented by Penny Haxell at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). Here $G$ and $H$ are graphs on the same vertex set, so the components of $H$ (copies of $K_4$) partition the vertices; asking whether $G\cup H$ is 4-colourable for all such $H$ amounts to asking whether a graph of maximum degree $2$ is strongly $4$-colourable, i.e. for every partition of its vertices into sets of size $4$ it has a proper colouring in which each set receives four distinct colours. If $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_5$'s, then $G\cup H$ is 5-colourable; if $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_3$'s, $G\cup H$ need not be 3-colourable. This is a special case of a general question on the strong chromatic number: if $G$ has maximum degree $d$ and $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_{2d}$'s, is $G\cup H$ $(2d)$-colourable? The value $2d$ would be best possible, and Haxell proved that $G\cup H$ is $(3d-1)$-colourable when $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_{3d-1}$'s.
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_cubic_truncation_strong_6_edge_coloring
title: Problem 4.1
statement_text:
Is it true that every diamond-free claw-free cubic graph is strongly 6-edge-colorable?
In other words, is it true that $\chi^{\prime}_{s}(T(G))=6$ for every cubic graph $G$?
context_text: Problem presented by František Kardoš at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A strong edge colouring assigns colours to the edges so that any two edges that are adjacent or joined by an edge receive distinct colours (i.e. a proper colouring of the square of the line graph); the strong chromatic index $\chi'_s(G)$ is the minimum number of colours. A graph is claw-free if it has no induced $K_{1,3}$, and diamond-free if it has no diamond ($K_4$ minus an edge) as a subgraph. The truncation $T(G)$ of a cubic graph $G$ is the cubic graph obtained by replacing each vertex by a triangle; it is well known that the diamond-free claw-free cubic graphs are exactly the truncations of cubic graphs, which explains the equivalence of the two formulations. Lv, Li and Zhang proved that every claw-free subcubic graph other than the triangular prism has $\chi'_s(G)\le8$; Lin and Lin improved this to $7$, with an infinite family of tight examples, all of which contain diamonds. Han and Cui proved that truncated prisms are strongly 6-edge-colourable.
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_cubic_2_homogeneous_coloring_4_colors
title: Problem 5.1
statement_text:
If a cubic graph admits a $2$-homogeneous coloring,
then $4$ colors are always sufficient.
context_text: Problem presented by Borut Lužar and Roman Soták at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A $k$-homogeneous colouring is a proper vertex colouring in which exactly $k$ colours appear in the open neighbourhood of every vertex. A graph has a $1$-homogeneous colouring if and only if it is bipartite. Not every cubic graph has a $2$-homogeneous colouring: for example, a cubic graph containing as a subgraph a triangular prism with one edge of a triangle subdivided does not. Bipartite cubic graphs admit a $2$-homogeneous colouring with at most $6$ colours (Janicová, Madaras, Soták and Lužar), and the problem asks for the minimum number of colours that suffices for every cubic graph admitting a $2$-homogeneous colouring; a weaker version, for bipartite cubic graphs only, appeared in the earlier paper. The statement is proposed as a conjecture based on preliminary research.
notes: Stated as a declarative conjecture inside a labeled Problem environment; a weaker bipartite version appeared in prior work [2].
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_cubic_2_homogeneous_coloring_finite_exceptions
title: Problem 5.2
statement_text: There is a finite number of connected bridgeless cubic graphs that do not admit a $2$-homogeneous coloring.
context_text: Problem presented by Borut Lužar and Roman Soták at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A $k$-homogeneous colouring is a proper vertex colouring in which exactly $k$ colours appear in the open neighbourhood of every vertex. A graph has a $1$-homogeneous colouring if and only if it is bipartite. Not every cubic graph has a $2$-homogeneous colouring: for example, a cubic graph containing as a subgraph a triangular prism with one edge of a triangle subdivided does not. The proposers ask which cubic graphs admit a $2$-homogeneous colouring and, based on preliminary research, conjecture that only finitely many connected bridgeless cubic graphs fail to admit one (they also conjecture that $4$ colours always suffice when one exists).
notes: Stated as a declarative conjecture inside a labeled Problem environment.
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_bridgeless_2_flow_4_flow_pair
title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: Each bridgeless graph admits a $2$-flow $\varphi_{2}$ and a $4$-flow $\varphi_{4}$ such that for any edge $e$, if $\varphi_{2}(e)=0$, then $|\varphi_{4}(e)|\geq 2$.
context_text: Conjecture presented by Jozef Rajník at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). For an integer $k\ge2$, a $k$-flow of a graph is an orientation of the edges with integer values $\varphi(e)$, $|\varphi(e)|<k$ (zero allowed), such that at every vertex the incoming and outgoing sums are equal; a circular $r$-flow is a real-valued flow with $1\le|f(e)|\le r-1$ on every edge. The conjecture implies Tutte's 5-flow conjecture, since $(5\varphi_2+\varphi_4)/2$ is then a circular $5$-flow. It generalises Seymour's approach in the proof of the 6-flow theorem, where a pair of a 2-flow and a 3-flow played a crucial role: besides forbidding the pair of values $(0,0)$ on an edge, the conjecture also forbids $(0,\pm1)$. Such a pair is called a $1/2$-flow-pair. It has been verified for all cyclically 4-edge-connected snarks up to $34$ vertices, all snarks with circular flow number $5$ on $36$ vertices, and snarks of oddness $4$ up to $44$ vertices.
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_bicritical_snarks_almost_group_connected
title: Problem 7.1
statement_text: Every bicritical snark is almost-$\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}$-connected and almost-$\mathbb{Z}_{4}$-connected.
context_text: Problem presented by Nikolay Ulyanov at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025), following the terminology of Jaeger, Linial, Payan and Tarsi. Let $G$ be a directed graph and $A$ a non-trivial abelian group; the boundary of $f:E\to A$ is $\partial f(x)=\sum_{e\text{ leaving }x}f(e)-\sum_{e\text{ entering }x}f(e)$. A map $b:V\to A$ with $\sum_x b(x)=0$ is admissible if $b=\partial f$ for some $f:E\to A\setminus\{0\}$, and $G$ is $A$-connected if every such $b$ is admissible; $G$ is almost-$A$-connected if every such $b$ is admissible except $b=0$ (i.e. $G$ has no nowhere-zero $A$-flow, but all other boundaries are admissible). Here a snark is a cubic, non-3-edge-colourable, cyclically 4-edge-connected graph of girth at least $5$; it is bicritical if removing any two distinct vertices yields a 3-edge-colourable graph, and critical if this holds for any two adjacent vertices. Non-3-edge-colourable cubic graphs have neither a nowhere-zero $\mathbb{Z}_4$-flow nor a nowhere-zero $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-flow. By exhaustive search, the Petersen graph and both Blanuša snarks on $18$ vertices are almost-$\mathbb{Z}_2^2$- and almost-$\mathbb{Z}_4$-connected, whereas Tietze's graph, all snarks on $24$ vertices (all non-bicritical) and the smallest critical non-bicritical snarks on $32$ vertices are not. The problem emerged from exploring the House of Graphs snark database.
notes: Stated as a declarative conjecture inside a labeled Problem environment.
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

name: AX_hypergraph_ramsey_polynomial_iterated_blowup
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: For a $3$-graph $H$, there exists a constant $c$ depending only on $H$ such that $r(H,K_{n}^{(3)})\leq n^{c}$ for all $n$ if and only if $H$ is a subgraph of an iterated blowup of an edge.
context_text: A $k$-graph is a $k$-uniform hypergraph and $K_n^{(k)}$ is the complete $k$-graph on $n$ vertices. The off-diagonal Ramsey number $r(H,K_n^{(k)})$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N^{(k)}$ contains a red copy of $H$ or a blue $K_n^{(k)}$. A blowup of an edge is a complete tripartite $3$-graph, and an iterated blowup of an edge is either a blowup of an edge or is obtained from one by placing iterated blowups inside one or more of its parts; $H$ is iterated tripartite if it is a subgraph of an iterated blowup. For graphs ($k=2$), $r(H,K_n)$ always grows polynomially, but for $3$-graphs it need not: $r(K_4^{(3)},K_n^{(3)})\ge2^{\Omega(n\log n)}$, and even some linear $3$-graphs have superpolynomial Ramsey numbers. The 'if' direction (polynomial growth for iterated tripartite $H$) follows from work of Erdős and Hajnal; the problem was first raised explicitly by Conlon at an AIM workshop in 2015, and the conjecture proposes a full classification. A $3$-graph is tightly connected if any two edges are joined by a sequence of edges in which consecutive edges share two vertices, and tight components are the maximal tightly connected subgraphs. The authors prove the conjecture for tightly connected $H$ (if $H$ is tightly connected and not tripartite then $r(H,K_n^{(3)})\ge2^{\Omega(n^{2/3})}$) and for $H$ with at most two tight components (if moreover $H$ is not iterated tripartite then $r(H,K_n^{(3)})\ge2^{\Omega(\log^2 n)}$).
notes: First author (Conlon) posed the problem at a 2015 AIM workshop (ref [5]); the formal conjecture as stated here appears to be the paper's own formulation.
paper_title: When are off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers polynomial?

name: AX_hypergraph_ramsey_tower_tightly_connected
title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: If $k>s$ and $H$ is a $k$-graph which is $s$-tightly connected and not $k$-partite, then there exists a positive constant $c$ such that $r(H,K_{n}^{(k)})\geq t_{s}(n^{c})$, where the tower function $t_{i}(x)$ is defined by $t_{1}(x)=x$ and $t_{i}(x)=2^{t_{i-1}(x)}$ for all $i\geq 2$.
context_text: A $k$-graph is a $k$-uniform hypergraph and $K_n^{(k)}$ is the complete $k$-graph on $n$ vertices. The off-diagonal Ramsey number $r(H,K_n^{(k)})$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N^{(k)}$ contains a red copy of $H$ or a blue $K_n^{(k)}$. A $k$-graph is $s$-tightly connected if any two edges $e,f$ are joined by a sequence $e=e_0,e_1,\dots,e_t=f$ of edges with $|e_{i-1}\cap e_i|\ge s$ for all $i$, and it is $k$-partite if its vertices can be split into $k$ parts with every edge meeting each part once. The authors prove the case $s=2$: if $k\ge3$ and $H$ is a $2$-tightly connected $k$-graph that is not $k$-partite, then $r(H,K_n^{(k)})\ge2^{\Omega(n^{2/k})}$. They also propose a stronger conjecture: for $k>s$, the Ramsey number of the whole family $\mathcal{H}_s^{(k)}$ of $s$-tightly connected non-$k$-partite $k$-graphs versus $K_n^{(k)}$ is at least $t_s(n^c)$; since $r(K_n^{(s)},K_n^{(s)})\ge r(\mathcal{H}_s^{(k)},K_n^{(k)})$, this would show that the diagonal Ramsey number $r(K_n^{(s)},K_n^{(s)})$ has tower height at least $s-1$, matching the long-standing upper bound and settling perhaps the central open problem of hypergraph Ramsey theory. The authors call this conjecture likely difficult.
paper_title: When are off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers polynomial?

name: AX_reachability_network_min_transpositions
title: Problem 1
statement_text: What is the minimum number of transpositions needed in a $t$-reachable network? What if all transpositions are of the form $(1,\cdot)$?
context_text: A sequence of transpositions $T_1,\dots,T_\ell$ of $[n]$, $T_i=(a_i,b_i)$, is a $t$-reachability network ($t$-reachable network) if for every choice of $t$ distinct ordered points $x_1,\dots,x_t\in[n]$ some subsequence $T_{i_1},\dots,T_{i_{\ell'}}$ has composition $(a_{i_1},b_{i_1})\cdots(a_{i_{\ell'}},b_{i_{\ell'}})$ mapping $j\mapsto x_j$ for $1\le j\le t$; informally, $t$ counters starting at positions $1,\dots,t$ can be moved to any prescribed positions by performing or skipping each transposition in turn. An $n$-reachability network is a permutation network, which needs $\Theta(n\log n)$ transpositions (Waksman). Star transpositions are those of the form $(1,\cdot)$. For $t=1$, exactly $n-1$ transpositions are needed. The authors prove that the shortest $2$-reachability network has exactly $\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$ transpositions, and $\lceil3(n-1)/2\rceil$ when only star transpositions are allowed ($n\ge3$); for every $t\ge3$, a randomised construction gives $t$-reachability networks of length $(2+o_t(1))n$, with leading coefficient independent of $t$ (using star transpositions apart from a final network on the first $t$ positions). For star transpositions they prove a lower bound $(2-1/t)n-C_t$, tight up to additive constants for $t=2,3$. Even the asymptotics of the minimum length for large $t$ remain open, and there is still a gap between upper and lower bounds in the star case.
paper_title: Short reachability networks

name: AX_reachability_network_2_uniformity_lazy_transpositions
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: For $n\geq 2$, the minimum number of lazy transpositions in a 2-uniformity network is $2n-3$.
context_text: A sequence of transpositions $T_1,\dots,T_\ell$ of $[n]$, $T_i=(a_i,b_i)$, is a $t$-reachability network ($t$-reachable network) if for every choice of $t$ distinct ordered points $x_1,\dots,x_t\in[n]$ some subsequence $T_{i_1},\dots,T_{i_{\ell'}}$ has composition $(a_{i_1},b_{i_1})\cdots(a_{i_{\ell'}},b_{i_{\ell'}})$ mapping $j\mapsto x_j$ for $1\le j\le t$; informally, $t$ counters starting at positions $1,\dots,t$ can be moved to any prescribed positions by performing or skipping each transposition in turn. An $n$-reachability network is a permutation network, which needs $\Theta(n\log n)$ transpositions (Waksman). Star transpositions are those of the form $(1,\cdot)$. A lazy transposition $(a,b,p)$ is the random permutation equal to $(a,b)$ with probability $p$ and to the identity otherwise. A sequence of independent lazy transpositions $T_1,\dots,T_\ell$ is a $t$-uniformity network if the probability that $T_1\cdots T_\ell$ maps $(1,\dots,t)$ to $(x_1,\dots,x_t)$ is the same for every tuple of $t$ distinct elements of $[n]$; every $t$-uniformity network yields a $t$-reachability network, and the shortest $2$-reachability network has $\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$ transpositions. The authors construct a $2$-uniformity network of length $2n-3$: $(1,2,\frac12),(1,3,\frac2n),(1,2,\frac12),(1,4,\frac2{n-1}),\dots,(1,2,\frac12),(1,n,\frac23),(1,2,\frac12)$, prove that $2$-uniformity networks using only star transpositions need at least $1.6n-C$ of them, and conjecture that $2n-3$ is optimal (it would match nicely with selection networks). A footnote in the final version states that, after a preliminary version was put on arXiv, this conjecture was proven by Janzer, Johnson and Leader ('Partial shuffles by lazy swaps'), which also separates $2$-reachability from $2$-uniformity without the star restriction.
notes: The paper states that after a preliminary version was posted on arXiv, Conjecture 1 was proven (by unspecified authors in the truncated text); it may no longer be open.
paper_title: Short reachability networks

name: AX_odd_cycle_orientations_avoidable
title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: All orientations of odd cycles are avoidable.
context_text: A digraph $F$ is avoidable if there is a function $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) of minimum out-degree at least $k$. This is the directed analogue of Thomassen's conjecture, which in this language states that every undirected graph containing a cycle is avoidable (with minimum degree instead of out-degree); no forest is avoidable there. For undirected graphs all odd cycles are trivially avoidable, since every graph of minimum degree at least $2k-1$ has a bipartite subgraph of minimum degree at least $k$; for digraphs no such reduction exists, as Thomassen constructed digraphs of arbitrarily large minimum out-degree in which every directed cycle is odd. The authors prove that all orientations of $C_3$ and $C_5$ are avoidable (directed cycles of all lengths were known to be avoidable, by Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl), while no one-directed complete bipartite graph (all arcs from one side to the other; this includes anti-directed even cycles) and no oriented forest is avoidable. A positive resolution would yield that every digraph of large minimum out-degree has a subdigraph of still large minimum out-degree whose underlying graph has large odd girth, a directed analogue of the existence of bipartite subgraphs of high minimum degree.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

name: AX_height_function_digraphs_not_avoidable
title: Question 6.2
statement_text: Are all digraphs which allow a height function not avoidable?
context_text: A digraph $F$ is avoidable if there is a function $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) of minimum out-degree at least $k$. This is the directed analogue of Thomassen's conjecture, which in this language states that every undirected graph containing a cycle is avoidable (with minimum degree instead of out-degree); no forest is avoidable there. A height function of a digraph $D$ is a map $h:V(D)\to\mathbb{Z}$ with $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$ (so a digraph allows one if and only if, in every cycle of the underlying graph, the numbers of forward and backward arcs are equal). The authors prove that all orientations of $C_3$ and $C_5$ are avoidable (directed cycles of all lengths were known to be avoidable, by Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl), while no one-directed complete bipartite graph (all arcs from one side to the other; this includes anti-directed even cycles) and no oriented forest is avoidable. All digraphs shown not to be avoidable in the paper (one-directed complete bipartite graphs and oriented forests) allow a height function, which motivates asking whether allowing a height function characterizes, or at least implies, non-avoidability. The simplest digraph with a height function whose avoidability is unknown is the orientation of $C_4$ formed by two parallel directed paths of length two.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

name: AX_c4_orientations_avoidable
title: Question 6.3
statement_text: Which orientations of $C_{4}$ are avoidable?
context_text: A digraph $F$ is avoidable if there is a function $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) of minimum out-degree at least $k$. This is the directed analogue of Thomassen's conjecture, which in this language states that every undirected graph containing a cycle is avoidable (with minimum degree instead of out-degree); no forest is avoidable there. The undirected $C_4$ is avoidable (Thomassen's conjecture is known for $4$-cycles). The authors prove that no one-directed complete bipartite graph (all arcs going from one side to the other) is avoidable; in particular the anti-directed orientation of $C_4$ (alternating directions) is not avoidable, whereas the directed $C_4$ is avoidable (Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl proved that all directed cycles are). A height function of a digraph $D$ is a map $h:V(D)\to\mathbb{Z}$ with $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$ (so a digraph allows one if and only if, in every cycle of the underlying graph, the numbers of forward and backward arcs are equal). The authors ask whether digraphs allowing a height function are never avoidable; the simplest digraph with a height function whose avoidability is unknown is the orientation of $C_4$ consisting of two parallel directed paths of length two. They believe this is the most difficult orientation of $C_4$ and that resolving the height-function question would likely also answer this one.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

name: AX_eulerian_avoidable_digraphs_characterization
title: Eulerian-avoidability characterization
statement_text: Which digraphs are Eulerian-avoidable?
context_text: A digraph is Eulerian if every vertex has the same in-degree as out-degree. A digraph $F$ is Eulerian-avoidable if there is $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every Eulerian digraph with minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph (one with no copy of $F$) with minimum out-degree at least $k$; in the general (non-Eulerian) setting, $F$ is called avoidable. A digraph is $d$-regular if every vertex has in- and out-degree $d$, and $F$ is regular-avoidable if there is $d_F$ such that every $d_F(k)$-regular digraph contains an $F$-free subdigraph of minimum out-degree $k$; the authors prove that a digraph is regular-avoidable if and only if it is not a grounded forest (an oriented forest having a height function, i.e. $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$, that is constant on the vertices of in-degree at least $2$). In the general setting the characterization of avoidable digraphs is wide open (all orientations of $C_3$ and $C_5$ are avoidable, but no one-directed complete bipartite graph and no oriented forest is). Eulerian host digraphs are intermediate between the two settings, and the authors suggest that this question might yield a new approach to the undirected Thomassen conjecture (every graph containing a cycle is avoidable with respect to minimum degree). They propose as a starting point whether every orientation of $C_4$ is Eulerian-avoidable.
notes: Stated as a prose question immediately preceding the numbered Question 6.4; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

name: AX_c4_orientations_eulerian_avoidable
title: Question 6.4
statement_text: Is every orientation of $C_{4}$ Eulerian-avoidable?
context_text: A digraph is Eulerian if every vertex has the same in-degree as out-degree. A digraph $F$ is Eulerian-avoidable if there is $d_F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every Eulerian digraph with minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph with minimum out-degree at least $k$; without the Eulerian restriction on the host, $F$ is avoidable. In the general setting the authors show that the anti-directed $C_4$ (alternating directions) is not avoidable, the directed $C_4$ is avoidable (all directed cycles are, by Dellamonica, Koubek, Martin and Rödl), and the avoidability of the orientation formed by two parallel directed paths of length two is open. A digraph is $d$-regular if every vertex has in- and out-degree $d$, and $F$ is regular-avoidable if there is $d_F$ such that every $d_F(k)$-regular digraph contains an $F$-free subdigraph of minimum out-degree $k$; the authors prove that a digraph is regular-avoidable if and only if it is not a grounded forest (an oriented forest having a height function, i.e. $h(v)=h(u)+1$ for every arc $(u,v)$, that is constant on the vertices of in-degree at least $2$). The Eulerian setting sits between the two and might give new insight into Thomassen's undirected conjecture; this question is proposed as a starting point.
paper_title: Extending Thomassen's conjecture to directed graphs

name: AX_cyclic_clique_minor_min_degree_bound
title: Question 1.2
statement_text: Could it be that $f(\ell)=O(\ell\sqrt{\log\ell})$, matching the bound for standard minors from [Kos82, dlV83]?
context_text: A graph $H$ is a cyclic minor of $G$ if $H$ is isomorphic to a graph obtained from a Hamiltonian subgraph of $G$ (a subgraph $G'$ with a Hamiltonian cycle $C$) by contracting some of the edges of the Hamiltonian cycle $C$. Using $k$-linked subgraphs one can show that large minimum degree forces a large clique as a cyclic minor, so $f(\ell)$, the smallest integer $\delta$ such that every graph of minimum degree at least $\delta$ contains $K_\ell$ as a cyclic minor, is well defined. The authors prove $f(4)=3$, $6\le f(5)\le8$ (the icosahedron has minimum degree $5$ and no $K_5$ minor) and $f(\ell)=O(\ell^2)$. The question is whether the order $\ell\sqrt{\log\ell}$, which is the known bound for ordinary $K_\ell$ minors (Kostochka; de la Vega), also suffices for cyclic minors. The paper's main result refines a theorem of Gupta, Kahn and Robertson: every graph of minimum degree $k\ge2$ has a cycle $C$ with at least $k+1$ vertices having at least $k$ neighbours in $C$, and some edges of $C$ can be contracted in $G[V(C)]$ to obtain minimum degree at least $\lceil(k+2)/2\rceil$, so large minimum degree forces a cyclic minor of large minimum degree.
paper_title: Lollipops, dense cycles and chords

name: AX_lollipop_active_path_complete_graph_criterion
title: Question 4.1
statement_text: Is there a simple criterion for a sequence of vertices to be an active path of $K_n$ (with respect to a Hamiltonian cycle $c_1c_2\dots c_nc_1$ of $K_n$)?
context_text: A chord of a path or cycle $Q$ is an edge joining two non-consecutive vertices of $Q$. Given a cycle $C=c_1c_2\dots c_tc_1$ of $G$, define sets $\mathcal{S}_1,\mathcal{S}_2,\dots$ of Hamiltonian paths of $G[V(C)]$ starting at $c_1$: $\mathcal{S}_1=\{c_1c_2\dots c_t,\ c_1c_tc_{t-1}\dots c_2\}$, and for each $Q=c_1\dots u\in\mathcal{S}_i$ and each $v$ such that $uv$ is a chord of $Q$, letting $w$ be the neighbour of $v$ on the subpath $vQu$, if $vw$ is an edge of $C$ then the path $c_1QvuQw$ (follow $Q$ to $v$, jump to $u$, follow $Q$ backwards to $w$) is put in $\mathcal{S}_{i+1}$. A path is active if it lies in some $\mathcal{S}_i$, and a vertex $u\ne c_1$ is active if it is the end of an active path. These notions come from the lollipop method (lollipops are a path and a cycle sharing exactly one vertex, the end of the path): for an optimal lollipop with cycle $C$, every active vertex has all its neighbours in $V(C)$, which yields many vertices of high degree in $C$ and hence cycles with many chords. Not every Hamiltonian path starting at $c_1$ is active: in $K_6$ with the Hamiltonian cycle $C=c_1c_2\dots c_6c_1$, the path $c_1c_2c_5c_4c_3c_6$ is not active, and there are $6$ non-active paths among the $120$ Hamiltonian paths starting at $c_1$. The question asks, for $K_n$ with $C$ a Hamiltonian cycle $c_1c_2\dots c_nc_1$, for a simple characterisation of the sequences of vertices that are active paths.
paper_title: Lollipops, dense cycles and chords

name: AX_lollipop_active_vertices_optimal_cycle
title: Question 4.2
statement_text: Is there a simple way to compute all the active vertices in the cycle of an optimal lollipop?
context_text: A lollipop in $G$ is a pair $(P,C)$ where $P=p_1\dots p_s$ ($s\ge1$) is a path, $C=c_1\dots c_tc_1$ ($t\ge3$) is a cycle, $p_s=c_1$ and $V(P)\cap V(C)=\{c_1\}$; it is optimal if no lollipop has a vertex set strictly containing $V(P)\cup V(C)$ and, among lollipops on the same vertex set, $C$ is as long as possible. A chord of a path or cycle $Q$ is an edge joining two non-consecutive vertices of $Q$. Given a cycle $C=c_1c_2\dots c_tc_1$ of $G$, define sets $\mathcal{S}_1,\mathcal{S}_2,\dots$ of Hamiltonian paths of $G[V(C)]$ starting at $c_1$: $\mathcal{S}_1=\{c_1c_2\dots c_t,\ c_1c_tc_{t-1}\dots c_2\}$, and for each $Q=c_1\dots u\in\mathcal{S}_i$ and each $v$ such that $uv$ is a chord of $Q$, letting $w$ be the neighbour of $v$ on the subpath $vQu$, if $vw$ is an edge of $C$ then the path $c_1QvuQw$ (follow $Q$ to $v$, jump to $u$, follow $Q$ backwards to $w$) is put in $\mathcal{S}_{i+1}$. A path is active if it lies in some $\mathcal{S}_i$, and a vertex $u\ne c_1$ is active if it is the end of an active path. For an optimal lollipop $(P,C)$ in a graph of minimum degree $k\ge2$, every active vertex has all its neighbours in $V(C)$, and the authors show that $C$ has at least $k$ active vertices (at least $k+1$ if $c_1$ has fewer than $k$ neighbours in $C$); this gives a cycle with at least $k+1$ vertices of degree at least $k$ in $C$, hence at least $(k+1)(k-2)/2$ chords, and allows contracting edges of $C$ into a dense cyclic minor. Finding an optimal lollipop is NP-hard and there may be exponentially many active paths; the authors' polynomial algorithm only computes enough active paths with distinct ends. In the lollipop argument, the number of distinct active vertices (and thus of chords) grows with the girth of the host graph.
paper_title: Lollipops, dense cycles and chords

name: AX_min_degree_3_cycle_linear_chords
title: Question 4.3
statement_text: Is there a constant $c>0$ such that every graph with minimum degree 3 contains a cycle of length $\ell$ with at least $c\ell$ chords?
context_text: A chord of a cycle is an edge joining two non-consecutive vertices of the cycle, and the length of a cycle is its number of vertices (equivalently edges). Gupta, Kahn and Robertson proved that every graph of minimum degree at least $k\ge2$ has a cycle with at least $(k+1)(k-2)/2$ chords, which is tight for $K_{k+1}$. For minimum degree $3$ alone one cannot ask for many chords: a disjoint union of copies of $K_4$ has no cycle with more than two chords. The authors observe that in their lollipop argument the number of distinct active vertices, and thus of chords, increases with the girth $g$ of the graph, which suggests relating the number of chords to the length of the cycle. They say they are very far from answering this, as even the relaxation where $c\ell$ is replaced by $f(\ell)$ for some function $f$ tending to infinity seems unclear.
paper_title: Lollipops, dense cycles and chords

name: AX_quasi_isometry_multiplicative_to_additive_classes
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a class of connected graphs, closed under contracting edges and subdividing edges. For all $L,C$ there exists $C^{\prime}$ such that if there is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry from a graph $G$ to a member of $\mathcal{C}$, then there is a $(1,C^{\prime})$-quasi-isometry from $G$ to a member of $\mathcal{C}$.
context_text: Graphs may be infinite and have no loops or parallel edges. For graphs $G,H$ and $L,C\ge0$, a map $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry if $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)+C$ and $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))+C$ for all $u,v$ (whenever the right-hand distance is finite), and every vertex of $H$ is at distance at most $C$ from $\phi(V(G))$. The conjecture is motivated by the theorem of Chepoi, Dragan, Newman, Rabinovich and Vaxès (also proved by Kerr) that an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a tree implies a $(1,C')$-quasi-isometry to a tree, and by a question of Georgakopoulos about planar graphs. Some closure of $\mathcal{C}$ is necessary: subdividing every edge of $H$ once gives a $(2,0)$-quasi-isometry to $H$, and contracting a matching gives a $(3,0)$-quasi-isometry, so $\mathcal{C}$ must be more or less closed under subdivision and contraction. The authors prove that for all $L,C,k$ there is $C'$ such that an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry from $G$ to a graph $H$ of path-width at most $k$ yields a $(1,C')$-quasi-isometry from $G$ to a graph obtained from $H$ by subdividing and contracting edges (even the same map works after putting integer weights on the edges of $H$), and they can prove the conjecture when $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of connected outerplanar graphs. A result of Davies, Hatzel and Hickingbotham shows that the path-width restriction cannot simply be dropped in the weighted statement, although this does not disprove the conjecture. The case of tree-width at most two is open, even in the weaker form where the target may have tree-width at most some $k$.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. II. Path-width and additive quasi-isometry

name: AX_sparse_graph_cut_small_chromatic_number
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: For every integer $k$ and every graph $G$ on at least $k$ vertices, if $$|E(G)|<k|V(G)|-\tfrac{k(k+1)}{2},$$ then $G$ admits a cut $X$ with $\chi(G[X])<k$. In particular, $\ell_{k}=k$.
context_text: A cut (or separator) of a graph $G$ is a set $X\subseteq V(G)$ such that $G\setminus X$ is disconnected. For an integer $k$, $\ell_k$ is the supremum of the reals $\ell$ such that every sufficiently large graph (as a function of $k$ and $\ell$) with average degree less than $2\ell$ has a cut $X$ with $\chi(G[X])<k$. A minimum-degree argument gives $\ell_k\ge k/2$, and joining a $k$-clique completely to an independent set of size $n-k$ gives an $n$-vertex graph with exactly $kn-\frac{k(k+1)}{2}$ edges in which every cut contains the clique, so $\ell_k\le k$; the conjectured edge bound is exactly the one of this example. It is folklore that $\ell_1=1$; Chen and Yu proved that every $n$-vertex graph with fewer than $2n-3$ edges has a stable cut, so $\ell_2=2$; Bogdanov et al. conjectured that fewer than $3n-6$ edges forces a bipartite cut ($\ell_3=3$). This conjecture is the natural generalization formulated by the authors, whose main purpose is to show that it is far from correct: they prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $k$, $\ell_k\le(1+\varepsilon)\frac{k}{2}$, so $\ell_k\sim k/2$, and indeed that there are arbitrarily large graphs of average degree $(1+o(1))k$ in which every cut contains a $k$-clique (which also rules out the stronger version asking for a $(k-2)$-degenerate cut). They ask for the smallest $k$ for which the conjecture fails, in particular whether it already fails for $k=3$.
notes: This conjecture is introduced by the paper's own authors and immediately refuted within the same paper: Theorem 1.4 shows $\ell_k \leq (1+\varepsilon)\frac{k}{2}$ for all sufficiently large $k$, so that asymptotically $\ell_k \sim \frac{k}{2}$ rather than $\ell_k = k$.
paper_title: On cuts of small chromatic number in sparse graphs

name: AX_circuit_distance_polygons_np_hard
title: Conjecture 21
statement_text: Circuit Distance is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard for polygons.
context_text: Let $P=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d : A\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b}\}$ be a polytope given by $A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times d}$ and $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{Q}^m$. A circuit of $P$ is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{g}$ such that $A_I\mathbf{g}=0$ for some $(d-1)\times d$ submatrix $A_I$ of $A$ of rank $d-1$ (all edge directions are circuits; for polygons, i.e. $d=2$, circuits are exactly the edge directions). A circuit move from $\mathbf{x}\in P$ goes to $\mathbf{x}+\alpha\mathbf{g}$ for a circuit $\mathbf{g}$ with $\alpha>0$ maximal such that the point stays in $P$, and a circuit walk of length $k$ is a sequence of $k$ circuit moves. The problem Circuit Distance takes as input such a polytope, two vertices $\mathbf{s}$ and $\mathbf{t}$ of $P$ and an integer $k\ge0$, and asks whether there is a circuit walk from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ of length at most $k$. Circuit walks underlie circuit augmentation schemes for linear programming, which generalize the simplex method. The authors prove that the monotone variant (walks that strictly improve a linear objective $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{x}$ at each step and end at a $\mathbf{c}$-maximal vertex) is NP-hard already for polygons, and even NP-hard to approximate within $m^{1-\varepsilon}$; they remark that their techniques seem likely to extend to the non-monotone setting, but this requires some technical innovation. This is discrete geometry / optimization rather than graph theory.
notes: Polygons are 2-dimensional polytopes; in this case circuit directions coincide with edge directions (as noted in Observation 9 of the paper).
paper_title: Short circuit walks in fixed dimension

name: AX_clique_ramsey_minimizer_complete_graph
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: For all $s \leq t$, $r_{K_s}(K_t) = \binom{r(K_t)}{s}$.
context_text: A graph $G$ is $H$-Ramsey if every two-colouring of its edges contains a monochromatic copy of $H$, and the $F$-Ramsey number $r_F(H)$ is the minimum number of copies of $F$ in an $H$-Ramsey graph; $F$ a single vertex gives the Ramsey number and $F=K_2$ the size Ramsey number. $r(K_t)$ is the usual Ramsey number of $K_t$, so $K_{r(K_t)}$ is $K_t$-Ramsey and $r_{K_s}(K_t)\le\binom{r(K_t)}{s}$. Chvátal observed that $r_{K_2}(K_t)=\binom{r(K_t)}{2}$, i.e. the complete graph on $r(K_t)$ vertices minimises the number of edges among $K_t$-Ramsey graphs. Sam Spiro asked whether the analogue holds for $r_{K_s}(K_t)$, and the authors conjecture that it does, i.e. that $K_{r(K_t)}$ minimises the number of copies of $K_s$ among $K_t$-Ramsey graphs. The condition $s\le t$ is necessary, since there are $K_{t+1}$-free $K_t$-Ramsey graphs (Folkman), giving $r_{K_s}(K_t)=0$ for $s>t$. The authors prove the case $s=3$ for all sufficiently large $t$, via the result that for an absolute constant $K$ every graph of chromatic number at least $r$ in which every edge lies in at least $K$ triangles has at least $\binom r3$ triangles. For general $s\le t$ they prove $r_{K_s}(K_t)\ge2^{s(t-1)/2-1}$, and they do not believe their techniques extend to $s\ge4$.
paper_title: Triangle Ramsey numbers of complete graphs

name: AX_clique_ramsey_minimizer_q_colors
title: q-color generalization of Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: The $q$-color generalization of the conjecture that $r_{K_s}(K_t)=\binom{r(K_t)}{s}$ for all $s\le t$ holds: for all $q\ge2$ and $s\le t$, the minimum number of copies of $K_s$ in a graph whose every $q$-colouring of the edges contains a monochromatic $K_t$ equals $\binom{r_q(K_t)}{s}$, where $r_q(K_t)$ is the $q$-color Ramsey number of $K_t$.
context_text: A graph $G$ is $H$-Ramsey if every two-colouring of its edges contains a monochromatic copy of $H$, and the $F$-Ramsey number $r_F(H)$ is the minimum number of copies of $F$ in an $H$-Ramsey graph; $F$ a single vertex gives the Ramsey number and $F=K_2$ the size Ramsey number. $r(K_t)$ is the usual Ramsey number of $K_t$, so $K_{r(K_t)}$ is $K_t$-Ramsey and $r_{K_s}(K_t)\le\binom{r(K_t)}{s}$. Chvátal observed that $r_{K_2}(K_t)=\binom{r(K_t)}{2}$, i.e. the complete graph on $r(K_t)$ vertices minimises the number of edges among $K_t$-Ramsey graphs. In the $q$-colour setting, $H$-Ramsey means that every $q$-colouring of the edges contains a monochromatic copy of $H$, and $r_q(K_t)$ is the least $n$ such that every $q$-colouring of $E(K_n)$ contains a monochromatic $K_t$. The authors conjecture $r_{K_s}(K_t)=\binom{r(K_t)}{s}$ for all $s\le t$ (two colours) and prove it for $s=3$ and $t$ sufficiently large. They note that the $q$-colour generalizations of Chvátal's theorem, of their $s=3$ result and of their basic lemmas (a $K_t$-Ramsey graph has chromatic number at least $r(K_t)$, and in a minimal $K_t$-Ramsey graph every edge lies in a $K_t$) hold by the same proofs, and they also conjecture the $q$-colour generalization of the main conjecture. The paper does not write the $q$-colour statement explicitly; the formulation above is the natural one.
notes: Stated in prose without a formal label. The paper text reads 'the q-color generalization of Theorem 1.2', which is almost certainly a typo for 'Conjecture 1.2', since no Theorem 1.2 exists in this paper. No explicit formula for the q-color version is given in the extracted text.
paper_title: Triangle Ramsey numbers of complete graphs

name: AX_tea_sharing_optimal_sequence_exponential_length
title: Question 6.1
statement_text: For every finite graph $G$, every ${w\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{V(G)}}$, and every ${v\in V(G)}$, is there always a ${(w,v)}$-optimal sequence whose length is at most $2^{{\left\lvert{V(G)}\right\rvert}}$?
context_text: A weight distribution on $G$ is a function $w\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V(G)}$ (the amount of tea at each vertex). A sharing move on a finite nonempty set $T\subseteq V(G)$ inducing a connected subgraph replaces $w(x)$ by the average $w(T)/|T|$ for every $x\in T$ and leaves other vertices unchanged. With $\mathcal{R}(w)$ the set of distributions reachable from $w$ by finite sequences of sharing moves, $w^*(v)=\sup\{w'(v):w'\in\mathcal{R}(w)\}$, and a finite sequence $(T_1,\dots,T_m)$ of sharing moves is $(w,v)$-optimal if applying it to $w$ yields a distribution $w'$ with $w'(v)=w^*(v)$. The authors prove that starting from one unit of tea at a vertex $r$, a vertex at distance $d$ never gets more than $1/(d+1)$ (attained by one sharing move along a shortest path), and that for every finite graph a $(w,v)$-optimal sequence always exists (whereas on infinite graphs it may not); but it is unclear whether the length of a shortest optimal sequence is bounded by a computable function of $|V(G)|$, even for $w\in\{0,1\}^{V(G)}$, and they do not know how to prove existence without the Axiom of Choice. One approach to a positive answer would be to show that some optimal sequence never repeats a sharing move; however, there is a finite tree with a distribution $w$ and vertex $v$ for which every optimal sequence contains a move that is a subset of a later move.
paper_title: Sharing tea on a graph

name: AX_strong_coloring_number_bramble_polynomial_expansion
title: Question 2
statement_text: Is it true that for every graph class $\mathcal{C}$ with polynomial expansion, there exists a polynomial function $f$ such that for every integer $r\geqslant 0$ and every graph $G\in\mathcal{C}$, $$\mathrm{scol}_{r}(G)\leqslant f(r,\mathrm{bn}_{r}(G))?$$
context_text: A graph $H$ is a depth-$r$ minor of $G$ if it is obtained from a subgraph of $G$ by contracting pairwise disjoint connected subgraphs of radius at most $r$; $\nabla_r(G)$ is the maximum of $|E(H)|/|V(H)|$ over depth-$r$ minors $H$ of $G$, and a class $\mathcal{C}$ has polynomial expansion if $\nabla_r(G)\le f(r)$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, $r\ge0$, for some polynomial $f$. Given a linear order $\pi$ of $V(G)$, a vertex $u$ is strongly $r$-reachable from $v$ if $\pi(u)\le\pi(v)$ and some path of length at most $r$ joins $v$ to $u$ with all internal vertices $w$ satisfying $\pi(w)>\pi(v)$; the strong $r$-coloring number $\mathrm{scol}_r(G)$ is the minimum over $\pi$ of the maximum over $v$ of the number of vertices strongly $r$-reachable from $v$. Two vertex sets touch if they share a vertex or are joined by an edge; a bramble is a set of pairwise touching connected vertex sets, its order is the minimum size of a set meeting all its elements, and a depth-$r$ bramble is one whose elements each induce a subgraph of radius at most $r$; the depth-$r$ bramble number $\mathrm{bn}_r(G)$ is the maximum order of a depth-$r$ bramble ($\mathrm{bn}_\infty(G)=\mathrm{scol}_\infty(G)$ is treewidth plus one). The authors prove $\mathrm{bn}_r(G)\le\mathrm{scol}_{4r+1}(G)$, and that in a class with polynomial expansion $\mathrm{bn}_r$ (and the related depth-$r$ tangle number, linkedness and well-linkedness) is bounded by a polynomial in $r$. A positive answer to this question would therefore answer positively the open problem of Joret and Wood asking whether every class with polynomial expansion has strong $r$-coloring numbers bounded by a polynomial in $r$ (which would characterize polynomial expansion). The polynomial expansion assumption is essential: over all graphs, $\mathrm{scol}_r(G)$ cannot be bounded by any function of $r$ and $\mathrm{bn}_{g(r)}(G)$, for any function $g$ (graphs of large minimum degree and large girth have $\mathrm{bn}_s(G)=2$).
paper_title: Shallow brambles

name: AX_fat_minor_quasi_isometry_trees_planar
title: Informal question: validity of Conjecture 1.2 for trees and planar graphs
statement_text: Is the Georgakopoulos–Papasoglu conjecture (for all $c\ge0$ there exist $L,C\ge0$ such that every graph $G$ that does not contain $H$ as a $c$-fat minor admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with no $H$ minor) true when $H$ is a tree, or more generally when $H$ is a planar graph?
context_text: Graphs may be infinite and have no loops or parallel edges; distances are shortest-path distances. A map $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry if $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)+C$ and $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))+C$ whenever these distances are finite, and every vertex of $H$ is within distance $C$ of $\phi(V(G))$. $G$ contains $H$ as a $c$-fat minor if there are pairwise vertex-disjoint non-null connected subgraphs $\eta(x)$ of $G$, one for each vertex and each edge $x$ of $H$, such that for each edge $uv$ of $H$ there are edges of $G$ from $\eta(uv)$ to $\eta(u)$ and to $\eta(v)$, and $\mathrm{dist}_G(\eta(x),\eta(y))>c$ for all distinct $x,y$ except when one is a vertex of $H$ incident with the other, an edge. If $G$ contains $H$ as a $c$-fat minor with $c\ge L(L+C)+C$, then every graph to which $G$ is $(L,C)$-quasi-isometric contains $H$ as a minor; Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu conjectured the converse for every $H$. It is known for $H=K_3$ (Manning), $K_{1,m}$, $K_{2,3}$, $K_4^-$ and $K_{2,t}$, but was disproved in general by Davies, Hickingbotham, Illingworth and McCarty, and also for the octahedron by Albrechtsen, Distel and Georgakopoulos. In the version of the paper examined, the authors say it may be true for all trees $H$ as far as they know. Their main result is a coarse analogue of the Robertson–Seymour path-width theorem: for every finite tree $H$ there is $k$ such that for every $c$ there are $L,C$ such that every graph with no $c$-fat $H$-minor is $(L,C)$-quasi-isometric to a graph of line-width at most $k$ (line-width extends path-width to infinite graphs via decompositions indexed by a linear order), and conversely. This does not settle the conjecture for trees, whose conclusion asks for a quasi-isometric graph with no $H$ minor.
notes: Appears as a parenthetical remark in the introduction rather than a formally labelled environment.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. III. Excluding a fat tree

name: AX_coarse_menger_bounded_genus
title: Informal conjecture: coarse Menger for bounded genus
statement_text: It might be true that the coarse Menger conjecture holds for graphs of bounded genus, that is: for all integers $g,k\geq0$ and $c\geq1$ there exists $\ell\geq0$ such that for every graph $G$ of genus at most $g$ and all $S,T\subseteq V(G)$, either there are $k+1$ paths between $S$ and $T$ pairwise at distance at least $c$, or there is a set $X\subseteq V(G)$ with $|X|\leq k$ such that every path between $S$ and $T$ contains a vertex at distance at most $\ell$ from some member of $X$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. Menger's theorem gives either $k+1$ vertex-disjoint $S$–$T$ paths or a set of at most $k$ vertices meeting all of them; the coarse Menger conjecture, proposed independently by Albrechtsen, Huynh, Jacobs, Knappe and Wollan and by Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu, asks for paths pairwise far apart: for all $k\ge0$ and $c\ge1$ there is $\ell$ such that every graph $G$ and $S,T\subseteq V(G)$ have either $k+1$ $S$–$T$ paths pairwise at distance at least $c$, or a set $X$ of at most $k$ vertices such that every $S$–$T$ path passes within distance $\ell$ of $X$. It holds for $k=1$, and for bounded-degree graphs when $c=2$, but three of the authors showed it is false for every $k\ge2$ and fixed $c\ge3$ (even allowing $|X|$ to be any constant depending on $k,c$). Their counterexamples have unbounded genus and unbounded path-width. In this paper the authors prove the conjecture for graphs excluding a fixed near-outerplanar graph as a minor, hence for graphs of bounded path-width (exclude a large tree) and for series-parallel graphs (exclude $K_4$), whereas it fails for bounded tree-width. The bounded-genus case is open; some progress is announced in a subsequent paper of the series.
notes: Stated as a possibility in running prose ("it might be true … but this is open"); no formal conjecture label.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. V. The coarse Menger conjecture in bounded path-width

name: AX_coarse_menger_bounded_genus_surfaces
title: Conjecture 1.2 (Coarse Menger conjecture for surfaces)
statement_text:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a fixed surface. For all integers $k,c\geq 0$ there exists $\ell>0$ with the following property. Let $G$ be a graph that embeds on $\mathcal{S}$ and let $S,T\subseteq V(G)$. Then either

$\bullet$ there are $k+1$ paths between $S,T$, pairwise $c$-distant; or

$\bullet$ there is a set $X\subseteq V(G)$ with $|X|\leq k$ such that every path between $S,T$ contains a vertex with distance at most $\ell$ from some member of $X$.
context_text: Graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges. The distance between two vertices, vertex sets or subgraphs is the number of edges of a shortest path with one end in each, and they are $c$-distant if their distance is at least $c$; a path between $S,T$ is a path with one end in $S$ and the other in $T$. Menger's theorem is the case $c=1$, $\ell=0$ (disjoint paths versus a separating set of $k$ vertices). The original coarse Menger conjecture, the same statement for all graphs, was proposed by Albrechtsen, Huynh, Jacobs, Knappe and Wollan, and independently by Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu; it holds for $k=1$, for $c=2$ in graphs of bounded degree, and for graphs of bounded path-width, but Nguyen, Scott and Seymour showed it false for all $k\ge2$, even with $c=3$ and maximum degree three (and even if $|X|$ may be an arbitrary function of $k$). Their counterexamples have unbounded genus, so the conjecture might hold for planar graphs or graphs on a fixed surface. As a first step, the authors prove it for planar $G$ drawn with all vertices of $S\cup T$ on the infinite region: then either there are $k+1$ paths between $S,T$ pairwise $(c+1)$-distant, or at most $k$ connected subgraphs, with diameters summing to at most $200k^3c$, meet every path between $S$ and $T$; in this case they also obtain a linear-time algorithm to test for $k+1$ pairwise far-apart paths.
notes: The paper proves a special case (Theorem 1.3): the conjecture holds when $G$ is planar and all vertices of $S\cup T$ lie on the infinite region, with the blocking structure being at most $k$ connected subgraphs whose diameters sum to at most $200k^3c$.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. VI. Distant paths across a disc

name: AX_coarse_treewidth_additive_quasi_isometry
title: Open question on Theorem 1.2 with $L=1$
statement_text: We do not know whether the following holds with $L=1$: for all $k,r$, there exist $L,C\ge1$ such that if $G$ admits a tree-decomposition $(T,(B_t:t\in V(T)))$ such that for each $t\in V(T)$, $B_t$ is the union of at most $k$ sets each with diameter at most $r$ in $G$, then $G$ admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with tree-width at most $k$.
context_text: Graphs may be infinite, and $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)$ is the number of edges of a shortest $u$–$v$ path in $G$ ($\infty$ if none). The diameter of $X\subseteq V(G)$ in $G$ is the maximum of $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)$ over $u,v\in X$. For $L,C\ge0$, a map $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry if $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)+C$ whenever $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)$ is finite, $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))+C$ whenever $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))$ is finite, and every vertex of $H$ is at distance at most $C$ from $\phi(V(G))$; with $L=1$ it is called additive. Tree-decompositions may be indexed by infinite trees. Berger and Seymour proved that if $G$ is connected and has a tree-decomposition whose bags all have diameter at most $r$ in $G$, then $G$ admits a $(1,6r+1)$-quasi-isometry to a tree. The authors extend this to bounded tree-width: for all $k,r$ there exist $L,C\ge1$ such that if $G$ has a tree-decomposition each of whose bags is the union of at most $k$ sets of diameter at most $r$ in $G$, then $G$ admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with tree-width at most $k$ (the tree-width bound $k$ cannot be lowered to $k-1$). They remark that calling this an extension of the Berger–Seymour result is something of a stretch, since they do not know whether one can take $L=1$. For path-decompositions (and line-decompositions, the extension of path-decompositions to infinite graphs indexed by linearly ordered sets) they can take $L=1$, using a result from a companion paper.
notes: Stated as a parenthetical remark in the introduction rather than a labelled conjecture/question environment. Only the first 4000 characters of the introduction were provided; additional open problems later in the paper may not be captured.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. I. Coarse tree-width
