name: AX_small_doubling_sumset_covering_family
title: Conjecture 15
statement_text: Let $G$ be an abelian group of order $n$ and let $s\le n$. There exist collections $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ of subsets of $G$ such that $\log|\mathcal{F}_\ell|=\tilde{O}(2^{\ell})$ and $\min_{F\in\mathcal{F}_\ell}|F|=\tilde{\Omega}(2^{\ell}s)$, and such that for every $A\subseteq G$ with $|A|=s$ and $|A+A|\leq K|A|$, there exists $\ell\leq\log_{2}K$ and $F\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ such that $A+A\supseteq F$.
context_text: $A+A=\{a+b: a,b\in A\}$ is the sumset, $|A+A|\le K|A|$ means that $A$ has doubling at most $K$, and $\tilde{O},\tilde{\Omega}$ hide polylogarithmic factors in $n$. The authors' main covering lemma proves this with weaker parameters: there are $C,c>0$ and collections $\mathcal{F}_\ell$ with $|\mathcal{F}_\ell|\le\exp\left(C\min\left(2^{2\ell}(\log n)^2,\sqrt{2^\ell s(\log n)^{3/2}}\right)\right)$ and $\min_{F\in\mathcal{F}_\ell}|F|\ge c2^\ell s/\ell^2$ with the same covering property; in particular, it answers Lovett's question by giving a collection of $\exp(O((\log n)^2))$ sets of size at least $\epsilon n$ such that $A+A$ contains one of them whenever $|A|\ge\delta n$. The motivation is graph-theoretic: in the random Cayley graph $G(p)$ (vertex set $G$, $x\sim y$ iff $y-x\in S$, where each pair $\{x,-x\}$ is put in $S$ independently with probability $p$) and the random Cayley sum graph $G^+(p)$ ($x\sim y$ iff $x+y\in S$, each element in $S$ with probability $p$), a set $A$ is independent in $G^+(p)$ exactly when $A+A$ avoids $S$, so the collections $\mathcal{F}_\ell$ act as a union-bound cover: $G^+(p)$ has no independent set of size $s$ whp if $\sum_\ell\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}_\ell}(1-p)^{|F|}=o(1)$. With the covering lemma the authors show that the independence numbers of $G(p)$ and $G^+(p)$ are $\tilde{O}(p^{-3/2})$ whp for abelian $G$ and $p\le 1/2$, the first improvement on the exponent $p^{-2}$; the conjectured optimal cover would characterize the independence number of sparse random Cayley graphs up to logarithmic factors, in line with Alon's conjecture that it is $\tilde{O}(p^{-1})$ whp.
notes: The statement text as extracted appears truncated: the clause 'such that and such that' suggests that the size or complexity conditions on the collections $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ were lost in the source extraction. The mathematical content may be incomplete or garbled.
paper_title: Random Cayley graphs and random sumsets

name: AX_induced_saturated_no_finite_infinite_family
title: Problem 21
statement_text: Is there an infinite family $\mathcal{G}$ of finite graphs, not containing cliques or independent sets, such that for all $H\in\mathcal{G}$, there is no finite $H$-induced-saturated graph?
context_text: A graph $G$ (on at least two vertices) is $H$-induced-saturated if it has no induced copy of $H$ but perturbing any pair (deleting an edge or adding a non-edge) creates an induced copy of $H$. No such graph exists when $H$ is a clique or an independent set on more than two vertices, and Martin and Smith showed there is no finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graph; finite $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\ne1,4$. The authors prove that every finite graph $H$ that is not a clique or an independent set admits a countably infinite $H$-induced-saturated graph, and even one such that every locally finite perturbation (toggling a nonempty set of pairs with every vertex in finitely many of them) creates an induced copy of $H$. In the finite case the classification is widely open: besides $P_4$, cliques and independent sets, no finite graph $H$ is known to have no finite $H$-induced-saturated graph, so it is asked whether there are infinitely many non-trivial such $H$.
paper_title: Infinite induced-saturated graphs

name: AX_induced_saturated_flip_graph_disconnected
title: Problem 22
statement_text: For a finite graph $H$ and integer $n$, let $G_{H,n}$ denote the graph with the $H$-free graphs on vertex set $[n]$ as vertices, and with an edge between $G,G^{\prime}\in V(G_{H,n})$ if and only if $|E(G)\triangle E(G^{\prime})|=1$. For which $H$ is $G_{H,n}$ disconnected for all sufficiently large $n$?
context_text: A graph $G$ (on at least two vertices) is $H$-induced-saturated if it has no induced copy of $H$ but perturbing any pair (deleting an edge or adding a non-edge) creates an induced copy of $H$. No such graph exists when $H$ is a clique or an independent set on more than two vertices, and Martin and Smith showed there is no finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graph; finite $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\ne1,4$. Here $H$-free means having no induced copy of $H$, and $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$. An $H$-induced-saturated graph on $[n]$ is exactly an isolated vertex of $G_{H,n}$, so showing that $G_{H,n}$ is disconnected may be easier than finding induced-saturated graphs. Using the inductive definition of cographs, $G_{P_4,n}$ is connected for every $n\ge1$, consistent with the non-existence of finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graphs. The problem was suggested by Torsten Ueckerdt.
paper_title: Infinite induced-saturated graphs

name: AX_induced_saturated_countable_tournament_arc_reversal
title: Problem 23
statement_text: For which finite tournaments $H$, does there exist a countable tournament $G$ that does not contain $H$ as subtournament, yet any tournament obtained from $G$ by changing the direction of a single arc does contain $H$?
context_text: A graph $G$ (on at least two vertices) is $H$-induced-saturated if it has no induced copy of $H$ but perturbing any pair (deleting an edge or adding a non-edge) creates an induced copy of $H$. No such graph exists when $H$ is a clique or an independent set on more than two vertices, and Martin and Smith showed there is no finite $P_4$-induced-saturated graph; finite $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\ne1,4$. For tournaments, the natural perturbation is reversing the direction of an arc, and $G$ contains $H$ if some subtournament of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. When $H$ is the directed triangle there is no finite example, but an infinite one exists: the transitive tournament on $\mathbb{Q}$ with $q\to q'$ iff $q<q'$, since reversing an arc $q\to q'$ creates a directed triangle with any $r$ such that $q<r<q'$. When $H$ is the transitive tournament on $3$ vertices, the directed triangle itself is a finite example. The paper settles the analogous question for graphs (a countable example exists iff $H$ is not a clique or an independent set).
paper_title: Infinite induced-saturated graphs

name: AX_induced_saturated_infinite_tournament_perturbation
title: Conjecture 24
statement_text: Let $T$ be a finite tournament. If $T$ is not transitive, then there exists a countably infinite $T$-free tournament $S_{T}$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $S_{T}$ has an induced copy of $T$.
context_text: Graphs may be countably infinite. A locally finite perturbation of a graph $G$ is obtained by perturbing (toggling) a nonempty, possibly infinite, set of pairs such that every vertex lies in only finitely many perturbed pairs. The paper's main theorem: if a finite graph $H$ is not a clique or an independent set, there is a countably infinite $H$-free graph $G_H$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_H$ contains an induced copy of $H$ (in particular $G_H$ is $H$-induced-saturated). For tournaments, perturbing a pair means reversing the arc between them, and a locally finite perturbation reverses a nonempty set of arcs with every vertex in finitely many of them; $T$-free means that no subtournament is isomorphic to $T$, and induced copy means subtournament. The conjecture is proposed as the tournament analogue of the main theorem. Local finiteness forces $S_T$ to be infinite, and the non-transitivity condition is necessary because every tournament on $2^n$ vertices contains a transitive subtournament on $n$ vertices.
paper_title: Infinite induced-saturated graphs

name: AX_induced_saturated_infinite_hypergraph
title: Conjecture 25
statement_text: Let $k\geq 3$ be an integer, and let $H$ be a finite $k$-uniform hypergraph. If $H$ has both an edge and a non-edge, then there exists a countably infinite $k$-uniform hypergraph $G_{H}$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_{H}$ has an induced copy of $H$.
context_text: Graphs may be countably infinite. A locally finite perturbation of a graph $G$ is obtained by perturbing (toggling) a nonempty, possibly infinite, set of pairs such that every vertex lies in only finitely many perturbed pairs. The paper's main theorem: if a finite graph $H$ is not a clique or an independent set, there is a countably infinite $H$-free graph $G_H$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_H$ contains an induced copy of $H$ (in particular $G_H$ is $H$-induced-saturated). For a $k$-uniform hypergraph, a single perturbation adds or removes one hyperedge (a $k$-set of vertices), and a locally finite perturbation does this for a nonempty set of $k$-sets with each vertex in finitely many of them; an induced copy of $H$ is a set of $|V(H)|$ vertices whose induced subhypergraph is isomorphic to $H$. The conjecture is called the strongest proposed extension of the main theorem to hypergraphs, and having both an edge and a non-edge is the analogue of not being a clique or independent set. As stated in the paper the conjecture does not explicitly require $G_H$ itself to contain no induced copy of $H$; by analogy with the main theorem this is presumably intended.
paper_title: Infinite induced-saturated graphs

name: AX_induced_saturated_infinite_edge_colored_clique
title: Conjecture 26
statement_text: Let $k\geq 2$ be an integer, and let $c$ be a $k$-colouring of the edges of a finite clique $K$ such that there is an edge of every colour. Then there is a colouring $\chi$ of the edges of the complete countably infinite graph such that every locally finite perturbation contains a copy of $K$ with colouring $c$.
context_text: Graphs may be countably infinite. A locally finite perturbation of a graph $G$ is obtained by perturbing (toggling) a nonempty, possibly infinite, set of pairs such that every vertex lies in only finitely many perturbed pairs. The paper's main theorem: if a finite graph $H$ is not a clique or an independent set, there is a countably infinite $H$-free graph $G_H$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $G_H$ contains an induced copy of $H$ (in particular $G_H$ is $H$-induced-saturated). For a $k$-colouring of the edges of a (finite or infinite) complete graph, a locally finite perturbation changes the colours on the edges of a nonempty locally finite subgraph (every vertex incident with finitely many recoloured edges). A copy of $K$ with colouring $c$ is a set of $|V(K)|$ vertices on which the colouring is isomorphic to $c$. The requirement that every colour appears in $c$ is the analogue of $H$ being neither a clique nor an independent set (the case $k=2$ with colours edge and non-edge is the main theorem). As stated in the paper the conjecture does not explicitly require $\chi$ itself to contain no copy of $K$ with colouring $c$; by analogy with the main theorem this is presumably intended.
paper_title: Infinite induced-saturated graphs

name: AX_coarse_menger_distance_2_paths
title: Open case: Coarse Menger Conjecture for c=2
statement_text: It is unknown whether the coarse Menger conjecture holds when $c = 2$: for all integers $k \geq 1$ there exists $\ell > 0$ such that for every graph $G$ and $S, T \subseteq V(G)$, either there are $k$ paths between $S, T$ pairwise at distance at least $2$, or there is a set $X \subseteq V(G)$ with $|X| \leq k-1$ such that every $S$-$T$ path contains a vertex within distance $\ell$ of some member of $X$.
context_text: Here $\mathrm{dist}_G(X,Y)$ is the number of edges of a shortest path of $G$ with one end in $X$ and the other in $Y$, and two paths are at distance at least $c$ if their vertex sets are; in particular, paths pairwise at distance at least $2$ are vertex-disjoint with no edge between any two of them. The coarse Menger conjecture of Albrechtsen, Huynh, Jacobs, Knappe and Wollan, and independently Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu, asserts the displayed dichotomy for all integers $k,c\ge1$ (for $c=1$ it is Menger's theorem, with $\ell=0$); both groups proved it for $k=2$. The authors showed earlier that it is false for every $k\ge3$ already with $c=3$, even for graphs of maximum degree three. The case $c=3$ is special since a positive result for $c=3$ and some $k$ would give it for all $c\ge3$ and the same $k$, by applying it to the $c$-th power of $G$. The remaining case $c=2$ is open, and the authors say they have nothing to say about it. In this paper they also refute the weaker version where $|X|\le k-1$ is replaced by $|X|\le m$ for a constant $m(k,c)$, even for $c=k=3$. For bounded maximum degree, a $c=2$ statement is known (Gartland, Korhonen and Lokshtanov; Hendrey, Norin, Steiner and Turcotte): for every $\Delta$ there is $C$ such that either there are $k$ $S$–$T$ paths pairwise at distance at least two or some set $X$ with $|X|<kC$ meets every $S$–$T$ path.
notes: Stated as a passing remark in the introduction; no formal conjecture label. Refers specifically to the strong-form Conjecture 1.1 restricted to c=2.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. IV. A counterexample to the weak coarse Menger conjecture

name: AX_regular_4_critical_no_critical_edge
title: Problem 5.2
statement_text: Does there exist a $6$-regular $(4,1)$-graph?
context_text: A vertex, edge or set of edges of a graph $G$ is critical if its removal yields a graph with smaller chromatic number than $G$; a graph $G$ with $\chi(G)=k$ is $k$-vertex-critical if every vertex is critical. A $(k,r)$-graph is a $k$-vertex-critical graph in which no set of at most $r$ edges is critical; so a $(4,1)$-graph is a 4-vertex-critical graph with no critical edge, i.e. removing any single edge leaves a graph that is still not 3-colorable. Dirac conjectured in 1970 that $(k,1)$-graphs exist for every $k\ge4$, and Erdős (1985) asked whether $(k,r)$-graphs exist for all $k\ge4$ and $r\ge1$. The authors prove that $(k,r)$-graphs exist for all $k\ge5$ and $r\ge1$ (with order $n$ and $r=\Omega(n^{1/3})$), so the only remaining open case of both Dirac's and Erdős's problems is $k=4$; in particular it is open whether a $(4,1)$-graph exists at all. Their circulant constructions cannot settle $k=4$, and they lean towards thinking that no circulant $(4,1)$-graph exists. They prove that every $(4,r)$-graph has edge-connectivity, hence minimum degree, at least $3r+3$ and maximum degree at most $|V(G)|-(2r+3)$; thus a $(4,1)$-graph has minimum degree at least $6$, and the sparsest option left is a 6-regular graph, which makes the search for 6-regular examples natural from a computational viewpoint.
paper_title: Critical edge sets in vertex-critical graphs

name: AX_cyclic_permutation_swap_diameter_prime
title: Conjecture 3.4
statement_text: $t(n)=n-2$ if and only if $n$ is prime.
context_text: A cyclic permutation of order $n$ is an arrangement of $1,\dots,n$ on a circle, up to rotation; equivalently, with $c=(1,2,\dots,n)\in S_n$ and $C_n=\langle c\rangle$, it is a coset $[\pi]=\pi C_n$ of a permutation $\pi\in S_n$. The sorting time $t([\pi])$ is the minimum number of swaps of two (not necessarily adjacent) entries needed to transform $[\pi]$ into the trivial cyclic permutation $[c]$, and $t(n)=\max_{\pi\in S_n}t([\pi])$ is the diameter of the (vertex-transitive) graph on cyclic permutations of order $n$ in which two are adjacent when they differ by one swap. Writing $\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)$ for the number of cycles of $\sigma\in S_n$, one has $t([\pi])=\min_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}(n-\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma))$. Since every permutation has a cyclic shift with a fixed point, $t(n)\le n-2$. For $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$ (the units of $\mathbb{Z}_n$), let $\pi_{n,a}\in S_n$ be the permutation $i\mapsto a\cdot i \pmod n$ (identifying $[n]$ with $\mathbb{Z}_n$). Using $\pi_{n,g}$ for a suitable generator $g$, the authors prove $t(p^k)\ge p^k-k-1$ for every odd prime $p$, hence $t(n)=n-2$ for every prime $n$; they also prove $t(n)\ge n-O(\log n)$ in general. Computer experiments show that for $n\le 11$ the upper bound $n-2$ is attained only for prime $n$, so the conjecture is that the converse also holds. It would follow from the stronger conjecture that if $n>2$ and $\max_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)=2$ then $n$ is prime and $\pi=\pi_{n,a}$ for some $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$; both have been verified for $n\le11$.
paper_title: Circular sorting

name: AX_cyclic_permutation_swap_diameter_extremal
title: Conjecture 3.6
statement_text: If $n>2$ and $\pi\in S_n$ satisfies $\max_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)=2$, then $n$ is prime and $\pi(i)\equiv a\cdot i \pmod n$ for all $i$, for some $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$.
context_text: A cyclic permutation of order $n$ is an arrangement of $1,\dots,n$ on a circle, up to rotation; equivalently, with $c=(1,2,\dots,n)\in S_n$ and $C_n=\langle c\rangle$, it is a coset $[\pi]=\pi C_n$ of a permutation $\pi\in S_n$. The sorting time $t([\pi])$ is the minimum number of swaps of two (not necessarily adjacent) entries needed to transform $[\pi]$ into the trivial cyclic permutation $[c]$, and $t(n)=\max_{\pi\in S_n}t([\pi])$ is the diameter of the (vertex-transitive) graph on cyclic permutations of order $n$ in which two are adjacent when they differ by one swap. Writing $\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)$ for the number of cycles of $\sigma\in S_n$, one has $t([\pi])=\min_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}(n-\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma))$. Since every permutation has a cyclic shift with a fixed point, $t(n)\le n-2$. For $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$ (the units of $\mathbb{Z}_n$), let $\pi_{n,a}\in S_n$ be the permutation $i\mapsto a\cdot i \pmod n$ (identifying $[n]$ with $\mathbb{Z}_n$). Using $\pi_{n,g}$ for a suitable generator $g$, the authors prove $t(p^k)\ge p^k-k-1$ for every odd prime $p$, hence $t(n)=n-2$ for every prime $n$; they also prove $t(n)\ge n-O(\log n)$ in general. The condition $\max_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)=2$ means exactly $t([\pi])=n-2$; the authors show that it forces every $\sigma\in\pi C_n$ to have cycle structure $(n-1,1)$ (a unique fixed point). The conjecture characterizes the extremal permutations as the multiplication maps $\pi_{n,a}$ (the hypothesis depends only on the coset $\pi C_n$ while the conclusion, as literally stated in the paper, depends on the representative $\pi$, since $\pi_{n,a}c^j$ is $i\mapsto a(i+j)$; presumably $[\pi]=[\pi_{n,a}]$ is meant). It implies the conjecture that $t(n)=n-2$ if and only if $n$ is prime, and both conjectures have been verified for $n\le 11$.

name: AX_cyclic_permutation_swap_diameter_monotone
title: Question 3.9
statement_text: Is the function $t(n)$ monotone?
context_text: A cyclic permutation of order $n$ is an arrangement of $1,\dots,n$ on a circle, up to rotation; equivalently, with $c=(1,2,\dots,n)\in S_n$ and $C_n=\langle c\rangle$, it is a coset $[\pi]=\pi C_n$ of a permutation $\pi\in S_n$. The sorting time $t([\pi])$ is the minimum number of swaps of two (not necessarily adjacent) entries needed to transform $[\pi]$ into the trivial cyclic permutation $[c]$, and $t(n)=\max_{\pi\in S_n}t([\pi])$ is the diameter of the (vertex-transitive) graph on cyclic permutations of order $n$ in which two are adjacent when they differ by one swap. Writing $\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma)$ for the number of cycles of $\sigma\in S_n$, one has $t([\pi])=\min_{\sigma\in\pi C_n}(n-\mathrm{cyc}(\sigma))$. Since every permutation has a cyclic shift with a fixed point, $t(n)\le n-2$. For $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$ (the units of $\mathbb{Z}_n$), let $\pi_{n,a}\in S_n$ be the permutation $i\mapsto a\cdot i \pmod n$ (identifying $[n]$ with $\mathbb{Z}_n$). Using $\pi_{n,g}$ for a suitable generator $g$, the authors prove $t(p^k)\ge p^k-k-1$ for every odd prime $p$, hence $t(n)=n-2$ for every prime $n$; they also prove $t(n)\ge n-O(\log n)$ in general. For powers of 2 they show $t(2^k)\ge 2^k-(2k-1)$ for $k\ge3$, and for $n=2p^k$ ($p$ an odd prime) $t(n)\ge n-2k-2$. If $t(n)$ were monotone, these bounds for prime powers could be transferred to other integers. However, adding a fixed point to a permutation may decrease its sorting time: $t([\pi_{11,3}])=9$, while extending $\pi_{11,3}$ to $S_{12}$ by fixing $12$ gives sorting time $8$.

name: AX_partition_polytope_diameter_4_thirds
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: There exists a constant $c$ such that for any positive integers $n$ and $\kappa_1 \geq \cdots \geq \kappa_n$, the partition polytope $\mathrm{PP}(\kappa_1, \ldots, \kappa_n)$ has diameter at most $\lceil 4\kappa_1/3 \rceil + c$.
context_text: For nonnegative integers $\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_n$ with $\kappa_1+\dots+\kappa_n=m$, the partition polytope $\mathrm{PP}(\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_n)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{nm}$ is defined by $\sum_{j=1}^m y_{ij}=\kappa_i$ for every $i\le n$, $\sum_{i=1}^n y_{ij}=1$ for every $j\le m$, and $y_{ij}\ge0$; its vertices are exactly the incidence matrices of the assignments $p:[m]\to[n]$ of $m$ items to $n$ clusters with cluster sizes $\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_n$. Its (combinatorial) diameter is the diameter of its edge graph (the graph of vertices and edges of the polytope). Two vertices $p,p'$ are adjacent if and only if their clustering difference graph (the digraph on the clusters $[n]$ with an arc from $p(j)$ to $p'(j)$ for each item $j$, loops suppressed) is a single directed cycle, i.e. $p'$ is obtained from $p$ by one cyclic exchange of items between clusters; so the diameter is the maximum, over pairs of assignments of the same shape, of the minimum number of cyclic exchanges transforming one into the other. Partition polytopes generalise Birkhoff polytopes ($n=m$, all $\kappa_i=1$, diameter $2$). Borgwardt showed the diameter is at most $\kappa_1+\kappa_2$; the authors improve this to $\kappa_1+\lceil\kappa_2/2\rceil\le\lceil3\kappa_1/2\rceil$ (and to $3$ when $\kappa_1=2$), while the known lower bound, noted by Borgwardt, is $\lceil4\kappa_1/3\rceil$. They suspect the true value is closer to the lower bound; the natural approach of proving diameter at most $4$ when $\kappa_1=3$ fails, as they show by an explicit example, so new techniques would be needed.
paper_title: Improved Decomposition Bounds for Partition Polytopes and Odd-Covers

name: AX_shotgun_assembly_second_threshold_all_radii
title: Informal Conjecture (second phase transition for all radii)
statement_text: It seems likely that for every radius $r$ there should be a second phase transition around some threshold $t=t(n)$. By which we mean that, if $p=\omega(t(n))$, then $G\in\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is with high probability reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods, while if $p=o(t(n))$ and $p=\omega(n^{-\frac{2r+1}{2r}})$, then with high probability $G$ is not reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods.
context_text: For a graph $G$, a vertex $v$ and an integer $r\ge1$, the $r$-neighbourhood $N^{(G)}_r(v)$ is the subgraph induced by the vertices at distance at most $r$ from $v$, unlabelled except for the root $v$. Graphs $G,H$ have isomorphic $r$-neighbourhoods if there is a bijection $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ such that for every $v$ there is an isomorphism $N^{(G)}_r(v)\to N^{(H)}_r(\phi(v))$ mapping $v$ to $\phi(v)$; $G$ is reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods ($r$-reconstructible) if every graph with $r$-neighbourhoods isomorphic to those of $G$ is isomorphic to $G$ (the shotgun assembly problem). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. At every radius $r$ there is a first phase transition around $p=n^{-\frac{2r+1}{2r}}$: below it every component lies inside an $r$-ball and $G$ is $r$-reconstructible, while slightly above it two disjoint paths on $2r+1$ vertices appear as components, which have the same $r$-neighbourhoods as disjoint $P_{2r}$ and $P_{2r+2}$, so $G$ is not $r$-reconstructible. The authors prove the second phase transition for all $r\ge3$: for $r=3$ it lies at $\frac{\log^2 n}{n(\log\log n)^3}$, and for $4\le r\le\log n$ at $\frac{\log n}{rn}$ (up to constant factors). For $r=2$ they show reconstructibility for $p\ge n^{-2/3-\delta}$ and non-reconstructibility for $\omega(n^{-5/4})\le p\le\frac13n^{-3/4}\log^{1/4}n$; for $r=1$, Huang and Tikhomirov showed reconstructibility for $n^{-1/2}\log^Cn\le p\le c$, and the authors show non-reconstructibility for $\omega(n^{-3/2})\le p\le\sqrt{\log n/(25n)}$. So the conjecture remains open for $r=1,2$.
notes: Proved within the paper for $r\geq 3$; remains open for $r=1,2$. The conjecture as universally quantified over all $r$ is therefore still open.
paper_title: Shotgun assembly of random graphs

name: AX_shotgun_assembly_second_threshold_radius_2
title: Question
statement_text: Determine when $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is 2-reconstructible. Is there a threshold around $n^{-3/4}$ (up to a polylogarithmic factor)?
context_text: For a graph $G$, a vertex $v$ and an integer $r\ge1$, the $r$-neighbourhood $N^{(G)}_r(v)$ is the subgraph induced by the vertices at distance at most $r$ from $v$, unlabelled except for the root $v$. Graphs $G,H$ have isomorphic $r$-neighbourhoods if there is a bijection $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ such that for every $v$ there is an isomorphism $N^{(G)}_r(v)\to N^{(H)}_r(\phi(v))$ mapping $v$ to $\phi(v)$; $G$ is reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods ($r$-reconstructible) if every graph with $r$-neighbourhoods isomorphic to those of $G$ is isomorphic to $G$ (the shotgun assembly problem). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. Since $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ has diameter at most 2 for $p=\omega(\sqrt{\log n/n})$, it is then trivially 2-reconstructible. Gaudio and Mossel showed 2-reconstructibility w.h.p. for $n^{-3/5+\varepsilon}\le p\le n^{-1/2-\varepsilon}$ or $p\ge n^{-1/2+\varepsilon}$, and non-reconstructibility for $n^{-1+\varepsilon}\le p\le n^{-3/4-\varepsilon}$. The authors prove that $G\in\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is w.h.p. 2-reconstructible if $p=o(n^{-5/4})$ or $p\ge n^{-2/3-\delta}$ for some constant $\delta>0$, and w.h.p. not 2-reconstructible if $p=\omega(n^{-5/4})$ and $p\le\frac13n^{-3/4}\log^{1/4}n$. The remaining gap is $n^{-3/4}\log^{1/4}n\lesssim p\lesssim n^{-2/3-\delta}$, while for every $r\ge3$ the authors determine the threshold of the second transition.
paper_title: Shotgun assembly of random graphs

name: AX_1_independent_percolation_q3_signs_model
title: Conjecture 6.2
statement_text: For $p>0.55$, among models in $\mathcal{D}_{\geq p}(Q_{3})$ the signs model minimises the probability that $Q_{3}$ is connected.
context_text: A bond percolation model on a graph $G$ is a probability distribution on the spanning subgraphs of $G$ (edges present in the random subgraph are open). It is 1-independent if, for any two sets of edges $S_1,S_2$ such that no edge of $S_1$ shares a vertex with an edge of $S_2$, the states of the edges in $S_1$ are independent of the states of the edges in $S_2$. $\mathcal{D}_{\ge p}(G)$ denotes the class of 1-independent bond percolation models on $G$ in which each edge is open with probability at least $p$. $Q_n$ is the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph on $\{0,1\}^n$. The signs model on $Q_3$ assigns each vertex independently the sign $+$ with probability $\theta$ and $-$ otherwise, an edge being open iff both endpoints have the same sign; it is 1-independent and each edge is open with probability $p=\theta^2+(1-\theta)^2$. The question of which models in $\mathcal{D}_{\ge p}(Q_n)$ minimise the probability that $Q_n$ is connected is open already for $n=3$ (for $n=2$ the minimisers are known and are not signs models unless $p=1$). Computational evidence strongly suggests that the signs model is the minimiser on $Q_3$ for $p>0.55$, while for smaller $p$ other models do worse, and for $p<0.516$ there are models that are disconnected almost surely. The authors note that if the signs model is optimal on $Q_3$ for $p\ge0.5720$, then their renormalisation argument would improve their bounds to $p_{\mathrm{giant}}\le0.5720$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}p_{\max}(\mathbb{Z}^n)\le0.5720$, where $p_{\max}(G)$ is the supremum of the $p$ for which some model in $\mathcal{D}_{\ge p}(G)$ does not percolate (has no infinite component with positive probability).
paper_title: Improved bounds for 1-independent percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^n$

name: AX_1_independent_percolation_hypercube_giant_threshold
title: Problem 6.4
statement_text: What is the value of $p_{\mathrm{giant}}$, the threshold for the asymptotically almost sure existence of a giant component in the hypercube $Q_n$ under any 1-independent bond percolation model with edge probability at least $p$?
context_text: A bond percolation model on a graph $G$ is a probability distribution on the spanning subgraphs of $G$ (edges present in the random subgraph are open). It is 1-independent if, for any two sets of edges $S_1,S_2$ such that no edge of $S_1$ shares a vertex with an edge of $S_2$, the states of the edges in $S_1$ are independent of the states of the edges in $S_2$. $\mathcal{D}_{\ge p}(G)$ denotes the class of 1-independent bond percolation models on $G$ in which each edge is open with probability at least $p$. $Q_n$ is the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph on $\{0,1\}^n$. The threshold is defined as $p_{\mathrm{giant}}=\inf\{p:\exists C>0,\ \lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal{D}_{\ge p}(Q_n)}\mathbb{P}_\mu(Q_n\text{ has a component of size}\ge C\cdot2^n)=1\}$. The authors prove $p_{\mathrm{giant}}\le0.5847$: when every edge of $Q_n$ is open with probability at least $0.5847$ and $n$ is large, there is a component containing a constant fraction of the vertices with high probability. The best lower bound is $1/2$, from a simple construction of Balister and Bollobás. Falgas-Ravry and Pfenninger conjectured that $p_{\mathrm{giant}}=1/2$, more precisely that for all $p>1/2$, under every model in $\mathcal{D}_{\ge p}(Q_n)$, $Q_n$ has a component of size at least $\big(\frac{1+\sqrt{2p-1}}{2}-o(1)\big)2^n$ with probability $1-o(1)$. In the independent model the analogous threshold is around $1/n$ (Erdős–Spencer, Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi).
paper_title: Improved bounds for 1-independent percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^n$

name: AX_negative_p_energy_path_minimum
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every connected graph $G$ of order $n$ and $p\geq 2$, $$\mathcal{E}^{-}_{p}(G)\geq\mathcal{E}^{-}_{p}(K_{n}).$$
context_text: For a graph $G$ with adjacency eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$ and a real $p\ge1$, the positive $p$-energy is $\mathcal{E}^+_p(G)=\sum_{\lambda_i>0}\lambda_i^p$ and the negative $p$-energy is $\mathcal{E}^-_p(G)=\sum_{\lambda_i<0}|\lambda_i|^p$; their sum $\mathcal{E}_p(G)$ is the $p$-th power of the Schatten $p$-norm of the adjacency matrix, and $\mathcal{E}_1$ is the usual graph energy. Since $K_n$ has eigenvalue $-1$ with multiplicity $n-1$, $\mathcal{E}^-_p(K_n)=n-1$. Tang, Liu and Wang conjectured that $\mathcal{E}^+_p(G)\ge\mathcal{E}^+_p(P_n)$ for every connected $G$ of order $n$ and $p\ge2$, and the authors pose this negative analogue; both generalise the conjecture of Elphick, Farber, Goldberg and Wocjan that $\min\{\mathcal{E}^+_2(G),\mathcal{E}^-_2(G)\}\ge n-1$ for connected $G$ (known: at least $n-\gamma(G)\ge n/2$ by Zhang, and at least $3n/4$ for $n\ge4$ by Akbari, Kumar, Mohar and Pragada). The authors settle the present conjecture for $p\ge4$: every connected graph $G\not\cong K_n$ of order $n$ has $\mathcal{E}^-_p(G)\ge n$ when $p\ge4$; the case $2\le p<4$ remains open. They also prove $\mathcal{E}^+_p(G)\ge(4/3)^{p/4}n$ for $p\ge4$ and connected $G$ of order $n\ge4$.
notes: The theorem-environment text captures only the preamble clause; the displayed formula $\mathcal{E}^{-}_{p}(G)\geq\mathcal{E}^{-}_{p}(P_{n})$ is reconstructed from the stated analogy with Conjecture 1, the generalisation claim for Conjecture 3, and the fact that Theorem 1 (proved bound $\mathcal{E}_{p}^{-}(G)\geq n$ for $p\geq 4$, $G\ncong K_n$) is said to settle this conjecture for $p\geq 4$. The case $2\leq p<4$ remains open.
paper_title: Vertex Partitioning and $p$-Energy of Graphs

name: AX_merge_width_radius_1_chi_bounded
title: Question 1.4
statement_text: Is the class $\{G:\operatorname{mw}_{1}(G)\leqslant k\}$, with $k$ arbitrary, $\chi$-bounded?
context_text: Merge-width (Dreier and Toruńczyk) is defined through merge sequences: for a graph $G$, a merge sequence is $(\mathcal{P}_1,R_1),\dots,(\mathcal{P}_m,R_m)$ where each $\mathcal{P}_i$ is a partition of $V(G)$, $\mathcal{P}_1$ is the partition into singletons, $\mathcal{P}_m=\{V(G)\}$, each $\mathcal{P}_i$ is coarser than or equal to $\mathcal{P}_{i-1}$; $R_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq R_m\subseteq\binom{V(G)}{2}$ are sets of resolved pairs; and for any two (possibly equal) parts $A,B\in\mathcal{P}_i$, the unresolved pairs between $A$ and $B$ (those not in $R_i$) are either all edges or all non-edges of $G$. Its radius-$r$ width is the maximum, over all steps $i\ge2$ and vertices $v$, of the number of parts of $\mathcal{P}_{i-1}$ reachable from $v$ by a path of length at most $r$ in the graph $(V(G),R_i)$ of resolved pairs. The radius-$r$ merge-width $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)$ is the minimum radius-$r$ width of a merge sequence for $G$, and a class has bounded merge-width if there is $f$ with $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le f(r)$ for all $G$ in the class and all $r$. Bounded merge-width generalises bounded expansion and bounded twin-width, and is stable under first-order transductions. A class is $\chi$-bounded if the chromatic number of its graphs is bounded by a function of their clique number $\omega$. The authors prove that every graph with $\operatorname{mw}_2(G)\le k$ and $\omega(G)\le t$ has $\chi(G)\le(t+1)!\,k^{2t-2}$, so bounded merge-width classes are $\chi$-bounded; radius $2$ is used in a single lemma (a colouring lemma for structurally $\omega$-bounded merge sequences), the rest of the proof needs only radius $1$, and it is unclear whether radius $2$ is necessary. A negative answer would require a class of bounded radius-1 merge-width and bounded clique number (possibly triangle-free) with unbounded chromatic number; such a class must contain arbitrarily large bicliques, since graphs of bounded radius-1 merge-width without $K_{t,t}$ subgraph are degenerate, and must have bounded symmetric difference (every induced subgraph has two vertices whose neighbourhoods differ on a bounded set). Shift graphs, a classical example of triangle-free graphs with large chromatic number, do not have bounded radius-1 merge-width.
paper_title: $χ$-Boundedness and Neighbourhood Complexity of Bounded Merge-Width Graphs

name: AX_merge_width_transduction_neighborhood_complexity
title: Conjecture 1.7
statement_text: A class $\mathcal{C}$ has bounded merge-width if and only if every first-order transduction of $\mathcal{C}$ has linear neighbourhood complexity.
context_text: Merge-width (Dreier and Toruńczyk) is defined through merge sequences: for a graph $G$, a merge sequence is $(\mathcal{P}_1,R_1),\dots,(\mathcal{P}_m,R_m)$ where each $\mathcal{P}_i$ is a partition of $V(G)$, $\mathcal{P}_1$ is the partition into singletons, $\mathcal{P}_m=\{V(G)\}$, each $\mathcal{P}_i$ is coarser than or equal to $\mathcal{P}_{i-1}$; $R_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq R_m\subseteq\binom{V(G)}{2}$ are sets of resolved pairs; and for any two (possibly equal) parts $A,B\in\mathcal{P}_i$, the unresolved pairs between $A$ and $B$ (those not in $R_i$) are either all edges or all non-edges of $G$. Its radius-$r$ width is the maximum, over all steps $i\ge2$ and vertices $v$, of the number of parts of $\mathcal{P}_{i-1}$ reachable from $v$ by a path of length at most $r$ in the graph $(V(G),R_i)$ of resolved pairs. The radius-$r$ merge-width $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)$ is the minimum radius-$r$ width of a merge sequence for $G$, and a class has bounded merge-width if there is $f$ with $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le f(r)$ for all $G$ in the class and all $r$. Bounded merge-width generalises bounded expansion and bounded twin-width, and is stable under first-order transductions. The neighbourhood complexity of $G$ is $\pi_G(p)=\max_{X\subseteq V(G),|X|=p}\#\{N(v)\cap X : v\notin X\}$, extended to classes by taking the maximum over the class; it is linear if $\pi(p)=O(p)$. A first-order transduction maps a graph to the graphs obtained by colouring its vertices with a bounded number of unary predicates, defining new edges by a fixed first-order formula, and taking an induced subgraph. The authors prove that every graph with $\operatorname{mw}_2(G)\le k$ has $\pi_G(p)\le k2^{k+2}p$ (radius $2$ is optimal since $k$-degenerate graphs have bounded radius-1 merge-width but neighbourhood complexity $\Theta(p^k)$); since bounded merge-width is preserved by transductions, this gives the left-to-right implication. Reidl, Villaamil and Stavropoulos showed that linear neighbourhood complexity of balls of every radius characterises bounded expansion among subgraph-closed classes, but balls are meaningless for dense graphs of diameter $2$, hence the use of transductions. Proving the conjecture would imply that flip-width and merge-width are equivalent, as conjectured by Dreier and Toruńczyk, since bounded flip-width also gives linear neighbourhood complexity and is closed under transductions; the authors also suggest the analogous question for flip-width.
paper_title: $χ$-Boundedness and Neighbourhood Complexity of Bounded Merge-Width Graphs

name: AX_regular_independence_edge_deletion_cubic_infinite
title: Question 4.1
statement_text: Do there exist infinitely many $3$-edge colourable cubic graphs $G$ such that for all edges $(u,v),(x,y)\in E(G)$, $\alpha(G)=\alpha(G-\{u,v,x,y\})$?
context_text:
An $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraph has its vertex set partitioned into $r$ parts, each edge containing exactly one vertex of each part; a matching is a set of pairwise disjoint edges, $
u$ is the matching number and $	au$ the vertex cover number. Ryser conjectured $	au\le(r-1)
u$ for such hypergraphs (true for $r=2$ by Kőnig and $r=3$ by Aharoni, open for $r\ge4$), and Lovász (1975) conjectured the stronger statement that every such hypergraph with at least one edge has $r-1$ vertices whose deletion reduces the matching number. The line hypergraph $\mathcal{L}(G)$ of a graph $G$ has the edges of $G$ as vertices and, for each vertex $v$ of $G$, the set of edges incident to $v$ as an edge; $
u(\mathcal{L}(G))=\alpha(G)$, and if $G$ is $r$-regular and $r$-edge-colourable then $\mathcal{L}(G)$ is $r$-partite $r$-uniform. Deleting vertices $e_1,\dots,e_{k}$ of $\mathcal{L}(G)$ corresponds to forbidding the endpoints of these edges in an independent set of $G$. The authors disprove Lovász's conjecture for $r=3$: in the Biggs–Smith graph (a cubic distance-transitive graph on $102$ vertices), for every two edges $uv,xy$ there is a maximum independent set avoiding $u,v,x,y$. With a computer, the authors verified that the Biggs–Smith graph is the unique cubic edge-transitive graph on at most $166$ vertices with this property, that the $168$-vertex graph F168D of the Foster census also has it, that these are the only two cubic edge-transitive examples on at most $300$ vertices, and that no cubic graph on at most $20$ vertices has it. Each such $3$-edge-colourable cubic graph gives a counterexample to Lovász's conjecture; the question asks whether there are infinitely many.
paper_title: A Counterexample to a Conjecture of Lovász

name: AX_positive_square_energy_at_least_n
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: Let $G$ be a connected graph of order $n$ and size $m$. If $m\geq n+1$, then $$s^{+}(G)\geq n.$$
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $n$ is the order and $m$ the size (number of edges). The eigenvalues of $G$ are those of its adjacency matrix, $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$. The positive square energy $s^+(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the positive eigenvalues, and the negative square energy $s^-(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the negative eigenvalues (so $s^+(G)+s^-(G)=2m$). Elphick, Farber, Goldberg and Wocjan conjectured that $\min\{s^+(G),s^-(G)\}\ge n-1$ for every connected graph $G$ of order $n$; this is known for regular graphs, hyper-energetic graphs (hence almost all graphs), and with weaker bounds $n-\gamma(G)$ ($\gamma$ the domination number) and $3n/4$ in general. The super-additivity of square energy over vertex partitions suggests an inductive proof, but the bound $n-1$ is not preserved well under such arguments, which motivates asking when the stronger $s^+(G)\ge n$ holds. Trees have $s^+=n-1$, and unicyclic graphs ($m=n$) can have $s^+<n$ (e.g. cycles of length $1\bmod4$), hence the condition $m\ge n+1$. The conjecture holds for regular graphs and graphs with 1-energy at least $2n$, and has been verified for all connected graphs with at most 9 vertices and for all graphs in the Mathematica database with $n\le100$ and $m\ge n+1$. The authors prove it for claw-free graphs (connected with maximum degree at least 3) and for graphs of diameter 2. The analogue for $s^-$ fails.
paper_title: Refinement of a conjecture on positive square energy of graphs

name: AX_positive_square_energy_unicyclic_odd_cycle
title: Conjecture 9.1
statement_text: If $G$ is a unicyclic graph of order $n$ whose cycle has odd length $k$, then $s^{+}(G)>n>s^{-}(G)$ if $k\equiv 3\pmod 4$, and $s^{+}(G)<n<s^{-}(G)$ if $k\equiv 1\pmod 4$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $n$ is the order and $m$ the size (number of edges). The eigenvalues of $G$ are those of its adjacency matrix, $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$. The positive square energy $s^+(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the positive eigenvalues, and the negative square energy $s^-(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the negative eigenvalues (so $s^+(G)+s^-(G)=2m$). Elphick, Farber, Goldberg and Wocjan conjectured that $\min\{s^+(G),s^-(G)\}\ge n-1$ for every connected graph $G$ of order $n$; this is known for regular graphs, hyper-energetic graphs (hence almost all graphs), and with weaker bounds $n-\gamma(G)$ ($\gamma$ the domination number) and $3n/4$ in general. A unicyclic graph is a connected graph with exactly one cycle (so $m=n$). The authors compute cycles exactly: $s^+(C_n)=s^-(C_n)=n$ for even $n$; for $n\equiv3\pmod4$, $s^+(C_n)=n-1+\sec(\pi/n)>n$ and $s^-(C_n)=n+1-\sec(\pi/n)<n$; for $n\equiv1\pmod4$ the roles are exchanged. Unicyclic graphs are believed to be among the hardest cases of the Elphick–Farber–Goldberg–Wocjan conjecture, and this computation together with computer search (no counterexample on at most 9 vertices) leads to the conjecture.
paper_title: Refinement of a conjecture on positive square energy of graphs

name: AX_positive_square_energy_equality_trees
title: Conjecture 9.2
statement_text: Let $G$ be a connected graph of order $n$. $s^{+}(G)=n-1$ if and only if $G$ is a tree. $s^{-}(G)=n-1$ if and only if $G$ is a tree or a complete graph.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $n$ is the order and $m$ the size (number of edges). The eigenvalues of $G$ are those of its adjacency matrix, $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$. The positive square energy $s^+(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the positive eigenvalues, and the negative square energy $s^-(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the negative eigenvalues (so $s^+(G)+s^-(G)=2m$). Elphick, Farber, Goldberg and Wocjan conjectured that $\min\{s^+(G),s^-(G)\}\ge n-1$ for every connected graph $G$ of order $n$; this is known for regular graphs, hyper-energetic graphs (hence almost all graphs), and with weaker bounds $n-\gamma(G)$ ($\gamma$ the domination number) and $3n/4$ in general. The conjecture characterizes the equality cases $s^+(G)=n-1$ and $s^-(G)=n-1$ in the Elphick–Farber–Goldberg–Wocjan conjecture. For a tree, which is bipartite, $s^+=s^-=m=n-1$; for the complete graph $K_n$, the eigenvalues are $n-1$ and $-1$ (with multiplicity $n-1$), so $s^-(K_n)=n-1$. No counterexample was found among graphs on at most 9 vertices.
paper_title: Refinement of a conjecture on positive square energy of graphs

name: AX_positive_square_energy_equals_n_unicyclic
title: Conjecture 9.3
statement_text: Let $G$ be a connected graph of order $n$ such that $s^{+}(G)=n$. Then $G$ is a bipartite unicyclic graph.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $n$ is the order and $m$ the size (number of edges). The eigenvalues of $G$ are those of its adjacency matrix, $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$. The authors conjecture that $s^+(G)\ge n$ for every connected graph with $m\ge n+1$, and believe that equality never holds there, i.e. that $s^+(G)=n$ can only occur when $m\le n$. Bipartite unicyclic graphs (connected, with exactly one cycle, of even length) have symmetric spectrum, so $s^+=s^-=m=n$ for them; e.g. $s^+(C_n)=n$ for even $n$. No counterexample was found among graphs on at most 9 vertices.
paper_title: Refinement of a conjecture on positive square energy of graphs

name: AX_positive_square_energy_clique_number_3
title: Conjecture 9.4
statement_text: For any connected graph $G$ of order $n$ and $\omega(G)\geq 3$, we have $s^{+}(G)\geq n$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $n$ is the order and $m$ the size (number of edges). The eigenvalues of $G$ are those of its adjacency matrix, $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$. The positive square energy $s^+(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the positive eigenvalues, and the negative square energy $s^-(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the negative eigenvalues (so $s^+(G)+s^-(G)=2m$). If the clique number $\omega(G)$ is large one expects $s^+(G)$ to be large, which suggests this refinement of the Elphick–Farber–Goldberg–Wocjan conjecture. It would follow from the authors' conjectures that $s^+(G)\ge n$ whenever $m\ge n+1$ and that unicyclic graphs whose cycle has length $3\pmod4$ satisfy $s^+(G)>n$ (a connected graph with a triangle either has $m\ge n+1$ or is unicyclic with a triangle). The bottleneck is unicyclic graphs with a triangle: the authors' proof for claw-free unicyclic graphs (a triangle with three pendant paths) was already quite a challenge. No counterexample was found among graphs on at most 9 vertices.
paper_title: Refinement of a conjecture on positive square energy of graphs

name: AX_positive_square_energy_maximal_planar_3n
title: Conjecture 9.5
statement_text: The following hold: Let $G$ be a maximal planar graph of order $n\geq 10$. Then $s^{+}(G)\geq 3n$. Let $G$ be a maximal outerplanar graph of order $n\geq 8$. Then $s^{+}(G)\geq 2n$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $n$ is the order and $m$ the size (number of edges). The eigenvalues of $G$ are those of its adjacency matrix, $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$. The positive square energy $s^+(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the positive eigenvalues, and the negative square energy $s^-(G)$ is the sum of the squares of the negative eigenvalues (so $s^+(G)+s^-(G)=2m$). Elphick, Farber, Goldberg and Wocjan conjectured that $\min\{s^+(G),s^-(G)\}\ge n-1$ for every connected graph $G$ of order $n$; this is known for regular graphs, hyper-energetic graphs (hence almost all graphs), and with weaker bounds $n-\gamma(G)$ ($\gamma$ the domination number) and $3n/4$ in general. A maximal planar graph is a planar graph to which no edge can be added while preserving planarity (a triangulation), and a maximal outerplanar graph is defined similarly with outerplanarity (all vertices on the outer face). Elphick and Linz noted that the Elphick–Farber–Goldberg–Wocjan conjecture holds for maximal planar graphs and asked whether $s^+(G)\ge3(n-2)$ and $s^-(G)\le3(n-2)$ for connected maximal planar graphs with $n\ge3$. Based on computations and super-additivity, the authors propose this as possibly more accessible. The coefficients cannot be improved: the maximal planar graph $C_{n-2}\vee\overline{K_2}$ (join of a cycle with two non-adjacent vertices) has $s^+=3n+O(\sqrt n)$, and the maximal outerplanar fan $K_1\vee P_{n-1}$ has $s^+\le2n+O(\sqrt n)$.
paper_title: Refinement of a conjecture on positive square energy of graphs

name: AX_induced_even_cycle_saturation_edge_addition
title: Question 1.7
statement_text: Let $t\geq 6$ be an integer. Does there exist a graph $G$ with $E(\overline{G})\neq\varnothing$ such that $G$ is $C_{2t-2}$-free but $G+e$ has an induced subgraph isomorphic to $C_{2t-2}$ for every $e\in E(\overline{G})$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $\overline{G}$ is the complement of $G$, $G-e$ removes an edge $e\in E(G)$ and $G+e$ adds a non-edge $e\in E(\overline{G})$. $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, and $G$ is $H$-induced-saturated if $G$ is $H$-free, $G-e$ contains an induced $H$ for every $e\in E(G)$, and $G+e$ contains an induced $H$ for every $e\in E(\overline{G})$. $C_t$ is the cycle on $t$ vertices. For paths, $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\notin\{1,4\}$ (Martin–Smith, Bonamy et al., Dvořák). For odd cycles, the line graph of $K_{t,t}$ is $C_{2t-1}$-induced-saturated (Behrens et al.). For even cycles, examples are known only for $C_4$ (icosahedron), $C_6$ ($C_5\square C_5$), $C_8$ (dodecahedron) and $C_{10}$ (a 28-vertex graph found by computer); existence is wide open for even cycles on 12 or more vertices. The authors prove the 'removal half': for every $t\ge5$ there is a graph $G_t$ with at least one edge that is $C_{2t-2}$-free but such that $G_t-e$ has an induced $C_{2t-2}$ for every edge $e$. This question asks for the other half, the edge-addition condition, which the authors see as a good start towards extending their methods to the full induced saturation problem for long even cycles. In the paper the question is written with '$H$-free'; from the context $H$ is the cycle $C_{2t-2}$.
paper_title: Halfway to induced saturation for even cycles

name: AX_induced_even_cycle_saturation_polynomial_size
title: Question 1.8
statement_text: Does there exist a polynomial $f$ such that for every $t\geq 3$, there is a graph $G$ on at most $f(t)$ vertices with $E(G)\neq\varnothing$, such that $G$ is $C_{2t-2}$-free but $G-e$ has an induced subgraph isomorphic to $C_{2t-2}$ for every $e\in E(G)$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $\overline{G}$ is the complement of $G$, $G-e$ removes an edge $e\in E(G)$ and $G+e$ adds a non-edge $e\in E(\overline{G})$. $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, and $G$ is $H$-induced-saturated if $G$ is $H$-free, $G-e$ contains an induced $H$ for every $e\in E(G)$, and $G+e$ contains an induced $H$ for every $e\in E(\overline{G})$. $C_t$ is the cycle on $t$ vertices. For paths, $P_t$-induced-saturated graphs exist iff $t\notin\{1,4\}$ (Martin–Smith, Bonamy et al., Dvořák). For odd cycles, the line graph of $K_{t,t}$ is $C_{2t-1}$-induced-saturated (Behrens et al.). For even cycles, examples are known only for $C_4$ (icosahedron), $C_6$ ($C_5\square C_5$), $C_8$ (dodecahedron) and $C_{10}$ (a 28-vertex graph found by computer); existence is wide open for even cycles on 12 or more vertices. The authors prove the 'removal half': for every $t\ge5$ there is a graph $G_t$ with at least one edge that is $C_{2t-2}$-free but such that $G_t-e$ has an induced $C_{2t-2}$ for every edge $e$. The graphs $G_t$ constructed by the authors have a number of vertices doubly exponential in $t$, and they do not even know a reason to expect more than linearly many vertices to be needed; this question asks whether polynomially many suffice. In the paper the question is written with '$H$-free'; from the context $H$ is the cycle $C_{2t-2}$.
paper_title: Halfway to induced saturation for even cycles

name: AX_largest_clique_minor_opt_approximation
title: Open Problem: polytime $f(\mathrm{OPT})$-approximation for largest complete minor
statement_text: It is open whether finding the size of a largest complete minor admits a polynomial-time $f(\mathrm{OPT})$-approximation algorithm.
context_text: The problem takes a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and asks for the largest $t$ (denoted $\mathrm{OPT}$) such that $K_t$ is a minor of $G$. A polynomial-time $f(\mathrm{OPT})$-approximation algorithm would, for some function $f$ independent of $n$, output in polynomial time a value within a factor $f(\mathrm{OPT})$ of the optimum (for instance, finding a $K_t$ minor or certifying that there is no $K_{f(t)}$ minor). Testing for a fixed $K_t$ minor is fixed-parameter tractable (Robertson–Seymour, time $f(t)n^3$; Korhonen, Pilipczuk and Stamoulis, $f(t)n^{1+o(1)}$), but computing the largest complete minor is NP-hard (Eppstein), has no PTAS unless P $=$ NP (Wahlén), and the best known polynomial-time approximation factor is $O(\sqrt n)$ (Alon, Lingas and Wahlén). The paper studies the analogue for ordered graphs (graphs with a linear order on the vertices), where an interval minor is obtained by deleting edges and contracting pairs of consecutive vertices: deciding whether an ordered graph has a $K_t$ interval minor is NP-complete, but the authors give a polynomial-time $f(t)$-approximation algorithm with $f$ triply exponential in $t$, based on delayed decompositions.
notes: Stated in the introduction as a known open problem without a labelled environment and without explicit attribution to specific authors; captured because the authors explicitly flag it as open and use it to motivate the paper.
paper_title: A Polynomial-Time Approximation Algorithm for Complete Interval Minors

name: AX_one_crossing_5_critical_degree_four
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: Every 5-critical graph in ${\cal C}$ contains a vertex of degree four.
context_text: Graphs are simple; ${\cal C}$ is the class of graphs that can be drawn in the plane with at most one crossing (such graphs also embed in the projective plane and the torus), and a graph is $5$-critical if $\chi(G)=5$ and every proper subgraph is $4$-colorable. A subgraph $K$ is separating if $G-V(K)$ is disconnected. Every $5$-critical graph has minimum degree at least four, and degree-four vertices can be handled inductively: if $G\ne K_5$ is $5$-critical with a vertex $v$ of degree four, $v$ has two non-adjacent neighbours $x,y$, and deleting $v$ and identifying $x$ with $y$ gives (when the crossing is not on $vx,vy$) a non-$4$-colorable graph in ${\cal C}$ containing a smaller $5$-critical graph. This conjecture says the base case of this induction is only $K_5$, i.e. there is no $5$-critical graph in ${\cal C}$ of minimum degree at least five; it is supported by computer experiments. The authors' main conjecture states that if $G$ has no separating triangle and has a drawing in the plane with one crossing in which every vertex not incident with the two crossed edges has degree at least five, then $G$ is $4$-colorable; they verify it by computer for all graphs with at most $28$ vertices. Since $5$-critical graphs have no separating cliques, that conjecture implies this one.
paper_title: On a conjecture concerning 4-coloring of graphs with one crossing

name: AX_one_crossing_4_colorable_degree_5
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: If a graph $G$ does not contain separating triangles and has a drawing in the plane with one crossing such that all vertices not incident with the crossed edges have degree at least five, then $G$ is 4-colorable.
context_text: Graphs are simple; a triangle is separating if deleting its vertices disconnects the graph; the condition says that only the (at most four) endpoints of the two crossed edges may have degree less than five. This is the central conjecture of the paper, which the authors verify by computer enumeration for all graphs with at most $28$ vertices. It strengthens the Four Color Theorem to graphs drawable with one crossing under a minimum degree condition, and implies that every $5$-critical graph (i.e. $\chi=5$ and all proper subgraphs $4$-colorable) drawable with at most one crossing has a vertex of degree four, since $5$-critical graphs have no separating cliques. The assumption on separating triangles cannot be dropped: gluing a copy of the icosahedron at each vertex of any graph drawable with one crossing yields such a graph of minimum degree at least five. Consequences include that every graph drawable with one crossing and without the $4$-wheel $W_4$ as a subgraph would be $4$-colorable. Any non-$4$-colorable graph drawn with one crossing has the four endpoints of the crossed edges forming a clique, and the authors reduce the conjecture to showing that no $4$-candidate (a near-triangulation of a disk bounded by a $4$-cycle, with every triangle facial and every internal vertex of degree at least five) forbids all colorings using four distinct colors on its outer $4$-cycle.
paper_title: On a conjecture concerning 4-coloring of graphs with one crossing

name: AX_one_crossing_4_connected_degree_four
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: Every non-4-colorable graph in ${\cal C}_{0}$ has an internal vertex of degree four.
context_text: Graphs are simple. ${\cal C}_0\subseteq{\cal C}$ consists of the graphs obtained from a $4$-connected plane triangulation by choosing two distinct facial triangles $xuv$ and $yuv$ sharing an edge $uv$ and adding the edge $xy$; $x,y,u,v$ are the external vertices and all others are internal. This is an equivalent form of the authors' main conjecture, that every graph without separating triangles that has a drawing in the plane with one crossing in which all vertices not incident with the crossed edges have degree at least five is $4$-colorable, just as the Four Color Theorem reduces to triangulations. Assuming the main conjecture, the authors show that every non-$4$-colorable graph in ${\cal C}_0$ can be obtained from $K_5$ by a sequence of expansion operations staying among non-$4$-colorable graphs of ${\cal C}_0$, which yields a relatively efficient enumeration algorithm; however, some $5$-critical graphs drawable with one crossing are not in ${\cal C}_0$. The main conjecture is verified by computer for graphs with at most $28$ vertices.
paper_title: On a conjecture concerning 4-coloring of graphs with one crossing

name: AX_one_crossing_bichromatic_forbidding_diamond_generation
title: Conjecture 30
statement_text: Every bichromatic-forbidding 4-candidate can be obtained from the diamond by a sequence of the operations (A), (B) and (C) described below.
context_text: A canvas is a plane graph whose outer face is bounded by a cycle of length at least four and all of whose other faces are triangles; a $4$-candidate is a canvas whose outer face is bounded by a $4$-cycle $K=x_1x_2x_3x_4$, in which every triangle bounds a face and every internal vertex (not on the outer face) has degree at least five. It is bichromatic-forbidding if it has no $4$-coloring with $\varphi(x_1)=\varphi(x_3)$ and $\varphi(x_2)=\varphi(x_4)$. The diamond is the $4$-cycle with one chord. The three operations, each turning a $4$-candidate $H$ with outer cycle $Q=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ into a larger $4$-candidate $G$ that is bichromatic-forbidding if and only if $H$ is, are: (A) add a cycle $x_1y_1x_2y_2x_3y_3x_4y_4$ around $H$ with edges $v_ix_i$, $v_ix_{i-1}$, $v_iy_{i-1}$, then a new outer $4$-cycle $u_1u_2u_3u_4$ with edges $u_iy_{i-1}$, $u_ix_i$, $u_iy_i$ (indices mod $4$); (B) if $Q$ is induced, add a new outer $4$-cycle $u_1u_2u_3u_4$ with edges $u_iv_i$ and $u_iv_{i+1}$ for all $i$; (C) if $Q$ is induced, $\deg_H v_1,\deg_H v_2\ge5$ and $v_1v_2u_1$ is the inner triangle on the edge $v_1v_2$, delete the edge $v_1v_2$ and add new vertices $u_2,u_3,u_4$ forming the outer $4$-cycle $u_1u_2u_3u_4$ with edges $u_iv_i$, $u_iv_{i+1}$ for $i\in\{2,3,4\}$ ($v_5=v_1$). These candidates arise in the authors' study of their conjecture that graphs without separating triangles, drawn in the plane with one crossing so that all vertices not incident with the crossed edges have degree at least five, are $4$-colorable: by computer enumeration, no $4$-candidate with at most $28$ vertices forbids rainbow colorings (all four colors on $K$), and only the diamond forbids diagonal colorings. In contrast, there are infinitely many bichromatic-forbidding $4$-candidates, produced from the diamond by (A), (B), (C), and the enumeration up to $28$ vertices supports the conjecture that these are all of them.
paper_title: On a conjecture concerning 4-coloring of graphs with one crossing

name: AX_rooted_kk_minor_free_unrealizable_colorings
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: For every integer $k\geq 3$, there exists a set $X$ of vertices and a set $C$ of $k$-colorings of $X$ such that no $X$-rooted-$K_{k}$-minor-free graph $G$ realizes $C$.
context_text: A set of $k$-colorings of a set $X$ of vertices is a set $C$ of functions $f:X\to[k]$ closed under permutations of the colours ($f\in C$ implies $\pi\circ f\in C$ for every permutation $\pi$ of $[k]$). A graph $G$ realizes $C$ if $X\subseteq V(G)$ and a function $f:X\to[k]$ belongs to $C$ if and only if $f$ extends to a proper $k$-coloring of $G$. For $X\subseteq V(G)$, an $X$-rooted minor of $G$ is a minor whose model can be chosen so that every branch set contains a vertex of $X$; $G$ is $X$-rooted-$H$-minor-free if $H$ is not an $X$-rooted minor of $G$. DeVos and Seymour proved that every set of $3$-colorings of a cyclically ordered set $X$ is realized by a plane graph with $X$ on the outer face in that order, hence by an $X$-rooted-$K_4$-minor-free $K_5$-minor-free graph; this limits the method of reducible configurations for $3$-coloring. The authors generalise this: for every $k\ge3$, every set $C$ of $k$-colorings of any $X$ is realized by some $X$-rooted-$K_{k+1}$-minor-free $K_{k+2}$-minor-free graph, so reducible configurations cannot exploit global properties when fewer colours are used than Hadwiger's conjecture postulates. The conjecture says this does not extend to $X$-rooted-$K_k$-minor-free graphs. It is a weakening of Holroyd's strengthening of Hadwiger's conjecture: if $G$ is $k$-colorable and every $k$-coloring of $G$ uses all $k$ colours on $X$, then $K_k$ is an $X$-rooted minor of $G$; Holroyd proved this for $k=3$ and Martinsson and Steiner for $k=4$.
paper_title: A note on extendable sets of colorings and rooted minors

name: AX_random_embedding_faces_gnp_logarithmic
title: Conjecture 1.13
statement_text: Let $p = p(n)$ be the probability of edges in $G(n,p)$. The expected number of faces in a random embedding of a random graph $G \in G(n,p)$ is $(1 + o(1))\ln(pn^{2})$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. Known bounds: Stahl showed $\mathbb{E}[F]\le n+\ln n$ for $K_n$ and $\le n\ln n$ for any $n$-vertex graph; Campion Loth and Mohar proved $\mathbb{E}[F]\le\frac{\pi^2}{6}n$ for every graph; Mauk and Stahl conjectured $2\ln n+O(1)$ for $K_n$, and the authors prove $\mathbb{E}[F]\le 10\ln n+2$ for $K_n$ (and $\le 3.65\ln n$ for very large $n$), tight up to the constant factor. For the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$ (with $p=p(n)$ allowed to depend on $n$), the authors prove that the expected number of faces of a random embedding is at most $H_n^2+1/p$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number, and they get a logarithmic bound for random sparse graphs (via random graphs with a fixed degree sequence). In the light of these results and Monte Carlo experiments they conjecture that a logarithmic bound holds for any usual model of random graphs, with the precise constant given here; note that $pn^2/2$ is the expected number of edges. Extending their proof for complete graphs to arbitrary random graphs seems to require further ideas. They also state the analogous conjecture $(1+o(1))\ln M$ for the random graph $G(n,M)$ with $n$ vertices and $M$ edges.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic

name: AX_random_embedding_faces_gnp_all_p
title: Conjecture 9.1
statement_text: For any $p(n) : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow [0,1]$, almost all graphs in $G(n,p)$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}[F] = O(\log(n))$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. Here $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of a random embedding of a fixed graph $G$, and the statement asks that, for every edge probability $p=p(n)$, with probability tending to 1 a graph $G\sim G(n,p)$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[F(G)]=O(\log n)$. The authors prove that the expected number of faces of a random embedding of $G(n,p)$ is at most $H_n^2+1/p$ ($H_n$ the harmonic number), so by Markov's inequality almost all dense graphs ($p\ge 1/\mathrm{polylog}\,n$) have a polylogarithmic expected number of faces (about $(\ln n)^2$ for constant $p$), and they show that random sparse graphs have a logarithmic expected number of faces. This leads them to conjecture that the logarithmic property holds for almost all graphs without any density condition. It would follow from their stronger conjecture that the expected number of faces of a random embedding of $G\in G(n,p)$ is $(1+o(1))\ln(pn^2)$.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic

name: AX_random_embedding_faces_dense_logarithmic
title: Conjecture 9.3
statement_text: Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices with minimum vertex degree $\Omega(n)$. Then $G$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[F] = \Theta(\log(n))$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. Known bounds: Stahl showed $\mathbb{E}[F]\le n+\ln n$ for $K_n$ and $\le n\ln n$ for any $n$-vertex graph; Campion Loth and Mohar proved $\mathbb{E}[F]\le\frac{\pi^2}{6}n$ for every graph; Mauk and Stahl conjectured $2\ln n+O(1)$ for $K_n$, and the authors prove $\mathbb{E}[F]\le 10\ln n+2$ for $K_n$ (and $\le 3.65\ln n$ for very large $n$), tight up to the constant factor. Campion Loth, Halasz, Masařík, Mohar and Šámal gave a large family of $n$-vertex graphs with $\mathbb{E}[F]=\Theta(n)$, but all have maximum degree $O(1)$; the authors were unable to find dense graphs with that many expected faces. The conjecture asks that every $n$-vertex graph with minimum degree at least $cn$ (for a fixed constant $c>0$) has $\mathbb{E}[F]=\Theta(\log n)$. The authors' logarithmic bound for $K_n$ (together with a matching lower bound) confirms it for complete graphs; the general dense case remains open.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic

name: AX_random_embedding_faces_nonorientable_complete
title: Conjecture 9.5
statement_text: The expected number of faces in a non-orientable random embedding of the complete graph $K_{n}$ is at most $\ln(n) + O(1)$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. A non-orientable random embedding is defined by choosing a random rotation system together with a random signature, giving each edge a sign $+$ or $-$ independently with probability $1/2$ (edges of sign $-$ are twisted, i.e. traversing them reverses the local orientation); $F^-$ denotes its number of faces. For orientable random embeddings of $K_n$, Mauk and Stahl conjectured $\mathbb{E}[F]=2\ln n+O(1)$, and the authors prove $\mathbb{E}[F]\le 10\ln n+2$ (and $\le 3.65\ln n$ for very large $n$), tight up to the constant factor. Computer data suggest a similar logarithmic behaviour for non-orientable random embeddings of $K_n$, with the smaller constant conjectured here.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic

name: AX_random_embedding_faces_nonorientable_vs_orientable
title: Conjecture 9.6
statement_text: Let $F^{-}$ be the random variable for the average number of faces in a non-orientable random embedding of some graph $G$. Then $\mathbb{E}[F^{-}] \leq \mathbb{E}[F]$.
context_text: Every 2-cell embedding of a connected graph $G$ in an orientable closed surface is described, up to homeomorphism, by a rotation system: a cyclic ordering $R_v$ of the edges (half-edges) at each vertex $v$, giving the clockwise order around $v$; so $G$ has exactly $\prod_v(d(v)-1)!$ such embeddings. A random embedding of $G$ is one chosen uniformly among them, and $F$ (or $F(G)$) denotes its number of faces, so $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is the expected number of faces of $G$ (equivalently, by Euler's formula, its average genus); a random embedding of a random graph means first drawing $G$ from the model and then a random embedding of $G$. A non-orientable random embedding is defined by choosing a random rotation system together with a random signature, giving each edge a sign $+$ or $-$ independently with probability $1/2$ (edges of sign $-$ are twisted, i.e. traversing them reverses the local orientation); $F^-$ denotes its number of faces. The conjecture asserts that for every graph $G$ the expected number of faces of a non-orientable random embedding is at most that of an orientable random embedding. The authors note that it is an easy exercise to check it on toy models, such as the chain of triangles joined by cut edges; for the dipole (two vertices joined by $m$ parallel edges) an analysis of their random process gives $\mathbb{E}[F^-]\le\frac12\mathbb{E}[F]+1$; computer data on more general graphs give evidence for small $n$. They also conjecture $\mathbb{E}[F^-]\le\ln n+O(1)$ for $K_n$, compared with the orientable value conjectured to be $2\ln n+O(1)$.
paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic

name: AX_defective_coloring_blowup_chromatic_ratio
title: Problem 1.4
statement_text: Determine $\sup\left\{\frac{\chi(G)}{\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})} : G \text{ is a graph and } d\ge 0\right\}$, i.e. the smallest value of $c$ for which the inequality $\chi(G)\leq c\cdot\chi^{d}(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ always holds.
context_text: For an integer $d\ge0$, a colouring of $G$ is $d$-defective if every colour class induces a subgraph of maximum degree at most $d$ (each vertex has at most $d$ neighbours of its own colour), and the $d$-defective chromatic number $\chi^d(G)$ is the minimum number of colours in a $d$-defective colouring. $G\boxtimes K_{d+1}$ is the strong product, i.e. the blowup of $G$ obtained by replacing each vertex by a clique of size $d+1$ and joining all vertices of the cliques of $u$ and $v$ whenever $uv\in E(G)$. Lifting a proper colouring of $G$ gives $\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})\le\chi(G)$ always. Guo, Kang and Zwaneveld conjectured that equality $\chi(G)=\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ always holds (true for $d\le1$, perfect graphs, and $\chi(G)\le4$). The authors disprove it: for every $d\ge2$ there is a graph $G$ with $\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})\le k:=2d^3+2d^2+d+3$ but $\chi(G)>k$; for $d=2$ this gives a ratio $\frac{30}{29}$, so the supremum is at least $\frac{30}{29}$. They also prove $\chi(G)\le2\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_d)\le2\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ for all $G$ and $d\ge1$, so the supremum is at most $2$. By bootstrapping, for all $d\equiv2\pmod 3$ and $k\equiv0\pmod{30}$ there is $G$ with $\chi(G)=k\ge\frac{30}{29}\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$, so assuming $\chi(G)$ or $d$ large does not bring the ratio arbitrarily close to $1$.
notes: The theorem environment statement is truncated to 'Determine' in the source; the full problem is reconstructed from the immediately preceding context.
paper_title: Defective coloring of blowups

name: AX_intersectionwise_chi_guarding_classes
title: Question 1 (Intersectionwise χ-guarding)
statement_text: Which graph classes have the property that their graph-intersection with every $\chi$-bounded class of graphs is $\chi$-bounded?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, and classes are hereditary (closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs). A class $\mathcal{C}$ is $\chi$-bounded if there is a non-decreasing $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$. The intersection of graphs $G_1,\dots,G_k$ is $(\bigcap_iV(G_i),\bigcap_iE(G_i))$, and the graph-intersection $\mathcal{G}_1\cap\dots\cap\mathcal{G}_k$ of classes is the class of all graphs $G_1\cap\dots\cap G_k$ with $G_i\in\mathcal{G}_i$. A class $\mathcal{A}$ is intersectionwise $\chi$-guarding if $\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{B}$ is $\chi$-bounded for every $\chi$-bounded class $\mathcal{B}$. Graph-union preserves $\chi$-boundedness (Gyárfás), but graph-intersection does not: intersection graphs of axis-parallel boxes in $\mathbb{R}^k$ form the $k$-fold graph-intersection of the class of interval graphs (which are perfect), and this is $\chi$-bounded for $k=2$ (Asplund and Grünbaum) but not for $k=3$ (Burling). The authors prove that decomposable classes (every graph is a union of $t$ graphs, each admitting a $k$-colouring whose colour classes induce graphs whose components have independence number less than $r$, for fixed $t,k,r$) are intersectionwise $\chi$-guarding, e.g. unit interval graphs and line graphs of bipartite graphs; that some $\chi$-bounded classes, such as trivially perfect graphs, are not; they derive necessary conditions on a finite set $\mathcal{H}$ for $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs to be intersectionwise $\chi$-guarding, and show that $H$-free graphs are intersectionwise $\chi$-guarding if and only if $H$ is $P_2$, $P_3$ or $rK_1$. The authors also study the companion notion of intersectionwise self-$\chi$-guarding classes, whose $k$-fold graph-intersections are $\chi$-bounded for every $k$.
