paper_title: Intersections of graphs and $χ$-boundedness

name: AX_oriented_graph_semidegree_non_antidirected_paths
title: Question 5.1
statement_text: Is it true that every oriented graph $G$ with $\delta^{0}(G)\geq k/2$ contains every orientation of the $k$-edge path, save for the antidirected orientations?
context_text: An oriented graph is a digraph with no loops and no directed cycles of length two; its minimum semidegree $\delta^0(G)$ is the minimum over all vertices of the in- and out-degrees. An orientation of the $k$-edge path is antidirected if consecutive arcs alternate in direction. Stein conjectured that every oriented graph with $\delta^0(G)>k/2$ contains every orientation of the $k$-edge path; Jackson proved this for directed paths (even with $\delta^0(G)\ge k/2$), and it is known for antidirected paths under stronger bounds (down to about $\frac12(k-1+\sqrt{k-3})$). The authors prove the case of paths with two blocks (maximal directed subpaths) under semidegree conditions, e.g. $\delta^0(G)\ge3k/4$ suffices for every two-block path with $k$ arcs. The $(k/2)$-blow-up of a directed cycle has $\delta^0=k/2$ and no antidirected $k$-arc path, and a regular tournament on $k+1$ vertices ($k$ even) has $\delta^0=k/2$ and, by Havet and Thomassé, contains every oriented $k$-arc path except (three small exceptions involving) the antidirected one, which motivated this question in an earlier version. In the final version the authors observe that the blow-up of a directed cycle in fact excludes every bouncing path for even $k$ (a path $p_0\dots p_k$ in which the two arcs $p_{2i}p_{2i+1}$ and $p_{2i+1}p_{2i+2}$ have opposite directions for every $i$, a class strictly containing the antidirected paths when $k\ge4$), so the question as stated has a negative answer for even $k\ge4$; they replace it by: does $\delta^0(G)\ge k/2$ force every orientation of the $k$-edge path except the bouncing paths when $k$ is even?
paper_title: Two-block paths in oriented graphs of large semidegree

name: AX_subcubic_triangle_free_fractional_19_7
title: Conjecture 1.6
statement_text: Every subcubic triangle-free graph avoiding $F^{(1)}_{14}$, $F^{(2)}_{14}$, $F_{11}$, and $F_{22}$ as subgraphs is fractionally $19/7$-colorable.
context_text: A graph is subcubic if it has maximum degree at most $3$. For a real $k$, $G$ is fractionally $k$-colorable if for some positive integers $a,b$ with $a/b\le k$ one can assign to each vertex a $b$-subset of $\{1,\dots,a\}$ with adjacent vertices receiving disjoint sets (equivalently, for every non-negative vertex weighting some independent set carries at least a $1/k$ fraction of the weight); the fractional chromatic number is the least such $k$. The excluded graphs are specific small subcubic triangle-free graphs given in the paper by figures: $F^{(1)}_{14}$ and $F^{(2)}_{14}$ are the two $14$-vertex graphs (one of them the generalized Petersen graph $P(7,2)$) that are the only connected graphs attaining Staton's bound $\alpha\ge5n/14$, and have fractional chromatic number $14/5$; $F_{11}$ and $F_{22}$ (on $11$ and $22$ vertices) have fractional chromatic number $11/4$; and $F^{(1)}_{19}$, $F^{(2)}_{19}$ (on $19$ vertices) have fractional chromatic number $19/7$. Dvořák et al. proved the Heckman–Thomas conjecture that every subcubic triangle-free graph is fractionally $14/5$-colorable, and Cames van Batenburg et al. conjectured that avoiding all six graphs $F^{(1)}_{14},F^{(2)}_{14},F_{11},F_{22},F^{(1)}_{19},F^{(2)}_{19}$ as subgraphs gives fractional $8/3$-colorability (which would imply the Heckman–Thomas planar conjecture). The authors prove that a subcubic triangle-free graph with no component isomorphic to $F^{(1)}_{14}$ or $F^{(2)}_{14}$ is fractionally $11/4$-colorable, which is tight because of $F_{11}$ and $F_{22}$. They propose this intermediate conjecture, the bound $19/7$ being attained by $F^{(1)}_{19}$ and $F^{(2)}_{19}$.
notes: PDF source — the bound $19/7$ and the excluded subgraphs are stated clearly in the text.
paper_title: 11/4-colorability of subcubic triangle-free graphs

name: AX_chromatic_threshold_odd_cycles_undirected
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: For which $\varepsilon>0$ and $k>0$ does there exist a bound $c$ such that each simple graph $G$ with minimum degree at least $\varepsilon|V(G)|$ either contains $C_{2k+1}$ as a subgraph or $\chi(G)\leq c$ (or both)?
context_text: The undirected question goes back to Erdős and Simonovits (1972), who asked whether graphs with no fixed odd cycle and large minimum degree have bounded chromatic number, for $C_3$ and $C_5$. Erdős, Hajnal and Simonovits showed that for $C_3$ no bound exists if $\varepsilon<1/3$; Thomassen answered affirmatively for $C_3$ when $\varepsilon>1/3$ and for all longer odd cycles for every $\varepsilon>0$ (Brandt and Thomassé showed triangle-free graphs with minimum degree at least $|V(G)|/3$ are even $4$-colourable), and for even cycles an affirmative answer follows from a result of Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov (large graphs with linearly many edges contain large complete bipartite subgraphs). The general version for any fixed forbidden graph, the chromatic threshold, was completely resolved by Allen, Böttcher, Griffiths, Kohayakawa and Morris. Thus the question is fully answered in the literature: such a bound exists if and only if $k\ge2$, or $k=1$ and $\varepsilon\ge1/3$. The paper studies a directed analogue, and its main theorem (via replacing each edge by two anti-parallel arcs) recovers Thomassen's result for odd cycles of length at least five.
notes: Presented as background context; the specific cases addressed by Thomassen [11,12] are resolved, but the fully general formulation is posed by the paper authors as a unifying question.
paper_title: Orientations of cycles in digraphs of high chromatic number and high minimum out-degree

name: AX_chromatic_threshold_digraph_cycle_orientations
title: Question 1.2
statement_text: Which orientations of cycles are contained in every digraph (without loops or parallel arcs) with high minimum out-degree (at least $\varepsilon|V(D)|$ for a fixed $\varepsilon>0$) and high chromatic number?
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs, but may have anti-parallel arcs (directed $2$-cycles); $\chi(D)$ is the chromatic number of the underlying undirected graph, and $H$ is contained in $D$ if it is a subdigraph. An orientation of a graph $G$ picks exactly one of the arcs $uv,vu$ for each edge $uv$. A block of an orientation $C$ of a cycle is a maximal connected subdigraph containing no $\rightarrow\leftarrow$ or $\leftarrow\rightarrow$, i.e. a maximal directed subpath (a directed cycle has a single block); its length is its number of arcs. The authors' main theorem: for fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and $k\ge2$ and an orientation $C$ of a $k$-cycle, there is $c\ge1$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\chi(D)\ge c$ and minimum out-degree at least $\varepsilon|V(D)|$ contains $C$ if and only if $C$ has at least three blocks, or two blocks both of length at least two; the negative direction uses directed shift graphs augmented to have large minimum out-degree. This question, the directed analogue of the chromatic threshold of cycles, is thus fully answered in the same paper. By reversing arcs the theorem also holds for high minimum in-degree, and by doubling edges it implies Thomassen's undirected result for odd cycles of length at least five. The undirected question goes back to Erdős and Simonovits (1972), who asked whether graphs with no fixed odd cycle and large minimum degree have bounded chromatic number, for $C_3$ and $C_5$. Erdős, Hajnal and Simonovits showed that for $C_3$ no bound exists if $\varepsilon<1/3$; Thomassen answered affirmatively for $C_3$ when $\varepsilon>1/3$ and for all longer odd cycles for every $\varepsilon>0$ (Brandt and Thomassé showed triangle-free graphs with minimum degree at least $|V(G)|/3$ are even $4$-colourable), and for even cycles an affirmative answer follows from a result of Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov (large graphs with linearly many edges contain large complete bipartite subgraphs). The general version for any fixed forbidden graph, the chromatic threshold, was completely resolved by Allen, Böttcher, Griffiths, Kohayakawa and Morris.
notes: This question is fully resolved within the same paper by Theorem 1.3; included because it is a labelled question environment and the central research question.
paper_title: Orientations of cycles in digraphs of high chromatic number and high minimum out-degree

name: AX_chromatic_threshold_digraph_fixed_subdigraph
title: Question 4.1
statement_text: For which fixed digraphs $H$ does there exist a constant $c_{\varepsilon}\geq 1$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ such that every digraph $D$ without loops or parallel arcs with $\chi(D)\geq c_{\varepsilon}$ and minimum out-degree at least $\varepsilon|V(D)|$ contains $H$ as a subdigraph?
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs, but may have anti-parallel arcs (directed $2$-cycles); $\chi(D)$ is the chromatic number of the underlying undirected graph, and $H$ is contained in $D$ if it is a subdigraph. An orientation of a graph $G$ picks exactly one of the arcs $uv,vu$ for each edge $uv$. A block of an orientation $C$ of a cycle is a maximal connected subdigraph containing no $\rightarrow\leftarrow$ or $\leftarrow\rightarrow$, i.e. a maximal directed subpath (a directed cycle has a single block); its length is its number of arcs. The authors' main theorem: for fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and $k\ge2$ and an orientation $C$ of a $k$-cycle, there is $c\ge1$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\chi(D)\ge c$ and minimum out-degree at least $\varepsilon|V(D)|$ contains $C$ if and only if $C$ has at least three blocks, or two blocks both of length at least two; the negative direction uses directed shift graphs augmented to have large minimum out-degree. So the main theorem answers this question for orientations of cycles. Since every sufficiently large graph with a linear number of edges contains a large complete bipartite subgraph (Alon, Krivelevich, Sudakov), a Ramsey-type argument colouring arcs by their direction between the two sides gives a large complete bipartite subdigraph with all arcs oriented from one side to the other; hence the answer is affirmative for every subdigraph $H$ of such a uniformly oriented complete bipartite digraph. Directed cycles, and orientations of cycles obtained from a directed cycle by reversing a single arc, are negative examples.
paper_title: Orientations of cycles in digraphs of high chromatic number and high minimum out-degree

name: AX_chromatic_threshold_digraph_minimum_epsilon
title: Question 4.2
statement_text: For a fixed digraph $H$, what is the minimum value $\varepsilon_{H}\geq 0$ such that there exists a constant $c\geq 1$ such that every digraph $D$ without loops or parallel arcs with $\chi(D)\geq c$ and minimum out-degree at least $\varepsilon_{H}|V(D)|$ contains $H$ as a subdigraph?
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs, but may have anti-parallel arcs (directed $2$-cycles); $\chi(D)$ is the chromatic number of the underlying undirected graph, and $H$ is contained in $D$ if it is a subdigraph. An orientation of a graph $G$ picks exactly one of the arcs $uv,vu$ for each edge $uv$. A block of an orientation $C$ of a cycle is a maximal connected subdigraph containing no $\rightarrow\leftarrow$ or $\leftarrow\rightarrow$, i.e. a maximal directed subpath (a directed cycle has a single block); its length is its number of arcs. The authors' main theorem: for fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and $k\ge2$ and an orientation $C$ of a $k$-cycle, there is $c\ge1$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\chi(D)\ge c$ and minimum out-degree at least $\varepsilon|V(D)|$ contains $C$ if and only if $C$ has at least three blocks, or two blocks both of length at least two; the negative direction uses directed shift graphs augmented to have large minimum out-degree. The question is well defined for every digraph $H$, since the statement trivially holds with $\varepsilon_H=1$. The quantity $\varepsilon_H$ is a directed analogue of the chromatic threshold of undirected graphs (for which the general problem was resolved by Allen, Böttcher, Griffiths, Kohayakawa and Morris; e.g. it is $1/3$ for the triangle by Erdős–Hajnal–Simonovits and Thomassen), and the main theorem characterises the orientations of cycles with $\varepsilon_H=0$. The authors also suggest variants of these questions where large chromatic number is replaced by large dichromatic number (the minimum number of acyclic sets, i.e. inducing no directed cycle, partitioning $V(D)$, introduced by Neumann-Lara).
notes: The authors note that $\varepsilon_H = 1$ is always an upper bound, so the quantity is well-defined for all digraphs $H$.
paper_title: Orientations of cycles in digraphs of high chromatic number and high minimum out-degree

name: AX_quasi_clique_minor_gap_infimum
title: Question 1.6
statement_text: What is the infimum $c$ such that for any large enough $t$, there is a graph that admits a quasi-$K_{t}$-minor but no $K_{ct}$-minor?
context_text: A graph admits a $K_p$-minor if it has $p$ non-empty, pairwise disjoint bags $B_1,\dots,B_p$ of vertices, each inducing a connected subgraph, with an edge between $B_i$ and $B_j$ for all $i\ne j$; it admits a quasi-$K_p$-minor (a notion of Las Vergnas and Meyniel) if it has $p$ non-empty pairwise disjoint bags such that $B_i\cup B_j$ induces a connected subgraph for all $i\ne j$ (the bags themselves need not be connected). A colouring is frozen if any two colour classes induce a connected subgraph; the colour classes of a frozen $p$-colouring form a quasi-$K_p$-minor. Las Vergnas and Meyniel conjectured that every graph with a quasi-$K_t$-minor has a $K_t$-minor; this is known for $t\le10$. Trivially every graph with a quasi-$K_{2t}$-minor has a $K_t$-minor (merge bags in pairs), so $c\ge\frac12$. The authors strongly disprove the conjecture: for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $t$ large enough, there is a graph with a quasi-$K_t$-minor but no $K_{(2/3+\varepsilon)t}$-minor, so $c\le\frac23$. In an addendum, they note that the same construction had been discovered independently earlier (by Reed, and by Böhme, Kostochka and Thomason), without the implications on quasi-minors.
paper_title: On a recolouring version of Hadwiger's conjecture

name: AX_kt_minor_free_recoloring_single_class
title: Question 1.7
statement_text: Is there a constant $c^{\prime}$ such that for every $t$, all the $c^{\prime}\cdot t$-colourings of a graph with no $K_{t}$-minor form a single equivalence class?
context_text: All colourings are proper vertex colourings. Given a $k$-colouring, a Kempe chain is a maximal connected subgraph induced by two colours (a vertex with no neighbour of the second colour is a chain by itself), and a Kempe change swaps the two colours on one Kempe chain; two $k$-colourings are Kempe equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a sequence of Kempe changes, and 'equivalence class' refers to this equivalence on the set of $k$-colourings. Meyniel proved that all $5$-colourings of a planar graph are Kempe equivalent, and Las Vergnas and Meyniel extended this to $K_5$-minor-free graphs and conjectured that for every $t$ all $t$-colourings of a graph with no $K_t$-minor are Kempe equivalent. The authors disprove this: for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $t$ large enough there is a graph with no $K_t$-minor whose $(\frac32-\varepsilon)t$-colourings are not all Kempe equivalent (it has a frozen colouring, in which any two colour classes induce a connected subgraph), so $c'\ge\frac32$ if such a constant exists. The best known upper bound comes from the result of Kostochka and of Thomason that graphs with no $K_t$-minor have degeneracy $O(t\sqrt{\log t})$, combined with the fact that all $k$-colourings of a $d$-degenerate graph are Kempe equivalent for $k>d$.
paper_title: On a recolouring version of Hadwiger's conjecture

name: AX_domination_packing_ratio_bounded_given_class
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Given a graph class $\mathcal{G}$, is there a constant $c_{\mathcal{G}}$ such that $$\frac{\gamma(G)}{\rho(G)}\leqslant c_{\mathcal{G}}\quad\text{ for each }\quad G\in\mathcal{G}~{}~{}?$$
context_text: The dominating number $\gamma(G)$ is the minimum size of a set of vertices whose closed neighborhoods cover $V(G)$; the packing number $\rho(G)$ is the maximum size of a set of vertices whose closed neighborhoods are pairwise disjoint (equivalently, pairwise at distance at least $3$). Always $\gamma(G)\ge\rho(G)$, and $\gamma(G)\le\Delta(G)\rho(G)$. The two parameters are optima of integer programs whose linear relaxations are dual, so a constant bound on $\gamma/\rho$ bounds the integrality gap of both programs. Known bounded classes include $K_{q,r}$-minor-free graphs, graphs of bounded Euler genus, classes of bounded weak colouring number $\mathrm{wcol}_2$, and bounded twin-width; the authors prove bounds $\gamma\le7\rho$ for $2$-degenerate graphs, $\gamma\le3\rho$ for AT-free graphs, $\gamma\le32\rho$ for unit-disk graphs, $\gamma\le k\rho$ for treewidth at most $k$, $\gamma\le10\rho$ for planar graphs and $\gamma\le4k^2\rho$ for twin-width at most $k$. On the other hand the ratio is unbounded for Cartesian products $K_n\square K_n$ ($\gamma=n$, $\rho=1$), for split graphs (hence chordal graphs) and for $3$-degenerate graphs (which also gives classes of bounded VC-dimension with unbounded ratio). The question is asked for each class $\mathcal{G}$ separately; it remains open e.g. for homogeneously orderable graphs, chordal bipartite graphs, and intersection graphs of axis-parallel rectangles in the plane or boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$. For subcubic connected graphs, Henning et al. conjectured $\gamma\le2\rho+1$.
paper_title: On graph classes with constant domination-packing ratio

name: AX_domination_packing_ratio_bounded_characterization
title: Question 9.1
statement_text: Characterize those graph classes $\mathcal{G}$ for which there is a constant $c_{\mathcal{G}}$ such that $\dfrac{\gamma(G)}{\rho(G)}\leqslant c_{\mathcal{G}}$ for each $G\in\mathcal{G}$.
context_text: The dominating number $\gamma(G)$ is the minimum size of a set of vertices whose closed neighborhoods cover $V(G)$; the packing number $\rho(G)$ is the maximum size of a set of vertices whose closed neighborhoods are pairwise disjoint (equivalently, pairwise at distance at least $3$). Always $\gamma(G)\ge\rho(G)$, and $\gamma(G)\le\Delta(G)\rho(G)$. The two parameters are optima of integer programs whose linear relaxations are dual, so a constant bound on $\gamma/\rho$ bounds the integrality gap of both programs. Known bounded classes include $K_{q,r}$-minor-free graphs, graphs of bounded Euler genus, classes of bounded weak colouring number $\mathrm{wcol}_2$, and bounded twin-width; the authors prove bounds $\gamma\le7\rho$ for $2$-degenerate graphs, $\gamma\le3\rho$ for AT-free graphs, $\gamma\le32\rho$ for unit-disk graphs, $\gamma\le k\rho$ for treewidth at most $k$, $\gamma\le10\rho$ for planar graphs and $\gamma\le4k^2\rho$ for twin-width at most $k$. On the other hand the ratio is unbounded for Cartesian products $K_n\square K_n$ ($\gamma=n$, $\rho=1$), for split graphs (hence chordal graphs) and for $3$-degenerate graphs (which also gives classes of bounded VC-dimension with unbounded ratio). Since $2$-degenerate graphs, which are not sparse in the sense of bounded weak colouring numbers (they contain all $1$-subdivisions of graphs), have bounded ratio while $3$-degenerate graphs do not, no characterization purely in terms of sparsity is possible, although previous results had suggested that sparsity (e.g. bounded weak colouring numbers) might be the key property. The authors call this a major open problem.

paper_title: On graph classes with constant domination-packing ratio

name: AX_rainbow_cycle_average_degree_loglog_factor
title: Question 10.1
statement_text: Is the $\log\log n$ factor necessary in order to guarantee a rainbow cycle, in the theorem that there exists $C>0$ such that every properly edge-coloured graph on $n\ge3$ vertices with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ contains a rainbow cycle? That is, does average degree $C\log n$ suffice?
context_text: An edge-colouring is proper if the edges at each vertex have distinct colours, and a subgraph is rainbow if no colour appears on more than one of its edges; $d(G)$ is the average degree and logarithms are natural. Keevash, Mubayi, Sudakov and Verstraëte asked how large the average degree of a properly edge-coloured $n$-vertex graph must be to guarantee a rainbow cycle; they showed that $\Omega(\log n)$ is needed, still the best lower bound, and upper bounds improved from $O(n^{1/3})$ through $e^{(\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}}$, $O(\log^4n)$ and $(\log n)^{2+o(1)}$ to $O(\log^2n)$. The authors prove that there is $C>0$ such that every properly edge-coloured graph on $n\ge3$ vertices with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ contains a rainbow cycle, tight up to the $\log\log n$ factor. The proof first passes to a robust sublinear expander subgraph and then randomly splits the colour palette into two parts, showing that most vertices are reachable by rainbow walks in each part; this approach needs the $\log\log n$ term, since there are properly edge-coloured robust sublinear expanders (built from Hamming graphs) with average degree $\log n(\log\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ in which random colour subsampling with probability $\frac12$ leaves no large component w.h.p. The authors view this as circumstantial evidence that the factor might be needed, and note that the transposition question ($t(k)$ for $\mathcal{S}_k$) might help decide it.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

name: AX_rainbow_expander_color_separated_spanning_decomposition
title: Question 10.2
statement_text: Does there exist a constant $C>0$ such that the edges of any $n$-vertex properly edge-coloured robust sublinear expander $G$ with average degree at least $C\log n$ can be decomposed into two spanning connected subgraphs in such a way that every colour appears on only one of them?
context_text: An edge-colouring is proper if the edges at each vertex have distinct colours, and a subgraph is rainbow if no colour appears on more than one of its edges; $d(G)$ is the average degree and logarithms are natural. Keevash, Mubayi, Sudakov and Verstraëte asked how large the average degree of a properly edge-coloured $n$-vertex graph must be to guarantee a rainbow cycle; they showed that $\Omega(\log n)$ is needed, still the best lower bound, and upper bounds improved from $O(n^{1/3})$ through $e^{(\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}}$, $O(\log^4n)$ and $(\log n)^{2+o(1)}$ to $O(\log^2n)$. The authors prove that there is $C>0$ such that every properly edge-coloured graph on $n\ge3$ vertices with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ contains a rainbow cycle, tight up to the $\log\log n$ factor. A graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is a robust sublinear expander if for every $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, every non-empty $U\subseteq V(G)$ with $|U|\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ and every set $F$ of at most $(\varepsilon/3)\,d(G)\,|U|$ edges, the neighbourhood of $U$ in $G-F$ (vertices outside $U$ adjacent to $U$) has size at least $(\varepsilon/3)|U|$. Every graph contains a robust sublinear expander subgraph $H$ with $d(H)/\log|V(H)|$ comparable to $d(G)/\log|V(G)|$. The most natural approach, assigning each colour independently with probability $\frac12$ to one of the two subgraphs, fails: there are properly edge-coloured robust sublinear expanders of average degree $\log n(\log\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ (from Hamming graphs) for which both resulting subgraphs are disconnected w.h.p. A positive answer would not quite suffice to remove the $\log\log n$ factor from the rainbow-cycle theorem; what would suffice is a pair of vertices joined by rainbow paths in both subgraphs, which would follow if the two subgraphs were (weaker) robust sublinear expanders rather than just connected.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

name: AX_group_subset_signed_product_identity
title: Question 10.3
statement_text: Given a positive integer $n$, what is the smallest number $d=d(n)$ so that in any group $G$ of size $|G|=n$, given any subset $S\subseteq G$ of size $|S|\geq d$, we can always find a solution to $g_{1}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdot\ldots\cdot g_{m}^{\varepsilon_{m}}=e$ with distinct $g_{1},\ldots,g_{m}\in S$ as well as $\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{m}\in\{-1,1\}$ and $m\geq 1$.
context_text: For a group $(G,\cdot)$ with identity $e$, a subset $S$ is dissociated if there is no solution to $g_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots g_m^{\varepsilon_m}=e$ with distinct $g_i\in S$, $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$ and $m\ge1$; the additive dimension $\dim A$ of a finite set $A$ is the largest size of a dissociated subset of $A$, and $\dim G$ equals the plus-minus weighted Davenport constant $D_\pm(G)$. A Cayley-graph argument links this to rainbow cycles, and the rainbow-cycle theorem gives $\dim A=O(K\log|A|\log\log|A|)$ whenever $|A\cdot A|\le K|A|$ (a non-abelian version of Sanders' theorem $\dim A=O(K\log|A|)$ for abelian groups), hence $\dim G=O(\log|G|\log\log|G|)$ for every finite group with $|G|\ge3$; for abelian groups $\dim G\le\lceil\log_2|G|\rceil$, which fails for non-abelian groups since $\dim\mathcal{S}_3^k\ge\frac{3}{\log_26}\log_2|\mathcal{S}_3^k|$. Equivalently, $d(n)-1$ is the maximum of $\dim G=D_\pm(G)$ over groups of order $n$. The authors' bound gives $d(n)\le O(\log n\log\log n)$, and $d(n)\ge\Omega(\log n)$ is easy; it is unclear whether the $\log\log n$ factor is necessary. The case $G=\mathcal{S}_k$ is of particular interest, since every $k$-element group embeds in $\mathcal{S}_k$ and the best lower bounds on $d(n)$ come from dissociated sets of transpositions. This question is not about graphs, but it is connected to rainbow cycles in properly edge-coloured Cayley graphs.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

name: AX_transpositions_product_identity_minimum
title: Question 10.4
statement_text: Given $k\geq 2$, determine the minimum number $t=t(k)$ such that any set of $t$ transpositions in $\mathcal{S}_{k}$ contains a non-empty subset whose elements can be multiplied in some order to give the identity.
context_text: $\mathcal{S}_k$ is the symmetric group on $k$ elements. Equivalently, $t(k)-1$ is the additive dimension of the set of all transpositions of $\mathcal{S}_k$, i.e. the largest size of a set of transpositions with no non-empty subset whose elements multiply, in some order, to the identity; since a transposition is its own inverse, this is the same as being dissociated (no solution to $g_1^{\pm1}\cdots g_m^{\pm1}=e$ with distinct $g_i$). For a group $(G,\cdot)$ with identity $e$, a subset $S$ is dissociated if there is no solution to $g_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots g_m^{\varepsilon_m}=e$ with distinct $g_i\in S$, $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$ and $m\ge1$; the additive dimension $\dim A$ of a finite set $A$ is the largest size of a dissociated subset of $A$, and $\dim G$ equals the plus-minus weighted Davenport constant $D_\pm(G)$. A Cayley-graph argument links this to rainbow cycles, and the rainbow-cycle theorem gives $\dim A=O(K\log|A|\log\log|A|)$ whenever $|A\cdot A|\le K|A|$ (a non-abelian version of Sanders' theorem $\dim A=O(K\log|A|)$ for abelian groups), hence $\dim G=O(\log|G|\log\log|G|)$ for every finite group with $|G|\ge3$; for abelian groups $\dim G\le\lceil\log_2|G|\rceil$, which fails for non-abelian groups since $\dim\mathcal{S}_3^k\ge\frac{3}{\log_26}\log_2|\mathcal{S}_3^k|$. The authors show $k(\log k)^{1-o(1)}\le t(k)\le O(k(\log k)^2)$; the upper bound comes from applying the rainbow-cycle theorem (every properly edge-coloured $n$-vertex graph with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ has a rainbow cycle) to a Cayley graph on $k!$ vertices, where $\log\log(k!)$ costs a factor $\log k$, while earlier rainbow-cycle bounds gave nothing better than the trivial $t(k)\le\binom{k}{2}$. These transposition sets give the best known lower bounds for the maximum additive dimension of groups of order $n$, and the question might help decide whether the $\log\log n$ factor is needed in the rainbow-cycle theorem.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

name: AX_annulus_digraph_winding_one_crossing_free
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: Let $G$ be a strongly 2-connected digraph drawn (possibly with crossings) in an annulus $\Sigma$, such that every directed cycle has winding number one around the annulus in the natural sense. Then $G$ can be drawn in $\Sigma$ without crossings, such that every directed cycle has winding number one.
context_text: In this paper a digraph has no loops or parallel edges, but directed cycles of length two are allowed. A digraph is strongly 2-connected if (in the usual sense; the paper does not define it) it has at least three vertices and remains strongly connected after deleting any one vertex. A digraph $G$ is weightable if one can assign a real weight $w(e)$ to each edge $e$ such that $\sum_{e\in E(C)}w(e)=1$ for every directed cycle $C$. Drawing in an annulus is the same as drawing in the plane avoiding the origin; in such a drawing each edge subtends a fraction $w(e)$ of a full turn around the origin, so $G$ is weightable if and only if it can be drawn (possibly with crossings) in an annulus so that every directed cycle has winding number one. The conjecture arises from a theorem of Thomassen: if $G$ is acyclic with sources $a,b$ and sinks $c,d$ (all distinct) and every other vertex has in- and out-degree at least two, then exactly one holds: there are vertex-disjoint directed paths from $a$ to $c$ and from $b$ to $d$, or $G$ can be drawn in a closed disc with $a,b,c,d$ in order on the boundary. Viewing this as a drawing in a rectangle with sources on the north side and sinks on the south side, and gluing north to south (identifying $a=d$, $b=c$), gives an annulus in which crossings can be removed iff every directed cycle winds exactly once; the conjecture asks whether this extends to strongly 2-connected digraphs. The author states that this would be a pretty extension of Thomassen's theorem but that he cannot prove it. Checking the case where all weights are equal ($\ell$-cyclic digraphs, in which every directed cycle has length $\ell$) gives no evidence, since no $\ell$-cyclic digraph is strongly 2-connected; the paper instead gives a construction of all 3-cyclic digraphs.
paper_title: When all directed cycles have length three

name: AX_weightable_digraphs_np_characterization
title: Informal Question (NP-characterization of weightable digraphs)
statement_text: Can we give a construction for all weightable digraphs (i.e., an NP-characterization)?
context_text: In this paper a digraph has no loops or parallel edges, but directed cycles of length two are allowed. A digraph is strongly 2-connected if (in the usual sense; the paper does not define it) it has at least three vertices and remains strongly connected after deleting any one vertex. A digraph $G$ is weightable if one can assign a real weight $w(e)$ to each edge $e$ such that $\sum_{e\in E(C)}w(e)=1$ for every directed cycle $C$. Drawing in an annulus is the same as drawing in the plane avoiding the origin; in such a drawing each edge subtends a fraction $w(e)$ of a full turn around the origin, so $G$ is weightable if and only if it can be drawn (possibly with crossings) in an annulus so that every directed cycle has winding number one. The author shows that $G$ is weightable if and only if no subdigraph of $G$ is a weak $k$-double cycle with $k\ge3$ (a notion from the theory of even directed cycles), by the same proof as for even digraphs but over the reals instead of $GF(2)$; this excluded-subdigraph characterization is a co-NP characterization. He also shows that every weightable digraph has a $\{0,1\}$-valued weighting. An NP-characterization would be an explicit construction producing exactly the weightable digraphs. For strongly 2-connected digraphs, the author's conjecture that any such digraph drawable in an annulus with all directed cycles of winding number one can be redrawn there without crossings would give such a construction, but it remains open; the paper gives a construction for the special case of 3-cyclic digraphs (all directed cycles of length three), and the case of 4-cyclic digraphs is open.
notes: Stated as prose question in the introduction without a labelled environment.
paper_title: When all directed cycles have length three

name: AX_induced_subdivision_containment_subcubic_planar_dichotomy
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: For any subcubic graph $H$, $H$-\textsc{ISC} is in $\mathsf{P}$ if and only if $H$ is planar.
context_text: A subcubic graph has maximum degree at most 3. $H$ is an induced subdivision of $G$ if some subdivision of $H$ (obtained by replacing edges by paths) is isomorphic to an induced subgraph of $G$; $H$-ISC ($H$-Induced Subdivision Containment), for fixed $H$, takes a graph $G$ as input and asks whether $H$ is an induced subdivision of $G$. The conjecture is stated under the assumption $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$. Polynomial algorithms are known for several planar $H$: $K_{2,3}$ (via Chudnovsky and Seymour's Three-In-A-Tree algorithm), the net (a triangle with a pendant vertex at each vertex), $K_4$, and disjoint unions of a fixed number of triangles; $K_5$ and some trees give NP-complete cases. Chudnovsky, Seymour, Trotignon and Le asked whether $H$-ISC is polynomial for every subcubic $H$. The paper answers this negatively, exhibiting a 66-vertex non-planar subcubic graph $H$ (built from 1-subdivisions of $K_{3,3}$) for which $H$-ISC is NP-complete; the proof derives from the NP-completeness of Induced 2-Disjoint Paths (finding two mutually induced paths between two given terminal pairs) in string graphs, which exclude the 1-subdivision of every non-planar graph as an induced minor. The conjecture proposes that planarity is exactly the dividing line among subcubic graphs.
notes: The 'only if' direction (NP-hardness for non-planar subcubic $H$) implicitly assumes $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$.
paper_title: Induced Disjoint Paths Without an Induced Minor

name: AX_induced_disjoint_paths_variants_complexity_gap
title: Informal Question on Complexity Gap Between Induced Disjoint Paths Variants
statement_text: Is there a hereditary graph class in which Induced $k$-Disjoint Paths is NP-complete but Induced Disjoint $S$–$T$ Paths with $|S|=|T|=k$ is polynomial-time solvable? The case $k=2$ is of particular interest.
context_text: In Induced $k$-Disjoint Paths (the linkage variant) one is given a graph $G$ and $k$ terminal pairs $(s_1,t_1),\dots,(s_k,t_k)$ and asks for paths $P_1,\dots,P_k$, $P_i$ joining $s_i$ to $t_i$, that are mutually induced, i.e. $G[\bigcup_i V(P_i)]$ is exactly the disjoint union of the paths (they are vertex-disjoint and no edge of $G$ joins two of them). In Induced Disjoint $S$–$T$ Paths (the flow variant) one is given disjoint sets $S,T\subseteq V(G)$ with $|S|=|T|$ and asks for $|S|$ mutually induced paths each with one end in $S$ and the other in $T$. Without the induced requirement both problems are polynomial (Robertson–Seymour, respectively Menger's theorem); the induced variants are NP-complete in general for $k=2$ and $|S|=|T|=2$. Induced Disjoint $S$–$T$ Paths with $|S|=|T|=k$ reduces to $k!$ calls of Induced $k$-Disjoint Paths, so for constant $k$ it is in principle easier. The authors observe that the polynomial algorithms in the literature (planar graphs, bounded genus, bounded mim-width, claw-free graphs, (theta, wheel)-free graphs) tend to apply to Induced $k$-Disjoint Paths, while hardness proofs, including theirs for string graphs (intersection graphs of curves in the plane) of bounded degree and twin-width, tend to apply already to Induced Disjoint $S$–$T$ Paths with $|S|=|T|=k$. A hereditary class is one closed under taking induced subgraphs.
notes: Appears in running prose with 'we wonder if' in the preamble to the open questions section (context before Conjecture 1.5); no labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Induced Disjoint Paths Without an Induced Minor

name: AX_multidimensional_ramsey_r2_superexponential
title: Problem 4.1
statement_text: Fix $r,d\geq 2$. Is $R_{2}(2,n)$ superexponential in $n$?
context_text: The Cartesian product $G\square H$ has vertex set $V(G)\times V(H)$, with $(x,y)$ adjacent to $(x',y')$ iff $x=x'$ and $yy'\in E(H)$, or $xx'\in E(G)$ and $y=y'$; in the $d$-fold product $\square^dK_N$ of copies of $K_N$, an edge joining two vertices that differ only in coordinate $i$ is in direction $i$. A colouring of the edges of $\square^dK_n$ is monochromatic in every direction if, for each $i$, all edges in direction $i$ have the same colour (colours may differ between directions). $R_r(d,n)$ is the least $N$ such that every $r$-colouring of the edges of $\square^dK_N$ contains a copy of $\square^dK_n$ that is monochromatic in every direction. Iterating Ramsey's theorem gives a tower-type bound; the authors prove the doubly exponential bound $R_r(d,n)\le r^{r^{C_drn^d}}$, whereas random colourings only give a singly exponential lower bound. They ask whether there is a simple exponential upper bound or the numbers grow faster. The problem is stated in the paper as 'Fix $r,d\ge2$. Is $R_2(2,n)$ superexponential in $n$?'; the quantifier over $r,d$ suggests that $R_r(d,n)$ in general is meant, with $R_2(2,n)$ (two colours, two dimensions) as the first case.
paper_title: A multidimensional Ramsey Theorem

name: AX_multidimensional_ramsey_r2_vs_erdos_szekeres
title: Problem 4.2
statement_text: Does there exist $C>0$ such that $\log R_{2}(2,n)\leq(\log M_{2}(n))^{C}$?
context_text: The Cartesian product $G\square H$ has vertex set $V(G)\times V(H)$, with $(x,y)$ adjacent to $(x',y')$ iff $x=x'$ and $yy'\in E(H)$, or $xx'\in E(G)$ and $y=y'$; in the $d$-fold product $\square^dK_N$ of copies of $K_N$, an edge joining two vertices that differ only in coordinate $i$ is in direction $i$. A colouring of the edges of $\square^dK_n$ is monochromatic in every direction if, for each $i$, all edges in direction $i$ have the same colour (colours may differ between directions). $R_r(d,n)$ is the least $N$ such that every $r$-colouring of the edges of $\square^dK_N$ contains a copy of $\square^dK_n$ that is monochromatic in every direction. A $d$-dimensional array is an injective function $f:A_1\times\dots\times A_d\to\mathbb{R}$ with $A_i\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$; it is monotone if, for each direction $i$, all its $1$-dimensional subarrays in direction $i$ are increasing, or all are decreasing. $M_d(n)$, the multidimensional Erdős–Szekeres number of Fishburn and Graham, is the least $N$ such that every $d$-dimensional array on $[N]^d$ contains a monotone subarray of size $[n]^d$. Colouring an edge $xy$ according to whether $f(x)<f(y)$ shows $M_2(n)\le R_2(2,n)$. Bucić, Sudakov and Tran proved $M_2(n)\le2^{2^{(2+o(1))n}}$ and doubly exponential bounds for $d=3$; the authors prove $R_r(d,n)\le r^{r^{C_drn^d}}$ and $M_d(n)\le2^{n^{C_dn^{d-1}}}$ for all $d$, but for both quantities a gap between singly and doubly exponential bounds remains. The authors ask whether $R_2(2,n)$ can be bounded above by a function of $M_2(n)$, for example by this polynomial relation between the logarithms.
notes: The statement as supplied appears to have a missing closing parenthesis: $(\log(M_{2}(n))^{C}$ is reproduced verbatim from the source.
paper_title: A multidimensional Ramsey Theorem

name: AX_triangle_free_chromatic_spectral_radius_log
title: Conjecture 1.7
statement_text: Every triangle-free graph $G$ satisfies $\chi(G)\leq(1+o(1))\frac{\rho(G)}{\ln\rho(G)}$.
context_text: Here $\rho(G)$ is the spectral radius of $G$, i.e. of its adjacency matrix, and the $o(1)$ term is a function of $\rho(G)$ tending to $0$ as $\rho(G)\to\infty$; $\chi_f$ denotes the fractional chromatic number. Molloy proved $\chi(G)\le(1+o(1))\frac{\Delta}{\ln\Delta}$ for triangle-free graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ (optimal up to a factor 2), and Wilf's classical bound gives $\chi(G)\le\rho(G)+1$ for connected $G$. Since $\rho(G)\le\Delta(G)$, and by Hayes every $d$-degenerate graph has $\rho(G)\le2\sqrt{d(\Delta(G)-d)}$, the spectral radius lies between the degeneracy and the maximum degree and can be much smaller than $\Delta$. The authors prove the fractional version: every triangle-free $G$ satisfies $\chi_f(G)\le(1+o(1))\frac{\rho(G)}{\ln\rho(G)}$, saving a $\ln\rho(G)$ factor over Wilf's bound and strengthening the fractional form of Molloy's bound; they see this as a first step from Molloy's bound towards Harris's conjecture that every triangle-free $d$-degenerate graph has $\chi_f(G)=O(d/\ln d)$, and ask for the same bound for the chromatic number.
paper_title: Local Shearer bound

name: AX_f2n_two_coloring_no_monochromatic_subspace
title: Conjecture 5.1
statement_text: There exists $C>0$ and a two-coloring of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}\setminus\{0\}$ such that there is no subspace $H$ of size $Cn$ for which all nonzero elements of the subspace are monochromatic.
context_text: $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is the $n$-dimensional vector space over the field with two elements; a subspace $H$ has $2^{\dim H}$ elements, so a subspace of size $Cn$ has dimension about $\log_2(Cn)$. A Cayley graph on a group $G$ with symmetric generating set $S$ has vertex set $G$, with $x\sim y$ iff $xy^{-1}\in S$; a graph on $N$ vertices is $C$-Ramsey if its clique number and independence number are both at most $C\log N$. Alon conjectured that there is a constant $C$ such that every finite group has a $C$-Ramsey Cayley graph. On $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ (with $N=2^n$), if all nonzero elements of a subspace lie in $S$ (resp. outside $S$), that subspace is a clique (resp. an independent set), so a $C$-Ramsey Cayley graph gives a two-coloring of $\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus\{0\}$ (in $S$ or not) with no monochromatic subspace of size larger than about $Cn$; the conjecture is thus a consequence of Alon's conjecture for $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, proposed as an intermediate step. By the finite unions theorem, every two-coloring of $\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus\{0\}$ has a monochromatic subspace of any fixed size once $n$ is large, which is why uniform random Cayley graphs on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have clique number $\Theta(\log N\log\log N)$. The best lower bound the authors know, adapted from Sanders' bounds for Rado's theorem, is a monochromatic subspace of size a bounded number of iterated logarithms of $n$, so the true bound may be much smaller than $Cn$. The authors prove Alon's conjecture for abelian groups of order $N$ for almost all $N$ (including $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ for $p\ge5$), but it remains wide open for $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and $\mathbb{F}_3^n$.
paper_title: On the clique number of random Cayley graphs and related topics

name: AX_padded_strings_unavoidable_substring_sets
title: Question 8.3
statement_text: For which sets $\mathcal{S}$ of strings is it true that there is a constant $c=c(\mathcal{S})\in\mathbb{N}$ such that every $c$-padded string $S$ contains either a string in $\mathcal{S}$ or the reverse of a string in $\mathcal{S}$ as a consecutive substring?
context_text: Strings are binary (over $\{0,1\}$). For $c\in\mathbb{N}$, a string is $c$-padded if it starts and ends with at least $c$ zeroes but is not the all-zero string. Graph motivation: a strand is a graph obtained from a path $P$ by adding a vertex $x$ (the neck) with at least one neighbour in $P$; it is a $c$-strand if $x$ is not adjacent to the first and last $c$ vertices of $P$. A $c$-tassel is obtained from at least $c$ disjoint copies of a $c$-strand by identifying their necks. A family $\mathcal{H}$ is tasselled if there is $c$ such that every $c$-tassel contains (as induced subgraphs) all components of some $H\in\mathcal{H}$. The paper proves that for finite $\mathcal{H}$, the class of $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs is clean (its only induced-subgraph obstructions to bounded treewidth are the basic ones: large cliques, complete bipartite graphs, subdivided walls and their line graphs) if and only if $\mathcal{H}$ is tasselled. A strand with neck $v$ and path $p_1\dots p_t$ is encoded by the string $S_{P,v}=b_1\dots b_t$ with $b_i=1$ iff $p_i$ is adjacent to $v$ (unique up to reversal); strands of a $c$-tassel give exactly the $c$-padded strings. When every graph of $\mathcal{H}$ is itself a tassel, deciding whether $\mathcal{H}$ is tasselled amounts to this question about the set $\mathcal{S}$ of their strings. A set $\mathcal{S}$ with the property is called a $c$-unavoidable language. The only singleton $c$-unavoidable languages are $\{0\cdots01\}$ (up to reversal) and $\{0\cdots0\}$, while larger ones seem hard to describe (e.g. $\{00011, 0001000, 1010, 010010, 111, 110011, 11011, 110010011, 00010011001000\}$ is 3-unavoidable); for finite $\mathcal{S}$ the property is decidable by a finite test. Unlike the classical unavoidable languages, whose minimal members are finite, minimal $c$-unavoidable languages may be infinite: $\{01^k0:k\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is 1-unavoidable but no proper subset is.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions XIII. Basic obstructions in $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs for finite $\mathcal{H}$

name: AX_hypercube_subcube_partitions_matchings_counting
title: Problem 1.1
statement_text:
Determine or estimate the functions 
(i) $m(d)$,     (ii) $m^{\prime}(d)$,
    (iii) $f(d)$,
    (iv) $f_{\leq 2}(d).$
context_text: $Q_d=\{0,1\}^d$ is the $d$-dimensional hypercube. $f(d)$ is the number of partitions (tilings) of the vertex set of $Q_d$ into classes each spanning a subcube (a set of vertices obtained by fixing some coordinates and letting the others vary), and for $S\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,d\}$, $f_S(d)$ counts those partitions in which every class has dimension in $S$; thus $f_{\le2}(d)$ counts partitions into singletons, edges and 2-dimensional subcubes, $f_2(d)$ partitions into 2-dimensional subcubes only, and $f_{0,r}(d)$ partitions into singletons and $r$-dimensional subcubes. $m(d)=f_1(d)$ and $m'(d)=f_{\le1}(d)$ are the numbers of perfect matchings and of all matchings of $Q_d$. Write $n=2^{d-1}$ (the size of each side of the bipartite graph $Q_d$) and $N=(d/e)^n$, a rough estimate of $m(d)$. The trivial hierarchy is $m(d)\le m'(d)\le f_{\le2}(d)\le f(d)$. Problem (i) is classical: Graham and Harary computed $m(1),\dots,m(5)=1,2,9,272,589185$, and Östergård and Pettersson computed $m(6)$ and $m(7)$; the first values of $f(d)$ from $d=0$ are $1,2,8,154,89512,71319425714$ (OEIS A018926). Problem (iii) was raised by Gadouleau at the 29th British Combinatorial Conference in 2022, and (iv) is introduced by the authors as a closely related variant. The authors prove $e^{n/2d}N\le m(d)\le 2^{(1+o(1))\log d\cdot n/(2d)}N$, $m'(d)=m(d)\,2^{\Theta(n/\sqrt d)}$ (so $m'(d)/m(d)$ is subexponential in $n$), $c^n m'(d)\le f_{\le2}(d)$ for some constant $c>1$ (so $f_{\le2}(d)/m'(d)$ and $f(d)/m(d)$ are at least exponential in $n$), $f(d)\le(d+1)^n\le e^{n+n/d}N$ (so $f(d)/m(d)$ is at most exponential), and for every fixed $r\ge2$, $N^{r/2^{r-1}-o(1)}\le f_{0,r}(d)\le f_{\{0\}\cup\{r,r+1,\dots\}}(d)\le N^{r/2^{r-1}+o(1)}$. These give the main term of $m(d)$ and partial answers to the other parts.
notes: Part (iii) attributed to Gadouleau (2022, unpublished talk); parts (i), (ii), (iv) are the authors' own formulations.
paper_title: Partitioning the hypercube into smaller hypercubes

name: AX_hypercube_subcube_partitions_ratio_growth
title: Problem 1.2
statement_text:
What is the order of magnitude of the
following ratios? In particular, which one of them is an
exponential function of $n$? 
(i) $m^{\prime}(d)/m(d)$,   (ii) $f_{\leq 2}(d)/m^{\prime}(d)$,
  (iii) $f(d)/f_{\leq 2}(d),$    (iv) $f(d)/m(d)$.
context_text: $Q_d=\{0,1\}^d$ is the $d$-dimensional hypercube. $f(d)$ is the number of partitions (tilings) of the vertex set of $Q_d$ into classes each spanning a subcube (a set of vertices obtained by fixing some coordinates and letting the others vary), and for $S\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,d\}$, $f_S(d)$ counts those partitions in which every class has dimension in $S$; thus $f_{\le2}(d)$ counts partitions into singletons, edges and 2-dimensional subcubes, $f_2(d)$ partitions into 2-dimensional subcubes only, and $f_{0,r}(d)$ partitions into singletons and $r$-dimensional subcubes. $m(d)=f_1(d)$ and $m'(d)=f_{\le1}(d)$ are the numbers of perfect matchings and of all matchings of $Q_d$. Write $n=2^{d-1}$ (the size of each side of the bipartite graph $Q_d$) and $N=(d/e)^n$, a rough estimate of $m(d)$. The hierarchy $m(d)\le m'(d)\le f_{\le2}(d)\le f(d)$ holds by definition, and 'exponential function of $n$' refers to $n=2^{d-1}$. The authors prove $e^{n/2d}N\le m(d)\le 2^{(1+o(1))\log d\cdot n/(2d)}N$, $m'(d)=m(d)\,2^{\Theta(n/\sqrt d)}$ (so $m'(d)/m(d)$ is subexponential in $n$), $c^n m'(d)\le f_{\le2}(d)$ for some constant $c>1$ (so $f_{\le2}(d)/m'(d)$ and $f(d)/m(d)$ are at least exponential in $n$), $f(d)\le(d+1)^n\le e^{n+n/d}N$ (so $f(d)/m(d)$ is at most exponential), and for every fixed $r\ge2$, $N^{r/2^{r-1}-o(1)}\le f_{0,r}(d)\le f_{\{0\}\cup\{r,r+1,\dots\}}(d)\le N^{r/2^{r-1}+o(1)}$. Hence the paper answers (i) (subexponential), (ii) (at least exponential) and (iv) (exponential in $n$); part (iii), whether $f(d)/f_{\le2}(d)$ is subexponential, remains open and is asked separately by the authors.
paper_title: Partitioning the hypercube into smaller hypercubes

name: AX_hypercube_subcube_partitions_dimension_2_asymptotics
title: Problem 1.9
statement_text: Determine the asymptotic behaviour of the number $f_{2}(d).$
context_text: $Q_d=\{0,1\}^d$ is the $d$-dimensional hypercube. $f(d)$ is the number of partitions (tilings) of the vertex set of $Q_d$ into classes each spanning a subcube (a set of vertices obtained by fixing some coordinates and letting the others vary), and for $S\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,d\}$, $f_S(d)$ counts those partitions in which every class has dimension in $S$; thus $f_{\le2}(d)$ counts partitions into singletons, edges and 2-dimensional subcubes, $f_2(d)$ partitions into 2-dimensional subcubes only, and $f_{0,r}(d)$ partitions into singletons and $r$-dimensional subcubes. $m(d)=f_1(d)$ and $m'(d)=f_{\le1}(d)$ are the numbers of perfect matchings and of all matchings of $Q_d$. Write $n=2^{d-1}$ (the size of each side of the bipartite graph $Q_d$) and $N=(d/e)^n$, a rough estimate of $m(d)$. The authors prove that for every fixed $r\ge2$, $N^{r/2^{r-1}-o(1)}\le f_{0,r}(d)\le N^{r/2^{r-1}+o(1)}$, which for $r=2$ gives $f_{0,2}(d)=N^{1+o(1)}$; since $f_2(d)\le f_{0,2}(d)$, the upper bound $f_2(d)\le N^{1+o(1)}$ holds. It is natural to ask what happens when only 2-dimensional subcubes are allowed, and the authors believe that the same bound holds, i.e. $f_2(d)=N^{1+o(1)}$, but the lower bound is not proved.
paper_title: Partitioning the hypercube into smaller hypercubes

name: AX_hypercube_subcube_partitions_dimension_2_bound
title: Informal conjecture on $f_2(d)$
statement_text: The number $f_2(d)$ of partitions of the vertex set of $Q_d$ into 2-dimensional subcubes satisfies the same bound as $f_{0,2}(d)$, namely $N^{1-o(1)}\le f_2(d)\le N^{1+o(1)}$, where $N=(d/e)^{2^{d-1}}$.
context_text: $Q_d=\{0,1\}^d$ is the $d$-dimensional hypercube. $f(d)$ is the number of partitions (tilings) of the vertex set of $Q_d$ into classes each spanning a subcube (a set of vertices obtained by fixing some coordinates and letting the others vary), and for $S\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,d\}$, $f_S(d)$ counts those partitions in which every class has dimension in $S$; thus $f_{\le2}(d)$ counts partitions into singletons, edges and 2-dimensional subcubes, $f_2(d)$ partitions into 2-dimensional subcubes only, and $f_{0,r}(d)$ partitions into singletons and $r$-dimensional subcubes. $m(d)=f_1(d)$ and $m'(d)=f_{\le1}(d)$ are the numbers of perfect matchings and of all matchings of $Q_d$. Write $n=2^{d-1}$ (the size of each side of the bipartite graph $Q_d$) and $N=(d/e)^n$, a rough estimate of $m(d)$. name: AX_hypercube_subcube_partitions_ratio_subexponential
title: Problem 1.10
statement_text:
Is it true that
$f(d)/f_{\leq 2}(d)$ is subexponential in $n$?
context_text: $Q_d=\{0,1\}^d$ is the $d$-dimensional hypercube. $f(d)$ is the number of partitions (tilings) of the vertex set of $Q_d$ into classes each spanning a subcube (a set of vertices obtained by fixing some coordinates and letting the others vary), and for $S\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,d\}$, $f_S(d)$ counts those partitions in which every class has dimension in $S$; thus $f_{\le2}(d)$ counts partitions into singletons, edges and 2-dimensional subcubes, $f_2(d)$ partitions into 2-dimensional subcubes only, and $f_{0,r}(d)$ partitions into singletons and $r$-dimensional subcubes. $m(d)=f_1(d)$ and $m'(d)=f_{\le1}(d)$ are the numbers of perfect matchings and of all matchings of $Q_d$. Write $n=2^{d-1}$ (the size of each side of the bipartite graph $Q_d$) and $N=(d/e)^n$, a rough estimate of $m(d)$. The hierarchy $m(d)\le m'(d)\le f_{\le2}(d)\le f(d)$ holds by definition, and the authors ask which of the ratios is exponential in $n$. The authors prove $e^{n/2d}N\le m(d)\le 2^{(1+o(1))\log d\cdot n/(2d)}N$, $m'(d)=m(d)\,2^{\Theta(n/\sqrt d)}$ (so $m'(d)/m(d)$ is subexponential in $n$), $c^n m'(d)\le f_{\le2}(d)$ for some constant $c>1$ (so $f_{\le2}(d)/m'(d)$ and $f(d)/m(d)$ are at least exponential in $n$), $f(d)\le(d+1)^n\le e^{n+n/d}N$ (so $f(d)/m(d)$ is at most exponential), and for every fixed $r\ge2$, $N^{r/2^{r-1}-o(1)}\le f_{0,r}(d)\le f_{\{0\}\cup\{r,r+1,\dots\}}(d)\le N^{r/2^{r-1}+o(1)}$. So the remaining case is the ratio $f(d)/f_{\le2}(d)$. Evidence that small subcubes matter: the authors show $f_{\{0,1,3,4,\dots\}}(d)\le\exp(20n/d^{1/4})\,m(d)$, so excluding 2-dimensional subcubes reduces the count to essentially the number of perfect matchings.

name: AX_unavoidability_bounded_average_degree_polynomial
title: Problem 6
statement_text: Let $\alpha$ be a positive real number. Does there exist a polynomial $P_{\alpha}$ such that $\operatorname{unvd}(D)\leqslant P_{\alpha}(|V(D)|)$ for every digraph with maximum average degree at most $\alpha$?
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. Bucić, Letzter and Sudakov asked whether acyclic digraphs of bounded maximum average degree are linearly unavoidable. Draganić et al. proved this for $k$-th powers of directed paths, but Fox, He and Wigderson showed it fails in general: for every $\Delta\ge2$ and large $n$ there is an acyclic digraph with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\ge n^{\Omega(\Delta^{2/3}/\log^{5/3}\Delta)}$. This problem asks whether polynomial unavoidability still holds (the digraphs are implicitly acyclic). The companion question is which families of bounded maximum average degree are linearly unavoidable.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments

name: AX_unavoidability_linear_blowup_closure
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: If $\cal F$ is linearly unavoidable and has bounded maximum average degree, then ${\cal F}[k]$ is also linearly unavoidable.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. The $k$-blow-up $D[k]$ of $D$ replaces each vertex by an independent set of $k$ vertices, with arcs from the copies of $u$ to the copies of $v$ for every arc $uv$ of $D$ (the paper's formal definition additionally restricts these arcs to pairs of copies with distinct indices), and $\mathcal{F}[k]=\{D[k]:D\in\mathcal{F}\}$. The bounded maximum average degree condition is necessary: the disjoint union of a transitive tournament of order $\lfloor\log n\rfloor+1$ and isolated vertices is $n$-unavoidable, but its $k$-blow-up has maximum average degree $k\lfloor\log n\rfloor$, hence unavoidability at least about $n^{k/2}/2$. The conjecture holds for directed paths (by the result of Draganić et al. on powers of directed paths), and the authors prove it for oriented trees and forests: the $k$-blow-up of an oriented tree of order $n$ is $(2^{10+18k}\cdot kn)$-unavoidable.

name: AX_unavoidability_tree_blowup_optimal_constant
title: Problem 8
statement_text: What is the infimum of all the constants $C$ such that for every large enough integer $n$, the $k$-blow-up of every oriented tree of order $n$ is $(C^{k}\cdot kn)$-unavoidable?
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). name: AX_unavoidability_vertex_deletion_ratio_bounded
title: Conjecture 9
statement_text: There exists a constant $C$ such that $\operatorname{unvd}(D)\leqslant C\cdot\operatorname{unvd}(D-v)$ for every acyclic digraph $D$ and for every vertex $v$ of $D$.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. Sumner's conjecture states that every oriented tree of order $n>1$ is $(2n-2)$-unavoidable; it is known for large $n$, and Häggkvist and Thomason proved that oriented trees are linearly unavoidable. For a source or sink $x$ of an acyclic digraph $D$, a simple induction argument gives $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le2\,\mathrm{unvd}(D-x)$, which yields the Erdős–Moser bound $2^{n-1}$. The conjecture asserts that deleting an arbitrary vertex can only decrease the unavoidability by a constant factor. Together with Sumner's conjecture it would imply that every $k$-extension of an oriented tree of order $n$ is $C^k(2n-2)$-unavoidable (an acyclic digraph $D$ is a $k$-extension of $A$ if $D-S=A$ for some set $S$ of $k$ vertices), and more generally that $k$-extensions of a linearly unavoidable family are linearly unavoidable.

name: AX_unavoidability_tree_extensions_exponential
title: Conjecture 10
statement_text: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every integer $k$, every $k$-extension of an oriented tree of order $n$ is $C^{k}(2n-2)$-unavoidable.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). The conjecture would follow from Sumner's conjecture together with the conjecture that there is a constant $C$ such that $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C\,\mathrm{unvd}(D-v)$ for every acyclic digraph $D$ and every vertex $v$ (true with $C=2$ when $v$ is a source or sink). The authors prove a weaker result: every $k$-extension of a sufficiently large oriented tree (or forest) $F$ is $(2\cdot3^{\binom{2k+2}{2}}\cdot|V(F)|)$-unavoidable.

name: AX_unavoidability_linear_extension_closure
title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: If $\cal F$ is linearly unavoidable, then the family of $k$-extensions of digraphs in $\cal F$ is also linearly unavoidable.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). name: AX_unavoidability_forest_extensions_rate
title: Problem 12
statement_text: What is the minimum function $f$ such that every $k$-extension of every forest of order $n$ is $(2^{f(k)}\cdot n)$-unavoidable?
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. An acyclic digraph $D$ is a $k$-extension of $A$ if $D-S=A$ for some set $S$ of $k$ vertices (the added vertices). Forests here are oriented forests (orientations of forests, including arcless digraphs). The authors prove that every $k$-extension of a sufficiently large oriented forest $F$ is $(2\cdot3^{\binom{2k+2}{2}}|V(F)|)$-unavoidable, so $f(k)$ is at most quadratic in $k$, and they show that some $k$-extensions of the arcless digraph on $n$ vertices have unavoidability $2^kn-o(n)$, so $f$ is at least linear. name: AX_hypercube_statistic_lambda_d_1_limit
title: Conjecture on $\lambda(d,1)$
statement_text: $\lambda(d,1)=(1+o(1))/e$ where the $o(1)$-term tends to $0$ as $d$ tends to infinity.
context_text: Let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube, with vertices the binary vectors of length $n$; a subcube $Q_d$ of $Q_n$ is the set of vertices obtained by fixing $n-d$ coordinates and letting the other $d$ vary. For $A\subseteq V(Q_n)$ and $d\le n$, $\lambda(n,d,s,A)$ is the fraction of $d$-dimensional subcubes of $Q_n$ that contain exactly $s$ vertices of $A$, $\lambda(n,d,s)$ is its maximum over all $A$, and $\lambda(d,s)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda(n,d,s)$ (the limit exists since $\lambda(n,d,s)$ is non-increasing in $n$). The problem is motivated by Goldwasser and Hansen's work on hypercubes and by edge-statistics (inducibility-type) results for graphs. Clearly $\lambda(d,s)=\lambda(d,2^d-s)$ and $\lambda(d,0)=1$, and $\lambda(d,2^{d-1})=1$ (take the vertices of even weight). For $s=1$ the authors (following Goldwasser and Hansen) show $\lambda(d,1)\ge(1-2^{-d})^{2^d-1}$, which tends to $1/e\approx0.37$, and also $\lambda(d,1)\ge2/(d+1)$ (vertices of Hamming weight divisible by $d+1$). For upper bounds they can only prove a weaker bound coming from the tight value $\lambda(d+2,d,1)=3/4$ for $d\ge6$; with more care $\lambda(d,1)<3/4$ for every fixed $d$, still far from $1/e$. Known estimates (with flag-algebra upper bounds of Baber): $2/3\le\lambda(2,1)\le0.68572$, $0.5\le\lambda(3,1)\le0.61005$, $0.4\le\lambda(4,1)\le0.60254$. The authors suspect that the lower bound is asymptotically sharp.

name: AX_hypercube_statistic_lambda_tight_bounds
title: Open problem on tight bounds for $\lambda(d,s)$
statement_text: Obtain tight bounds for $\lambda(d,s)$ for essentially all admissible values of $d$ and $s$.
context_text: Let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube, with vertices the binary vectors of length $n$; a subcube $Q_d$ of $Q_n$ is the set of vertices obtained by fixing $n-d$ coordinates and letting the other $d$ vary. For $A\subseteq V(Q_n)$ and $d\le n$, $\lambda(n,d,s,A)$ is the fraction of $d$-dimensional subcubes of $Q_n$ that contain exactly $s$ vertices of $A$, $\lambda(n,d,s)$ is its maximum over all $A$, and $\lambda(d,s)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda(n,d,s)$ (the limit exists since $\lambda(n,d,s)$ is non-increasing in $n$). The problem is motivated by Goldwasser and Hansen's work on hypercubes and by edge-statistics (inducibility-type) results for graphs. Clearly $\lambda(d,s)=\lambda(d,2^d-s)$ and $\lambda(d,0)=1$, and $\lambda(d,2^{d-1})=1$ (take the vertices of even weight). The authors prove that $\lambda(d,s)=1$ if and only if $s\in\{0,2^{d-1},2^d\}$, and for $1<s<2^{d-1}$ that $\lambda(d,s)\le\lambda(d+2,d,s)=\pi(d+2,\omega(s))\le(1-\frac{1}{4s-1})(1+\frac{1}{d+1})$, where $\pi(m,k)$ is the edge density of the Turán graph $T(m,k)$ and $\omega(s)$ is the clique number of the generalized Johnson graph $J(4s,2s,s)$ ($2s$-subsets of a $4s$-set, adjacent when they meet in exactly $s$ elements); in particular $\lambda(d,s)\le1-\Omega(1/s)$ for $0<s<d/8$. Probabilistic lower bounds: $\lambda(d,s)\ge c_d$ for all admissible $d,s$, where $c_d\approx0.289$ is the probability that a random $d\times d$ binary matrix with independent nonzero rows is nonsingular over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and $\lambda(d,s)\ge1-\frac1s$ when $s$ is a power of 2; so the bounds are close when $s$ is divisible by a large power of 2. They also ask for the infimum of $\lambda(d,s)$ over all admissible $d,s$, and whether it is $c_d(1+o(1))$ for large $d$, and suspect $\lambda(d,1)=(1+o(1))/e$.

name: AX_odd_minor_free_clustered_chromatic_treedepth
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every graph $H$, $\chi_{\star}(\mathcal{G}_H^{\mathrm{odd}})\leq 2\,\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)-2$ and $\chi_{\Delta}(\mathcal{G}_H^{\mathrm{odd}})=\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)-1$.
context_text: A colouring has clustering $k$ if each monochromatic component has at most $k$ vertices. The clustered chromatic number $\chi_\star(\mathcal{G})$ of a class $\mathcal{G}$ is the minimum $c$ such that for some $k$ every graph of $\mathcal{G}$ is $c$-colourable with clustering $k$; the defective chromatic number $\chi_\Delta(\mathcal{G})$ is the minimum $c$ such that for some $d$ every graph of $\mathcal{G}$ is $c$-colourable with monochromatic components of maximum degree at most $d$. An $H$-model in $G$ is a family $(T_x:x\in V(H))$ of vertex-disjoint subtrees with an edge between $T_x$ and $T_y$ for each $xy\in E(H)$; it is odd if some $2$-colouring of the union of the trees and these connecting edges properly colours each $T_x$ and has a monochromatic edge between $T_x$ and $T_y$ for each $xy\in E(H)$. $H$ is an odd-minor of $G$ if $G$ has an odd $H$-model; $\mathcal{G}_H^{\mathrm{odd}}$ is the class of graphs with no $H$ odd-minor and $\mathcal{G}_H$ the class of $H$-minor-free graphs. The connected tree-depth $\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)$ is the minimum vertex-height (number of vertices on a longest root-to-leaf path) of a rooted tree $T$ on $V(H)$ such that $H$ is a subgraph of the closure of $T$ (pairs in ancestor–descendant relation); it equals the tree-depth unless $H$ has two components of maximum tree-depth, in which case it is one more. For minors, $\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)-1=\chi_\Delta(\mathcal{G}_H)\le\chi_\star(\mathcal{G}_H)\le3\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)-3$ (Ossona de Mendez, Oum and Wood; Norin, Scott, Seymour and Wood; Liu), and Norin et al. conjectured $\chi_\star(\mathcal{G}_H)\le2\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)-2$, which is tight for some $H$. The authors prove the odd-minor analogue $\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)-1\le\chi_\Delta(\mathcal{G}_H^{\mathrm{odd}})\le\chi_\star(\mathcal{G}_H^{\mathrm{odd}})\le3\cdot2^{\overline{\mathrm{td}}(H)}-4$; also $\chi_\star(\mathcal{G}_H^{\mathrm{odd}})\le3\chi_\Delta(\mathcal{G}_H^{\mathrm{odd}})$ by a result of Liu and Wood.

name: AX_positive_square_energy_lower_bound_4n_5
title: Informal Conjecture (improved linear bound)
statement_text: We believe the bound $s(G)\ge\frac{3n}{4}$ for every connected graph $G$ of order $n\ge4$ can be improved to $\frac{4n}{5}$ using more intricate partitioning of the graph $G$ and applying the superadditivity of $s^+$ and $s^-$ over vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs.
context_text: Graphs are simple. Let $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of $G$. The positive and negative square energies are $s^+(G)=\sum_{\lambda_i>0}\lambda_i^2$ and $s^-(G)=\sum_{\lambda_i<0}\lambda_i^2$, and the square energy is $s(G)=\min\{s^+(G),s^-(G)\}$. Since $s(G)=|E(G)|$ for bipartite graphs, Elphick, Farber, Goldberg and Wocjan conjectured that every connected graph of order $n$ satisfies $s(G)\ge n-1$; it is known for several classes including regular graphs, and the best previous general bound was $\sqrt n$. The authors prove that if $H_1,\dots,H_k$ are vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs of $G$ then $s^+(G)\ge\sum_i s^+(H_i)$ and $s^-(G)\ge\sum_i s^-(H_i)$, and deduce, by partitioning a connected graph into connected pieces, the first linear bound $s(G)\ge\frac{3n}{4}$ for connected $G$ of order $n\ge4$. They believe $\frac{4n}{5}$ is reachable with a more intricate partition, but did not do it because they believe more ideas are needed to reach $n-1$.

name: AX_split_digraph_strong_2_kernel_half
title: Open question on strong 2-kernels in split digraphs
statement_text: Does every split digraph $G$ with no sources admit a strong 2-kernel of size at most $|G|/2$?
context_text: Digraphs are finite with no loops or parallel edges; an oriented graph is a digraph with no directed cycle of length two. A set $X$ $k$-covers $Y$ if for every $y\in Y$ there are $x\in X$ and a directed path of length at most $k$ from $x$ to $y$; a $k$-kernel is a stable set that $k$-covers $V(G)$ (a 2-kernel is also called a quasi-kernel); a source is a vertex of in-degree zero, and $|G|$ is the number of vertices. A split digraph is an oriented graph $G$ whose vertex set has a partition $(S,T)$ (a split) with $S$ stable and $G[T]$ a tournament. Given such a split, a 2-kernel $K$ is strong if for every $v\in T$, either some vertex of $K$ 1-covers $v$ (is $v$ or an in-neighbour of $v$), or some vertex of $K\cap T$ 2-covers $v$. The Erdős–Székely small quasi-kernel conjecture (1976) asserts that every digraph with no source has a 2-kernel of size at most $|G|/2$. Langlois, Meunier, Rizzi, Vialette and Zhou proved the bound $2|G|/3$ for split digraphs with no sources, and the authors prove the conjecture for split digraphs: every split digraph with no sources has a 2-kernel of size at most $|G|/2$ (indeed it suffices that $S\ne\emptyset$ and no vertex of $S$ is a source). Strong 2-kernels appear in their proof; they remark in passing that they do not know whether this result remains true if one asks for a strong 2-kernel of size at most $|G|/2$.

name: AX_genus_approximation_spherical_density_regime
title: Open Problem (Spherical Density Regime)
statement_text: Determine whether efficient constant-factor approximation algorithms exist for the genus of graphs with average degree at most 6 (spherical density regime), or prove that approximating the genus in this regime is hard.
context_text: The genus $g(G)$ of a graph is the minimum genus of an orientable surface in which $G$ embeds; deciding whether $g(G)\le k$ is NP-complete (Thomassen), even for cubic graphs, and a constant-factor approximation means a polynomial-time algorithm producing an embedding (or an integer) within a constant factor of $g(G)$. Graphs whose genus is $\Theta(n)$, which includes graphs of average degree at least $d$ for some constant $d>6$, admit a constant-factor approximation by Euler's formula; the best known general algorithm (Kawarabayashi and Sidiropoulos) approximates the Euler genus within a factor $O(\hat g^{255}\log^{189}n)$, giving an $O(n^{1-\alpha})$ factor for the genus. Following an approach of Mohar, the authors split genus approximation into four regimes: spherical density (average degree at most 6), bounded average degree with hyperbolic density (average degree between constants $6<\delta<\Delta$, where a constant factor is easy but improving it may be hard), intermediate density (unbounded average degree and $o(n^2)$ edges), and dense graphs (at least $\alpha n^2$ edges), for which the paper gives an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme. In the spherical density regime, described as probably the most interesting, there is no evidence that efficient constant-factor approximation algorithms exist, and resolving it is called the major open problem; Mohar (2018) conjectured that approximating the genus of cubic graphs is APX-hard, i.e. that approximation in this range is hard.
notes: Stated in prose: 'resolving this is the major open problem'; no formal labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme for the genus of dense graphs

name: AX_chromatic_cochromatic_gap_three_small_clique
title: Problem 1.5
statement_text: Let $k\geq 5$. Is there a graph $G_{k}$ with $\omega(G_{k})<5$, $\zeta(G_{k})=k$ and $\chi(G_{k})=\zeta(G_{k})+3$?
context_text: The cochromatic number $\zeta(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the minimum size of a partition of $V(G)$ into homogeneous sets, i.e. sets that are independent or cliques; clearly $\zeta(G)\le\chi(G)$, and $\omega(G)$ is the clique number. Erdős, Gimbel and Straight (1988) conjectured that every graph $G$ with $\omega(G)<5$ and $\zeta(G)>3$ satisfies $\chi(G)\le\zeta(G)+2$ (Erdős problem no. 762), their own examples of $K_5$-free graphs with $\chi(G)>\zeta(G)+2$ all having $\zeta(G)\le3$; Erdős and Gimbel (1993) also asked whether there are only finitely many graphs with $\omega(G)<5$ and $\chi(G)>\zeta(G)+2$. The authors disprove the conjecture and answer the finiteness question negatively by proving that there are infinitely many graphs $G$ with $\omega(G)<5$, $\zeta(G)=4$ and $\chi(G)=7$. The question left open is whether the conclusion of the Erdős–Gimbel–Straight conjecture remains false when $\zeta(G)$ is required to be large, i.e. whether a gap $\chi-\zeta=3$ is possible with $\omega<5$ for every value $k\ge5$ of the cochromatic number.
paper_title: On the difference between the chromatic and cochromatic number

name: AX_clustered_coloring_strong_product_path_tight
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: For any fixed integer $c \geq 2$, there exists an integer $t$ such that for infinitely many graphs $H$ with treewidth $t$ and paths $P$, every $c$-colouring of $H \boxtimes P$ has clustering $\Omega(|V(H \boxtimes P)|^{c/(c^2-c+1)})$.
context_text: A $c$-colouring assigns one of at most $c$ colours to each vertex, adjacent vertices being allowed the same colour. It has clustering $k$ if the largest monochromatic component (component of the subgraph induced by one colour class) has $k$ vertices. $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is the strong product: vertex set $V(H_1)\times V(H_2)$, distinct $(u,v),(u',v')$ adjacent if $u=u'$ or $uu'\in E(H_1)$, and $v=v'$ or $vv'\in E(H_2)$. Products of a bounded-treewidth graph with a path are motivated by product structure theorems (e.g. planar graphs are subgraphs of such products), and graphs of treewidth $t$ are properly $(t+1)$-colourable, so only $c<(t+1)^2$ is interesting. With $n=|V(H_1\boxtimes H_2)|$, the authors prove the following. With 2 colours, clustering $\Theta(n^{2/3})$ is optimal, even when one factor is a path. With 3 colours and $H_2$ of bounded degree, $\Theta(n^{3/7})$ is optimal, with a lower-bound construction where $H_2$ is a path. For every $c$, if $H_1,H_2$ have treewidth at most $t$ and $H_2$ has maximum degree at most $\Delta$, then $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is $c$-colourable with clustering $O(n^{c/(c^2-c+1)})$. Conversely, for $c\ge3$ there are graphs $H$ of treewidth $c$ and paths $P$ for which every $c$-colouring of $H\boxtimes P$ has clustering $\Omega(n^{1/(c-2/3)})$. The conjecture states that the upper bound is tight with the bounded-degree factor a path. It holds for $c=2$ ($c/(c^2-c+1)=2/3$) and $c=3$ ($3/7$) by the results above, so it is open for $c\ge4$.

paper_title: Clustered Colouring of Graph Products

name: AX_clustered_coloring_strong_product_exponent_tight
title: Conjecture 8
statement_text: There exists a positive integer $t$ such that for infinitely many graphs $H_1, H_2$ with treewidth $t$, every $3$-colouring of $H_1 \boxtimes H_2$ has clustering $\Omega(|V(H_1 \boxtimes H_2)|^{4/7})$.
context_text: A $c$-colouring assigns one of at most $c$ colours to each vertex, adjacent vertices being allowed the same colour. It has clustering $k$ if the largest monochromatic component (component of the subgraph induced by one colour class) has $k$ vertices. $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is the strong product: vertex set $V(H_1)\times V(H_2)$, distinct $(u,v),(u',v')$ adjacent if $u=u'$ or $uu'\in E(H_1)$, and $v=v'$ or $vv'\in E(H_2)$. Products of a bounded-treewidth graph with a path are motivated by product structure theorems (e.g. planar graphs are subgraphs of such products), and graphs of treewidth $t$ are properly $(t+1)$-colourable, so only $c<(t+1)^2$ is interesting. With $n=|V(H_1\boxtimes H_2)|$, the authors prove the following. With 2 colours, clustering $\Theta(n^{2/3})$ is optimal, even when one factor is a path. With 3 colours: if one factor has bounded degree, $\Theta(n^{3/7})$ is optimal. Without degree restriction, they prove that for any $H_1,H_2$ of treewidth at most $t$, $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is 3-colourable with clustering $O(n^{4/7})$. They also give infinitely many pairs $H_1,H_2$ of treewidth 2 for which every 3-colouring has clustering $\Omega(n^{1/2})$.
