name: AX_convex_drawings_vs_pseudocircular_drawings
title: Open problem: convex drawings vs. pseudocircular drawings
statement_text: The relation between convex drawings and pseudocircular drawings remains open.
context_text: All drawings are simple topological drawings of the complete graph $K_n$ in the plane or on the sphere: vertices are distinct points, edges are simple curves joining their endpoints and containing no other vertex, every two edges share at most one point (a common endpoint or a proper crossing), and no three edges cross at a point. The three edges among three vertices (a triangle) do not cross, so they split the plane into two sides (closures of the two components); a side is convex if every edge with both endpoints in it is drawn entirely inside it. A drawing is convex if every triangle has a convex side, and hereditary-convex if one can choose a convex side for each triangle so that whenever a triangle lies inside the chosen convex side of another triangle, its own chosen side does too (convex drawings form the second level of the convexity hierarchy of Arroyo, McQuillan, Richter and Salazar, between topological and hereditary-convex drawings). A drawing is pseudocircular if its edges can be extended to pseudocircles (simple closed curves) such that any two pseudocircles either cross exactly twice or are disjoint; it is pseudospherical if moreover every two pseudocircles intersect and, for any two edges $e\neq f$, the pseudocircle extending $e$ crosses $f$ at most once. Arroyo, Richter and Sunohara gave a topological drawing that is not pseudocircular and proved that the hereditary-convex drawings are exactly the pseudospherical drawings. The analogous relation for (non-hereditary) convex drawings, e.g. whether they are characterized by some class of pseudocircular drawings, has not been established.

name: AX_toroidal_5_choosability_critical_6_critical
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: A graph drawn on the torus is critical for 5-choosability if and only if it is $6$-critical.
context_text: A list assignment $L$ gives each vertex a set of colours; it is a $k$-list assignment if all lists have size at least $k$, and an $L$-colouring is a proper colouring with each vertex coloured from its list. $G$ is $k$-choosable if it has an $L$-colouring for every $k$-list assignment $L$. $G$ is critical for $k$-choosability if it is not $k$-choosable but every proper subgraph is; it is critical for $k$-list colouring if for some $k$-list assignment $L$ it has no $L$-colouring but every proper subgraph has one; it is $k$-critical if it is a minimal graph of chromatic number at least $k$. Thomassen proved that exactly four 6-critical graphs embed on the torus, so these characterise 5-colourability of toroidal graphs; Postle proved that 5-choosability on any fixed surface is characterised by finitely many minimal obstructions, but explicit lists are known only for the sphere (none) and the projective plane ($K_6$ only), and it is unknown whether the torus has any obstruction to 5-choosability beyond the four 6-critical graphs. A non-contractible triangle is a triangle forming a non-contractible curve; a cyclic system of non-contractible triangles is a cyclic sequence of distinct, pairwise homotopic (laminar) non-contractible triangles $C_1,\dots,C_m$ such that, for each $i$ (with $C_{m+1}=C_1$), some cylindrical region of the torus between $C_i$ and $C_{i+1}$ contains no other triangle of the system; its spacing is the maximum, over these $m$ regions (cut open into a cylinder), of the distance between their two boundary triangles. The authors prove by computer-assisted enumeration that a toroidal graph containing a cyclic system of non-contractible triangles of spacing at most four is critical for 5-choosability iff it is one of Thomassen's four 6-critical graphs ($K_7$ being the only such graph critical for 5-list colouring but not for 5-choosability). The conjecture says that the cyclic-system assumption can be dropped. It is equivalent to the statement that a toroidal graph is 5-choosable if and only if it is 5-colourable.
paper_title: Towards Characterization of 5-List-Colorability of Toroidal Graphs

name: AX_toroidal_5_choosability_equals_5_colorable
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: A toroidal graph is $5$-choosable if and only if it is $5$-colorable.
context_text: A list assignment $L$ gives each vertex a set of colours; it is a $k$-list assignment if all lists have size at least $k$, and an $L$-colouring is a proper colouring with each vertex coloured from its list. $G$ is $k$-choosable if it has an $L$-colouring for every $k$-list assignment $L$. $G$ is critical for $k$-choosability if it is not $k$-choosable but every proper subgraph is; it is critical for $k$-list colouring if for some $k$-list assignment $L$ it has no $L$-colouring but every proper subgraph has one; it is $k$-critical if it is a minimal graph of chromatic number at least $k$. A non-contractible triangle is a triangle forming a non-contractible curve; a cyclic system of non-contractible triangles is a cyclic sequence of distinct, pairwise homotopic (laminar) non-contractible triangles $C_1,\dots,C_m$ such that, for each $i$ (with $C_{m+1}=C_1$), some cylindrical region of the torus between $C_i$ and $C_{i+1}$ contains no other triangle of the system; its spacing is the maximum, over these $m$ regions (cut open into a cylinder), of the distance between their two boundary triangles. The authors prove by computer-assisted enumeration that a toroidal graph containing a cyclic system of non-contractible triangles of spacing at most four is critical for 5-choosability iff it is one of Thomassen's four 6-critical graphs ($K_7$ being the only such graph critical for 5-list colouring but not for 5-choosability). The conjecture is equivalent to the statement that a graph drawn on the torus is critical for 5-choosability if and only if it is 6-critical, i.e. that the only minimal obstructions to 5-choosability on the torus are Thomassen's four 6-critical graphs; it would be a choosability analogue of Thomassen's characterisation of 5-colourability on the torus.
paper_title: Towards Characterization of 5-List-Colorability of Toroidal Graphs

name: AX_toroidal_5_choosability_edge_width_4
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: Every graph drawn on the torus with edge-width at least four is 5-choosable.
context_text: A list assignment $L$ gives each vertex a set of colours; it is a $k$-list assignment if all lists have size at least $k$, and an $L$-colouring is a proper colouring with each vertex coloured from its list. $G$ is $k$-choosable if it has an $L$-colouring for every $k$-list assignment $L$. $G$ is critical for $k$-choosability if it is not $k$-choosable but every proper subgraph is; it is critical for $k$-list colouring if for some $k$-list assignment $L$ it has no $L$-colouring but every proper subgraph has one; it is $k$-critical if it is a minimal graph of chromatic number at least $k$. The edge-width of a graph drawn on a surface is the length of its shortest non-contractible cycle; edge-width at least four means in particular no non-contractible triangles. The authors conjecture that a toroidal graph is 5-choosable iff it is 5-colourable, and prove it for graphs containing a cyclic system of non-contractible triangles of spacing at most four; graphs of edge-width at least four are the complementary case, and this conjecture would be an important step. Postle proved that the edge-width of a graph critical for 5-list colouring is at most logarithmic in its genus, so the conjecture holds with four replaced by a sufficiently large constant.
paper_title: Towards Characterization of 5-List-Colorability of Toroidal Graphs

name: AX_toroidal_5_choosability_prism_canvas_spacing
title: Conjecture 8
statement_text: There is no critical prism-canvas of spacing at least five.
context_text: A list assignment $L$ gives each vertex a set of colours, and an $L$-colouring is a proper colouring from the lists. For a subgraph $T$ of $G$, $G$ is $T$-critical with respect to $L$ if $G\neq T$ and for every proper subgraph $G'\supseteq T$ some $L$-colouring of $T$ extends to $G'$ but not to $G$. A prism-canvas $(F,T_1,T_2,L)$ consists of a connected graph $F$ drawn on the sphere with two distinct faces bounded by triangles $T_1,T_2$ (equivalently, drawn in a cylinder with $T_1,T_2$ as boundaries) and a list assignment with $|L(v)|\ge5$ for every $v\notin V(T_1\cup T_2)$; it is critical if $F$ is $(T_1\cup T_2)$-critical with respect to $L$, and its spacing is the distance between $T_1$ and $T_2$ in $F$. Postle proved that there is an integer $D$ such that every critical prism-canvas has spacing less than $D$ (i.e. for spacing at least $D$ every $L$-colouring of $T_1\cup T_2$ extends to $F$); his $D$ is not explicit, roughly 100. Every critical prism-canvas is obtained from its skeleton ($T_1\cup T_2$ plus a shortest path between them) by pasting chordless critical cycle-canvases (5-list-assigned disk drawings that are critical with respect to their boundary cycle) of circumference at most $2d+6$ into its faces. Using an enumeration of chordless critical cycle-canvases of circumference at most 14, the authors obtained 510, 2719, 300 and 5 candidates for critical prism-canvases of spacing 1, 2, 3 and 4; the rapid decrease suggests $D=5$, which is the conjecture. Such canvases are the building blocks of toroidal graphs critical for 5-list colouring.
paper_title: Towards Characterization of 5-List-Colorability of Toroidal Graphs

name: AX_even_hole_free_independent_set_polynomial
title: Open Problem: Polynomial-time MWIS on even-hole-free graphs
statement_text: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm for the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem on even-hole-free graphs?
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four; a graph is even-hole-free if it has no hole of even length. The tree independence number of a tree decomposition is the maximum, over its bags, of the independence number of the subgraph induced by the bag, and the tree independence number of $G$ is the minimum of this over all tree decompositions of $G$. On even-hole-free graphs Maximum Weight Clique is polynomial, whereas for Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) and Coloring the existence of polynomial-time algorithms remains open, in stark contrast with perfect graphs, for which polynomial algorithms (Grötschel, Lovász and Schrijver) have been known since 1981. The authors prove that every $n$-vertex even-hole-free graph has tree independence number $O(\log^{10}n)$, and that such a decomposition can be computed in quasi-polynomial time $2^{O(\log^{20}n)}$. Consequently MWIS (and many other problems, e.g. Feedback Vertex Set and $k$-Coloring for fixed $k$) can be solved in quasi-polynomial time $2^{O(\log^c n)}$ on even-hole-free graphs, so they are not NP-hard unless every problem in NP has a quasi-polynomial algorithm; earlier, a quasi-polynomial-time $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation was known. The authors stress that polynomial algorithms would need significant new ideas: even an $O(\log n)$ bound on the tree independence number would only give quasi-polynomial time.
notes: Stated in prose in the introduction without a labelled theorem environment; the paper provides quasi-polynomial-time progress but leaves polynomial-time open.
paper_title: Tree Independence Number IV. Even-hole-free Graphs

name: AX_even_hole_free_coloring_polynomial
title: Open Problem: Polynomial-time Coloring on even-hole-free graphs
statement_text: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm for the Coloring problem (computing the chromatic number) on even-hole-free graphs?
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four; a graph is even-hole-free if it has no hole of even length. The tree independence number of a tree decomposition is the maximum, over its bags, of the independence number of the subgraph induced by the bag, and the tree independence number of $G$ is the minimum of this over all tree decompositions of $G$. On even-hole-free graphs Maximum Weight Clique is polynomial, whereas for Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) and Coloring the existence of polynomial-time algorithms remains open, in stark contrast with perfect graphs, for which polynomial algorithms (Grötschel, Lovász and Schrijver) have been known since 1981. The authors prove that every $n$-vertex even-hole-free graph has tree independence number $O(\log^{10}n)$, and that such a decomposition can be computed in quasi-polynomial time $2^{O(\log^{20}n)}$. For every fixed $k$, $k$-Coloring is solvable on even-hole-free graphs (since $K_{k+1}$ is not $k$-colorable and $K_t$-free even-hole-free graphs have logarithmic treewidth, this even gives a polynomial algorithm for fixed $k$), but the complexity of Coloring with $k$ part of the input, i.e. computing the chromatic number, is not settled by these results and remains open.

name: AX_alon_tarsi_orientation_half_out_degree
title: Question 6.1
statement_text: Does every graph $G$ have a spanning subgraph with an Alon-Tarsi orientation in which each vertex $v$ has out-degree at least $\frac{1}{2}(\deg_{G}(v)-1)$?
context_text: For an orientation $D$ of a graph $G$, a spanning subgraph of $G$ is Eulerian (with respect to $D$) if every vertex has equal in- and out-degree in it; $EE(D)$ and $EO(D)$ count the Eulerian subgraphs with an even, resp. odd, number of edges, and $D$ is an Alon-Tarsi orientation if $EE(D)\neq EO(D)$. The Alon-Tarsi number $\operatorname{AT}(G)$ is the minimum $k$ such that $G$ has an Alon-Tarsi orientation of maximum out-degree less than $k$; Alon and Tarsi proved that the list chromatic number satisfies $\mathrm{ch}(G)\le\operatorname{AT}(G)$. Given $F:V(G)\to2^{\mathbb{N}}$, an orientation $D$ of $G$ is $F$-avoiding if $\deg^+_D(v)\notin F(v)$ for every vertex $v$. Akbari et al. conjectured that $G$ has an $F$-avoiding orientation whenever $|F(v)|\le\frac12(\deg_G(v)-1)$ for every $v$ (sharp, e.g. for $K_{2k+1}$), and proved that if some spanning subgraph $H$ of $G$ has an Alon-Tarsi orientation $D$ with $|F(v)|\le\deg^+_D(v)$ for every $v$, then $G$ has an $F$-avoiding orientation. A positive answer would therefore prove that conjecture for every graph, in a stronger form (combined with a result of Huang, Wong and Zhu on $\operatorname{AT}(K_n-N)$ for a maximum matching $N$, this approach already proves the conjecture for complete graphs). The authors prove the conjecture with coefficient roughly $\frac13$ instead of $\frac12$ (and $\sqrt2-1$ when the maximum degree is $e^{o(\delta)}$). An affirmative answer would also imply that every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with maximum degree $\Delta$ has a subgraph $H$ with at least $|E(G)|-n/2$ edges satisfying $\operatorname{AT}(H)\le\lfloor\frac12\Delta+\frac32\rfloor$. If the answer is negative, one can still ask the same question with $-1$ replaced by an arbitrary constant $-C$.
paper_title: List-avoiding orientations

name: AX_alon_tarsi_matching_removal_half_delta
title: Question 6.2
statement_text: Does there exist a constant $C$ such that every graph $G$ of maximum degree $\Delta$ has a matching $M$ such that $\operatorname{AT}(G-M)\leq\frac{1}{2}\Delta+C$?
context_text: For an orientation $D$ of a graph $G$, a spanning subgraph of $G$ is Eulerian (with respect to $D$) if every vertex has equal in- and out-degree in it; $EE(D)$ and $EO(D)$ count the Eulerian subgraphs with an even, resp. odd, number of edges, and $D$ is an Alon-Tarsi orientation if $EE(D)\neq EO(D)$. The Alon-Tarsi number $\operatorname{AT}(G)$ is the minimum $k$ such that $G$ has an Alon-Tarsi orientation of maximum out-degree less than $k$; Alon and Tarsi proved that the list chromatic number satisfies $\mathrm{ch}(G)\le\operatorname{AT}(G)$. The question is motivated by the authors' question whether every graph has a spanning subgraph with an Alon-Tarsi orientation in which every vertex $v$ has out-degree at least $\frac12(\deg_G(v)-1)$ (related to $F$-avoiding orientations), a positive answer to which would give a subgraph $H$ with at least $|E(G)|-n/2$ edges and $\operatorname{AT}(H)\le\lfloor\frac12\Delta+\frac32\rfloor$. The requirement that $M$ be a matching is inspired by two results showing that removing a matching can lower a coloring bound: Zhu proved that planar graphs have Alon-Tarsi number at most $5$ (tight), while Grytczuk and Zhu showed that every planar graph has a matching $M$ with $\operatorname{AT}(G-M)\le4$; and although $\chi(G)\le\Delta+1$ is tight for cliques, every graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ has a matching $M$ with $\chi(G-M)\le\lceil\frac{\Delta+1}{2}\rceil$. If the answer is affirmative one may ask for the optimal $C$; it cannot be smaller than $\frac12$, since for odd $n$ and any maximum matching $M$ of $K_n$, $\operatorname{AT}(K_n-M)=\frac{n+1}{2}$.
paper_title: List-avoiding orientations

name: AX_s_color_connected_vertices_asymptotic
title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: For any $1\leq s\leq\frac{\sqrt{r}}{\log r}$ and $n$ large enough we have $f(n,r,s)=\frac{s^{2}(\log r)^{1-o_{r}(1)}}{r}\cdot n$.
context_text: For integers $1\le s\le r$, $f(n,r,s)$ is the maximum number of vertices one can guarantee to connect using edges of at most $s$ colours in any $r$-edge colouring of $K_n$, i.e. the largest $m$ such that every $r$-edge colouring of $K_n$ has a set $S$ of $s$ colours whose edges span a connected subgraph on at least $m$ vertices (for $s=1$ this is the Gerencsér–Gyárfás largest monochromatic component problem, $f(n,r,1)\approx n/(r-1)$). Here $o_r(1)$ is a term tending to $0$ as $r\to\infty$. Combining results of Liu, Morris and Prince with theirs, the authors show that for $n$ large compared to $r$: $f(n,r,s)=\Theta(2^s/r)\cdot n$ for $s\le(1-o_r(1))\log\log r$ (tight up to an absolute constant factor between 4 and 8 depending on divisibility properties of $r$); $f(n,r,s)=\widetilde{\Theta}_r(s^2/r)\cdot n$ for $s\le\sqrt r$ (tight up to a $\log r$ factor); $\Theta(n)$ for $s=\Theta(\sqrt r)$; $(1-e^{-\Theta(s^2/r)})n$ for $s\ge\sqrt{r\log r}$; and $n$ for $s\ge r/2$. The least precise part is the $\log r$ gap for $s\le\sqrt r$; since their lower bound for $s\approx\log\log r$ shows that a factor $(\log r)^{1-o_r(1)}$ is necessary there, they conjecture the precise form stated here throughout $s\le\sqrt r/\log r$.
paper_title: The power of many colours

name: AX_s_color_connected_vertices_transition
title: Question 4.3
statement_text: Given $n$ and $r$, what is the smallest value of $s$ for which $f(n,r,s)=g(n,r,s)$?
context_text: For integers $1\le s\le r$, $f(n,r,s)$ is the maximum number of vertices one can guarantee to connect using edges of at most $s$ colours in any $r$-edge colouring of $K_n$, i.e. the largest $m$ such that every $r$-edge colouring of $K_n$ has a set $S$ of $s$ colours whose edges span a connected subgraph on at least $m$ vertices (for $s=1$ this is the Gerencsér–Gyárfás largest monochromatic component problem, $f(n,r,1)\approx n/(r-1)$). $g(n,r,s)$ is the minimum, over $r$-edge colourings of $K_n$, of the maximum over sets $S$ of $s$ colours of the number of vertices incident to at least one edge with colour in $S$ (for $s=1$ this is equivalent to the classical problem of covering the edges of $K_n$ by $r$ cliques, and $g(n,r,1)=\frac{1+o_r(1)}{\sqrt r}n$). Always $f(n,r,s)\le g(n,r,s)$. For $s=1$ the two functions are very different ($f\approx n/r$, $g\approx n/\sqrt r$), and the authors show they behave differently for $s\ll\sqrt r/\log r$ but similarly for $s\ge\sqrt{r\log r}$ (both are $(1-e^{-\Theta(s^2/r)})n$). Equality $f(n,r,s)=g(n,r,s)$ holds for $s\ge(r-1)/2$, and it already seems non-trivial to decide it for $s=r/2-1$ ($r$ even). For $s\ll\sqrt r$ and $n$ large there is a gap of at least about a factor $\sqrt2$, since $g(n,r,s)\ge\frac{(1+o_r(1))s}{\sqrt r}n$ while $f(n,r,s)\le\frac{(1+o_r(1))s}{\sqrt{2r}}n$.
paper_title: The power of many colours

name: AX_intersecting_hypergraph_cover_number_min_edges
title: Question 4.4
statement_text: Let $r\geq 2s-1\geq 3$ be integers. What is the minimum number of edges in an $r$-vertex $s$-uniform intersecting hypergraph with cover number equal to $s$?
context_text: A hypergraph is intersecting if any two of its edges share a vertex, and its cover number is the minimum size of a vertex set meeting every edge. For $r$ unrestricted this is the question of Erdős and Lovász (from their 1975 paper introducing the Local Lemma) on the minimum number of edges in an $s$-uniform intersecting hypergraph with cover number $s$, solved by Kahn in 1994, who showed the answer is linear in $s$; the new feature here is that the number of vertices is restricted to $r$. The condition $r\ge 2s-1$ is necessary (if $r\le 2s-2$, any $s-1$ vertices form a cover), and for $r=2s-1$ the answer is $\binom{2s-1}{s}$ (only the complete hypergraph works). A double counting argument shows that at least $\binom{r}{s-1}/\binom{r-s}{s-1}\ge e^{s(s-1)/(2(r-s))}$ edges are needed, so the answer grows much faster than linearly when $s\gg\sqrt{r\log r}$. The motivation is the function $g(n,r,s)$, the minimum over $r$-edge colourings of $K_n$ of the maximum number of vertices incident to an edge with colour in some set of $s$ colours; the authors essentially solve a weakening in which the uniformity may be somewhat larger than the cover number bound, and a good answer would give more precise bounds on $g(n,r,s)$.
paper_title: The power of many colours

name: AX_intersecting_hypergraph_subset_edges_minimum
title: Question 4.5
statement_text: What is the minimum number of edges in an $r$-vertex intersecting hypergraph if any subset of $m$ vertices needs to contain at least $t$ edges?
context_text: A hypergraph is intersecting if any two of its edges share a vertex, and its cover number is the minimum size of a vertex set meeting every edge. An edge is contained in a vertex subset if it is a subset of it. $g(n,r,s)$ is the minimum, over $r$-edge colourings of $K_n$, of the maximum over sets $S$ of $s$ colours of the number of vertices incident to at least one edge with colour in $S$ (for $s=1$ this is equivalent to the classical problem of covering the edges of $K_n$ by $r$ cliques, and $g(n,r,1)=\frac{1+o_r(1)}{\sqrt r}n$). Always $f(n,r,s)\le g(n,r,s)$. The authors show that determining $g(n,r,s)$ is equivalent to an extremal problem on intersecting (multi-)hypergraphs on the $r$ colours: from a colouring, each vertex $v$ of $K_n$ gives the edge consisting of the colours at $v$, which is intersecting, and conversely an $r$-vertex intersecting hypergraph $H$ in which every set of $r-s$ vertices contains at least $t$ edges yields $g(n,r,s)\le n-t\lfloor n/|E(H)|\rfloor$; only edges of size at least $s+1$ are useful, and they mostly use $(s+1)$-uniform $H$. Hence, if multi-hypergraphs are allowed, the question (for $m=r-s$) is essentially equivalent to determining $g(n,r,s)$, and most of the authors' results on $g$ come from results on this question.
paper_title: The power of many colours

name: AX_intersecting_hypergraph_uniform_subset_edge_counts
title: Question 4.6
statement_text: For which values of $r,s$ does there exist an $r$-vertex, $(s+1)$-uniform intersecting hypergraph in which all sets of size $r-s$ contain the same positive number of edges?
context_text: A hypergraph is intersecting if any two of its edges share a vertex, and its cover number is the minimum size of a vertex set meeting every edge. $g(n,r,s)$ is the minimum, over $r$-edge colourings of $K_n$, of the maximum over sets $S$ of $s$ colours of the number of vertices incident to at least one edge with colour in $S$ (for $s=1$ this is equivalent to the classical problem of covering the edges of $K_n$ by $r$ cliques, and $g(n,r,1)=\frac{1+o_r(1)}{\sqrt r}n$). Always $f(n,r,s)\le g(n,r,s)$. The authors show that determining $g(n,r,s)$ is equivalent to an extremal problem on intersecting (multi-)hypergraphs on the $r$ colours: from a colouring, each vertex $v$ of $K_n$ gives the edge consisting of the colours at $v$, which is intersecting, and conversely an $r$-vertex intersecting hypergraph $H$ in which every set of $r-s$ vertices contains at least $t$ edges yields $g(n,r,s)\le n-t\lfloor n/|E(H)|\rfloor$; only edges of size at least $s+1$ are useful, and they mostly use $(s+1)$-uniform $H$. If an $(s+1)$-uniform intersecting $H$ has every set of $r-s$ vertices containing the same number of edges, this gives $g(n,r,s)\le\left(1-\binom{r-s-1}{s}/\binom{r}{s}\right)n$, which is tight under some divisibility conditions; the authors use the complete $(s+1)$-uniform hypergraph to obtain their precise result at the end of the range. The question has a design-like flavour, asking for a somewhat pseudorandom intersecting hypergraph; approximate versions give approximate results on $g(n,r,s)$.
paper_title: The power of many colours

name: AX_sparse_host_hereditary_turan_number
title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: Given a hereditary property $\mathcal{P}$ which misses a bipartite graph and a $(c,t)$-sparse graph $\Gamma$, determine $\mathrm{ex}(\Gamma,\mathcal{P})$.
context_text: A graph $\Gamma$ on $n$ vertices is $(c,t)$-sparse if for all vertex subsets $A,B$ (not necessarily disjoint) with $|A|,|B|\ge t$ we have $e(A,B)\le(1-c)|A||B|$, where $e(A,B)$ counts the pairs $(a,b)\in A\times B$ with $ab\in E(\Gamma)$. A hereditary property is a class of graphs closed under induced subgraphs; it is assumed nontrivial (contains all edgeless graphs and misses some graph). For a hereditary property $\mathcal{P}$, $\mathrm{ex}(\Gamma,\mathcal{P})$ is the maximum number of edges of a subgraph $G\subseteq\Gamma$ that belongs to $\mathcal{P}$; for a graph $H$, $\mathcal{P}_H$ is the property of not containing $H$ as an induced subgraph. For $\Gamma=K_n$ and the property of not containing $H$ as a subgraph, this is the usual Turán number. The random graph $G(n,p)$ with fixed $0<p<1$ is with high probability $(c,t)$-sparse for any fixed $c<1-p$ and $t\ge C'\log n$, and a graph is $K_{t,t}$-free if and only if it is $(1/t^2,t)$-sparse, so the problem unifies Turán problems in dense random or pseudorandom hosts and induced Turán problems in $K_{t,t}$-free graphs. Alon, Krivelevich and Samotij asked to show $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P})\le n^{2-\varepsilon}$ when $\mathcal{P}$ misses a bipartite graph. Calling a bipartite graph $H=(A\cup B,E)$ $d$-bounded if some $1\le\ell\le d$ vertices of $A$ are complete to $B$ and all other vertices of $A$ have degree at most $d$, the authors prove that every subgraph of a $(c,t)$-sparse $\Gamma$ with at least $Ct^{1/d}n^{2-1/d}$ edges contains a copy of $H$ that is induced in $\Gamma$, which answers that question; they determine $\mathrm{ex}(\Gamma,\mathcal{P}_H)$ up to a constant factor for trees $H$ and for suitable $K_{s,r}$ when $\Gamma$ is a dense random graph or a Paley graph with a square number of vertices.
paper_title: The largest subgraph without a forbidden induced subgraph

name: AX_sparse_host_hereditary_turan_even_cycles
title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: For every $c>0$ and integer $\ell$ there exists $C>1$, such that if $\Gamma$ is a $(c,t)$-sparse graph then $\mathrm{ex}(\Gamma,\mathcal{P}_{C_{2\ell}})\leq Ct^{1-1/\ell}n^{1+1/\ell}$.
context_text: A graph $\Gamma$ on $n$ vertices is $(c,t)$-sparse if for all vertex subsets $A,B$ (not necessarily disjoint) with $|A|,|B|\ge t$ we have $e(A,B)\le(1-c)|A||B|$, where $e(A,B)$ counts the pairs $(a,b)\in A\times B$ with $ab\in E(\Gamma)$. A hereditary property is a class of graphs closed under induced subgraphs; it is assumed nontrivial (contains all edgeless graphs and misses some graph). For a hereditary property $\mathcal{P}$, $\mathrm{ex}(\Gamma,\mathcal{P})$ is the maximum number of edges of a subgraph $G\subseteq\Gamma$ that belongs to $\mathcal{P}$; for a graph $H$, $\mathcal{P}_H$ is the property of not containing $H$ as an induced subgraph. For $\Gamma=K_n$ and the property of not containing $H$ as a subgraph, this is the usual Turán number. The authors give the general lower bound $\mathrm{ex}(\Gamma,\mathcal{P}_H)\ge\frac12e(\Gamma)\,\mathrm{ex}(\chi(\overline{\Gamma}),\mathcal{F}_H)/\binom{\chi(\overline{\Gamma})}{2}$, where a clique quotient of $H$ is the graph obtained by contracting each part of a partition of $V(H)$ into cliques, and $\mathcal{F}_H$ is the family of bipartite clique quotients of $H$. For $H=C_{2\ell}$, $\mathcal{F}_H$ consists of all cycles of length between $\ell$ and $2\ell$, and graphs on $n$ vertices of girth larger than $2\ell$ have at most $\frac12n^{1+1/\ell}+\frac12n$ edges (Alon, Hoory and Linial), a bound conjectured to be tight up to a constant factor and known to be so for $\ell\in\{2,3,5\}$. This motivates the conjectured upper bound. For comparison, the authors prove $\mathrm{ex}(\Gamma,\mathcal{P}_T)\le Ctn$ for every tree $T$, which is tight.
paper_title: The largest subgraph without a forbidden induced subgraph

name: AX_acyclic_subgraph_chromatic_oriented_function
title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: What is the minimum integer $f(k)$ such that every $f(k)$-chromatic oriented graph has an acyclic $k$-chromatic subgraph?
context_text: An oriented graph is an orientation of a simple graph (no 2-cycles), a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph, its chromatic number is that of the underlying undirected graph, and a subgraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. Burr conjectured that every $(2k-2)$-chromatic oriented graph contains a copy of every oriented tree on $k$ vertices (for tournaments this is Sumner's conjecture, resolved for large $k$ by Kühn, Mycroft and Osthus); Burr proved that chromatic number $(k-1)^2$ suffices, improved to $k^2/2-k/2+1$ by Addario-Berry, Havet, Sales, Reed and Thomassé. They observed that a $k$-chromatic oriented graph with no directed cycle contains every oriented tree of order $k$, and suggested that finding acyclic subgraphs of high chromatic number could yield improved bounds towards Burr's conjecture. Partitioning the edges into forward and backward edges of a vertex ordering gives two acyclic subgraphs, so $\chi(G_1\cup G_2)\le\chi(G_1)\chi(G_2)$ yields $f(k)\le k^2$, refined to $f(k)\le k^2-2k+2$, but substantially improving this seems to require new ideas. The authors show that the tournament version $g(k)$ (the minimum $g$ such that every $g$-vertex tournament has an acyclic $k$-chromatic subgraph) satisfies $k^{4/3-o(1)}\le g(k)\le k^{9/5+o(1)}$; since $f(k)\ge g(k)$, this approach cannot give bounds better than $k^{4/3-o(1)}$ for Burr's conjecture.
paper_title: Acyclic subgraphs of tournaments with high chromatic number

name: AX_acyclic_subgraph_chromatic_tournament_exponent
title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: Every $n$-vertex tournament has an acyclic subgraph with chromatic number at least $n^{3/4-o(1)}$. That is, $g(k)\le k^{4/3+o(1)}$.
context_text: An oriented graph is an orientation of a simple graph (no 2-cycles), a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph, its chromatic number is that of the underlying undirected graph, and a subgraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. $g(k)$ is the minimum integer such that every $g(k)$-vertex tournament has an acyclic subgraph of chromatic number $k$ (a question of Nassar and Yuster, who proved $k^{8/7}/4\le g(k)\le k^2-(2-1/\sqrt2)k+2$ and conjectured $g(k)=o(k^2)$). The authors prove that every $n$-vertex tournament has an acyclic subgraph with chromatic number at least $n^{5/9-o(1)}$, i.e. $g(k)\le k^{9/5+o(1)}$, and construct (via a random orientation defined from a projective plane, following Rödl and Winkler) an $n$-vertex tournament in which every acyclic subgraph has chromatic number $O(n^{3/4}\log n)$, i.e. $g(k)=\Omega((k/\log k)^{4/3})$. They suspect the lower bound is closer to the truth. They also wonder whether the following simpler tournament attains the same bound: for $n=q^2$, on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ orient $ij$ ($i<j$) from $i$ to $j$ unless $q$ divides $i-j$, in which case from $j$ to $i$ (used by Nassar and Yuster for their lower bound).
paper_title: Acyclic subgraphs of tournaments with high chromatic number

name: AX_rainbow_stacking_random_colorings_sharp_threshold
title: Problem 3.1
statement_text: Determine whether or not there exists a function $r_{0}\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that the following holds. For each $n\geq 1$, let $\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m}\colon\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathcal{C}_{r}$ be independent uniformly random $r$-edge-colorings. If $r=r(n)$ satisfies $r(n)<r_{0}(n)$, then with high probability, there does not exist a rainbow stacking of $\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m}$. If $r=r(n)$ satisfies $r(n)>r_{0}(n)$, then with high probability, there exists a rainbow stacking of $\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m}$.
context_text: Let $\mathfrak{S}_n$ be the symmetric group on $[n]$, $K_n$ the complete graph on $[n]$, and $\mathcal{C}_r$ a set of $r$ colours. A rainbow stacking of edge-colourings $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_m:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathcal{C}_r$ is a tuple $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m)\in\mathfrak{S}_n^m$ such that for each edge $e$ the colours $\chi_1(\sigma_1^{-1}(e)),\dots,\chi_m(\sigma_m^{-1}(e))$ are all distinct; informally, the $m$ coloured copies of $K_n$ are stacked on top of each other so that no edge lies above another edge of the same colour. Here $m\ge2$ is fixed, the colourings are independent and uniformly random, and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to $1$ as $n\to\infty$. The authors prove that for any $\omega(n)\to\infty$, there is w.h.p. no rainbow stacking if $r\le\frac{m\binom{n}{2}}{2\log(n!)}-\frac{\omega(n)}{(\log n)^2}$, and w.h.p. there is one if $r\ge\frac{m\binom{n}{2}}{2\log(n!)}+\frac{2m-1}{3}+\frac{m}{2\log n}+\frac{\omega(n)}{(\log n)^2}$. So the transition occurs within an interval of length roughly $(2m-1)/3$ around a critical value of order $n/\log n$, and the problem asks whether it is even sharper, i.e. governed by a single threshold function $r_0$. The authors compare with the $2$-point concentration of the independence number of $G(n,1/2)$, which is less dramatic since that quantity is only $O(\log n)$.
paper_title: Rainbow Stackings of Random Edge-Colorings

name: AX_rainbow_stacking_odd_complete_proper_colorings
title: Question 3.3
statement_text: Is it true that when $n$ is odd, every pair of proper edge-colorings of $K_{n}$ admits a rainbow stacking?
context_text: Let $\mathfrak{S}_n$ be the symmetric group on $[n]$, $K_n$ the complete graph on $[n]$, and $\mathcal{C}_r$ a set of $r$ colours. A rainbow stacking of edge-colourings $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_m:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathcal{C}_r$ is a tuple $(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_m)\in\mathfrak{S}_n^m$ such that for each edge $e$ the colours $\chi_1(\sigma_1^{-1}(e)),\dots,\chi_m(\sigma_m^{-1}(e))$ are all distinct; informally, the $m$ coloured copies of $K_n$ are stacked on top of each other so that no edge lies above another edge of the same colour. The question concerns $m=2$ proper edge-colourings (no two edges sharing a vertex get the same colour), with any number of colours. The authors show that not every pair of proper edge-colourings has a rainbow stacking: if $n=2^k-2$ with $k\ge2$, removing two pairs $\{u_1,v_1\}$, $\{u_2,v_2\}$ with $u_1+v_1=u_2+v_2$ from $\mathbb{F}_2^k$ and colouring each edge $\{x,y\}$ by $x+y$ gives two proper colourings of $K_n$ with no rainbow stacking (a construction from transversals in Latin squares). This Cayley sum-graph construction does not work for large $n\ne2^k-2$, by a result of Müyesser and Pokrovskiy. Motivated by this and by Ryser's conjecture on transversals in Latin squares of odd order, the authors ask about odd $n$. The answer is yes for $n=3$ (by inspection) and $n=5$ (by computer search); a general resolution seems difficult, and it may be easier to start with proper colourings in which no colour appears many times.
paper_title: Rainbow Stackings of Random Edge-Colorings

name: AX_erdos_szekeres_collinear_variant_ell_dependence
title: Open Problem (Introduction)
statement_text: Determine the correct dependence of $ES_{\ell}(n)$ on $\ell$.
context_text: A planar point set is in convex position if it is the vertex set of a convex polygon. For $\ell,n\ge3$, $ES_\ell(n)$ is the minimum $N$ such that every set of $N$ points in the plane contains either $\ell$ collinear points or $n$ points in convex position; thus $ES_3(n)=ES(n)$ is the classical Erdős–Szekeres number for point sets in general position, for which $2^{n-2}+1\le ES(n)\le 4^{n+o(n)}$ (Erdős and Szekeres conjectured the lower bound to be tight, and Suk proved $ES(n)=2^{n+o(n)}$). The authors prove that there is a constant $C>0$ such that $(3\ell-1)\cdot2^{n-5}<ES_\ell(n)<\ell^2\cdot2^{n+C\sqrt{n\log n}}$ for all $\ell,n\ge3$, so the dependence on $\ell$ is between linear and quadratic. Their proof goes through a new cups-caps theorem for arbitrary point sets, which implies that for fixed $n$ and $\ell\to\infty$, $ES_\ell(n)=O(\ell)$, best possible up to constants; the joint dependence on $\ell$ remains open.
notes: Stated in running prose at the end of the introduction: "It remains an interesting open problem to determine the correct dependence of $ES_{\ell}(n)$ on $\ell$."
paper_title: Big line or big convex polygon

name: AX_multicolor_ramsey_hypergraph_tower_height
title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: Given a fixed $k$-uniform hypergraph $G$, determine the integer $h$ (if it exists) such that $r(G;q)$ grows as a tower of height $h$ as $q$ tends to infinity.
context_text: For a $k$-uniform hypergraph ($k$-graph) $G$, the $q$-color Ramsey number $r(G;q)$ is the minimum $N$ such that every coloring of the edges of the complete $k$-graph $K_N^{(k)}$ with $q$ colors contains a monochromatic copy of $G$. The tower function is $\mathrm{tw}_1(x)=x$ and $\mathrm{tw}_h(x)=2^{\mathrm{tw}_{h-1}(x)}$, and a function $f(q)$ grows as a tower of height $h$ if $\mathrm{tw}_h(\Omega(q^c))\le f(q)\le\mathrm{tw}_h(O(q^C))$ for some constants $c,C>0$. Not every function grows as a tower of some height, but it may be natural to guess that $r(G;q)$ always does. For graphs, $r(G;q)$ grows as a tower of height $1$ if $G$ is bipartite with at least two edges and as a tower of height $2$ otherwise. For $3$-graphs, Abbott and Williams showed that $r(K_4^{(3)};q)$ grows as a tower of height $3$, and Axenovich, Gyárfás, Liu and Mubayi showed that $r(G;q)$ is polynomial if and only if $G$ is tripartite and asked which $3$-graphs have double-exponential $r(G;q)$. The authors resolve the problem for $k=3$: they define an explicit nested family of classes $\mathcal{U}$ of $3$-graphs (via collapsing vertex sets that no edge meets in exactly two vertices) and show that for every $3$-graph $G$ with at least two edges, $r(G;q)$ grows as a tower of height $1$ if $G$ is tripartite, of height $2$ if $G\in\mathcal{U}$ is not tripartite, and of height $3$ otherwise. For higher uniformities the problem is open; the authors tentatively conjecture that $r(G;q)$ grows as a tower of some height for every fixed uniform hypergraph $G$, and do not know the answer even for the $4$-graph on $A\cup B$ ($|A|=|B|=t\ge3$) whose edges are the $4$-sets meeting $A$ and $B$ in two vertices each (it is between exponential and double exponential).
paper_title: The growth rate of multicolor Ramsey numbers of $3$-graphs

name: AX_multicolor_ramsey_3_graph_every_exponent
title: Problem 4.1
statement_text: Does there exist, for every $\ell\geq 1,$ a $3$-uniform hypergraph $G_{\ell}$ with $r(G_{\ell};q)=2^{q^{\ell+o(1)}}$?
context_text: For a $k$-uniform hypergraph ($k$-graph) $G$, the $q$-color Ramsey number $r(G;q)$ is the minimum $N$ such that every coloring of the edges of the complete $k$-graph $K_N^{(k)}$ with $q$ colors contains a monochromatic copy of $G$. The tower function is $\mathrm{tw}_1(x)=x$ and $\mathrm{tw}_h(x)=2^{\mathrm{tw}_{h-1}(x)}$, and a function $f(q)$ grows as a tower of height $h$ if $\mathrm{tw}_h(\Omega(q^c))\le f(q)\le\mathrm{tw}_h(O(q^C))$ for some constants $c,C>0$. In a $3$-graph $G$, a set $U\subseteq V(G)$ with $2\le|U|<|V(G)|$ is collapsible if no edge meets $U$ in exactly two vertices; collapsing $U$ gives the $3$-graph $H$ on $(V(G)\setminus U)\cup\{v^*\}$ whose edges are the edges of $G$ disjoint from $U$ and the triples $xyv^*$ such that $xyu\in E(G)$ for some $u\in U$, and $G$ is then reducible to $(H,G[U])$. $\mathcal{U}_0$ is the class of tripartite $3$-graphs, $\mathcal{U}_1$ the class of $3$-graphs having a vertex set meeting every edge in exactly one vertex, and for $i>1$, $\mathcal{U}_i$ is the largest class containing $\mathcal{U}_{i-1}$ and every $3$-graph reducible to some $(H,F)$ with $H\in\mathcal{U}_{i-1}$ and $F\in\mathcal{U}_i$; $\mathcal{U}=\bigcup_i\mathcal{U}_i$. The authors prove that for a $3$-graph $G$ with at least two edges, $r(G;q)=q^{\Theta(1)}$ if $G\in\mathcal{U}_0$; $2^{\Omega(q)}\le r(G;q)\le2^{O(q^\ell\log q)}$ if $G\in\mathcal{U}_\ell\setminus\mathcal{U}_0$; and $2^{2^{q/2}}\le r(G;q)\le2^{2^{O(q\log q)}}$ if $G\notin\mathcal{U}$. So for non-tripartite $G\in\mathcal{U}$ the lower and upper bounds often have different powers of $q$ in the exponent. Writing $\mathrm{Star}^{(3)}(h)$ for the $3$-graph on $h$ vertices whose edges are all triples containing a fixed vertex, it is easy to see that $r(\mathrm{Star}^{(3)}(4);q)=2^{q^{1+o(1)}}$, and the authors construct a $3$-graph $G$ with $r(G;q)=2^{q^{2+o(1)}}$ (blow up a non-central vertex of $\mathrm{Star}^{(3)}(4)$ into a set of $4$ vertices spanning a copy of $\mathrm{Star}^{(3)}(4)$). For each $\ell\ge3$ there are $3$-graphs $G_\ell$ for which their best upper bound is of the form $2^{q^{\ell+o(1)}}$, and they ask whether this can be tight. Even for the Fano plane only $2^{\Omega(q)}\le r(\mathrm{Fano};q)\le2^{O(q^2\log q)}$ is known.
paper_title: The growth rate of multicolor Ramsey numbers of $3$-graphs

name: AX_kt_minor_free_hypergraph_chromatic_bound
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every integer $t\geq 2$ we have $h(t)=\left\lceil\frac{3}{2}(t-1)\right\rceil$. In other words, if a hypergraph $H$ does not contain $K_{t}$ as a minor, then $\chi(H)\leq\left\lceil\frac{3}{2}(t-1)\right\rceil$.
context_text: A hypergraph is a finite vertex set with a set of hyperedges, each a subset of size at least $2$ (no loops). A proper colouring assigns colours to vertices so that no hyperedge is monochromatic, and $\chi(H)$ is the least number of colours needed (the usual chromatic number for graphs). A set $W$ of vertices is connected if for every partition of $W$ into non-empty $X,Y$ some hyperedge contained in $W$ meets both $X$ and $Y$. $H_2$ is a minor of $H_1$ if it can be obtained from $H_1$ by repeatedly taking subhypergraphs and contracting a hyperedge $e$ (identifying all vertices of $e$ into one vertex, discarding hyperedges contained in $e$ and merging parallel copies). Equivalently, $H_1$ contains a $K_t$ minor if there are $t$ disjoint non-empty connected sets $B_1,\dots,B_t$ such that for all $i\ne j$ some hyperedge is contained in $B_i\cup B_j$ and meets both. $h(t)$ denotes the largest chromatic number of a hypergraph with no $K_t$ minor, and $g(t)$ the analogue for graphs (Hadwiger's conjecture says $g(t)=t-1$). The author shows $h(t)$ is finite with $\lceil\frac32(t-1)\rceil\le h(t)\le 2g(t)$, hence $h(t)=O(t\log\log t)$ by the Delcourt–Postle bound on $g(t)$; so Hadwiger's conjecture does not extend verbatim to hypergraphs. The lower bound comes from the complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on $3(t-1)$ vertices, which has no $K_t$ minor and chromatic number $\lceil\frac32(t-1)\rceil$ (its independent sets have size at most $2$). The conjecture is proved for hypergraphs with independence number at most $2$, and remains open even for $t=3$, where the best known upper bound is $4$.
paper_title: Coloring hypergraphs with excluded minors

name: AX_kt_minor_free_hypergraph_3_colorable
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Is every $K_{3}$-minor-free hypergraph $3$-colorable?
context_text: A hypergraph is a finite vertex set with a set of hyperedges, each a subset of size at least $2$ (no loops). A proper colouring assigns colours to vertices so that no hyperedge is monochromatic, and $\chi(H)$ is the least number of colours needed (the usual chromatic number for graphs). A set $W$ of vertices is connected if for every partition of $W$ into non-empty $X,Y$ some hyperedge contained in $W$ meets both $X$ and $Y$. $H_2$ is a minor of $H_1$ if it can be obtained from $H_1$ by repeatedly taking subhypergraphs and contracting a hyperedge $e$ (identifying all vertices of $e$ into one vertex, discarding hyperedges contained in $e$ and merging parallel copies). Equivalently, $H_1$ contains a $K_t$ minor if there are $t$ disjoint non-empty connected sets $B_1,\dots,B_t$ such that for all $i\ne j$ some hyperedge is contained in $B_i\cup B_j$ and meets both. $h(t)$ denotes the largest chromatic number of a hypergraph with no $K_t$ minor, and $g(t)$ the analogue for graphs (Hadwiger's conjecture says $g(t)=t-1$). The author conjectures $h(t)=\lceil\frac32(t-1)\rceil$ for all $t\ge2$, which for $t=3$ predicts that every $K_3$-minor-free hypergraph is $3$-colourable; the matching lower bound comes from the complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on $6$ vertices, which has no $K_3$ minor and chromatic number $3$. This is the smallest open case of the conjecture: the best known upper bound for $K_3$-minor-free hypergraphs is $4$, from the author's general bound $h(t)\le 2g(t)$ (with $g(3)=2$).
paper_title: Coloring hypergraphs with excluded minors

name: AX_erdos_hajnal_polynomial_rodl_hereditary_families
title: Conjecture 10
statement_text: For each proper hereditary family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs there are $C_{\mathcal{F}},d_{\mathcal{F}}>0$ such that if $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, every graph on $n$ vertices which is $\varepsilon^{d_{\mathcal{F}}}$-close to $\mathcal{F}$ contains an $\varepsilon$-homogeneous set of size at least $\varepsilon^{C_{\mathcal{F}}}n$.
context_text: A family of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs, and proper if it does not contain all graphs. A set of vertices $S$ is homogeneous if it is a clique or an independent set, and $\varepsilon$-homogeneous if the edge density of $G[S]$ is at most $\varepsilon$ or at least $1-\varepsilon$. A graph on $n$ vertices is $\alpha$-close to a family $\mathcal{F}$ if one can add or delete at most $\alpha n^2/2$ edges to obtain a graph in $\mathcal{F}$. A family $\mathcal{F}$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property if there is $c>0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{F}$ has a homogeneous set of size at least $n^{c}$; the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture is equivalent to every proper hereditary family having this property. $\mathcal{F}$ has the polynomial Rödl property if there is $C$ such that for every $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{F}$ has an $\varepsilon$-homogeneous set of size at least $\varepsilon^{C}n$. The conjecture defines the polynomial close Rödl property, which clearly implies the polynomial Rödl property. The authors prove that a hereditary family has the Erdős–Hajnal property if and only if it has the polynomial close Rödl property; hence this conjecture is equivalent to the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture, and holds for every hereditary family already known to have the Erdős–Hajnal property.
paper_title: Equivalence between Erdős-Hajnal and polynomial Rödl and Nikiforov conjectures

name: AX_meyniel_cop_number_k_uniform_hypergraph
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: Let $H$ be a connected $k$-graph on $n$ vertices. Then $c(H) = O\!\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{n}{k}}\right)$.
context_text: A $k$-graph is a $k$-uniform hypergraph. In the game of Cops and Robber on a hypergraph $H$, the first player places $m$ cops on vertices, then the second player places a robber; the players then alternate, and in each turn a player may move each of its pieces to a vertex sharing a hyperedge with its current vertex (or leave it in place); positions are known to both players and the cops win if a cop eventually occupies the robber's vertex. The cop number $c(H)$ is the minimum $m$ such that $m$ cops have a winning strategy (for $k=2$ this is the usual cop number of a graph). Meyniel's conjecture states that every connected $n$-vertex graph has cop number $O(\sqrt{n})$. Replacing each hyperedge by a clique shows that the hypergraph game is the graph game on a restricted class of graphs; conversely, blowing up each vertex of a graph $G$ into $k$ vertices and each edge $uv$ into the hyperedge formed by the $2k$ copies of $u$ and $v$ gives a $2k$-graph with the same cop number on $k|V(G)|$ vertices, so there are $k$-graphs with $c(H)=\Omega(\sqrt{n/k})$. The conjecture asserts that this simple construction is the worst case. It generalises Meyniel's conjecture, and for any $k=n^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha<1$ it even implies Meyniel's conjecture. As supporting evidence, the authors prove a bound $O(\sqrt{n/k}\log n)$ for $k$-graphs with suitable uniform expansion properties, and show that with high probability the binomial random $k$-graph satisfies this bound for a broad range of parameters.

paper_title: Catching a robber on a random $k$-uniform hypergraph

name: AX_cover_free_families_optimal_size
title: Problem 5.1 (cover-free families)
statement_text: Are there $(1,r)$-cover-free families $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(t)$ with $t\in\mathcal{O}(r^{2}\log\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert/\log r)$?
context_text: A family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ is $(w,r)$-cover-free if for all $A_1,\dots,A_w\in\mathcal{F}$ and all $B_1,\dots,B_r\in\mathcal{F}\setminus\{A_1,\dots,A_w\}$ one has $\bigcap_{i=1}^w A_i\not\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^r B_i$; in particular $(1,r)$-cover-free means that no set of the family is covered by the union of $r$ other sets. $\mathcal{P}(t)$ denotes the power set of a $t$-element ground set, and $t(n,w,r)$ is the minimum $t$ such that some $(w,r)$-cover-free family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(t)$ has $n$ sets. Known bounds give $\Omega(r^{w+1}\log n/\log r)\le t(n,w,r)\le\mathcal{O}(r^{w+1}\log n)$ for fixed $w$ and $r$ not too large ($r=\mathcal{O}(n^{w/(w+1)})$); for $w=1$ the lower bound $t(n,1,r)=\Omega(\min\{n, r^2\log n/\log r\})$ is due to D'yachkov–Rykov and Füredi, and the authors extend it to $t(n,w,r)=\Omega(\min\{n^w,r^{w+1}\log n/\log r\})$ for fixed $w$. The question asks whether the lower bound is tight for $w=1$, closing the longstanding $\log r$ gap. The motivation in the paper is graph reconstruction with maximal independent set queries (each query is a vertex set $Q$ and the answer is a maximal independent set of $G[Q]$): the minimum number of queries of a deterministic non-adaptive algorithm reconstructing every $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ lies between $t(n,2,2\Delta-2)$ and $t(n,2,2\Delta)$, which yields the bounds $\Omega(\Delta^3\log n/\log\Delta)$ and $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^3\log n)$, with the same gap.

paper_title: Lower bounds for graph reconstruction with maximal independent set queries

name: AX_graph_reconstruction_mis_queries_randomized_nonadaptive
title: Problem 5.2 (randomised non-adaptive optimality)
statement_text: Is there a randomised non-adaptive algorithm which uses $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{2}\log(n/\Delta))$ maximal independent set queries to reconstruct any graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ with high probability?
context_text: In graph reconstruction with maximal independent set (MIS) queries, an algorithm must determine all edges of a hidden graph $G$ on a known vertex set $V$ of size $n$, where each query is a set $Q\subseteq V$ and the answer is some maximal independent set of the induced subgraph $G[Q]$ (chosen by an adversary). An algorithm is non-adaptive if its queries are fixed in advance, adaptive if each query may depend on previous answers; a randomised algorithm need only succeed with high probability (lower bounds are for success probability at least $1/2$). Konrad, O'Sullivan and Traistaru showed that $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^2\log n)$ random non-adaptive queries reconstruct graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ with high probability, and that $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^3\log n)$ deterministic non-adaptive queries suffice. The authors prove that every randomised non-adaptive algorithm needs $\Omega(\Delta^2\log(n/\Delta))$ queries (and every randomised adaptive one $\Omega(\Delta^2\log(n/\Delta)/\log\Delta)$, answering a question of Konrad, O'Sullivan and Traistaru who had shown $\Omega(\Delta^2+\log n)$). The question asks whether the non-adaptive lower bound is tight, i.e. whether the gap between $\log n$ and $\log(n/\Delta)$ can be closed.
notes: Parser assigned the label 'Problem 5.0' to all three problems in Section 5; this is likely Problem 5.2 or the second of several unnumbered problems.
paper_title: Lower bounds for graph reconstruction with maximal independent set queries

name: AX_graph_reconstruction_mis_queries_adaptive_deterministic
title: Problem 5.3 (adaptive vs non-adaptive gap)
statement_text: Is there a deterministic adaptive algorithm that uses $o(\Delta^{3}\log(n/\Delta))$ maximal independent set queries to reconstruct any graph of maximum degree $\Delta$?
context_text: In graph reconstruction with maximal independent set (MIS) queries, an algorithm must determine all edges of a hidden graph $G$ on a known vertex set $V$ of size $n$, where each query is a set $Q\subseteq V$ and the answer is some maximal independent set of the induced subgraph $G[Q]$ (chosen by an adversary). An algorithm is non-adaptive if its queries are fixed in advance, adaptive if each query may depend on previous answers; a randomised algorithm need only succeed with high probability (lower bounds are for success probability at least $1/2$). Konrad, O'Sullivan and Traistaru showed that $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^2\log n)$ random non-adaptive queries reconstruct graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ with high probability, and that $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^3\log n)$ deterministic non-adaptive queries suffice. In fact their argument gives $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^3\log(n/\Delta))$ deterministic non-adaptive queries, and the authors prove that deterministic non-adaptive algorithms need $\Omega(\Delta^3\log n/\log\Delta)$ queries (via cover-free families). For adaptive algorithms the known upper bounds are the same as in the non-adaptive case, while the best lower bound drops to $\Omega(\Delta^2\log(n/\Delta)/\log\Delta)$ in both the deterministic and randomised settings. This gap suggests that adaptive algorithms might perform better than non-adaptive ones, which the question asks to confirm in the deterministic case.

name: AX_off_diagonal_3_ramsey_pair_complexity
title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: There exists an absolute constant $a>0$ such that, for all $3$-graphs $G$ and $H$, $r^{p}(G,H)\geq r(G,H)^{a}$ whenever $p>r(G,H)^{o(1)}$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_N^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $N$ vertices and $K_{n,n,n}^{(3)}$ the complete $3$-partite $3$-graph with three parts of size $n$. The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue coloring of the edges of $K_N^{(3)}$ contains a red copy of $G$ or a blue copy of $H$; subscripts in $O_H$, $\Theta_H$, $\Omega_s$ mean that the implied constants depend on $H$ or $s$. A (3-uniform) pair construction on vertex set $[N]$ is a red/blue coloring $\chi_{f,g}$ of $K_N^{(3)}$ obtained from two functions $f:\binom{[N]}{2}\to[p]$ and $g:[p]^3\to\{\text{red},\text{blue}\}$ by setting $\chi_{f,g}(\{i,j,k\})=g(f(i,j),f(j,k),f(k,i))$ for $i<j<k$; the parameter $p$ is its complexity. Then $r^p(G,H)$ is the smallest $n$ such that every pair construction on $K_n^{(3)}$ of complexity at most $p$ contains a red copy of $G$ or a blue copy of $H$. Stepping-up constructions (where $f(i,j)$ is the index of the most significant binary digit in which $i$ and $j$ differ, complexity typically $O(\log N)$) and inducibility constructions (random $f$, constant complexity) are pair constructions, as are both constructions of this paper. The conjecture says that if there is a Ramsey coloring of order $N$, then there is one of order $N^{\Omega(1)}$ of much smaller complexity, which would explain the prevalence of such constructions and might shed light on the growth rates of $r(H,K_n^{(3)})$. The authors also show that polylogarithmic complexity does not suffice in general: $r^p(K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})\le 2^{O(n\log p)}$, so complexity $2^{\Omega(n)}$ is needed to reach $r(K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})^{\Omega(1)}$.
paper_title: On off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers

name: AX_off_diagonal_3_ramsey_purely_exponential
title: Conjecture 4.3
statement_text: There exists a $3$-graph $H$ for which $r(H,K_{n}^{(3)})=2^{\Theta_{H}(n)}$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_N^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $N$ vertices and $K_{n,n,n}^{(3)}$ the complete $3$-partite $3$-graph with three parts of size $n$. The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue coloring of the edges of $K_N^{(3)}$ contains a red copy of $G$ or a blue copy of $H$; subscripts in $O_H$, $\Theta_H$, $\Omega_s$ mean that the implied constants depend on $H$ or $s$. Fox and He showed $r(H,K_n^{(3)})=2^{\Theta_H(n\log n)}$ when $H$ is the link of an odd cycle (the link of a graph $G$ is the $3$-graph on $V(G)\cup\{u\}$, $u$ a new vertex, with edges $e\cup\{u\}$ for $e\in E(G)$), and this paper extends the $2^{\Omega_H(n\log n)}$ lower bound to many more $3$-graphs (including tight cycles of length not divisible by 3), with a matching upper bound for many of them. Strangely, no $3$-graph $H$ with $r(H,K_n^{(3)})=2^{\Theta_H(n)}$ is known. Call $H$ $123$-inducible if there is an ordering of $V(H)$ and a labelling of the pairs covered by edges of $H$ with $1,2,3$ such that for every edge $uvw$ with $u<v<w$, $uv$ is labelled 1, $vw$ is labelled 2 and $uw$ is labelled 3; Erdős and Hajnal proved that if $H$ is not $123$-inducible then $r(H,K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})\ge 2^{\Omega_H(n)}$. The authors construct (by gluing the links of two paths on 12 vertices along some vertices without sharing edges) a $3$-graph $H$ that is not $123$-inducible, so $r(H,K_n^{(3)})\ge 2^{\Omega_H(n)}$, but to which their $2^{\Omega(n\log n)}$ lower bound does not apply; they suggest it as a promising candidate. For families the rate is attainable: for the family of links of nonbipartite graphs, the Ramsey number is $2^{\Theta(n)}$.
paper_title: On off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers

name: AX_off_diagonal_3_ramsey_superpolynomial_exponent
title: Conjecture 4.6
statement_text: For every $c>0$, there exists $s$ such that $r(K_{s}^{(3)},K_{n}^{(3)})\geq 2^{\Omega_{s}(n^{c})}$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_N^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $N$ vertices and $K_{n,n,n}^{(3)}$ the complete $3$-partite $3$-graph with three parts of size $n$. The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue coloring of the edges of $K_N^{(3)}$ contains a red copy of $G$ or a blue copy of $H$; subscripts in $O_H$, $\Theta_H$, $\Omega_s$ mean that the implied constants depend on $H$ or $s$. For fixed $s$, Conlon, Fox and Sudakov showed $2^{cn\log n}\le r(K_s^{(3)},K_n^{(3)})\le 2^{Cn^{s-2}\log n}$. The outstanding question on off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers is whether some fixed $3$-graph $H$ has $r(H,K_n^{(3)})\ge 2^{\omega(n\log n)}$; the authors believe this already holds for $H=K_4^{(3)}$ but their methods do not suffice, and they conjecture the much stronger statement here. They note that it fails with $K_{n,n,n}^{(3)}$ in place of $K_n^{(3)}$, since $r(H,K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})\le 2^{O_H(n^2)}$ for every $H$ (and even $2^{O_H(n^{2-\epsilon})}$ for some $\epsilon>0$ depending on $H$). They also ask which growth rates are possible for fixed $H$ (e.g. $2^{\Theta_H(\sqrt n)}$ or $2^{\Theta_H(n\log\log n)}$), noting that for the family of links of nonbipartite graphs the rate $2^{\Theta(n)}$ occurs.
paper_title: On off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers

name: AX_off_diagonal_3_ramsey_linear_subexponential
title: Conjecture 4.7
statement_text: There is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that $r(F,K_{n}^{(3)})\leq 2^{O_{F}(n^{C})}$ for every fixed linear $3$-graph $F$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_N^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $N$ vertices and $K_{n,n,n}^{(3)}$ the complete $3$-partite $3$-graph with three parts of size $n$. The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue coloring of the edges of $K_N^{(3)}$ contains a red copy of $G$ or a blue copy of $H$; subscripts in $O_H$, $\Theta_H$, $\Omega_s$ mean that the implied constants depend on $H$ or $s$. A $3$-graph is linear if any two of its edges share at most one vertex. It was a folklore conjecture that $r(F,K_n^{(3)})$ is polynomial in $n$ for every linear $F$ (it is known that $r(F,K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})$ is polynomial for linear $F$, by Fox and He). The authors disprove it: for all large $k$ there is a linear $3$-graph $F$ on $k$ vertices with $r(F,K_n^{(3)})>2^{c(\log n)^{\sqrt{k}/(128\log^5 k)}}$, $c>0$ depending on $k$. For linear $F$ on $s$ vertices, the arguments of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov give $r(F,K_n^{(3)})\le 2^{n^{s-\Omega(s^{1/2})}}$, and the authors believe the much stronger subexponential bound conjectured here may be true. They mention possible strengthenings, with $n^C$ replaced by $n^{o(1)}$, or with linear $3$-graphs replaced by $123$-inducible ones ($H$ is $123$-inducible if there is an ordering of $V(H)$ and a labelling by $1,2,3$ of the pairs covered by edges such that every edge $uvw$, $u<v<w$, has $uv,vw,uw$ labelled $1,2,3$ respectively), but are less certain about these.
paper_title: On off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers

name: AX_off_diagonal_3_ramsey_tripartite_nlogn
title: Informal conjecture on tripartite off-diagonal Ramsey numbers
statement_text: It may be the case that $r(H,K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})\leq 2^{O_{H}(n\log n)}$ for all $H$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_N^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $N$ vertices and $K_{n,n,n}^{(3)}$ the complete $3$-partite $3$-graph with three parts of size $n$. The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue coloring of the edges of $K_N^{(3)}$ contains a red copy of $G$ or a blue copy of $H$; subscripts in $O_H$, $\Theta_H$, $\Omega_s$ mean that the implied constants depend on $H$ or $s$. It is easy to see that $r(H,K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})\le 2^{O_H(n^2)}$ for every $3$-graph $H$, and using methods of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov one can show that for every $H$ there is $\epsilon>0$ with $r(H,K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})\le 2^{O_H(n^{2-\epsilon})}$. On the other hand the authors prove $r(H,K_{n,n,n}^{(3)})\ge 2^{\Omega_H(n\log n)}$ for many $H$ (e.g. links of odd cycles and tight cycles of length not divisible by 3), tight in several cases. They suspect that $2^{O_H(n\log n)}$ is the truth for all $H$, which would go some way towards explaining why the threshold $2^{\Theta(n\log n)}$ is so hard to surpass in lower-bound constructions for $r(H,K_n^{(3)})$.
notes: Introduced with 'We suspect that it may even be the case' in the discussion following Conjecture 4.6.
paper_title: On off-diagonal hypergraph Ramsey numbers

name: AX_oriented_triangle_free_acyclic_number_sqrt
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: $\vec{a}(n)=\Theta(\sqrt{n\log n})$.
context_text: An oriented graph is a digraph with no loops and no directed $2$-cycles (an orientation of a simple graph); it is triangle-free if its underlying graph has no triangle. The acyclic number $\vec{\alpha}(D)$ is the maximum order of an acyclic induced subdigraph of $D$, and the dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. $\vec{a}(n)$ is the minimum of $\vec{\alpha}(D)$ and $\vec{t}(n)$ the maximum of $\vec{\chi}(D)$ over all oriented triangle-free graphs $D$ of order $n$; they are the directed analogues of the minimum independence number and of Erdős's maximum chromatic number $t(n)=\Theta(\sqrt{n/\log n})$ of triangle-free graphs of order $n$. Since $\vec{\chi}(D)\ge n/\vec{\alpha}(D)$ and $\vec{t}(n)\le t(n)$, the authors obtain, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $n$ large, $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}-\varepsilon\right)\sqrt{n\log n}\le\vec{a}(n)\le\frac{107}{8}\sqrt{n}\log n$ (the upper bound from a well-chosen orientation of $G(n,p)$ with $p=c_0/\sqrt n$) and $\frac{8}{107}\frac{\sqrt n}{\log n}\le\vec{t}(n)\le(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)\sqrt{n/\log n}$. The authors believe that a similar analysis of an orientation of the triangle-free process $G_\triangle$ would give acyclic number $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$, which motivates the conjecture. They also construct an oriented triangle-free graph on $25$ vertices with dichromatic number $3$, and show that every oriented triangle-free graph of order at most $17$ is $2$-dicolourable.
paper_title: Minimum acyclic number and maximum dichromatic number of oriented triangle-free graphs of a given order

name: AX_oriented_triangle_free_dichromatic_number_max
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: $\vec{t}(n)=\Theta\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}\right)$.
context_text: An oriented graph is a digraph with no loops and no directed $2$-cycles (an orientation of a simple graph); it is triangle-free if its underlying graph has no triangle. The acyclic number $\vec{\alpha}(D)$ is the maximum order of an acyclic induced subdigraph of $D$, and the dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. $\vec{a}(n)$ is the minimum of $\vec{\alpha}(D)$ and $\vec{t}(n)$ the maximum of $\vec{\chi}(D)$ over all oriented triangle-free graphs $D$ of order $n$; they are the directed analogues of the minimum independence number and of Erdős's maximum chromatic number $t(n)=\Theta(\sqrt{n/\log n})$ of triangle-free graphs of order $n$. Since $\vec{\chi}(D)\ge n/\vec{\alpha}(D)$ and $\vec{t}(n)\le t(n)$, the authors obtain, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $n$ large, $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}-\varepsilon\right)\sqrt{n\log n}\le\vec{a}(n)\le\frac{107}{8}\sqrt{n}\log n$ (the upper bound from a well-chosen orientation of $G(n,p)$ with $p=c_0/\sqrt n$) and $\frac{8}{107}\frac{\sqrt n}{\log n}\le\vec{t}(n)\le(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)\sqrt{n/\log n}$.
