name: AX_coloring_graph_polynomial_determination
title: Problem 11
statement_text: For which graphs $H$ does there exist an $H^{\prime}$ such that $\pi_{G}^{(H^{\prime})}$ determines $\pi_{G}^{(H)}$ for every graph $G$?
context_text: All colourings are proper, and a $k$-colouring uses colours from $\{1,\dots,k\}$. The $k$-colouring graph $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ has the $k$-colourings of $G$ as vertices, two being adjacent if they differ at exactly one vertex of $G$. For graphs $G,H$, the generalised chromatic polynomial $\pi_G^{(H)}(k)$ (introduced by Asgarli, Krehbiel, Levinson and Russell) is the number of vertex subsets of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ inducing a subgraph isomorphic to $H$, as a function of $k$; the authors prove it is always a polynomial in $k$. Thus $\pi_G^{(K_1)}$ is the chromatic polynomial and $\pi_G^{(K_2)}$ counts edges of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$. Here $\pi_G^{(H')}$ determines $\pi_G^{(H)}$ if any two graphs $G_1,G_2$ with $\pi_{G_1}^{(H')}=\pi_{G_2}^{(H')}$ satisfy $\pi_{G_1}^{(H)}=\pi_{G_2}^{(H)}$ (the interesting case being $H'\ne H$; the paper does not say so explicitly). Asgarli et al. conjectured that $\pi_G^{(K_2)}$ determines $\pi_G^{(K_1)}$, which remains unverified. The authors show that for connected $H$ there is a finite family $\mathcal{F}(H)$ of graphs, not containing $H$ and not depending on $G$, such that $\{\pi_G^{(F)}:F\in\mathcal{F}(H)\}$ determines $\pi_G^{(H)}$, which motivates asking when a single graph suffices. Since $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ is an induced subgraph of the Cartesian product of $|V(G)|$ copies of $K_k$, the problem is only interesting when $H$ is an induced subgraph of such a product.
paper_title: A note on graphs of $k$-colourings

name: AX_coloring_graph_polynomial_random_graph_distinguishing
title: Problem 12
statement_text: Is there a finite set of graphs $H_{1},\dotsc,H_{t}$ such that, for almost every $G\in\mathcal{G}(n,\frac{1}{2})$, if $\pi_{G^{\prime}}^{(H_{i})}=\pi_{G}^{(H_{i})}$ for all $i$ then $G^{\prime}\cong G$?
context_text: All colourings are proper, and a $k$-colouring uses colours from $\{1,\dots,k\}$. The $k$-colouring graph $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ has the $k$-colourings of $G$ as vertices, two being adjacent if they differ at exactly one vertex of $G$. For graphs $G,H$, the generalised chromatic polynomial $\pi_G^{(H)}(k)$ (introduced by Asgarli, Krehbiel, Levinson and Russell) is the number of vertex subsets of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ inducing a subgraph isomorphic to $H$, as a function of $k$; the authors prove it is always a polynomial in $k$. Thus $\pi_G^{(K_1)}$ is the chromatic polynomial and $\pi_G^{(K_2)}$ counts edges of $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$. $\mathcal{G}(n,\frac12)$ is the random graph on $n$ vertices with each edge present independently with probability $1/2$. The authors prove that for every $n$-vertex graph $G$ and every $k>5n^2$, $\mathcal{C}_k(G)$ determines $G$ up to isomorphism (confirming two conjectures of Asgarli et al.), but that no finite family of generalised chromatic polynomials is a complete graph invariant. Bollobás, Pebody and Riordan conjectured that almost every graph is determined by its chromatic polynomial; this problem is a weakening of that conjecture, asking whether finitely many generalised chromatic polynomials suffice for typical graphs.
paper_title: A note on graphs of $k$-colourings

name: AX_even_hole_diamond_free_tree_independence
title: Conjecture 1.6
statement_text: The class of (even hole, diamond)-free graph has bounded tree-$\alpha$.
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least 4, and it is even if its length is even; a class is ($H_1,H_2,\dots$)-free if no graph in it contains any $H_i$ as an induced subgraph (for holes: no even hole as an induced subgraph). A diamond is $K_4$ minus an edge. A pyramid consists of a vertex $a$, a triangle $b_1b_2b_3$ disjoint from $a$, and three paths $P_1,P_2,P_3$ from $a$ to $b_1,b_2,b_3$ such that any two of them induce a hole (so at least two of them have length at least 2). The independence number of a tree decomposition is the maximum independence number $\alpha$ of the subgraph induced by a bag, and the tree independence number tree-$\alpha(G)$ is the minimum of this over all tree decompositions of $G$. Graphs of bounded tree-$\alpha$ admit polynomial-time algorithms for Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS), and bounded tree-$\alpha$ implies that treewidth is bounded by a function of the clique number $\omega$ in every induced subgraph ($(\mathrm{tw},\omega)$-boundedness); Dallard, Milanič and Štorgel conjectured that the converse holds for hereditary classes. The paper's main result is that the class of ($C_4$, diamond, theta, pyramid, prism, even wheel)-free graphs, which contains all (even hole, diamond, pyramid)-free graphs, has bounded tree-$\alpha$, yielding a polynomial-time MWIS algorithm and confirming the Dallard–Milanič–Štorgel conjecture for this class. The conjecture drops the pyramid-free condition. (Even hole, diamond)-free graphs are known to be colourable in polynomial time (via a decomposition by star cutsets and 2-joins showing they always have a simplicial vertex or a vertex of degree 2), but no polynomial-time MWIS algorithm is yet known for them; the authors believe their central-bag method may extend to this class. Allowing pyramids destroys the polynomial bound on the number of minimal separators used in some earlier approaches.
paper_title: Tree independence number I. (Even hole, diamond, pyramid)-free graphs

name: AX_even_hole_kt_free_logarithmic_treewidth
title: Conjecture 1.7
statement_text: The class of (even hole, $K_{t}$)-free graph has logarithmic treewidth.
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least 4, and it is even if its length is even; a class is ($H_1,H_2,\dots$)-free if no graph in it contains any $H_i$ as an induced subgraph (for holes: no even hole as an induced subgraph). A diamond is $K_4$ minus an edge. A pyramid consists of a vertex $a$, a triangle $b_1b_2b_3$ disjoint from $a$, and three paths $P_1,P_2,P_3$ from $a$ to $b_1,b_2,b_3$ such that any two of them induce a hole (so at least two of them have length at least 2). A class has logarithmic treewidth if (in the usual sense, not spelled out in the paper) there is a constant $c$ such that every $n$-vertex graph in the class has treewidth at most $c\log n$; here $t$ is fixed and the constant may depend on $t$. It is known (Cameron et al.) that (even hole, $K_3$)-free graphs have treewidth at most 5, whereas the layered wheel construction shows that (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs have unbounded treewidth; layered wheels contain many diamonds, and (even hole, diamond, $K_4$)-free graphs, and more generally even-hole-free graphs excluding a clique and a certain family of graphs containing diamonds, have bounded treewidth. Also, for each $t$, (even hole, diamond, pyramid, $K_t$)-free graphs have bounded treewidth. Logarithmic treewidth is known to hold if one additionally forbids the family of generalized $k$-pyramids, and a forthcoming paper of some of the authors works towards logarithmic treewidth for even-hole-free graphs. Status note (November 2026): proved by Chudnovsky, Gartland, Hajebi, Lokshtanov and Spirkl ('Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions XV. Even-hole-free graphs have logarithmic treewidth', arXiv 2402.14211, 2024), as reported in arXiv 2407.08927.
paper_title: Tree independence number I. (Even hole, diamond, pyramid)-free graphs

name: AX_induced_cycle_packing_bounded_mis_polynomial
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: Maximum Independent Set is solvable in polynomial time in $\mathcal{O}_{k}$-free graphs.
context_text: Let $\mathcal{O}_k$ denote the family of all graphs consisting of the disjoint union of $k$ cycles; a graph is $\mathcal{O}_k$-free if it contains no graph of $\mathcal{O}_k$ as an induced subgraph, equivalently if it does not contain $k$ independent cycles, i.e. $k$ pairwise vertex-disjoint cycles with no edge between any two of them. Thus $G$ is $\mathcal{O}_k$-free if and only if its induced cycle packing number $\mathrm{icp}(G)$, the maximum number of pairwise independent cycles, is less than $k$. Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a maximum-size set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices. The authors prove that every $n$-vertex $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graph with no $K_{t,t}$ subgraph has a feedback vertex set of size $O_{t,k}(\log n)$, hence treewidth $O_{t,k}(\log n)$, so that MIS (and many other NP-hard problems) is polynomial in such sparse $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs. For general $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs they give a quasi-polynomial algorithm for MIS, running in time $n^{O(k^2\log n+f(k))}$, which excludes NP-completeness unless a complexity-theoretic collapse occurs and makes the conjecture quite likely. Note that Maximum Clique is NP-hard in $\mathcal{O}_2$-free graphs (complements of graphs without $K_{3,3}$ subgraph are $\mathcal{O}_2$-free), and that MIS is known to be polynomial in graphs with bounded odd cycle packing number (maximum number of vertex-disjoint odd cycles).
paper_title: Sparse graphs with bounded induced cycle packing number have logarithmic treewidth

name: AX_induced_cycle_packing_sparse_twin_width
title: Open Question: bounded twin-width for sparse $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs
statement_text: Is there a function $f:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every $\mathcal{O}_{k}$-free graph that does not contain $K_{t,t}$ as a subgraph has twin-width at most $f(t,k)$?
context_text: Let $\mathcal{O}_k$ denote the family of all graphs consisting of the disjoint union of $k$ cycles; a graph is $\mathcal{O}_k$-free if it contains no graph of $\mathcal{O}_k$ as an induced subgraph, equivalently if it does not contain $k$ independent cycles, i.e. $k$ pairwise vertex-disjoint cycles with no edge between any two of them. Thus $G$ is $\mathcal{O}_k$-free if and only if its induced cycle packing number $\mathrm{icp}(G)$, the maximum number of pairwise independent cycles, is less than $k$. Twin-width (Bonnet, Kim, Thomassé, Watrigant) is defined via contraction sequences: starting from $G$, repeatedly merge two vertices into one, marking as red the edges from the new vertex to vertices that were adjacent to exactly one of the two merged vertices (red edges are kept through later merges); the twin-width is the least $d$ such that $G$ can be reduced to a single vertex while every intermediate graph has red degree at most $d$. The authors prove that every $n$-vertex $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graph with no $K_{t,t}$ subgraph has treewidth (even feedback vertex set number) $O_{t,k}(\log n)$, which is optimal: there are $\mathcal{O}_2$-free graphs without $K_{2,3}$ subgraph whose treewidth is logarithmic, and the class of $\mathcal{O}_2$-free graphs without $K_{3,3}$ subgraph has unbounded treewidth, yielding a new family of hereditary classes of unbounded treewidth with no induced subdivision of a large wall or its line graph. They leave open whether bounded twin-width holds in this sparse setting.
notes: Stated in prose in the introduction without a labelled theorem environment; language is explicit ('we leave as an open question').
paper_title: Sparse graphs with bounded induced cycle packing number have logarithmic treewidth

name: AX_induced_cycle_packing_odd_mis_tractable
title: Informal conjecture: MIS tractable in bounded-iocp graphs
statement_text: Maximum Independent Set could be tractable in graphs with bounded $\mathrm{iocp}$ (induced odd cycle packing number).
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a maximum-size set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices. Two cycles are independent if they are vertex-disjoint and no edge joins them. For a graph $G$, $\mathrm{ocp}(G)$ (odd cycle packing number) is the maximum number of vertex-disjoint odd cycles of $G$, $\mathrm{icp}(G)$ (induced cycle packing number) is the maximum number of pairwise independent cycles, and $\mathrm{iocp}(G)$ (induced odd cycle packing number) is the maximum number of pairwise independent odd cycles; bounded $\mathrm{iocp}$ is thus a much weaker requirement than bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ or bounded $\mathrm{icp}$. MIS is polynomial in bipartite graphs ($\mathrm{ocp}=0$), and it is known (Fiorini et al.) to be polynomial for bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$. The authors conjecture that MIS is polynomial in $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs, i.e. graphs with $\mathrm{icp}<k$ (they prove it in quasi-polynomial time in general, and polynomial time when $K_{t,t}$ subgraphs are excluded), and remark that tractability for bounded $\mathrm{iocp}$ would be a surprising and formidable generalisation of both. Already the case $\mathrm{iocp}\le1$ is an intriguing open question: graphs with $\mathrm{iocp}\le1$ contain all complements of disk graphs and of unit ball graphs, so a polynomial algorithm would settle whether Maximum Clique is in P for disk graphs and unit ball graphs; recognizing graphs with $\mathrm{iocp}\le1$ is NP-complete.
notes: Stated as a speculative remark in prose ('As far as we can tell, MIS could even be tractable in graphs with bounded iocp'); authors treat it seriously as a potential generalisation.
paper_title: Sparse graphs with bounded induced cycle packing number have logarithmic treewidth

name: AX_tournament_anti_sidorenko_orientation_every_tree
title: Conjecture 1.12
statement_text: For every undirected tree, there exists some orientation that has the tournament anti-Sidorenko property.
context_text: For digraphs $D$ and $T$, the homomorphism density $t_D(T)=h_D(T)/v(T)^{v(D)}$ is the fraction of all maps $V(D)\to V(T)$ that are homomorphisms (send arcs to arcs). A digraph $D$ with $e(D)$ arcs is tournament anti-Sidorenko if $t_D(T)\le 2^{-e(D)}$ for every tournament $T$ (equivalently, every $n$-vertex tournament has at most $2^{-e(D)}n^{v(D)}$ labeled copies of $D$), i.e. $D$ is never more frequent than in a uniformly random tournament; it is tournament Sidorenko if $t_D(T)\ge(1-o(1))2^{-e(D)}$ for all tournaments $T$ (the $o(1)$ is due to tournaments having no loops). Examples of anti-Sidorenko digraphs are directed paths and directed cycles of length not divisible by 4. The authors show that a $k$-vertex tournament anti-Sidorenko digraph has at most $(1+o(1))k\log_2k$ arcs, which is tight. For trees, any orientation having a homomorphism to a single arc is tournament Sidorenko; they characterize orientations of stars $K_{1,s}$: such an orientation is tournament anti-Sidorenko if and only if the centre's in-degree and out-degree differ by at most one. The conjecture asks whether every undirected tree has an anti-Sidorenko orientation; the authors prove it for all trees with at most one vertex of even degree.
paper_title: Variations on Sidorenko's conjecture in tournaments

name: AX_pure_pairs_blockade_transversal_triangle_polynomial
title: Question 1.3
statement_text: Do there exist $c, \varepsilon > 0$ with the following property? Let $\mathcal{B} = (B_1, B_2, B_3)$ be a blockade in a graph $G$, and let $W$ be its width. If there is no $\mathcal{B}$-transversal triangle, then there exist distinct $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $X \subseteq B_i$ and $Y \subseteq B_j$, such that $X, Y$ is a pure pair, and $|X| \geq \varepsilon W$ and $|Y| \geq \varepsilon W^c$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A pure pair is a pair $X,Y$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (every vertex of $X$ adjacent to every vertex of $Y$) or anticomplete (no edges between them). A blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ in $G$ is a sequence of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ (the blocks); its width $W$ is the minimum size of a block and its length is $k$. A copy of $H$ in $G$ is an induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; it is $\mathcal{B}$-transversal if it has exactly one vertex in each block. So a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal triangle is a triangle with one vertex in each of $B_1,B_2,B_3$. By a theorem of Erdős, Hajnal and Pach one always gets a pure pair with $|X|,|Y|\ge\varepsilon W^c$; the question asks for one side of linear size. It is a variant of a conjecture of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov. Settling it was the authors' initial goal, but they could not; it is easy to reduce it to the sparse case where, for all distinct $i,j$, every vertex of $B_i$ has at most $|B_j|/100$ neighbours in $B_j$ (and 100 can be replaced by any number). A blockade has local degree $\lambda$ if $\lambda$ is the maximum, over distinct $i,j$ and $v\in B_i$, of the number of neighbours of $v$ in $B_j$; it is $(x,y)$-cohesive if for all distinct $i,j$ there are no $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ with $|X|\ge x$, $|Y|\ge y$ and $X$ anticomplete to $Y$. The authors prove that for every cycle $H$ of length $k\ge 4$ there are $\varepsilon,c>0$ such that every blockade $(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ of width $W$ with local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ that is $(\varepsilon W,\varepsilon W^c)$-cohesive contains a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$; the same statement for $k=3$ is open and equivalent to this question.
paper_title: Pure pairs. IX. Transversal trees

name: AX_pure_pairs_blockade_polynomial_ordered_graphs
title: Informal: which graphs H admit polynomial-size pure pairs
statement_text: For which ordered graphs $H$ can we get $|X| \geq \varepsilon W$ and $|Y| \geq \varepsilon W^c$ (for some $c, \varepsilon > 0$ depending only on $H$) as the pure pair conclusion, i.e. such that for every graph $G$ and every blockade $\mathcal{B} = (B_1, \ldots, B_{|H|})$ of width $W$ in $G$, either there is an ordered $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$, or there are distinct $i, j$ and $X \subseteq B_i$, $Y \subseteq B_j$ such that $X, Y$ is a pure pair with $|X| \geq \varepsilon W$ and $|Y| \geq \varepsilon W^c$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A pure pair is a pair $X,Y$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (every vertex of $X$ adjacent to every vertex of $Y$) or anticomplete (no edges between them). A blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ in $G$ is a sequence of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ (the blocks); its width $W$ is the minimum size of a block and its length is $k$. A copy of $H$ in $G$ is an induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; it is $\mathcal{B}$-transversal if it has exactly one vertex in each block. An ordered graph is a graph $H$ with a fixed linear ordering $v_1,\dots,v_k$ of its vertices; an ordered $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$ in a blockade $(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ is a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy $J$ with an isomorphism $\phi:H\to J$ such that $\phi(v_i)\in B_i$ for all $i$. Erdős, Hajnal and Pach proved that for every ordered graph $H$ there exist $c,\varepsilon>0$ such that for every graph $G$ and every blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ of width $W$ with $k=|H|$, either there is an ordered $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$, or there are distinct $i,j$ and $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ forming a pure pair with $|X|,|Y|\ge\varepsilon W^c$. The authors ask for which $H$ one side of the pure pair can be made linear in $W$. Taking $c=1$ (both sides linear) is possible only for graphs $H$ with at most two vertices; the version with $|X|\ge\varepsilon W$ and $|Y|\ge\varepsilon W^c$ is called more promising. For $H$ a triangle this is an open question (a variant of a conjecture of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov). A blockade has local degree $\lambda$ if $\lambda$ is the maximum, over distinct $i,j$ and $v\in B_i$, of the number of neighbours of $v$ in $B_j$; it is $(x,y)$-cohesive if for all distinct $i,j$ there are no $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ with $|X|\ge x$, $|Y|\ge y$ and $X$ anticomplete to $Y$. In the sparse setting the paper gives partial answers: for every ordered tree $H$ with $k\ge 2$ vertices there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that every blockade of width $W$ with local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ that is $(\varepsilon W,\varepsilon W^{1/(k-1)})$-cohesive contains an ordered transversal copy of $H$; for ordered caterpillars (trees whose vertices of degree more than one lie on one path) $W^{1/(k-1)}$ can be replaced by $W^{1/d}$ with $d$ the maximum degree of $H$, and for an ordered star with $t\ge 3$ leaves this fails for every exponent $c>1/t$.
notes: PDF source — the exact threshold formulas around this informal question may be partially garbled; overall intent is clear from context.
paper_title: Pure pairs. IX. Transversal trees

name: AX_pure_pairs_blockade_strong_transversal_characterization
title: Informal: characterization of graphs with the strong transversal property
statement_text: Which graphs $H$ have the strong transversal property, i.e., for which $H$ does there exist $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every graph $G$ with an $(\varepsilon W, \varepsilon W)$-cohesive blockade $\mathcal{B} = (B_1, \ldots, B_{|H|})$ of local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ contain a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A pure pair is a pair $X,Y$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (every vertex of $X$ adjacent to every vertex of $Y$) or anticomplete (no edges between them). A blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ in $G$ is a sequence of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ (the blocks); its width $W$ is the minimum size of a block and its length is $k$. A copy of $H$ in $G$ is an induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; it is $\mathcal{B}$-transversal if it has exactly one vertex in each block. A blockade has local degree $\lambda$ if $\lambda$ is the maximum, over distinct $i,j$ and $v\in B_i$, of the number of neighbours of $v$ in $B_j$; it is $(x,y)$-cohesive if for all distinct $i,j$ there are no $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ with $|X|\ge x$, $|Y|\ge y$ and $X$ anticomplete to $Y$. A graph $H$ has the strong transversal property if there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that for every graph $G$, every blockade $(B_1,\dots,B_{|H|})$ in $G$ of width $W$, with local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ and $(\varepsilon W,\varepsilon W)$-cohesive, contains a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$. A sparse random graph of large girth shows that such $H$ must be a forest, but not all forests have it. The authors prove: if every component of $H$ has the property so does $H$ (the converse is false); paths have it; a path with two extra vertices attached to its last vertex has it when $|H|>4$, and with $t$ extra vertices attached to its last vertex when $|H|>2^t(t^2-t+1)$; a path with three extra vertices attached to each end does not; and $H$ does not have it if it has a vertex of degree $d$ with $2^{d-1}\ge|H|$. In particular the property is not closed under induced subgraphs: the star $K_{1,3}$ fails it but adding an isolated vertex gives a forest that has it, and any forest gets the property after adding enough isolated vertices. No complete characterization is known.
notes: Posed as a driving question for Section 2 without a formal label or environment.
paper_title: Pure pairs. IX. Transversal trees

name: AX_hitting_max_stable_sets_forest_free
title: Conjecture 1.8
statement_text: For every forest $H$, there exists a function $f:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ such that every $H$-free graph $G$ satisfies $\eta(G)\leq f(\omega(G))$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $H$-free means with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hitting set of $G$ is a set of vertices meeting every maximum stable set of $G$ (equivalently, whose removal decreases $\alpha(G)$), and $\eta(G)$ is the minimum size of a hitting set. A class $\mathcal{C}$ is $\eta$-bounded if there is $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\eta(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, and polynomially $\eta$-bounded if moreover $f(x)=x^d$ for some $d\in\mathbb{N}$. The notion parallels $\chi$-boundedness: $G$ is perfect if and only if $\eta(H)\le\omega(H)$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$, there are graphs with arbitrarily large girth and $\eta$, and every hereditary polynomially $\eta$-bounded class satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture. This conjecture is proposed as the analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture for $\eta$-boundedness, motivated by the existence of graphs with large girth and large $\eta$. It holds easily for stars ($K_{1,s}$-free graphs satisfy $\eta(G)\le\omega(G)^s$, because a vertex of degree $d$ yields a hitting set of size $d+1$) and for induced subgraphs of $P_4$ ($P_4$-free graphs are perfect). The authors prove it for $P_5$, for every graph $H$ having a vertex incident with all its edges (e.g. disjoint unions of a star and isolated vertices), and for trees obtained from a star by subdividing at most one edge once; it remains open even for trees of diameter three, for $P_6$, and for the disjoint union of two stars. They also propose the stronger polynomial version (for every forest $H$ there is $d$ with $\eta(G)\le\omega(G)^d$ for $H$-free $G$).
paper_title: Hitting all maximum stable sets in $P_5$-free graphs

name: AX_hitting_max_stable_sets_pt_free
title: Conjecture 1.13
statement_text: For every integer $t\geq 6$, the class of $P_{t}$-free graphs is $\eta$-bounded.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $H$-free means with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hitting set of $G$ is a set of vertices meeting every maximum stable set of $G$ (equivalently, whose removal decreases $\alpha(G)$), and $\eta(G)$ is the minimum size of a hitting set. A class $\mathcal{C}$ is $\eta$-bounded if there is $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\eta(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, and polynomially $\eta$-bounded if moreover $f(x)=x^d$ for some $d\in\mathbb{N}$. The notion parallels $\chi$-boundedness: $G$ is perfect if and only if $\eta(H)\le\omega(H)$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$, there are graphs with arbitrarily large girth and $\eta$, and every hereditary polynomially $\eta$-bounded class satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture. The authors conjecture, as an analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, that for every forest $H$ the $H$-free graphs are $\eta$-bounded; this is easy for stars ($K_{1,s}$-free graphs satisfy $\eta(G)\le\omega(G)^s$, since a vertex of degree $d$ gives $\eta\le d+1$) and for induced subgraphs of $P_4$ (perfect graphs). The main result of the paper is that $P_5$-free graphs are $\eta$-bounded, with a proof much longer than the classical Gyárfás path argument that gives $\chi$-boundedness of $P_t$-free graphs for every $t$ (the bound obtained is super-exponential). Whether $P_t$-free graphs are $\eta$-bounded for $t\ge6$ remains open.
paper_title: Hitting all maximum stable sets in $P_5$-free graphs

name: AX_hitting_max_stable_sets_p5_polynomial
title: Conjecture 1.17
statement_text: There exists $d\in\mathbb{N}$ such that every $P_{5}$-free graph $G$ satisfies $\eta(G)\leq\omega(G)^{d}$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $H$-free means with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hitting set of $G$ is a set of vertices meeting every maximum stable set of $G$ (equivalently, whose removal decreases $\alpha(G)$), and $\eta(G)$ is the minimum size of a hitting set. A class $\mathcal{C}$ is $\eta$-bounded if there is $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\eta(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, and polynomially $\eta$-bounded if moreover $f(x)=x^d$ for some $d\in\mathbb{N}$. The notion parallels $\chi$-boundedness: $G$ is perfect if and only if $\eta(H)\le\omega(H)$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$, there are graphs with arbitrarily large girth and $\eta$, and every hereditary polynomially $\eta$-bounded class satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture. The authors prove that $P_5$-free graphs are $\eta$-bounded, but with a super-exponential bound (they say it would be interesting even to obtain a singly exponential bound), and that $H$-free graphs are polynomially $\eta$-bounded whenever $H$ is a proper induced subgraph of $P_5$. This conjecture is the $P_5$ case of their conjecture that $H$-free graphs are polynomially $\eta$-bounded for every forest $H$; it is singled out because, by the Erdős–Hajnal connection above, it would imply the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for $P_5$-free graphs.
paper_title: Hitting all maximum stable sets in $P_5$-free graphs

name: AX_hitting_max_stable_sets_mt_polynomial
title: Conjecture 1.20
statement_text: For every integer $t\geq 3$, $M_{t}$-free graphs are polynomially $\eta$-bounded.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $H$-free means with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hitting set of $G$ is a set of vertices meeting every maximum stable set of $G$ (equivalently, whose removal decreases $\alpha(G)$), and $\eta(G)$ is the minimum size of a hitting set. A class $\mathcal{C}$ is $\eta$-bounded if there is $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\eta(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, and polynomially $\eta$-bounded if moreover $f(x)=x^d$ for some $d\in\mathbb{N}$. The notion parallels $\chi$-boundedness: $G$ is perfect if and only if $\eta(H)\le\omega(H)$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$, there are graphs with arbitrarily large girth and $\eta$, and every hereditary polynomially $\eta$-bounded class satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture. $M_t$ denotes the $1$-regular graph on $2t$ vertices, i.e. a matching of $t$ edges (so $M_t$-free means no induced matching of size $t$). The authors prove that $H$-free graphs are polynomially $\eta$-bounded whenever $H$ has maximum degree at most one and at most four vertices of degree one (this covers $M_2$, an induced subgraph of $P_5$). They conjecture this natural strengthening for all $t$, although, strikingly, it is not even known whether $M_3$-free graphs are $\eta$-bounded.
paper_title: Hitting all maximum stable sets in $P_5$-free graphs

name: AX_hitting_max_stable_sets_two_stars
title: Open problem on $\eta$-boundedness for disjoint union of two stars
statement_text: It remains open whether the disjoint union of two stars satisfies the $\eta$-analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, i.e. whether the class of $(S_{a}\cup S_{b})$-free graphs is $\eta$-bounded for all $a,b\geq 1$, where $S_a$ denotes the star $K_{1,a}$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $H$-free means with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hitting set of $G$ is a set of vertices meeting every maximum stable set of $G$ (equivalently, whose removal decreases $\alpha(G)$), and $\eta(G)$ is the minimum size of a hitting set. A class $\mathcal{C}$ is $\eta$-bounded if there is $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\eta(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, and polynomially $\eta$-bounded if moreover $f(x)=x^d$ for some $d\in\mathbb{N}$. The notion parallels $\chi$-boundedness: $G$ is perfect if and only if $\eta(H)\le\omega(H)$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$, there are graphs with arbitrarily large girth and $\eta$, and every hereditary polynomially $\eta$-bounded class satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture. The authors conjecture, as an analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, that for every forest $H$ the $H$-free graphs are $\eta$-bounded; this is easy for stars ($K_{1,s}$-free graphs satisfy $\eta(G)\le\omega(G)^s$, since a vertex of degree $d$ gives $\eta\le d+1$) and for induced subgraphs of $P_4$ (perfect graphs). For $\chi$-boundedness it is straightforward that a forest satisfies the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture if and only if all its components do; the authors do not know whether the analogous statement holds for $\eta$-boundedness, and in particular whether the disjoint union of two stars satisfies it. As a weakening they prove that $H$-free graphs are $\eta$-bounded whenever $H$ has a vertex incident with all edges of $H$ (a star plus isolated vertices).
notes: Stated as 'it remains open' in prose following Conjecture 1.13, without a labelled environment.
paper_title: Hitting all maximum stable sets in $P_5$-free graphs

name: AX_universal_graph_bounded_density_edge_count
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: For every $d\in\mathbb{Q}$, $d>1$, and $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there exists a graph $G$ with $$e(G)\leq Cn^{2-1/d}$$ edges which is $\mathcal{H}_{d}(n)$-universal, where $C=C(d)$.
context_text: A graph $G$ is universal for a family $\mathcal{H}$ if every $H\in\mathcal{H}$ is a (not necessarily induced) subgraph of $G$. The density of a graph $H$ is $m(H)=\max_{H'\subseteq H}e(H')/v(H')$, and $\mathcal{H}_d(n)$ is the family of all $n$-vertex graphs of density at most $d$ (it contains graphs of maximum degree at most $2d$, $d$-degenerate graphs and graphs of arboricity $d$; density at most $d$ implies $\lfloor2d\rfloor$-degeneracy). The authors initiate the study of universality for graphs of bounded density, aiming to unify results for bounded-degree graphs, forests and degenerate graphs. A counting argument shows $e(G)=o(n^{2-1/d})$ is not enough, even restricted to graphs of bounded maximum degree, so the conjectured bound would be optimal up to $C$. The condition $d>1$ is needed: for density at most $1$ (essentially forests) $\Theta(n\log n)$ edges are necessary and sufficient. Previously Allen, Böttcher and Liebenau gave $O_d(n^{2-1/\lfloor2d\rfloor}\log^{1/(2d)+o(1)}n)$. The authors construct $\mathcal{H}_d(n)$-universal graphs with $C(d)\,n^{2-1/(\lceil d\rceil+1)}$ edges; for the subfamily of graphs of maximum degree at most $D$ they obtain $n^{2-1/d}2^{C\sqrt{\log n}}$ edges for rational $d>1$, and the optimal $C(D,d)\,n^{2-1/d}$ when $d$ is an integer. They call this conjecture the main remaining open problem.
notes: The complete edge bound $e(G)\leq Cn^{2-1/d}$ appears in the introduction prose; the theorem-environment extraction was truncated. Statement reconstructed from the introduction.
paper_title: Universality for graphs with bounded density

name: AX_prime_cayley_graph_joined_union_decomposition
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Given a graph $\Gamma$, can we decompose it as the joined union of smaller graphs?
context_text: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected. A homogeneous set (module) of a graph $\Gamma$ is a set $X$ of vertices such that every vertex outside $X$ is adjacent to all or to none of the vertices of $X$; it is non-trivial if $2\le|X|<|V(\Gamma)|$, and $\Gamma$ is prime if it has no non-trivial homogeneous set. For a graph $G$ on vertices $v_1,\dots,v_d$ and graphs $G_1,\dots,G_d$, the joined union $G[G_1,\dots,G_d]$ is obtained from the disjoint union of $G_1,\dots,G_d$ by joining every vertex of $G_i$ to every vertex of $G_j$ whenever $v_iv_j$ is an edge of $G$ (the wreath or lexicographic product is the case where all $G_i$ are equal). Each $G_i$ is a homogeneous set of $G[G_1,\dots,G_d]$, and conversely a graph has a non-trivial homogeneous set iff it can be written as such a joined union with some $G_i$ having more than one vertex, so the question amounts to deciding whether $\Gamma$ is prime; this is classically studied through modular decomposition, and homogeneous sets can be found in polynomial time. The question is motivated by the study of phase oscillators on multilayer networks, where a joined-union decomposition lets solutions of a reduced system be broadcast to the full network. The paper answers it for Cayley graphs: if $S\ne\emptyset$ and $S\ne G\setminus\{1\}$, then $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$ has a non-trivial homogeneous set iff $G$ has a non-trivial subgroup $H$ such that $Hc\subseteq S$ for every $c\in S\setminus H$; moreover a vertex-transitive graph that is neither complete nor edgeless is a non-trivial wreath product iff it is not prime.
notes: The paper answers this question in the special case of Cayley graphs; the general question for arbitrary graphs is classical and studied via modular decomposition theory.
paper_title: On prime Cayley graphs

name: AX_prime_cayley_graph_finite_ring_characterization
title: Question 4.28
statement_text: For a finite commutative ring $R$, when is the unitary Cayley graph $X_R=\mathrm{Cay}((R,+),R^{\times})$ prime?
context_text: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected. A homogeneous set (module) of a graph $\Gamma$ is a set $X$ of vertices such that every vertex outside $X$ is adjacent to all or to none of the vertices of $X$; it is non-trivial if $2\le|X|<|V(\Gamma)|$, and $\Gamma$ is prime if it has no non-trivial homogeneous set. For a finite commutative ring $R$ with group of units $R^\times$, the unitary Cayley graph $X_R=\mathrm{Cay}((R,+),R^\times)$ has vertex set $R$, with $x$ and $y$ adjacent iff $y-x$ is a unit. For a subgroup $S$ of $R^\times$ with $-1\in S$, the authors show that if $\mathrm{Cay}(R,S)$ is connected and its complement is connected, then it is prime iff the pair $(R,S)$ has no non-trivial quotient, and a non-prime such graph has a non-trivial ideal that is a homogeneous set. For $X_R$, since $X_{R_1\times R_2}\cong X_{R_1}\times X_{R_2}$ (tensor product) and units are detected modulo the Jacobson radical, $X_R$ is not prime unless $R$ is semisimple, i.e. a product of finite fields $k_1\times\dots\times k_d$, in which case $X_R\cong\prod_iK_{|k_i|}$. The paper answers the question completely: $X_R$ is prime iff $R=\mathbb{F}_2$, or $R\cong\prod_{i=1}^dk_i$ with $d\ge2$ fields $k_i$ at most one of which has size $2$.
notes: This question appears to be answered within the paper via Theorem 4.35; it is posed as the key structural question leading to the main results.
paper_title: On prime Cayley graphs

name: AX_prime_cayley_graph_tensor_product_complete
title: Question 4.31
statement_text: Let $n_{1},\ldots,n_{d}$ be positive integers. When is $\prod_{i=1}^{d}K_{n_{i}}$ prime?
context_text: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected. A homogeneous set (module) of a graph $\Gamma$ is a set $X$ of vertices such that every vertex outside $X$ is adjacent to all or to none of the vertices of $X$; it is non-trivial if $2\le|X|<|V(\Gamma)|$, and $\Gamma$ is prime if it has no non-trivial homogeneous set. The tensor (direct, Kronecker) product $\prod_{i=1}^dK_{n_i}$ has as vertices the $d$-tuples $(s_1,\dots,s_d)$ with $0\le s_i\le n_i-1$, two tuples being adjacent iff they differ in every coordinate. The question arises from unitary Cayley graphs: for a finite commutative ring $R$, $X_R=\mathrm{Cay}((R,+),R^\times)$ (adjacency when the difference is a unit) is prime only if $R$ is a product of finite fields $k_1\times\dots\times k_d$, and then $X_R\cong\prod_iK_{|k_i|}$, so primeness of $X_R$ reduces to this question with $n_i=|k_i|$. For $d=1$, $K_n$ is not prime unless $n\le2$. For $d\ge2$ the complement of the product is connected, and the authors show the product is connected iff at most one $n_i$ equals $2$. When every $n_i$ is the size of a finite field, they conclude that the product is prime iff it is connected, i.e. iff at most one $n_i=2$. The paper does not explicitly treat general $n_i$ (for instance $n_i=6$), for which the ring-theoretic argument does not directly apply.
notes: This question is addressed by Theorem 4.35 within the paper; it is the combinatorial core to which the algebraic problem of Question 4.28 is reduced.
paper_title: On prime Cayley graphs

name: AX_digraph_forward_connected_pairs_approximation_ratio
title: Problem 1
statement_text: What is the value of $r_{t}$?
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. With $t(D)$ the maximum number of forward couples over all orders, the ordered ratio $r_t$ is the infimum of $t(D)/n^2$ over strong digraphs $D$ on $n$ vertices as $n\to\infty$. The scheduled ratio $r_s$ is defined similarly by injectively assigning times to the arcs and counting couples joined by a path with increasing times (temporal paths); the authors show $r_t\le r_s$. An out-tree is an orientation of a tree in which a root reaches every vertex, an in-tree is the reverse; a bi-tree $T$ is obtained by identifying the roots of an in-tree $T^-$ and an out-tree $T^+$ that share no other vertex (every $x\in T^-$ reaches every $y\in T^+$), and it is balanced if $|T^+|=|T^-|$. The authors prove that every strong $n$-vertex digraph has a balanced bi-tree of size at least $n/3-1$, computable in $O(n^2)$ time, so both $T^-$ and $T^+$ have size about $n/6$; ordering the vertices along it gives at least $n^2/36$ forward couples, a $1/18$-approximation for the Forward Connected Pairs Problem (FCPP: find an order maximizing the number of forward couples), which is thus in APX (it is NP-hard, as it contains Hamilton path). Hence $r_t\ge1/36>0$, the central result of the paper; the exact values of $r_t$ and $r_s$ are asked for, and whether $r_t$ can be bounded below by an interesting function of $r_s$.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

name: AX_digraph_strong_balanced_bitree_linear_constant
title: Problem 2
statement_text: What is the maximum $c_{b}$ for which every strongly connected directed graph on $n$ vertices has a balanced bi-tree of size at least $c_{b}.n$?
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. An out-tree is an orientation of a tree in which a root reaches every vertex, an in-tree is the reverse; a bi-tree $T$ is obtained by identifying the roots of an in-tree $T^-$ and an out-tree $T^+$ that share no other vertex (every $x\in T^-$ reaches every $y\in T^+$), and it is balanced if $|T^+|=|T^-|$. The authors prove that every strong $n$-vertex digraph has a balanced bi-tree of size at least $n/3-1$, computable in $O(n^2)$ time, so both $T^-$ and $T^+$ have size about $n/6$; ordering the vertices along it gives at least $n^2/36$ forward couples, a $1/18$-approximation for the Forward Connected Pairs Problem (FCPP: find an order maximizing the number of forward couples), which is thus in APX (it is NP-hard, as it contains Hamilton path). Here the size of a bi-tree is its number of vertices, so $c_b\ge1/3$. A construction of Balliu et al. gives strong digraphs in which every bi-tree has $|T^-|\le n/3+O(1)$ or $|T^+|\le n/3+O(1)$, leaving a factor $2$ gap. The authors also ask the analogous question for in-out-branchings, where the in- and out-branchings need only be arc-disjoint.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

name: AX_digraph_left_maximal_dfs_tree_complexity
title: Problem 3
statement_text: Can we compute a left-maximal dfs-tree in $o(n^{2})$ time in minimally strongly connected digraphs? What about the complexity in the general case?
context_text: A digraph is strongly connected if every vertex reaches every other, and minimally strongly connected if every arc $xy$ is the unique directed $x$–$y$ path (such digraphs have at most $2n-2$ arcs). A depth-first search (dfs) tree of $D$ is a spanning out-tree $T$ (a root reaching all vertices) with a left-right order on the children of each node such that arcs of $D$ between disjoint subtrees of two children go from right to left. It is left-maximal if at every node the sizes of the child subtrees are non-increasing from left to right. The authors show that a left-maximal dfs tree rooted at any vertex reaching all others exists and can be computed in $O(n^2)$ time in minimally strongly connected digraphs (by repeatedly computing strongly connected components and out-section sizes); from it a balanced cyclic separator (a circuit $C$ with a partition $I,C,O$, no arc from $I$ to $O$, and $|I\cup C|,|C\cup O|\ge n/3$) is obtained in linear time, yielding a balanced bi-tree of linear size. Computing the left-maximal dfs tree is the bottleneck of their algorithm; they feel that a linear-time algorithm for the separator should be achievable, but computing a left-maximal dfs tree in linear time could be more challenging.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

name: AX_digraph_forward_connected_pairs_request_approximation
title: Problem 4
statement_text: Is there a polytime constant approximation algorithm for RFCPP?
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. In the Request Forward Connected Pairs Problem (RFCPP), the input is a strong digraph $D=(V,A)$ and a set $R\subseteq\binom{V}{2}$ of requested unordered pairs, and one seeks a vertex order maximizing the number of pairs $\{x,y\}\in R$ such that $(x,y)$ or $(y,x)$ is a forward couple; FCPP is the case $R=\binom{V}{2}$, which the authors show is in APX ($1/18$-approximation via balanced bi-trees). The paper shows that one cannot always satisfy a linear fraction of $R$: on the complete binary tree of height $n$ with each edge replaced by a 2-cycle (on $2^{n+1}-1$ vertices) there is a set of $n2^{n-1}$ requests of which at most $2^n$ can be realized, i.e. only a logarithmic ratio; the authors could not find instances where a $1/\log n$ ratio is impossible. The question of a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation (relative to the optimum) remains open.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

name: AX_digraph_strong_forward_cover_log_n
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: Every strong digraph $D$ on $n$ vertices has a $O(\log n)$ size forward cover.
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. A forward cover of $D$ is a set of vertex orders $\le_1,\dots,\le_k$ such that for every pair $\{x,y\}$ of vertices, $(x,y)$ or $(y,x)$ is a forward couple in some $\le_i$. The conjecture is motivated by the request version of the forward connected pairs problem: on the complete binary tree with every edge doubled into a 2-cycle, some request sets can only be satisfied in a logarithmic fraction by one order, yet $2n$ orders suffice to make every pair of leaves forward connected. It holds for bi-oriented graphs (undirected graphs with each edge replaced by two opposite arcs), by splitting a spanning tree at a centroid and recursing. The conjecture would imply that every RFCPP instance has an order satisfying a $1/O(\log n)$ fraction of the requests. A possible approach is to find $O(\log n)$ bi-trees (an in-tree and an out-tree glued at their roots) such that every pair has one vertex in the in-tree and the other in the out-tree of one of them.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

name: AX_sparse_hypergraph_ramsey_double_exponential_degree
title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: For a 3-uniform $n$-vertex hypergraph $H$ with $d_{1}(H)=d$, $r(H;q)\leq\exp^{(2)}(O_{q}(d))n$.
context_text: For a $k$-uniform hypergraph $H$ and $0\le i<k$, the $i$-skeleton $H^{(i)}$ is the $(i+1)$-uniform hypergraph on $V(H)$ whose edges are all $(i+1)$-sets contained in some edge of $H$, and the $i$-th skeletal degeneracy $d_i(H)$ is the degeneracy of $H^{(i)}$ (the least $d$ such that every subhypergraph of $H^{(i)}$ has minimum degree at most $d$); thus $d_1(H)$, the skeletal degeneracy, is the degeneracy of the graph obtained by replacing every edge of $H$ by a clique, and $d_{k-1}(H)$ is the usual degeneracy of $H$. The $q$-color Ramsey number $r(H;q)$ is the least $N$ such that every $q$-coloring of the edges of the complete $k$-uniform hypergraph $K^{(k)}_N$ contains a monochromatic copy of $H$, and $\exp^{(k)}(x)$ is the exponential tower of height $k$ with $x$ on top: $\exp^{(1)}(x)=2^x$, $\exp^{(k)}(x)=2^{\exp^{(k-1)}(x)}$. Answering a question of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov (a hypergraph analogue of the Burr–Erdős conjecture proved by Lee), the authors prove that $k$-uniform hypergraphs with bounded skeletal degeneracy have linear Ramsey number; for $k\ge4$ their proof gives $r(H;q)\le\exp^{(k-1)}(O_{k,q}(d))n$ with $d=d_1(H)$, which is generally expected to be best possible. For $k=3$ it only gives $r(H;q)\le\exp^{(2)}(O_q(d\log d))n$, improved to $\exp^{(2)}(O_q(d))n$ when the 1-skeleton $H^{(1)}$ has bounded chromatic number; the conjecture is that the $\log d$ factor can always be removed. A similar statement is known (Bradač, Fox, Sudakov) with $d_1(H)$ replaced by the square root of the number of edges, and the conjecture would be stronger since $d_1(H)\le O(\sqrt{e(H)})$.
paper_title: Ramsey and Turán numbers of sparse hypergraphs

name: AX_sparse_hypergraph_turan_exponent_max_degree
title: Conjecture 6.2
statement_text: There is a constant $c_{k}>0$ such that for every $k$-uniform $k$-partite hypergraph $H$, $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)\leq O_{H}\left(n^{k-\frac{c_{k}}{d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)}}\right).$
context_text: For a $k$-uniform hypergraph $H$ and $0\le i<k$, the $i$-skeleton $H^{(i)}$ is the $(i+1)$-uniform hypergraph on $V(H)$ whose edges are all $(i+1)$-sets contained in some edge of $H$, and the $i$-th skeletal degeneracy $d_i(H)$ is the degeneracy of $H^{(i)}$ (the least $d$ such that every subhypergraph of $H^{(i)}$ has minimum degree at most $d$); thus $d_1(H)$, the skeletal degeneracy, is the degeneracy of the graph obtained by replacing every edge of $H$ by a clique, and $d_{k-1}(H)$ is the usual degeneracy of $H$. The Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$ is the maximum number of edges of an $H$-free $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices. The authors prove that for every $k$-uniform $k$-partite $H$ with at least two edges, $\Omega_k(n^{k-C_k/d_1(H)})\le\mathrm{ex}(n,H)\le O_H(n^{k-c_k/d_1(H)^{k-1}})$; the upper bound is tight in terms of $d_1$ for the complete $k$-partite $k$-uniform hypergraph $K^{(k)}_{d,\dots,d}$, and the lower bound is tight for the bipartite hedgehog $H^{(k)}_d$ (each edge of $K_{d,d}$ extended to a $k$-edge by $k-2$ new vertices), so $d_1$ alone does not determine the Turán exponent. With $d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)=\max_{1\le i<k}d_i(H)$, one has $d_1(H)\le d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)\le d_1(H)^{k-1}$, and the authors prove $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)\ge\Omega_k(n^{k-C_k/d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)})$ for every $k$-partite $H$ with at least two edges. The conjecture states that this lower bound is tight up to the constant, i.e. that $d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)$ controls the Turán exponent of $k$-partite $k$-uniform hypergraphs, as degeneracy is conjectured to do for bipartite graphs (Erdős's conjecture $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)=O(n^{2-1/d})$ for $d$-degenerate bipartite $H$).
paper_title: Ramsey and Turán numbers of sparse hypergraphs

name: AX_sparse_hypergraph_turan_latin_square_exponent
title: Conjecture 6.4
statement_text: Let $L$ be a $d\times d$ Latin square. Define $H_{L}$ to be the 3-uniform 3-partite hypergraph on vertex set $[d]\sqcup[d]\sqcup[d]$ where $(i,j,k)\in E(H_{L})$ if and only if $L(i,j)=k$. Then $\mathrm{ex}(n,H_{L})=n^{3-\Theta(1/d)}$.
context_text: For a $k$-uniform hypergraph $H$ and $0\le i<k$, the $i$-skeleton $H^{(i)}$ is the $(i+1)$-uniform hypergraph on $V(H)$ whose edges are all $(i+1)$-sets contained in some edge of $H$, and the $i$-th skeletal degeneracy $d_i(H)$ is the degeneracy of $H^{(i)}$ (the least $d$ such that every subhypergraph of $H^{(i)}$ has minimum degree at most $d$); thus $d_1(H)$, the skeletal degeneracy, is the degeneracy of the graph obtained by replacing every edge of $H$ by a clique, and $d_{k-1}(H)$ is the usual degeneracy of $H$. The Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$ is the maximum number of edges of an $H$-free 3-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices. A $d\times d$ Latin square $L$ is a $d\times d$ array filled with symbols from $[d]$ such that each symbol occurs exactly once in each row and each column. The authors prove $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)\le O_H(n^{3-c/d_1(H)^2})$ for every 3-partite 3-uniform $H$, and conjecture that in general $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)\le O_H(n^{k-c_k/d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)})$ for $k$-partite $k$-uniform $H$, where $d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)=\max_{1\le i<k}d_i(H)$; a matching lower bound $\Omega(n^{k-C_k/d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)})$ is proved. The hardest cases should be those with a large gap between $d_{\mathsf{max}}(H)$ and $d_1(H)^{k-1}$, and Latin squares give such an example: $d_1(H_L),d_2(H_L)=\Theta(d)$, yet their theorem only gives $\mathrm{ex}(n,H_L)\le O(n^{3-c/d^2})$. Indeed the 1-skeleton of $H_L$ is $K_{d,d,d}$, the same as that of the complete 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraph $K^{(3)}_{d,d,d}$, and their techniques find $H_L$ only by finding the much larger $K^{(3)}_{d,d,d}$, which contains every 3-partite hypergraph with at most $d$ vertices in each part.
paper_title: Ramsey and Turán numbers of sparse hypergraphs

name: AX_sparse_hypergraph_turan_dense_linear_subhypergraph
title: Conjecture 6.5
statement_text: There is a constant $c>0$ such that for all $d\geq 4$ the following holds. If $G$ is a (not necessarily linear) 3-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with at least $n^{3-c/d}$ edges, then there is a linear subhypergraph of $G$ with $d$ vertices and at least $d^{2}/100$ edges.
context_text: A hypergraph is linear if any two of its edges share at most one vertex; a subhypergraph of $G$ on $d$ vertices is a set of $d$ vertices together with some of the edges of $G$ inside it. For a $d\times d$ Latin square $L$ (each symbol of $[d]$ once in each row and each column), $H_L$ is the 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraph on $[d]\sqcup[d]\sqcup[d]$ with edges $(i,j,k)$ such that $L(i,j)=k$; it is linear, with $3d$ vertices and $d^2$ edges. The authors conjecture that $\mathrm{ex}(n,H_L)=n^{3-\Theta(1/d)}$, where $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)$ is the maximum number of edges of an $H$-free 3-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices, but their methods only find $H_L$ in hypergraphs with $n^{3-c/d^2}$ edges, by finding the complete 3-partite hypergraph $K^{(3)}_{d,d,d}$, which is far from linear. They suggest it would still be interesting to find some Latin square (not a specific one), or even some large part of one, in any hypergraph of density $n^{3-c/d}$, and propose this weaker conjecture, which they are still unable to prove. Without the linearity requirement it is easy: a hypergraph generalization of the Kővári–Sós–Turán argument (Erdős) shows that every 3-uniform hypergraph with at least $n^{3-c/d}$ edges contains $K^{(3)}_{1,(d-1)/2,(d-1)/2}$, a non-linear hypergraph with $d$ vertices and $(d-1)^2/4$ edges.
paper_title: Ramsey and Turán numbers of sparse hypergraphs

name: AX_ell_holed_graphs_structure_small_ell
title: Open Problem: characterisation of ℓ-holed graphs for ℓ ∈ {4, 5, 6}
statement_text: Give a complete structural description of $\ell$-holed graphs (graphs in which every hole has length exactly $\ell$) with no clique cutset and no universal vertex for $\ell \in \{4, 5, 6\}$, analogous to the one the authors obtain for $\ell \geq 7$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; a hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and for $\ell\ge4$ a graph is $\ell$-holed if all its holes have length exactly $\ell$ (chordal graphs, which have no holes, are trivially $\ell$-holed). A clique cutset is a set $X$ inducing a complete graph such that $G\setminus X$ is disconnected, and a universal vertex is adjacent to all other vertices. Gluing two $\ell$-holed graphs along a clique, or adding a universal vertex, preserves being $\ell$-holed, so the task reduces to graphs with no clique cutset and no universal vertex. A bipartite graph between cliques $X,Y$ is a half-graph if $X$ and $Y$ can be ordered so that each vertex of one side is adjacent to an initial segment of the other side. A blow-up of an $\ell$-cycle has vertex set partitioned into non-empty cliques $W_1,\dots,W_\ell$, with edges only between cyclically consecutive $W_i$, each $G[W_{i-1},W_i]$ a half-graph and, for each $i$, $G[W_i,W_{i+1}]$ and $G[W_i,W_{i-1}]$ compatible (together a half-graph between $W_i$ and $W_{i-1}\cup W_{i+1}$). The authors prove that for $\ell\ge7$ a graph with no clique cutset and no universal vertex is $\ell$-holed if and only if it is a blow-up of an $\ell$-cycle or a blow-up of a more complex structure they call an $\ell$-framework (generalizing pyramids, thetas and prisms whose relevant paths all have the same length). They were not able to do this for $\ell=4,5,6$; for $\ell=5$, such graphs were studied in algebraic combinatorics and commutative algebra (Woodroofe), but no complete description is known.
