name: AX_near_eulerian_triangulation_precoloring_polynomial
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: For every positive integer $\ell$, there is a polynomial-time algorithm that given a planar near-Eulerian-triangulation $G$ with the outer face of length at most $\ell$ and a precoloring $\varphi$ of the vertices incident with the outer face decides whether $\varphi$ extends to a 4-coloring of $G$.
context_text: A planar near-Eulerian-triangulation is a plane graph in which all faces except possibly the outer one have length three and all vertices not incident with the outer face have even degree; equivalently, it is a patch (connected plane graph whose inner faces are triangles) that is 3-colorable, and when 2-connected its proper 3-coloring is unique up to permuting colors. A $4$-coloring is a proper coloring with $4$ colors, and a precoloring of the outer face extends if it is the restriction of a 4-coloring of $G$. Deciding 4-colorability of Eulerian triangulations of a fixed surface is the long-term motivation; the disk case with precolored boundary is the basic case of the usual cutting approach for graphs on surfaces. The authors give linear-time algorithms when the outer face is a cycle of length at most five, and when the outer face is a cycle of bounded length whose vertices all have odd degree and the precoloring uses only three colors. In general they only obtain a necessary topological condition (viability: the precoloring, together with the 3-coloring of $G$, must lift to a color- and hue-preserving homomorphism into the infinite triangular grid), shown sufficient when $G$ has an independent set $U$ disjoint from the outer cycle such that all inner faces of $G-U$ have length four. They conjecture that this condition combined with further ideas resolves the disk case in full.
paper_title: Precoloring extension in planar near-Eulerian-triangulations

name: AX_near_eulerian_triangulation_precoloring_separated_faces
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: For every positive even integer $\ell$, there exists an integer $d$ such that the following claim holds. Let $G$ be a planar near-Eulerian-triangulation with the outer face bounded by a cycle $C$ of length $\ell$ and let $U$ be an independent set disjoint from $C$ such that $G-U$ is bipartite. Moreover, suppose that $G-U$ has a set $S$ of $d$ faces of length at least six such that there is no 4-cycle in $G-U$ separating a face of $S$ from the outer face, and for distinct faces $s_{1},s_{2}\in S$, the distance between $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ in $G-U$ is at least $d$ and there is no closed walk of length less than $\ell$ in $G-U$ separating both $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ from the outer face. Then any viable 4-coloring of $C$ extends to a 4-coloring of $G$.
context_text: A planar near-Eulerian-triangulation is a plane graph in which all faces except possibly the outer one have length three and all vertices not incident with the outer face have even degree; equivalently, it is a patch (connected plane graph whose inner faces are triangles) that is 3-colorable, and when 2-connected its proper 3-coloring is unique up to permuting colors. A $4$-coloring is a proper coloring with $4$ colors, and a precoloring of the outer face extends if it is the restriction of a 4-coloring of $G$. A hued graph is a graph with a fixed proper 3-coloring $\psi$ (its hue) with values in $\mathbb{Z}_3$; a dappled graph is a hued graph with in addition a proper 4-coloring $\varphi$ with values in $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$, and homomorphisms of dappled graphs must preserve edges, hues and colors. The dappled triangular grid $T$ has vertex set $\mathbb{Z}^2$, $(i_1,j_1)$ adjacent to $(i_2,j_2)$ iff $(i_2-i_1,j_2-j_1)\in\{\pm(1,0),\pm(0,1),\pm(1,1)\}$, hue $(i+j)\bmod 3$ and color $(i\bmod 2,j\bmod 2)$. A 4-coloring $\varphi$ of a connected hued graph $C$ (here the outer cycle with the hue inherited from the 3-coloring of $G$) is viable if the resulting dappled graph has a homomorphism to $T$; equivalently, the induced map of $C$ to $K_3\times K_4$ (drawn as a triangulation of the torus whose universal cover is $T$) is a contractible closed walk. The authors show that viability is a necessary condition for a precoloring of the outer face to extend, and that it is checkable in linear time. Faces of $G-U$ (the plane graph obtained by deleting $U$) have even length since $G-U$ is bipartite; the authors prove that viability is sufficient when all inner faces of $G-U$ have length four. The conjecture asserts that it is also sufficient in a 'sufficiently generic' situation where $G-U$ has many long faces that are far apart and not separated from the outer face by short cycles or walks. It is proposed as a step towards the companion conjecture that for every fixed $\ell$ precoloring extension of an outer face of length at most $\ell$ in planar near-Eulerian-triangulations is decidable in polynomial time.
paper_title: Precoloring extension in planar near-Eulerian-triangulations

name: AX_neighborhood_complexity_planar_tight_bound
title: Problem 41
statement_text: Determine the profile and neighborhood complexities of planar graphs up to a constant factor. For profile complexity, it is known to be in $\Omega(r^{3})$ and in $\mathcal{O}(r^{4})$. For neighborhood complexity, it is known to be in $\Omega(r^{2})$ and in $\mathcal{O}(r^{4})$.
context_text: For a vertex $v$ of $G$, $N^r[v]$ is the ball of radius $r$ around $v$ (vertices at distance at most $r$). The neighborhood complexity of a graph class $\mathcal{C}$ is the minimum function $f$ such that for every $G\in\mathcal{C}$, every non-empty $A\subseteq V(G)$ and every integer $r\ge0$, $|\{N^r[v]\cap A: v\in V(G)\}|\le f(r)|A|$ (for subgraph-closed classes, its existence characterizes bounded expansion). The profile of a vertex $u$ on $A$ at distance $r$ is the $|A|$-tuple of distances $\mathrm{dist}(u,a)$, $a\in A$, with values larger than $r$ replaced by $+\infty$; the profile complexity of $\mathcal{C}$ is the minimum $f$ such that the number of distinct profiles on $A$ at distance $r$ is at most $f(r)|A|$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, non-empty $A$ and $r$. Profile complexity is an upper bound on neighborhood complexity. Sokołowski proved the bound $|\{N^r[v]\cap A\}|=\mathcal{O}(r^7|A|^3)$ for planar graphs and conjectured that their neighborhood complexity is polynomial in $r$. The authors prove this: the profile (hence neighborhood) complexity of planar graphs is $\mathcal{O}(r^4)$, and they construct planar graphs (of bounded treewidth) showing that the profile complexity is $\Omega(r^3)$, which yields an $\Omega(r^2)$ lower bound for neighborhood complexity. They also show that $K_t$-minor-free graphs have profile complexity $\mathcal{O}_t(r^{t^2-1})$ and graphs of Euler genus $g$ have profile complexity $\mathcal{O}_g(r^5)$, whereas $1$-planar graphs do not have polynomial neighborhood complexity.
paper_title: Neighborhood complexity of planar graphs

name: AX_neighborhood_complexity_kt_minor_free_polynomial
title: Problem 42
statement_text: Are the profile and neighborhood complexities of $K_{t}$-minor-free graphs in $r^{\operatorname{\mathcal{O}}(t)}$?
context_text: For a vertex $v$ of $G$, $N^r[v]$ is the ball of radius $r$ around $v$ (vertices at distance at most $r$). The neighborhood complexity of a graph class $\mathcal{C}$ is the minimum function $f$ such that for every $G\in\mathcal{C}$, every non-empty $A\subseteq V(G)$ and every integer $r\ge0$, $|\{N^r[v]\cap A: v\in V(G)\}|\le f(r)|A|$ (for subgraph-closed classes, its existence characterizes bounded expansion). The profile of a vertex $u$ on $A$ at distance $r$ is the $|A|$-tuple of distances $\mathrm{dist}(u,a)$, $a\in A$, with values larger than $r$ replaced by $+\infty$; the profile complexity of $\mathcal{C}$ is the minimum $f$ such that the number of distinct profiles on $A$ at distance $r$ is at most $f(r)|A|$ for all $G\in\mathcal{C}$, non-empty $A$ and $r$. Profile complexity is an upper bound on neighborhood complexity. The authors prove that for every $t\ge1$ the profile complexity (hence the neighborhood complexity) of $K_t$-minor-free graphs is $\mathcal{O}_t(r^{t^2-1})$, so every proper minor-closed class has polynomial neighborhood complexity; for planar graphs they get $\mathcal{O}(r^4)$. The question asks whether the exponent of $r$ can be made linear in $t$ instead of quadratic.
paper_title: Neighborhood complexity of planar graphs

name: AX_heroes_complete_multipartite_delta_1_2_2
title: Question 1.4
statement_text: Is $\Delta(1,2,2)$ a hero in oriented complete multipartite graphs?
context_text: Digraphs have no digons, loops or multi-arcs. The dichromatic number of a digraph is the minimum number of sets in a partition of its vertices into sets inducing acyclic subdigraphs. A digraph is $H$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to $H$, and $H$ is a hero in a class $\mathcal{C}$ if the $H$-free digraphs of $\mathcal{C}$ have bounded dichromatic number. An oriented complete multipartite graph is an orientation of a complete multipartite graph. $TT_k$ is the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices; for tournaments $H_1,H_2$, $\Delta(1,H_1,H_2)$ is obtained from disjoint copies of $H_1$ and $H_2$ plus a vertex $x$, with all arcs from $x$ to $H_1$, from $H_1$ to $H_2$, and from $H_2$ to $x$; integers stand for transitive tournaments, so $\Delta(1,2,2)=\Delta(1,TT_2,TT_2)$ is a 5-vertex tournament. $H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ is the disjoint union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ with all arcs from $H_1$ to $H_2$. Berger et al. characterized heroes in tournaments; since oriented complete multipartite graphs contain all tournaments, a hero there must be a hero in tournaments. The paper shows that $\Delta(1,2,C_3)$, $\Delta(1,C_3,2)$, $\Delta(1,2,3)$ and $\Delta(1,3,2)$ are not heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs (disproving a conjecture of Aboulker, Charbit and Naserasr), and that $K_1$, $H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ and $\Delta(1,1,H_1)$ are heroes whenever $H_1,H_2$ are. Hence heroes in this class are characterized up to the status of $\Delta(1,2,2)$: if it is not a hero, the heroes are exactly those generated by these three rules; if it is, $\Delta(1,2,2)$ must be added as a base case. A remark in the final version states that, after submission, Walczak proved that non-interlaced ordered graphs have unbounded chromatic number, which together with a theorem of the paper implies that $\Delta(1,2,2)$ is not a hero, though the authors did not yet claim this as a theorem since that proof was not yet published.
paper_title: Heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs

name: AX_heroes_k1_join_delta_1_1_h
title: Question 5.4
statement_text: Let $H$ and $F$ be digraphs such that $\Delta(1,1,H)$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(F)$ and $H$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_{1}+F)$. Then $\Delta(1,1,H)$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_{1}+F)$.
context_text: Digraphs have no digons, loops or multi-arcs. The dichromatic number of a digraph is the minimum number of sets in a partition of its vertices into sets inducing acyclic subdigraphs. A digraph is $H$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to $H$; $Forb_{ind}(F)$ is the class of $F$-free digraphs, and $H$ is a hero in a class $\mathcal{C}$ if the $H$-free digraphs of $\mathcal{C}$ have bounded dichromatic number. $K_1$ is the one-vertex digraph and $G_1+G_2$ denotes disjoint union; $\bar{K}_t$ is the digraph on $t$ vertices with no arc, $TT_k$ the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices, and $\vec{P}_3$ the directed path on 3 vertices. $\Delta(1,1,H)$ is obtained from a copy of $H$ plus two vertices $x,y$ with the arc $xy$, all arcs from $y$ to $H$ and all arcs from $H$ to $x$. Oriented complete multipartite graphs are exactly $Forb_{ind}(K_1+TT_2)$. The paper proves the analogous transfer statement for $H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ (disjoint union with all arcs from $H_1$ to $H_2$): if $H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(F)$ and $H_1,H_2$ are heroes in $Forb_{ind}(K_1+F)$, then $H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_1+F)$. Knowing heroes in $Forb_{ind}(F)$ does not in general help with $Forb_{ind}(K_1+F)$ (every digraph is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_1)$ and in $Forb_{ind}(TT_2)$, while very few are heroes in $Forb_{ind}(K_1+TT_2)$), and heroes in $Forb_{ind}(\bar{K}_t)$ were shown to coincide with heroes in tournaments by a hard proof. A positive answer to this question would show that heroes in $Forb_{ind}(F)$ for $F=\bar{K}_t+TT_2$ or $F=\bar{K}_t+\vec{P}_3$ are the same as in oriented complete multipartite graphs (up to the status of $\Delta(1,2,2)$).
paper_title: Heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs

name: AX_tournament_local_chromatic_out_neighborhood_degeneracy
title: Question 10
statement_text: Does there exist, for each integer $d$, an integer $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there is a vertex $v$ for which $G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]$ has degeneracy at least $d$?
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. For degeneracy, they show that for every $k$ there is a $k$-regular graph $G$ and a tournament $T$ on its vertex set with every $G[N^+_T(v)]$ a forest, whereas if $G$ has degeneracy at least $12k$ then some two vertices $x,y$ have $G[N^+_T(\{x,y\})]$ of degeneracy at least $k-1$. Since in their counterexamples the out-neighbourhoods induce bipartite graphs, which can still have high degeneracy, the authors have been unable to determine whether high chromatic number forces an out-neighbourhood of high degeneracy, and ask this question.
paper_title: Chromatic number is not tournament-local

name: AX_tournament_local_chromatic_out_neighborhood_cycle
title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: For every graph $G$ with sufficiently large chromatic number, and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there exists a vertex $v$ such that $G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]$ contains a cycle.
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. For degeneracy, they show that for every $k$ there is a $k$-regular graph $G$ and a tournament $T$ on its vertex set with every $G[N^+_T(v)]$ a forest, whereas if $G$ has degeneracy at least $12k$ then some two vertices $x,y$ have $G[N^+_T(\{x,y\})]$ of degeneracy at least $k-1$. The authors ask whether, for each $d$, sufficiently large chromatic number forces some out-neighbourhood $G[N^+_T(v)]$ of degeneracy at least $d$. They suspect that this is true for $d=2$, i.e. that some out-neighbourhood must induce a subgraph containing a cycle (a graph has degeneracy at least $2$ exactly when it contains a cycle).
paper_title: Chromatic number is not tournament-local

name: AX_tournament_local_chromatic_random_tournament
title: Conjecture 12
statement_text: For every positive integer $k$, there exists a $\chi$ such that if $T$ is the uniformly random tournament on vertex set $[N]$, then with high probability (as $N\to\infty$), for every graph $G$ on $[N]$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant\chi$ there is a vertex $v\in[N]$ for which $\chi(G[N^{+}_{T}(v)])\geqslant k$.
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. The tournaments in these counterexamples are very structured; the authors conjecture that, with high probability, a uniformly random tournament $T$ cannot be used instead, i.e. that the Scott–Seymour statement holds for almost every tournament.
notes: The statement as extracted likely contains a typographical omission: '$G[N^{+}_{T}(v)]\geqslant k$' should read '$\chi(G[N^{+}_{T}(v)])\geqslant k$'.
paper_title: Chromatic number is not tournament-local

name: AX_tournament_local_chromatic_sublog_threshold_3
title: Conjecture 13
statement_text: There exists $f(N)$ satisfying $f(N)=o(\log N)$ such that for every $N$-vertex graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\geqslant f(N)$, and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, there is a vertex $v$ for which $\chi(G[N^{+}_{T}(v)])\geqslant 3$.
context_text: For a tournament $T$ and a vertex $v$, $N^+_T(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; for a set $U$, $N^+_T(U)=\bigcup_{v\in U}N^+_T(v)$ (it may contain vertices of $U$). A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$; its degeneracy is the least such $d$. Scott and Seymour conjectured that for every $k$ there is $\chi$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ and every tournament $T$ on the same vertex set, some vertex $v$ has $\chi(G[N^+_T(v)])\ge k$ (the fractional-chromatic version holds). The authors disprove this for $k\ge3$ in a strong form: for every $\chi$ there are arbitrarily large $N$ and a (triangle-free) graph $G$ and tournament $T$ on the same $N$-vertex set with $\chi(G)=\chi$ such that $\chi(G[N^+_T(U)])\le2$ for every set $U$ of at most $\frac{\log N}{2\chi^2}$ vertices. Conversely, the bound on $|U|$ is close to optimal: $T$ has a dominating set $S$ of size at most $\lceil\log_2N\rceil$, so if $\chi(G)\ge\chi$ some collection of at most $\lceil\log_2(N)/\lfloor\chi/2-1\rfloor\rceil$ out-neighbourhoods has union inducing a subgraph of chromatic number at least $3$. The authors ask whether $o(\log(N)/\chi)$ out-neighbourhoods (as $\chi\to\infty$) suffice, and in particular conjecture that a single out-neighbourhood suffices once $\chi(G)$ exceeds some $f(N)=o(\log N)$. Note that out-neighbourhoods inducing independent sets for all $v$ force $\chi(G)\le3$.
paper_title: Chromatic number is not tournament-local

name: AX_complete_topological_graph_linear_disjoint_edges
title: Optimal disjoint-edges bound in complete simple topological graphs
statement_text: Is it true that every complete $n$-vertex simple topological graph contains $\Omega(n)$ pairwise disjoint edges?
context_text: A topological graph is a graph drawn in the plane with vertices as points and edges as non-self-intersecting arcs between their endpoints, not passing through other vertices, any two edges sharing an interior point crossing properly there (no tangencies); it is simple if every two edges intersect at most once (a shared endpoint counts). Two edges are disjoint if they share no endpoint and do not cross. A complete topological graph is a drawing of $K_n$. Aichholzer et al. showed that every complete $n$-vertex simple topological graph contains $\Omega(n^{1/2})$ pairwise disjoint edges, and whether this can be improved to $\Omega(n)$ is open. In the Turán-type direction, Pach and Tóth showed that $n$-vertex simple topological graphs with no $k\ge3$ pairwise disjoint edges have $O(n\log^{4k-8}n)$ edges and conjectured $O_k(n)$ (Conway's thrackle conjecture is the case $k=2$). Using a homogeneous regularity lemma for intersection graphs of pseudo-segments (curves pairwise meeting at most once, no three through a point), the authors improve this to $n(\log n)^{O(\log k)}$ edges, and deduce that every $n$-vertex simple topological graph with at least $2n^{1+\epsilon}$ edges has $n^{\Omega(\epsilon/\log\log n)}$ pairwise disjoint edges, improving the $\Omega(\log^{1+\delta}n)$ bound of Fox and Sudakov for dense graphs.
notes: Stated in passing as an open problem without a labelled theorem environment; PDF source.
paper_title: A structure theorem for pseudo-segments and its applications

name: AX_mwis_qptas_forest_subdivision_free
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: For every forest $H$ of maximum degree at most three, MWIS admits a QPTAS and a subexponential-time algorithm in the class of graphs that do not contain any subdivision of $H$ as an induced subgraph.
context_text: In Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS), the input is a graph $G$ with a weight function $w:V(G)\to\mathbb{N}$, and one seeks an independent set $X$ maximizing $w(X)=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)$. A QPTAS (quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme) is an algorithm that, given $(G,w)$ and an accuracy parameter $\varepsilon>0$, computes a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of the optimum in time exponential in a polynomial of $\log|V(G)|$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}$; a subexponential-time algorithm solves the problem exactly in time $2^{o(n)}$ on $n$-vertex graphs. $G$ is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; a subdivided claw is a subdivision of $K_{1,3}$, and $H$ is treated as a fixed graph (constants may depend on $H$). MWIS is not known to be APX-hard or SUBEXP-hard on $H$-free graphs exactly when every component of $H$ is a path or a subdivided claw, and for all such $H$ the paper gives a QPTAS and an exact algorithm in time $2^{O(|V(G)|^{8/9}\log|V(G)|)}$ on $H$-free graphs. The conjecture generalizes this to excluding all induced subdivisions of a forest of maximum degree at most three. The paper proves it when $H$ is a forest with at most three vertices of degree three (with a $2^{O(|V(G)|^{40/41}\log|V(G)|)}$ subexponential bound); as a side result it also handles graphs with no induced cycle of length at least $t$. The final version of the paper mentions later work (Majewski et al. 2022, Gartland et al.) giving simpler proofs and a quasipolynomial-time exact algorithm when every component of $H$ is a path or a subdivided claw.
paper_title: Quasi-polynomial time approximation schemes for the Maximum Weight Independent Set Problem in H-free graphs

name: AX_pt_free_3_coloring_polynomial_linear_forests
title: Converse to Theorem 1.1 (3-Coloring dichotomy for $H$-free graphs)
statement_text: If every component of $H$ is a path, then the $3$-Coloring Problem restricted to $H$-free graphs can be solved in polynomial time.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A graph $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. The $k$-Coloring Problem asks whether an input graph has a proper colouring with $k$ colours; the List-$k$-Coloring Problem asks, given $G$ and lists $L(v)\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$, whether $G$ has a proper colouring with each $v$ coloured from $L(v)$. $rP_s$ denotes the disjoint union of $r$ paths on $s$ vertices and $H_1+H_2$ the disjoint union. Holyer, and Kamiński and Lozin, proved that if $H$ has a component which is not a path, then 3-Coloring is NP-hard on $H$-free graphs (via claws, i.e. line graphs, and via graphs of large girth). The statement is the converse, which the paper describes as wide open rather than conjecturing it; it asks whether 3-Coloring is polynomial-time solvable on $H$-free graphs whenever $H$ is a linear forest (disjoint union of paths), so that the 'easy' and 'hard' cases of $H$ would be completely distinguished for $k=3$. The paper itself settles the analogous dichotomy for List-$k$-Coloring for every $k>4$: it is polynomial on $H$-free graphs if $H$ is an induced subgraph of $rP_3$ or of $P_5+rP_1$ for some $r$, and NP-hard otherwise (assuming P $\ne$ NP); in particular List-$k$-Coloring is polynomial on $rP_3$-free graphs for all fixed $k,r$.
notes: Not a labelled environment; the open problem is identified by the remark 'The converse to Theorem 1.1 is wide open.' The statement of the converse is implicit and reconstructed from Theorem 1.1.
paper_title: List-$k$-Coloring $H$-free graphs for all $k>4$

name: AX_h_free_coloring_dichotomy_all_k
title: Full dichotomy for $k$-Coloring on $H$-free graphs ($k\geq 3$)
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 3$, characterise the graphs $H$ for which the $k$-Coloring Problem restricted to $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable versus NP-hard.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A graph $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. The $k$-Coloring Problem asks whether an input graph has a proper colouring with $k$ colours; the List-$k$-Coloring Problem asks, given $G$ and lists $L(v)\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$, whether $G$ has a proper colouring with each $v$ coloured from $L(v)$. $rP_s$ denotes the disjoint union of $r$ paths on $s$ vertices and $H_1+H_2$ the disjoint union. For 3-Coloring, Holyer and Kamiński–Lozin showed NP-hardness on $H$-free graphs whenever some component of $H$ is not a path, and the converse is wide open; in general, for the $k$-Coloring Problem no value $k\ge3$ is known for which the polynomial cases of $H$ are completely separated from the NP-hard ones. For List-$k$-Coloring this was also the case until Hajebi, Li and Spirkl settled $k=5$, and the present paper settles all $k>4$: assuming P $\ne$ NP, List-$k$-Coloring on $H$-free graphs is polynomial if and only if $H$ is an induced subgraph of $rP_3$ or of $P_5+rP_1$ for some $r\ge1$ (NP-hardness coming from $P_6$ for $k>3$ and $P_4+P_2$ for $k>4$).

name: AX_clean_classes_t_clock_free
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: For every fixed $t \geq 1$, the family of $t$-clock-free graphs is clean.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, and $G$ is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. The $t$-basic obstructions are $K_{t+1}$, $K_{t,t}$, subdivisions of the $(t\times t)$-wall, and line graphs of subdivisions of the $(t\times t)$-wall; all have treewidth $t$. A graph is $t$-clean if it contains no $t$-basic obstruction as an induced subgraph. A class $\mathcal{C}$ is clean if there is $f$ such that every $t$-clean graph in $\mathcal{C}$ has treewidth at most $f(t)$, i.e. large treewidth forces a large basic obstruction. The class of all graphs is not clean, because of Pohoata–Davies graphs, layered wheels and occultations, and neither is the class of wheel-free graphs. A hole is an induced cycle of length at least 4. A clock is a hole $C$ plus a vertex $v\notin C$ (its center) whose neighbours on $C$ include two non-adjacent vertices. A $t$-clock is a clock with two neighbours $x,y\in V(C)$ of $v$ at distance at least $t$ along $C$, so 2-clocks are exactly the clocks and the classes of $t$-clock-free graphs grow with $t$. Clocks appear in all three known non-basic constructions. Earlier, the authors and coauthors proved that (clock, prism, pyramid)-free graphs form a clean class. The main result of this paper is that the class of clock-free graphs is clean, which settles $t\le2$. The conjecture asserts the strengthening for every fixed $t$, where only clocks whose center has two neighbours far apart on the hole are excluded.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions XIV. Non-adjacent neighbours in a hole

name: AX_clean_classes_finite_family_characterization
title: Question: finite families yielding clean H-free classes
statement_text: For which finite families $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs is the class of all $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs clean?
context_text: A graph is $\mathcal{H}$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{H}$. For a positive integer $t$, the $t$-basic obstructions are the complete graph $K_t$, the complete bipartite graph $K_{t,t}$, all subdivisions of the $(t\times t)$-wall $W_{t\times t}$ (the standard subcubic planar grid-like graph whose subdivisions are used in grid-minor theorems), and the line graphs of all subdivisions of $W_{t\times t}$; a graph is $t$-clean if it contains no $t$-basic obstruction as an induced subgraph, and a class $\mathcal{C}$ is clean if for every $t$ there is $w(t)$ such that every $t$-clean graph in $\mathcal{C}$ has treewidth at most $w(t)$. A subdivided star forest is a forest in which every component has at most one vertex of degree more than two. The class of all graphs is not clean, while proper minor-closed classes, classes of bounded maximum degree (Korhonen) and graphs with no long hole are clean. The authors prove that the class of $H$-free graphs is clean if and only if $H$ is a subdivided star forest; a characterization of all families $\mathcal{H}$ giving clean classes would amount to a full grid-type theorem for induced subgraphs, which is out of reach, so finite families are the natural next step. Any finite $\mathcal{H}$ containing a subdivided star forest yields a clean class, but the converse fails: if $H$ is the unique double star on six vertices (two adjacent vertices of degree 3, the smallest tree that is not a subdivided star), then $\{H,K_3\}$-free graphs form a clean class. The authors announce that an upcoming paper by four of them gives a full description of the finite families $\mathcal{H}$ for which the class of $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs is clean.

name: AX_flip_distance_complexity_binary_trees_rotation
title: Complexity of Rotation Distance Between Binary Search Trees
statement_text: What is the computational complexity of computing the rotation distance between two binary search trees (equivalently, the flip distance between two triangulations of a convex polygon)?
context_text: A rotation in a binary search tree is the local restructuring operation that makes a child the parent of its former parent while preserving the in-order of the keys; the rotation distance between two binary search trees on the same keys is the minimum number of rotations transforming one into the other. Via the classical Catalan bijection mapping a triangulation of a convex polygon to its dual tree, this equals the flip distance between triangulations, where a flip replaces the diagonal of a quadrilateral formed by two adjacent triangles by the other diagonal; equivalently, it is the distance between two vertices on the skeleton (graph of vertices and edges) of the associahedron. The authors stress that the complexity status of this problem is widely open: it is not known to be NP-hard, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known either; only a simple polynomial-time 2-approximation and several fixed-parameter algorithms are known. In contrast, flip distances between triangulations of arbitrary point sets or polygons are NP-hard. This is one of the main motivations of the paper, which proves that computing shortest paths on the skeleton of polymatroids (generalized permutohedra, of which associahedra are examples) is NP-hard, even for very simple polymatroids in $\mathbb{R}^n$ defined by $O(n)$ inequalities, and hard to approximate when the polymatroid is given by a submodular-function oracle.
notes: Stated in prose as 'another widely open question'; not a newly posed problem but an existing open question highlighted as a primary motivation. PDF source — math notation appears clean for this item.
paper_title: Shortest paths on polymatroids and hypergraphic polytopes

name: AX_flip_distance_complexity_rectangulations
title: Complexity of Flip Distance Between Rectangulations
statement_text: What is the computational complexity of computing the flip distance between two rectangulations of a unit square?
context_text: A rectangulation is a tessellation of the unit square into disjoint axis-aligned rectangles; modulo a natural equivalence, rectangulations are in bijection with classes of pattern-avoiding permutations. As for triangulations, flip graphs on rectangulations can be defined, and they are skeletons (graphs of vertices and edges) of polytopes; the flip distance between two rectangulations is their distance in this flip graph. These polytopes belong to the family of quotientopes and are polymatroids (generalized permutohedra), so computing flip distances between rectangulations is a special case of computing shortest paths on the skeleton of a polymatroid. The authors prove that the latter is NP-hard in general, even for very simple polymatroids defined by $O(n)$ inequalities, but state that the complexity of the flip distance problems between rectangulations is open (as is, famously, the rotation distance between binary search trees, i.e. flip distance on the associahedron).
notes: Stated in prose as 'The complexity of these problems is open.' PDF source — math notation appears clean for this item.
paper_title: Shortest paths on polymatroids and hypergraphic polytopes

name: AX_treedepth_bound_treewidth_binary_tree_path
title: Open Problem: sharpness of the treedepth bound in Theorem 1
statement_text: Czerwiński, Nadara and Pilipczuk proved that every graph of treewidth less than $t$ with no complete binary tree of height $h$ as a minor and no $2^b$-vertex path (as a subgraph) has treedepth $O(thb)$. Whether this bound $O(thb)$ can be improved remains an open problem.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; paths are not required to be induced. Treedepth $\mathrm{td}(G)$ is the minimum height of a rooted forest $F$ on $V(G)$ such that every edge of $G$ joins a vertex to one of its ancestors in $F$; one has $\mathrm{tw}(G)+1\le\mathrm{pw}(G)+1\le\mathrm{td}(G)$. Each parameter is approximated by an obstruction: treedepth by the longest path (a graph with an $\ell$-vertex path has treedepth greater than $\log_2\ell$, and one with no such path has treedepth less than $\ell$), pathwidth by the largest height of a complete binary tree minor, treewidth by the largest grid minor. Kawarabayashi and Rossman showed that every graph of treewidth less than $k$ with no height-$k$ complete binary tree minor and no $2^k$-vertex path has treedepth $O(k^5\log^2 k)$, and the bound $O(thb)$ above improves this (it is stated by its authors for $t=h=b$, but the proof works in general). It also follows by combining two results: Groenland, Joret, Nadara and Walczak proved that treewidth less than $t$ and no complete binary tree minor of height $h$ give pathwidth $O(th)$, and the present paper proves that every graph of pathwidth less than $a$ with no $2^b$-vertex path has treedepth at most $10ab$. Each of these two bounds is sharp up to a constant factor (for the second, blow up each vertex of a path on $2^{b-c}$ vertices into a clique of size $a/2=2^{c-1}$ and each edge into a complete bipartite graph), but it is unknown whether their combination $O(thb)$ is optimal.
notes: Stated as prose without a labelled theorem environment. PDF source — exponent notation inferred from context.
paper_title: Tight bound on treedepth in terms of pathwidth and longest path

name: AX_ramsey_number_arbitrary_growth_rate_approximation
title: Conjecture 10
statement_text: For all functions $f(n) : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $n \leq f(n) \leq r(K_n)$ and for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there is a sequence of graphs $(G_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfying $|V(G_n)| = n$ and $(1-\varepsilon)f(n) \leq r(G_n) \leq (1+\varepsilon)f(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
context_text: The Ramsey number $r(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the least $N$ such that every red-blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic copy of $G$; every $n$-vertex graph has $n\le r(G)\le r(K_n)$. Pavez-Signé, Piga and Sanhueza-Matamala proved that for every $f$ with $n\le f(n)\le r(K_n)$ there are connected $n$-vertex graphs $G_n$ with $r(G_n)=\Theta(f(n))$, and conjectured that the $G_n$ can moreover be $k$-connected; this paper proves it: for every $k\ge2$ there is $C_k$ such that one can take $G_n$ $k$-connected with $f(n)\le r(G_n)\le C_kf(n)$. With $\mathcal{R}_n=\{r(G):|V(G)|=n\}$ and $\mathcal{R}^c_n$ the same set restricted to connected $G$, Pavez-Signé et al. asked whether $\mathcal{R}_n=[n,r(K_n)]$ and $\mathcal{R}^c_n=[\lceil 4n/3\rceil-1,r(K_n)]$ (which would allow hitting any growth rate exactly), and whether the multiplicative gaps in $\mathcal{R}^c_n$ are $1+o(1)$. This conjecture asks the latter even without the connectivity constraint, i.e. that any prescribed growth rate can be approximated within a factor $1\pm\varepsilon$. The authors suggest edge deletion as a possible route: Wigderson conjectured that deleting an edge changes the Ramsey number by at most a constant factor, and perhaps, at least for dense graphs, some edge deletion changes it only by a factor $1+o(1)$.
notes: PDF source; mathematical notation is clean.
paper_title: Graphs with arbitrary Ramsey number and connectivity

name: AX_non_averaging_sets_n_quarter_tight
title: Informal Conjecture on h(n)
statement_text: The current best lower bound $h(n) = \Omega(n^{1/4})$ on the maximum size $h(n)$ of a non-averaging subset of $[n]$ is tight, i.e., $h(n) = \Theta(n^{1/4})$.
context_text: A subset $A$ of $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ is non-averaging if no element of $A$ is the average of two or more other elements of $A$, and $h(n)$ denotes the maximum size of a non-averaging subset of $[n]$ (the Erdős–Straus non-averaging sets problem). Straus showed $h(n)\ge e^{c\sqrt{\log n}}$ and, with Erdős, $h(n)=O(n^{2/3})$; Abbott improved the lower bound to $\Omega(n^{1/10})$ and then $\Omega(n^{1/5})$, and the current best lower bound $\Omega(n^{1/4})$ follows from a simple construction of Bosznay: for a fixed integer $q$, the integers $n_i=iq^3+i(i+1)/2$, $i=1,\dots,q-1$, form a non-averaging subset of $[n]$ with $n=q^4$. Erdős and Sárközy (1990) proved $h(n)\le n^{1/2+o(1)}$, and methods based on the auxiliary function $H(n)$ (the largest size of two subsets of $[n]$ whose sets of subset sums share no non-zero element; $h(n)\le2H(n)+2$) cannot go below $\sqrt{n}$. Using a homogeneous strengthening of the Szemerédi–Vu theorem on generalized arithmetic progressions in subset sums, the authors prove $h(n)\le Cn^{\sqrt2-1}(\log n)^2$, the first polynomial improvement. They suspect the lower bound $n^{1/4}$ to be the truth.
notes: Stated as running prose: 'The current best lower bound, h(n) = Ω(n^{1/4}), which we suspect to be tight'. No labelled conjecture environment.
paper_title: Homogeneous structures in subset sums and non-averaging sets

name: AX_degree_bounded_classes_polynomial_bounding_function
title: Polynomial degree-bounding function for hereditary degree-bounded classes
statement_text: Is there always a polynomial degree-bounding function for every hereditary degree-bounded class of graphs? That is, for every hereditary degree-bounded class $\mathcal{F}$, does there exist a polynomial $g$ such that $d(G) \leq g(\tau(G))$ for every $G \in \mathcal{F}$?
context_text: $d(G)$ is the average degree of $G$, and the biclique number $\tau(G)$ is the largest $s$ such that $G$ contains $K_{s,s}$ as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph. A class is hereditary if closed under induced subgraphs; a hereditary class $\mathcal{F}$ is degree-bounded if there is a function $g$ (a degree-bounding function) with $d(G)\le g(\tau(G))$ for all $G\in\mathcal{F}$. For instance, by Kierstead and Penrice the class of graphs with no induced copy of a fixed tree $T$ is degree-bounded, and Scott, Seymour and Spirkl showed it is polynomially degree-bounded. The authors' main theorem says that every $K_{s,s}$-free graph of average degree at least $k^{Cs^3}$ contains an induced $C_4$-free subgraph of average degree at least $k$; as a consequence every hereditary degree-bounded class $\mathcal{F}$ has a degree-bounding function $C_{\mathcal{F}}^{s^3}$, the first bound of any type. The analogous question for $\chi$-boundedness (Esperet's conjecture) has a negative answer by Briański, Davies and Walczak. The authors believe that for every $k$ there is a polynomial $p_k(s)$ such that every $K_{s,s}$-free graph with $d(G)\ge p_k(s)$ contains an induced $C_4$-free subgraph of average degree at least $k$, which would give a positive answer.
notes: Stated in prose in the abstract and in the introduction without a labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Induced $C_4$-free subgraphs with large average degree

name: AX_degree_bounded_classes_c4_free_polynomial
title: Polynomial bound in k for C4-free subgraphs
statement_text: Does there exist a polynomial $p(k)$ such that every graph with average degree at least $p(k)$ contains a $C_4$-free subgraph with average degree at least $k$?
context_text: Here subgraphs are not necessarily induced, and $C_4$-free means containing no $4$-cycle as a subgraph. This is the first nontrivial case of Thomassen's 1983 conjecture that for all $g,k$ there is $f(g,k)$ such that every graph of average degree at least $f(g,k)$ has a subgraph of girth at least $g$ and average degree at least $k$ (proved by Kühn and Osthus for girth $5$, i.e. $C_4$-free, and open for $g\ge7$). Writing $f(k,6)$ for the least $d$ such that every graph of average degree at least $d$ has a $C_4$-free subgraph of average degree at least $k$, the best known bounds, due to Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov, are $k^{3-o(1)}\le f(k,6)\le k^{O(k^2)}$; the question is whether $f(k,6)\le k^{O(1)}$. The authors consider the induced analogue in $K_{s,s}$-free graphs, where average degree $k^{Cs^3}$ forces an induced $C_4$-free subgraph of average degree $k$.
notes: Stated in prose in the introduction without a labelled theorem environment; the gap between the lower bound $k^{3-o(1)}$ and the upper bound $k^{Ck^2}$ makes this a natural open problem.
paper_title: Induced $C_4$-free subgraphs with large average degree

name: AX_pure_pairs_sparse_excluded_linear_side
title: Possibility 1.6
statement_text: For all $c > 0$, there exists $\xi > 0$ with the following property. For every graph $H$ with congestion at most $\xi$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every graph $G$ with $|G| > 1$ that is $H$-free and $\bar{H}$-free, there is a pure pair $A, B$ in $G$ with $|A| \geq \varepsilon|G|$ and $|B| \geq \varepsilon|G|^{1-c}$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices, $\bar H$ is the complement of $H$, and $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. A pure pair in $G$ is a pair $A,B$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (all edges between them present) or anticomplete (no edges). The congestion of a graph $H$ with at least one edge is the maximum of $1-(|J|-1)/|E(J)|$ over all subgraphs $J$ of $H$ with at least one edge (and $0$ if $H$ has no edge); it is $0$ iff $H$ is a forest, and small congestion means roughly large girth and maximum average degree only slightly above $2$. By Erdős, Hajnal and Pach, for every $H$ there are $\varepsilon,b>0$ such that every $H$-free and $\bar H$-free $G$ has a pure pair with both sides of size at least $\varepsilon|G|^b$, and the authors ask when $b$ can be close to $1$. Their main theorem: if $c>0$ and one of $H,\bar H$ has congestion at most $c/(9+15c)$, then there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that every $H$-free and $\bar H$-free graph $G$ with $|G|>1$ has a pure pair with $|A|,|B|\ge\varepsilon|G|^{1-c}$; conversely, if both $H$ and $\bar H$ have congestion more than $c$, no such $\varepsilon$ exists. For forests $H$ (congestion $0$) both sides can be linear (Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour, Spirkl), and in an earlier paper they showed that for $H$ of branch-length at least $4c^{-1}+5$ one side can be linear and the other of size $\varepsilon|G|^{1-c}$. This "possibility" asks whether the same strengthening (one side linear) holds under small congestion; the authors were unable to decide it. Their proof does not give it because one step must shrink the blocks of the structure by factors polynomial in $|G|$ rather than by constant factors.

paper_title: Pure pairs. VIII. Excluding a sparse graph

name: AX_pure_pairs_sparse_excluded_stronger_coherence
title: Open question on Theorem 3.3 with stronger coherence
statement_text: Let $\beta\ge2$ be an integer, let $H$ be a $\beta$-buildable graph, and let $c>1/\lfloor(\beta-3)/3\rfloor$. Is it true that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that every $\varepsilon$-sparse $(\varepsilon|G|^{1-c},\varepsilon|G|)$-coherent graph $G$ with $|G|>1$ contains $H$ (as an induced subgraph)?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices, $\bar H$ is the complement of $H$, and $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. A pure pair in $G$ is a pair $A,B$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (all edges between them present) or anticomplete (no edges). The congestion of a graph $H$ with at least one edge is the maximum of $1-(|J|-1)/|E(J)|$ over all subgraphs $J$ of $H$ with at least one edge (and $0$ if $H$ has no edge); it is $0$ iff $H$ is a forest, and small congestion means roughly large girth and maximum average degree only slightly above $2$. A graph $G$ is $\varepsilon$-sparse if every vertex has degree less than $\varepsilon|G|$, and $(\gamma,\delta)$-coherent if there is no anticomplete pair $A,B$ with $|A|\ge\gamma$ and $|B|\ge\delta$. Adding a handle to a graph means adding an induced path $P$ of length at least two between two existing vertices, whose internal vertices are new and have degree two. $H$ is $\beta$-buildable if it can be built from a two-vertex graph with no edges by repeatedly adding handles of length at least $\beta$; graphs of small congestion are induced subgraphs of such graphs. The authors prove the statement with the hypothesis $(\varepsilon|G|^{1-c},\varepsilon|G|^{1-c})$-coherent; since every such graph is also $(\varepsilon|G|^{1-c},\varepsilon|G|)$-coherent, the question asks whether a weaker hypothesis suffices. This proven version is the sparse core of their main theorem: if one of $H,\bar H$ has congestion at most $c/(9+15c)$, every $H$-free and $\bar H$-free graph has a pure pair with both sides of size at least $\varepsilon|G|^{1-c}$. The weaker coherence hypothesis suffices for almost all of their proof, and an affirmative answer would be a step towards the possibility that one side of the pure pair can be taken linear.
notes: PDF source — stated as prose ('we do not know whether') without a labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Pure pairs. VIII. Excluding a sparse graph

name: AX_vertex_critical_edge_robust_fixed_k
title: Open case of Erdős's problem for fixed small k
statement_text: For every fixed $k \geq 4$ and arbitrarily large $r$, does there exist a $k$-chromatic vertex-critical graph $G$ such that $\chi(G - R) = k$ for every $R \subseteq E(G)$ with $|R| \leq r$?
context_text: A graph $G$ is $k$-chromatic vertex-critical if $\chi(G)=k$ but $\chi(G-v)=k-1$ for every vertex $v$, and $k$-chromatic edge-critical if $\chi(G-e)=k-1$ for every edge $e$; an edge $e$ is critical if $\chi(G-e)<\chi(G)$. Dirac conjectured in 1970 that for every $k\ge4$ there is a $k$-chromatic vertex-critical graph with no critical edge; this was proved by Brown ($k=5$), Lattanzio ($k\ge5$ with $k-1$ not prime) and Jensen (all $k\ge5$), leaving only $k=4$ open. Erdős (1985) asked for the strengthening that for every $k\ge4$ and every $r$ there is a $k$-chromatic vertex-critical graph that remains $k$-chromatic after deleting any $r$ edges (Problem 5.14 in Jensen and Toft's book). Little was known for $r\ge2$. The authors prove that for every $r$ there is $k_0(r)$ such that the answer is yes for every $k\ge k_0(r)$, using uniform hypergraphs that have a perfect matching after deleting any vertex but are locally sparse; the case where $k\ge4$ is fixed and $r$ tends to infinity remains open.
notes: Stated in prose without a labelled environment: 'Our result still leaves open Erdős' question when k ≥ 4 is fixed as a small value and r tends to infinity, and this remains an interesting open case of the problem.'
paper_title: Vertex-critical graphs far from edge-criticality

name: AX_regular_graph_top_eigenvalues_limit_points
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: For any $d \geq 3$ and any fixed $k$, the set of all limit points of the vectors $(\lambda_1(G_i), \lambda_2(G_i), \ldots, \lambda_k(G_i))$ for an infinite sequence $G_i$ of $d$-regular graphs is exactly the set $$B(d,k) = \{(\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_k) : d = \mu_1 \geq \mu_2 \geq \mu_3 \geq \ldots \geq \mu_k \geq 2\sqrt{d-1}\}.$$
context_text: For a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, $\lambda_1(G)\ge\lambda_2(G)\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n(G)$ are the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix; for $d$-regular $G$, $\lambda_1(G)=d$, and the Alon–Boppana bound gives $\lambda_2(G)\ge(1-o(1))2\sqrt{d-1}$. Answering a question of Sarnak, the authors prove that for every $d\ge3$ the set of limit points of $\lambda_2(G_i)$ over infinite sequences of $d$-regular graphs $G_i$ is exactly $[2\sqrt{d-1},d]$, i.e. the case $k=2$ of this conjecture. The inclusion of the set of limit points in $B(d,k)$ follows from the known fact that for fixed $d$ and $k$, every sufficiently large $d$-regular graph has at least $k$ eigenvalues at least $2\sqrt{d-1}-o(1)$; the authors could not decide whether every point of $B(d,k)$ is a limit point even for $k=3$. They prove that every point of $B(d,k)$ with $\mu_k\ge2\sqrt{d-1}+1/\sqrt{d-1}$ is a limit point of $d$-regular graphs, and that every point of $B(d,k)$ is a limit point if the graphs are only required to have maximum degree at most $d$.
paper_title: The limit points of the top and bottom eigenvalues of regular graphs

name: AX_separating_path_system_strong_2n
title: Problem 3
statement_text: Does every graph on $n$ vertices admit a strongly-separating path system of size $2n$?
context_text: A path separates an edge $e$ from an edge $f$ if it contains $e$ but not $f$. A collection $\mathcal{P}$ of paths of $G$ is a strongly-separating path system if for any two distinct edges $e,f$ there are paths $P_e,P_f\in\mathcal{P}$ with $e\in P_e$, $f\notin P_e$, $f\in P_f$, $e\notin P_f$ (weakly-separating if some path contains exactly one of $e,f$); its size is the number of paths. The question, due to Katona, is how many paths are needed; Falgas-Ravry, Kittipassorn, Korándi, Letzter and Narayanan (weak version) and Balogh, Csaba, Martin and Pluhár (strong version) conjectured that $O(n)$ paths always suffice for $n$-vertex graphs, and Letzter proved $O(n\log^\star n)$. The paper confirms the conjecture: every graph on $n$ vertices admits a strongly-separating path system of size $19n$ (using Pósa rotation–extension to reduce to graphs with a Hamiltonian path). This bound is likely far from optimal: Balogh et al. showed that $K_{\varepsilon n,(1-\varepsilon)n}$ cannot be strongly separated by fewer than $2(1-2\varepsilon)n$ paths, and no graph with a larger lower bound is known, suggesting that $2n$ might suffice. Determining the exact constant is challenging even for cliques.
paper_title: Separating the edges of a graph by a linear number of paths

name: AX_separating_path_system_rainbow_cover_linear
title: Problem 4
statement_text: Does every properly edge-colored graph $G$ admit $O(|V(G)|)$ rainbow paths that cover $E(G)$?
context_text: A proper edge-coloring gives distinct colors to edges sharing an endpoint, and a rainbow path is a path with no two edges of the same color. A path separates an edge $e$ from an edge $f$ if it contains $e$ but not $f$. A collection $\mathcal{P}$ of paths of $G$ is a strongly-separating path system if for any two distinct edges $e,f$ there are paths $P_e,P_f\in\mathcal{P}$ with $e\in P_e$, $f\notin P_e$, $f\in P_f$, $e\notin P_f$ (weakly-separating if some path contains exactly one of $e,f$); its size is the number of paths. The question, due to Katona, is how many paths are needed; Falgas-Ravry, Kittipassorn, Korándi, Letzter and Narayanan (weak version) and Balogh, Csaba, Martin and Pluhár (strong version) conjectured that $O(n)$ paths always suffice for $n$-vertex graphs, and Letzter proved $O(n\log^\star n)$. The paper proves this conjecture, with $19n$ paths. The rainbow question arose in the authors' first attempts and, as far as they know, has not been stated before. An affirmative answer would give another proof of the linear bound: take a path decomposition of $G$ into $O(n)$ paths, split each path into two matchings, form two graphs each containing one matching of each path (the matchings properly color them), and combine rainbow path covers of these two graphs with the original decomposition. The authors can verify the version where paths are replaced by trails.
paper_title: Separating the edges of a graph by a linear number of paths

name: AX_tournament_clique_number_simultaneous_ordering
title: Question 3.5
statement_text: Is it true that for every tournament $T$, there exists $\prec\in\mathfrak{S}(T)$ such that $\prec$ is both a $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}$-ordering and a $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-ordering?
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. $\mathfrak{S}(T)$ is the set of orderings of $V(T)$; an ordering $\prec$ is an $\overrightarrow{\omega}$-ordering if $\omega(T^{\prec})=\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)$ and a $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-ordering if $\chi(T^{\prec})=\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)$. Using the inequality $\chi(T^{\prec})/\omega(T^{\prec})\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)\le\chi(T^{\prec})$ of Nguyen, Scott and Seymour, valid for every ordering of a tournament, the authors show that every $\overrightarrow{\omega}$-ordering $\prec$ of a tournament $T$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)\le\chi(T^{\prec})\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)^2$. The question asks whether a single ordering can simultaneously witness both the clique number and the dichromatic number; the authors say they have no reason to believe it, but could not find a counterexample.

name: AX_tournament_clique_number_substitution_polynomial_bounded
title: Question 3.10
statement_text: Is it true that if a class of tournaments $\mathcal{T}$ is polynomially $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-bounded, then so is $\mathcal{T}^{subst}$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). A class (always closed under induced subdigraphs) is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)\le f(\overrightarrow{\omega}(D))$ for every $D$ in the class, polynomially so if $f$ can be taken polynomial. A digraph $D$ is obtained from $D_1$ by substituting $D_2$ for a vertex $u$ of $D_1$ if $D$ is obtained from $D_1-u$ and a disjoint copy of $D_2$ by adding, for each $v\ne u$, all arcs from $V(D_2)$ to $v$ if $uv\in A(D_1)$, all arcs from $v$ to $V(D_2)$ if $vu\in A(D_1)$, and no arc if $u,v$ are non-adjacent; $\mathcal{C}^{subst}$ is the closure of the class $\mathcal{C}$ under substitution. For tournaments $T_1,T_2,T_3$, $\Delta(T_1,T_2,T_3)$ is obtained from disjoint copies of them by adding all arcs from $T_1$ to $T_2$, from $T_2$ to $T_3$ and from $T_3$ to $T_1$ (an integer $k$ stands for $TT_k$, and $\Delta(1,1,1)=\overrightarrow{C_3}$). name: AX_tournament_clique_number_twin_width_bounded
title: Conjecture 3.12
statement_text: Let $k\geq 1$. The class of tournaments with twin-width at most $k$ is $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-bounded.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. A contraction sequence of a structure $S$ on $n$ vertices is a sequence of partitions $\mathcal{P}_n,\dots,\mathcal{P}_1$ of $V(S)$ from singletons to a single part, each obtained by merging two parts of the previous one; the error degree of a part $X$ is the number of other parts $Y$ not homogeneous to $X$, and $\operatorname{tww}(S)$ is the minimum over contraction sequences of the maximum error degree. name: AX_tournament_clique_number_twin_width_ordering
title: Conjecture 3.13
statement_text: There exists a function $f$ such that for every tournament $T$, there exists an ordering $\prec^{*}$ of $V(T)$ such that $\omega(T^{\prec^{*}})\leq f(\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T))$ and $\operatorname{tww}(T,\prec^{*})\leq f(\operatorname{tww}(T))$.

name: AX_tournament_clique_number_bst_ordering
title: Conjecture 3.16
statement_text: There exists a function $f$ such that, for every tournament $T$, there exists a $BST$-ordering $\prec$ of $T$ such that $\omega(T^{\prec})\leq f(\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T))$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. $N^-(x)$ and $N^+(x)$ denote the in- and out-neighbourhood of $x$. Following Geniet and Thomassé, a BST-ordering of a tournament $T$ is (informally) obtained from a rooted binary search tree on $V(T)$ in which, for every vertex $x$, the left child of $x$ and its descendants lie in $N^-(x)$ and the right child of $x$ and its descendants lie in $N^+(x)$; the ordering is the left-to-right order of this tree (recursively: pick $x$, put $N^-(x)$ to its left and $N^+(x)$ to its right, and order both sides in the same way). name: AX_tournament_clique_number_gyarfas_sumner_backedge
title: Conjecture 4.3 (Gyárfás-Sumner for Tournaments)
statement_text: A tournament $H$ is $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\chi}}$-binding if and only if $H$ has a backedge graph which is a forest.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. name: AX_ordered_graph_matching_free_chi_bounded
title: Conjecture 4.11
statement_text: Let $(M,\prec)$ be an ordered graph with maximum degree $1$. Then the class of $(M,\prec)$-free ordered graphs is $\chi$-bounded.
context_text: An ordered graph is a pair $(G,\prec)$ where $\prec$ is a total order of $V(G)$; $(H,\prec_H)$ is an induced ordered subgraph of $(G,\prec_G)$ if there is an injection $\phi:V(H)\to V(G)$ preserving both the order and adjacency/non-adjacency, and $(G,\prec_G)$ is $(M,\prec)$-free if it has no induced ordered subgraph isomorphic to $(M,\prec)$. An ordered graph of maximum degree $1$ is an ordered matching (possibly with isolated vertices). A class of ordered graphs is $\chi$-bounded if the class of their underlying graphs is, i.e. $\chi$ is bounded by a function of $\omega$. Briański, Davies and Walczak studied which excluded ordered graphs yield $\chi$-bounded classes and, according to the authors, claimed in a personal communication to have proven that excluding any ordered matching does. The motivation comes from tournaments (orientations of complete graphs): for an ordering $\prec$ of a tournament $T$, the backedge graph $T^{\prec}$ has an edge $uv$ when $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc; with $\overrightarrow{\chi}$ the dichromatic number and $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)=\min_{\prec}\omega(T^{\prec})$, the authors show that the class of $F$-free tournaments has $\overrightarrow{\chi}$ bounded by a function of $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ if and only if the class of ordered graphs excluding all ordered backedge graphs $(F^{\prec},\prec)$ of $F$ is $\chi$-bounded. Hence the conjecture would imply that every tournament with a backedge graph of maximum degree $1$ is $\overrightarrow{\chi}$-binding.

name: AX_tournament_clique_number_domination_cluster
title: Conjecture 5.3 (Large dom implies an ω̄-cluster)
statement_text: There exist two functions $f$ and $\ell$ such that, for every integer $k$, every tournament $T$ with $\operatorname{dom}(T)\geq f(k)$ contains a subtournament $X$ with $|X|\leq\ell(k)$ and $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(X)\geq k$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops, no parallel arcs and no 2-cycles (digons); a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph and $TT_n$ is the transitive tournament on $n$ vertices. The dichromatic number $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph. For an ordering (total order) $\prec$ of $V(D)$, the backedge graph $D^{\prec}$ is the undirected graph on $V(D)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc (a backward arc). One has $\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)=\min_{\prec}\chi(D^{\prec})$, and the authors define the clique number of $D$ as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)=\min_{\prec}\omega(D^{\prec})$, so that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(D)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(D)$ and $\overrightarrow{\omega}$ of a symmetric digraph equals the clique number of its underlying graph. $N^+(v)$ is the out-neighbourhood of $v$; a dominating set of a tournament $T$ is a set $X$ such that every vertex outside $X$ has an in-neighbour in $X$, and $\operatorname{dom}(T)$ is the minimum size of a dominating set; the authors show $\operatorname{dom}(T)\le\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\le\overrightarrow{\chi}(T)$. name: AX_tournament_clique_number_local_global
title: Conjecture 5.6
statement_text: There exists a function $g$ such that, for every integer $t$, if $T$ is a tournament such that for every $v\in V(T)$, $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(N^{+}(v))\leq t$, then $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\leq g(t)$.

name: AX_tournament_clique_number_bounded_witness
title: Question 5.9
statement_text: Is there a function $\ell$ such that, for every tournament $T$, if $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\geq k$, then $T$ has a subtournament $A$ such that $|A|\leq\ell(k)$ and $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(A)\geq k$.

name: AX_tournament_clique_number_critical_infinitely_many
title: Conjecture 5.10

name: AX_sublinear_separators_product_structure_tree_depth
title: Conjecture (product structure with bounded tree-depth and tight clique size)
statement_text: For any hereditary graph class $\mathcal{G}$ that admits $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ separators, every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is a subgraph of the strong product of a graph $H$ with bounded tree-width and a complete graph of size $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; a class is hereditary if it is closed under induced subgraphs, and $G$ is contained in $H$ if $G$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $H$. A balanced separator of an $n$-vertex graph $G$ is a set $S\subseteq V(G)$ such that every component of $G-S$ has at most $n/2$ vertices; the separation-number $\operatorname{sep}(G)$ is the minimum size of a balanced separator, and $\operatorname{sep}(\mathcal{G})\in O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ (the class admits $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ separators) means that $n$-vertex graphs of $\mathcal{G}$ have separation-number $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$, for some fixed $\epsilon\in(0,1)$. The strong product $A\boxtimes B$ has vertex set $V(A)\times V(B)$, distinct $(v,x),(w,y)$ being adjacent if ($v=w$ and $xy\in E(B)$) or ($x=y$ and $vw\in E(A)$) or ($vw\in E(A)$ and $xy\in E(B)$); $K_m$ is the complete graph on $m$ vertices and $\operatorname{tw}$ denotes treewidth. The tree-depth $\operatorname{td}(H)$ is the minimum number of vertices on a root–leaf path of a rooted forest whose closure (ancestor–descendant pairs made adjacent) contains $H$. Examples: proper minor-closed classes ($\epsilon=1/2$) and touching graphs of $d$-dimensional balls ($\epsilon=1/d$). The authors prove that for $0<\delta<\epsilon<1$, every $n$-vertex graph of such a class is contained in $H\boxtimes K_m$ with $\operatorname{td}(H)$ bounded (in terms of $\epsilon,\delta$) and $m\in O(n^{1-\epsilon+\delta})$, and with $\delta=0$ if $\operatorname{td}(H)\in O(\log\log n)$ is allowed; using isoperimetric inequalities for grids they show that both the dependence on $\delta$ and the $O(\log\log n)$ bound are best possible, so bounded tree-depth cannot be combined with $m\in O(n^{1-\epsilon})$. Whether exponent gap $0$ and bounded treewidth of $H$ can be achieved simultaneously is open. It is known for minor-closed classes with $\epsilon=1/2$, and it holds with $\operatorname{tw}(H)\le1$ for classes of bounded maximum degree; the authors prove it for several further classes (e.g. map graphs) and leave open touching graphs of 3-dimensional spheres, $k$-crossing-degenerate and $k$-gap-planar graphs, string graphs and graphs of bounded layered treewidth. The hereditary hypothesis is essential: the analogous statement for single graphs $G$ with $\operatorname{td}(G)\in O(\sqrt{n})$ is false.

name: AX_f_free_induced_girth_preserving_bounded
title: Girth Conjecture (strengthening of Theorem 3)
statement_text: For every triangle-free graph $F$, there is a constant $c_F$ and graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large chromatic number and the same girth as $F$ such that every $F$-free induced subgraph of $G$ is $c_F$-colourable.
context_text: Here $G$ is $F$-free if it contains no induced copy of $F$. The authors prove that for every graph $F$ with at least one edge there are a constant $c_F$ and graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large chromatic number with the same clique number as $F$ in which every $F$-free induced subgraph is $c_F$-colourable, generalizing results of Carbonero, Hompe, Moore and Spirkl (disproving the Galvin–Rödl/Esperet conjecture) and of Briański, Davies and Walczak; in particular a triangle-free $F$ yields a triangle-free $G$. It is natural to ask whether $G$ can also have the same girth as $F$; the authors conjecture so but could not prove it, and in their concluding section state the conjecture in the more general form: for every graph $F$ with at least one cycle there are $b_F$ and graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large chromatic number and the same girth as $F$ whose $F$-free induced subgraphs are $b_F$-colourable. As a weaker result, they prove the analogue with odd girth (length of a shortest odd cycle): for every nonbipartite $F$ there are such $G$ with the same odd girth as $F$. A necessary condition, that graphs of girth at least $g$ form a vertex Ramsey class, holds by a theorem of Nešetřil and Rödl. Their construction (adding edges according to residues of distances in a base graph) unavoidably creates many $4$-cycles, so even the case $F=C_5$ would be very interesting.

name: AX_induced_menger_bounded_degree_linear_separator
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: For every $d, \Delta \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists a constant $C = C(d, \Delta) > 0$ such that the following holds. If $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $G$ is a graph with $\Delta(G) \leq \Delta$ and $X, Y \subseteq V(G)$, then there exists either (1) $k$ $X$-$Y$-paths pairwise at distance at least $d$ in $G$, or (2) a set of less than $Ck$ vertices in $G$ which separates $X$ and $Y$.
context_text: An $X$–$Y$ path has one end in $X$ and the other in $Y$ (a single vertex of $X\cap Y$ counts); a set $Z$ separates $X$ and $Y$ if it meets every $X$–$Y$ path; $\Delta(G)$ is the maximum degree, and the distance between two paths is the minimum distance in $G$ between their vertices. By Menger's theorem there are either $k$ disjoint $X$–$Y$ paths or fewer than $k$ separating vertices. Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu, and Albrechtsen et al., conjectured a coarse Menger theorem: for every $k$ there is $c=c(k)$ such that for every $d$ there are either $k$ disjoint $X$–$Y$ paths pairwise at distance at least $d$, or a set $Z$ of fewer than $k$ vertices whose ball $B_G(Z,cd)$ of radius $cd$ separates $X$ and $Y$ (the case $k=2$ is known); Albrechtsen et al. even conjectured that $c$ can be taken independent of $k$. In graphs of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ the ball has fewer than $\Delta^{cd+1}k$ vertices, so this stronger version would imply the present conjecture. The authors prove the first non-trivial case $d=2$ (pairwise non-adjacent paths, equivalently $k$ paths whose union is an induced subgraph): either there are $k$ pairwise non-adjacent $X$–$Y$ paths or fewer than $2^{\chi'_s(G)}k$ vertices separate $X$ and $Y$, where $\chi'_s(G)\le2\Delta(G)(\Delta(G)-1)+1$ is the strong chromatic index (minimum number of induced matchings partitioning $E(G)$). They also prove the $d=2$ statement for graphs excluding $K_r$ as a topological minor. The conjecture remains open for $d\ge3$.
notes: PDF source. The $d = 2$ case is proved within the paper (Theorem 1.5); the conjecture for $d \geq 3$ remains open.
paper_title: On an induced version of Menger's theorem

name: AX_2_extremal_digraphs_hajos_characterization
title: Conjecture 9.2
statement_text: A digraph is 2-extremal if and only if it is in $\mathcal{H}_2$.
context_text: Digraphs are finite, without loops or parallel arcs, but may contain digons (a digon $[x,y]$ is the pair of arcs $xy,yx$); a symmetric odd cycle is an odd cycle with every edge replaced by a digon. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum number of parts in a partition of $V(D)$ into sets inducing acyclic subdigraphs. For distinct vertices $x,y$, $\lambda(x,y)$ is the maximum number of arc-disjoint directed $xy$-paths, and $\lambda(D)=\max_{x\ne y}\lambda(x,y)$ is the maximum local arc-connectivity; Neumann-Lara proved $\vec{\chi}(D)\le\lambda(D)+1$. A digraph $D$ is $k$-extremal if it is strong (strongly connected), its underlying graph is $2$-connected, and $\vec{\chi}(D)=\lambda(D)+1=k+1$. The directed Hajós join of $D_1$ and $D_2$ with respect to arcs $uv_1\in A(D_1)$ and $v_2w\in A(D_2)$ is obtained from the disjoint union of $D_1-uv_1$ and $D_2-v_2w$ by identifying $v_1$ and $v_2$ and adding the arc $uw$. A 2-Hajós tree join is built from a tree $T$ embedded in the plane with at least two edges, a partition $(A,B)$ of $E(T)$ such that every leaf-to-leaf path of $T$ contains an even number of edges of $B$, the circular ordering $z_1,\dots,z_\ell$ of the leaves of $T$ given by the embedding, and for each edge $u_iv_i\in A$ a digraph $D_i$ containing the digon $[u_i,v_i]$, meeting $T$ exactly in $\{u_i,v_i\}$, the $D_i$ being otherwise pairwise disjoint: replace each edge $u_iv_i\in A$ by $D_i-[u_i,v_i]$, each edge of $B$ by a digon, and add the directed cycle $z_1\to z_2\to\dots\to z_\ell\to z_1$. $\mathcal{H}_2$ is the smallest class of digraphs containing all symmetric odd cycles and closed under directed Hajós joins and 2-Hajós tree joins; checking that its members are 2-extremal is routine. The authors' main theorem characterizes, for $k\ge3$, the digraphs with $\vec{\chi}(D)=\lambda(D)+1=k+1$ (a block of a strong component lies in a class generated from bidirected odd wheels when $k=3$, or from the symmetric complete digraph on $k+1$ vertices when $k\ge4$, by directed Hajós joins and (ordinary) Hajós tree joins), and shows that the 1-extremal digraphs are exactly the directed cycles; the case $k=2$ (dichromatic number $3$) is left open and this conjecture proposes its characterization, generalizing Mohar's directed Brooks theorem and the undirected result of Stiebitz and Toft.

name: AX_happy_triples_bound_small_max_degree
title: Open problem on happy triples for $l < k/2$
statement_text: It would be interesting to consider the best upper bound on the number of happy triples in a graph with $k$ edges and maximum degree at most $l$, for the regime when $l < k/2$.
context_text: In a graph $G$, a set $\{u,v,w\}$ of three vertices is a happy triple if $G[\{u,v,w\}]$ has at least two edges. The authors prove that a graph with $k$ edges and maximum degree at most $l\ge k/2$ has at most $\binom{l}{2}+\binom{k-l+1}{2}$ happy triples, and that this is best possible: for $l>k/2$ it is attained by joining the centres of the stars $K_{1,l-1}$ and $K_{1,k-l}$ by an edge, and for $l=k/2$ by $K_{2,l}$ (for $l\ge k$ the maximum is $\binom{k}{2}$, attained by $K_{1,k}$). This bound is used to count triangles with two edges of the same colour, in the authors' improved bounds for the triangle case of Aharoni's rainbow generalisation of the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture. For $l<k/2$ the question is open; the authors' computer program (a dynamic programming upper bound) gives little insight: for example, for $l=3$ and $k=3t$ the value it outputs is the number of happy triples of $K_{t,3}$, which does not have maximum degree $3$ for $t\ge4$.
