name: AX_cube_complex_boundary_distance_rigidity
title: Question 1
statement_text: Under what conditions is a finite $k$-dimensional cube complex $X \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ reconstructible up to combinatorial type from its boundary distances?
context_text: A cube complex is a (regular) CW complex whose $n$-cells are $n$-cubes glued along cubical faces by combinatorial isometries; its dimension is the largest dimension of a cube, and distances are measured in the graph metric of its $1$-skeleton. For $X$ embedded in $\mathbb{R}^k$ (with $k$ its dimension; otherwise reconstruction is trivial), the boundary $\partial X$ is its topological boundary, which for finite complexes does not depend on the embedding, and the boundary distances are the pairwise distances, in the whole $1$-skeleton, between labelled vertices of $\partial X$; reconstructing up to combinatorial type means determining $X$ up to a cell-preserving isomorphism. Haslegrave proved that a planar quadrangulation of a disc with all internal vertices of degree at least $4$ is determined by its boundary distances, and the degree condition is necessary. A cube complex is CAT(0) if it is simply connected and the link of every vertex is a flag simplicial complex (any set of pairwise adjacent vertices spans a simplex: Gromov's link condition, i.e. nonpositive curvature); for disc quadrangulations this is exactly Haslegrave's degree condition. The authors answer the question for $k=3$: every finite CAT(0) cube complex embeddable in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is reconstructible from its boundary distances, and examples show that both simple connectivity and the flag condition are needed; they also show that every finite CAT(0) cube complex of dimension at most $2$ is reconstructible (with a combinatorial notion of boundary, no embedding being needed). They conjecture that for every $k\ge4$ every finite CAT(0) cube complex embeddable in $\mathbb{R}^k$ is reconstructible, and more generally that for every $k\ge3$ every finite CAT(0) cube complex is, noting difficulties in generalising their thickening step.
paper_title: Boundary rigidity of 3D CAT(0) cube complexes

name: AX_connectivity_code_torus_product_cycles
title: Open Problem: m(C_t × C_s) for all t, s
statement_text: Determine $m(C_t \times C_s)$ for all $t, s$.
context_text: The symmetric difference of two graphs $(V,E_1)$ and $(V,E_2)$ on the same vertex set is $(V,E_1\oplus E_2)$. For a graph $H$, a connectivity code for $H$ is a collection of spanning subgraphs of $H$ such that the symmetric difference of any two distinct members is a connected spanning subgraph of $H$, and $m(H)$ is the maximum size of a connectivity code for $H$. Here $C_t\times C_s$ is the Cartesian (box) product of two cycles (the $t$ by $s$ torus), which is $4$-regular and $4$-edge-connected. In general $2^{\lfloor k'(H)/2\rfloor}\le m(H)\le 2^{k'(H)}$, where $k'(H)$ is the edge-connectivity (the lower bound via Nash-Williams' tree packing), so $4\le m(C_t\times C_s)\le16$. Equality $m(H)=2^{k'(H)}$ holds for complete graphs and, as shown by Bai, Gao, Ma and Wu (who asked about larger tori), $m(C_3\times C_3)=16$; the authors prove it also holds for every $d$-regular mild expander. On the other hand they show that for $s>(2^t+1)2^{t-1}$ the $(t+1)$-regular, $(t+1)$-edge-connected graph $K_t\times C_s$ has $m\le 2^t$; in particular $m(C_3\times C_s)\le8$ for all $s>36$, which answers the question of Bai et al. but does not determine the exact value; they note that determining $m(C_t\times C_s)$ for all $t,s$ remains open.
notes: PDF source; $\times$ denotes the Cartesian (box) product of graphs. The special case $t=3$ ($K_3=C_3$) is resolved by Proposition 3.2; all other cases remain open.
paper_title: Connectivity Graph-Codes

name: AX_levine_hat_intersecting_success_vanishes
title: Conjecture 2.1
statement_text: $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t)$ tends to $0$ as $t$ grows.
context_text: Let $B=\{0,1\}^n$ and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a family of subsets of $B$ (winning sets). In the $t$-player game each player is assigned a uniformly random point of $B$, sees the points of the other players but not her own, and then all players simultaneously name a set of $\mathcal{W}$; they succeed if every player named a set containing her own point. A strategy is a $t$-tuple $(f_1,\dots,f_t)$ with $f_i:B^{t-1}\to\mathcal{W}$, its winning set is the set of $x\in B^t$ with $x_i\in f_i(x^{-i})$ for all $i$ ($x^{-i}$ is $x$ with the $i$-th coordinate deleted), $p(t,n)$ is the maximum uniform measure of such a winning set and $p(t)=\lim_{n\to\infty}p(t,n)$. Three choices of $\mathcal{W}$: dictators $\{x:x_i=1\}$ (this is Levine's hat game: each player has a stack of $n$ random black/white hats and must point to a black hat on her own head), giving $p_{\mathrm{dict}}$; all intersecting families (sets $W$ such that any $x,y\in W$ have a coordinate $i$ with $x_i=y_i=1$), giving $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}$; and all balanced monotone families (up-sets containing exactly half of $\{0,1\}^n$), giving $p_{\mathrm{monotone}}$. Since every dictator is intersecting and every maximal intersecting family is balanced monotone, $p_{\mathrm{monotone}}(t)\ge p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t)\ge p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)$. Levine's conjecture is that $p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$; known bounds are $0.35\le p_{\mathrm{dict}}(2)\le0.361607$ and $p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)=\Omega(1/\log t)$, and the authors prove $p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t+1)<p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)$ for all $t\ge1$. This conjecture is the strengthening of Levine's conjecture where winning sets are all intersecting families. It is equivalent to the graph statement $\lim_{t\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar{\alpha}(K(n)^{\square t})=0$, where $K(n)$ is the Kneser graph on $\{0,1\}^n$. Changing the order of the limits gives an uninteresting question, since for fixed $n$, $p(t,n)\to0$.
paper_title: The success probability in Levine's hat problem, and independent sets in graphs

name: AX_levine_hat_intersecting_kneser_independence
title: Conjecture 2.6
statement_text: $$\lim_{t \to \infty} \lim_{n \to \infty} \bar{\alpha}\!\left(K(n)^{\square t}\right) = 0.$$
context_text: The Kneser graph $K(n)$ has vertex set $\{0,1\}^n$, with $x\sim y$ when their supports are disjoint (no $i$ with $x_i=y_i=1$); its independent sets are exactly the intersecting families. The Hamming product $G_1\square\cdots\square G_t$ has vertex set $V(G_1)\times\cdots\times V(G_t)$, two tuples being adjacent if they differ in exactly one coordinate $i$ and are adjacent in $G_i$ there (the usual Cartesian product); $G^{\square t}$ is the $t$-fold power. $\bar{\alpha}(G)=\alpha(G)/|V(G)|$. This is a graph-theoretic restatement of the conjecture that $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t)\to0$, coming from a generalization of Levine's hat game: $t$ players each receive a uniformly random point of $\{0,1\}^n$, each sees all points but her own, and they simultaneously each name an intersecting family; they win if each named family contains her own point. An independent set of $K(n)^{\square t}$ meets every one-dimensional fiber of $(\{0,1\}^n)^t$ in an intersecting family, exactly as a winning set of a strategy does, which gives the authors' observation $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t,n)=\bar{\alpha}(K(n)^{\square t})$, where $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t,n)$ is the maximum success probability and $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t)$ its limit as $n\to\infty$. Since every dictator family $\{x:x_i=1\}$ is intersecting, the conjecture implies Levine's hat conjecture (where players must name a dictator, i.e. point to a black hat in a stack of $n$ random black/white hats), which asserts that the success probability tends to $0$ as $t\to\infty$.

name: AX_independence_ratio_random_subset_gap_positive
title: Conjecture 2.8
statement_text: $\varepsilon^*(\alpha) > 0$ for all $\alpha \in (0, 1/2)$.
context_text: For a graph $G$ let $\mu$ be the uniform probability measure on $V(G)$, $\bar{\alpha}(G)=\max_I\mu(I)$ over independent sets $I$. Let $\mathcal{D}_r$ be the set of probability distributions on subsets $R\subseteq[r]$ in which every $i\in[r]$ belongs to $R$ with probability $1/2$ and all these events are positively correlated, and $\mathcal{D}=\bigcup_r\mathcal{D}_r$. Define $\alpha^*(G)=\max E_{R\sim D}\left[\max_I\mu\left(I\cap\bigcup_{i\in R}V_i\right)\right]$, the outer maximum being over $r$, $D\in\mathcal{D}_r$ and partitions $V(G)=V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_r$ (parts may be empty), the inner one over independent sets $I$ of $G$. Let $\varepsilon^*(\alpha)=\inf_{G:\,\bar{\alpha}(G)\ge\alpha}\{\bar{\alpha}(G)-\alpha^*(G)\}$. The authors show that this conjecture would imply that $\bar{\alpha}(K(n)^{\square t})$ tends to $0$ (as $t\to\infty$, after $n\to\infty$), where $K(n)$ is the Kneser graph on $\{0,1\}^n$ (vectors adjacent when their supports are disjoint) and $\square$ the Cartesian (Hamming) product, and hence Levine's conjecture that the success probability in his hat game (each of $t$ players has a stack of random black/white hats, sees all other hats and must point to a black hat on her own head; all must succeed) tends to $0$ as $t$ grows. The authors do not know whether the conjecture holds even when $D$ is the binomial distribution, or when each $V_i$ is a single vertex (which is the conjecture $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha)>0$ about a uniformly random subset of vertices).
notes: PDF source — some definitions in Section 2.4 rely on notation that may be partially garbled; the conjecture statement itself is clearly readable.
paper_title: The success probability in Levine's hat problem, and independent sets in graphs

name: AX_independence_ratio_binomial_subset_gap_positive
title: Conjecture 2.9
statement_text: $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha) > 0$ for all $\alpha \in (0, 1/2)$. In other words, there exists a monotone non-decreasing function $\varepsilon^{**} : (0,1/2) \to (0,1/2)$ such that the following holds: if $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices with maximum independent set of size $\alpha n$, $W$ is a binomial random subset of $V(G)$, and $I_W$ is the maximal independent set contained in $W$, then $$\alpha^{**}(G) = E_W\!\left[|I_W|/n\right] \leq \alpha - \varepsilon^{**}(\alpha).$$
context_text: For a graph $G$ let $\mu$ be the uniform probability measure on $V(G)$, $\bar{\alpha}(G)=\max_I\mu(I)$ over independent sets $I$. $\alpha^{**}(G)=E_W[\max_I\mu(I\cap W)]$, where $W$ is a uniformly random subset of $V(G)$ (each vertex included independently with probability $1/2$) and $I$ ranges over independent sets of $G$; that is, $\alpha^{**}(G)$ is the expected independence number of the random induced subgraph $G[W]$ divided by $n$. $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha)=\inf_{G:\,\bar{\alpha}(G)\ge\alpha}\{\bar{\alpha}(G)-\alpha^{**}(G)\}$; in the second formulation, $I_W$ denotes a maximum independent set of $G[W]$. This is the special case, where each part of the partition is a single vertex, of the authors' more general conjecture $\varepsilon^*(\alpha)>0$ for positively correlated random unions of parts, which would imply Levine's hat conjecture; the authors call it a fundamental problem in the study of independent sets in graphs. They prove it for $\alpha>1/4$: if $\alpha(G)=(1/4+\tau)n$ with $0<\tau<1/4$ then $\alpha^{**}(G)\le1/4+\tau-\tau^2/3$; and for regular graphs with $\alpha>1/8$: for every $\tau>0$ there is $g(\tau)>0$ such that every regular $G$ with $\alpha(G)=(1/8+\tau)n$ has $\alpha^{**}(G)\le1/8+\tau-g(\tau)$. It remains open below these thresholds. The best known upper bound, from $G(n,p)$, is $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha)<\alpha2^{-\Omega(1/\alpha)}$.
paper_title: The success probability in Levine's hat problem, and independent sets in graphs

name: AX_ramsey_sqrt_edges_bound_multicolor
title: Informal Problem: extending the $\sqrt{m}$ Ramsey bound to more than two colors for graphs
statement_text: It would be interesting to extend the result $r_2(G; 2) \leq 2^{c\sqrt{m}}$ (for any graph $G$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices) to more than two colors.
context_text: For a $k$-uniform hypergraph $H$ and an integer $q$, $r_k(H;q)$ is the $q$-color Ramsey number: the minimum $N$ such that every $q$-coloring of the edges of the complete $k$-uniform hypergraph $K_N^{(k)}$ contains a monochromatic copy of $H$; so $r_2(G;q)$ is the usual $q$-color Ramsey number of a graph $G$. Erdős and Graham conjectured that among graphs with $m=\binom n2$ edges the clique $K_n$ has the largest Ramsey number; Erdős made the weaker conjecture that $r_2(G;2)\le 2^{c\sqrt m}$ for every graph $G$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, which is sharp by the lower bound $r_2(n;2)>\sqrt2^{\,n}$ for cliques. Sudakov proved this conjecture, but his argument only works for two colors. The present paper proves the hypergraph analogue for every fixed number of colors: for $k\ge 3$ and fixed $q$, every $k$-uniform hypergraph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices has $r_k(H;q)\le\mathrm{tw}_k(C_{k,q}\sqrt m)$, where $\mathrm{tw}_1(x)=x$ and $\mathrm{tw}_k(x)=2^{\mathrm{tw}_{k-1}(x)}$, tight for $q\ge4$ (resolving a problem of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov); the graph case $k=2$ with $q\ge3$ colors is what the remark leaves open, the natural target being $r_2(G;q)\le 2^{c_q\sqrt m}$ for every graph $G$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices.
notes: Stated as a brief remark in the introduction without a labelled environment.
paper_title: Ramsey numbers of hypergraphs of a given size

name: AX_set_coloring_ramsey_zero_rate_equality
title: Informal Conjecture (Equality in Theorem 1.1 near the zero-rate threshold)
statement_text: We suspect that there may even be equality in the bound $R(q+1; r, s) \geq A_q(r, s) + 1$ when $s$ is sufficiently close to $(1 - 1/q)r$, i.e., $R(q+1; r, s) = A_q(r, s) + 1$, though our methods fall somewhat short of proving this.
context_text: For positive integers $n,r,s$ with $r>s$, the set-coloring Ramsey number $R(n;r,s)$ is the minimum $N$ such that whenever every edge of $K_N$ receives a set of $s$ colors from a palette of $r$ colors, there is a monochromatic $K_n$, i.e. $n$ vertices such that all edges between them share a common color. $A_q(m,d)$ is the maximum size of a code $C\subseteq[q]^m$ in which any two codewords differ in at least $d$ coordinates (Hamming distance at least $d$); by Plotkin, codes of positive rate exist for $d<(1-1/q-\varepsilon)m$ but not for $d\ge(1-1/q)m$. Conlon, Fox, He, Mubayi, Suk and Verstraëte proved that $R(q+1;r,s)\ge A_q(r,s)+1$ for all positive integers $q,r,s$ with $r>s$, and that for fixed $q$ the value $s/r=1-1/q$ is a threshold: $R(q+1;r,s)$ grows exponentially in $r$ below it and is bounded above it. The present paper proves a near-converse close to the threshold: for every $q$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $c>0$ such that if $s\le(1-1/q)r$ and $j=(1-1/q)r-s+1$ then $R(q+1;r,s)\le\max((1+\varepsilon)A_q(r,s-cj),\varepsilon s)$, the maximum being unnecessary when $q$ and $r\ge q$ are powers of the same prime. So the two problems are essentially equivalent near the zero-rate threshold, and the authors suspect that the lower bound is exactly tight there.
notes: PDF source — stated as running prose ('We suspect that there may even be equality in Theorem 1.1 when s is sufficiently close to (1−1/q)r'); math notation is readable in context but PDF extraction may garble some symbols.
paper_title: Set-coloring Ramsey numbers and error-correcting codes near the zero-rate threshold

name: AX_vantage_sign_patterns_r_dependence_gap
title: Gap in $r$-dependence of sign-pattern bound
statement_text: For tuples of $m$ functions on $\mathbb{R}^N$, each a linear combination of at most $r$ terms $g^{1/s}$ with $g$ a polynomial of degree at most $\Delta$ that is nonnegative on $\mathbb{R}^N$, the number of distinct proper sign patterns is at most $2(2s^{r-2}\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N 2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$, which is exponential in $r$. Any such bound must have at least a linear dependence on $r$ if it is to depend polynomially on $m$. It would be interesting to close this gap.
context_text: For a tuple $\mathcal{F}=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of real functions on $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, the sign pattern of $x$ is $(\mathrm{sgn} f_1(x),\dots,\mathrm{sgn} f_m(x))\in\{0,1,-1\}^m$, and it is proper if no entry is $0$. Warren's theorem bounds the number of proper sign patterns of $m$ polynomials of degree at most $\Delta$ in $N$ variables by $2(2\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$. As an analogue, the authors prove that if each $f_i$ is of the form $\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}a_{i,j}g_{i,j}^{1/s}$ with $r_i\le r$ ($r\ge2$), real coefficients $a_{i,j}$ and polynomials $g_{i,j}$ of degree at most $\Delta$ that are nonnegative on $\mathbb{R}^N$, then the number of proper sign patterns is at most $2(2s^{r-2}\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$, a bound exponential in $r$. They use it to count the orderings of a set of candidate points by the sum of Euclidean distances to $k$ vantage points. The authors show that the dependence on $r$ cannot be removed: with $N=1$ and $\Delta=s=2$ fixed, the functions $f_{\vec a}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i\big(\sqrt{(x-i)^2+\delta^2}-\sqrt{(x-i)^2}\big)$ with $\vec a\in\{-1,1\}^\ell$ and small $\delta>0$ satisfy $\mathrm{sgn} f_{\vec a}(j)=a_j$ for $j\in[\ell]$, so with $\ell=2^m$ one obtains $m$ such functions with $r=2^{m+1}$ realizing all $2^m$ proper sign patterns. Informally, this forces at least a linear dependence on $r$ for a bound polynomial in $m$, far below the exponential dependence of their bound. This is real algebraic geometry rather than graph theory.
notes: Stated informally in prose; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Ordering Candidates via Vantage Points

name: AX_vantage_square_roots_sum_components_gap
title: Gap in connected-component count for sums of square roots
statement_text: For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ a linear combination of $r$ square roots of everywhere-positive quadratic polynomials, the number of connected components of $\mathbb{R} \setminus V(f)$ is at most $2^{r-1}+1$, while at least $2r-1$ components are achievable. It would be interesting to narrow the gap between this linear lower bound and the exponential upper bound.
context_text: For a tuple $\mathcal{F}=(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of real functions on $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, the sign pattern of $x$ is $(\mathrm{sgn} f_1(x),\dots,\mathrm{sgn} f_m(x))\in\{0,1,-1\}^m$, and it is proper if no entry is $0$. Warren's theorem bounds the number of proper sign patterns of $m$ polynomials of degree at most $\Delta$ in $N$ variables by $2(2\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$. As an analogue, the authors prove that if each $f_i$ is of the form $\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}a_{i,j}g_{i,j}^{1/s}$ with $r_i\le r$ ($r\ge2$), real coefficients $a_{i,j}$ and polynomials $g_{i,j}$ of degree at most $\Delta$ that are nonnegative on $\mathbb{R}^N$, then the number of proper sign patterns is at most $2(2s^{r-2}\Delta)^N\sum_{\ell=0}^N2^\ell\binom{m}{\ell}$, a bound exponential in $r$. They use it to count the orderings of a set of candidate points by the sum of Euclidean distances to $k$ vantage points. This is a simpler companion problem with $N=m=1$ and $\Delta=s=2$: for $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ a linear combination of $r$ square roots of everywhere-positive quadratic polynomials, the number of proper sign patterns is trivially at most $2$, so one counts instead the connected components of $\mathbb{R}\setminus V(f)$, where $V(f)=\{x: f(x)=0\}$ is the zero set. A multiplication-by-conjugates argument, as in the proof of their sign-pattern bound, gives at most $2^{r-1}+1$ components, while $f(x)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}(-1)^ia_i^{1/10}\big(\sqrt{x^2+a_i^2}-a_i\big)$ with $0<a_1<\dots<a_{r-1}$ growing extremely quickly has $2r-1$ components. This is real algebraic geometry rather than graph theory.
notes: PDF source — mathematical expressions (e.g. $2^{r-1}+1$ vs $2r-1$) may be garbled; values interpreted from the authors' explicit statement 'linear lower bound and exponential upper bound'.
paper_title: Ordering Candidates via Vantage Points

name: AX_vantage_protrusive_ordering_5_points
title: Five-point protrusive-but-not-witnessed construction
statement_text: Does there exist a set $C$ of $5$ points such that some protrusive ordering of $C$ is not in $\Psi(C)$?
context_text: For a set $C=\{c_1,\dots,c_n\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ of candidate points and a finite multiset $V=\{v_1,\dots,v_k\}$ of vantage points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $D_V(x)=\sum_{i}\|x-v_i\|$ (Euclidean distance). If the values $D_V(c_1),\dots,D_V(c_n)$ are distinct, $V$ witnesses the ordering of $C$ by increasing $D_V$. $\Psi(C)$ is the set of orderings of $C$ witnessed by some finite multiset $V$ (of any size). A tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is protrusive if for every $i<n$ the point $x_{i+1}$ is not in the convex hull of $x_1,\dots,x_i$. By the triangle inequality every ordering in $\Psi(C)$ is protrusive, and the authors prove that $\Psi(C)$ is exactly the set of protrusive orderings of $C$ when $d=1$, when $|C|\le4$, and when $C$ is the vertex set of a vertex-transitive polytope. In the other direction they construct a $6$-point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (the vertices of an equilateral triangle together with three points just outside the midpoints of its sides, in convex position) for which some protrusive ordering is not in $\Psi(C)$, and ask whether $5$ points suffice. The formal question does not fix the dimension; the $6$-point example is planar. This is combinatorial geometry rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Ordering Candidates via Vantage Points

name: AX_tournament_strong_eh_backedge_forest
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: A tournament has the strong EH-property if and only if it admits a numbering for which the backedge graph is a forest.
context_text: Tournaments are finite; a tournament $G$ is $H$-free if it has no subtournament isomorphic to $H$. A pure pair in a tournament $G$ is an ordered pair $(A,B)$ of disjoint vertex sets such that every vertex of $B$ is adjacent from every vertex of $A$ (all edges go from $A$ to $B$); its order is $\min(|A|,|B|)$. A tournament $H$ has the strong EH-property if there is $c>0$ such that every $H$-free tournament $G$ with $|G|>1$ has a pure pair of order at least $c|G|$; this implies the (weak) EH-property, that some $\tau>0$ makes every $H$-free tournament $G$ contain a transitive subtournament on $|G|^\tau$ vertices (the tournament Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asserts that all tournaments have it). For a numbering $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $H$, the backedge graph is the ordered graph on $V(H)$ in which, for $i<j$, $v_iv_j$ is an edge (a backedge) iff the edge of $H$ is directed from $v_j$ to $v_i$. $D_5$ is the unique $5$-vertex tournament in which every vertex has out-degree two. For graphs, the authors previously proved that a graph $H$ has the analogous strong property (linear pure pairs in graphs excluding $H$ and $\overline{H}$ as induced subgraphs) if and only if $H$ or $\overline{H}$ is a forest. For tournaments they prove one direction: every tournament with the strong EH-property admits a numbering whose backedge graph is a forest. They initially found the converse unlikely, but tried hard to disprove it and failed, and pose it as a conjecture. They are far from proving it: the tournament $P_7^-$ has a backedge graph that is a forest with four edges, yet they cannot even show it has the weak EH-property. They prove that tournaments with a numbering with at most three backedges have the strong EH-property (except one undecided case), so every tournament with at most six vertices has it except three undecided ones, and give a seven-vertex tournament $P_7$ without it.
paper_title: Pure pairs. X. Tournaments and the strong Erdos-Hajnal property

name: AX_tournament_strong_eh_three_backedges_d5
title: Informal question: can the D5-freeness hypothesis in Theorem 1.6 be dropped?
statement_text: Let $H$ be a tournament that admits a numbering $(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ for which the backedge graph $B$ has at most three edges. The authors prove that if moreover $H$ is $D_5$-free (that is, there do not exist $1\le a<b<c<d<e\le n$ with $E(B)=\{v_av_d,v_av_e,v_bv_e\}$), then $H$ has the strong EH-property. Perhaps the $D_5$-freeness condition can be omitted, but that remains open.
context_text: Tournaments are finite; a tournament $G$ is $H$-free if it has no subtournament isomorphic to $H$. A pure pair in a tournament $G$ is an ordered pair $(A,B)$ of disjoint vertex sets such that every vertex of $B$ is adjacent from every vertex of $A$ (all edges go from $A$ to $B$); its order is $\min(|A|,|B|)$. A tournament $H$ has the strong EH-property if there is $c>0$ such that every $H$-free tournament $G$ with $|G|>1$ has a pure pair of order at least $c|G|$; this implies the (weak) EH-property, that some $\tau>0$ makes every $H$-free tournament $G$ contain a transitive subtournament on $|G|^\tau$ vertices (the tournament Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asserts that all tournaments have it). For a numbering $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $H$, the backedge graph is the ordered graph on $V(H)$ in which, for $i<j$, $v_iv_j$ is an edge (a backedge) iff the edge of $H$ is directed from $v_j$ to $v_i$. $D_5$ is the unique $5$-vertex tournament in which every vertex has out-degree two. The two forms of the $D_5$ condition are equivalent since, up to isomorphism, $D_5$ has only one backedge graph with three edges, and $D_5$ itself has the strong EH-property (Berger, Choromanski, Chudnovsky and Zerbib). The open case is thus a tournament with three backedges that contains $D_5$, i.e. whose backedge graph is $\{v_av_d,v_av_e,v_bv_e\}$ for some $a<b<c<d<e$. Every tournament with the strong EH-property admits a numbering whose backedge graph is a forest, and the authors conjecture the converse; the three-backedge theorem is a small step in this direction.
paper_title: Pure pairs. X. Tournaments and the strong Erdos-Hajnal property

name: AX_separable_index_pattern_avoiding_polynomial
title: Question 1.2
statement_text: Is the maximum separable index among permutations avoiding a pattern of size $k$ polynomial in $k$?
context_text: A permutation $\sigma$ contains a pattern $\pi$ (of size $k$) if some $k$ entries of $\sigma$ appear in the same relative order as the entries of $\pi$, and avoids $\pi$ otherwise. Separable permutations are those obtained from the trivial permutation $1$ by repeatedly taking direct sums (placing two permutation matrices as diagonal blocks) and skew sums (antidiagonal blocks); equivalently they are the permutations avoiding $2413$ and $3142$, or those whose permutation graph is a cograph. The separable index $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$ is the smallest $k$ such that $\sigma$ is a product (composition) of $k$ separable permutations. The authors' main theorem is that every permutation avoiding a fixed pattern $\pi$ of size $k$ is a product of at most $2^{2^{O(k)}}$ separable permutations; conversely, products of a bounded number of separable permutations avoid some pattern, since there are only $2^{O(cn)}$ products of $c$ of them on $n$ elements. For specific patterns the bound is much lower (avoiding the decreasing pattern of length $k$ gives separable index $O(\log k)$), but from Fox's lower bounds on the growth of pattern-avoiding classes, for almost all patterns of size $k$ the maximum separable index of permutations avoiding it is at least $\Omega(k^{1/4-\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. The question asks whether a polynomial upper bound holds; as an easier first step, the authors suggest bringing the upper bound down to singly exponential.
paper_title: Factoring Pattern-Free Permutations into Separable ones

name: AX_separable_index_parameterized_complexity
title: Question 1.3
statement_text: What is the parameterised complexity of computing $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$, and of approximating it within a constant factor?
context_text: A permutation $\sigma$ contains a pattern $\pi$ (of size $k$) if some $k$ entries of $\sigma$ appear in the same relative order as the entries of $\pi$, and avoids $\pi$ otherwise. Separable permutations are those obtained from the trivial permutation $1$ by repeatedly taking direct sums (placing two permutation matrices as diagonal blocks) and skew sums (antidiagonal blocks); equivalently they are the permutations avoiding $2413$ and $3142$, or those whose permutation graph is a cograph. The separable index $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$ is the smallest $k$ such that $\sigma$ is a product (composition) of $k$ separable permutations. Given $\sigma$ and $k$, the main theorem yields an FPT approximation: there is a pattern $\pi$ (of size exponential in $k$) avoided by every product of $k$ separable permutations, while every permutation avoiding $\pi$ has separable index at most $f(k)$; running the Guillemot–Marx pattern recognition algorithm then either shows that $\sigma$ contains $\pi$, so $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)>k$, or that $\sigma$ avoids $\pi$, so $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)\le f(k)$. The approximation function $f$ is triple exponential in $k$. The authors ask whether this can be improved, possibly up to an exact FPT algorithm parameterised by $\mathrm{sep}(\sigma)$, and whether a constant-factor approximation is possible.
paper_title: Factoring Pattern-Free Permutations into Separable ones

name: AX_random_graph_correspondence_chromatic_n_logn
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: For every fixed positive $p \leq 1$, Erdős-Rényi random graph $G(n, 1-p)$ a.a.s. has correspondence chromatic number $\Theta(n/\log n)$.
context_text: $G(n,1-p)$ is the Erdős–Rényi random graph in which each pair of vertices is an edge independently with probability $1-p$ (so for $p<1$ it is dense; for $p=1$ it is edgeless and the statement is degenerate). Correspondence coloring (DP-coloring, Dvořák and Postle) generalizes list coloring: a correspondence assignment $(L,M)$ gives each vertex $v$ a list $L(v)$ and each edge $uv$ a (not necessarily perfect) matching $M_{uv}$ between $\{u\}\times L(u)$ and $\{v\}\times L(v)$; an $(L,M)$-coloring picks $\varphi(v)\in L(v)$ for every $v$ such that $(u,\varphi(u))$ and $(v,\varphi(v))$ are not matched in $M_{uv}$ for any edge $uv$; the correspondence chromatic number is the least $\ell$ such that $G$ is $(L,M)$-colorable for every assignment with all $|L(v)|\ge\ell$. Lower bound: $G(n,1-p)$ a.a.s. has independence number $O(\log n)$, so already $\chi=\Omega(n/\log n)$, and Bernshteyn's bound $\Omega(d/\log d)$ for graphs of average degree $d$ gives the same. The authors prove the upper bound $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ a.a.s., which matches the Hadwiger number $\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ of $G(n,p)$ and thus supports Linear Hadwiger's conjecture for correspondence coloring. Both extreme kinds of assignment need only $O(n/\log n)$ colors: list assignments (the list chromatic number of $G(n,1-p)$ is $O(n/\log n)$ a.a.s.) and uniformly random assignments with perfect matchings, for which they show that even $K_n$ is a.a.s. colorable with $\Theta(n/\log n)$ colors. The authors hope the conjecture is false, as this would separate list and correspondence chromatic numbers in a new way.
notes: PDF source; special characters (Erdős-Rényi) rendered via ASCII in extraction but mathematical content is unambiguous.
paper_title: Correspondence coloring of random graphs

name: AX_ramsey_goodness_books_threshold_not_tight
title: Informal Belief on Non-Optimality of p-Goodness Bound
statement_text: The bound $n \geq 2^{k^{10p}}$, which the authors prove sufficient for the $k$-book $B_{k,n}$ to be $p$-good (i.e. $r(K_p,B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+1$ for all $k,p\ge2$ and $n\ge 2^{k^{10p}}$), is not best possible.
context_text: The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the least $N$ such that every $N$-vertex graph contains $G$ or its complement contains $H$. Burr showed $r(G,H)\ge(\chi(G)-1)(|V(H)|-1)+s(G)$ for connected $H$ with at least $s(G)$ vertices, where $s(G)$ is the minimum size of a colour class in a proper $\chi(G)$-colouring of $G$; $H$ is $G$-good if equality holds, and $p$-good if moreover $G=K_p$, i.e. $r(K_p,H)=(p-1)(|V(H)|-1)+1$. For $n\ge k\ge1$, the $k$-book $B_{k,n}$ is the $n$-vertex graph consisting of a clique $K_k$ (the spine) and $n-k$ further vertices, pairwise non-adjacent, each adjacent to all of the spine. Nikiforov and Rousseau proved, using Szemerédi's regularity lemma, that $B_{k,n}$ is $p$-good for $n$ sufficiently large, with a tower-type bound, and asked for the best possible $n$. The authors give a regularity-free proof with the bound $n\ge2^{k^{10p}}$ and say they do not expect it to be best possible. In their concluding remarks they ask for the Ramsey goodness threshold, i.e. the smallest $n$ with $r(K_p,B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+1$: a random construction shows it is at least $(k/\log p)^{cp}$ for an absolute constant $c>0$, and it would be interesting to determine whether, for fixed $p$, the correct behaviour is polynomial or exponential in $k$. Improving the bound to one single-exponential in both $k$ and $p$ would give progress on a conjecture of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov on empty pairs in triangle-free graphs.
notes: PDF source — exponent reconstructed as $k^{10p}$ from surrounding proof; stated in prose as 'We do not expect the bound $n \geq 2k^{10p}$ to be best possible'.
paper_title: Ramsey goodness of books revisited

name: AX_ramsey_goodness_regularity_free_proof
title: Question on Eliminating the Regularity Lemma from Nikiforov–Rousseau's General Theorem
statement_text: Is it possible to completely eliminate the use of the regularity lemma from the proof of the general Ramsey goodness theorem of Nikiforov and Rousseau (Theorem 2.1 of their paper 'Ramsey goodness and beyond', Combinatorica 2009)?
context_text: The Ramsey number $r(G,H)$ is the least $N$ such that every $N$-vertex graph contains $G$ or its complement contains $H$. Burr showed $r(G,H)\ge(\chi(G)-1)(|V(H)|-1)+s(G)$ for connected $H$ with at least $s(G)$ vertices, where $s(G)$ is the minimum size of a colour class in a proper $\chi(G)$-colouring of $G$; $H$ is $G$-good if equality holds, and $p$-good if moreover $G=K_p$, i.e. $r(K_p,H)=(p-1)(|V(H)|-1)+1$. For $n\ge k\ge1$, the $k$-book $B_{k,n}$ is the $n$-vertex graph consisting of a clique $K_k$ (the spine) and $n-k$ further vertices, pairwise non-adjacent, each adjacent to all of the spine. Using Szemerédi's regularity lemma (hence with tower-type quantitative bounds), Nikiforov and Rousseau proved a very general goodness theorem, the most general result in the field, giving tight bounds on $r(G,H)$ for several families of sparse graphs $G,H$ with $|V(G)|<\delta|V(H)|$; it implies for instance that clique subdivisions and large planar graphs are $p$-good, and that $r(B_{p-1,\delta n},B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+1$ for large $n$. The authors avoid the regularity lemma for special cases: $B_{k,n}$ is $p$-good for $n\ge2^{k^{10p}}$, and for a complete $p$-partite graph $G$ with parts $a_1\le\dots\le a_{p-1}\le t$ and $a_p\le\delta n$, $r(G,B_{k,n})=(p-1)(n-1)+a_1$ if and only if $a_1=a_2=1$, with double-exponential bounds on $1/\delta$. They ask how far these ideas can be pushed, since a regularity-free proof of the general theorem would likely give much better quantitative bounds.
notes: Posed in prose in the introduction as 'for example, is it possible to completely eliminate the use of the regularity lemma from the proof of [28, Theorem 2.1]?'.
paper_title: Ramsey goodness of books revisited

name: AX_planar_square_root_np_complete
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: The $\mathcal{H}$-square-root problem is NP-complete for the class $\mathcal{H}$ of planar graphs.
context_text: The square $H^2$ of a graph $H$ has the same vertices, two vertices being adjacent iff their distance in $H$ is at most $2$; a square root of $G$ is a graph $H$ with $H^2=G$ (a graph can have several, e.g. $K_5$ has $C_5$ and $K_{1,4}$). For a graph class $\mathcal{H}$, the $\mathcal{H}$-square-root problem asks, given $G$, whether $G$ has a square root belonging to $\mathcal{H}$. It is polynomial for bipartite, outerplanar and proper interval graphs, graphs of girth at least $6$, and trees, cacti and block graphs, and NP-complete for all graphs (Motwani and Sudan), graphs of girth at least $5$, chordal graphs and split graphs. Since these hard classes are relatively dense, it was asked whether the problem becomes polynomial for sparse classes. The authors answer no: the problem (and even its promise version) is NP-complete for the class of $6$-apex graphs, i.e. graphs that become planar after deleting at most $6$ vertices, a minor-closed class at the bottom of the bounded-expansion hierarchy of sparse classes. They ask whether the apex vertices are necessary and believe that already the planar case is hard.
paper_title: Square roots of nearly planar graphs

name: AX_minor_free_underlying_treewidth_polynomial_treedepth
title: Question 1
statement_text: Can the upper bound $\operatorname{utw}(\mathcal{G}_{X})\le 2^{\operatorname{td}(X)+1}-4$ be improved? In particular, is $\operatorname{utw}(\mathcal{G}_{X})$ at most a polynomial function of $\operatorname{td}(X)$?
context_text: The strong product $G_1\boxtimes G_2$ has vertex set $V(G_1)\times V(G_2)$, with $(v,x)(w,y)$ an edge if $v=w$ and $xy\in E(G_2)$, or $x=y$ and $vw\in E(G_1)$, or $vw\in E(G_1)$ and $xy\in E(G_2)$; thus $H\boxtimes K_c$ is $H$ with each vertex blown up into a clique $K_c$. The treedepth $\mathrm{td}(X)$ of a graph $X$ is the minimum height (number of vertices on a root-to-leaf path) of a rooted forest $F$ on $V(X)$ such that every edge of $X$ joins a vertex to one of its ancestors in $F$; arbitrarily large graphs can have bounded treedepth. $\mathcal{G}_X$ is the class of $X$-minor-free graphs, and the underlying treewidth $\mathrm{utw}(\mathcal{G})$ of a graph class $\mathcal{G}$ (Campbell et al.) is the least integer $k$ such that, for some function $f$, every $G\in\mathcal{G}$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $H\boxtimes K_{f(\mathrm{tw}(G))}$ for some graph $H$ of treewidth at most $k$. The authors prove that for every graph $X$ there is $c$ such that every $X$-minor-free graph $G$ with $\mathrm{tw}(G)<t$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $H\boxtimes K_{ct}$ for some $H$ of treewidth at most $2^{\mathrm{td}(X)+1}-4$; together with a lower-bound construction this gives $\mathrm{td}(X)-2\le\mathrm{utw}(\mathcal{G}_X)\le2^{\mathrm{td}(X)+1}-4$, so underlying treewidth and treedepth of the excluded minor are tied. Combined with the Grid-Minor Theorem, for planar $X$ every $X$-minor-free graph is a subgraph of $H\boxtimes K_c$ with $\mathrm{tw}(H)\le2^{\mathrm{td}(X)+1}-4$. Earlier, Campbell et al. showed $\mathrm{utw}(\mathcal{G}_{K_t})=t-2$ and $\mathrm{utw}(\mathcal{G}_{K_{s,t}})=s$ for $t\ge\max\{s,3\}$. The question asks whether the exponential gap between the lower and upper bounds can be closed.
paper_title: The grid-minor theorem revisited

name: AX_topological_minor_free_treewidth_product_structure
title: Question 2
statement_text: Is there a function $f$ such that for every graph $X$ there exists a function $c$ such that for every positive integer $t$ and for every graph $G$ with $\operatorname{tw}(G)<t$ that does not contain $X$ as a topological minor, there exists a graph $H$ of treewidth at most $f(\operatorname{td}(X))$ such that $G$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $H\boxtimes K_{c(t)}$?
context_text: The strong product $G_1\boxtimes G_2$ has vertex set $V(G_1)\times V(G_2)$, with $(v,x)(w,y)$ an edge if $v=w$ and $xy\in E(G_2)$, or $x=y$ and $vw\in E(G_1)$, or $vw\in E(G_1)$ and $xy\in E(G_2)$; thus $H\boxtimes K_c$ is $H$ with each vertex blown up into a clique $K_c$. The treedepth $\mathrm{td}(X)$ of a graph $X$ is the minimum height (number of vertices on a root-to-leaf path) of a rooted forest $F$ on $V(X)$ such that every edge of $X$ joins a vertex to one of its ancestors in $F$; arbitrarily large graphs can have bounded treedepth. The authors prove the analogous statement for excluded minors: for every graph $X$ there is $c$ such that every $X$-minor-free graph $G$ with $\mathrm{tw}(G)<t$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $H\boxtimes K_{ct}$ with $\mathrm{tw}(H)\le2^{\mathrm{td}(X)+1}-4$, and they ask whether it extends to excluded topological minors. Campbell et al. showed that a monotone class has bounded underlying treewidth if and only if it excludes some fixed topological minor, and proved the weakening of this question with $\mathrm{tw}(H)\le f(\mathrm{td}(X))$ replaced by $\mathrm{tw}(H)\le|V(X)|$; this is tight for complete graphs (the underlying treewidth of $K_t$-topological-minor-free graphs is $t$ for $t\ge5$), which gives the question for complete $X$. They also proved it for $X=K_{s,t}$ with $s\le3$ (open for $s\ge4$), and that the underlying treewidth of $P_k$-free graphs is $\lfloor\log_2k\rfloor-1$, good evidence since $\mathrm{td}(P_k)=\lceil\log_2(k+1)\rceil$. A positive answer would also generalise the result that every graph of treewidth $t$ and maximum degree $\Delta$ is a subgraph of $T\boxtimes K_{24t\Delta}$ for a tree $T$ (the case $X=K_{1,\Delta+1}$).

name: AX_minor_free_p_centered_coloring_polynomial
title: Question 3
statement_text: Is there a function $g$ such that for every graph $X$, there is a constant $c$ such that for every $X$-minor-free graph $G$, $\chi_{p}(G)\leqslant c\cdot p^{g(\operatorname{td}(X))}$ for every $p\geqslant 1$?
context_text: For an integer $p\ge1$, a vertex colouring of $G$ is $p$-centered if every connected subgraph of $G$ either receives more than $p$ colours or contains a colour appearing exactly once in it; the $p$-centered chromatic number $\chi_p(G)$ is the least number of colours of such a colouring. Centered colourings characterize classes of bounded expansion and are central in parameterized algorithms on them; if $\mathrm{tw}(G)\le t$ then $\chi_p(G)\le\binom{p+t}{t}$, which is tight. The strong product $G_1\boxtimes G_2$ has vertex set $V(G_1)\times V(G_2)$, with $(v,x)(w,y)$ an edge if $v=w$ and $xy\in E(G_2)$, or $x=y$ and $vw\in E(G_1)$, or $vw\in E(G_1)$ and $xy\in E(G_2)$; thus $H\boxtimes K_c$ is $H$ with each vertex blown up into a clique $K_c$. The treedepth $\mathrm{td}(X)$ of a graph $X$ is the minimum height (number of vertices on a root-to-leaf path) of a rooted forest $F$ on $V(X)$ such that every edge of $X$ joins a vertex to one of its ancestors in $F$; arbitrarily large graphs can have bounded treedepth. The authors prove that for planar $X$ every $X$-minor-free graph is a subgraph of $H\boxtimes K_c$ with $\mathrm{tw}(H)\le2^{\mathrm{td}(X)+1}-4$ and $c=c(X)$, which gives $\chi_p(G)\le c\cdot p^{f(\mathrm{td}(X))}$; using a product structure with an extra path factor, they obtain the same for apex $X$ (graphs $X$ with a vertex $u$ such that $X-u$ is planar). They also prove an analogous bound for weak colouring numbers $\mathrm{wcol}_r$ for every excluded minor $X$, via chordal partitions, but cannot adapt this technique to $p$-centered colourings for arbitrary $X$, since they do not know how to use chordal partitions to build $p$-centered colourings.

name: AX_ramsey_multiplicity_polite_integers
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: Every sufficiently large integer is polite.
context_text: For a graph $H$ on $t$ vertices, $m(H,n)$ is the minimum number of monochromatic labeled copies of $H$ over all red/blue colorings of $E(K_n)$, and the Ramsey multiplicity constant is $c(H)=\lim_{n\to\infty}m(H,n)/(n)_t$, where $(n)_t=n(n-1)\cdots(n-t+1)$. A random coloring gives $c(H)\le 2^{1-e(H)}$ (graphs attaining this are called common). For $H$ connected with chromatic number $k$, the Turán coloring (red graph a disjoint union of $k-1$ balanced cliques, blue graph the complete $(k-1)$-partite graph) gives $c(H)\le(k-1)^{1-t}$. A connected graph $H$ is a (two-color) bonbon if, for all large $n$, the Turán coloring with $\chi(H)-1$ parts is, up to permuting colors and vertices, the unique coloring of $E(K_n)$ minimizing the number of monochromatic copies of $H$. For $q\ge3$ colors, $r_{q-1}(k)$ is the $(q-1)$-color Ramsey number of $K_k$, $r(a,b)$ is the two-color off-diagonal Ramsey number (least $r$ such that every red/blue coloring of $E(K_r)$ has a red $K_a$ or a blue $K_b$) and $r(k)=r(k,k)$; a Ramsey coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}$ is a red/blue coloring of its edges with no monochromatic $K_k$. A $q$-coloring of $E(K_n)$ is Ramsey-blowup-like if some color class is a disjoint union of $r_{q-1}(k)-1$ balanced cliques and the other colors contain no monochromatic $K_k$; a connected $t$-vertex graph $H$ with clique number $k$ is a $q$-color bonbon if for all large $n$ every $q$-coloring of $E(K_n)$ minimizing the number of monochromatic copies of $H$ is Ramsey-blowup-like (then $c_q(H)=(r_{q-1}(k)-1)^{1-t}$). A positive integer $k$ is polite if $r(k,\lceil k/2\rceil)\le 2^{-31}r(k,k)$ and $\frac{r(k,k)-1}{r(k,k-1)}\ge 1+25\left(\frac{r(k,\lceil k/2\rceil)}{r(k,k)}\right)^{1/4}$. The authors prove that if $k$ is a sufficiently large polite integer and $t$ is large enough in terms of $k$, then the graph obtained from $K_k$ by adding $t-k$ pendant edges is a 3-color bonbon; the conjecture would make this unconditional for all large $k$. It would follow from natural conjectures on the growth of Ramsey numbers: $r(k,\lceil k/2\rceil)=o(r(k,k))$, which gives the first inequality for large $k$, together with the Burr–Erdős conjecture $r(k,k)\ge(1+c)r(k,k-1)$ for an absolute $c>0$; but it seems out of reach, the best known lower bound on $r(k,k)-r(k,k-1)$ being far weaker.

name: AX_ramsey_multiplicity_mixed_blowup_coloring
title: Conjecture 5.3
statement_text: There exist a mixed blowup coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}[2]$ for infinitely many $k$.
context_text: The setting is Ramsey multiplicity: minimizing the number of monochromatic copies of a fixed graph $H$ over colorings of $E(K_n)$. For $q\ge3$ colors, $r_{q-1}(k)$ is the $(q-1)$-color Ramsey number of $K_k$, $r(a,b)$ is the two-color off-diagonal Ramsey number (least $r$ such that every red/blue coloring of $E(K_r)$ has a red $K_a$ or a blue $K_b$) and $r(k)=r(k,k)$; a Ramsey coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}$ is a red/blue coloring of its edges with no monochromatic $K_k$. A $q$-coloring of $E(K_n)$ is Ramsey-blowup-like if some color class is a disjoint union of $r_{q-1}(k)-1$ balanced cliques and the other colors contain no monochromatic $K_k$; a connected $t$-vertex graph $H$ with clique number $k$ is a $q$-color bonbon if for all large $n$ every $q$-coloring of $E(K_n)$ minimizing the number of monochromatic copies of $H$ is Ramsey-blowup-like (then $c_q(H)=(r_{q-1}(k)-1)^{1-t}$). For a graph $G$, $G[s]$ is its $s$-blowup (each vertex replaced by an independent set of $s$ vertices, each edge by a complete bipartite graph); here $K_{r(k)-1}[s]$ is the complete $(r(k)-1)$-partite graph with parts of size $s$. A mixed blowup coloring is a red/blue coloring of $E(K_{r(k)-1}[s])$ with no monochromatic $K_k$ that is not the blowup of a Ramsey coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}$. Mixed blowup colorings would show that, in the 3-color case, the Ramsey-blowup coloring is not the unique extremizer (any of them can serve as the red/blue part of an equally good 3-coloring), which is why $q$-color bonbons are defined via Ramsey-blowup-like colorings. The authors show that a mixed blowup coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}[2]$ exists if and only if one exists for every $s\ge2$, if and only if some 2-coloring of $E(K_{r(k)-2})$ extends to two distinct Ramsey colorings of $K_{r(k)-1}$. They cannot do this for any $k$: $r(k)$ is known only for $k=3,4$, and for both the Ramsey coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}$ is unique with all vertices of equal red and blue degree. They expect special values of $k$ with a unique structured (e.g. Paley) Ramsey coloring, hence conjecture existence only for infinitely many $k$; for the off-diagonal case $r(3,4)=9$ such colorings exist.
paper_title: Ramsey multiplicity and the Turán coloring

name: AX_ramsey_multiplicity_lollipop_bonbon
title: Conjecture 5.4
statement_text: If $k\geq 4$ and $t$ is sufficiently large in terms of $k$, then any $(k,t)$-generalized lollipop is a two-color bonbon.
context_text: For a graph $H$ on $t$ vertices, $m(H,n)$ is the minimum number of monochromatic labeled copies of $H$ over all red/blue colorings of $E(K_n)$, and the Ramsey multiplicity constant is $c(H)=\lim_{n\to\infty}m(H,n)/(n)_t$, where $(n)_t=n(n-1)\cdots(n-t+1)$. A random coloring gives $c(H)\le 2^{1-e(H)}$ (graphs attaining this are called common). For $H$ connected with chromatic number $k$, the Turán coloring (red graph a disjoint union of $k-1$ balanced cliques, blue graph the complete $(k-1)$-partite graph) gives $c(H)\le(k-1)^{1-t}$. A connected graph $H$ is a (two-color) bonbon if, for all large $n$, the Turán coloring with $\chi(H)-1$ parts is, up to permuting colors and vertices, the unique coloring of $E(K_n)$ minimizing the number of monochromatic copies of $H$. A graph is $k$-critical (in the paper's convention) if it has chromatic number $k$ and some edge whose deletion lowers the chromatic number. A $(k,t)$-generalized lollipop is a graph on $t$ vertices containing a $K_k$ whose deletion leaves a forest, i.e. $K_k$ with trees comprising $t-k$ vertices attached to its vertices; for such graphs the Turán coloring gives $c(H)\le(k-1)^{1-t}$. The authors prove that adding $t-h$ pendant edges to a $k$-critical graph $H_0$ on $h$ vertices yields a bonbon when $k\ge4$ and $t\ge(1000kh)^{10}h^{10k}$; their technique needs $t$ at least exponential in $k$, and for $H_0=K_k$ some lower bound is necessary since adding $o(k^2/\log k)$ pendant edges does not give a bonbon (the random coloring is better). The conjecture extends this from pendant edges to arbitrary attached trees. They also single out the special case of the lollipop $L_{k,t}$ ($K_k$ with a path of $t-k$ edges attached at one vertex), and ask whether, for $H_0=K_k$, $t$ polynomial in $k$ suffices.
paper_title: Ramsey multiplicity and the Turán coloring

name: AX_heroic_sets_bounded_dichromatic_finite_families
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Which finite families $F$ of digraphs are $\vec{\chi}$-finite?
context_text: Digraphs are finite and simple (no digons). A digraph is $F$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to a member of $F$. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum number of colours in a colouring of $V(D)$ in which every colour class induces an acyclic digraph. A family $F$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if there is a constant $c$ such that all $F$-free digraphs have dichromatic number at most $c$. This question is the digraph analogue of the study of $\chi$-bounded hereditary classes, and was first studied systematically by Aboulker, Charbit and Naserasr. They showed that every $\vec{\chi}$-finite family contains an oriented forest (a digraph whose underlying graph is a forest) and a hero in tournaments, i.e. a digraph $H$ such that $H$-free tournaments have bounded dichromatic number (heroes in tournaments were characterized by Berger et al.). They also conjectured, as a directed analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, that $\{H,F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite whenever $F$ is an oriented forest and $H$ a transitive tournament. The paper contributes results on heroes in $F$-free digraphs for oriented stars $F$, for $F=rK_1+\vec{P}_3$, and for two orientations of brooms.
notes: Stated without a parenthetical attribution in the theorem header; the surrounding prose credits Aboulker, Charbit, and Naserasr [2] with first systematically studying this question.
paper_title: On heroes in digraphs with forbidden induced forests

name: AX_heroes_oriented_star_delta_1_m_m
title: Open problem: hero status of $\Delta(1,m,m')$ for degree-4 oriented stars
statement_text: Determine for which integers $m, m' \geq 1$ the set $\{\Delta(1, m, m'), F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite when $F$ is an oriented star of degree $4$.
context_text: Digraphs are finite and simple: between two vertices at most one of the arcs $uv$, $vu$ is present (no digons). A digraph is $\mathcal{F}$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{F}$. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every colour class induces an acyclic digraph (no monochromatic directed cycle). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if there is a constant $c$ such that all $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs have dichromatic number at most $c$, and $H$ is a hero in $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs if $\{H\}\cup\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite (heroes in tournaments, i.e. in $\{2K_1\}$-free digraphs, are simply called heroes). $D_1+D_2$ is the disjoint union and $rD$ the disjoint union of $r$ copies; $TT_k$ is the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices; $D_1\Rightarrow D_2$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$; $\Delta(D_1,D_2,D_3)$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2+D_3$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$, from $D_2$ to $D_3$ and from $D_3$ to $D_1$, and an integer $k$ in this notation stands for $TT_k$. Berger et al. characterized heroes in tournaments: $H$ is a hero iff $H=K_1$, or $H=H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ with $H_1,H_2$ heroes, or $H=\Delta(1,H_1,m)$ or $\Delta(1,m,H_1)$ with $m\ge1$ and $H_1$ a hero. An oriented star of degree $t$ is an orientation of $K_{1,t}$. Aboulker, Charbit and Naserasr showed that every $\vec{\chi}$-finite family contains an oriented forest and a hero in tournaments, and Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour proved that $\{H,F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite whenever $F$ is an oriented star and $H$ is a transitive tournament. The authors prove that if $F$ is an oriented star of degree at least 5, then transitive tournaments are the only heroes in $F$-free digraphs. They also prove that if $F$ has degree exactly 4 and $\{H,F\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite, then $H$ is a transitive tournament or $H=\Delta(1,m,m')$ for some $m,m'\ge1$, i.e. a vertex $v$ together with transitive tournaments $A$ on $m$ and $B$ on $m'$ vertices, with $v\to A\to B\to v$. Whether these tournaments $\Delta(1,m,m')$ are actually heroes in $F$-free digraphs is left open.

name: AX_heroes_delta_1_2_2_k1_p2_free
title: Open problem: hero status of $\Delta(1,2,2)$
statement_text: Determine whether $\Delta(1,2,2)$ is a hero in $\{K_1 + \vec{P}_2\}$-free digraphs, i.e., whether $\{\Delta(1,2,2),\, K_1 + \vec{P}_2\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite.
context_text: Digraphs are finite and simple: between two vertices at most one of the arcs $uv$, $vu$ is present (no digons). A digraph is $\mathcal{F}$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{F}$. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every colour class induces an acyclic digraph (no monochromatic directed cycle). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if there is a constant $c$ such that all $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs have dichromatic number at most $c$, and $H$ is a hero in $\mathcal{F}$-free digraphs if $\{H\}\cup\mathcal{F}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite (heroes in tournaments, i.e. in $\{2K_1\}$-free digraphs, are simply called heroes). $D_1+D_2$ is the disjoint union and $rD$ the disjoint union of $r$ copies; $TT_k$ is the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices; $D_1\Rightarrow D_2$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$; $\Delta(D_1,D_2,D_3)$ is obtained from $D_1+D_2+D_3$ by adding all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$, from $D_2$ to $D_3$ and from $D_3$ to $D_1$, and an integer $k$ in this notation stands for $TT_k$. Berger et al. characterized heroes in tournaments: $H$ is a hero iff $H=K_1$, or $H=H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ with $H_1,H_2$ heroes, or $H=\Delta(1,H_1,m)$ or $\Delta(1,m,H_1)$ with $m\ge1$ and $H_1$ a hero. $\vec{P}_m$ is the directed path on $m$ vertices (so $K_1+\vec{P}_2$ is an arc plus an isolated vertex). Harutyunyan, Le, Newman and Thomassé showed that every hero in tournaments is a hero in $rK_1$-free digraphs. In contrast, Aboulker, Aubian and Charbit showed that if $F$ contains $K_1+\vec{P}_2$, then $\Delta(1,2,\vec{C}_3)$, $\Delta(1,\vec{C}_3,2)$, $\Delta(1,2,3)$ and $\Delta(1,3,2)$ are not heroes in $F$-free digraphs ($\vec{C}_3$ is the cyclic triangle). They also proved that $\{H,K_1+\vec{P}_2\}$ is $\vec{\chi}$-finite if $H=K_1$, or $H=H_1\Rightarrow H_2$ with both $H_i$ heroes in $\{K_1+\vec{P}_2\}$-free digraphs, or $H=\Delta(1,1,H_1)$ with $H_1$ such a hero; with their negative result, this characterizes heroes in $\{K_1+\vec{P}_2\}$-free digraphs except for $H=\Delta(1,2,2)$. The present paper proves the same sufficient conditions for $\{H,rK_1+\vec{P}_3\}$ for every $r$, which again leaves only $\Delta(1,2,2)$ undecided, for both forbidden digraphs.

name: AX_tournament_flash_rainbow_edge_coloring_exact
title: Conjecture 1.7
statement_text: For all positive integers $l$ and $k$, $t(l, k) = l^{k-1}$.
context_text: A tournament is an orientation of a complete graph, and a directed walk is a sequence of vertices $x_0,\dots,x_l$ with $x_{i-1}x_i$ a directed edge for each $i$ (vertices and edges may repeat). Given a colouring $c$ of the edges, an $l$-flash is a directed walk $x_0,\dots,x_l$ with $c(x_0x_1),\dots,c(x_{l-1}x_l)$ all equal, and a $k$-rainbow is a directed walk $y_0,\dots,y_k$ with $c(y_0y_1),\dots,c(y_{k-1}y_k)$ all distinct (any number of colours may be used). $t(l,k)$ is the smallest integer such that every edge colouring of any tournament with more than $t(l,k)$ vertices contains an $l$-flash or a $k$-rainbow, and $f(l,k)$ is the same quantity restricted to transitive tournaments (i.e. to colourings of the pairs of $[n]$, with walks along increasing vertices). Lefmann, Rödl and Thomas showed $f(l,k)\ge l^{k-1}$ (label vertices by strings of $\{1,\dots,l\}^{k-1}$ in lexicographic order and colour $uv$, $u<v$, by an index where $u$ is smaller than $v$) and conjectured $f(l,k)=l^{k-1}$; they proved it for $l\le2$ or $k\le4$ or $l\ge(3k)^{2k}$, and the authors prove it for $l\ge k^3(\log k)^{1+o(1)}$. Since $t(l,k)\ge f(l,k)\ge l^{k-1}$, this conjecture is a tournament strengthening of theirs. The authors prove $t(l,k)\le(1+2/\sqrt{l})^k l^{k-1}$, which confirms it asymptotically for $l=\omega(k^2)$, and $t(l,k)\le D_\varepsilon k(\log k)^{1+\varepsilon}l^{k-1}$; they also show that for $l\ge2$, $k\ge3$ some tournament with $f(l,k)-1$ vertices has no good colouring, so transitive tournaments are not the worst. They note the conjecture remains wide open for every $l\ge2$, $k\ge3$, and that the case $l=2$ together with their results would give it for $l\ge k^3(\log k)^{1+o(1)}$.
paper_title: Flashes and rainbows in tournaments

name: AX_kromatic_claw_free_grassmannian_subvariety
title: Grassmannian Subvariety Construction Problem
statement_text: For each claw-free incomparability graph $G$, there should exist a subvariety of the Grassmannian whose cohomology class is represented by $X_G$ and whose K-theoretic structure sheaf class is represented by $\overline{X}_G$. It would be very interesting to have an explicit construction of such subvarieties.
context_text: For a graph $G$, Stanley's chromatic symmetric function is $X_G=\sum_\kappa\prod_{v\in V(G)}x_{\kappa(v)}$, the sum over all proper colourings $\kappa:V(G)\to\mathbb{N}$. The Kromatic symmetric function $\overline{X}_G=\sum_\kappa\prod_{v\in V(G)}\prod_{i\in\kappa(v)}x_i$ is its $K$-theoretic analogue, where now $\kappa$ ranges over all proper set colourings, assigning to each vertex a non-empty finite set of colours so that adjacent vertices receive disjoint sets. The incomparability graph of a poset $P$ has vertex set $P$, two elements being adjacent when they are incomparable; it is claw-free (no induced $K_{1,3}$) exactly when $P$ is $(3+1)$-free. In the ring of symmetric functions, viewed as the cohomology of Grassmannians, Schur functions $s_\lambda$ represent Schubert classes; in $K$-theory they are replaced by symmetric Grothendieck functions $\overline{s}_\lambda$, representing structure sheaves of Schubert varieties. Gasharov proved that $X_G$ is Schur-positive for every claw-free incomparability graph $G$; the authors' main result lifts this to $K$-theory: $\overline{X}_G$ is a positive sum of symmetric Grothendieck functions. Since all known proofs of Gasharov's theorem are representation-theoretic or combinatorial, the authors suggest that both results should have a topological interpretation, and propose finding explicit subvarieties realising them. In contrast they show that Kromatic symmetric functions of paths are not positive in several $K$-analogues of the $e$-basis, so the Stanley–Stembridge conjecture does not lift in this way. This is a speculative remark in algebraic combinatorics rather than a precise conjecture.

paper_title: The Kromatic Symmetric Function: A $K$-theoretic Analogue of $X_G$

name: AX_minor_free_choosability_trivial_bound_characterization
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Characterize the class $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs $H$ such that $f_\ell(H') = v(H')-1$ for all $H' \subseteq H$.
context_text: For a graph $H$, $f_\chi(H)$ and $f_\ell(H)$ denote the maximum chromatic number and the maximum list chromatic number (choosability $\chi_\ell$: the least $k$ such that a proper colouring from the lists exists whenever every list has at least $k$ colours) over all $H$-minor-free graphs; $v(H)$ is the number of vertices and $H'\subseteq H$ ranges over all subgraphs. Since $K_{v(H)-1}$ is $H$-minor-free, $f_\ell(H)\ge f_\chi(H)\ge v(H)-1$, and Seymour's $H$-Hadwiger conjecture asserts $f_\chi(H)=v(H)-1$. So $\mathcal{H}$ is the largest subgraph-closed class on which the list-colouring version of the $H$-Hadwiger conjecture holds with this trivial bound; the problem is posed in the spirit of perfect graphs, where restricting to a hereditary class yields a structural description. Restricting to subgraph-closed classes is needed since, by the authors, adding enough isolated vertices to any graph $F$ yields $H$ with $f_\ell(H)=v(H)-1$. Known facts: $f_\ell(K_t)\ge2t-o(t)$ and $f_\ell(K_{s,t})\ge(1-o(1))(2s+t)$ for large $s\le t$ (so large complete and complete bipartite graphs are not in $\mathcal{H}$), while Norin and Turcotte showed $f_\ell(H)=v(H)-1$ for large bipartite $H$ of bounded maximum degree in a class with strongly sublinear separators. The authors prove $f_\ell(H)\ge(1-\varepsilon)(v(H)+\kappa(H))$ for all large $H$ ($\kappa$ = vertex-connectivity), which implies that graphs in $\mathcal{H}$ have $o(n^2)$ edges, and that almost every $n$-vertex graph with $\lceil Cn\log n\rceil$ edges has $f_\ell(H)\ge(2-\varepsilon)n$.
paper_title: On the choosability of $H$-minor-free graphs

name: AX_random_embedding_expected_faces_third_n
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: For any simple graph $G$ of order $n$, $E[F] \leq \frac{1}{3}n + 1$.
context_text: An embedding is a 2-cell embedding of $G$ in an orientable closed surface, considered up to homeomorphisms inducing the identity on $G$; embeddings correspond bijectively to rotation systems, i.e. a choice of a cyclic ordering of the half-edges (darts) at each vertex. $F$ is the number of faces of an embedding chosen uniformly at random, equivalently obtained by choosing a uniformly random local rotation independently at each vertex; by Euler's formula, bounding $\mathbb{E}[F]$ is equivalent to bounding the average genus. Stahl proved $\mathbb{E}[F]\le n\log n$ for simple graphs, and Halasz, Masařík, Šámal and the present authors conjectured an $O(n)$ bound. The paper confirms it, proving $\mathbb{E}[F]\le n(H_{2\mu}+1)$ ($H_k$ the harmonic number) for $n$-vertex multigraphs with maximum edge-multiplicity $\mu$, which is tight up to a constant factor, and $\mathbb{E}[F]\le\frac{\pi^2}{6}n$ for simple graphs; no simple graphs are known coming close to that constant. A chain of triangles joined by cut edges has $\mathbb{E}[F]=\frac13 n+1$, and the authors conjecture this is optimal.
notes: PDF source; fraction $\frac{1}{3}$ appears as '1\n3' in raw PDF text but context is unambiguous.
paper_title: Expected number of faces in a random embedding of any graph is at most linear

name: AX_forest_free_polynomial_chi_good
title: Informal Conjecture (every forest is good)
statement_text: Perhaps every forest is good (i.e., for every forest $H$, the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded).
context_text: A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hereditary class (closed under induced subgraphs) is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded if $f$ can be taken to be a polynomial; a graph $H$ is good if the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture asserts that for every forest $H$ the class of $H$-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded; it remains open. Esperet's conjecture that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class is polynomially $\chi$-bounded was disproved by Briański, Davies and Walczak, so the question is which hereditary classes are polynomially $\chi$-bounded, and in particular whether the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture can be strengthened to polynomial $\chi$-boundedness. The only trees known to be good are those not containing the five-vertex path $P_5$, and it is not known whether $P_5$ is good; it is not even known that a forest whose components are all good is good. The authors prove that if $H$ is a good forest then so is the disjoint union of $H$ and $P_4$ (e.g. $2P_4$-free graphs satisfy $\chi\le\omega^{16}$), and more generally results for disjoint unions of good forests with paths or brooms (a $(k,d)$-broom is a $k$-vertex path with $d$ extra vertices attached to one end).
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VI. Adding a four-vertex path

name: AX_broom_nondominating_copy_no_scattering
title: Conjecture 2.3
statement_text: Let $\psi,\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ be non-decreasing polynomials, let $q\geq 0$ be an integer, and let $H$ be a broom. Then there is a non-decreasing polynomial $\phi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that if $G$ is a graph, and $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$, and $G$ contains no $(\psi,q)$-scattering, then $G$ contains a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of $H$.
context_text: For $X\subseteq V(G)$, $\chi(X)$ and $\omega(X)$ denote $\chi(G[X])$ and $\omega(G[X])$; copies are induced subgraphs; a set is complete (anticomplete) to another if every (no) vertex of the first is adjacent to every vertex of the second. A $(k,d)$-broom is the tree obtained from a $k$-vertex path with one end $v$ by adding $d$ new vertices adjacent to $v$; a broom is a $(k,d)$-broom for some $k,d$. For a non-decreasing $\psi$ and an integer $q\ge0$, a $(\psi,q)$-scattering in $G$ is a triple $(v,P,Q)$ with $P,Q\subseteq V(G)$ disjoint, $v\notin P\cup Q$ complete to $P$ and anticomplete to $Q$, $\chi(P)>\psi(\omega(P))$, and $\chi(Q)>qr+\psi(\omega(Q))$, where $r$ is the maximum over $u\in P$ of the chromatic number of the set of neighbours of $u$ in $Q$. For a non-decreasing $\sigma$, a subgraph $P$ of $G$ is $\sigma$-nondominating if some set $X\subseteq V(G)\setminus V(P)$ anticomplete to $V(P)$ has $\chi(X)>\sigma(\omega(X))$. Excluding scatterings is a weakening of excluding a forest $H_1$ built from good pieces, used to show that unions of good forests with brooms or paths are polynomially $\chi$-bounded ($\chi\le$ a polynomial of $\omega$ on $H$-free graphs). The authors prove the weaker statement in which, under the same hypotheses, $G$ contains a copy of the broom $H$ and a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of a given path $J$; the conjecture asks for a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of the broom itself, an appealing strengthening they could not prove. From the path version they deduce that paths are self-isolating; by the same argument the conjecture would imply that brooms are self-isolating.

paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VI. Adding a four-vertex path

name: AX_forest_free_multibounding_chi_bound
title: Conjecture 1.6
statement_text: Every forest is multibounding.
context_text: $H$-free means having no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and $K_d(t)$ denotes the complete $d$-partite graph with all parts of size $t$ (excluded here as a subgraph, not necessarily induced). A graph $H$ is multibounding if for every $d\ge1$ there is a polynomial $f(t)$ such that, for all $t\ge1$, every $H$-free graph $G$ with no $K_d(t)$ subgraph satisfies $\chi(G)\le f(t)$. Taking $t=1$ ($K_d(1)=K_d$) shows that every multibounding graph is a forest satisfying the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture (for every forest $H$ and every $k$, $H$-free graphs with no $K_k$ have bounded chromatic number), so this conjecture strengthens Gyárfás–Sumner; conversely, every forest satisfying the polynomial version of Gyárfás–Sumner (chromatic number polynomial in the clique number for $H$-free graphs) is multibounding. For $d=2$ the statement is known for every forest: Rödl proved that $H$-free graphs with no $K_{t,t}$ subgraph have bounded chromatic number, and Scott, Seymour and Spirkl made the bound polynomial in $t$. Previously trees of radius two were known to be multibounding; the paper proves that paths and brooms (a path with leaves added at one end) are multibounding, and that a forest whose components are all multibounding is multibounding.
notes: Explicitly introduced with 'We propose: 1.6 Conjecture' in the paper.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VIII. Excluding a path and a complete multipartite graph

name: AX_neighborly_boxes_limit_one_half
title: Conjecture on the asymptotic of n(2,d)
statement_text: For every $2\leqslant k\leqslant d$, $n(k,d)\leqslant n(k-1,d-1)+n(k,d-1)$ (the 'Pascal Triangle' conjecture). Together with the lower bound $n(2,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$, this would imply $\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{n(2,d)}{d^2}=\frac{1}{2}$.
context_text: A standard box in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a product $K_1\times\cdots\times K_d$ of closed intervals. Two standard boxes $K,L$ are $k$-neighborly if $d-k\leqslant\dim(K\cap L)\leqslant d-1$, and a family of standard boxes is $k$-neighborly if every two of its members are. For $1\leqslant k\leqslant d$, $n(k,d)$ is the maximum size of a $k$-neighborly family of standard boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$; equivalently (Alon), it is the maximum number of vertices of a complete graph whose edges can be covered by $d$ complete bipartite subgraphs so that every edge is covered at least once and at most $k$ times. Zaks proved $n(1,d)=d+1$ via the Graham–Pollak theorem, and $n(d,d)=2^d$. The authors prove $n(k,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^k}{k!}$; for $k=2$ this gives $n(2,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$, improving the previous $d^2/4$, while determining the asymptotic order of $n(2,d)$ was noted to be hard by Alon and by Huang–Sudakov. In the final section they pose the Pascal Triangle conjecture, supported by Gurobi computations for $d\leqslant 8$ and by the fact that the analogous inequality holds for the values $\overline{m}(k,d)$ given by their explicit constructions. The Pascal inequality gives $n(2,j)-n(2,j-1)\leqslant j$, hence $n(2,d)\leqslant(d+1)+\binom{d}{2}$, which combined with the lower bound yields the limit $1/2$.

paper_title: New bounds on the maximum number of neighborly boxes in R^d

name: AX_neighborly_boxes_limit_exists
title: Open question on existence of lim n(2,d)/d^2
statement_text: Does $\lim_{d\to\infty} \frac{n(2,d)}{d^2}$ exist?
context_text: A standard box in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a product $K_1\times\cdots\times K_d$ of closed intervals. name: AX_planar_odd_degree_linear_forests_matching
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every planar graph $G$ of odd maximum degree $\Delta \geq 7$ the edges of $G$ can be partitioned into $\frac{\Delta-1}{2}$ linear forests and one matching.
context_text: A linear forest is a forest whose components are paths, and the linear arboricity $\mathrm{la}(G)$ is the minimum number of linear forests whose union is $G$. For planar graphs, $\mathrm{la}(G)\le\lceil(\Delta+1)/2\rceil$ (Wu, and Wu and Wu), and Cygan et al. proved $\mathrm{la}(G)=\lceil\Delta/2\rceil$ when $\Delta\ge9$ and conjectured it for $\Delta\ge5$. For odd $\Delta$ the equality $\mathrm{la}(G)=\lceil\Delta/2\rceil$ already holds, which leaves freedom (each vertex has a linear forest with at most one incident edge) that the conjecture tries to exploit by replacing one linear forest by a matching. The conjecture implies chromatic index $\Delta$ (colour each linear forest with two colours and the matching with one more), so it fails for $\Delta\in\{3,5\}$ ($K_4$ and the icosahedron with one edge subdivided). It holds for $\Delta\ge11$ by combining Vizing's theorem that planar graphs with $\Delta\ge8$ have chromatic index $\Delta$ (remove one colour class, a matching) with the result of Cygan et al. The paper proves that every planar graph of maximum degree at most $9$ can be partitioned into $4$ linear forests and a matching, settling $\Delta=9$; the case $\Delta=7$ remains open (it would strengthen the result of Sanders and Zhao that planar graphs of maximum degree $7$ have chromatic index $7$), and the authors think it needs a different, more global argument.
paper_title: Partitioning edges of a planar graph into linear forests and a matching

name: AX_path_induced_rooted_tree_polynomial_chi
title: Polynomial bounds for path-induced copy theorem (1.2)
statement_text: For every rooted tree $(T,r)$ and integer $t\ge1$, graphs with no path-induced copy of $(T,r)$ and no clique of size $t$ have bounded chromatic number. Is there any hope for a comparable strengthening of this result, giving a polynomial bound (in $t$) on the chromatic number of graphs with no path-induced copy of a rooted tree $(T,r)$ and with clique number at most $t$?
context_text: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture says that for every tree $T$ and integer $t\ge1$, graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $T$ and no clique of size $t$ have bounded chromatic number; it is proved for a few families of trees but open in general. A rooted tree $(T,r)$ is a tree $T$ with a distinguished vertex $r$; an isomorphism $\phi$ from $T$ to a (not necessarily induced) subgraph of $G$ is a path-induced copy of $(T,r)$ if for every path $P$ of $T$ with one end $r$, the image of $P$ under $\phi$ is an induced path of $G$ (this lies between subgraph and induced subgraph). The authors prove that the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture holds when excluding a path-induced copy of $(T,r)$ instead of an induced copy of $T$: graphs with no path-induced copy of $(T,r)$ and no clique of size $t$ have chromatic number bounded by a function of $(T,r)$ and $t$. In the analogous setting where $K_{t,t}$ is excluded as a subgraph, Scott, Seymour and Spirkl proved that for every tree $T$ there is a polynomial $f(t)$ such that graphs with no induced $T$ and no $K_{t,t}$ subgraph have average degree at most $f(t)$ (improving Kierstead–Penrice and Rödl). With only bounded clique number one must bound the chromatic number rather than the average degree, since $K_{n,n}$ has no $K_3$ and no path-induced copy of $P_4$; but one can still ask for a polynomial bound. Polynomial bounds in $t$ have recently been shown for a few trees, including every tree that does not contain the five-vertex path $P_5$ as an induced subgraph, but $P_5$ appears to be a sticking point: the best known bound for $P_5$-free graphs of clique number $t$ is the slightly superpolynomial $\chi\le t^{\log_2 t}$. Since a graph contains a path-induced copy of a path rooted at an end if and only if it contains that path as an induced subgraph, polynomial bounds here even for $P_5$ would require improving the $P_5$ bound.

paper_title: A note on the Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture

title: Polynomial bounds for the Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture
statement_text: It is possible that the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture holds with polynomial bounds; that is, for every tree $T$ there is a polynomial $f$ such that every graph with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $T$ and no clique of size $t$ has chromatic number at most $f(t)$.

Polynomial bounds in $t$ have recently been shown for a few trees, including every tree that does not contain the five-vertex path $P_5$ as an induced subgraph, but $P_5$ appears to be a sticking point: the best known bound for $P_5$-free graphs of clique number $t$ is the slightly superpolynomial $\chi\le t^{\log_2 t}$. name: AX_graph_codes_even_edges_density_vanishes
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a family of graphs closed under isomorphism. Is it true that $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity if and only if $\mathcal{H}$ contains a graph with an even number of edges? Equivalently: is it true that for any fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges, $d_H(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity?
context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. The author shows $d_{K_{1,2k}}(n)=\Theta_k(n^{-k})$ and $d_{M_{2k}}(n)=\Theta_k(n^{-k})$ for stars and matchings with $2k$ edges, $d_H(n)\le|V(H)|/n$ when $H$ is obtained from two copies of a graph by identifying the vertices of an independent set, and $d_{\mathcal{K}}(n)\ge2^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ for the family $\mathcal{K}$ of all cliques. The question asks whether this parity obstruction is the only one. It remains wide open; an interesting special case is $H=K_4$. A related conjecture of Gowers (any constant fraction of all graphs on $[n]$ contains $G_2\subseteq G_1$ whose difference is a clique) is stronger than $d_{\mathcal{K}}(n)\to0$, which is also open.

name: AX_graph_codes_k4_density_vanishes
title: Informal question: is $d_{K_4}(n) = o(1)$?
statement_text: Is it true that $d_{K_4}(n) = o(1)$?
context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. $K_4$ has $6$ edges, so this is a special case of the question whether $d_H(n)\to0$ for every fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges, which remains wide open.
