name: AX_graph_codes_linear_even_h_bounds
title: Open problem: tighter bounds for linear graph-codes
statement_text: Establish tighter bounds for the maximum possible cardinality of a linear family of graphs on $[n]$ in which no symmetric difference is a copy of a fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges.
context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. A linear family is a family of graphs on $[n]$ closed under symmetric difference (a linear subspace of $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$). For every graph $H$ with an even number of edges, a Ramsey argument shows that a linear (or affine) $H$-code has size $o(2^{\binom n2})$, in fact a fraction $O(\log\log n/\log n)$ of all graphs, but these bounds are very weak. As a model of a tight result, the author proves that the minimum co-dimension of a linear space of graphs on $n$ vertices containing no clique is exactly $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.

name: AX_graph_codes_cube_length_interval_vectors
title: Open problem: binary vectors with cube-length forbidden symmetric difference
statement_text: What is the maximum possible cardinality of a collection of binary vectors whose coordinates are indexed by the elements of the ordered set $[n]$, where no symmetric difference of two distinct members of the collection forms an interval of length which is a cube of an integer?
context_text: This is a variant of graph-codes (families of graphs on $[n]$ none of whose pairwise symmetric differences lies in a forbidden family) where codewords are binary vectors indexed by $[n]$ and the forbidden symmetric differences are the characteristic vectors of intervals of $[n]$ whose length is a perfect cube. The answer is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ generated by these interval vectors; this graph has $2^n$ vertices and is triangle-free by Fermat's Last Theorem for cubes. Its independence number is $o(2^n)$ by the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem and its extensions, applied to the induced subgraph on the characteristic vectors of the intervals $[i]=\{1,\dots,i\}$, $0\le i\le n$. The question asks for the true order of magnitude. It is a combinatorial coding question rather than graph theory proper.

context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. Lower bounds on $d_H(n)$ in the paper come from proper colourings of the Cayley graph, built from edge colourings of $K_n$: for instance, an edge colouring of $K_n$ with $n^{o(1)}$ colours in which no copy of $K_4$ has every colour appearing an even number of times, combined with the parity check matrix of a BCH code, gives $d_{K_4}(n)\ge n^{-o(1)}$. This motivates asking for the minimum number of colours in an edge colouring of $K_n$ such that every copy of $H$ (or of any member of $\mathcal{H}$) meets some colour class in an odd number of edges, which the author calls an interesting variant of classical Ramsey questions.
paper_title: Graph-codes

name: AX_even_hole_free_chordal_modulator
title: Informal Conjecture (chordal modulator characterization for even-hole-free graphs)
statement_text: Every chordal graph of clique number at most three modulates even-hole-free graphs.
context_text: Containment means as an induced subgraph. A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and a graph is even-hole-free if it has no hole of even length; a chordal graph is a graph with no hole. A $t$-basic obstruction is one of $K_t$, $K_{t,t}$, a subdivision of the $(t\times t)$-wall, or the line graph of such a subdivision, and a graph is $t$-clean if it contains no $t$-basic obstruction. A graph $H$ modulates a class $\mathcal{G}$ if for every positive integer $t$ there is $w(t)$ such that every $t$-clean $H$-free graph in $\mathcal{G}$ has treewidth at most $w(t)$. For even-hole-free graphs, being $t$-clean is equivalent to being $K_t$-free, so $H$ modulates even-hole-free graphs iff for every $t$, even-hole-free graphs with no $H$ and no clique of size $t$ have bounded treewidth. Sintiari and Trotignon constructed (even-hole, $K_4$)-free graphs of arbitrarily large treewidth and with no short holes (layered wheels), which shows that a graph $H$ can modulate even-hole-free graphs only if $H$ is chordal with clique number at most three; the authors say the converse may also be true. They prove the case of clique number at most two, i.e. every forest modulates even-hole-free graphs, and they show that forests are exactly the graphs modulating the larger class of (theta, prism)-free graphs. Extending to all chordal graphs of clique number at most three remains open.
notes: Stated as "as far as we know, the converse may also be true" in the introduction; confirmed open by the subsequent remark "while the former remains open".
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions VIII. Excluding a forest in (theta, prism)-free graphs

name: AX_point_set_random_distances_reconstruction_threshold
title: Informal conjecture on sharp threshold for linear-proportion reconstruction
statement_text: Let $V$ be a set of $n$ points on the real line, and suppose the graph of known pairwise distances $(V,\mathcal{P})$ is distributed as $\mathcal{G}(n,(1+\varepsilon)/n)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is a constant. Then with high probability there is a reconstructible set of size $\Omega_\varepsilon(n)$; that is, the correct threshold for the existence of a reconstructible set of size $\Omega(n)$ is $p=(1+\varepsilon)/n$.
context_text: Let $V\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a set of $n$ labelled points, and suppose that only the distances $|u-v|$ for pairs $uv$ in a set $\mathcal{P}\subseteq\binom{V}{2}$ are known, where $(V,\mathcal{P})$ is the binomial random graph $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ (each distance is revealed independently with probability $p$); the point set itself is arbitrary. A set $U\subseteq V$ is reconstructible if the positions of its points can be deduced up to isometry, equivalently all pairwise distances within $U$ can be deduced from the known ones; whp means with probability tending to 1. Benjamini and Tzalik showed that $V$ is whp fully reconstructible when $p=C\log n/n$ for a large constant $C$. The authors prove that whp there is a reconstructible set of size $\Omega(n)$ if $p\ge 42/n$, and of size $(1-o(1))n$ if $pn\to\infty$, with a sharp hitting-time result for full reconstruction. Since for $p=c/n$ with $c<1$ all components have size $O(\log n)$, $1/n$ is a weak threshold for a linear-size reconstructible set; the authors conjecture a sharp threshold at $1/n$, where the giant component of $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ appears. Their approach (via cycles of length at most $0.9\log n$) cannot give a constant better than $9$, and bootstrapping would not reach $(1+\varepsilon)/n$, since most pairs are then only in cycles of length $\Omega(\log(n)/\varepsilon)$.
notes: Appears in footnote 2 as an informal belief. Section 4 (open problems) is not present in the extracted text, so additional conjectures from that section may be missing.
paper_title: Reconstructing a point set from a random subset of its pairwise distances

name: AX_forest_free_polynomial_chi_bounded
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: For every forest $H$, there is a polynomial $f$ such that $\chi(G) \leq f(\omega(G))$ for every $H$-free graph $G$.
context_text: A graph $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$; $\omega(G)$ is the clique number. A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs, and $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all its members. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture asserts that for every forest $H$ the class of $H$-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded; Kierstead and Penrice proved it for trees of radius two. Esperet conjectured that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class admits a polynomial bounding function $f$; this has been disproved in general but remains open for classes excluding a forest, where together with Gyárfás–Sumner it gives the present conjecture. It is known only for a few classes of trees. The authors note that a polynomial bound for the five-vertex path $P_5$ (whose best known bound is $\omega^{\log_2\omega}$) would imply the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for $P_5$. Rödl proved that for every forest $H$, $H$-free graphs with no $K_{t,t}$ subgraph have bounded chromatic number, and the authors (with Spirkl) showed this bound can be taken polynomial in $t$, a special case of this conjecture.
notes: Stated in the paper without a parenthesised attribution; it is a natural combination of Conjecture 1.1 and Esperet's conjecture restricted to forest-free classes.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number. V. Excluding a tree of radius two and a complete multipartite graph

name: AX_path_free_polynomial_chi_tau_d
title: Question: Extending Theorem 1.6 to paths
statement_text: Is it true that if $H$ is a path, then for every integer $d \geq 1$, there is a polynomial $f$ such that $\chi(G) \leq f(\tau_d(G))$ for every $H$-free graph $G$?
context_text: A graph $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$; $\omega(G)$ is the clique number. A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs, and $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all its members. For an integer $d\ge1$, $\tau_d(G)$ is the largest $t$ such that $G$ has a subgraph (not necessarily induced) isomorphic to the complete $d$-partite graph with every part of size $t$; thus $\tau_1(G)=|G|$, $\tau_2(G)$ is the largest $t$ with $K_{t,t}\subseteq G$, and $\tau_d(G)\ge\lfloor\omega(G)/d\rfloor$. Rödl proved that for every forest $H$ there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\tau_2(G))$ for every $H$-free $G$; for $H$ a path, a polynomial $f$ was obtained by Bonamy, Bousquet, Pilipczuk, Rzążewski, Thomassé and Walczak, and the authors (with Spirkl) proved it for every forest. The main result of the paper is that for every tree $H$ of radius two and every integer $d\ge1$ there is a polynomial $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\tau_d(G))$ for every $H$-free graph $G$ (a strengthening of the Kierstead–Penrice theorem). A referee suggested this question, extending that result to paths, another family of trees known to satisfy the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture (that $H$-free graphs are $\chi$-bounded for every forest $H$). Proving such a statement for a forest $H$ and all $d$ would imply that $H$ satisfies the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture.
notes: Explicitly labelled as an open question suggested by a referee and incorporated into the paper.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number. V. Excluding a tree of radius two and a complete multipartite graph

name: AX_hereditary_tau_d_bounded_implies_polynomial_esperet
title: Question: Polynomial bound analogue of Esperet's conjecture for $\tau_d$
statement_text: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a hereditary class of graphs, and $d \geq 1$. Suppose that there is a function $f$ such that $\chi(G) \leq f(\tau_d(G))$ for each $G \in \mathcal{C}$. Can we always choose $f$ to be a polynomial? What if $d = 2$?
context_text: A graph $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$; $\omega(G)$ is the clique number. A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs, and $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for all its members. For an integer $d\ge1$, $\tau_d(G)$ is the largest $t$ such that $G$ has a subgraph (not necessarily induced) isomorphic to the complete $d$-partite graph with every part of size $t$; thus $\tau_1(G)=|G|$, $\tau_2(G)$ is the largest $t$ with $K_{t,t}\subseteq G$, and $\tau_d(G)\ge\lfloor\omega(G)/d\rfloor$. Esperet conjectured that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class has a polynomial bounding function; this was disproved in general (Briański, Davies and Walczak) but remains open for classes excluding a forest. A referee suggested this analogue for $\tau_d$ in place of $\omega$. It is motivated by the paper's main result: for every tree $H$ of radius two and every integer $d\ge1$ there is a polynomial $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\tau_d(G))$ for every $H$-free graph $G$, and by the earlier result of the authors with Spirkl that for every forest $H$ there is $c>0$ with $\chi(G)\le\tau_2(G)^c$ for every $H$-free $G$.
notes: Explicitly labelled as an open question suggested by a referee and incorporated into the paper.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number. V. Excluding a tree of radius two and a complete multipartite graph

name: AX_independent_set_reconfiguration_diameter_k4_cubic
title: Conjecture 4
context_text: For a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, the ($k$-)configuration graph $\mathcal{R}_k(G)$ has the independent sets of size $k$ of $G$ as vertices, two of them being adjacent if one is obtained from the other by a token jump, i.e. by removing one vertex and adding another vertex (Token Jumping model). $D(n,k)$ is the maximum, over all $n$-vertex graphs $G$, of the diameter of a connected component of $\mathcal{R}_k(G)$, i.e. the maximum length of a shortest reconfiguration sequence between two $k$-independent sets. The authors prove $D(n,k)\le\binom{n}{k-1}$, $D(n,2)=n-2$ (the complement of the path being the unique extremal graph), and, via the hypergraph removal lemma, $D(n,k)=o(n^{k-1})$ for $k\ge3$; their lower bounds also hold for Token Sliding. For $k=3$ they give an almost tight construction $D(n,3)\ge n^2/e^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ (related to the $(6,3)$-problem and built from 3-AP-free sets), and in general $D(n,k)\ge n^{2\lfloor k/3\rfloor}/e^{O_k(\sqrt{\log n})}$. They could not show that lower and upper bounds almost match for $k\ge4$: in particular it is open whether the 4-configuration graph can have super-quadratic diameter, while the upper bound is $o(n^3)$. As a first step towards super-quadratic diameter one needs many copies of $K_4$ no two sharing a triangle, and Gowers and Janzer showed that there are $n$-vertex graphs with $n^{k-1-o(1)}$ copies of $K_k$ such that every $K_{k-1}$ lies in at most one of them, which might suggest $D(n,k)=n^{k-1-o(1)}$ in general.
paper_title: Extremal Independent Set Reconfiguration

name: AX_independent_set_reconfiguration_diameter_max_k
title: Question 8
statement_text: What is the asymptotic behavior of $\max_k D(n, k)$?
context_text: For a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, the ($k$-)configuration graph $\mathcal{R}_k(G)$ has the independent sets of size $k$ of $G$ as vertices, two of them being adjacent if one is obtained from the other by a token jump, i.e. by removing one vertex and adding another vertex (Token Jumping model). $D(n,k)$ is the maximum, over all $n$-vertex graphs $G$, of the diameter of a connected component of $\mathcal{R}_k(G)$, i.e. the maximum length of a shortest reconfiguration sequence between two $k$-independent sets. The authors prove $D(n,k)\le\binom{n}{k-1}$, $D(n,2)=n-2$ (the complement of the path being the unique extremal graph), and, via the hypergraph removal lemma, $D(n,k)=o(n^{k-1})$ for $k\ge3$; their lower bounds also hold for Token Sliding. The asymptotic lower bounds they prove for fixed $k$ (such as $D(n,k)\ge n^{2\lfloor k/3\rfloor}/e^{O_k(\sqrt{\log n})}$) may fail when $k$ grows with $n$. Building on a construction from the CoRe Challenge 2022, they show that there are graphs on $10n$ vertices whose configuration graph for independent sets of size $3n$ is a path of length $\Theta(4^n)$, and more generally that $D(n,k)=\Omega(2^{n/5})$ for every $k$ with $3n/10\le k\le2n/5$; they find it surprising that this exponential bound holds for such a range of $k$, which raises the question of the maximum over $k$.
paper_title: Extremal Independent Set Reconfiguration

name: AX_dope_matrices_generic_conditions_ert_sufficient
title: Conjecture on Sufficiency of Conditions E, R, T for Generic Tuples
statement_text: When $\Lambda$ is generic, Conditions E, R, and T are necessary and sufficient for an $m \times (n+1)$ matrix to be the multiplicity matrix of some polynomial $P$ with respect to $\Lambda$.
context_text: For a complex polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ and an $m$-tuple $\Lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m)$ of distinct complex numbers, Nathanson's multiplicity matrix $M_P(\Lambda)=(\mu_{ij})_{i\in[1,m],j\in[0,n]}$ has $\mu_{ij}$ equal to the multiplicity of $\lambda_i$ as a root of the $j$-th derivative $P^{(j)}$; the dope matrix $D_P(\Lambda)$ is the $\{0,1\}$-matrix recording which entries are nonzero, and $M_P(\Lambda)$ can be recovered from it. Necessary conditions are: Condition E, the entries are nonnegative integers; Condition R (rows), if $\mu_{ij}>0$ then $j<n$ and $\mu_{i,j+1}=\mu_{ij}-1$; Condition C (columns), $\sum_i\mu_{ij}\le n-j$ for each $j$; and Condition T (tail), for each $k\in[0,n]$ there are at most $k$ nonzero entries in the last $k+1$ columns, which is stronger than C and is necessary for $m\le2$. A tuple $\Lambda$ is generic if its entries satisfy no nontrivial integer polynomial relation (e.g. a random tuple); all generic $m$-tuples give the same set of dope matrices. The authors prove that E, R, T are necessary and sufficient for $m=2$ (for every pair $\Lambda$), and hence count the $2\times(n+1)$ dope matrices ($\binom{2n+1}{n}$); for $m>2$, E, R, C are far from sufficient (for large $m=n$, almost all matrices satisfying them are not multiplicity matrices). In dope-matrix form the conjecture says that, for $m\ge3$ and generic $\Lambda$, the dope matrices are exactly the $m\times(n+1)$ $\{0,1\}$-matrices satisfying Condition T. It is consistent with computations for $m=3$, $n\le6$, it would give a linear recurrence for the number of generic dope matrices, and the authors' theorem that generic tuples maximize the number of dope matrices is a quick consequence of it. This is a problem about polynomials rather than graphs. Status note (November 2026): a note added in the revision of the paper states that Bisain has since proved this conjecture ('Generic classification and asymptotic enumeration of dope matrices', arXiv 2209.13811, 2022).
notes: Stated in running prose in Section 3 without a labelled theorem environment; the authors write 'we conjecture that when $\Lambda$ is generic, Conditions E, R, and T are necessary and sufficient'.
paper_title: Counting Dope Matrices

name: AX_list_total_coloring_delta_plus_2
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: Every simple graph $G$ satisfies $\chi''_\ell(G) \leq \Delta(G) + 2$.
context_text: A total coloring of $G$ colors its vertices and edges so that adjacent vertices, adjacent (incident to a common vertex) edges, and a vertex and an incident edge always receive different colors; $\chi''(G)$ is the minimum number of colors of a total coloring. $G$ is totally $k$-choosable if, for every assignment of lists of $k$ colors to its vertices and edges, there is a total coloring giving each element a color from its own list, and the list total chromatic number $\chi''_\ell(G)$ is the minimum such $k$; so $\chi''(G)\le\chi''_\ell(G)$, and greedily $\chi''_\ell\le 2\Delta+1$, while $\chi''\ge\Delta+1$. This is the list analogue of the Total Coloring Conjecture of Behzad and Vizing ($\chi''(G)\le\Delta(G)+2$), in the same way as Vizing's conjecture $\chi'_\ell\le\Delta+1$ is the list version of Vizing's theorem; the List Coloring Conjecture even asserts $\chi''(G)=\chi''_\ell(G)$ for every simple graph. Graphs are simple. For planar graphs it was known when $\Delta\ge 9$ or $\Delta\le3$; the authors prove that every planar graph of maximum degree at most 8 is totally 10-choosable, hence the conjecture holds for all planar graphs with $\Delta\ge 8$.
notes: PDF source — math notation reconstructed from Unicode. No citation appears in the conjecture header; the paper proves this conjecture for planar graphs with $\Delta \geq 8$ as its central result.
paper_title: Every planar graph with $Δ\geqslant 8$ is totally $(Δ+2)$-choosable

name: AX_z3_flow_critical_density_genus_coefficient
title: Problem 1.6
statement_text: What is the smallest constant $\alpha$ such that every $Z_3$-flow-critical graph $G$ satisfies $|E(G)| \leq \frac{5}{2}|V(G)| + \alpha g(G) + O(1)$?
context_text: Graphs may have parallel edges but no loops. For an abelian group $A$, an $A$-flow of $G$ assigns to each edge an orientation and a value in $A$ so that at every vertex the sum of incoming values equals the sum of outgoing values; it is nowhere-zero if no edge gets $0$. $Z_3$ is the cyclic group of order 3. A graph $G$ is $Z_3$-flow-critical if it is connected, has no nowhere-zero $Z_3$-flow, but every proper contraction of $G$ (in particular $G/e$ for every edge $e$, loops being removed) has one; flow-critical graphs are the duals of colour-critical graphs. The Euler genus $g(G)$ is the minimum Euler genus of a surface (sphere with $h$ handles and $c$ crosscaps has Euler genus $2h+c$) in which $G$ embeds. Dualising Kostochka–Yancey gives $|E(G)|\le\frac{5|V(G)|-8}{2}$ for planar $Z_3$-flow-critical graphs, which is tight for infinitely many planar graphs, while the graph $K^+_{3,n-3}$ ($K_{3,n-3}$ plus an edge between two vertices of degree $n-3$) is $Z_3$-flow-critical with $3n-8$ edges and has Euler genus $\lceil\frac{n-5}{2}\rceil$; Li et al. conjectured $|E(G)|\le3|V(G)|-8$ for $|V(G)|\ge7$ and proved $|E(G)|\le4|V(G)|-10$ for $G\neq K_2$. The authors prove $|E(G)|\le\frac{5|V(G)|+5g(G)-8}{2}$ for every $Z_3$-flow-critical graph, so $\alpha\le5/2$, while $K^+_{3,n-3}$ shows $\alpha\ge1$; the coefficient $5/2$ of $|V(G)|$ cannot be lowered, but the dependence on the genus is likely not optimal.
paper_title: On density of $Z_3$-flow-critical graphs

name: AX_directed_sidorenko_bipartite_homomorphism
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: If $B$ is a bipartite oriented graph with a homomorphism $B \to \vec{K}_2$, then $B$ has the directed Sidorenko property.
context_text: An oriented graph is a simple graph with each edge oriented; $\vec K_2$ is the single arc (directed edge). For oriented graphs $B,G$, a homomorphism $B\to G$ is a vertex map sending every arc $(x,y)$ of $B$ to an arc $(f(x),f(y))$ of $G$, and the homomorphism density $t(B,G)$ is the fraction of all maps $V(B)\to V(G)$ that are homomorphisms (similarly $t(A,H)$ for undirected graphs). An oriented graph $B$ has the directed Sidorenko property if $t(B,G)\ge t(\vec K_2,G)^{e(B)}$ for every oriented graph $G$, i.e. $G$ contains at least as many copies of $B$ as expected in a random oriented graph of the same edge density. This is a directed analogue of Sidorenko's conjecture, which asserts $t(A,H)\ge t(K_2,H)^{e(A)}$ for every bipartite graph $A$ and every graph $H$. Having a homomorphism to $\vec K_2$ (i.e. every vertex of $B$ is a source or a sink) is necessary, since otherwise $B$ has no copy in the complete bipartite graph with all arcs oriented from one side to the other. For a bipartite undirected graph $A=(A_1\sqcup A_2,E)$ with a fixed ordered bipartition and a bipartite graph $H=(U_1\sqcup U_2,F)$, $t_{\mathrm{bip}}(A,H)$ is the fraction of maps $f$ with $f(A_i)\subseteq U_i$ ($i=1,2$) that are homomorphisms; $A$ has the asymmetric Sidorenko property if $t_{\mathrm{bip}}(A,H)\ge t_{\mathrm{bip}}(K_2,H)^{e(A)}$ for every bipartite $H$, i.e. the count of copies of $A$ respecting sides is at least that expected in a random bipartite graph of the same bipartite density $|F|/(|U_1||U_2|)$. Such a homomorphism gives the underlying graph $\overline B$ of $B$ a bipartition (preimages of the tail and of the head of $\vec K_2$), and the authors prove that $B$ has the directed Sidorenko property if and only if $\overline B$ has the asymmetric Sidorenko property; thus the conjecture is equivalent to the asymmetric Sidorenko conjecture.
notes: PDF source.
paper_title: A note on directed analogues of the Sidorenko and forcing conjectures

name: AX_directed_sidorenko_forcing_cycle_homomorphism
title: Conjecture 1.7
statement_text: If $B$ is an oriented graph with a homomorphism to an edge and whose underlying undirected graph has a cycle, then $B$ has the directed forcing property.
context_text: An oriented graph is a simple graph with each edge oriented; $\vec K_2$ is the single arc (directed edge). For oriented graphs $B,G$, a homomorphism $B\to G$ is a vertex map sending every arc $(x,y)$ of $B$ to an arc $(f(x),f(y))$ of $G$, and the homomorphism density $t(B,G)$ is the fraction of all maps $V(B)\to V(G)$ that are homomorphisms (similarly $t(A,H)$ for undirected graphs). A sequence of oriented graphs $(G_n)$ is quasirandom with density $p$ if its directed graphons (the step functions $W_{G_n}:[0,1]^2\to\{0,1\}$ obtained by splitting $[0,1]$ into $v(G_n)$ equal intervals and setting $W_{G_n}(x,y)=1$ on $I_i\times I_j$ iff $(i,j)$ is an arc) converge in cut norm to a constant. An oriented graph $B$ has the directed forcing property if, for every $p\in[0,1]$, every sequence of oriented graphs $(G_n)$ with $t(\vec K_2,G_n)\to p/2$ and $t(B,G_n)\to(p/2)^{e(B)}$ (the values for a random orientation of a random graph of edge density $p$) is $p$-quasirandom. This is a directed analogue of the forcing conjecture of Skokan and Thoma, which states that an undirected graph is forcing (counts of it at the random value force quasirandomness) if and only if it is bipartite and contains a cycle. The authors prove that having a homomorphism to $\vec K_2$ (every vertex of $B$ is a source or a sink) and having a cycle in the underlying undirected graph $\overline B$ are both necessary for the directed forcing property, and that, for $B$ with a homomorphism to $\vec K_2$, $B$ has the directed forcing property if and only if $\overline B$ (with the bipartition given by the homomorphism) has the asymmetric forcing property, the analogous property for bipartite graphs with ordered sides counted side-respectingly.
notes: PDF source.
paper_title: A note on directed analogues of the Sidorenko and forcing conjectures

name: AX_sidorenko_asymmetric_classical_equivalent
title: Equivalence of asymmetric and classical Sidorenko properties
statement_text: It is conjectured that the asymmetric Sidorenko property and the classical Sidorenko property are equivalent for bipartite graphs.
context_text: For graphs $A,H$, the homomorphism density $t(A,H)$ is the fraction of all maps $V(A)\to V(H)$ that send edges to edges; a bipartite graph $A$ has the (classical) Sidorenko property if $t(A,H)\ge t(K_2,H)^{e(A)}$ for every graph $H$, and Sidorenko's conjecture asserts that every bipartite graph has it. For a bipartite undirected graph $A=(A_1\sqcup A_2,E)$ with a fixed ordered bipartition and a bipartite graph $H=(U_1\sqcup U_2,F)$, $t_{\mathrm{bip}}(A,H)$ is the fraction of maps $f$ with $f(A_i)\subseteq U_i$ ($i=1,2$) that are homomorphisms; $A$ has the asymmetric Sidorenko property if $t_{\mathrm{bip}}(A,H)\ge t_{\mathrm{bip}}(K_2,H)^{e(A)}$ for every bipartite $H$, i.e. the count of copies of $A$ respecting sides is at least that expected in a random bipartite graph of the same bipartite density $|F|/(|U_1||U_2|)$. The asymmetric Sidorenko property implies the classical one (apply it to the bipartite double cover of $H$, with two copies of $V(H)$ and an edge between copies of $u$ and $v$ whenever $uv\in E(H)$), so it is a priori stronger. There is no known black-box reduction in the other direction, but essentially all bipartite graphs known to have the Sidorenko property are also known to have the asymmetric one (e.g. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov observed it for bipartite graphs with a vertex complete to the other side). The question matters for the paper because the authors show that the directed Sidorenko property of an oriented graph with a homomorphism to an arc is equivalent to the asymmetric Sidorenko property of its underlying bipartite graph.
notes: Reported as a widely held community belief without explicit attribution to specific authors; no formal labelled environment.
paper_title: A note on directed analogues of the Sidorenko and forcing conjectures

name: AX_turan_h_free_bounded_matching_number
title: Extension to H-free graphs
statement_text: Determine the maximum possible number of edges of an $H$-free graph on $n$ vertices with matching number at most $s$, for general forbidden subgraphs $H$ (extending the authors' solution of the case $H = K_{k+1}$).
context_text: The matching number of $G$ is the maximum size of a matching, and $H$-free means containing no (not necessarily induced) copy of $H$. Turán's theorem gives the maximum number $t(n,k)$ of edges of a graph on $n$ vertices with clique number at most $k$ (attained by the balanced complete $k$-partite Turán graph $T(n,k)$), and the Erdős–Gallai theorem the maximum number of edges with matching number at most $s$. Let $G(n,k,s)$ be the complete $k$-partite graph on $n$ vertices with $k-1$ classes of sizes as equal as possible and total size $s$, plus one class of size $n-s$, and $g(n,k,s)$ its number of edges. The authors prove the common generalization: for $n\ge2s+1$, the maximum number of edges of a graph on $n$ vertices with clique number at most $k$ (i.e. $K_{k+1}$-free) and matching number at most $s$ is $\max\{t(2s+1,k),g(n,k,s)\}$. They suggest extending this to other forbidden graphs $H$, and prove, using Simonovits's result on color-critical graphs, that if $H$ is color-critical (has an edge whose deletion decreases its chromatic number) with chromatic number $k+1>2$, then for $s>s_0(H)$ and $n>n_0(s)$ the maximum is $g(n,k,s)$. The general case (other $H$, smaller parameters) is left open.
notes: No labeled environment; posed as a research direction at the start of Section 3, partially addressed by Proposition 3.1 in the same section.
paper_title: Turán graphs with bounded matching number

name: AX_segment_graphs_kr_free_linear_induced
title: Problem 1.2
statement_text: Fix an integer $r \geq 4$. Is it true that every $K_r$-free segment graph on $n$ vertices has an induced subgraph on $\Omega_r(n)$ vertices which is $K_{r-1}$-free?
context_text: A string graph (resp. segment graph) is the intersection graph of a family of continuous curves (resp. straight line segments) in the plane: vertices are the curves, adjacent when they intersect. A topological graph is $r$-quasiplanar if no $r$ of its edges pairwise cross; a longstanding conjecture states that $r$-quasiplanar graphs on $n$ vertices have $O_r(n)$ edges, known for $r\le4$ (Ackerman for $r=4$). Removing small discs around the vertices of an $r$-quasiplanar graph yields a $K_r$-free string graph on its edges; a natural approach would be to colour it with few colours so that each colour class is planar or $K_4$-free, but this fails: there are $K_3$-free segment graphs of arbitrarily large chromatic number (Pawlik et al., from Burling's construction), and Krawczyk and Walczak built $K_r$-free string graphs needing $\Omega_r(\log\log n)$ colours if each class must induce a $K_{r-1}$-free graph. The question here asks for a single large $K_{r-1}$-free induced subgraph instead. Suk showed (building on McGuinness) that every $K_r$-free segment graph on $n$ vertices has a $K_{r-1}$-free induced subgraph on $\Omega_r(n/\log n)$ vertices. The authors prove that every $K_r$-free string graph on $n$ vertices has a $K_{r-1}$-free induced subgraph on $cn/\log^2 n$ vertices and use this to improve the edge bound for $r$-quasiplanar graphs; the linear bound for segment graphs remains open. They also conjecture the analogous linear bound for $K_r$-free circle graphs (where the bound $\Omega(n/\log r)$ follows from Davies' colouring result) and for intersection graphs of axis-parallel boxes.
paper_title: Quasiplanar Graphs, String Graphs, and the Erdos-Gallai Problem

name: AX_linear_growth_tree_strong_product_subgraph
title: Conjecture 14
statement_text: There exist functions $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for any $c \geq 1$, every graph $G$ with growth $f_G(r) \leq cr$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $T \boxtimes K_{g(c)}$ for some tree $T$ with growth $f_T(r) \leq h(c)r$.
context_text: The growth of a (possibly infinite) graph $G$ is the function $f_G:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ where $f_G(r)$ is the supremum of $|V(H)|$ over all subgraphs $H$ of $G$ of radius at most $r$; a class has linear growth if this is $O(r)$. The strong product $A\boxtimes B$ has vertex set $V(A)\times V(B)$, with $(v,w)$ and $(v',w')$ adjacent if ($vv'\in E(A)$ and $w=w'$) or ($v=v'$ and $ww'\in E(B)$) or ($vv'\in E(A)$ and $ww'\in E(B)$). Thus $T\boxtimes K_t$ is the blow-up of $T$ obtained by replacing each vertex by a $K_t$ and each edge by a $K_{t,t}$. The authors' main result is that every graph with $f_G(r)\le cr$ has treewidth at most $49c^2+30c$. Such a graph also has maximum degree at most $c-1$, so known results give that it is a subgraph of $T\boxtimes K_{\lfloor 882c^3\rfloor}$ for some tree $T$. But $T$ may have exponential growth (e.g. a complete binary tree), and then so does the product. The conjecture asks for a tree of linear growth instead. This would roughly characterise graphs of linear growth, since every subgraph $H$ of $T\boxtimes K_{g(c)}$ then has $f_H(r)\le g(c)h(c)r$. The authors make the analogous conjecture for polynomial growth $f_G(r)\le cr^d$, with a product of $d$ trees of linear growth and a clique $K_{g(c,d)}$.
paper_title: Graphs of Linear Growth have Bounded Treewidth

name: AX_random_graph_hereditary_extremal_probability_range
title: Open Problem (characterizing edge probabilities for Theorem 1.1)
statement_text: Characterize all edge probabilities $p = p(n)$ for which the following holds whp for the random graph $G=G(n,p)$: $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})=\left(1-\frac{1}{k-1}+o(1)\right)p\binom{n}{2}$, where $\mathcal{P}$ is a non-trivial hereditary property and $k=k(\mathcal{P})$ is the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in $\mathcal{P}$.
context_text: A graph property $\mathcal{P}$ is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs (and isomorphism); it is non-trivial if it contains all edgeless graphs and misses some graph. For a graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})$ is the maximum number of edges of a subgraph of $G$ (not necessarily induced) that belongs to $\mathcal{P}$. $k=k(\mathcal{P})\ge2$ is the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in $\mathcal{P}$, $G(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and whp means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. The authors prove that for every fixed $p\in(0,1)$, whp $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P})=(1-\frac{1}{k-1}+o(1))p\binom n2$, and that the same holds whenever $n^{-c}\le p\le1-n^{-c}$ for a constant $c=c(\mathcal{P})>0$. For principal monotone properties (avoiding a single graph as a subgraph) the exact range of $p$ is known (Conlon–Gowers, Schacht), but hereditary properties are far more general (e.g. perfect graphs, or graphs with no induced copy of a given graph). The authors note that it is not difficult to find hereditary (even monotone) properties for which the fraction of edges of $G(n,p)$ lying in a maximum subgraph with the property changes, whp, several times as $p=p(n)$ increases from 0 to 1; presumably the answer depends on $\mathcal{P}$.
notes: PDF source; stated as an informal open problem in the concluding remarks without a labelled environment.
paper_title: Largest subgraph from a hereditary property in a random graph

name: AX_random_graph_hereditary_extremal_bipartite_asymptotics
title: Open Problem (accurate estimate in the bipartite case)
statement_text: Provide a more accurate estimate for $\mathrm{ex}(G, \mathcal{P})$, $G=G(n,p)$, when the non-trivial hereditary property $\mathcal{P}$ misses a bipartite graph (i.e., when $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P}) = o(n^2)$ whp).
context_text: A graph property $\mathcal{P}$ is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs (and isomorphism); it is non-trivial if it contains all edgeless graphs and misses some graph. For a graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})$ is the maximum number of edges of a subgraph of $G$ (not necessarily induced) that belongs to $\mathcal{P}$. $k=k(\mathcal{P})\ge2$ is the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in $\mathcal{P}$, $G(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and whp means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. The authors prove that for every fixed $p\in(0,1)$, whp $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P})=(1-\frac{1}{k-1}+o(1))p\binom n2$, and that the same holds whenever $n^{-c}\le p\le1-n^{-c}$ for a constant $c=c(\mathcal{P})>0$. For principal monotone properties (avoiding a single graph as a subgraph) the exact range of $p$ is known (Conlon–Gowers, Schacht), but hereditary properties are far more general (e.g. perfect graphs, or graphs with no induced copy of a given graph). When $\mathcal{P}$ misses a bipartite graph, $k(\mathcal{P})=2$ and the theorem only gives $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P})=o(n^2)$ whp, without the precise order of magnitude. The authors suggest that it is plausible that $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})\le n^{2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(\mathcal{P})>0$ in this case.

paper_title: Largest subgraph from a hereditary property in a random graph

name: AX_random_graph_hereditary_extremal_polynomial_saving
title: Informal Conjecture (polynomial saving in the bipartite case)
statement_text: It seems plausible that in the bipartite case (the non-trivial hereditary property $\mathcal{P}$ misses some bipartite graph) one has, for $G=G(n,p)$ whp, $\mathrm{ex}(G, \mathcal{P}) \leq n^{2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\mathcal{P}) > 0$.
context_text: A graph property $\mathcal{P}$ is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs (and isomorphism); it is non-trivial if it contains all edgeless graphs and misses some graph. For a graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})$ is the maximum number of edges of a subgraph of $G$ (not necessarily induced) that belongs to $\mathcal{P}$. $k=k(\mathcal{P})\ge2$ is the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in $\mathcal{P}$, $G(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and whp means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. name: AX_subdigraph_half_vertices_min_outdegree_gap
title: Open problem: closing the gap for $d(s)$
statement_text: It remains an interesting open problem to close the gap between the lower and upper bounds: $\Omega(\log s) < \frac{s}{2} - d(s) < O(\sqrt{s\log s})$, where $d(s)$ denotes the largest integer such that every $2n$-vertex digraph of minimum out-degree at least $s$ contains an $n$-vertex subdigraph of minimum out-degree at least $d(s)$.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs (opposite arcs $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ are allowed), and an $n$-vertex subdigraph means the subdigraph $D[X]$ induced by an $n$-set $X$. Alon (2006) asked whether there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that every $2n$-vertex digraph of minimum out-degree at least $s$ contains an $n$-vertex subdigraph of minimum out-degree at least $\frac{s}{2}-c$, and proved by a probabilistic argument the weaker bound $\frac{s}{2}-O(\sqrt{s\log s})$. The authors answer Alon's problem negatively with an explicit recursive construction: for infinitely many $n$ there is a $2n$-vertex tournament with minimum out-degree $s=n-1$ in which every $n$-vertex subdigraph has minimum out-degree at most $\frac{s}{2}-(\frac12+o(1))\log_3 s$. Together these give the stated bounds $\Omega(\log s)<\frac{s}{2}-d(s)<O(\sqrt{s\log s})$; the true order of $\frac{s}{2}-d(s)$ remains open.
notes: Stated in prose without a labelled environment; PDF source may garble some exponent notation.
paper_title: Subdigraphs of prescribed size and outdegree

name: AX_c4_diamond_theta_prism_bounded_treewidth
title: Conjecture 1.6
statement_text: For all $t > 0$ there exists $c_t \geq 0$ such that $\mathrm{tw}(G) \leq c_t$ for every ($C_4$, diamond, theta, prism, even wheel, $K_t$)-free graph $G$.
context_text: $\mathcal{H}$-free means with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{H}$. A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four and $C_4$ is the hole of length four; the diamond is $K_4$ minus an edge. A theta consists of two non-adjacent vertices $a,b$ and three paths of length at least two from $a$ to $b$ whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and anticomplete. A pyramid consists of a vertex $a$, a triangle $b_1b_2b_3$ and three paths $P_i$ from $a$ to $b_i$ such that the sets $P_i\setminus\{a\}$ are pairwise disjoint and anticomplete and at least two $P_i$ have length at least two. A prism consists of two disjoint triangles $a_1a_2a_3$, $b_1b_2b_3$ and three paths $P_i$ from $a_i$ to $b_i$ such that the only edges between distinct $P_i,P_j$ are $a_ia_j$ and $b_ib_j$. A wheel $(H,w)$ is a hole $H$ and a vertex $w$ with at least three pairwise non-adjacent neighbours in $H$; a line wheel is a hole $H$ and a vertex $v\notin H$ whose neighbours in $H$ form two disjoint edges; an even wheel is a line wheel or a wheel $(H,w)$ with $|N(w)\cap H|$ even and $N(w)\cap H$ not a single edge. Thetas, prisms and even wheels contain even holes. The authors prove that ($C_4$, diamond, theta, pyramid, prism, even wheel, $K_t$)-free graphs have bounded treewidth, hence so do (even hole, diamond, pyramid, $K_t$)-free graphs; this is sharp since Sintiari and Trotignon constructed (even hole, pyramid, $K_4$)-free graphs (containing diamonds) of unbounded treewidth. Sintiari and Trotignon conjectured that (even hole, diamond, $K_4$)-free graphs have bounded treewidth; the present conjecture is a slight generalization, obtained by no longer excluding pyramids, and the authors prove many intermediate results in this generality.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions IV. (Even hole, diamond, pyramid)-free graphs

name: AX_grid_ramsey_rectangle_vs_clique
title: Grid Ramsey Problem (gr(G_{2x2}, K_n))
statement_text: What is the minimum $N$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the Cartesian product $K_N \square K_N$ contains either a red rectangle or a blue $K_n$?
context_text: The $N\times N$ grid graph $G_{N\times N}=K_N\square K_N$ has vertex set $[N]\times[N]$, two vertices being adjacent when they share exactly one coordinate; a rectangle is a $2\times2$ subgrid, i.e. four vertices $(x,y),(x,y'),(x',y'),(x',y)$ with the four axis-parallel edges between them. $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $2$-edge-colouring of $G_{N\times N}$ contains a red rectangle or a blue $K_n$ (a clique of $G_{N\times N}$ lies in a single row or column). Via the bipartite $3$-graph $B^{(3)}(N,N)$ on $[2N]$ (all triples meeting both halves), whose triples correspond to the edges of the grid, rectangles correspond to copies of $K_4^{(3)}$ and $n$-cliques to copies of $S_n^{(3)}$; hence $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $2$-colouring of $B^{(3)}(N,N)$ has a red $K_4^{(3)}$ or a blue $S_n^{(3)}$, and $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})\le2\,\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$. The authors introduce this grid Ramsey problem as the key tool for estimating $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})$, and prove $2^{c\log^2n}\le\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)\le2^{c'n^{2/3}\log n}$ for positive constants $c,c'$; the exact growth rate remains open. They note a curious similarity with the lower bound $2^{c(\log r)^{2.5}/\sqrt{\log\log r}}$ for the grid case of Shelah's cube lemma ($r$ colours), without finding any connection.
notes: PDF source — stated verbatim in the abstract and introduction as a novel problem of independent interest; math notation reconstructed from PDF extraction.
paper_title: Hypergraph Ramsey numbers of cliques versus stars

name: AX_grid_ramsey_equals_hypergraph_clique_star
title: Informal Conjecture: r(K^(3)_4, S^(3)_n) and gr(G_{2x2}, K_n) have the same order
statement_text: We strongly believe that $r(K^{(3)}_4, S^{(3)}_n)$ and $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times 2}, K_n)$ are of roughly the same order.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_s^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $s$ vertices, $K_4^{(3)}-e$ is $K_4^{(3)}$ minus one edge (three triples on four vertices), and the star $3$-graph $S_n^{(3)}$ has $n+1$ vertices and all $\binom{n}{2}$ triples containing a given vertex. The Ramsey number $r(H_1,H_2)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $3$-graph on $N$ vertices contains $H_1$ or its complement contains $H_2$ (equivalently, every red/blue colouring of the triples of $K_N^{(3)}$ has a red $H_1$ or a blue $H_2$). The $N\times N$ grid graph $G_{N\times N}=K_N\square K_N$ has vertex set $[N]\times[N]$, two vertices being adjacent when they share exactly one coordinate; a rectangle is a $2\times2$ subgrid, i.e. four vertices $(x,y),(x,y'),(x',y'),(x',y)$ with the four axis-parallel edges between them. $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $2$-edge-colouring of $G_{N\times N}$ contains a red rectangle or a blue $K_n$ (a clique of $G_{N\times N}$ lies in a single row or column). Rectangles in $G_{N\times N}$ correspond to copies of $K_4^{(3)}$ and $n$-cliques to copies of $S_n^{(3)}$ in the bipartite $3$-graph $B^{(3)}(N,N)\subseteq K_{2N}^{(3)}$, which gives $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})\le2\,\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$. No direct implication between the lower bounds is known, but the authors glue together copies of their lower-bound construction for $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ to obtain one for $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})$ of comparable size; both quantities satisfy $2^{c\log^2n}\le\cdot\le2^{c'n^{2/3}\log n}$. This intermediate growth (between polynomial and exponential) contrasts with $r(K_s^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})=2^{\Theta(n)}$ for $s\ge5$ and with the Erdős–Hajnal polynomial-to-exponential transition phenomenon for Ramsey numbers against cliques.
notes: PDF source — explicit 'we strongly believe' language in the introduction; math notation reconstructed from PDF extraction.
paper_title: Hypergraph Ramsey numbers of cliques versus stars

name: AX_hypergraph_ramsey_k4_minus_edge_star
title: Informal Conjecture: r(K^(3)_{4-e}, S^(3)_n) = Theta(n^2 / log n)
statement_text: The close connection between $r(K_4^{(3)}-e, S^{(3)}_n)$ and $r(K_3, K_n)$ suggests that $r(K_4^{(3)}-e, S^{(3)}_n) = \Theta\!\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n}\right)$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_s^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $s$ vertices, $K_4^{(3)}-e$ is $K_4^{(3)}$ minus one edge (three triples on four vertices), and the star $3$-graph $S_n^{(3)}$ has $n+1$ vertices and all $\binom{n}{2}$ triples containing a given vertex. The Ramsey number $r(H_1,H_2)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $3$-graph on $N$ vertices contains $H_1$ or its complement contains $H_2$ (equivalently, every red/blue colouring of the triples of $K_N^{(3)}$ has a red $H_1$ or a blue $H_2$). The paper studies $r(K_s^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})$ for fixed $s$ and growing $n$, the regime left open by Fox and He. By the Lovász Local Lemma the authors obtain $c\frac{n^2}{\log^2n}\le r(K_4^{(3)}-e,S_n^{(3)})\le c'\frac{n^2}{\log n}$, which parallels the graph Ramsey number $r(K_3,K_n)=\Theta(n^2/\log n)$. They believe that the upper bound is the truth and that a proof may be possible through a careful analysis of the $(K_4^{(3)}-e)$-free process, but do not pursue this. For comparison, they show $2^{c\log^2n}\le r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})\le2^{c'n^{2/3}\log n}$ and $r(K_s^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})=2^{\Theta(n)}$ for $s\ge5$.
notes: PDF source — conjectural language 'suggests' and 'it seems likely'; $K^{(3)}_{4-e}$ denotes the complete 3-uniform hypergraph on 4 vertices minus one edge; math notation reconstructed from PDF extraction.

name: AX_intersection_graphs_asymptotic_dimension_tight
title: Optimal bound question
statement_text: Is it possible to decrease the bound $2n+1$ to $n$ in the following result: for every metric space $(X,d)$ of Assouad–Nagata dimension $n$ and every $f:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{Z}_+$, the family of intersection graphs of $f$-space-filling systems of subsets of $X$ has asymptotic dimension at most $2n+1$ (or at least in its special case: for every $\alpha\ge1$, the class of intersection graphs of systems of compact convex sets of aspect ratio at most $\alpha$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has asymptotic dimension at most $2n+1$)?
context_text: For a cover $\mathcal{U}$ of a metric space $(X,d)$, its Lebesgue number is the supremum of $r\ge0$ such that every ball of radius $r$ lies in some member of $\mathcal{U}$, and its mesh is the supremum of the diameters of its members. A function $D:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}_+$ is an $n$-dimensional control function for $X$ if for every $r>0$ there is a cover $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}_1\cup\dots\cup\mathcal{U}_{n+1}$ of $X$ with mesh at most $D(r)$, Lebesgue number at least $r$, and each $\mathcal{U}_i$ consisting of pairwise disjoint sets. The asymptotic dimension of $X$ is the least $n$ admitting such a $D$, and the Assouad–Nagata dimension is the least $n$ for which $D(r)=Kr$ works for some $K>1$ ($\mathbb{R}^n$ has Assouad–Nagata dimension $n$). A graph is viewed as the metric space of its vertices with the shortest-path distance, and a class of graphs has asymptotic dimension at most $n$ if a single $n$-dimensional control function works for all its members. The intersection graph of a system $\mathcal{S}$ of sets has vertex set $\mathcal{S}$, two sets being adjacent when they intersect. For $f:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{Z}_+$, $\mathcal{S}$ is $f$-space-filling if all its sets have finite diameter and for all $r,s>0$ and $x\in X$, the ball $B(x,r)$ meets at most $f(r/s)$ pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal{S}$ of diameter at least $s$. The aspect ratio of $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is its diameter divided by its height (the least distance between two parallel hyperplanes enclosing $S$). Without such fatness restrictions there is no bound: graphs obtained from bipartite graphs by subdividing each edge once are intersection graphs of boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ but have unbounded asymptotic dimension. The authors prove the upper bound $2n+1$ and remark that it is likely not optimal: interval graphs (intersection graphs of balls in $\mathbb{R}^1$) have asymptotic dimension $1$ rather than $3$. Since $n$-dimensional grids have asymptotic dimension $n$ and are touching graphs of balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the bound cannot go below $n$.
notes: PDF source — stated as 'it is natural to ask' without a labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Asymptotic dimension of intersection graphs

name: AX_forest_free_polynomial_chi_omega_power
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: For every forest $H$, there exists $c > 0$ such that $\chi(G) \leq \omega(G)^c$ for every $H$-free graph $G$.
context_text: $H$-free means having no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and $\omega(G)$ is the clique number. A hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for some function $f$ and all $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded if $f$ can be taken polynomial. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture states that $H$-free graphs are $\chi$-bounded for every forest $H$; Esperet conjectured that every $\chi$-bounded class is polynomially $\chi$-bounded, which was disproved by Briański, Davies and Walczak. The present conjecture would follow from both and is still open; the authors call it beautiful. It has been proved only for a much smaller collection of forests than the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, including (by the authors) every $P_5$-free tree, but not for any tree containing $P_5$ ($P_k$ is the $k$-vertex path). For $H=P_5$ the best previous bound was exponential, $\chi(G)\le\frac{5}{27}3^{\omega(G)}$ for $\omega(G)\ge3$ (Esperet, Lemoine, Maffray, Morel), and the paper proves the near-polynomial bound $\chi(G)\le\omega(G)^{\log_2\omega(G)}$. Every forest $H$ satisfying the conjecture also satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (every $H$-free graph $G$ has $\alpha(G)\omega(G)\ge|G|^c$ for some $c>0$), whose smallest open case is $H=P_5$.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number. IV. A near-polynomial bound for excluding the five-vertex path

name: AX_twin_width_matrices_infinite_fields
title: Open question on twin-width over infinite fields
statement_text: An intriguing question concerns the existence of such results (almost linear-time multiplication of matrices of bounded twin-width given by twin-decompositions, known over finite fields) over infinite fields (starting with $\mathbb{Q}$). We do not have a direct definition of twin-width of matrices over $\mathbb{Q}$ based on contraction sequences. However linear-minor freeness naturally carries to infinite fields, and thus, it is natural to consider that a class of matrices over $\mathbb{Q}$ has bounded twin-width if its closure under linear minors is not the set of all matrices. This can be equivalently stated via the notion of grid rank of a matrix $M$, i.e., the largest $k$ for which there is a $k\times k$ subdivision of $M$ in which every block has rank at least $k$. We believe that computing the product of two matrices over $\mathbb{Q}$ with bounded grid rank should be done in almost quadratic time, however, we lack a structural decomposition as in the finite field case.
context_text: Matrices have ordered rows and columns, and a matrix class is a set of matrices closed under taking submatrices. A linear minor of a matrix $M$ over a field is a matrix obtained by a succession of replacements of two consecutive rows, or two consecutive columns, by a linear combination of them; equivalently, one partitions the columns into intervals and picks one column vector in the span of each part, then does the same with the rows (over $\mathbb{F}_2$ this amounts to deletions and sums of consecutive rows or columns, called parity minors). A class excludes $M$ as a linear minor if $M$ is not a linear minor of any matrix of the class; a $k\times k$ subdivision (or $k$-division) partitions the rows and the columns into $k$ intervals each. Over a finite field, twin-width of matrices is defined by contraction sequences, and the authors prove that a matrix class over a finite field has bounded twin-width if and only if it excludes some matrix as a linear minor. They also give an algorithm that, given two $n\times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q$ as twin-decompositions (a compact tree-based representation derived from contraction sequences) of width at most $d$, computes a twin-decomposition of their product in time $q^{2d+o(d)}n$, with entries then queryable in time $O(1/\varepsilon)$ after $2^{O_q(d)}n^{1+\varepsilon}$ preprocessing. The question is whether analogous results hold over infinite fields. The authors note that a linear minor of a matrix of grid rank $k$ has grid rank at most $k$, and that a class has bounded grid rank if and only if it excludes some matrix as a linear minor.
