paper_title: Twin-width V: linear minors, modular counting, and matrix multiplication

name: AX_monochromatic_subset_sums_density_tight
title: Conjecture on tightness of the upper bound for all r ≥ 3
statement_text: We suspect that our upper bound $c_r \leq \left(1-\frac{1}{2b_0}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{2rb_0-r}\right)$ is also tight for all $r \geq 3$, where $b_0 > 1$ is the unique root of $b^r - 2rb + r - 1 = 0$.
context_text: For a set $A$ of positive integers, the logarithmic density of $A$ up to $x$ is $d_\ell(A;x)=\frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{a\in A,\,a\le x}1/a$ (natural logarithm), and the upper logarithmic density is $\bar{d}_\ell(A)=\limsup_{x\to\infty}d_\ell(A;x)$. The set of subset sums of $A$ is $\Sigma(A)=\{\sum_{s\in S}s : S\subseteq A\}$ (sums of distinct elements of $A$). For an integer $r\ge2$, $c_r=\min_{\mathbb{N}=A_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup A_r}\max_{i\in[r]}\bar{d}_\ell(\Sigma(A_i))$, the minimum being over all partitions (r-colorings) of the positive integers into $r$ parts; equivalently, $c_r$ is the largest real such that every $r$-coloring of the positive integers has a color class whose set of subset sums has upper logarithmic density at least $c_r$. Erdős asked for the value of $c_2$, noting that it is at least $1/2$ and less than $1$. The authors prove for every $r\ge2$ the upper bound $c_r\le\left(1-\frac{1}{2b_0}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{2rb_0-r}\right)$, with $b_0>1$ the unique root of $b^r-2rb+r-1$ greater than $1$, and show that it is tight for $r=2$, giving $c_2=(2+\sqrt{3})/4\approx0.93301$. They conjecture tightness for all $r\ge3$; their lower-bound method seems to work if an auxiliary coloring arising in the proof is assumed to be cyclic (the $i$-th monochromatic interval has color $i \bmod r$), which is automatic for $r=2$ but not in general.
notes: Stated in prose without a labelled environment: 'We suspect that our upper bound is also tight for all r ≥ 3, but our methods do not seem sufficient for proving this.' PDF extraction may have garbled exponent notation (2^r vs 2r) in the formula.
paper_title: The upper logarithmic density of monochromatic subset sums

name: AX_clique_3_triangle_free_induced_bounded
title: Question 3.1
statement_text: Are there graphs with clique number $3$ and arbitrarily large chromatic number whose all triangle-free induced subgraphs have chromatic number at most $3$?
context_text: A conjecture (attributed to Esperet, and earlier to Galvin and Rödl) stated that for all $k,r$ there is $n$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\ge n$ and $\omega(G)\le k$ has an induced subgraph $H$ with $\chi(H)\ge r$ and $\omega(H)=2$; it is the induced analogue of Rödl's theorem that large chromatic number forces a triangle-free (not necessarily induced) subgraph of large chromatic number. The authors disprove it for all $r\ge5$: for every $n$ there is a graph with $\chi(G)\ge n$ and $\omega(G)\le3$ all of whose triangle-free induced subgraphs have chromatic number at most $4$. The case $r\le3$ holds, since by Scott and Seymour graphs with no induced odd cycle of length at least $5$ have chromatic number bounded by a function of the clique number, so every graph of large chromatic number with bounded clique number contains an induced odd cycle of length at least $5$ (triangle-free with chromatic number $3$). Thus $r=4$ is the only open case, and this question, first asked by James Davies, asks whether it fails as well (with clique number $3$).
notes: First asked by James Davies (private communication), as acknowledged in the paper.
paper_title: A counterexample to a conjecture about triangle-free induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number

name: AX_odd_dicycle_free_digraph_dichromatic_bounded
title: Question 3.2
statement_text: Is there a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every digraph $D$ with no induced directed cycle of odd length, we have $\vec{\chi}(D) \leq f(\omega(D))$?
context_text: Digraphs are simple: between two distinct vertices there is at most one arc, in one direction (no digons). The clique number $\omega(D)$ is that of the underlying undirected graph. A $k$-dicolouring of $D$ partitions $V(D)$ into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph, and the dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the least such $k$. For undirected graphs, Scott and Seymour proved that excluding induced odd cycles of length at least $5$ bounds the chromatic number by a function of the clique number. The authors show the directed analogue fails: for every $n$ there is a digraph with $\vec{\chi}(D)\ge n$, $\omega(D)\le3$ and no induced directed cycle of odd length at least $5$. This question asks whether excluding all induced directed cycles of odd length (including directed triangles) suffices. The paper states, in its final version, that the authors subsequently answered it in the negative (Carbonero, Hompe, Moore and Spirkl, Digraphs with all induced directed cycles of the same length are not $\vec{\chi}$-bounded).
notes: The paper states that Questions 3.2 and 3.4 were subsequently answered in the negative by the same authors in arXiv:2203.15575.
paper_title: A counterexample to a conjecture about triangle-free induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number

name: AX_four_families_free_logarithmic_treewidth
title: Conjecture 1.10
statement_text: For all $t \geq 0$ there exists $c = c(t)$ such that if $G$ is a graph with no $K_t$, no $K_{t,t}$, no subdivision of $W_{t \times t}$ and no line graph of a subdivision of $W_{t \times t}$ as induced subgraphs, then $\mathrm{tw}(G) \leq c \log(|V(G)|)$.
context_text: The $(t\times t)$-wall $W_{t\times t}$ is the standard planar hexagonal-grid-like graph of maximum degree three and treewidth $t$; the line graph $L(F)$ of a graph $F$ has vertex set $E(F)$, two edges being adjacent when they share an end; excluded graphs are excluded as induced subgraphs. Complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs, subdivided walls and line graphs of subdivided walls all have unbounded treewidth, and it was asked whether excluding $K_t$, $K_{t,t}$, subdivisions of $W_{t\times t}$ and their line graphs as induced subgraphs bounds the treewidth by a constant $c(t)$. Sintiari and Trotignon answered negatively: for every $\ell$ there is a (theta, triangle)-free graph of treewidth at least $\ell$ (a theta consists of two non-adjacent vertices joined by three induced paths of length at least two whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and anticomplete; subdivisions of large walls contain thetas and their line graphs contain triangles). Their graphs have a number of vertices exponential in the treewidth, unlike walls and their line graphs, and they conjectured that (theta, triangle)-free graphs have treewidth $O(\log|V(G)|)$. The authors prove this, and more generally that for each $t$ graphs excluding $K_t$ and all three-path-configurations have treewidth at most $c_t\log|V(G)|$, which is asymptotically best possible. This conjecture is the corresponding variant for the four basic families; the bounded-degree version (Aboulker et al.: bounded degree and no induced subdivided $W_{k\times k}$ or its line graph imply bounded treewidth) is still open.
notes: PDF source — math appears clean.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions III. Three-path-configurations and logarithmic treewidth

name: AX_5_coloring_p4_rp3_free_complexity
title: Open Problem: 5-Coloring complexity for H-free graphs with a P4 component
statement_text: The complexity of the $5$-Coloring Problem restricted to $H$-free graphs remains open when $H$ has exactly one connected component $C$ isomorphic to $P_4$, and $H - V(C)$ is an induced subgraph of $rP_3$ containing at least one edge for some $r \geq 1$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. $G+H$ is the disjoint union of $G$ and $H$, $rH$ is the disjoint union of $r$ copies of $H$, $P_t$ is the path on $t$ vertices, and $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. For fixed $k$, the List-$k$-Coloring Problem asks, given $G$ and lists $L(v)\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$, whether $G$ has a proper colouring with each $v$ coloured from $L(v)$; the $k$-Coloring Problem is the special case $L(v)=\{1,\dots,k\}$. Both are NP-complete for $k\ge3$, and on $H$-free graphs they remain NP-complete if $H$ contains a cycle or a claw, so only disjoint unions of paths are of interest. Known results: 5-Coloring is NP-complete on $P_6$-free graphs (Huang) and on $(P_5+P_2)$-free graphs (Chudnovsky, Huang, Spirkl, Zhong). List-$k$-Coloring is polynomial on $(P_5+rP_1)$-free graphs for all $k,r$, and List-5-Coloring is NP-complete on $(P_4+P_2)$-free graphs. The authors prove that List-5-Coloring (hence 5-Coloring) is polynomial on $rP_3$-free graphs for every $r$, which gives a full dichotomy for List-5-Coloring: it is polynomial on $H$-free graphs iff $H$ is an induced subgraph of $rP_3$ or of $P_5+rP_1$. They also prove that $k$-Coloring is NP-complete on $2P_4$-free graphs (hence on $rP_4$-free graphs, $r\ge2$) for every $k\ge5$. Combining these results, the complexity of 5-Coloring (without lists) on $H$-free graphs remains open exactly in the stated case, where $H$ has exactly one component $C$ isomorphic to $P_4$ and $H-V(C)$ is an induced subgraph of $rP_3$ with at least one edge (for instance $H=P_4+P_2$ or $P_4+P_3$).
notes: Stated implicitly as a remaining open case after Theorem 7; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Complexity dichotomy for List-5-Coloring with a forbidden induced subgraph

name: AX_list_coloring_rp3_free_np_hard
title: Open Question: NP-hardness of List-k-Coloring on rP3-free graphs
statement_text: Does there exist $k \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the List-$k$-Coloring Problem restricted to $rP_3$-free graphs is NP-hard?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. $G+H$ is the disjoint union of $G$ and $H$, $rH$ is the disjoint union of $r$ copies of $H$, $P_t$ is the path on $t$ vertices, and $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. For fixed $k$, the List-$k$-Coloring Problem asks, given $G$ and lists $L(v)\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$, whether $G$ has a proper colouring with each $v$ coloured from $L(v)$; the $k$-Coloring Problem is the special case $L(v)=\{1,\dots,k\}$. Both are NP-complete for $k\ge3$, and on $H$-free graphs they remain NP-complete if $H$ contains a cycle or a claw, so only disjoint unions of paths are of interest. Known polynomial cases on $rP_3$-free graphs: 3-Coloring for every fixed $r$ (Broersma, Golovach, Paulusma, Song), and $k$-Coloring on $rP_2$-free graphs for all fixed $k,r$. The authors prove that List-5-Coloring restricted to $rP_3$-free graphs is polynomial for every $r$, which completes a dichotomy for List-5-Coloring on $H$-free graphs. Two of the three main ingredients of their proof (frugality of colourings and the handling of certain $P_3$'s) hold for List-$k$-Coloring on $rP_3$-free graphs for every $k$, but the third fails to extend to $k\ge6$, and they could not decide whether List-$k$-Coloring is NP-hard on $rP_3$-free graphs for some $k$. In contrast, they show that $k$-Coloring (even without lists) is NP-complete on $2P_4$-free graphs for all $k\ge5$.
notes: Stated in running prose at the end of Section 1; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Complexity dichotomy for List-5-Coloring with a forbidden induced subgraph

name: AX_cell_3_colorable_3_flowable_subcontraction
title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: If $G$ is a universally cell 3-colorable graph which does not have a subcontraction isomorphic to $K^+_{3,n-3}$ for some $n \geq 7$, then $G$ is 3-flowable.
context_text: Graphs are finite multigraphs. A drawing of $G$ maps vertices to distinct points of the plane and edges to curves between their endpoints, with finitely many intersection points (edges may cross each other or themselves arbitrarily, and need not be simple drawings); its cells are the maximal connected regions of the plane minus the drawing. A cell $k$-coloring colors the cells with $k$ colors so that two cells sharing a segment of an edge get different colors. $G$ is universally cell $3$-colorable if every drawing of $G$ in the plane has a cell $3$-coloring. $G$ is $k$-flowable if it has a nowhere-zero $k$-flow, i.e. an orientation with arc weights in $\mathbb{Z}_k\setminus\{0\}$ satisfying flow conservation at every vertex. For $X\subseteq V(G)$, $G/X$ is obtained by replacing $X$ by a single new vertex $v_X$ joined by one edge to $u$ for each edge $uv$ with $u\notin X$, $v\in X$ (edges inside $X$ disappear; $X$ need not be connected); a subcontraction of $G$ is any graph obtained by a finite sequence of such identifications. $K^+_{3,n-3}$ is the $n$-vertex graph obtained from $K_{3,n-3}$ by adding an edge between two vertices of the part of size $3$. For planar graphs, universal cell $3$-colorability is equivalent to $3$-flowability; in general every $3$-flowable graph and every $4$-edge-connected graph is universally cell $3$-colorable, and the equivalence also holds for graphs of maximum degree at most $3$ and for $K_{3,3}$-minor-free graphs. The authors show that $K^+_{3,n-3}$ is universally cell $3$-colorable but not $3$-flowable for every $n\ge7$, and that universal cell $3$-colorability is closed under subcontractions. Having found no other examples beyond simple modifications of these, they conjecture that excluding them as subcontractions restores the equivalence. A positive answer would imply Tutte's 3-flow conjecture (every $4$-edge-connected graph is $3$-flowable), since $4$-edge-connectivity is preserved by subcontractions and $K^+_{3,n-3}$ has a vertex of degree $3$.
paper_title: Coloring Drawings of Graphs

name: AX_lazy_transpositions_shuffle_t_counters_exact
title: Problem 3
statement_text: Does $U_t(n) = tn - \binom{t+1}{2}$?
context_text: A lazy transposition $(a,b,p)$ is the random permutation equal to the transposition $(a,b)$ with probability $p$ and to the identity otherwise. Think of $t$ distinguishable counters placed initially in positions $1,\dots,t$ among $n$ positions; a lazy transposition $(a,b,p)$ swaps the contents of positions $a$ and $b$ (possibly a counter and an empty position) with probability $p$. A sequence of independent lazy transpositions is a $(t,n)$-shuffle if the final placement of the counters is uniformly distributed over all $t!\binom{n}{t}$ possibilities, and $U_t(n)$ is the minimum length of a $(t,n)$-shuffle; $U(n)=U_n(n)$ is the minimum length of a sequence whose composition is a uniformly random permutation of $S_n$. Simple sweeping and divide-and-conquer constructions give $U_t(n)\le tn-\binom{t+1}{2}$. For $t=n$ the question is the problem of Fitzsimons and of Angel and Holroyd whether $U(n)=\binom n2$, which the authors answer negatively: $U(n)\le(1-\varepsilon)\binom n2$ for $n\ge6$ and $U(n)\le\frac23\binom n2+O(n\log n)$. Note that the paper also answers this question negatively for every $3\le t\le n$ with $n\ge6$: $U_t(n)\le(1-\varepsilon)(tn-\binom{t+1}{2})$ for an absolute $\varepsilon>0$. For $t=2$, they found no $(2,n)$-shuffle with fewer than $2n-3=2n-\binom32$ lazy transpositions and conjecture that $U_2(n)=2n-3$ for $n\ge2$.
notes: PDF source — binomial-coefficient notation garbled in raw extraction; LaTeX reconstructed from context. The paper also proves (Theorem 4) that for $3\leq t\leq n$ the bound can likewise be beaten by a constant factor, so the answer is negative for all $t\geq 3$.
paper_title: Perfect shuffling with fewer lazy transpositions

name: AX_threshold_ramsey_multiplicity_paths_exact
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: For sufficiently large $k$, if $k$ is even, then $m(P_k) = k!/2$ and if $k$ is odd, then $m(P_k) = \frac{k-1}{4}(k-1)!$.
context_text: $P_k$ is the path on $k$ vertices. The Ramsey number $r(H)$ is the least $n$ such that every two-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $H$, and the threshold Ramsey multiplicity $m(H)$ is the minimum number of monochromatic copies of $H$ over all two-colourings of the edges of $K_{r(H)}$. Gerencsér and Gyárfás showed $r(P_k)=k-1+\lfloor k/2\rfloor$. Harary and Prins, who determined $m$ for stars ($m(K_{1,k})=1$ for $k$ even and $2k$ for $k\ge3$ odd), asked for $m$ of paths and cycles. The authors prove $m(P_k)\ge(ck)^k$ and $m(C_k)\ge(ck)^k$ for an absolute constant $c>0$. The conjectured values come from the colouring $\chi(a,b)$ of $K_{a+b}$ on $A\cup B$ ($|A|=a$, $|B|=b$) in which $A$ and $B$ are blue cliques and all $A$–$B$ edges are red: with $a_0=k-1$ and $b_0=\lfloor k/2\rfloor-1$, $\chi(a_0,b_0)$ has no monochromatic $P_k$; for $k$ even, $\chi(a_0+1,b_0)$ and $\chi(a_0,b_0+1)$ on $r(P_k)$ vertices each have exactly $k!/2$ monochromatic $P_k$, and for $k$ odd, $\chi(a_0,b_0+1)$ has exactly $\frac{k-1}{4}(k-1)!$. These show the lower bound is tight up to $c$, and the authors conjecture they are optimal for large $k$. They make an analogous conjecture for cycles.
notes: PDF source — fraction $\frac{k-1}{4}$ reconstructed from line-break artifact in extraction.
paper_title: Threshold Ramsey multiplicity for paths and even cycles

name: AX_rodl_h_free_restricted_union_cover
title: Union cover variant (open problem)
statement_text: For every graph $H$, and all $\varepsilon > 0$, there is an integer $N$ such that for every $H$-free graph $G$, $V(G)$ is the union of at most $N$ $\varepsilon$-restricted subsets (not necessarily pairwise disjoint).
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, and $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$. A set $X\subseteq V(G)$ is $\varepsilon$-restricted if one of $G[X]$, $\overline{G}[X]$ has maximum degree at most $\varepsilon|X|$, and weakly $\varepsilon$-restricted if one of them has at most $\varepsilon|X|^2$ edges. Rödl's theorem says that every $H$-free graph has a (weakly) $\varepsilon$-restricted set of linear size, and applying it repeatedly easily shows that $V(G)$ can be partitioned into a bounded number of weakly $\varepsilon$-restricted subsets. The main theorem of the paper is the much harder statement that for every $H$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ such that the vertex set of every $H$-free graph can be partitioned into at most $N$ $\varepsilon$-restricted subsets; some parts must sometimes have size at most two (e.g. in a large star). The union-cover statement is described as midway between these two results. The authors remark that it does not seem easy to prove directly and, as far as they know, does not imply their partition theorem. Since a partition is in particular a covering by not necessarily disjoint sets, the statement follows from the partition theorem proved in the paper; it is not presented as an open problem.
notes: Stated as a passing remark without a labelled environment; the authors signal it is open and non-trivial but do not explicitly phrase it as a conjecture or question.
paper_title: Strengthening Rodl's theorem

name: AX_random_irregular_subgraph_property_range
title: Informal Conjecture on Property (*) for d = o(n/log n)
statement_text: For every $d$-regular graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $d=o(n/\log n)$, with high probability the irregular random subgraph $H=H(G)$ satisfies $m(H,k)=(1+o(1))n/(d+1)$ for all $0\leq k\leq d$.
context_text: For a graph $H$ and an integer $k\ge0$, $m(H,k)$ is the number of vertices of degree $k$ in $H$. Given a $d$-regular graph $G$, the irregular random subgraph $H=H(G)$ (introduced by Frieze, Gould, Karoński and Pfender) is obtained by choosing independent uniform weights $x(v)\in[0,1]$ for the vertices and keeping an edge $uv$ of $G$ if and only if $x(u)+x(v)\ge1$; every vertex then has degree $k$ in $H$ with probability exactly $1/(d+1)$, so $\mathbb{E}[m(H,k)]=n/(d+1)$, and the question is concentration. Alon and Wei asked whether every $d$-regular $n$-vertex graph has a spanning subgraph $H$ with $m(H,k)=(1+o(1))\frac{n}{d+1}$ for all $0\le k\le d$ (and conjectured the stronger $|m(H,k)-\frac{n}{d+1}|\le2$). Frieze et al. showed the random model works for $d\le(n/\log n)^{1/4}$; the authors prove it with high probability for $d=o(n^{1/2})$ by the second moment method and for all $d=o(n/(\log n)^{12})$ via the martingale Bernstein inequality. They conjecture the range extends to $d=o(n/\log n)$, and believe that for $d=\omega(n/\log n)$ the model fails, so new ideas would be needed for the Alon–Wei question in the full range.
notes: Stated in prose without a labelled theorem environment: 'We conjecture that with high probability for all d = o(n/log n), the irregular random subgraph H satisfies Property *'.
paper_title: On random irregular subgraphs

name: AX_arithmetic_hyperbolic_surface_diameter_log_volume
title: Informal conjecture on the actual diameter
statement_text: Let $\Gamma\subset\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ be a co-compact arithmetic lattice of co-volume $V_\Gamma$ coming from the proper units of an Eichler order. The almost-diameter bound $\min_{\gamma\in\Gamma}d(\gamma z,w)\le(1+o(1))\log 3V_\Gamma$ (for every $w\in\mathbb{H}$ and almost every $z\in\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$) is sharp, and one may speculate whether the actual diameter of the hyperbolic surface $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ is around the same length, i.e. $(1+o(1))\log 3V_\Gamma$.
context_text: Here $\mathbb{H}$ is the hyperbolic upper half-plane with hyperbolic distance $d$, and $\Gamma$ is a co-compact arithmetic lattice of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of co-volume $V_\Gamma$ stemming from the proper units of an Eichler order $R$ of level $Q$ in a quaternion algebra over $\mathbb{Q}$ of reduced discriminant $D$; the size of a matrix is measured by its Frobenius norm. The author proves that for almost every $w$, $\sup_{z\in\mathbb{H}}\min_{\gamma\in\Gamma}d(\gamma z,w)\le(2+o(1))\log 3V_\Gamma$, so the diameter of $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ is at most $(2+o(1))\log 3V_\Gamma$; and, if $Q$ is square-free, or assuming Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture for $\Gamma_0(DQ)$ or a sup-norm conjecture for exceptional eigenforms, that for every $w$ almost every $z$ is within distance $(1+o(1))\log 3V_\Gamma$ of the orbit $\Gamma w$ (the almost diameter), which is sharp. Consequently such $\Gamma$ (for almost every embedding, and for every embedding under those conditions) is generated by its elements of Frobenius norm $O_\varepsilon(V_\Gamma^{2+\varepsilon})$. A diameter of $(1+o(1))\log 3V_\Gamma$ would imply generation by elements of norm $O_\varepsilon(V_\Gamma^{1+\varepsilon})$, on equal footing with the author's result that $\Gamma_0(Q)$ is generated by its elements of Frobenius norm $O_\varepsilon(Q^{1+\varepsilon})$.
notes: PDF source — stated with hedged language ('one may speculate') but refers to a precise mathematical quantity and has a non-trivial stated implication.
paper_title: Small diameters and generators for arithmetic lattices in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ and certain Ramanujan graphs

name: AX_groups_uniform_twin_width_strictly_stronger
title: Informal Conjecture (uniform twin-width strictly stronger than twin-width)
statement_text: Uniform twin-width is strictly stronger than twin-width, i.e. there are groups with finite twin-width and infinite uniform twin-width.
context_text: Twin-width is a graph (and ordered 0–1 matrix) parameter: a graph has twin-width at most $k$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex by successively merging two vertices, marking as red the edges to vertices adjacent to only one of the two merged parts, so that every intermediate graph has red degree at most $k$; for an ordered 0–1 matrix, rows and columns are merged only between consecutive ones. A finitely generated group has finite twin-width if some (equivalently every) Cayley graph has finite twin-width (this is invariant under quasi-isometry for bounded-degree graphs); equivalently, there is a total order $<$ on $\Gamma$ such that for every $x\in\Gamma$ the permutation matrix of the right-multiplication action of $x$ on $(\Gamma,<)$ has finite twin-width (for permutations, finite width in the sense of Guillemot and Marx, i.e. avoiding some pattern), which also defines finite twin-width for non-finitely generated groups. The uniform twin-width of $\Gamma$ is the minimum over total orders $<$ of $\sup_{g\in\Gamma}$ of the twin-width of the action of $g$ on $(\Gamma,<)$, i.e. it requires a bound on these twin-widths that is uniform over all $g$, so finite uniform twin-width implies finite twin-width. Finite uniform twin-width is preserved by group extensions (hence direct and semidirect products), infinite direct products and sums, direct limits, finite-index supergroups, quotients by finite subgroups and wreath products, and the authors show that abelian, solvable and polynomial-growth groups, lamplighter groups and automorphism groups of trees have finite uniform twin-width. The converse implication is not established. A proposed candidate separating the two notions is the group of finitely supported permutations of $\mathbb{Z}$: it has finite twin-width, but finite uniform twin-width for it would imply a universal bound on the uniform twin-width of finite groups and, more generally, of elementary amenable groups, which the authors find unlikely.
notes: Stated in prose in Section 1.2 with 'We conjecture that'.
paper_title: Twin-width VII: groups

name: AX_groups_infinite_twin_width_explicit_construction
title: Question (explicit group with infinite twin-width)
statement_text: Can we find a more explicit construction of a group with infinite twin-width, or one with a direct proof that twin-width is infinite?
context_text: Twin-width is a graph (and ordered 0–1 matrix) parameter: a graph has twin-width at most $k$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex by successively merging two vertices, marking as red the edges to vertices adjacent to only one of the two merged parts, so that every intermediate graph has red degree at most $k$; for an ordered 0–1 matrix, rows and columns are merged only between consecutive ones. A finitely generated group has finite twin-width if some (equivalently every) Cayley graph has finite twin-width (this is invariant under quasi-isometry for bounded-degree graphs); equivalently, there is a total order $<$ on $\Gamma$ such that for every $x\in\Gamma$ the permutation matrix of the right-multiplication action of $x$ on $(\Gamma,<)$ has finite twin-width (for permutations, finite width in the sense of Guillemot and Marx, i.e. avoiding some pattern), which also defines finite twin-width for non-finitely generated groups. The authors construct a finitely generated group with infinite twin-width, using Osajda's theorem on embedding graphs into groups; this disproves the 'small conjecture' (that every small hereditary graph class, i.e. with at most $n!\,c^n$ labelled graphs on $n$ vertices, has bounded twin-width). The construction starts from a sequence of bounded-degree graphs with unbounded twin-width (which exist by counting: almost all $3$-regular graphs have large twin-width) and relies largely on probabilistic methods. No explicit or deterministic construction of bounded-degree graphs with unbounded twin-width is known; since the subgraphs of a Cayley graph of a group with infinite twin-width form a bounded-degree class of unbounded twin-width, a more explicit group, or one with a direct proof of infinite twin-width, could solve that problem and significantly help understanding twin-width.
notes: Stated as a question in prose at the end of Section 1.3.
paper_title: Twin-width VII: groups

name: AX_sparse_twin_width_queue_number_separation
title: Open Problem (separating twin-width and queue number on sparse graphs)
statement_text: Separating twin-width and queue number on sparse graphs is an open problem.
context_text: The queue number of a graph is the least $t$ such that, for some vertex order, the edges can be partitioned into $t$ sets none containing two nested edges $xy,uv$ with $x<u<v<y$. Twin-width is a graph (and ordered 0–1 matrix) parameter: a graph has twin-width at most $k$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex by successively merging two vertices, marking as red the edges to vertices adjacent to only one of the two merged parts, so that every intermediate graph has red degree at most $k$; for an ordered 0–1 matrix, rows and columns are merged only between consecutive ones. A finitely generated group has finite twin-width if some (equivalently every) Cayley graph has finite twin-width (this is invariant under quasi-isometry for bounded-degree graphs); equivalently, there is a total order $<$ on $\Gamma$ such that for every $x\in\Gamma$ the permutation matrix of the right-multiplication action of $x$ on $(\Gamma,<)$ has finite twin-width (for permutations, finite width in the sense of Guillemot and Marx, i.e. avoiding some pattern), which also defines finite twin-width for non-finitely generated groups. Bounded tree-width implies bounded queue number, which implies bounded twin-width. Queue number is also a group invariant (via Cayley graphs), and is characterised by excluding decreasing sequences in the adjacency matrix for some vertex ordering, which allows a uniform queue number for groups to be defined in analogy with uniform twin-width; many results of the paper also hold for queue number. Yet the authors know no group with finite twin-width and infinite queue number (nor for the uniform variants), and they state that separating bounded twin-width and bounded queue number on sparse graphs (e.g. bounded-degree graphs) is an open problem.
notes: Explicitly declared an open problem in Section 1.4.
paper_title: Twin-width VII: groups

name: AX_counting_perfect_matchings_alpha_2_hard
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: The problem of counting perfect matchings in input graphs of independence number $2$ is $\#P$-complete.
context_text: The independence number of a graph is the maximum size of an independent set; graphs of independence number $2$ include all complements of triangle-free graphs. In the Exact Matching problem (EM), introduced by Papadimitriou and Yannakakis, one is given a graph whose edges are coloured red or blue and an integer $k$, and asks whether there is a perfect matching with exactly $k$ red edges; it is in RP (Mulmuley, Vazirani and Vazirani) but no deterministic polynomial algorithm is known in general. The authors give deterministic algorithms for EM running in time $n^{2^{O(\alpha)}}$ on graphs of independence number $\alpha$ (and similarly for bipartite graphs of bounded bipartite independence number). They note that for all graph classes on which EM was previously known to be polynomial (planar graphs, $K_{3,3}$-minor-free graphs, graphs of bounded genus, complete and complete bipartite graphs) perfect matchings can also be counted in polynomial time; in contrast, they are not aware of polynomial counting schemes even for graphs of independence number $2$, and conjecture that counting is hard there. In the conclusion they ask to prove this conjecture, or to find deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for EM on classes where counting perfect matchings is #P-hard.
notes: The paper text is truncated before Section 6 (open problems), so additional open problems stated there could not be extracted.
paper_title: Exact Matching in Graphs of Bounded Independence Number

name: AX_set_coloring_ramsey_chromatic_variant_equality
title: Informal Conjecture on R(n;r,s) vs R'(n;r,s) near Turán density
statement_text: We clearly have $R(n; r, s) \geq R'(n; r, s)$ and we believe that this estimate should be close to an equality when $s/r$ is close to the Turán density $1 - \frac{1}{n-1}$.
context_text: For positive integers $n,r,s$ with $r>s$, an $(r,s)$-coloring of $K_N$ assigns to every edge a set of exactly $s$ colors from a palette of $r$ colors; a monochromatic $n$-clique is a set of $n$ vertices such that all edges between them share a common color. The set-coloring Ramsey number $R(n;r,s)$ is the minimum $N$ such that every $(r,s)$-coloring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $n$-clique ($s=1$ is the classical multicolor Ramsey number). The variant $R'(n;r,s)$ is the minimum $N$ such that in every $(r,s)$-coloring of $K_N$ some color class (the graph of edges whose set contains that color) has chromatic number at least $n$; since a $K_n$ forces chromatic number $n$, $R(n;r,s)\ge R'(n;r,s)$. The authors show $R'(n;r,s)=A_{n-1}(r,s)+1$, where $A_q(r,s)$ is the maximum size of a $q$-ary code of length $r$ with minimum Hamming distance at least $s$. For fixed $n$, counting edges against the Turán number shows that $R(n;r,s)$ is bounded by a constant when $s/r\ge1-\frac{1}{n-1}+\epsilon$, whereas codes show that it grows exponentially in $r$ when $s/r\le1-\frac{1}{n-1}-\epsilon$; so the Turán density $1-\frac{1}{n-1}$ of $K_n$ is a threshold. The near-equality is confirmed for $s=r-1$ by Alon, Erdős, Gunderson and Molloy, and equality $R=R'=A_{n-1}(r,s)+1$ holds whenever suitable balanced partitions exist (each color class then being a Turán graph). The authors note that the bound $R\ge R'$ can be far from the truth in other regimes, since by the Singleton bound $A_{n-1}(r,s)\le(n-1)^{r-s+1}$ is only polynomial in $n$, while $R(n;r,s)$ can grow exponentially in $n$.

paper_title: Set-coloring Ramsey numbers via codes

name: AX_littlewood_offord_geometric_nonzero_vectors
title: Question 1
statement_text: Assuming only that each $a_i \neq 0$, what geometric constraints can be imposed on a set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ which imply non-trivial uniform upper bounds on $\Pr(X \in S)$?
context_text: Here $X=a_1\xi_1+\dots+a_n\xi_n$ where $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$ are vectors and $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n$ are i.i.d. Rademacher random variables ($\Pr(\xi_i=1)=\Pr(\xi_i=-1)=1/2$). The classical Erdős–Littlewood–Offord theorem gives $\max_x\Pr(X=x)=O(1/\sqrt{n})$ when every $a_i\neq0$ (and $O(1/\sqrt n)$ for falling in a unit interval when $|a_i|\ge1$, in dimension 1). The paper introduces a new generalisation to $\mathbb{R}^d$: bound $\Pr(X\in S)$ uniformly over all choices of nonzero $a_i$, for a fixed set $S$. Since no assumption is made on the sizes of the $a_i$, the question is much more about the geometry of $S$ than about spatial anti-concentration of $X$; for a smooth manifold $S$ any answer must work both at a local scale (where $S$ looks like an affine subspace) and globally. If $S$ contains a line segment then $\Pr(X\in S)\ge1/2$ is possible, and highly oscillatory sets (such as the graph of $x\mapsto\sin(2\pi x)$) are also obstacles. Costello had shown $\Pr(X\in S)\le n^{-1/2+o(1)}$ for a parabola in $\mathbb{R}^2$. The authors' main answer: if $S$ is definable with respect to an o-minimal structure (for instance any semi-algebraic set, or any set defined by Boolean combinations of equalities and inequalities involving polynomials, the exponential and restricted analytic functions) and contains no line segment, then $\Pr(X\in S)\le n^{-1/2+o(1)}$. This is probability / additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Geometric and o-minimal Littlewood-Offord problems

name: AX_littlewood_offord_o_minimal_sqrt_n
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ be definable with respect to an o-minimal structure and contain no line segment, and let $X=a_1\xi_1+\dots+a_n\xi_n$ with nonzero $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and i.i.d. Rademacher $\xi_i$. Then $\Pr(X \in S) \leq C_S/\sqrt{n}$, for some $C_S$ depending only on $S$.
context_text: Here $X=a_1\xi_1+\dots+a_n\xi_n$ where $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$ are vectors and $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n$ are i.i.d. Rademacher random variables ($\Pr(\xi_i=1)=\Pr(\xi_i=-1)=1/2$). The classical Erdős–Littlewood–Offord theorem gives $\max_x\Pr(X=x)=O(1/\sqrt{n})$ when every $a_i\neq0$ (and $O(1/\sqrt n)$ for falling in a unit interval when $|a_i|\ge1$, in dimension 1). The authors prove: if $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ is definable with respect to an o-minimal structure (this includes every semi-algebraic set, i.e. Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and inequalities, and more generally sets built from polynomials, the exponential and restricted analytic functions) and contains no line segment, then for every $\alpha>0$ and $n$ large enough in terms of $\alpha$ and $S$, every choice of nonzero $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$ gives $\Pr(X\in S)\le n^{-1/2+\alpha}$. The conjecture asks for the optimal bound $\Pr(X\in S)\le C_S/\sqrt{n}$ in this same setting, matching the Erdős–Littlewood–Offord point-concentration bound. They prove it when $S$ has a generic intersection property, which covers convex or irreducible algebraic plane curves in $\mathbb{R}^2$, irreducible complex algebraic curves in $\mathbb{C}^2\cong\mathbb{R}^4$, and the boundary of a 3-dimensional ball; the simplest open case is the unit 3-sphere in $\mathbb{R}^4$. A full resolution of the Gotsman–Linial conjecture on the average sensitivity of polynomial threshold functions would imply the conjecture for semi-algebraic sets not containing a line segment. This is probability / additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
paper_title: Geometric and o-minimal Littlewood-Offord problems

name: AX_oriented_tree_avoiding_2_coloring_complexity
title: Open Complexity Problem (2-F-PFC for oriented trees of maximum degree ≥ 3)
statement_text: Let $F$ be an oriented tree whose underlying undirected tree has maximum degree at least $3$. The complexity of the $2$-$F$-PFC (deciding whether a given planar digraph admits an $F$-free $2$-coloring) remains partially open. In particular, the complexity for those $F$ where successively deleting all leaves yields a star $K_{1,n}$ is not determined.
context_text: Digraphs are simple (orientations of graphs). A digraph is $F$-free if it has no induced subdigraph isomorphic to $F$, and a coloring $c:V(D)\to\{0,\dots,k-1\}$ is an $F$-free $k$-coloring if every color class induces an $F$-free subdigraph. The problem $k$-$F$-PFC (planar $F$-free $k$-coloring) asks, for fixed $F$ and $k$, whether a given planar digraph admits an $F$-free $k$-coloring. It is trivial for $k\ge4$ by the Four Color Theorem, polynomial whenever $F$ contains a (not necessarily directed) cycle (planar graphs admit $C_n$-free 2-colorings), and for $k=3$ every planar digraph has an $F$-free 3-coloring when $F$ has maximum degree at least 3 (planar graphs can be partitioned into 3 induced linear forests); so the interesting case is $F$ an oriented tree and $k\in\{2,3\}$. The authors prove that for every orientation $\vec P$ of the path $P_n$, the $2$-$\vec P$-PFC is polynomial for $n\le2$ and NP-complete for $n\ge3$, and the $3$-$\vec P$-PFC is polynomial for $n=1$ and NP-complete for $n\ge2$, even for acyclic inputs. Writing $\mathrm{lrem}(\vec T)$ for the oriented tree obtained from $\vec T$ by deleting all its leaves, they show that the $2$-$\mathrm{lrem}(\vec T)$-PFC reduces polynomially to the $2$-$\vec T$-PFC; hence the $2$-$F$-PFC is NP-hard whenever iterating $\mathrm{lrem}$ on $F$ reaches an oriented path of length 2 or 3 (number of edges). The remaining case is when iterating $\mathrm{lrem}$ reaches a star $K_{1,n}$. For undirected graphs, Broersma, Fomin, Kratochvíl and Woeginger showed that planar $F$-free 2-coloring is NP-hard if $F$ is a tree with at least two edges.
notes: Stated in prose in the introduction without a formal labelled environment. PDF source — math notation may be garbled.
paper_title: Colorings of oriented planar graphs avoiding a monochromatic subgraph

name: AX_large_chromatic_dense_minor_edge_density
title: Informal conjecture on improving the $g(t)$ lower bound
statement_text: The factor $1/4$ in $g(t) \geq t(t+2)/8$ can likely be significantly improved. However it appears to be quite challenging, for example, to show that every graph with chromatic number at least $t$ contains a minor on $t$ vertices with at most one tenth of all possible edges missing.
context_text: Graphs are simple. $g(t)$ is the largest integer such that every graph with chromatic number at least $t$ contains a minor with exactly $t$ vertices and at least $g(t)$ edges; Hadwiger's conjecture asserts $g(t)=\binom{t}{2}$. Since every graph with chromatic number at least $t$ has a subgraph of minimum degree at least $t-1$, and Mader showed that every graph of average degree at least $t-1$ has a minor on at most $t$ vertices with minimum degree at least $t/2$, one gets $g(t)\ge t(t+2)/8=\frac14\binom{t}{2}+o(t^2)$. The authors believe the factor $1/4$ can be significantly improved but find even density $9/10$ challenging. They concentrate instead on graphs $G$ with independence number $\alpha(G)\le2$ (where Hadwiger's conjecture would give a $K_{\lceil|V(G)|/2\rceil}$ minor and Duchet–Meyniel gives $K_{\lceil|V(G)|/3\rceil}$), and prove that such $G$ has a minor on $\lceil|V(G)|/2\rceil$ vertices missing fewer than $1/76$ of all possible edges (edge density at least $0.98688\ldots-o(1)$).
notes: Stated as a remark in the introduction without a labelled environment; language 'can likely' and 'appears to be quite challenging' signals authorial belief rather than a formal conjecture.
paper_title: Dense minors of graphs with independence number two

name: AX_twin_width_approximation_unordered_graphs
title: Open Challenge: Efficient Approximation of Twin-Width for Unordered Graphs
statement_text: Efficiently approximating twin-width (that is, returning an $f(d)$-sequence when the twin-width of the input is at most $d$) remains an open challenge for unordered graphs.
context_text: A trigraph is a graph some of whose edges are red (the others black). Contracting two (not necessarily adjacent) vertices $u,v$ of a trigraph merges them into a new vertex $w$, keeping $wx$ black if both $ux$ and $vx$ were black edges and making every other edge incident to $w$ red; the rest of the trigraph is unchanged. A contraction sequence of an $n$-vertex graph $G$ is a sequence of trigraphs $G=G_n,G_{n-1},\dots,G_1$ where $G_i$ has $i$ vertices and is obtained from $G_{i+1}$ by one contraction; it is a $d$-sequence if every $G_i$ has maximum red degree at most $d$, and the twin-width of $G$ is the minimum $d$ such that $G$ admits a $d$-sequence. An approximation algorithm should, given a graph of twin-width at most $d$, output an $f(d)$-sequence for some function $f$; the authors specify later that it is unknown whether this can be done, say, in fixed-parameter time (parameterized by $d$). Many algorithmic results on bounded twin-width (e.g. fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking) assume that an $O(1)$-sequence is given with the input. Efficient approximation is known for totally ordered binary structures and for the known classes of bounded twin-width (bounded tree-width or rank-width, proper minor-closed classes, hereditary proper subclasses of permutation graphs, etc.), but remains open for general unordered graphs. The authors suggest one reason it may be delicate: $\Omega(\log n)$-subdivisions of $n$-vertex graphs have bounded twin-width while $o(\log n)$-subdivisions do not.

paper_title: Twin-width VI: the lens of contraction sequences

name: AX_arrangement_graphs_4_critical_infinite_family
title: Belief on 4-vertex-critical arrangement graphs
statement_text: We believe that the corona construction (which extends a $\triangle$-saturated arrangement of pseudocircles with a pentagonal cell to a 4-chromatic arrangement by inserting one additional pseudocircle around the pentagonal cell) results in infinitely many 4-vertex-critical arrangement graphs.
context_text: An arrangement of pseudocircles is a family of simple closed curves on the sphere or in the plane, every two of which intersect at most twice. It is simple if no three curves share a point, and intersecting if every two curves intersect. Its arrangement graph is the planar graph whose vertices are the intersection points, with the curves subdivided into edges; for simple arrangements it is 4-regular, hence 4-colourable. A plane graph is $\triangle$-saturated if every edge is incident to exactly one triangular face, and an arrangement is $\triangle$-saturated if its arrangement graph is; the authors show that $\triangle$-saturated intersecting arrangements are 3-colourable. A $k$-chromatic graph is $k$-vertex-critical if deleting any vertex lowers the chromatic number, and $k$-edge-critical if deleting any edge does. The corona extension starts from a $\triangle$-saturated arrangement with a pentagonal cell. It inserts one new pseudocircle around the pentagon, crossing only the five pseudocircles bounding it, at edges incident to the pentagon's vertices. In the resulting 4-regular graph one face class consists of triangles and one pentagon, which forces independence number below $|V|/3$ and hence chromatic number 4. This gives an infinite family of 4-chromatic arrangements; Koester's arrangement of 7 circles, a 4-edge-critical 4-regular planar graph, arises this way. Because of similarities with Koester's crowning operation, the authors believe that many of these arrangement graphs are 4-vertex-critical. They prove a sufficient condition: if the arrangement graph is the medial graph of a cubic planar graph $H$ with a pentagonal face and a trihamiltonian 3-edge-colouring (each pair of colour classes forms a Hamiltonian cycle), then the corona extension is 4-vertex-critical, and even 4-edge-critical if $H$ has 5-fold rotational symmetry about the pentagon. They conjecture separately that there is an infinite family of 4-edge-critical simple arrangements of pseudocircles.
notes: Statement appears as running prose in the outline of Section 3; the exact family is defined later in that section, which is only partially present in the extracted text.
paper_title: Coloring circle arrangements: New $4$-chromatic planar graphs

name: AX_k6_minor_6_regular_graphs
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: Every non-null 6-regular graph has a $K_6$ minor.
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. By Mader's theorem every $n$-vertex graph ($n\ge4$) with more than $4n-10$ edges has a $K_6$ minor, and this is tight even with minimum degree six (add a vertex adjacent to everything in a planar triangulation on $n-1$ vertices with minimum degree five), so average degree eight is needed in general. The authors ask what happens if the maximum degree is close to the average degree, or the minimum degree is large: they found $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree six and maximum degree at most nine, and $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree five, maximum degree seven and average degree arbitrarily close to $98/15$ (details omitted). They also state as open that every non-null graph with minimum degree at least seven has a $K_6$ minor, and recall Jørgensen's conjecture that every $6$-connected graph with no $K_6$ minor becomes planar after deleting some vertex. Their main result is that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor. The present conjecture, open as far as the authors know, asks whether $6$-regularity alone forces a $K_6$ minor; they even believe this holds for every non-null graph with minimum degree at least six and maximum degree at most eight.
paper_title: Bipartite graphs with no $K_6$ minor

name: AX_k6_minor_min_6_max_8
title: Informal Conjecture: min degree $\geq 6$, max degree $\leq 8$ forces $K_6$ minor
statement_text: Every non-null graph with minimum degree at least six and maximum degree at most eight has a $K_6$ minor.
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. By Mader's theorem every $n$-vertex graph ($n\ge4$) with more than $4n-10$ edges has a $K_6$ minor, and this is tight even with minimum degree six (add a vertex adjacent to everything in a planar triangulation on $n-1$ vertices with minimum degree five), so average degree eight is needed in general. The authors ask what happens if the maximum degree is close to the average degree, or the minimum degree is large: they found $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree six and maximum degree at most nine, and $K_6$-minor-free graphs with minimum degree five, maximum degree seven and average degree arbitrarily close to $98/15$ (details omitted). They also state as open that every non-null graph with minimum degree at least seven has a $K_6$ minor, and recall Jørgensen's conjecture that every $6$-connected graph with no $K_6$ minor becomes planar after deleting some vertex. Their main result is that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor. This statement is stated parenthetically right after the authors' conjecture that every non-null $6$-regular graph has a $K_6$ minor, as a stronger belief ('as far as we know') that it implies.
