name: AX_k6_minor_bipartite_min_degree_5
title: Open Question: minimum degree five in Theorem 1.6
statement_text: We do not know whether ``six'' can be replaced by ``five'' in the theorem that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor; that is, does every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least five have a $K_6$ minor?
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. For bipartite graphs, average degree still does not help: $K_{4,n-4}$ has $4n-16$ edges and no $K_6$ minor, so no constant smaller than eight works for average degree. The authors prove that every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least six has a $K_6$ minor, via a strengthening amenable to induction: if $G$ has a bipartition $(A,B)$ with $|A|\ge|B|>0$ and every vertex of $A$ has degree at least six, then $G$ has a $K_6$ minor. They remark that minimum degree is more difficult than average degree to work with inductively. For comparison with $K_5$: every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least four has a $K_5$ minor, while for general graphs minimum degree six is needed for $K_5$ (planar graphs of minimum degree five exist).
notes: Stated in running prose without a labelled environment.
paper_title: Bipartite graphs with no $K_6$ minor

name: AX_k5_minor_bipartite_average_degree_5
title: Informal Conjecture: average degree $\geq 5$ and max degree $\leq 6$ forces $K_5$ minor in bipartite graphs
statement_text: Perhaps average degree at least five and maximum degree at most six will guarantee a $K_5$ minor in a bipartite graph.
context_text: All graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, and non-null means having at least one vertex. By Wagner's theorem every graph with $n\ge3$ vertices and more than $3n-6$ edges has a $K_5$ minor, and this is tight even for almost $6$-regular planar graphs. For bipartite graphs, $K_{3,n-3}$ has $3n-9$ edges and no $K_5$ minor (it is the only such extremal graph), so average degree alone behaves as in general; but every non-null bipartite graph with minimum degree at least four has a $K_5$ minor (a result also stated by Barát and Wood). Bounding the maximum degree alone does not give much: there are $n$-vertex bipartite graphs with average degree at least four and maximum degree at most five with no $K_5$ minor (take five disjoint copies of $K_{3,5}$, pick a degree-three vertex $v_i$ in the $i$th copy, add two new vertices adjacent to all of $v_1,\dots,v_5$, and take disjoint unions). The authors suggest that average degree at least five together with maximum degree at most six might force a $K_5$ minor in a bipartite graph, but state they have not worked this out.
notes: Phrased as 'perhaps ... but we have not worked this out'; quite tentative.
paper_title: Bipartite graphs with no $K_6$ minor

name: AX_r_free_digraphs_near_acyclic
title: Conjecture on r-free digraphs with r > 2n/3
statement_text: All $r$-free digraphs on $n$ vertices with $r > 2n/3$ are at most one edge away from being acyclic.
context_text: For a digraph $G$, a feedback arc set is a set of edges whose deletion leaves an acyclic digraph, and $\beta(G)$ is the minimum size of a feedback arc set. Ordering the vertices arbitrarily and deleting the smaller of the sets of forward and backward edges shows $\beta(G)\le m/2$ for any oriented graph with $m$ edges, and by Berger and Shor $\beta(G)\le m/2-\Omega(m^{3/4})$ always; the quantity $m/2-\beta(G)$ is called the directed surplus. A digraph is $r$-free if it contains no directed cycle of length at most $r$; "at most one edge away from being acyclic" means $\beta(G)\le1$. Previous work bounded $\beta(G)$ for $r$-free digraphs in terms of the number of non-adjacent pairs (Chudnovsky–Seymour–Sullivan, Sullivan, and Fox–Keevash–Sudakov, who proved $\beta(G)\le 800\gamma(G)/r^2$ where $\gamma(G)$ is the number of non-adjacent unordered pairs of vertices). The authors construct $r$-free digraphs $G$ on $n$ vertices with $\beta(G)\ge n^2/(r+1)^2$, so if every $r$-free digraph on $n$ vertices has $\beta(G)=O(1)$ then $r=\Omega(n)$. In the converse direction they pose this conjecture, and note it would be tight: for $n$ a multiple of $3$ there is an $(r-1)$-free digraph on $n$ vertices with $r=2n/3$ and $\beta(G)=2$.
notes: Stated in running prose with explicit 'we conjecture' language; no labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Extremal results on feedback arc sets in digraphs

name: AX_random_orientation_feedback_arc_surplus
title: Suspected directed surplus of a random B-free orientation (Remark 1.6)
statement_text: A random orientation of a $\mathcal{B}$-free undirected graph on $n$ vertices with $m = \mathrm{ex}(n, \mathcal{B})$ edges likely satisfies $\beta(G) = m/2 - \Omega(\sqrt{mn})$.
context_text: For a digraph $G$, a feedback arc set is a set of edges whose deletion leaves an acyclic digraph, and $\beta(G)$ is the minimum size of a feedback arc set. Ordering the vertices arbitrarily and deleting the smaller of the sets of forward and backward edges shows $\beta(G)\le m/2$ for any oriented graph with $m$ edges, and by Berger and Shor $\beta(G)\le m/2-\Omega(m^{3/4})$ always; the quantity $m/2-\beta(G)$ is called the directed surplus. For a family $\mathcal{B}$ of undirected graphs, a graph is $\mathcal{B}$-free if it contains no member of $\mathcal{B}$ as a subgraph, and the extremal number $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})$ is the maximum number of edges of a $\mathcal{B}$-free graph on $n$ vertices. The authors prove that if $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ then every digraph $G$ with $m$ edges whose underlying undirected graph is $\mathcal{B}$-free has $\beta(G)\le m/2-c\,m^{3/4+\varepsilon/(4(2-\varepsilon))}$, and that this is tight up to the constant when $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})=\Theta(n^{2-\varepsilon})$: a random orientation $G$ of an extremal $\mathcal{B}$-free graph on $n$ vertices with $m=\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})$ edges satisfies $\beta(G)\ge m/2-C\,m^{3/4+\varepsilon/(4(2-\varepsilon))}$, which for such $m$ equals $m/2-O(\sqrt{mn})$. They remark that the condition $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})=\Theta(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ is used only for convenience (the proof works under some mild conditions on $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})$), and suspect that in general such a random orientation satisfies $\beta(G)=m/2-\Omega(\sqrt{mn})$ (as written in the paper; since the remark is about the proof of the lower bound on $\beta(G)$, the intended meaning may be that the directed surplus of the random orientation is of order $\sqrt{mn}$).
notes: Stated with 'we suspect' in Remark 1.6; no labelled theorem environment. PDF math is readable.
paper_title: Extremal results on feedback arc sets in digraphs

name: AX_structured_graph_codes_f2c_odd_n
title: Open case of Theorem 3 for odd $n$
statement_text: Determine $M_{F_{2c}}(n)$ for odd $n \geq 5$. The upper bound $M_{F_{2c}}(n) \leq 2^{n-2}$ holds for all $n$, but the best construction for odd $n$ yields only $2^{n-2} - \binom{n-2}{(n-3)/2}$ graphs.
context_text: For graphs $G,G'$ on the same labeled vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, $G\oplus G'$ is the graph on $[n]$ whose edge set is the symmetric difference $E(G)\triangle E(G')$. For a class $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, a family $\mathcal{G}$ of graphs on $[n]$ is $\mathcal{F}$-good if $G\oplus G'\in\mathcal{F}$ for every two distinct $G,G'\in\mathcal{G}$, and $M_{\mathcal{F}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{F}$-good family on $[n]$ (a graph analogue of the code distance problem, in the spirit of the Simonovits–Sós problem). Here $\mathcal{F}_{2c}$ is the class of $2$-connected graphs. The upper bound $M_{\mathcal{F}_{2c}}(n)\le 2^{n-2}$ follows for every $n$ from a duality argument: the $2^{\binom{n-1}{2}+1}$ graphs in which vertex $n$ is isolated or adjacent only to $n-1$ have pairwise non-2-connected symmetric differences, and $M_{\mathcal{F}}(n)\cdot D_{\mathcal{F}}(n)\le 2^{\binom n2}$ where $D_{\mathcal{F}}(n)$ is the largest family with no symmetric difference in $\mathcal{F}$. For even $n$ the authors attain $2^{n-2}$ by taking, for every bipartition $\{K,L\}$ of $[n]$ with $|K|$ and $|L|$ even, the disjoint union of the complete graphs on $K$ and on $L$ (pairwise symmetric differences are complete bipartite graphs with both sides of size at least $2$). For odd $n$ this construction fails; for $n=3$ the bound is attained (a triangle and the empty graph), but for larger odd $n$ the best they obtain, by keeping only the bipartitions whose smaller class has odd size if $n\equiv1\pmod 4$ and even size if $n\equiv3\pmod 4$, has $2^{n-2}-\binom{n-2}{(n-3)/2}$ graphs.
notes: Stated as Remark 2 without a formal Problem/Conjecture environment; the authors do not explicitly conjecture the true value for odd $n$ but clearly identify it as an open case.
paper_title: Structured Codes of Graphs

name: AX_unit_segment_graphs_twin_width_delineated
title: Open Question (unit segment graphs delineation)
statement_text: Are unit segment graphs delineated (by twin-width)?
context_text: Unit segment graphs are the intersection graphs of segments of length $1$ in the plane (any directions). Twin-width is a graph parameter defined via contraction sequences (iteratively merging two vertices, recording inconsistent adjacencies as red edges; twin-width at most $d$ means the graph can be reduced to one vertex keeping red degree at most $d$); classes of bounded twin-width are monadically dependent. A class is monadically dependent if it does not first-order transduce the class of all finite graphs (a transduction colours the vertices with a bounded number of unary predicates and defines a new graph by a first-order formula); it is conjectured that these are exactly the hereditary classes with fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking, so that an effective form of delineation of $\mathcal{C}$ settles which hereditary subclasses of $\mathcal{C}$ have FPT model checking. A class $\mathcal{C}$ is delineated (by twin-width) if for every hereditary closure $\mathcal{D}$ of a subclass of $\mathcal{C}$, $\mathcal{D}$ has bounded twin-width if and only if $\mathcal{D}$ is monadically dependent. The authors prove that interval graphs and rooted directed path graphs are delineated, while segment graphs, directed path graphs, visibility graphs of simple polygons and even intersection graphs of axis-parallel segments with two distinct lengths are not. Towards the frontier, they show that $K_{t,t}$-free segment graphs and axis-parallel $H_t$-free unit segment graphs have bounded twin-width, where $H_t$ is the half-graph of height $t$ (vertices $a_1,\dots,a_t,b_1,\dots,b_t$ with $a_ib_j$ an edge iff $i\le j$, both sides independent) and freeness is with respect to semi-induced subgraphs (only edges between the two sides are prescribed); in contrast axis-parallel $H_4$-free two-lengthed segment graphs have unbounded twin-width, and (triangle-free) pure axis-parallel unit segment graphs were already known to have unbounded twin-width. The authors also ask the same question for visibility graphs of 1.5D terrains and for tournaments.
notes: Stated verbatim in the abstract: 'We leave as an open question whether unit segment graphs are delineated.'
paper_title: Twin-width VIII: delineation and win-wins

name: AX_planar_weak_coloring_number_quadratic_log
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: Planar graphs have $r$-th weak coloring numbers in $O(r^2 \log r)$.
context_text: For a linear ordering $\sigma$ of $V(G)$ and $r\ge0$, a vertex $u$ is weakly $r$-reachable from $v$ if there is a $u$–$v$ path of length at most $r$ all of whose vertices $w$ satisfy $u\le_\sigma w$ (so $v$ itself is weakly reachable from $v$); $\mathrm{wcol}_r(G,\sigma)$ is the maximum over $v$ of the number of vertices weakly $r$-reachable from $v$, and the $r$-th weak coloring number $\mathrm{wcol}_r(G)$ is the minimum of $\mathrm{wcol}_r(G,\sigma)$ over all orderings, so that $\mathrm{wcol}_1(G)$ is the coloring number (degeneracy plus one). The conjecture concerns the maximum of $\mathrm{wcol}_r(G)$ over planar graphs $G$, as a function of $r$. Graphs of treewidth at most $k$ have $\mathrm{wcol}_r\le\binom{r+k}{k}$, tight (Grohe, Kreutzer, Rabinovich, Siebertz, Stavropoulos), giving planar graphs with $\mathrm{wcol}_r=\Omega(r^2)$; the best upper bound for planar graphs is $\binom{r+2}{2}(2r+1)=O(r^3)$ (Van den Heuvel, Ossona de Mendez, Quiroz, Rabinovich, Siebertz). The authors prove that graphs of simple treewidth at most $k$ (subgraphs of $k$-trees built without using any $k$-clique twice) have maximum $\mathrm{wcol}_r$ of order $\Theta(r^{k-1}\log r)$, which gives planar graphs with $\mathrm{wcol}_r=\Omega(r^2\log r)$ and the tight bound $\Theta(r\log r)$ for outerplanar graphs. They believe the lower bound is the right order for planar graphs. Similar gaps ($\Omega(p^2\log p)$ vs $O(p^3\log p)$) exist for the $p$-centered chromatic number and fractional treedepth-fragility rate of planar graphs.
notes: PDF source; the statement notation is sufficiently clear despite possible garbling. Section 4 (open problems) is absent from the extracted text, so additional open problems beyond Conjecture 4 may exist in the full paper.
paper_title: Improved bounds for weak coloring numbers

name: AX_tree_bounded_growth_r_burnable
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: Let $T$ be a tree of growth $k$ and of order $n$. If $R$ is a finite set of integers such that $\{0, 1, \ldots, k\} \subseteq R$ and $\sum_{r \in R}(2r+1) \geq n$, then $T$ is $R$-burnable.
context_text: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected; $B(v,r)$ is the set of vertices at distance at most $r$ from $v$. In graph burning, in each round every unburned vertex with a burned neighbour becomes burned and then one new vertex is chosen to burn; the burning number $b(G)$ is the least $k$ such that all vertices are burned after $k$ rounds. The Burning Number Conjecture (BNC) states $b(G)\le\lceil\sqrt n\rceil$ for every connected graph of order $n$. Since the vertices burned after $p$ rounds are $\bigcup_i B(v_i,p-i)$, the BNC says that every connected $n$-vertex graph can be covered by balls of radii $0,1,\dots,\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1$. For a finite set $\mathcal{R}=\{r_1,\dots,r_p\}$ of non-negative integers (a set, not a multiset), $G$ is $\mathcal{R}$-burnable if there are vertices $v_1,\dots,v_p$ with $\bigcup_i B(v_i,r_i)=V(G)$. The growth of a connected graph is the smallest $k$ such that every vertex is within distance $k$ of some path $P$ of the graph (trees of growth $k$ are $k$-caterpillars; it suffices to consider trees, via spanning trees). Since $\sum_{r=0}^{\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1}(2r+1)=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil^2\ge n$, this conjecture strengthens the BNC for trees of growth $k$ whenever $\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1\ge k$. The authors prove that $b(T)\le\sqrt{n+c_k}$ for trees of growth at most $k$, with $c_k$ depending only on $k$, so the BNC is asymptotically true for them and reduces to finitely many cases for each $k$, and they state that analogous arguments extend this to the present conjecture. They also prove $b(G)\le\sqrt{4n/3}+1$ for every connected graph.
paper_title: Improved pyrotechnics : Closer to the burning graph conjecture

name: AX_poly_chi_bounded_hereditary_characterization
title: Question (which hereditary classes are poly-χ-bounded?)
statement_text: Which hereditary classes are poly-$\chi$-bounded?
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. Many classes are known to be $\chi$-bounded, but the proofs frequently give fast-growing binding functions, and it is natural to ask whether this is necessary. Esperet conjectured that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class is polynomially $\chi$-bounded, but this was recently disproved by Briański, Davies and Walczak, leaving the question of which hereditary classes are. As a contribution, the authors prove that for every $k$ the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole (an induced subgraph with $k$ components, each a cycle of length at least four) is polynomially $\chi$-bounded, and similar results when the cycles are required to be odd or of length four, or long or of length four.
notes: Posed as a guiding open question in the introduction after noting Esperet's conjecture was disproved; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

name: AX_poly_chi_bounded_odd_multihole_free
title: Open problem (poly-χ-bounded for k-multihole with only odd cycles)
statement_text: For any integer $k \geq 1$, is the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole in which all the cycles have odd length polynomially $\chi$-bounded?
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and a $k$-multihole of $G$ is an induced subgraph with exactly $k$ components, each a cycle of length at least four (so graphs with no $1$-multihole are chordal, hence perfect). Scott and Seymour showed that the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole in which all the cycles have odd length is $\chi$-bounded, but it contains the class of $\{P_5,C_5\}$-free graphs, which the authors cannot yet prove to be polynomially $\chi$-bounded. The same applies to excluding $k$-multiholes whose cycles all have length at least $\ell$. The authors prove polynomial $\chi$-boundedness once cycles of length four are also permitted as components: for each $k$, the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole in which every component has length four or odd length is polynomially $\chi$-bounded (and similarly with length four or at least $\ell$).
notes: Stated as an open limitation in the introduction; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

name: AX_forest_free_polynomial_chi_gyarfas_sumner_all_forests
title: Informal conjecture (polynomial Gyárfás–Sumner)
statement_text: It might be true that every forest $H$ is good, i.e., the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded (strengthening the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture from $\chi$-boundedness to polynomial $\chi$-boundedness).
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A forest $H$ is good if the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture says that for every forest $H$ the class of $H$-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded; the statement here is the strengthening to polynomial binding functions. It has been proved only for a few simple kinds of trees and some (not all) forests that are disjoint unions of these; for instance, trees of diameter three are good, and stars and four-vertex paths are good. It is not even known that the disjoint union of two good trees is good. The authors introduce self-isolation as a tool: if $H_1$ and $H_2$ are good forests and one of them is self-isolating, then their disjoint union is good, where a graph $H$ is self-isolating if for every non-decreasing polynomial $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ there is a polynomial $\phi$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$ has a set $A\subseteq V(G)$ with $\chi(G[A])>\psi(\omega(G[A]))$ such that either $G[A]$ is $H$-free, or $G$ contains an induced copy of $H$ whose vertex set is disjoint from $A$ and has no edges to $A$.
notes: Introduced with 'It might be true that'; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

name: AX_poly_chi_bounded_trees_disjoint_union
title: Open problem (disjoint union of good trees)
statement_text: It is not known that if trees $H_1$, $H_2$ are good (i.e., the class of $H_i$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded for $i=1,2$), then the disjoint union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is also good.
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A forest $H$ is good if the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded. It might be true that every forest is good (a polynomial strengthening of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture), but this is only proved for a few simple trees. For instance trees of diameter three are good, but as far as the authors know disjoint unions of them might not be. A graph $H$ is self-isolating if for every non-decreasing polynomial $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ there is a polynomial $\phi$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$ has a set $A\subseteq V(G)$ with $\chi(G[A])>\psi(\omega(G[A]))$ such that either $G[A]$ is $H$-free, or $G$ contains an induced copy of $H$ whose vertex set is disjoint from $A$ and has no edges to $A$. The authors show that if $H_1$ and $H_2$ are good forests and one of them is self-isolating, then their disjoint union is good; stars and four-vertex paths are good and self-isolating, so disjoint unions with them preserve goodness.
notes: Stated as 'It is not known that …'; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

name: AX_poly_chi_bounded_self_isolating_all
title: Question (are all graphs self-isolating?)
statement_text: Could it be that all graphs are self-isolating?
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A graph $H$ is self-isolating if for every non-decreasing polynomial $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ there is a polynomial $\phi$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$ has a set $A\subseteq V(G)$ with $\chi(G[A])>\psi(\omega(G[A]))$ such that either $G[A]$ is $H$-free, or $G$ contains an induced copy of $H$ whose vertex set is disjoint from $A$ and has no edges to $A$. If $H_1$ and $H_2$ are forests such that the classes of $H_1$-free and $H_2$-free graphs are polynomially $\chi$-bounded and one of them is self-isolating, then the class of graphs with no induced copy of the disjoint union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is polynomially $\chi$-bounded, which motivates the notion. A graph is self-isolating if all its components are; the only connected graphs known to be self-isolating are complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs (proved in the paper; the case of stars was proved earlier) and paths of arbitrary length. The authors know very few graphs with the property and none without it. If the polynomials $\phi,\psi$ in the definition are replaced by general functions, it is easy to show (by induction on $\omega(G)$) that all graphs have the property.
notes: Posed explicitly as a question in Section 2; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

name: AX_chordal_digraphs_dichromatic_construction_size
title: Open problem on construction size
statement_text: Let $\mathcal{C}_3$ be the class of digraphs containing neither the transitive tournament $TT_3$ nor an induced directed cycle of length at least 4. It would be interesting to know if the size of the authors' $(k+1)$-dichromatic example in $\mathcal{C}_3$ can be reduced below the current bound of $n^{2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}}$, which is larger than the $2^{\mathrm{poly}(|G_k|)}$ bound achieved by Zykov's construction for triangle-free graphs.
context_text: A $k$-dicolouring of a digraph $D$ is a partition of $V(D)$ into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph, and the dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the least such $k$; $\omega(D)$ is the clique number of the underlying graph. Carbonero, Hompe, Moore and Spirkl showed that digraphs with no induced directed cycle of odd length at least 5 are not $\vec{\chi}$-bounded, and asked whether digraphs in which every induced directed cycle has length 3 (directed analogues of chordal graphs) are. The authors answer negatively: for every $k$ there is a digraph in $\mathcal{C}_3$ (hence with no $K_4$, since every orientation of $K_4$ contains $TT_3$) with dichromatic number at least $k$. The construction generalizes Zykov's construction of triangle-free graphs of large chromatic number, where $G_{k+1}$ is built from $k$ disjoint copies of $G_k$ by adding, for each transversal set $I$ (one vertex per copy), a new vertex adjacent to all of $I$, giving size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(|G_k|)}$. In the directed case a single vertex cannot force a colour to be missed, and the authors attach directed triangles to independent sets repeatedly, which gives the much larger size $n^{2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}}$, where $n$ presumably denotes the number of vertices of the previous digraph $G_k$ (the paper does not say explicitly).
notes: PDF source — the size expression appears as 'n2poly(n)' in the extraction; the exact exponent tower has been reconstructed as $n^{2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}}$ based on the Lemma 3 bound $n^{4r}$ and the recursive structure, but may differ from the original LaTeX.
paper_title: Chordal directed graphs are not $χ$-bounded

name: AX_list_ramsey_chromatic_family_exact
title: Conjecture on $R_\ell(\mathcal{H}_s, k)$
statement_text: For $s \geq 2$, if $\mathcal{H}_s$ is the family of graphs with chromatic number greater than $s$, then $R_\ell(\mathcal{H}_s, k) = s^k + 1$.
context_text: For a list assignment $L:E(K_n)\to\binom{\mathbb{N}}{k}$ giving each edge of $K_n$ a set of $k$ colours, an $L$-colouring is an edge-colouring in which each edge $e$ receives a colour from $L(e)$. The $k$-colour list Ramsey number $R_\ell(H,k)$ (introduced by Alon, Bucić, Kalvari, Kuperwasser and Szabó) is the smallest $n$ such that there is some $L:E(K_n)\to\binom{\mathbb{N}}{k}$ for which every $L$-colouring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $H$; taking $L$ constant shows $R_\ell(H,k)\le R(H,k)$, the classical $k$-colour Ramsey number. (The paper works more generally with $r$-uniform hypergraphs.) For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs, $R_\ell(\mathcal{H},k)$ is the minimum $n$ such that some $L:E(K_n)\to\binom{\mathbb{N}}{k}$ forces, in every $L$-colouring of $K_n$, a monochromatic copy of some $H\in\mathcal{H}$. The authors state (proof omitted) that for $s\ge2$ and $\mathcal{H}_s$ the family of graphs with chromatic number greater than $s$, $\frac{1}{e}\cdot s^k\le R_\ell(\mathcal{H}_s,k)\le s^k+1$: the lower bound comes from their random construction for single graphs, which avoids every graph of chromatic number at least $\chi(H)$, and the upper bound from $R_\ell(\mathcal{H}_s,k)\le R(\mathcal{H}_s,k)=s^k+1$. They conjecture that the upper bound is the truth, i.e. that for this family the list Ramsey number equals the classical one.
paper_title: Multicolor list Ramsey numbers grow exponentially

name: AX_list_ramsey_exponential_constant_k3
title: Determine the exponential constant in $R_\ell(H,k)$
statement_text: It would be interesting to determine $\lim_{k\to\infty} R_\ell(H,k)^{1/k}$, even in just the case $H = K_3$.
context_text: For a list assignment $L:E(K_n)\to\binom{\mathbb{N}}{k}$ giving each edge of $K_n$ a set of $k$ colours, an $L$-colouring is an edge-colouring in which each edge $e$ receives a colour from $L(e)$. The $k$-colour list Ramsey number $R_\ell(H,k)$ (introduced by Alon, Bucić, Kalvari, Kuperwasser and Szabó) is the smallest $n$ such that there is some $L:E(K_n)\to\binom{\mathbb{N}}{k}$ for which every $L$-colouring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $H$; taking $L$ constant shows $R_\ell(H,k)\le R(H,k)$, the classical $k$-colour Ramsey number. (The paper works more generally with $r$-uniform hypergraphs.) Alon et al. proved that if $H$ is not bipartite, $e^{\sqrt{k\log(\chi(H)-1)/4}}\le R_\ell(H,k)\le(1-\pi(H)+o(1))^{-k\,m(H)}$, where $\pi(H)=\lim_n \mathrm{ex}(n,H)\binom{n}{2}^{-1}$ is the Turán density and $m(H)=\max_{H'\subseteq H,\,e(H')>1}\frac{e(H')-1}{v(H')-2}$. The authors prove the lower bound $R_\ell(H,k)\ge\frac{1}{e}(1-\pi(H))^{-k}$, so $R_\ell(H,k)$ is exponential in $k$ if and only if $H$ is not bipartite (and polynomial otherwise). Since $m(H)>1$ for non-bipartite $H$, the two exponential constants differ, and the results do not determine $\lim_{k\to\infty}R_\ell(H,k)^{1/k}$ or even show that it exists. For $H=K_3$ the bounds read $\frac{1}{e}\cdot2^k\le R_\ell(K_3,k)\le(4+o(1))^k$, whereas no exponential upper bound is known for the classical $R(K_3,k)$; showing $R_\ell(K_3,k)\le3.199^k$ would, by the best known lower bound for $R(K_3,k)$, give $R_\ell(K_3,k)<R(K_3,k)$.
notes: PDF source — the precise numerical bounds cited for $K_3$ may be garbled in extraction.
paper_title: Multicolor list Ramsey numbers grow exponentially

name: AX_kst_minor_free_choosable_k44_k35
title: Question 1
statement_text: Is every graph without a $K_{4,4}$-minor $7$-choosable? Is every graph without a $K_{3,5}$-minor $7$-choosable?
context_text: Graphs are finite, loopless and without parallel edges; $G\succeq F$ means $G$ contains $F$ as a minor. The list chromatic number $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $G$ has a proper coloring from any assignment of lists of size at least $k$ to its vertices ($G$ is then $k$-choosable). Woodall conjectured that for all $s,t\ge1$ every graph with no $K_{s,t}$-minor has $\chi(G)\le s+t-1$ (a weakening of Hadwiger's conjecture, also proposed by Seymour) and even $\chi_\ell(G)\le s+t-1$. The author refutes the list version in a strong form: for all $\varepsilon>0$ and $C\ge1$ there is $N$ such that for all $N\le s\le t\le Cs$ some $K_{s,t}$-minor-free graph has list chromatic number greater than $(1-\varepsilon)(2s+t)$ (so about $3t$ for $s=t$, versus the conjectured $2t-1$); the construction is probabilistic and the resulting values of $s,t$ are astronomically large. Known cases of the list conjecture: it holds for $s\le2$ and for $s=t=3$ (Woodall), and for $s=3,t=4$ since Jørgensen showed $K_{3,4}$-minor-free graphs are 5-degenerate; Kostochka and Prince showed $K_{3,t}$-minor-free graphs are $(t+3)$-choosable for $t\ge6300$, one more than conjectured; Kawarabayashi showed $K_{4,t}$-minor-free graphs are $4t$-choosable, and Jørgensen that $K_{4,4}$-minor-free graphs are 7-degenerate, hence 8-choosable. The author proposes $K_{4,4}$ and $K_{3,5}$ as the smallest open cases of Woodall's list conjecture, which predicts 7-choosability in both cases.
notes: PDF source — math notation is clear.
paper_title: Disproof of a Conjecture by Woodall

name: AX_kst_minor_free_choosable_2s_t
title: Question 2
statement_text: Is it true that for all integers $1 \leq s \leq t$, every graph $G$ with $G \not\succeq K_{s,t}$ satisfies $\chi_{\ell}(G) \leq 2s + t$?
context_text: Graphs are finite, loopless and without parallel edges; $G\succeq F$ means $G$ contains $F$ as a minor. The list chromatic number $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $G$ has a proper coloring from any assignment of lists of size at least $k$ to its vertices ($G$ is then $k$-choosable). Woodall conjectured that for all $s,t\ge1$ every graph with no $K_{s,t}$-minor has $\chi(G)\le s+t-1$ (a weakening of Hadwiger's conjecture, also proposed by Seymour) and even $\chi_\ell(G)\le s+t-1$. The author refutes the list version in a strong form: for all $\varepsilon>0$ and $C\ge1$ there is $N$ such that for all $N\le s\le t\le Cs$ some $K_{s,t}$-minor-free graph has list chromatic number greater than $(1-\varepsilon)(2s+t)$ (so about $3t$ for $s=t$, versus the conjectured $2t-1$); the construction is probabilistic and the resulting values of $s,t$ are astronomically large. The question asks whether the lower bound $(1-\varepsilon)(2s+t)$ is essentially tight for all $1\le s\le t$. Known upper bounds: by Delcourt and Postle, $K_t$-minor-free graphs are $O(t(\log\log t)^2)$-choosable, giving $O((s+t)(\log\log(s+t))^2)$ for $K_{s,t}$-minor-free graphs; for $t>(240s\log_2 s)^{8s\log_2 s+1}$ every $K_{s,t}$-minor-free graph is $(3s+t)$-degenerate, hence $(3s+t+1)$-choosable (Kostochka and Prince).

name: AX_kst_minor_free_choosable_woodall_fixed_s
title: Open problem: Woodall's conjecture for fixed s
statement_text: It remains an interesting open problem whether Woodall's conjecture (that every graph without a $K_{s,t}$-minor is $(s+t-1)$-choosable) remains true if $s$ is fixed and $t$ is sufficiently large in terms of $s$.
context_text: Graphs are finite, loopless and without parallel edges; $G\succeq F$ means $G$ contains $F$ as a minor. The list chromatic number $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $G$ has a proper coloring from any assignment of lists of size at least $k$ to its vertices ($G$ is then $k$-choosable). Woodall conjectured that for all $s,t\ge1$ every graph with no $K_{s,t}$-minor has $\chi(G)\le s+t-1$ (a weakening of Hadwiger's conjecture, also proposed by Seymour) and even $\chi_\ell(G)\le s+t-1$. The author refutes the list version in a strong form: for all $\varepsilon>0$ and $C\ge1$ there is $N$ such that for all $N\le s\le t\le Cs$ some $K_{s,t}$-minor-free graph has list chromatic number greater than $(1-\varepsilon)(2s+t)$ (so about $3t$ for $s=t$, versus the conjectured $2t-1$); the construction is probabilistic and the resulting values of $s,t$ are astronomically large. The disproof requires $s$ and $t$ of comparable size ($s\le t\le Cs$). For the chromatic number, Kostochka proved that $K_{s,t}$-minor-free graphs are $(s+t-1)$-colorable for every $s$ when $t\ge t_0(s)=O(s^3\log^3 s)$, but no analogous result is known for the list chromatic number; the best is that for $t>(240s\log_2 s)^{8s\log_2 s+1}$ such graphs are $(3s+t)$-degenerate, hence $(3s+t+1)$-choosable. For $s=3$, Kostochka and Prince obtained $(t+3)$-choosability for $t\ge6300$.

name: AX_kst_minor_free_choosable_woodall_smallest_counterexample
title: Open problem: smallest counterexample to Woodall's conjecture
statement_text: It would also be interesting to determine the smallest values of $s$ and $t$ (or of $s + t$) for which Woodall's conjecture (that every graph without a $K_{s,t}$-minor is $(s+t-1)$-choosable) fails.
context_text: Graphs are finite, loopless and without parallel edges; $G\succeq F$ means $G$ contains $F$ as a minor. The list chromatic number $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $G$ has a proper coloring from any assignment of lists of size at least $k$ to its vertices ($G$ is then $k$-choosable). Woodall conjectured that for all $s,t\ge1$ every graph with no $K_{s,t}$-minor has $\chi(G)\le s+t-1$ (a weakening of Hadwiger's conjecture, also proposed by Seymour) and even $\chi_\ell(G)\le s+t-1$. The author refutes the list version in a strong form: for all $\varepsilon>0$ and $C\ge1$ there is $N$ such that for all $N\le s\le t\le Cs$ some $K_{s,t}$-minor-free graph has list chromatic number greater than $(1-\varepsilon)(2s+t)$ (so about $3t$ for $s=t$, versus the conjectured $2t-1$); the construction is probabilistic and the resulting values of $s,t$ are astronomically large. Known cases of the list conjecture: it holds for $s\le2$ and for $s=t=3$ (Woodall), and for $s=3,t=4$ since Jørgensen showed $K_{3,4}$-minor-free graphs are 5-degenerate; Kostochka and Prince showed $K_{3,t}$-minor-free graphs are $(t+3)$-choosable for $t\ge6300$, one more than conjectured; Kawarabayashi showed $K_{4,t}$-minor-free graphs are $4t$-choosable, and Jørgensen that $K_{4,4}$-minor-free graphs are 7-degenerate, hence 8-choosable. The smallest cases left open are $K_{4,4}$ and $K_{3,5}$.

name: AX_acyclic_digraph_ramsey_bounded_degree_polynomial
title: Open problem on parameters governing $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H)$
statement_text: What natural parameters (analogous to degeneracy and vertex count for undirected graphs) determine the growth order of $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H)$ for acyclic digraphs? In particular, is $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H)$ polynomial or super-polynomial in $n$ when $H$ has bounded degree?
context_text: Digraphs are simple and oriented (no loops, parallel or anti-parallel edges). For an acyclic digraph $H$, the oriented Ramsey number $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H)$ is the least $N$ such that every tournament on $N$ vertices contains a copy of $H$ (more generally $\overrightarrow{r}_k(H)$ asks for a monochromatic copy in every $k$-edge-coloured tournament; acyclicity is needed since transitive tournaments contain no directed cycle); $n$ denotes the number of vertices and $\Delta$ the maximum degree of $H$. For undirected graphs, the Burr–Erdős conjecture (bounded-degeneracy graphs have linear Ramsey number) was proved by Lee, and the degeneracy $d$ and the number $n$ of vertices essentially govern $r_2(H)$: $r_2(H)\ge\max(n,2^{d/2})$, and Conlon, Fox and Sudakov conjectured $r_2(H)=2^{O(d)}n$ (known up to a $\log^2d$ factor in the exponent). Disproving the directed analogue of Burr–Erdős (a question of Bucić, Letzter and Sudakov), the authors construct, for every $\Delta\ge2$ and large $n$, acyclic $H$ with maximum degree $\Delta$ and $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H)\ge n^{\Omega(\Delta^{2/3}/\log^{5/3}\Delta)}$, while the worst case is at most $2^{O(\Delta\log^2(2n/\Delta))}$; typical bounded-degree acyclic digraphs have nearly linear oriented Ramsey number, and for $k\ge2$ colours there are acyclic $H$ of maximum degree 3 with $\overrightarrow{r}_k(H)\ge n^{\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)}$. They identify multiscale complexity as a relevant parameter: order $V(H)$ so that all edges go forward (a topological sorting), give each edge $v_i\to v_j$ the length $j-i$, and say $H$ has high multiscale complexity if for most dyadic scales $[2^t,2^{t+1})$ many edges have length in that scale; their upper bounds are stronger for low complexity, and their lower-bound digraphs (interval meshes) maximize it. They conjecture that super-polynomial growth $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H)\ge n^{\omega(1)}$ occurs already for one colour and some fixed $\Delta$.
notes: Stated as prose in the introduction (no formal theorem environment); also reiterated in the conclusion.
paper_title: Ramsey numbers of sparse digraphs

name: AX_triangle_removal_vs_dfl_growth
title: Informal Conjecture on similar growth of $N_{DFL}(\varepsilon)$ and $1/\delta_{TRL}(\varepsilon)$
statement_text: We suspect that $N_{DFL}(\varepsilon)$ and $1/\delta_{TRL}(\varepsilon)$ have similar growth.
context_text: The triangle removal lemma states that for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph with fewer than $\delta n^3$ triangles can be made triangle-free by deleting at most $\epsilon n^2$ edges; $\delta_{TRL}(\epsilon)$ is the largest such $\delta$. The diamond-free lemma states that for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $N$ such that for every $n\ge N$, every $n$-vertex graph in which each edge lies in a unique triangle has at most $\epsilon n^2$ edges; $N_{DFL}(\epsilon)$ is the smallest such $N$. It follows from the triangle removal lemma, giving $N_{DFL}(\epsilon)\le1/\delta_{TRL}(\epsilon/3)$. For both quantities the best lower bound is of the form $(1/\epsilon)^{c\log(1/\epsilon)}$ (from Behrend's construction), while the best upper bound is $1/\delta_{TRL}(\epsilon)\le\mathrm{tower}(O(\log(1/\epsilon)))$ (Fox), a tower of $2$'s. The authors prove supporting evidence: for fixed $0<c<1$, if $N_{DFL}(\epsilon)\le2^{\epsilon^{-c+o(1)}}$ then $\delta_{TRL}(\epsilon)\ge2^{-\epsilon^{-c/(1-c)+o(1)}}$. Their motivation is the triangle-free lemma: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $M$ such that every triangle-free graph $G$ has an $\epsilon$-approximate homomorphism (a map $V(G)\to V(F)$ sending all but at most $\epsilon|V(G)|^2$ edges to edges) to a triangle-free graph $F$ on at most $M$ vertices; with $M_{TFL}(\epsilon)$ the least such $M$, they show $M_{TFL}(\epsilon)\ge e^{\epsilon N_{DFL}(C\epsilon)/C}$, while $M_{TFL}(\epsilon)\le e^{O(\delta_{TRL}(\epsilon/C)^{-2})}$ is known; similar growth of $N_{DFL}$ and $1/\delta_{TRL}$ would thus give comparable bounds on $M_{TFL}$.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled; stated as 'We suspect' in running prose without a labelled environment. The PDF extraction appears truncated after the start of Section 2, so further conjectures or open problems in later sections may be missing.
paper_title: Removal lemmas and approximate homomorphisms

name: AX_implicit_representation_speed_sqrt_n_labels
title: Question (Section 3, implicit representation for speed $2^{O(n\log n)}$)
statement_text: Is it possible that hereditary families with speed $f(n) \leq 2^{O(n \log n)}$ always admit an implicit representation of size $O(n^{1/2} \log n)$?
context_text: A family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; $\mathcal{F}_n$ is the set of members of $\mathcal{F}$ with $n$ vertices, and the speed of $\mathcal{F}$ is $f(n)=|\mathcal{F}_n|$. An implicit representation of size $\ell(n)$ of $\mathcal{F}_n$ is a function assigning a label of $\ell(n)$ bits to each vertex of any graph $G\in\mathcal{F}_n$ so that the adjacency between any two vertices is determined by their labels (the labeling need not be efficiently computable); equivalently, there is a universal graph on $2^{\ell(n)}$ vertices containing every member of $\mathcal{F}_n$ as an induced subgraph. Necessarily $\ell(n)\ge\log_2|\mathcal{F}_n|/n$. Speed $2^{O(n\log n)}$ holds for many natural families, e.g. those whose vertices are points of a bounded-dimensional real space with adjacency determined by signs of bounded-degree polynomials (intersection graphs of segments or discs in the plane, for which economic implicit representations are not known). Hatami and Hatami showed that for every $\delta>0$ there are hereditary families with speed $f(n)\le 2^{O(n\log n)}$ for which any implicit representation requires labels of size at least $\Omega(n^{1/2-\delta})$, and asked whether the exponent $1/2$ can be improved. Alon proves that speed $f(n)\le 2^{(1/4-\varepsilon)n^2}$ already guarantees an implicit representation of size $O(n^{1-1/d}\log n)$ for some integer $d$ depending on $\varepsilon$, and asks whether $O(n^{1/2}\log n)$ always suffices in the $2^{O(n\log n)}$ speed range.
notes: Posed as an explicit question in Section 3 but without a labelled theorem environment; PDF source.
paper_title: Implicit representation of sparse hereditary families

name: AX_implicit_representation_speed_n23_labels
title: Question (Section 3, implicit representation for speed $2^{n^{1+\varepsilon}}$)
statement_text: If the speed of a hereditary family satisfies $f(n) < 2^{n^{1+\varepsilon}}$ for a sufficiently small fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, is there always an implicit representation of size at most $O(n^{2/3} \log n)$?
context_text: A family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; $\mathcal{F}_n$ is the set of members of $\mathcal{F}$ with $n$ vertices, and the speed of $\mathcal{F}$ is $f(n)=|\mathcal{F}_n|$. An implicit representation of size $\ell(n)$ of $\mathcal{F}_n$ is a function assigning a label of $\ell(n)$ bits to each vertex of any graph $G\in\mathcal{F}_n$ so that the adjacency between any two vertices is determined by their labels; equivalently, there is a universal graph on $2^{\ell(n)}$ vertices containing every member of $\mathcal{F}_n$ as an induced subgraph. Alon's main theorem: for any $\varepsilon>0$ there is an integer $d$ such that every hereditary family with speed $f(n)\le 2^{(1/4-\varepsilon)n^2}$ admits an implicit representation of size $O(n^{1-1/d}\log n)$, and for every $d>1$ this is tight up to the $\log n$ factor for some hereditary family. He asks whether tighter bounds hold when the speed grows more slowly: for speed $2^{O(n\log n)}$, whether $O(n^{1/2}\log n)$ always suffices (Hatami and Hatami showed $n^{1/2-\delta}$ may be needed there), and, as here, whether speed below $2^{n^{1+\varepsilon}}$ for a sufficiently small fixed $\varepsilon>0$ always allows labels of size $O(n^{2/3}\log n)$.
notes: Posed as an explicit question in Section 3 but without a labelled theorem environment; PDF source.
paper_title: Implicit representation of sparse hereditary families

name: AX_k_creature_free_polynomial_minimal_separators
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: There exists $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a $k$-creature, then $G$ has at most $|V(G)|^{f(k)}$ minimal separators.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A set $C\subseteq V(G)$ is a minimal separator if $G\setminus C$ has two distinct components $L,R$ with $N(L)=N(R)=C$; a class has the polynomial separator property if for some constant $c$ every member $G$ has at most $|V(G)|^c$ minimal separators (equivalently, polynomially many potential maximal cliques, which makes maximum weight independent set and more generally maximum weight induced subgraph of treewidth less than $k$ polynomial). For an integer $k\ge3$, a $k$-creature is a graph whose vertex set is $A\cup B\cup\{x_1,\dots,x_k\}\cup\{y_1,\dots,y_k\}$ where $G[A]$ and $G[B]$ are connected and $A$ is anticomplete to $B$ (no edges between them); for each $i$, $x_iy_i$ is an edge, $x_i$ has a neighbour in $A$ and none in $B$, and $y_i$ has a neighbour in $B$ and none in $A$; and $x_iy_j$ is not an edge for $i\neq j$ (edges among the $x_i$'s and among the $y_i$'s are unrestricted). Every $k$-creature contains a theta, a pyramid, a prism or a turtle (the paper's four basic configurations of paths forming holes), and the authors prove the conjecture of Chudnovsky, Thomassé, Trotignon and Vušković that graphs with none of these four as induced subgraphs have at most $|V(G)|^{18}$ minimal separators; this conjecture is a stronger generalisation. They prove the weaker version for immature $k$-creatures ($X=\{x_1,\dots,x_k\}$ and $Y=\{y_1,\dots,y_k\}$ with the $x_iy_i$ as the only $X$–$Y$ edges): excluding them gives $O(n^{2k-2})$ minimal separators. Even if true, the conjecture would not characterise the polynomial separator property: induced subgraphs of $k$-turtles with very long paths have it but contain $k$-creatures for arbitrarily large $k$.
notes: The paper proves a weaker version (Theorem 1.5) replacing $k$-creatures by the stricter notion of immature $k$-creatures.
paper_title: Graphs with polynomially many minimal separators

name: AX_convex_complete_geometric_k_planar_partition
title: Question 9
statement_text: Is the upper bound of $\frac{n}{\sqrt{2k}}$ on the number of $k$-planar subgraphs needed to partition the complete convex geometric graph $K(P)$ on $n$ points (more precisely, a partition into $\lceil\frac{n}{s}\rceil$ $\frac{(s-1)(s-2)}{2}$-planar subgraphs for every $s>2$) tight up to lower-order terms?
context_text: A geometric graph is a drawing of a graph in the plane with vertices at points in general position and edges as straight-line segments; two edges cross if they share a point in their relative interiors, and a geometric graph is $k$-planar (or $k$-plane) if each edge crosses at most $k$ other edges. For a point set $P$, $K(P)$ is the complete geometric graph on $P$, and a $k$-planar partition of $K(P)$ is a partition of its edges into $k$-planar subgraphs (an edge coloring in which each color class is $k$-planar); $P$ is in convex position here. The authors prove that for $n$ points in convex position, $K(P)$ admits a partition into at most $\frac{n}{\sqrt{2k}}$ $k$-planar subgraphs, obtained by grouping the $n$ edge slopes of a regular $n$-gon into $\lceil n/s\rceil$ circular intervals of size $s$, which gives $\frac{(s-1)(s-2)}{2}$-planar classes; conversely, using an improved crossing lemma for convex geometric graphs, at least $\frac{n-1}{4.93\sqrt{k}}$ subgraphs are required. For $k=1$ they prove the tight bound $\lceil n/3\rceil$ (for $n\ge5$). They ask in particular whether, when $k$ is far from $\frac{(s-1)(s-2)}{2}$, one can improve on $\lceil n/s\rceil$, and find this question surprisingly difficult; for $k=2$ they can show, with computer assistance, a lower bound of $\frac{3n}{10}$, almost matching the upper bound $\frac{n}{3}$, but omit this result from this version.
paper_title: Edge Partitions of Complete Geometric Graphs (Part 2)

name: AX_lipschitz_bijection_dictator_xor_inverse
title: Informal Question (Section 2)
statement_text: Does there exist a map $\phi$ from Dictator to XOR which is $C$-Lipschitz, where each output bit depends on at most $k$ input bits, and such that $\phi^{-1}$ is $o(\log n / \log k)$-Lipschitz as $n, k \to \infty$?
context_text: For Boolean functions $f,g:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$, a mapping from $f$ to $g$ is a bijection $\phi:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n$ with $f(x)=g(\phi(x))$ for all $x$. With $d$ the Hamming distance, $\phi$ is $C$-Lipschitz if $d(\phi(x),\phi(y))\le C\,d(x,y)$ for all $x,y$ (bi-Lipschitz if $\phi^{-1}$ is too). The output bit $\phi_j$ depends on input bit $x_i$ if $\phi_j(x)\ne\phi_j(x+e_i)$ for some $x$; $\phi$ is $k$-local if each output bit depends on at most $k$ input bits. Dictator is $x\mapsto x_1$ and XOR is $x\mapsto\sum_ix_i \bmod 2$. Rao and Shinkar constructed a $2$-Lipschitz $3$-local mapping from Dictator to XOR whose inverse is $O(\log n)$-Lipschitz, and asked whether an $O(1)$-local $O(1)$-bi-Lipschitz one exists. The authors answer negatively: if $\phi$ is $C$-Lipschitz and $k$-local then $\phi^{-1}$ is not $\delta\log n$-Lipschitz for some $\delta=\Omega(1/(k+\log C))$, and one may take $\delta=\Omega(1/\log(C+k))$ when $\phi$ is linear. Rao and Shinkar's linear construction shows that, for $C=2$, the optimal $\delta$ is $O(1/\log k)$, so the bound is tight for linear maps; for general maps only $\Omega(1/k)$ is known, which raises this question.
notes: Stated in running prose as 'This raises the following question:' without a labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Lipschitz bijections between boolean functions

name: AX_degenerate_graphs_polynomial_kempe_sequences
title: Polynomial Kempe sequences for degenerate graphs
statement_text: Can any two $k$-colorings of a $(k-1)$-degenerate graph on $n$ vertices always be connected by a sequence of Kempe changes whose length is polynomial in $n$?
context_text: Given a proper $k$-colouring of a graph, a Kempe chain is a connected component of the subgraph induced by two given colours, and a Kempe change swaps the two colours on one Kempe chain, giving another proper $k$-colouring; two colourings are Kempe equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a sequence of Kempe changes. A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$. Las Vergnas and Meyniel proved in 1981 that all $k$-colourings of a $d$-degenerate graph are Kempe equivalent when $k\ge d+1$ (the question is about the tight case $d=k-1$), but their proof yields sequences that may be exponential in the number $n$ of vertices. In the related setting of single-vertex recolourings with $k\ge d+2$ colours, Cereceda conjectured sequences of length $O(n^2)$ and Bousquet and Heinrich proved $O(n^{d+3})$, but their method does not extend to Kempe changes with one fewer colour. A polynomial bound would have many consequences since the lemma of Las Vergnas and Meyniel is used in several proofs. The authors prove polynomial bounds in related settings: if $G$ has treewidth at most $k-1$, any two $k$-colourings are equivalent up to $O(kn^2)$ Kempe changes; and the $\Delta$-colourings of an $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ are equivalent up to $O(n^2)$ Kempe changes unless $\Delta=3$ and some component is the 3-prism. They also study list colouring and bounded maximum average degree.
notes: PDF source — stated as an open question in the abstract and introduction without a labeled environment; no explicit attribution to prior authors.
paper_title: Kempe changes in degenerate graphs

name: AX_surface_k_dicolorability_complexity_4_5
title: Problem 4.4
statement_text: What is the complexity of $\Sigma$-$k$-\textsc{Dicolourability} for $k \in \{4, 5\}$ and $\Sigma$ different from the sphere?
context_text: Surfaces are closed. A $k$-dicolouring of a digraph is a partition of its vertex set into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph; the dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ for which $D$ is $k$-dicolourable. Digraphs may contain digons (pairs of opposite arcs), so that $\chi(G)=\vec{\chi}(\overleftrightarrow{G})$ for the bidirected graph $\overleftrightarrow{G}$ obtained by replacing each edge by a digon; a digraph is embeddable on $\Sigma$ if its underlying graph is. For a fixed surface $\Sigma$, $\Sigma$-$k$-Dicolourability is the problem: given a digraph $D$ embeddable on $\Sigma$, is $D$ $k$-dicolourable? A digraph is $(k+1)$-dicritical if $\vec{\chi}(D)=k+1$ and every proper subdigraph has dichromatic number at most $k$. The authors prove that only finitely many $(k+1)$-dicritical digraphs embed on a given surface for $k\ge6$, so $\Sigma$-$k$-Dicolourability is polynomial-time solvable for $k\ge6$; they show $\Sigma$-$2$-Dicolourability is NP-complete for every surface (already for planar digraphs), and $\Sigma$-$3$-Dicolourability is NP-complete since planar $3$-colourability is. On the sphere, the cases $k=4,5$ are trivial since planar graphs are $4$-colourable. The undirected analogue (testing $4$-colourability of graphs on a fixed surface other than the sphere) is also open. Along with this, the authors also ask whether there are infinitely many $6$-dicritical digraphs embeddable on $\Sigma$, and separately the complexity of the restriction to oriented graphs with $k=2$.
notes: Problem 4.4 is referenced in the introduction but the full text of Section 4 was not present in the PDF extraction; the statement is inferred from the surrounding context.
paper_title: On the dichromatic number of surfaces

name: AX_plane_graphs_weak_diameter_2_coloring
title: Question 6
statement_text: For a non-negative integer $r$, let $\mathcal{G}_r$ be the class of plane graphs with no separating triangles such that each vertex is at distance at most $r$ from a face of length at least four. Does $\mathcal{G}_r$ have weak diameter chromatic number at most two?
context_text: The weak diameter of a subgraph $H$ of $G$ is the maximum distance in $G$ (not in $H$) between vertices of $H$. For an integer $\ell\ge0$, a weak diameter-$\ell$ coloring of $G$ is a vertex coloring in which every monochromatic connected subgraph has weak diameter at most $\ell$, and a class $\mathcal{G}$ has weak diameter chromatic number at most $k$ if for some $\ell$ every graph of $\mathcal{G}$ has a weak diameter-$\ell$ coloring with at most $k$ colors. A separating triangle is a triangle whose removal disconnects the graph (one with vertices both inside and outside it in the plane drawing). The authors prove that for every surface the class of graphs drawn on it has weak diameter choosability (list version) at most three, and the class of triangle-free graphs drawn on it at most two; replacing weak diameter by diameter measured inside the monochromatic subgraph fails already for planar graphs. They suspect that a substantial relaxation of the triangle-free assumption suffices for two colors. Non-triangular faces are essential: in the $n\times n$ grid with a diagonal added in each face, the HEX lemma forces a monochromatic component of weak diameter at least $n-1$ in any 2-coloring. The question has a positive answer when the graph has exactly one non-triangular face, since plane graphs with all vertices at bounded distance from a fixed face have bounded treewidth and hence asymptotic dimension one.
paper_title: Weak diameter coloring of graphs on surfaces

name: AX_grid_arithmetic_progression_discrepancy_tight
title: Conjecture (Section 7)
statement_text: For any integer $d\geq 1$ and positive integers $N_1,\dots,N_d$, with $N=(N_1,\dots,N_d)$, $$\mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{A}_N) = \Theta_d\!\left(\max_{I \subseteq [d]} \left(\prod_{i \in I} N_i\right)^{\frac{1}{2|I|+2}}\right),$$ that is, the known lower bound for the discrepancy of arithmetic progressions in the grid $[N_1]\times\cdots\times[N_d]$ is tight up to a constant factor depending only on $d$.
context_text: For a finite set $\Omega$ and a family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets, a colouring is a map $\chi:\Omega\to\{1,-1\}$. With $\chi(A)=\sum_{x\in A}\chi(x)$, the discrepancy is $\mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{A})=\min_\chi\max_{A\in\mathcal{A}}|\chi(A)|$. An arithmetic progression in $d$ dimensions is a set $\{a+ib : i=0,\dots,l-1\}$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}^d$, $b\neq0$, $l\in\mathbb{N}$. $\mathcal{A}_N$ is the family of such progressions contained in the grid $[N_1]\times\cdots\times[N_d]$, where $N=(N_1,\dots,N_d)$, and $\prod_{i\in\emptyset}N_i=1$. In dimension 1, Roth's lower bound $cN^{1/4}$ and the Matoušek–Spencer upper bound determine the discrepancy up to a constant. Valkó proved $N^{d/(2d+2)}$ up to a $(\log N)^{5/2}$ factor for the cube $[N]^d$. The authors show $\mathrm{disc}=\Theta_d(N^{d/(2d+2)})$ for cubes, and $\Theta_d((N_1\cdots N_d)^{1/(2d+2)})$ for grids with comparable sides. For general grids with $N_1\cdots N_d\ge3$ they prove $c_d M\le\mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{A}_N)\le C_d\frac{\log(N_1\cdots N_d)}{\log\log(N_1\cdots N_d)}M$, where $M=\max_{I\subseteq[d]}(\prod_{i\in I}N_i)^{1/(2|I|+2)}$. The bounds differ by more than a constant in some regimes even for $d=2$, e.g. $N=(N,\sqrt N(\log N)^k)$. The conjecture is that the lower bound is tight, i.e. the sub-logarithmic factor can be removed. This is discrepancy theory rather than graph theory.
notes: Section 7 is not reproduced in the PDF extraction; the conjecture is described by reference in the paper's organization paragraph. The statement above is reconstructed from Theorem 1.3 and the prose description 'a conjecture that the lower bound for the discrepancy for grids in Theorem 1.3 is tight up to the constant factor'.
paper_title: Discrepancy of arithmetic progressions in grids

name: AX_active_clustering_clique_algorithm_optimal
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: For an $n$-set with a random partition with probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$, the clique algorithm has minimal average complexity among all AC algorithms.
context_text: An active clustering (AC) algorithm must recover an unknown partition of an $n$-set by queries asking an oracle whether two given items belong to the same class; it uses transitivity (never querying a pair whose relation is already implied) and stops once every class is known to be connected by positive answers and every pair of classes has received at least one negative answer. Its average complexity is the expected number of queries for a random input partition. In the model considered, each item independently belongs to class $C_i$ with probability $p_i$, for a fixed number $k$ of classes with $p_1\ge\dots\ge p_k$, $\sum_ip_i=1$. The clique algorithm processes items one by one and compares each new item with one representative of each block discovered so far, in decreasing order of block size, until it is added to a block or a new block is created. For uniformly random partitions the authors prove that an AC algorithm has minimal average complexity iff it is chordal (the graph of known negative answers between aggregated blocks stays chordal), and that all chordal algorithms, including the clique algorithm, have the same query distribution. For the $p_i$-model they prove that the clique algorithm makes $\mathbb{E}[X]\sim n\sum_{i=1}^kip_i$ queries, fewer than the algorithm choosing random unresolved pairs. The conjecture is that no AC algorithm does better on average in the $p_i$-model.
paper_title: Active clustering for labeling training data

name: AX_near_triangulation_4_coloring_extension_complexity
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm which, given a near-triangulation $G$ with the outer face bounded by a 4-cycle $C$ and a 4-coloring $\psi$ of $C$, correctly decides whether $\psi$ extends to a 4-coloring of $G$?
context_text: A near-triangulation is a connected plane graph in which all faces except the outer one have length three. By the Four Color Theorem every planar graph is 4-colourable, but many natural follow-up questions are wide open, and even very basic precoloring extension questions such as this one are unresolved. There exist infinitely many near-triangulations whose outer face is bounded by a $4$-cycle $C$ such that not every $4$-colouring of $C$ extends to a $4$-colouring of $G$, and the authors have no good guess at how such near-triangulations could be described. Some information is known: writing $n^\star_G(\psi)$ for the number of extensions of a colouring $\psi$ of $C=v_1v_2v_3v_4$, a standard Kempe chain argument shows that if the colouring $(1,2,1,2)$ extends, then $(1,2,3,2)$ or $(1,2,1,4)$ extends, and block-count reducibility gives linear inequalities that the vector of extension counts must satisfy (a cone in $\mathbb{R}^3$).
notes: PDF source — math notation may be garbled
paper_title: Coloring count cones of planar graphs

name: AX_plane_near_cubic_coloring_cone_b5
title: Conjecture 8
statement_text: Every plane near-cubic graph $\tilde{G}$ with $d(\tilde{G}) = 5$ satisfies $n_{\tilde{G}} \in B'_5$.
context_text: Graphs may have loops and parallel edges. A near-cubic graph $\tilde G=(G,v,\nu)$ is a connected graph $G$ with a vertex $v$ such that every other vertex has degree $3$, together with a numbering $\nu$ of the half-edges at $v$ by $0,\dots,\deg(v)-1$; it is plane if $G$ is plane and these half-edges appear in this clockwise order around $v$, and $d(\tilde G)=\deg(v)$. A $3$-edge-colouring of $\tilde G$ colours the edges with $1,2,3$ so that edges sharing a vertex other than $v$ get distinct colours; a $d$-precolouring is a map $\psi:\{0,\dots,d-1\}\to\{1,2,3\}$ in which each colour is used a number of times of the same parity as $d$, and $n_{\tilde G}(\psi)$ is the number of $3$-edge-colourings whose colours on the half-edges at $v$ are given by $\psi$. Dually, $n_{\tilde G}$ counts the extensions of $4$-colourings of the outer cycle of the near-triangulation $G^\star$ whose outer face corresponds to $v$. Using Kempe chains through $v$ (their endpoints and parities), the authors define for each $d$ a polyhedral coloring count cone $B_d\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{P}_d}$ ($\mathcal{P}_d$ the set of $d$-precolourings) and prove that $n_{\tilde G}\in B_{d(\tilde G)}$ for every plane near-cubic graph. The cone $B_5$ has exactly $12$ rays, spanned by $n_{\tilde R_{5,1}},\dots,n_{\tilde R_{5,12}}$ for explicit near-cubic graphs; the first eleven are plane, while $\tilde R_{5,12}$ is not (glued with the $5$-wheel it gives the Petersen graph), and $B'_5$ is the subcone spanned by the first eleven rays. The statement that no non-zero $n_{\tilde G}$ of a plane $\tilde G$ lies on the ray of $\tilde R_{5,12}$ is equivalent to the Four Color Theorem, so this conjecture strengthens it. Equivalently (as $B'_5$ has a single facet not shared with $B_5$): $3\sum_{i=0}^4 n_{\tilde G}(\psi^{a}_i)\ge\sum_{i=0}^4 n_{\tilde G}(\psi^{b}_i)$, where $\psi^a_i(j)$ and $\psi^b_i(j)$ are given, for $(j-i)\bmod5=0,1,2,3,4$, by $1,1,2,3,1$ and $1,2,1,1,3$ respectively. The authors verify it for all plane near-cubic graphs with fewer than $30$ vertices.
