paper_title: Coloring count cones of planar graphs

name: AX_polynomial_expansion_bounded_twin_width_speculation
title: Informal Conjecture (polynomial expansion and bounded twin-width)
statement_text: All classes of polynomial expansion may also have bounded twin-width.
context_text: Twin-width is defined via contraction sequences $G=G_n,G_{n-1},\dots,G_1$, where $G_{i-1}$ is obtained from $G_i$ by contracting two (not necessarily adjacent) vertices; for $u\in V(G_i)$ let $u(G)$ be the set of vertices of $G$ contracted into $u$, and let $uv$ be a red edge of $G_i$ if the pair $u(G),v(G)$ is not homogeneous in $G$ (neither all edges nor no edges between them). The twin-width of $G$ is the minimum $d$ such that some contraction sequence has red degree at most $d$ in every $G_i$ (twin-width 0 graphs are exactly the cographs). A class has bounded expansion if there is a function $f$ such that every $r$-shallow minor (minor obtained by contracting disjoint connected subgraphs of radius at most $r$ and deleting vertices and edges) of a graph in the class has edge density at most $f(r)$, and polynomial expansion if $f$ can be taken polynomial. The authors show that proper minor-closed classes (which have polynomial expansion) have bounded twin-width, and remark that, as far as they know, all classes of polynomial expansion may also have bounded twin-width. Bounded twin-width is incomparable with bounded degree, bounded expansion and nowhere denseness: cubic graphs have unbounded twin-width while cliques have twin-width 0. In their concluding questions they ask whether classes with polynomial expansion have bounded twin-width and, if so, whether contraction sequences can be computed efficiently, announcing as a first step that $t$-subdivisions of $n$-cliques have bounded twin-width if and only if $t=\Omega(\log n)$.
notes: Stated in hedged prose ('as far as we know … may also'); clearly conjectural but no labelled environment.
paper_title: Twin-width I: tractable FO model checking

name: AX_twin_width_nowhere_dense_fo_superclass
title: Question (common superclass for FPT FO model checking)
statement_text: Do bounded twin-width and nowhere dense classes admit a natural common superclass still admitting an FPT algorithm for FO model checking?
context_text: Twin-width is defined via contraction sequences $G=G_n,G_{n-1},\dots,G_1$, where $G_{i-1}$ is obtained from $G_i$ by contracting two (not necessarily adjacent) vertices; for $u\in V(G_i)$ let $u(G)$ be the set of vertices of $G$ contracted into $u$, and let $uv$ be a red edge of $G_i$ if the pair $u(G),v(G)$ is not homogeneous in $G$ (neither all edges nor no edges between them). The twin-width of $G$ is the minimum $d$ such that some contraction sequence has red degree at most $d$ in every $G_i$ (twin-width 0 graphs are exactly the cographs). FO model checking asks, given a first-order formula $\varphi$ and a graph (or binary structure) $G$, whether $G\models\varphi$; it is FPT on a class if solvable in time $f(|\varphi|)\cdot|G|^{O(1)}$. A class is nowhere dense if for every $r$ some graph is not an $r$-shallow minor of any member. FO model checking is FPT on bounded-degree graphs, graphs of locally bounded treewidth, $H$-minor-free graphs, classes of (locally) bounded expansion and finally nowhere dense classes (Grohe, Kreutzer and Siebertz). The authors prove that it is FPT on classes of bounded twin-width, given a contraction sequence witnessing it; this covers non-sparse classes such as bounded rank-width graphs, map graphs, $K_t$-free unit ball graphs, posets with antichains of bounded size and $d$-dimensional grids. Bounded twin-width is incomparable with nowhere denseness (even with structurally nowhere dense classes, i.e. FO transductions of nowhere dense ones), and in their Hasse diagram of classes with FPT FO model checking the two roughly subsume all current knowledge; the question is whether there is a natural common superclass of both on which FO model checking is still FPT.
notes: Posed as a rhetorical question in the caption of Figure 3, not in a labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Twin-width I: tractable FO model checking

name: AX_kt_minor_free_list_chromatic_2t
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Does every $K_t$-minor-free graph $G$ satisfy $\chi_\ell(G) \leq 2t$?
context_text: The list chromatic number $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the smallest $k$ such that $G$ has a proper coloring choosing each vertex's color from its list $L(v)$, for every assignment of lists with $|L(v)|\ge k$ for all $v$. Kawarabayashi and Mohar (2007) conjectured that there is an absolute constant $c$ such that every $K_t$-minor-free graph has $\chi_\ell(G)\le ct$ (List Hadwiger conjecture), and believed it holds with $c=\frac{3}{2}$; Barát, Joret and Wood had shown $c\ge\frac{4}{3}$ is necessary (a graph with no $K_{3t+2}$-minor and list chromatic number greater than $4t$). The best known upper bound is $O(t(\log\log t)^2)$ (Delcourt and Postle). Refuting the $\frac{3}{2}$ conjecture, this paper shows via a probabilistic construction that for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $t\ge t_0(\varepsilon)$ there is a graph with no $K_t$-minor and $\chi_\ell(G)\ge(2-\varepsilon)t$, so $c\ge 2$ is necessary. The author asks whether this lower-bound construction could be optimal up to the lower-order term, or whether a further improvement of the lower bound is possible.
paper_title: Improved lower bound for the list chromatic number of graphs with no $K_t$ minor

name: AX_sublinear_separators_fractional_treewidth_fragile
title: Informal Conjecture (fractional treewidth-fragility of sublinear-separator classes)
statement_text: All classes with sublinear separators are fractionally treewidth-fragile.
context_text: In this paper, For an $n$-vertex graph, a balanced separator is a set $X$ of vertices such that each component of $G-X$ has at most $2n/3$ vertices; a class $\mathcal{G}$ has strongly sublinear separators if every subgraph with at most $n$ vertices of a graph of $\mathcal{G}$ has a balanced separator of size $O(n^{1-\beta})$ for some fixed $\beta>0$ (by Dvořák and Norin these are exactly the classes of polynomial expansion). A multiset $\mathcal{Z}$ of vertex subsets of $G$ is an $(s,\delta)$-generic cover if every set of at most $s$ vertices is contained in at least $\delta|\mathcal{Z}|$ members of $\mathcal{Z}$; its treewidth is the maximum treewidth of $G[Z]$, $Z\in\mathcal{Z}$. A class is fractionally treewidth-fragile if there is a function $f$ such that every $G$ in the class has, for all positive integers $s,o$, an $(s,1-1/o)$-generic cover of treewidth at most $f(os)$ (equivalently, in the usual formulation: there is a system of vertex sets, each vertex lying in at most a $1/o$ fraction of them, whose deletion each leaves treewidth at most $f(o)$); it is efficiently fractionally treewidth-fragile if such a cover (of polynomial size) can be found in polynomial time. The author proves that, for every first-order expressible monotone maximization problem, efficiently fractionally treewidth-fragile classes admit a PTAS. These classes include all hereditary classes with sublinear separators and bounded maximum degree, all proper minor-closed classes, and many geometric graph classes such as intersection graphs of convex sets with bounded aspect ratio and bounded clique number in a fixed Euclidean space. The author remarks that it is possible, and the author has conjectured, that the property extends to all classes with sublinear separators (the phrase is used here without the word 'strongly', the paper's general notion being strongly sublinear separators).
notes: Stated in running prose as 'it is possible (and I have conjectured) that all classes with sublinear separators are fractionally treewidth-fragile'.
paper_title: Approximation metatheorems for classes with bounded expansion

name: AX_fo_minimization_approximation_bounded_expansion_ptas
title: Problem 6
statement_text: Do monotone minimization problems expressible in the first order logic admit constant factor approximation in all classes with bounded expansion? And PTASes in all efficiently fractionally treewidth-fragile graph classes?
context_text: For a finite index set $I$, a property $\pi$ of $I$-tuples $A_I=(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of vertex subsets of $G$ is expressible in first-order logic if it is the set of tuples satisfying a fixed first-order sentence using quantification over vertices, the adjacency predicate, equality and unary predicates $X_i$ interpreted as the sets $A_i$. Given a weight assignment $w(v,J)\ge0$ for each vertex $v$ and set $J\subseteq I$ of indices of the sets containing $v$ (with $w(v,\emptyset)=0$), the weight $w(A_I)$ is the sum over vertices of $w(v,\{i:v\in A_i\})$, and the problem is to optimise $w(A_I)$ over the tuples satisfying $\pi$. For a minimization problem, $\pi$ is monotone if supersets of valid solutions are valid (componentwise), and one minimises the weight. An $r$-shallow minor of $G$ is a graph obtained from a subgraph of $G$ by contracting pairwise vertex-disjoint subgraphs of radius at most $r$; a class has bounded expansion if there is a function $f$ such that for every $r\ge0$ every $r$-shallow minor of a graph in the class has average degree at most $f(r)$. A multiset $\mathcal{Z}$ of vertex subsets of $G$ is an $(s,\delta)$-generic cover if every set of at most $s$ vertices is contained in at least $\delta|\mathcal{Z}|$ members of $\mathcal{Z}$; its treewidth is the maximum treewidth of $G[Z]$, $Z\in\mathcal{Z}$. A class is fractionally treewidth-fragile if there is a function $f$ such that every $G$ in the class has, for all positive integers $s,o$, an $(s,1-1/o)$-generic cover of treewidth at most $f(os)$ (equivalently, in the usual formulation: there is a system of vertex sets, each vertex lying in at most a $1/o$ fraction of them, whose deletion each leaves treewidth at most $f(o)$); it is efficiently fractionally treewidth-fragile if such a cover (of polynomial size) can be found in polynomial time. A PTAS is a polynomial-time algorithm achieving approximation ratio $1+\varepsilon$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. The author proves, for monotone maximization problems (where subsets of valid solutions are valid) expressible in first-order logic, a linear-time constant-factor approximation in every class of bounded expansion and a PTAS in every efficiently fractionally treewidth-fragile class. The technique applies to minimization problems only with error bounded by a fraction of the total vertex weight rather than of the optimum, so these questions remain open for minimization; as a simplest case, it is unknown whether a PTAS exists for weighted vertex cover in fractionally treewidth-fragile graph classes.
paper_title: Approximation metatheorems for classes with bounded expansion

name: AX_fo_maximization_approximation_nowhere_dense
title: Problem 7
statement_text: Do monotone maximization problems expressible in the first order logic admit an $O(n^{o(1)})$-factor approximation for $n$-vertex graphs from nowhere-dense classes?
context_text: For a finite index set $I$, a property $\pi$ of $I$-tuples $A_I=(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of vertex subsets of $G$ is expressible in first-order logic if it is the set of tuples satisfying a fixed first-order sentence using quantification over vertices, the adjacency predicate, equality and unary predicates $X_i$ interpreted as the sets $A_i$. Given a weight assignment $w(v,J)\ge0$ for each vertex $v$ and set $J\subseteq I$ of indices of the sets containing $v$ (with $w(v,\emptyset)=0$), the weight $w(A_I)$ is the sum over vertices of $w(v,\{i:v\in A_i\})$, and the problem is to optimise $w(A_I)$ over the tuples satisfying $\pi$. Here $\pi$ is monotone if every componentwise subset of a tuple satisfying $\pi$ also satisfies $\pi$, and one maximises the weight. An $r$-shallow minor of $G$ is a graph obtained from a subgraph of $G$ by contracting pairwise vertex-disjoint subgraphs of radius at most $r$; a class has bounded expansion if there is a function $f$ such that for every $r\ge0$ every $r$-shallow minor of a graph in the class has average degree at most $f(r)$. A class is nowhere dense if for every $r\ge0$ there is $t$ such that $K_t$ is not an $r$-shallow minor of any graph in the class. The author proves that such problems admit a linear-time constant-factor approximation in every class of bounded expansion. Many results for classes with bounded expansion extend to nowhere-dense classes with constants replaced by $n^{o(1)}$ terms, but the paper's approach does not apply there because it relies on a quantifier elimination result specific to bounded-expansion classes, which leaves the question open.
paper_title: Approximation metatheorems for classes with bounded expansion

name: AX_random_embedding_expected_faces_linear
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: For every $n$-vertex simple graph $G$, the expected number of faces when selecting an orientable embedding of $G$ uniformly at random is $O(n)$.
context_text: An embedding means a $2$-cell embedding in some orientable surface, up to orientation-preserving homeomorphism fixing the graph; such embeddings of $G$ correspond bijectively to local rotations, i.e. a choice for each vertex $v$ of a cyclic permutation of the half-edges at $v$. A uniformly random embedding thus chooses independently a uniformly random rotation at every vertex; by Euler's formula, the expected number of faces determines the average genus. Stahl proved that the expected number of faces in a random embedding of any $n$-vertex graph is at most $n\log n$ (natural logarithm). The authors show that the dipole with $n$ parallel edges has exactly $H_{n-1}+\lceil n/2\rceil^{-1}$ expected faces ($H_{n-1}$ the harmonic sum), that every multistar (a loopless multigraph with a vertex incident with all edges) with $n$ nonleaf edges is within $2/(n+1)$ of this, and deduce that adding a new vertex of degree $d$ to an embedded graph creates at most $\log(d)+1$ new faces in expectation; hence $d$-regular, and more generally $d$-degenerate, $n$-vertex graphs have at most $n\log(d)$ expected faces. They also construct graph families with linearly many expected faces but found no family with superlinearly many, which led to this conjecture. For multigraphs with maximum edge-multiplicity $\mu$ they conjecture the bound $O(n\log(2\mu))$. Status note (November 2026): proved by Campion Loth and Mohar ('Expected number of faces in a random embedding of any graph is at most linear', arXiv 2202.07746, 2022), who show $\mathbb{E}[F]\le n(H_{2\mu}+1)$ for every $n$-vertex graph of maximum edge-multiplicity $\mu$, $H_k$ the $k$-th harmonic number; this confirms both this conjecture and its multigraph version.
paper_title: Random 2-cell embeddings of multistars

name: AX_c5_free_triangle_removal_exponent
title: Optimality of the $o(n^{3/2})$ bound in Corollary 1.4
statement_text: Is the exponent $3/2$ best possible in the following statement: every $n$-vertex $C_5$-free graph can be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges?
context_text: $C_k$ denotes the cycle of length $k$, and a graph is $C_5$-free if it contains no $5$-cycle as a subgraph. The Ruzsa–Szemerédi triangle removal lemma says an $n$-vertex graph with $o(n^3)$ triangles can be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^2)$ edges. Using a sparse regularity method, the authors prove a sparse $C_3$–$C_5$ removal lemma: an $n$-vertex graph with $o(n^2)$ copies of $C_4$ and $o(n^{5/2})$ copies of $C_5$ can be made $\{C_3,C_5\}$-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges. As corollaries, an $n$-vertex graph with $o(n^2)$ copies of $C_5$, and in particular every $n$-vertex $C_5$-free graph, can be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges. The authors do not know whether the exponent $3/2$ is best possible in the $C_5$-free statement. They show that the hypothesis $o(n^2)$ on the number of $C_5$'s cannot be relaxed to $o(n^{5/2})$ (there are graphs with $o(n^{2.442})$ copies of $C_5$ that cannot be made triangle-free by deleting $o(n^{3/2})$ edges). A matching lower bound would require a tripartite $C_5$-free graph between sets of order $n$ that is a union of $n^{3/2-o(1)}$ edge-disjoint triangles; their arithmetic approach would need a set $X\subseteq[n]$ of size $n^{1/2-o(1)}$ with, in particular, no nontrivial solution to $x+2y+2z=2u+3w$, which they cannot construct and which may not exist.
paper_title: The regularity method for graphs with few 4-cycles

name: AX_linear_equation_free_sets_sqrt_n
title: Improvement of the bound in Theorem 1.12
statement_text: Can the bound $o(\sqrt{n})$ for subsets of $[n]$ without a nontrivial solution to $x_1+x_2+2x_3=x_4+3x_5$ be improved to $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$?
context_text: Here $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, and a solution $(x_1,\dots,x_5)$ of $x_1+x_2+2x_3=x_4+3x_5$ is trivial if it has the form $(x,y,y,x,y)$ or $(y,x,y,x,y)$. A set without a nontrivial solution must be a Sidon set (no nontrivial solution to $x_1+x_2=x_4+x_5$, taking $x_3=x_5$), so the Sidon bound $(1+o(1))\sqrt{n}$ applies. Using a sparse removal lemma for $5$-cycles in $5$-partite graphs (an arithmetic application of their sparse regularity method, in the spirit of the deduction of Roth's theorem from the triangle removal lemma), the authors prove that every subset of $[n]$ without a nontrivial solution has size $o(\sqrt{n})$, and state as open whether this can be improved to $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.
paper_title: The regularity method for graphs with few 4-cycles

name: AX_odd_cycle_ramsey_multiplicity_exact
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: For any sufficiently large odd integer $k$, $m(C_k) = (k-1)!/2$.
context_text: The Ramsey number $r(H)$ is the minimum $n$ such that every two-coloring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $H$, and the threshold Ramsey multiplicity $m(H)$ is the minimum number of monochromatic copies of $H$ over all two-edge-colorings of $K_{r(H)}$. Harary and Prins asked for the determination of $m(P_k)$ and $m(C_k)$; for odd cycles Rosta and Surányi proved $m(C_k)\ge 2^{ck}$ and Károlyi and Rosta $m(C_k)\ge k^{ck}$, and the authors prove that $m(C_k)\ge(ck)^k$ for every odd $k$ and some constant $c>0$. For $a,b\ge1$, let $\chi(a,b)$ be the red/blue coloring of $K_{a+b}$ with vertex set $A\cup B$, $|A|=a$, $|B|=b$, where $A$ and $B$ are blue cliques and all edges between them are red. For odd $k\ge5$, $\chi(k-1,k-1)$ shows $r(C_k)>2k-2$, and $\chi(k,k-1)$ is a coloring of $K_{2k-1}=K_{r(C_k)}$ with exactly $(k-1)!/2$ monochromatic copies of $C_k$, all in the blue clique of order $k$. This shows that the $(ck)^k$ bound is tight up to the value of $c$, and the authors conjecture that this coloring is optimal for large odd $k$. Their proof goes through a stability lemma: every two-edge-coloring of $K_{2k-1}$ either has a regularity partition whose reduced graph contains a long monochromatic path, or is close to $\chi(k,k-1)$.
paper_title: Threshold Ramsey multiplicity for odd cycles

name: AX_twin_width_connected_domination_no_kernel
title: Open problem: no-kernel lower bound at twin-width 4 for Connected/Total k-Dominating Set
statement_text: Can one show that Connected $k$-Dominating Set and Total $k$-Dominating Set on graphs of twin-width at most $4$ do not admit a polynomial kernel (unless $\mathrm{coNP} \subseteq \mathrm{NP/poly}$), even when a $4$-sequence of the graph is given?
context_text: A partition sequence of an $n$-vertex graph $G$ is a sequence of partitions $\mathcal{P}_n,\dots,\mathcal{P}_1$ of $V(G)$, from all singletons to the single part $V(G)$, each obtained from the previous one by merging two parts. Two parts are homogeneous if either all or none of the pairs between them are edges. A $d$-sequence is a partition sequence in which every part of every $\mathcal{P}_i$ is non-homogeneous to at most $d$ other parts of $\mathcal{P}_i$, and the twin-width of $G$ is the least $d$ admitting a $d$-sequence. A kernel for a parameterized problem is a polynomial-time algorithm mapping each instance to an equivalent instance whose size is bounded by a function of the parameter $k$; it is polynomial if this function is polynomial. Connected $k$-Dominating Set asks for a dominating set of size at most $k$ inducing a connected subgraph, and Total $k$-Dominating Set for a set $D$ of size at most $k$ such that every vertex of $G$ (including those of $D$) has a neighbour in $D$. These problems are FPT on graphs given with an $O(1)$-sequence, by first-order model checking. The authors' main result is that, unless $\mathrm{coNP}\subseteq\mathrm{NP/poly}$, $k$-Dominating Set has no polynomial kernel on graphs of twin-width at most $4$, even when a $4$-sequence is given. Local gadget modifications of this reduction give the same lower bound for Connected $k$-Dominating Set and Total $k$-Dominating Set on graphs of bounded twin-width, but with a worse twin-width bound than $4$; more work would be needed to get it down to $4$. The paper also observes that most optimization and decision graph problems, including $k$-Dominating Set and Connected $k$-Dominating Set, are polynomial-time solvable on graphs of twin-width at most $1$.
notes: Implicit open problem stated in prose: 'More work would be necessary to get the lower bound for twin-width at most 4.' Confirmed by Table 1, which lists no 'no PK' entry for Connected k-Dominating Set at twin-width at most 4. PDF source — math notation may be partially garbled.
paper_title: Twin-width and polynomial kernels

name: AX_multiplicative_group_matrix_rank_sharp_bounds
title: Open problem: improved quantitative rank bounds
statement_text: It would be very interesting to get better lower bounds on the rank of $n\times n$ complex matrices whose non-diagonal entries lie in a multiplicative group $G\subseteq\mathbb{C}^*$ of rank at most $r$ and whose diagonal entries do not lie in $G$, even for cases where the rank of the multiplicative group is very small, for example when all non-diagonal elements are powers of two (and the diagonal elements are not).
context_text: All matrices are $n\times n$ complex matrices, and the rank of a multiplicative subgroup $G$ of $\mathbb{C}^*$ is its rank as an abelian group (the maximum number of multiplicatively independent elements; e.g. the powers of 2 form a group of rank 1). The authors' main theorem says that for all positive integers $r$ and $D$ there is $n_0(r,D)$ such that if $G$ has rank at most $r$, $M=(m_{ij})$ is an $n\times n$ matrix with $n\ge n_0$, $m_{ij}\in G$ for all $i\ne j$ and $m_{jj}\notin G$ for all $j$, then $\mathrm{rank}(M)\ge D$. The proofs rely on the Subspace Theorem of Evertse, Schlickewei and Schmidt; the first gives roughly $\log\log n\le rd^7$ for a matrix of rank $d$, and the second improves this to $\log n\le rd^8$, i.e. $d\ge(\log n/r)^{1/8}$, which the authors still consider weak. Even the special case of determining the minimum possible rank of an $n\times n$ matrix whose non-diagonal elements are powers of 2 and whose diagonal elements are not is intriguing: the minimum tends to infinity with $n$, but the lower bound is probably far from tight, and a Gram-matrix construction from the affine planes of $\mathbb{F}_3^d$ plus an extra point shows that it is at most $O(n^{1/3})$. Applications include the fact that distance sets of finite point sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$ generate multiplicative groups of high rank.

paper_title: Rank of matrices with entries from a multiplicative group

name: AX_kt_minor_free_universal_graph_separators
title: Open Problem (Section 1): Balanced Separator for $U_t$
statement_text: It is open whether the countable graph $U_t$ constructed by the authors (which contains every $K_t$-minor-free graph as an induced subgraph, has bounded minimum degree on finite subgraphs, bounded $r$-colouring numbers, and no subdivision of $K_{\aleph_0}$) satisfies (K2), that is, whether every finite $n$-vertex subgraph of $U_t$ has a balanced separator of order $O(\sqrt{n})$.
context_text: Graphs in the paper are countable (finite or countably infinite). A graph $U$ contains a class of graphs if every graph of the class is isomorphic to a subgraph of $U$. A separation of a graph $G$ is a pair $(G_1,G_2)$ of subgraphs with $G=G_1\cup G_2$, $E(G_1)\cap E(G_2)=\emptyset$ and both $V(G_1)\setminus V(G_2)$ and $V(G_2)\setminus V(G_1)$ nonempty; its order is $|V(G_1)\cap V(G_2)|$, and it is balanced if $|V(G_i)\setminus V(G_{3-i})|\le\frac23|V(G)|$ for $i=1,2$. For a total order $\preceq$ of $V(G)$, a vertex $w$ is strongly $r$-reachable from $v$ if there is a path $v=w_0,\dots,w_{r'}=w$ of length $r'\le r$ with $w\preceq v$ and $v\prec w_i$ for all internal $w_i$; the $r$-colouring number $\mathrm{col}_r(G)$ is the minimum over orders of the maximum number of vertices strongly $r$-reachable from a vertex. The authors argue that a graph containing every planar graph should share key properties of planar graphs: (K1) every finite subgraph has bounded minimum degree, (K2) every finite $n$-vertex subgraph has a balanced separator of order $O(\sqrt n)$ (as in the Lipton–Tarjan theorem), (K3) bounded $r$-colouring numbers for each $r$, (K4) no subdivision of the countably infinite complete graph $K_{\aleph_0}$. They show that any graph containing all planar graphs has $K_{\aleph_0}$ as a minor and contains subdivisions of every finite $K_t$, and construct graphs such as $\mathcal{T}_6\boxtimes P$ (strong product of a universal treewidth-6 graph with the one-way infinite path) containing all planar graphs and satisfying (K1)–(K3). For each $t\ge3$, using chordal partitions, they construct a graph $U_t$ containing every $K_t$-minor-free graph as an induced subgraph, with no $K_{\aleph_0}$ subdivision, which is $(t-1)(3t-7)$-degenerate and has $\mathrm{col}_r(U_t)\le(t-2)(t-1)(2r+1)$, so it satisfies (K1), (K3), (K4). For $t=5$ this covers planar graphs. Whether $U_t$ also satisfies (K2) is open; a weaker bound of $O(n^{3/4}\log n)$ on balanced separators follows from a result of Plotkin, Rao and Smith.
notes: Stated as 'It is open whether…' in running prose after Theorem 1.3; no labelled environment. PDF source — math notation appears readable.
paper_title: Universality in minor-closed graph classes

name: AX_bipartite_asymmetric_list_sizes_optimal
title: Problem 3
statement_text: Given $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$, what are optimal choices of $k_A \leq \Delta_A$ and $k_B \leq \Delta_B$ for which any bipartite graph $G = (V = A \cup B, E)$ with parts $A$ and $B$ having maximum degrees at most $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$, respectively, is $(k_A, k_B)$-choosable?
context_text: For a bipartite graph $G=(V=A\cup B,E)$ and positive integers $k_A,k_B$, a $(k_A,k_B)$-list-assignment gives every vertex of $A$ a list of $k_A$ colours and every vertex of $B$ a list of $k_B$ colours, and $G$ is $(k_A,k_B)$-choosable if for every such assignment there is a proper colouring giving each vertex a colour from its list (so $(k,k)$-choosability is ordinary $k$-choosability). Erdős, Rubin and Taylor showed that $K_{n,n}$ has choosability $(1+o(1))\log_2 n$, and Alon and Krivelevich conjectured in 1998 that there is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ is $k$-choosable for $k\ge C\log\Delta$; Johansson's theorem only gives $k\ge C\Delta/\log\Delta$. The problem is an asymmetric refinement of the Alon–Krivelevich conjecture, which it contains as the symmetric case; it is trivial when $k_A>\Delta_A$ or $k_B>\Delta_B$, hence the restriction $k_A\le\Delta_A$, $k_B\le\Delta_B$. The authors prove general sufficient conditions that are nearly sharp in very asymmetric cases, for instance that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and $\Delta$ large, every bipartite graph with maximum degree at most $\Delta$ is $((1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log_4\Delta,2)$- and $((1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta,\log\Delta)$-choosable. They also derive necessary conditions from the complete bipartite case via a connection with the extremal size of approximate Steiner systems, and show that the complete case is not always exactly extremal.
notes: PDF source — math notation verified readable.
paper_title: Asymmetric list sizes in bipartite graphs

name: AX_bipartite_asymmetric_list_sizes_krivelevich_alon
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text:
Let the positive integers $\Delta_A, \Delta_B, k_A, k_B$ satisfy one of the following.
(i) Given $\varepsilon > 0$, we have $\Delta_A, \Delta_B \geq \Delta_0$ for some $\Delta_0 = \Delta_0(\varepsilon)$, and $k_A \geq \Delta_A^\varepsilon$ and $k_B \geq \Delta_B^\varepsilon$.
(ii) For some absolute constant $C > 1$, $k_A \geq C \log \Delta_B$ and $k_B \geq C \log \Delta_A$.
(iii) $\Delta_A = \Delta_B = \Delta$, and, for some absolute constant $C > 0$, $k_B \geq C(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{1/k_A} \log\Delta$ or $k_A \geq C(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{1/k_B} \log\Delta$.
Then any bipartite graph $G = (V = A \cup B, E)$ with parts $A$ and $B$ having maximum degrees at most $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$, respectively, is $(k_A, k_B)$-choosable.
context_text: For a bipartite graph $G=(V=A\cup B,E)$ and positive integers $k_A,k_B$, a $(k_A,k_B)$-list-assignment gives every vertex of $A$ a list of $k_A$ colours and every vertex of $B$ a list of $k_B$ colours, and $G$ is $(k_A,k_B)$-choosable if for every such assignment there is a proper colouring giving each vertex a colour from its list (so $(k,k)$-choosability is ordinary $k$-choosability). Erdős, Rubin and Taylor showed that $K_{n,n}$ has choosability $(1+o(1))\log_2 n$, and Alon and Krivelevich conjectured in 1998 that there is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ is $k$-choosable for $k\ge C\log\Delta$; Johansson's theorem only gives $k\ge C\Delta/\log\Delta$. The authors propose these three concrete asymmetric analogues of the Alon–Krivelevich conjecture, motivated by the asymptotic behaviour of $(k_A,k_B)$-choosability of complete bipartite graphs, for which they prove that the conjecture holds. Condition (i) is weaker than the Alon–Krivelevich conjecture and conditions (ii) and (iii) are stronger; if true they would be close to best possible (for (i), no bound $k\ge f(\Delta)$ with $f(x)=O(\log x)$ can work when $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$ are far apart). They show that case (i) reduces to its symmetric form $\Delta_A=\Delta_B$, since every bipartite graph with $\Delta_B>\Delta_A^{2/\varepsilon}$ and $\Delta_A>(4/\varepsilon)^{1/\varepsilon}$ is $(\Delta_A^\varepsilon,\Delta_B^\varepsilon)$-choosable. Towards (iii) they prove that for $\Delta_A=\Delta_B=\Delta$ large, every such graph is $((1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log_4\Delta,2)$- and $((1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta,\log\Delta)$-choosable.
notes: PDF source — math notation verified readable. Three-part conjecture; each part is a separate asymmetric generalisation of Conjecture 2.
paper_title: Asymmetric list sizes in bipartite graphs

name: AX_triangle_free_planar_3_coloring_count
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: There exists a constant $c > 1$ such that every $n$-vertex triangle-free planar graph has at least $c^{n^{\log_{9/2} 3}}$ distinct proper 3-colorings.
context_text: By Grötzsch's theorem every triangle-free planar graph is 3-colorable. Thomassen conjectured that such graphs have exponentially many proper 3-colorings, and proved that every $n$-vertex triangle-free planar graph has at least $c^{n^{1/12}}$ of them for some constant $c>1$; he later disproved his exponential conjecture by exhibiting, for infinitely many $n$, $n$-vertex triangle-free planar graphs with at most $2^{15n/\log_2 n}$ 3-colorings. The authors improve this construction: for infinitely many $n$ there is an $n$-vertex triangle-free planar graph with at most $64^{n^{\log_{9/2} 3}}<64^{n^{0.731}}$ proper 3-colorings. Since it does not seem possible to improve the exponent $\log_{9/2}3\approx 0.731$ with the same method, they conjecture that this exponent is optimal, which is the matching lower bound stated here.
notes: PDF source — the exponent 'nlog9/23' in the raw extraction is read as $n^{\log_{9/2} 3}$, consistent with the stated numerical approximation $n^{0.731}$ and the analytic derivation in the proof.
paper_title: Triangle-free planar graphs with at most $64^{n^{0.731}}$ 3-colorings

name: AX_irregular_spanning_subgraph_regular_graphs
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: Every $d$-regular graph $G$ on $n$ vertices contains a spanning subgraph $H$ so that for every $k$, $0 \leq k \leq d$, $\left|m(H, k) - \frac{n}{d+1}\right| \leq 2$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. For a graph $H$ and an integer $k\ge0$, $m(H,k)$ denotes the number of vertices of degree $k$ in $H$, and $m(H)=\max_k m(H,k)$ is the maximum number of vertices of the same degree; a small value of $m(H)$ measures the irregularity of $H$ (every graph with at least two vertices has $m(H)\ge2$). If $G$ is $d$-regular on $n$ vertices, every spanning subgraph has degrees in $\{0,\dots,d\}$, so $m(H)\ge\frac{n}{d+1}$ by pigeonhole; the conjectures say that every graph has a spanning subgraph nearly as irregular as its degrees permit. If true, both conjectures (this one and its companion for minimum degree, resp. for $d$-regular graphs) are tight: the disjoint union of two $4$-cycles is an example, and an extra additive $1$ is needed even when $\frac{n}{d+1}$ is an integer, e.g. when $\lfloor\frac{d+1}{2}\rfloor\frac{n}{d+1}$ is odd, by parity of the number of odd-degree vertices. The authors could not prove it, but show an asymptotic version: if $d^3\log n=o(n)$, every $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices has a spanning subgraph $H$ with $m(H,k)=(1+o(1))\frac{n}{d+1}$ for all $0\le k\le d$; in general they get a spanning subgraph with $m(H)\le8\frac nd+2$.
notes: Source is PDF extraction; mathematical notation appears clean for this statement.
paper_title: Irregular Subgraphs

name: AX_irregular_spanning_subgraph_min_degree
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: Every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta$ contains a spanning subgraph $H$ satisfying $m(H) \leq \frac{n}{\delta+1} + 2$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. For a graph $H$ and an integer $k\ge0$, $m(H,k)$ denotes the number of vertices of degree $k$ in $H$, and $m(H)=\max_k m(H,k)$ is the maximum number of vertices of the same degree; a small value of $m(H)$ measures the irregularity of $H$ (every graph with at least two vertices has $m(H)\ge2$). If $G$ is $d$-regular on $n$ vertices, every spanning subgraph has degrees in $\{0,\dots,d\}$, so $m(H)\ge\frac{n}{d+1}$ by pigeonhole; the conjectures say that every graph has a spanning subgraph nearly as irregular as its degrees permit. If true, both conjectures (this one and its companion for minimum degree, resp. for $d$-regular graphs) are tight: the disjoint union of two $4$-cycles is an example, and an extra additive $1$ is needed even when $\frac{n}{d+1}$ is an integer, e.g. when $\lfloor\frac{d+1}{2}\rfloor\frac{n}{d+1}$ is odd, by parity of the number of odd-degree vertices. The authors could not prove it, but show that every graph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta$ has a spanning subgraph $H$ with $m(H)\le(1+o(1))\lceil\frac{n}{\delta+1}\rceil+2$ (with $o(1)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$), and with $m(H)\le\lceil\frac{n}{\delta+1}\rceil+2$ if $\delta^{1.24}\ge n$ and $n$ is large; in general they get $m(H)\le16\frac{n}{\delta}+4$. The companion conjecture for $d$-regular graphs asks for a spanning $H$ with $|m(H,k)-\frac{n}{d+1}|\le2$ for every $0\le k\le d$.
notes: Source is PDF extraction; mathematical notation appears clean for this statement.
paper_title: Irregular Subgraphs

name: AX_poly_chi_bounded_forests_known_complete
title: Informal remark on completeness of known forests satisfying Esperet's conjecture
statement_text: As far as we know (although it seems unlikely), the forests $H$ that are the disjoint union of a double star and a star-forest might be all the forests $H$ that satisfy Esperet's conjecture, i.e. for which there is a polynomial $f_H$ such that $\chi(G)\le f_H(\omega(G))$ for every $H$-free graph $G$.
context_text: A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A star is a tree with one vertex adjacent to all others, a star-forest is a forest whose components are stars, and a double star is a tree with exactly two internal (non-leaf) vertices, the most general tree with no five-vertex path. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture asserts that for every forest $H$ the class of $H$-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded ($\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for some function $f$); Esperet conjectured that every $\chi$-bounded class is polynomially $\chi$-bounded. For forests, the polynomial version is known for far fewer $H$; for instance it is open for the path $P_5$ (which would imply the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for $P_5$) and for two disjoint copies of $P_4$. Previously known cases were disjoint unions of copies of $K_2$ (Wagon), $H'$ plus a disjoint $K_2$ when $H'$ satisfies it (Schiermeyer), and a star with one edge subdivided once (Liu, Schroeder, Wang and Yu). The authors prove that adding a disjoint star to a forest satisfying the polynomial bound preserves it, and with their companion result for double stars deduce that every disjoint union of a double star and a star-forest satisfies it; the remark says these might be all such forests. If $\omega(G)$ is replaced by the largest $t$ with $K_{t,t}$ as a subgraph, all forests satisfy the polynomial bound.
notes: Authors signal explicit scepticism ('although it seems unlikely'), so this is a note on the limits of current knowledge rather than a firm conjecture.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number. II. Excluding a star-forest

name: AX_hat_guessing_degenerate_bounded
title: Informal Belief on Degeneracy Bound for Hat Guessing Number
statement_text: It seems plausible that there exists a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $d$-degenerate graph $G$, $\mathrm{HG}(G) \leq f(d)$.
context_text: In the hat guessing game on a simple graph $G$, each vertex is a player who receives a hat of one of $q$ colours, chosen arbitrarily; each player sees only the hat colours of its neighbours, and after agreeing on a deterministic strategy, all players simultaneously guess their own colour, without communication. The players win if at least one guesses correctly. The hat guessing number $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is the largest $q$ for which the players have a winning strategy. A graph is $d$-degenerate if every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $d$. The question whether such an $f$ exists was raised by Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Shangguan and Tamo, and the authors find it plausible. It would imply that the hat guessing number of planar graphs (which are $5$-degenerate) is bounded by an absolute constant, and more generally that $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is bounded by a function of the Hadwiger number (the order of the largest clique minor), since graphs with Hadwiger number $k$ are $O(k\sqrt{\log k})$-degenerate. It had been conjectured that planar graphs have hat guessing number at most $4$ and that $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is at most the Hadwiger number; the authors refute both with a planar graph of hat guessing number $12$ (a later construction reaches $14$), and note that the hat guessing number can be doubly exponential in the Hadwiger number.
paper_title: On the Hat Guessing Number of Graphs

name: AX_hat_guessing_random_graph_sublinear
title: Question on Typical Hat Guessing Number of G(n,1/2)
statement_text: What is the typical asymptotic behavior of the hat guessing number of the random graph $G(n,1/2)$? In particular, is $\mathrm{HG}(G(n,1/2))$ equal to $o(n)$ with high probability?
context_text: In the hat guessing game on a simple graph $G$, each vertex is a player who receives a hat of one of $q$ colours, chosen arbitrarily; each player sees only the hat colours of its neighbours, and after agreeing on a deterministic strategy, all players simultaneously guess their own colour, without communication. The players win if at least one guesses correctly. The hat guessing number $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is the largest $q$ for which the players have a winning strategy. $G(n,1/2)$ is the binomial random graph on $n$ vertices where each edge is present independently with probability $1/2$. It was known that with high probability $(2-o(1))\log_2 n\le\mathrm{HG}(G(n,1/2))\le n-(1+o(1))\log_2 n$; the authors improve the lower bound to $n^{1-o(1)}$ with high probability, leaving the true order of growth open.
paper_title: On the Hat Guessing Number of Graphs

name: AX_hat_guessing_universal_vertex_addition
title: Problem on Hat Guessing Number After Adding a Universal Vertex
statement_text: Establish an upper bound for $\mathrm{HG}(G')$ as a function of $\mathrm{HG}(G)$, where $G'$ is obtained from $G$ by adding a single vertex connected to all vertices of $G$, or show that no such function exists.
context_text: In the hat guessing game on a simple graph $G$, each vertex is a player who receives a hat of one of $q$ colours, chosen arbitrarily; each player sees only the hat colours of its neighbours, and after agreeing on a deterministic strategy, all players simultaneously guess their own colour, without communication. The players win if at least one guesses correctly. The hat guessing number $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is the largest $q$ for which the players have a winning strategy. Let $G'$ be obtained from $G$ by adding one vertex adjacent to all vertices of $G$. Using graphs $G_d(N)$ of He and Li, each of which has a unique vertex adjacent to all others and whose removal leaves disjoint copies of $G_{d-1}(N)$, the authors observe that for arbitrarily large $q=\mathrm{HG}(G)$ one can have $\mathrm{HG}(G')=q^2+q$, so adding a universal vertex can increase the hat guessing number to more than $q^2$. The question is whether $\mathrm{HG}(G')$ is bounded by some function of $\mathrm{HG}(G)$.
paper_title: On the Hat Guessing Number of Graphs

name: AX_divisible_subdivision_clique_minor_f_growth
title: Open Problem (asymptotic behavior of f(H,q))
statement_text: Determine or estimate the asymptotic behavior of the best possible bound for $f(H, q)$ such that every $K_f$-minor contains a subdivision of $H$ in which every edge is replaced by a path whose length is divisible by $q$.
context_text: Following the paper, a $K_f$-minor is a graph $G$ whose vertex set can be partitioned into $f$ sets (supernodes), each inducing a connected subgraph, with at least one edge between any two supernodes (equivalently for the questions below, a graph containing $K_f$ as a minor). The length of a path or cycle is its number of edges. The authors prove that for every graph $H$ of maximum degree at most $3$ and every positive integer $q$ there is a finite $f=f(H,q)$ such that every $K_f$-minor contains a subdivision of $H$ in which every edge is replaced by a path of length divisible by $q$. This applies to very sparse graphs, since there are $K_f$-minors of average degree arbitrarily close to $2$ in every subgraph, and to (weakly) expanding graphs, which have large clique minors. The degree condition is necessary (there are $K_f$-minors of maximum degree $3$ in which every path between two degree-$3$ vertices has length divisible by $q$), and residue $0$ cannot be replaced by another residue. The proof makes essentially no attempt to optimise $f(H,q)$; using Ramsey graphs for subdivisions as a seed gives some improvement, but the bound is still huge and surely far from optimal. For cycles the authors get a nearly tight bound $O(q\log q)$ (and $<4q$ for prime $q$).
notes: Stated twice: once after the remark following Theorem 1 ('the problem of determining its asymptotic behavior remains open') and once in the concluding remarks. PDF source — math notation appears clean.
paper_title: Divisible subdivisions

name: AX_divisible_subdivision_g_q_linear
title: Informal Conjecture (linearity of g(q))
statement_text: It seems plausible to believe that the lemma stating that every complete digraph on $\lceil 2q\ln q\rceil$ vertices with edge weights in $\mathbb{Z}_q$ contains a directed cycle of total weight divisible by $q$ is not tight, and that the function $g(q)$ (the smallest $g$ such that every $K_g$-minor contains a cycle of length divisible by $q$) is linear in $q$ for any integer $q$.
context_text: Following the paper, a $K_f$-minor is a graph $G$ whose vertex set can be partitioned into $f$ sets (supernodes), each inducing a connected subgraph, with at least one edge between any two supernodes (equivalently for the questions below, a graph containing $K_f$ as a minor). The length of a path or cycle is its number of edges. The authors prove that for every positive integer $q$ there is $g=g(q)=O(q\log q)$ such that every $K_g$-minor contains a cycle of length divisible by $q$, and that $g(q)<4q$ when $q$ is prime; together with the fact that expanders contain large clique minors, this settles a problem of Friedman and Krivelevich on cycle lengths in expanders. The proof reduces to a zero-sum problem: every complete digraph on $\lceil 2q\ln q\rceil$ vertices whose edges are weighted by elements of $\mathbb{Z}_q$ contains a directed cycle of total weight divisible by $q$ (shown with a random labelling and the union bound), and for prime $q$ already $2q-1$ vertices suffice, which gives the linear bound for primes. Linearity of $g(q)$ for every $q$ is suggested in the concluding remarks.
notes: Expressed via 'It seems plausible to believe'; clearly conjectural but no labelled environment. PDF source — math notation appears clean.
paper_title: Divisible subdivisions

name: AX_runsort_permuton_horizontal_uniformity_direct
title: Direct Proof of Horizontal Uniformity
statement_text: The pointwise density of $R$ in $C^+ = \{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2 : x < ye^{1-y}\}$ depends only on the vertical coordinate $y$ (``horizontal uniformity''). The authors state they do not know how to establish this directly, that is, without recourse to the explicit characterization of $R$.
context_text: An ascending run of a permutation is a maximal consecutive increasing subsequence (the runs of $351476298$ are $35,147,6,29,8$), and $\mathsf{runsort}(\pi)$ is the permutation obtained by sorting the runs of $\pi$ so that their smallest entries appear in increasing order (e.g. $\mathsf{runsort}(351476298)=147293568$). A permuton is a probability measure on $[0,1]^2$ with uniform marginals; a permutation $\pi\in S_n$ gives the permuton $\gamma_\pi$ with density $n$ on each square $[(i-1)/n,i/n)\times[(\pi_i-1)/n,\pi_i/n)$, and permutons are compared with the distance $d_\square(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)=\sup_B|\gamma_1(B)-\gamma_2(B)|$ over axis-parallel rectangles $B$. Answering a question of Alexandersson and Nabawanda, the authors prove that for $\pi$ uniform in $S_n$, $\gamma_{\mathsf{runsort}(\pi)}$ converges to the runsort permuton $\mathbf{R}$ defined by $\mathbf{R}(B)=\int_{B\cap\mathcal{C}^+}e^{y-1}\,dx\,dy+\int_{B\cap\mathcal{C}}(1-y)\,dy$, where $\mathcal{C}=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x=ye^{1-y}\}$ and $\mathcal{C}^+=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x<ye^{1-y}\}$. The singular part on the curve $\mathcal{C}$ comes from the first entries of the runs (half of the mass) and the absolutely continuous part on $\mathcal{C}^+$ from the remaining entries. The surprising fact that this density $e^{y-1}$ does not depend on $x$ is obtained only from the explicit computation; the authors say it is not combinatorially obvious and that they do not know a direct proof. In a generalized setting (sorting $\mathcal{F}$-runs defined by a prefix-closed family $\mathcal{F}$ of permutations) they also suggest finding conditions on $\mathcal{F}$ that guarantee some form of horizontal uniformity. This is a problem about permutations rather than graphs.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled. The open problem is implicit: find a direct combinatorial argument establishing horizontal uniformity without using the explicit formula for $R$. Section 6 (generalizations) is referenced in the introduction but not included in the extracted text, so additional items from that section may be missing.
paper_title: The runsort permuton

name: AX_friends_strangers_random_connectivity_threshold
title: Informal Conjecture (§1.2, Theorem 1.1 remarks)
statement_text: The threshold for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to be connected when $X, Y$ are independent random graphs in $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is determined by the isolated-vertex threshold: ``it seems that (as in the usual case of a binomial random graph) this local obstruction to connectedness tells essentially the whole story.'' Formally (the authors' conjecture): there exists an absolute constant $C>0$ such that if $p\ge Cn^{-1/2}$, then $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ is connected with high probability.
context_text: For simple graphs $X,Y$ on $n$ vertices, the friends-and-strangers graph $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has as vertices all bijections $\sigma:V(X)\to V(Y)$, two bijections being adjacent if one is obtained from the other by a friendly swap: exchanging the images of the endpoints of an edge $\{a,b\}$ of $X$ such that $\{\sigma(a),\sigma(b)\}$ is an edge of $Y$ (people placed on the vertices of $X$, two people may swap positions if they stand on adjacent vertices and are friends in $Y$). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph, $\mathcal{G}(K_{r,r},p)$ the random subgraph of $K_{r,r}$ keeping each edge with probability $p$, and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1. The authors prove that if $p\le(2^{-1/2}-\varepsilon)n^{-1/2}$ then $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ is disconnected with high probability, because it has isolated vertices, while if $p\ge\exp(2(\log n)^{2/3})n^{-1/2}$ it is connected with high probability; so the threshold is $n^{-1/2+o(1)}$. They conjecture that the gap is an artefact of the proof, stating formally in their concluding section that $p\ge Cn^{-1/2}$ suffices for some constant $C$, and also ask the finer hitting-time question: in the random graph process on pairs $(X_t,Y_t)$, is the first time $t_{\mathrm{conn}}$ at which $\mathrm{FS}(X_t,Y_t)$ is connected equal to (or $(1+o(1))$ times, or $O$ of) the first time $t_{\mathrm{iso}}$ at which it has no isolated vertices? They prove $t_{\mathrm{conn}}\le t_{\mathrm{iso}}\cdot n^{o(1)}$ w.h.p.

name: AX_friends_strangers_isolated_vertex_cutoff_coincide
title: Open Question (§1.2, Theorem 1.4 remarks)
statement_text: Do the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to avoid isolated vertices and the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to have exactly 2 connected components coincide when $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$? That is, is $d_{r,r} = \lceil (3r+1)/4 \rceil$ for all $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$?
context_text: For simple graphs $X,Y$ on $n$ vertices, the friends-and-strangers graph $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has as vertices all bijections $\sigma:V(X)\to V(Y)$, two bijections being adjacent if one is obtained from the other by a friendly swap: exchanging the images of the endpoints of an edge $\{a,b\}$ of $X$ such that $\{\sigma(a),\sigma(b)\}$ is an edge of $Y$ (people placed on the vertices of $X$, two people may swap positions if they stand on adjacent vertices and are friends in $Y$). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph, $\mathcal{G}(K_{r,r},p)$ the random subgraph of $K_{r,r}$ keeping each edge with probability $p$, and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1. If $X$ and $Y$ are bipartite on $n\ge3$ vertices, a parity argument (relating the sign of $\sigma^{-1}\tau$ to how the bipartitions are matched) shows that $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has at least 2 connected components, and $\mathrm{FS}(K_{r,r},K_{r,r})$ has exactly 2. For $r\ge2$, $d_{r,r}$ is the smallest nonnegative integer such that whenever $X,Y$ are subgraphs of $K_{r,r}$ (on its full vertex set) with minimum degrees $\delta(X),\delta(Y)\ge d_{r,r}$, $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has exactly 2 connected components. The authors prove $\lceil(3r+1)/4\rceil\le d_{r,r}\le\lceil(3r+2)/4\rceil$; the bounds coincide unless $r\equiv1\pmod4$. The lower bound is the minimum-degree cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ to have no isolated vertices; unlike the non-bipartite case (where the analogous $d_n$ satisfies $\frac35n-2\le d_n\le\frac9{14}n+2$ while isolated vertices already disappear at minimum degree $n/2$), this cutoff is essentially the connectivity cutoff, and in their concluding section the authors conjecture $d_{r,r}=\lceil(3r+1)/4\rceil$.

paper_title: Typical and Extremal Aspects of Friends-and-Strangers Graphs

name: AX_c4_free_counting_lemma_characterization
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: For which graphs $F$ is there an $F$-counting lemma in $C_4$-free graphs?
context_text: For a graph $F$, the authors make the notion of an $F$-counting lemma in $C_4$-free graphs precise as follows: $F$ is countable if for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that whenever $G$ is an $n$-vertex $C_4$-free graph on vertex set $V$ and $H\in[0,1]^{V\times V}$ is a symmetric matrix (an edge-weighted graph) with $\left|\frac{e_G(A,B)}{n^{3/2}}-\frac{e_H(A,B)}{n^2}\right|\le\delta$ for all $A,B\subseteq V$ (where $e_G(A,B)$ counts pairs $(x,y)\in A\times B$ with $xy\in E(G)$ and $e_H(A,B)=\sum_{x\in A,y\in B}H(x,y)$), then for every family $(A_v)_{v\in V(F)}$ of subsets of $V$ one has $\frac{\hom_{\mathbf{A}}(F,G)}{n^{|V(F)|-|E(F)|/2}}\ge\frac{\hom_{\mathbf{A}}(F,H)}{n^{|V(F)|}}-\epsilon$, where $\hom_{\mathbf{A}}(F,G)$ is the number of homomorphisms of $F$ to $G$ mapping each $v$ into $A_v$ and $\hom_{\mathbf{A}}(F,H)=\sum_{x_v\in A_v}\prod_{uv\in E(F)}H(x_u,x_v)$. This is a one-sided (lower-bound) sparse counting lemma, the scaling coming from the fact that $C_4$-free graphs have at most $(1/2+o(1))n^{3/2}$ edges; countability of $F$ yields an $F$-removal lemma in $C_4$-free graphs. In earlier work the authors proved that $C_5$ is countable. Here they show that every countable graph has girth at least $5$ (using the polarity graph), that trees and all cycles of length at least $5$ are countable, that adding a pendant edge preserves countability, and they give a recursive 'islands and bridges' construction producing many countable graphs of girth at least $5$ (e.g. chains of $5$-cycles and subdivisions of cliques), but they are far from a classification. They also note that it seems necessary that every subgraph $F'$ of $F$ satisfies $|E(F')|\le2|V(F')|-4$, which would imply that $d$-regular countable graphs have $d\le3$.
notes: Labeled '(Main question, informal)' in the paper; the informal qualifier refers to the prose level of precision, not the environment type.
paper_title: Which graphs can be counted in $C_4$-free graphs?

name: AX_zombie_number_leaf_attachment_invariance
title: Question 4.1
statement_text: For every graph $G$, and for a graph $G'$ obtained from $G$ by successively adding vertices of degree 1, does it always hold that $z(G') = z(G)$?
context_text: Graphs are connected. In the game of (deterministic) Zombies and Survivors, a variant of Cops and Robber, zombies play the role of cops and a single survivor the role of the robber; in each round every zombie must move along some shortest path (geodesic) towards the survivor (when several geodesics exist, the zombies may choose which one), and the zombies win if one of them moves onto the survivor's vertex. The zombie number $z(G)$ is the minimum number of zombies that can be placed in $G$ so as to ensure that the survivor is eventually captured, and the cop number $c(G)$ is the analogous minimum for cops (which can move freely to a neighbour or stay); clearly $c(G)\le z(G)$. The paper proves $z(G\,\square\,H)\le z(G)+z(H)$ for the Cartesian product, answering a question of Fitzpatrick et al., and gives graphs with cop number 2 and arbitrarily large zombie number. The authors interpret the question as asking whether zombies could gain an advantage by waiting individually for some pre-announced time at the start of the game before following the standard rules. The authors pose it, together with a question on subdivisions, as touching on whether, when the survivor plays to survive as long as possible, all $z(G)$ zombies are close to it at the time of capture.
paper_title: A note on deterministic zombies

name: AX_zombie_number_subdivision_increase
title: Question 4.2
statement_text: For any graph $G$, is there an integer $k$ such that, for $G'_k$ the graph obtained from $G$ by subdividing all edges $k$ times then adding the original edges, $z(G'_k) \geq z(G) + 1$?
context_text: Graphs are connected. In the game of (deterministic) Zombies and Survivors, a variant of Cops and Robber, zombies play the role of cops and a single survivor the role of the robber; in each round every zombie must move along some shortest path (geodesic) towards the survivor (when several geodesics exist, the zombies may choose which one), and the zombies win if one of them moves onto the survivor's vertex. The zombie number $z(G)$ is the minimum number of zombies that can be placed in $G$ so as to ensure that the survivor is eventually captured, and the cop number $c(G)$ is the analogous minimum for cops (which can move freely to a neighbour or stay); clearly $c(G)\le z(G)$. The paper proves $z(G\,\square\,H)\le z(G)+z(H)$ for the Cartesian product, answering a question of Fitzpatrick et al., and gives graphs with cop number 2 and arbitrarily large zombie number. In $G'_k$ each edge $uv$ of $G$ is kept and also replaced by a path from $u$ to $v$ with $k$ new internal vertices, so $G$ is an isometric subgraph of $G'_k$ and the original vertices keep their distances. The authors remark that, as far as they can tell, $k=5$ might be a valid answer for every graph $G$.

The follow-up remark 'it could be that 5 is a valid answer to Question 4.2 in any graph' suggests the question may additionally seek a universal constant $k$.

name: AX_convex_unit_distance_realization_gk
title: Open Question on Convex Unit Distance Realization of Graphs $G_k$
statement_text: Can the graphs $G_k$ arising from the authors' construction of convex polygons $P_k,Q_k$ with $\mathrm{ci}(P_k+Q_k)\ge(k+2)2^{k-1}$ be realized as convex unit distance graphs?
context_text: A finite planar point set is convexly independent if it is the vertex set of a convex polygon, and $\mathrm{ci}(X)$ is the largest size of a convexly independent subset of $X$; $P+Q=\{p+q:p\in P,q\in Q\}$ is the Minkowski sum. Tiwary proved $\mathrm{ci}(P+Q)=O((n+m)\log(n+m))$ for a convex $n$-gon $P$ and a convex $m$-gon $Q$, and the authors show this is sharp: they construct convexly independent sets $P_k,Q_k$ of size $2^k$ with $\mathrm{ci}(P_k+Q_k)\ge(k+2)2^{k-1}$. The graph $G_k=(U_k\sqcup V_k,E_k)$ is the bipartite graph of this construction: its vertices are the $2^{k+1}$ points of $P_k$ and $Q_k$ (each side in convex position), and its $(k+2)2^{k-1}$ edges are the pairs $(p,q)\in P_k\times Q_k$ whose midpoints $(p+q)/2$ form the convexly independent set. A convex unit distance graph is the graph of unit-distance pairs among the vertices of a convex polygon; the Erdős–Moser problem asks for the maximum number of unit distances in a convex $n$-gon, for which the best upper bound is $O(n\log n)$ (Füredi, Aggarwal). The authors observe that if $G_k$ could be embedded with $U_k,V_k$ as south-east chains in the quadrant $\{x_1\ge0,x_2\le0\}$ and all edge midpoints on the unit circle, one would get convex $2^{k+1}$-gons with $\Theta(k2^k)$ unit diagonals, i.e. a matching $\Theta(n\log n)$ lower bound for the convex unit distance problem. Such an embedding cannot be excluded by the known list of forbidden matrices of Aggarwal, none of which appears in $G_k$; if $G_k$ is not realizable, it would be interesting to find a new forbidden pattern in $G_k$. The authors could neither construct such embeddings nor find such a pattern. This is a question of discrete geometry.
notes: Stated in running prose without a labelled environment; a secondary conditional direction (finding forbidden patterns in $G_k$) is folded into the same passage.
paper_title: Convexly independent subsets of Minkowski sums of convex polygons

name: AX_forest_of_lanterns_pervasive
title: Conjecture: every forest of lanterns is pervasive
statement_text: Every forest of lanterns $H$ is pervasive; that is, for all $\nu, \ell \geq 0$ there exists $c$ such that every graph $G$ with $\omega(G) \leq \nu$ and $\chi(G) > c$ contains an induced subgraph isomorphic to an $(\geq \ell)$-subdivision of $H$.
context_text: A subdivision of $H$ is obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path joining $u,v$, these paths being internally disjoint; it is an $(\geq \ell)$-subdivision if each of these paths has at least $\ell+1$ edges. $\omega(G)$ is the clique number. A graph $H$ is pervasive in an ideal $\mathcal{C}$ (a class closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs) if for all $\nu,\ell\geq 0$ there is $c$ such that every $G\in\mathcal{C}$ with $\omega(G)\le\nu$ and $\chi(G)>c$ contains an induced $(\geq\ell)$-subdivision of $H$; pervasive means pervasive in the class of all graphs. Let $T$ be a tree with at least two vertices and add a new vertex $v$ adjacent to every leaf of $T$ (and possibly to some other vertices of $T$): the result is a lantern with pivot $v$ (the one- and two-vertex complete graphs also count as lanterns). A tree of lanterns is built by starting from a lantern and repeatedly taking a new lantern and identifying its pivot with some vertex of what has been built so far; a forest of lanterns is a graph whose components are trees of lanterns. All forests and all cycles are known to be pervasive. Combining results of Chalopin, Esperet, Li and Ossona de Mendez on the Burling (Pawlik et al.) graphs, which are triangle-free string graphs of unbounded chromatic number, a graph $H$ has a $(\geq 2)$-subdivision appearing as an induced subgraph in some Burling graph if and only if $H$ is a forest of lanterns; hence every pervasive graph is a forest of lanterns, and the authors suggest that perhaps the converse is true. An ideal is $\rho$-controlled if there is a nondecreasing $\phi$ such that $\chi(H)\le\phi(\chi^{\rho}(H))$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of a graph in the ideal, where $\chi^\rho(H)$ is the maximum chromatic number of a ball of radius $\rho$ in $H$. The paper proves that every forest of lanterns is pervasive in every $\rho$-controlled ideal ($\rho\geq 2$), and in the class of string graphs, but the question for the ideal of all graphs remains open.
notes: Stated as 'perhaps the converse is true' in the introduction and as an explicitly open problem in the abstract; no formal conjecture environment.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. V. Chandeliers and strings

name: AX_crossing_critical_max_degree_optimal_bounds
title: Optimal degree bounds $D_c$ for small $c$
statement_text: Determine the optimal values of $D_c$ for each $c \in \{2, 3, \ldots, 12\}$, where $D_c$ is the smallest integer such that every $c$-crossing-critical graph has maximum degree at most $D_c$.
context_text: Graphs are multigraphs by default (parallel edges allowed). The crossing number $\operatorname{cr}(G)$ is the minimum number of crossings in a drawing of $G$ in the plane. For a positive integer $c$, a graph is $c$-crossing-critical if $\operatorname{cr}(G)\ge c$ but every proper subgraph has crossing number less than $c$. Richter conjectured in 2003 that for every $c$ the maximum degree of $c$-crossing-critical graphs is bounded; Dvořák and Mohar disproved this for every $c\ge171$, non-constructively. The authors settle the question for all $c$: using Hliněný's bounded path-width result and the structural classification of large $c$-crossing-critical graphs by Dvořák, Hliněný and Mohar, they prove that there is an integer $D$ such that every $c$-crossing-critical graph with $c\le12$ has maximum degree at most $D$, while for every $c\ge13$ they construct 3-connected $c$-crossing-critical graphs with arbitrarily many vertices of arbitrarily large degree. Thus finite optimal bounds $D_c$ exist for $c\le 12$, but the proof is asymptotic and gives no explicit values. Known: $D_1=4$ (1-crossing-critical graphs are the subdivisions of $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$), $D_2\ge8$, and the optimal $D_2$ should be within reach using the characterization of 2-crossing-critical graphs by Bokal, Oporowski, Richter and Salazar; the remaining values are left to future investigations (the authors list this among their final open problems, for each $c\le12$).
notes: Stated as a future-work direction rather than a formally labelled open problem; Section 7 (open problems) was not included in the provided text excerpt.
paper_title: Bounded maximum degree conjecture holds precisely for $c$-crossing-critical graphs with $c \leq 12$

name: AX_treewidth_fragile_weighted_vertex_cover_ptas
title: Open Problem: PTAS for weighted minimization problems in fractionally treewidth-fragile classes
statement_text: For the minimization problems, we do not know whether fractional treewidth-fragility is sufficient even for the distance-1 problems. In particular, consider the Minimum Vertex Cover problem in fractionally treewidth-fragile graphs, or more generally in hereditary classes with sublinear separators: while the unweighted version can be dealt with by the local search method, we do not know whether there exists a PTAS for the weighted version of this problem.
context_text: A PTAS is an algorithm that, for each fixed $k$, returns in polynomial time a solution within a factor $1\pm1/k$ of the optimum. A set $S$ is a balanced separator of $G$ if every component of $G\setminus S$ has at most $|V(G)|/2$ vertices; a hereditary class has sublinear separators if, for some $c<1$, every graph in it has a balanced separator of size $O(|V(G)|^c)$ (e.g. planar graphs, proper minor-closed classes, many geometric classes). A class $\mathcal{G}$ is efficiently fractionally treewidth-fragile if there are a function $f$ and a polynomial-time algorithm that, given $k$ and $G\in\mathcal{G}$, returns sets $X_1,\dots,X_m\subseteq V(G)$ such that each vertex lies in at most $m/k$ of them, together with tree decompositions of each $G\setminus X_i$ of width at most $f(k)$; this holds for proper minor-closed classes, classes with sublinear separators and bounded maximum degree, and many geometric classes, and Dvořák conjectured that every hereditary class with sublinear separators is fractionally treewidth-fragile. Distance-1 problems are those where admissibility of a vertex set depends only on adjacencies (like independent set or vertex cover), while distance-$r$ problems involve dependencies over distance $r$. The paper's main result gives a PTAS, in every efficiently fractionally treewidth-fragile class, for all maximization problems on vertex-weighted graphs that are determined by distances at most $r$, (near-)monotone (subsets of admissible sets remain admissible, up to a bounded correction) and solvable in polynomial time on bounded treewidth (e.g. weighted maximum $r$-independent set), and a QPTAS for them in all hereditary classes with sublinear separators. Minimization problems such as Minimum Vertex Cover are not monotone in this sense; unweighted Minimum Vertex Cover has a PTAS in classes with sublinear separators by local search (Har-Peled and Quanrud), but the weighted case is open.
notes: Stated in running prose without a labelled environment; PDF extraction — surrounding math is clean but statement itself is purely verbal.
paper_title: Approximation schemes for bounded distance problems on fractionally treewidth-fragile graphs

name: AX_intersection_graphs_polynomial_weak_coloring_numbers
title: Question (polynomial weak coloring numbers for intersection graph classes)
statement_text: Are the $k$-th weak coloring numbers polynomial in $k$ for the following graph classes: intersection graphs of $t$-thin sets of (a) scaled and translated copies of the same centrally symmetric compact convex object, or comparable axis-aligned boxes; or (b) $b$-ball-like objects for some $b\geq 1$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. For a linear order $\prec$ of $V(G)$ and $k\ge0$, a vertex $u$ is weakly $k$-reachable from $v$ if $u\preceq v$ and some path of length at most $k$ from $v$ to $u$ has all internal vertices greater than $u$, and strongly $k$-reachable if moreover all internal vertices are greater than $v$; $\mathrm{wcol}_k(G)$ (resp. $\mathrm{scol}_k(G)$) is the minimum over $\prec$ of the maximum over $v$ of the number of vertices weakly (resp. strongly) $k$-reachable from $v$. For a finite set $S$ of objects in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the intersection graph has vertex set $S$ and edges between intersecting objects; $S$ is $t$-thin if every point of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the interior of at most $t$ objects ($t=1$: touching representation). An object $v$ is $b$-ball-like if it is compact convex with volume at least $1/b$ times that of a ball of diameter $\mathrm{diam}(v)$; axis-aligned boxes are comparable if for any two of them a translate of one is contained in the other. For these classes, ordering objects by non-increasing diameter gives $\mathrm{scol}_k(G)\le t(2k+1)^d$ in case (a) and $\le bt(2k+2)^d$ in case (b), i.e. polynomial in $k$ for fixed $d,t,b$. Joret and Wood conjectured that polynomial strong coloring numbers imply polynomial weak coloring numbers; Grohe et al. disproved this using subdivisions, but the authors ask whether it still holds for these natural classes. The paper itself answers it: for homothets of a centrally symmetric compact convex object and for $b$-ball-like objects, $\mathrm{wcol}_k(G)\le t\max(1,\lceil\log_2k\rceil)(4k-1)^d\binom{k+t5^d+2}{t5^d+2}$ (resp. a similar bound), which is polynomial in $k$; but touching graphs of comparable axis-aligned boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can have $\mathrm{wcol}_{2k}\ge2^{k+1}-1$, so for comparable boxes the answer is negative. They also show that the dependence on $t$ must be in the exponent in dimension at least $2$.
notes: Stated as a prose question without a labelled theorem environment. Theorem 3 of the paper gives polynomial (in $k$) upper bounds for scaled/translated centrally symmetric objects and $b$-ball-like objects, giving a positive partial answer; Theorem 4(i) shows exponential lower bounds for touching comparable axis-aligned boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$, giving a negative answer for that subclass. PDF source — surrounding math may be garbled in the extracted text.
paper_title: Weak Coloring Numbers of Intersection Graphs

name: AX_ladder_minor_bumping_universal_constant
title: Informal Conjecture on Universal N0 for Bumping a Ladder
statement_text: There exists a constant $N_0$ such that for every $k\ge1$, every $3$-connected graph containing a union of $N_0$ vertex-disjoint copies of the ladder $L_k$ as a minor contains $L_{k+1}$ as a minor. For all we know, this might even be true with $N_0 = 4$.
context_text: $L_k$ denotes the ladder with $k$ rungs, i.e. the $2\times k$ grid graph. The authors prove the 'bumping a ladder' theorem: for every integer $k\ge1$ there is an integer $N$ such that every $3$-connected graph containing a union of $N$ vertex-disjoint copies of $L_k$ as a minor contains $L_{k+1}$ as a minor. This generalizes the fact that a connected graph with two vertex-disjoint paths of order $k$ has a path of order $k+1$; combined with a theorem of Robertson and Seymour on packing disjoint copies of a planar minor, it gives that every $3$-connected graph without an $L_{k+1}$ minor has a set of boundedly many vertices whose removal destroys all $L_k$ minors. The $3$-connectivity is necessary: there is a $2$-connected graph with $8$ disjoint copies of $L_4$ and no $L_5$ minor. In their proof $N$ depends on $k$, but the authors expect this dependence is not necessary and conjecture a universal constant.
notes: Stated in prose immediately after Theorem 2 with the phrase 'We conjecture'; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Excluding a ladder

name: AX_poset_cover_graph_unavoidable_minors_characterization
title: Open Problem: Characterization of Unavoidable Graphs
statement_text: Obtain a full characterization of unavoidable graphs, where a graph $H$ is unavoidable if the cover graph of every poset with large enough dimension contains $H$ as a minor.
context_text: For a poset $P$, $y$ covers $x$ if $x<y$ and no $z$ satisfies $x<z<y$; the cover graph of $P$ is the graph on its ground set where two elements are adjacent if one covers the other (the Hasse diagram as an undirected graph). The dimension of $P$ is the least number of linear orders whose intersection is the order of $P$. A graph $H$ is unavoidable if the cover graph of every poset of large enough dimension contains $H$ as a minor; the class of unavoidable graphs is minor-closed. Kelly's classical construction gives posets of unbounded dimension whose cover graphs are planar and have pathwidth $3$, so every unavoidable graph is a minor of a graph from Kelly's construction (equivalently, of a graph obtained by gluing copies of $K_4$ along edges in a path-like way and subdividing once all their 'horizontal' edges, as depicted in the paper). The authors prove that posets whose cover graphs exclude a fixed ladder ($2\times k$ grid) as a minor have bounded dimension, so all ladders (and hence their minors, e.g. fans) are unavoidable; besides ladders, the only other known positive result is that $K_4$ is unavoidable. They conjecture that the necessary condition given by Kelly's construction is also sufficient.
notes: Stated in prose as 'it is an open problem'; no labelled environment. Conjecture 6 in the same paper proposes a conjectured answer.
paper_title: Excluding a ladder

name: AX_poset_cover_graph_unavoidable_minors_kelly
title: Conjecture 6
statement_text: A graph $H$ is unavoidable if and only if $H$ is a minor of some graph from Kelly's construction.
context_text: For a poset $P$, $y$ covers $x$ if $x<y$ and no $z$ satisfies $x<z<y$; the cover graph of $P$ is the graph on its ground set where two elements are adjacent if one covers the other (the Hasse diagram as an undirected graph). The dimension of $P$ is the least number of linear orders whose intersection is the order of $P$. A graph $H$ is unavoidable if the cover graph of every poset of large enough dimension contains $H$ as a minor; the class of unavoidable graphs is minor-closed. Kelly's classical construction gives posets of unbounded dimension whose cover graphs are planar and have pathwidth $3$, so every unavoidable graph is a minor of a graph from Kelly's construction (equivalently, of a graph obtained by gluing copies of $K_4$ along edges in a path-like way and subdividing once all their 'horizontal' edges, as depicted in the paper). The authors prove that posets whose cover graphs exclude a fixed ladder ($2\times k$ grid) as a minor have bounded dimension, so every ladder is unavoidable; the only other known positive result is that $K_4$ is unavoidable. The conjecture asserts that the necessary condition from Kelly's construction is also sufficient, which would give a full characterization of unavoidable graphs.
