name: AX_hitting_max_independent_sets_graph_chromatic
title: Informal Conjecture on Chromatic Number of $G_{m,t}$
statement_text: Let $m$ be even and $t$ a positive integer with $4t^2 \leq m$, and let $G_{m,t}$ be the graph whose vertices are the binary vectors of length $m$, two being adjacent iff their Hamming distance exceeds $m-2t$. Then the chromatic number of $G_{m,t}$ is $\Theta(t^2)$.
context_text: $G_{m,t}$ is the Cayley graph of $\mathbb{Z}_2^m$ with respect to the vectors of Hamming weight at least $m-2t+1$, and it contains the Kneser graph $K(m,m/2+1-t)$ as an induced subgraph. By a result of Kleitman its independence number is $\sum_{i=0}^{m/2-t}\binom mi$, and its maximum independent sets are exactly the $2^m$ Hamming balls of radius $m/2-t$. Alon uses it to show that the minimum size $h(G)$ of a set of vertices meeting every maximum independent set can be $\Theta(t^2)$ (via covering codes and discrepancy), which disproves a conjecture of Friedgut, Kalai and Kindler. The Kneser subgraph gives $\chi(G_{m,t})\ge 2t$, and the arguments of the paper give $\chi(G_{m,t})=O(t^2)$; Alon states that he raised the conjecture that the truth is $\Theta(t^2)$ more than ten years earlier, motivated by results of Alon, Hassidim, Lubetzky, Stav and Weinstein, and mentioned it in several lectures.
notes: Stated informally in the Remarks section (Section 3) without a labelled theorem environment; attributed to the author himself from more than ten years prior but cited only via lectures, not a prior publication.
paper_title: Hitting all maximum independent sets

name: AX_sunflower_bounded_vc_dimension_exponential
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: For $d \geq 1$ and $r \geq 3$, there is a constant $C = C(d, r)$ such that $f^d_r(k) \leq C^k$.
context_text: A $k$-set is a set with $k$ elements. Distinct sets $S_1,\dots,S_r$ form an $r$-sunflower if all their pairwise intersections are the same: $S_i\cap S_j=S_{i'}\cap S_{j'}$ for all $i\ne j$ and $i'\ne j'$. The VC-dimension of a family $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of a ground set $V$ is the largest $d$ for which some $d$-element set $S\subseteq V$ is shattered by $\mathcal{F}$, i.e. for every $B\subseteq S$ some $A\in\mathcal{F}$ has $A\cap S=B$. $f^d_r(k)$ is the least positive integer $m$ such that every family $\mathcal{F}$ of $k$-sets with $|\mathcal{F}|\ge m$ and VC-dimension at most $d$ contains an $r$-sunflower; it is at most the classical $f_r(k)$, defined without the dimension restriction, so the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture ($f_r(k)\le C(r)^k$) implies this weaker conjecture. Even $f^1_r(k)>(r-1)^{k-1}$ (root-to-leaf paths of a complete $(r-1)$-ary tree), so exponential growth is necessary. Using a result of Ding, Seymour and Winkler, the authors prove the case $d=1$, namely $f^1_r(k)\le r^{10k}$, and for $d\ge2$ they prove the slightly weaker bound $f^d_r(k)\le2^{10k(dr)^{2\log^*k}}$, where $\log^*$ is the iterated logarithm (logs in base 2); they also verify the sunflower conjecture for families cut out of planar point sets by pseudo-disks, and show that for bounded Littlestone dimension the corresponding function is only polynomial in $k$. This is a problem about set systems (hypergraphs).
notes: PDF source. Conjecture is explicitly labelled in the paper. The case $d=1$ is resolved by Theorem 1.2; the case $d \geq 2$ remains open.
paper_title: Sunflowers in set systems of bounded dimension

name: AX_k_colorable_deletion_clique_free_sharp
title: Conjecture on sharpness of Theorem 1.1
statement_text: For each integer $r \geq 3$ there is $c_r$ such that for all positive integers $n, k$ with $n$ sufficiently large in terms of $k$, $$h(n, k, K_r) = \Theta_r\!\left(\frac{n^2}{k^{(r-1)/(r-2)}}\right),$$ i.e., the upper bound $h(n, k, K_r) \leq c_r \dfrac{n^2}{k^{(r-1)/(r-2)}}$ is tight up to the constant factor $c_r$.
context_text: For a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, $h(G,k)$ is the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes $G$ $k$-colourable, and $h(n,k,H)$ is the maximum of $h(G,k)$ over all $n$-vertex graphs $G$ not containing $H$ as a subgraph (the case $k=1$ is the Turán problem; Erdős's conjecture that triangle-free graphs can be made bipartite by deleting $n^2/25$ edges is the case $H=K_3$, $k=2$). The authors prove $h(n,k,K_r)\le c_r n^2/k^{(r-1)/(r-2)}$ for every $r\ge3$ and all $n,k$, and prove the matching lower bound for $r=3$. For odd cycles they determine $h(n,k,C_{2r+1})$ up to a constant factor for $n$ large, using Alon's pseudorandom graphs of large odd girth for the lower bound. A corresponding dense pseudorandom $K_r$-free construction is not known for $r\ge4$ but is conjectured to exist, and it would imply this conjecture.
paper_title: Making an $H$-Free Graph $k$-Colorable

name: AX_k_colorable_deletion_odd_wheel_sharp
title: Conjecture on sharpness of Theorem 1.5
statement_text: For each positive integer $r$, the bound $$h(n, k, W_{2r+1}) \leq c_r \frac{n^2}{k^{2 - 1/(r+1)}}$$ is tight up to the constant factor $c_r$ depending on $r$.
context_text: For a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, $h(G,k)$ is the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes $G$ $k$-colourable, and $h(n,k,H)$ is the maximum of $h(G,k)$ over all $n$-vertex graphs $G$ not containing $H$ as a subgraph (the case $k=1$ is the Turán problem; Erdős's conjecture that triangle-free graphs can be made bipartite by deleting $n^2/25$ edges is the case $H=K_3$, $k=2$). The wheel $W_\ell$ consists of an $\ell$-cycle plus a vertex adjacent to all its vertices. For even wheels the authors show $h(n,k,W_\ell)$ is asymptotically the same as $h(n,k,K_3)$. For odd wheels, combining their methods for cliques ($h(n,k,K_r)\le c_rn^2/k^{(r-1)/(r-2)}$) and for graphs of large odd girth ($h(n,k,C_{2r+1})=O_r(n^2/k^{r+1})$, tight for large $n$), they prove $h(n,k,W_{2r+1})\le c_rn^2/k^{2-1/(r+1)}$ for $n\ge k\ge2$, and conjecture this is tight up to the constant factor depending on $r$.
paper_title: Making an $H$-Free Graph $k$-Colorable

name: AX_k_colorable_deletion_neighborhood_edge_cover
title: Question 2.1
statement_text: Given a graph $G$, how many edges of $G$ can we cover by the union of $k$ neighborhoods of vertices of $G$?
context_text: For a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, $u(G,k)$ is the maximum number of edges of the induced subgraph $G[N(v_1)\cup\dots\cup N(v_k)]$ over all choices of $k$ vertices $v_1,\dots,v_k$, and $m(n,k)$ is the minimum of $e(G)-u(G,k)$ over all $n$-vertex graphs $G$, i.e. the least $r$ such that in every $n$-vertex graph some $k$ neighbourhoods together induce all but at most $r$ edges. One has $m(n,1)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$, a strengthening of Mantel's theorem since $u(G,1)=0$ exactly when $G$ is triangle-free. Bounds on this quantity are the main tool for the authors' upper bounds on $h(n,k,H)$, the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes any $n$-vertex $H$-free graph $k$-colourable, when $H$ is a clique or an odd wheel. Via a random choice of the $k$ vertices they prove $m(n,k)\le n^2/(ek)$.
paper_title: Making an $H$-Free Graph $k$-Colorable

name: AX_k_colorable_deletion_mnk_asymptotics
title: Open problem on $m(n,k)$ for fixed $k \geq 2$
statement_text: What is the exact or asymptotic value of $m(n,k)$ for any fixed $k \geq 2$?
context_text: For a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$, $u(G,k)$ is the maximum number of edges of the induced subgraph $G[N(v_1)\cup\dots\cup N(v_k)]$ over all choices of $k$ vertices $v_1,\dots,v_k$, and $m(n,k)$ is the minimum of $e(G)-u(G,k)$ over all $n$-vertex graphs $G$, i.e. the least $r$ such that in every $n$-vertex graph some $k$ neighbourhoods together induce all but at most $r$ edges. One has $m(n,1)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$, a strengthening of Mantel's theorem since $u(G,1)=0$ exactly when $G$ is triangle-free. The authors prove $m(n,k)\le n^2/(ek)$ by choosing $k$ random vertices. An Erdős–Rényi random graph $G(n,c/k)$, with $c$ maximising $ce^{-c}-\frac c2e^{-2c}$, gives $m(n,k)\ge(1+o_k(1))(ce^{-c}-\frac c2e^{-2c})\frac{n^2}{k}$ for $n$ large in terms of $k$, which for $k$ large is within $20\%$ of the upper bound. They state that they have no idea what the exact or asymptotic value of $m(n,k)$ is for any fixed $k\ge2$.
notes: Stated as an informal open problem in the body of the paper without a labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Making an $H$-Free Graph $k$-Colorable

name: AX_link_hypergraph_ramsey_rate_odd_girth
title: Exact Ramsey growth rate dependence on G for link hypergraphs
statement_text: It would be interesting to determine the exact dependence on $G$ in the bounds $\Omega(1/g) \le \frac{\log r(L_G,\, K_n^{(3)})}{n \log n} \le O(s)$, where $G$ is a non-bipartite graph on $s$ vertices with odd girth $g \ge 3$.
context_text: A $k$-graph is a $k$-uniform hypergraph and $K_n^{(3)}$ the complete 3-graph on $n$ vertices; the Ramsey number $r(H,K_n^{(3)})$ is the least $N$ such that every 3-graph on $N$ vertices contains a copy of $H$ or an independent set of size $n$ (no edge inside). For a graph $G$, the link hypergraph $L_G$ is the 3-graph on $V(G)\cup\{u\}$ whose edges are the triples $\{u,v,w\}$ with $vw\in E(G)$ (so $L_{K_3}=K_4^{(3)}\setminus e$); a 3-graph is $L_G$-free iff the link of each vertex (the graph of pairs forming an edge with it) is $G$-free. The odd girth of a non-bipartite graph is the length of its shortest odd cycle. Logarithms are base 2 unless noted. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov showed $r(L_G,K_n^{(3)})=n^{\Theta(1)}$ if $G$ is bipartite and $r(L_G,K_n^{(3)})\ge2^{\Omega(n)}$ otherwise. The authors prove $r(L_G,K_n^{(3)})=n^{\Theta(n)}$ for every fixed non-bipartite $G$, solving in particular the Erdős–Hajnal problem for $K_4^{(3)}\setminus e$. The lower bound comes from a random 3-graph on $n^{\Omega(n/g)}$ vertices in which every link has odd girth greater than $g$ and the complement contains no $K^{(3)}_{n,n,n}$. The upper bound is $r(L_{K_s},K_n^{(3)})<(2n)^{sn}$. Together they give the stated bounds $n^{\Omega(n/g)}\le r(L_G,K_n^{(3)})\le n^{O(sn)}$ for $G$ on $s$ vertices with odd girth $g$. The authors further conjecture that for every non-bipartite $G$ there is a constant $c_G$ with $r(L_G,K_n^{(3)})=n^{(1+o(1))c_G n}$. They note that such constants, if they exist for odd cycles $C_g$, are bounded by an absolute constant, but it is unknown whether they tend to zero. This is hypergraph Ramsey theory.
notes: Stated as 'it would be interesting' in running prose without a labelled environment; PDF source.
paper_title: Independent sets in hypergraphs with a forbidden link

name: AX_hypergraph_independence_fk_order
title: Determine the order of f_k(N; s, t) in general
statement_text: Determine the order of $f_k(N; s, t)$ for all valid parameters $k \ge 3$, $s \ge k+1$, and $1 \le t \le \binom{s}{k}$.
context_text: A $k$-graph is a $k$-uniform hypergraph and $K_n^{(3)}$ the complete 3-graph on $n$ vertices; the Ramsey number $r(H,K_n^{(3)})$ is the least $N$ such that every 3-graph on $N$ vertices contains a copy of $H$ or an independent set of size $n$ (no edge inside). Erdős and Hajnal defined $f_k(N;s,t)$ as the minimum possible independence number of a $k$-graph on $N$ vertices in which any $s$ vertices span fewer than $t$ edges (for example $f_3(N;4,3)$ is essentially the inverse of $r(K_4^{(3)}\setminus e,K_n^{(3)})$). For fixed $k\ge3$ and $s\ge k+1$, they conjectured that as $t$ increases from $1$ to $\binom{s}{k}$, $f_k(N;s,t)$ grows first like a power of $N$, then beyond thresholds $h_1^{(k)}(s)<h_2^{(k)}(s)<\dots$ like a power of $\log N$, of $\log\log N$, and so on, up to the $(k-2)$-fold iterated logarithm; they also conjectured the value of the first threshold. That conjecture was solved for $k=3$ and infinitely many $s$ by Conlon–Fox–Sudakov, for $k\ge4$ by Mubayi–Razborov, and for $s=k+1$ by Mubayi–Suk. Despite this, the order of $f_k(N;s,t)$ has remained wide open. The authors prove that for every fixed $s\ge4$ and $t\in(e(s),E(s)]$, $f_3(N;s,t)=\Theta(\log N/\log\log N)$. Here $e(s)\le(0.266+o(1))\binom s3$ is the maximum number of edges of a 3-graph on $s$ vertices all of whose vertex links are bipartite, and $E(s)\ge(0.464-o(1))\binom s3$ is the maximum number of edges of a 3-graph $H$ on $s$ vertices with $r(H,K_n^{(3)})=n^{O(n)}$. This is hypergraph Ramsey theory.
notes: Framed in prose as 'the order of $f_k(N;s,t)$ has remained wide open'; no explicit labelled problem environment. Section 7, which the paper states contains explicit open problems, is absent from the PDF extraction.
paper_title: Independent sets in hypergraphs with a forbidden link

name: AX_tournament_path_powers_exponent_constant
title: Open Problem: exact constant in the exponent
statement_text: The maximum length $\ell$ such that every $n$-vertex tournament contains the $k$-th power of a directed path of length $\ell$ has the form $n/2^{\Theta(k)}$. It would be interesting to find the exact value of the constant factor in the exponent. Optimizing our proof can yield a lower bound of $n/2^{ck+o(k)}$ with $c\approx 3.9$, but is unlikely to give the correct bound.
context_text: The $k$-th power of the directed path $v_0v_1\dots v_\ell$ of length $\ell$ is the digraph on the same vertices with an arc $v_iv_j$ whenever $i<j\le i+k$; a tournament contains it if it contains it as a subdigraph. Every tournament has a directed Hamilton path, but Yuster showed that for every $k\ge2$ some $n$-vertex tournaments contain no $k$-th power of a path with more than $nk/2^{k/2}$ vertices; Yuster and then Girão proved that powers of paths of length $n^{0.295}$ (for squares), respectively $n^{1-o(1)}$ (for fixed $k$), always exist. The authors prove that every $n$-vertex tournament ($n\ge2$) contains the $k$-th power of a directed path of length $n/(2^{4k+6}k)$, using Kővári–Sós–Turán type arguments and median orderings. They also show that for $k\ge5$ and $n\ge k(k+1)2^k$ some $n$-vertex tournament contains no $k$-th power of a directed path of length $k(k+1)n/2^k$. So the answer is $n/2^{ck}$ up to lower-order terms, with the optimal $c$ between $1$ and about $3.9$.
notes: Stated in prose without a labelled environment; verbatim phrasing 'It would be interesting to find the exact value of the constant factor in the exponent.'
paper_title: Powers of paths in tournaments

name: AX_twin_width_mis_dominating_approximability
title: Informal conjecture on MIS approximability vs. Min Dominating Set
statement_text: Max Independent Set may have a very different approximability status than Min Dominating Set on bounded twin-width graphs.
context_text: Twin-width: a graph has twin-width at most $d$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex by successively contracting two vertices into one, where edges from the merged vertex to vertices adjacent to only part of it become 'red', so that every intermediate graph has red degree at most $d$; such a contraction sequence is a $d$-sequence, and bounded twin-width classes include planar graphs, bounded tree-width or clique-width graphs, and proper minor-closed classes. Max Independent Set (MIS) is Distance-$1$ MIS; Distance-$r$ MIS asks for a largest set of vertices pairwise at distance at least $r$; Min $r$-Dominating Set asks for a smallest set within distance $r$ of every vertex. The authors show that, when an $O(1)$-sequence is given, Min Dominating Set, Distance-$2$ MIS and more generally Min $r$-Dominating Set and Distance-$2r$ MIS admit polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximations, as bounded twin-width implies a constant integrality gap between packing and hitting for the corresponding hypergraphs; this does not cover MIS. Their evidence that MIS behaves differently: the self-improving reduction of Feige et al. preserves twin-width, so a constant-factor approximation for MIS on graphs of twin-width at most $d$ would yield a PTAS; MIS can be $O(1)$-approximated on $K_t$-free graphs of bounded twin-width, but not obviously when the clique number is unbounded. In contrast, on general graphs Min Dominating Set cannot be approximated within $(1-o(1))\ln n$ unless P$=$NP.

paper_title: Twin-width III: Max Independent Set, Min Dominating Set, and Coloring

name: AX_erdos_hajnal_c8_complement_c8
title: Erdős-Hajnal property for $\{C_8, \overline{C_8}\}$
statement_text: Does $\{C_8, \overline{C_8}\}$ have the Erdős-Hajnal property?
context_text: A graph $G$ is $\mathcal{H}$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{H}$; $\overline{H}$ denotes the complement of $H$ and $|G|$ the number of vertices. A set $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs has the Erdős–Hajnal property if there exists $\tau>0$ such that $\max(\alpha(G),\omega(G))\ge|G|^\tau$ for every $\mathcal{H}$-free graph $G$; the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asserts that every single graph has it. Excluding both $C_8$ and $\overline{C_8}$ is a stronger restriction than excluding $C_8$ alone, so the question is a weakening of the conjecture for $C_8$. The paper's main result is that $C_5$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property; with the same method the authors also prove that $\{C_6,\overline{C_6}\}$ and $\{C_7,\overline{C_7}\}$ have it, that $\{C,\overline{H}\}$ has it for every cycle $C$ and forest $H$, and that a cycle together with the complements of all cycles of length at least $\ell$ has it. They remark that it would be nice to know whether $\{C_8,\overline{C_8}\}$ has the property, but this remains open.
notes: Stated in running prose as 'it would be nice to know if the same is true for $\{C_8,\overline{C_8}\}$, but this remains open'; no formal theorem environment.
paper_title: Erdos-Hajnal for graphs with no 5-hole

name: AX_star_contraction_clique_minor_strategy_generality
title: Informal conjecture on the generality of the probabilistic minor strategy
statement_text: The random star-contraction strategy of the authors (colour each vertex red independently with probability $p$ and blue otherwise, let each blue vertex pick a uniformly random red neighbour, contract the resulting stars and delete isolated blue vertices, then analyse the minor obtained), or minor modifications of it, could provide a useful tool for finding clique minors in graphs under other structural restrictions as well.
context_text: $\alpha(G)$ denotes the independence number. Hadwiger's conjecture would imply that every $n$-vertex graph has a clique minor of order $n/\alpha(G)$. Kühn and Osthus, and Krivelevich and Sudakov, showed that $H$-free graphs for a bipartite $H$ (e.g. $K_{s,t}$-free graphs of average degree $d$, which have clique minors of order about $d^{1+2/(s-1)}$ up to log factors) have polynomially larger clique minors than general graphs, and Dvořák and Yepremyan extended this to triangle-free graphs. Using the strategy above, the authors prove that for every $s\ge3$ every $K_s$-free $n$-vertex graph with $\alpha(G)\le r$ has a clique minor of order at least $(n/r)^{1+\frac{1}{10(s-2)}}$ when $n/r$ is large, with the exponent tight up to the constant in front of $\frac1{s-2}$, answering a question of Dvořák and Yepremyan; they also use it for a short proof of the Kühn–Osthus result for $K_{s,t}$-free graphs. Since the approach works under these two quite different restrictions, they believe it should be useful under other structural restrictions as well. This is an informal belief rather than a precise mathematical conjecture.
paper_title: Clique minors in graphs with a forbidden subgraph

name: AX_ordered_pure_pairs_n_polylog
title: Informal belief on Conjecture 1.7 and polylog bound
statement_text: Korándi, Pach and Tomon conjectured: for every ordered forest bigraph $H$, there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that, if $G$ is an ordered bigraph that does not contain $H$ or its bicomplement, with $|V_1(G)|,|V_2(G)|\ge n$, then there is a pure pair $(Z_1,Z_2)$ with $Z_i\subseteq V_i(G)$ and $|Z_i|\ge\varepsilon n$ for $i=1,2$. Our guess is that this conjecture is false. Perhaps $n/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ might be true (that is, the same statement with $|Z_i|\ge n/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$)?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A bigraph is a graph with a distinguished bipartition $(V_1(G),V_2(G))$, and an ordered bigraph is a bigraph with a linear order on $V_1(G)$ and a linear order on $V_2(G)$ (equivalently, a $0/1$ matrix). An ordered bigraph $G$ contains $H$ if some induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$ via an isomorphism mapping $V_i(H)$ into $V_i(G)$ and preserving both orders (submatrix containment); the bicomplement of $H$ is obtained by reversing adjacency between every $v_1\in V_1$ and $v_2\in V_2$ (complementing the matrix). A pair $(Z_1,Z_2)$ of disjoint vertex sets is pure if $Z_1$ is complete or anticomplete to $Z_2$. A forest bigraph is one whose underlying graph is a forest. For unordered bigraphs the analogous statement holds and characterises forests (an earlier result of the authors), and Korándi, Pach and Tomon proved it for certain ordered $H$ with $|V_1(H)|\le2$. Their conjecture implies their weaker conjecture that linear pure pairs exist when $G$ excludes a single ordered bigraph $H$ such that both $H$ and its bicomplement are forests. The authors find it natural by analogy with the unordered case but guess it is false; they prove that, for every ordered forest bigraph $H$, excluding $H$ and its bicomplement forces a pure pair with $|Z_1|,|Z_2|\ge n^{1-o(1)}$, and indeed one with one side of size at least $\delta n$ and the other at least $\delta n^{1-c}$ for any fixed $c>0$.
notes: Stated as an informal belief/guess in running prose; no labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Pure pairs. VII. Homogeneous submatrices in 0/1-matrices with a forbidden submatrix

name: AX_map_isomorphism_quadratic_lower_bound
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: There is no $\varepsilon > 0$ for which there is an algorithm for testing isomorphism of maps of unrestricted genus in time $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$.
context_text: A map is an embedding of a connected graph in a closed compact surface such that every face is homeomorphic to an open disc; an isomorphism of maps is a bijection preserving the vertex-edge-face incidences, and $n$ denotes the size of the map (e.g. its number of darts). In the simultaneous conjugation problem, given permutations $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$ and $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_d$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, each family generating a transitive group, one seeks $\gamma$ with $\gamma\alpha_i\gamma^{-1}=\beta_i$ for all $i$; map isomorphism is the special case $d=2$ with $\alpha_1,\beta_1$ involutions acting on the darts. Map isomorphism is solvable in quadratic time, and in linear time on the sphere (Hopcroft and Wong) and for bounded genus; the authors compute generators of the automorphism group of a map of genus $g$ in time $f(g)n$. For unrestricted genus, simultaneous conjugation is solvable in $O(dn^2)$ (known since the 1970s) and in $O(n^2\log d/\log n+dn\log n)$ (recent), giving $O(n^2/\log n)$ for map isomorphism and automorphism, which is not considered truly subquadratic. This motivates the conjecture that no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm exists.
paper_title: Automorphism groups of maps in linear time

name: AX_map_isomorphism_superlinear_lower_bound
title: Open subproblem: conditional superlinear lower bound
statement_text: An interesting open subproblem is to prove a conditional ``truly superlinear'' lower bound for any of the problems of testing isomorphism of maps of unrestricted genus, computing the automorphism group of such maps, and simultaneous conjugation of permutations.
context_text: A map is an embedding of a connected graph in a closed compact surface such that every face is homeomorphic to an open disc; an isomorphism of maps is a bijection preserving the vertex-edge-face incidences, and $n$ denotes the size of the map (e.g. its number of darts). In the simultaneous conjugation problem, given permutations $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$ and $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_d$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, each family generating a transitive group, one seeks $\gamma$ with $\gamma\alpha_i\gamma^{-1}=\beta_i$ for all $i$; map isomorphism is the special case $d=2$ with $\alpha_1,\beta_1$ involutions acting on the darts. Map isomorphism is solvable in quadratic time, and in linear time on the sphere (Hopcroft and Wong) and for bounded genus; the authors compute generators of the automorphism group of a map of genus $g$ in time $f(g)n$. For unrestricted genus, simultaneous conjugation is solvable in $O(dn^2)$ (known since the 1970s) and in $O(n^2\log d/\log n+dn\log n)$ (recent), giving $O(n^2/\log n)$ for map isomorphism and automorphism, which is not considered truly subquadratic. The authors conjecture that map isomorphism for unrestricted genus has no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm. As partial progress towards lower bounds, the communication complexity of simultaneous conjugation is $\Omega(dn\log n)$ for $d>1$, and in the decision tree model the search version has an $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound; a conditional lower bound of the form $n^{1+\varepsilon}$ remains open.

paper_title: Automorphism groups of maps in linear time

name: AX_interactive_sum_choice_strict_non_complete
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: If any connected component of $G$ is not a complete graph, then $\chi_{ISC}(G) < \chi_{SC}(G)$.
context_text: A function $f:V(G)\to\mathbb{N}$ is a choice function for $G$ if $G$ has a proper colouring from the lists $L$ whenever $|L(v)|\ge f(v)$ for every vertex $v$; the sum choice number $\chi_{SC}(G)$ (Isaak) is the minimum of $\sum_vf(v)$ over choice functions. The interactive sum choice number $\chi_{ISC}(G)$ is defined by a game: all lists start empty; in each round Alice chooses a vertex $v$ and Bob adds to $L(v)$ a colour not already in it; the game stops as soon as $G$ has a proper colouring from the current lists, Alice trying to minimise and Bob to maximise the number of rounds; $\chi_{ISC}(G)$ is the number of rounds under optimal play. Clearly $\chi_{ISC}(G)\le\chi_{SC}(G)\le|V|+|E|$, the latter being the greedy bound; graphs attaining it are called sc-greedy. Equality $\chi_{ISC}=\chi_{SC}$ holds for complete graphs (Bob gives colours $1,2,\dots$ in order at every vertex), and hence for disjoint unions of complete graphs, while for example $\chi_{SC}(P_3)=5$ but $\chi_{ISC}(P_3)=4$. The authors confirm the conjecture for all sc-greedy graphs and show that the gap $\chi_{SC}-\chi_{ISC}$ grows with the number of vertices (in many cases linearly) for trees, unbalanced complete bipartite graphs and grids.

name: AX_minimal_complements_count_sqrt_n
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: We have that $T(n) = \widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{n})$. More generally, we have that $T(G) = \widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{|G|})$.
context_text: All groups are abelian. For subsets $W,C$ of a group $G$, $C$ is a complement for $W$ if $W+C=G$, and a minimal complement for $W$ if moreover no proper subset of $C$ is a complement for $W$; $C$ is a minimal complement in $G$ if it is a minimal complement for some $W\subseteq G$. For a finite abelian group $G$, $T(G)$ is the greatest $T$ such that every subset of $G$ of size at most $T$ is a minimal complement in $G$, and $T(n)$ is the minimum of $T(G)$ over abelian groups of order $n$. The authors prove $T(n)\ge\frac{n^{1/3}}{2(\log n/\log2)^{2/3}}$ (every non-empty $C$ with $|C|\le2^{2/3}n^{1/3}/(3e\log n)^{2/3}$ is a minimal complement), $\liminf_{n\to\infty}T(n)/\sqrt{n}\le\sqrt2$ (using groups with subgroups of suitable orders), and $T(G)=O(|G|^{3/4+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Here $f(n)=\widetilde{\Theta}(g(n))$ means $f(n)=\Omega(g(n)(\log n)^a)$ and $f(n)=O(g(n)(\log n)^b)$ for some integers $a,b$, i.e. equality up to polylogarithmic factors. The conjecture asks for the true order of $T(n)$ and $T(G)$, between these bounds. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

title: Question 8
statement_text: Is the behavior of $T(n)$ different when $n$ is prime? How much does $T(G)$ depend on the structure of $G$ in addition to the order of $G$?
context_text: All groups are abelian. name: AX_maximal_supplement_solid_subset_optimal
title: Question 9
statement_text: What is the optimal function $f$ such that every non-empty solid subset $C$ of a finite abelian group $G$ with $|C|\le f(|G|)$ is a maximal supplement in $G$?
context_text: $C$ is a supplement for $W$ if the translates $W+c$, $c\in C$, are pairwise disjoint, and a maximal supplement for $W$ if no proper superset of $C$ is a supplement for $W$; $C$ is a maximal supplement in $G$ if it is one for some $W$. A subset $C$ of $G$ is solid if it is not properly contained in any set $D$ with $D-D=C-C$; every maximal supplement must be solid, so small sets need not be maximal supplements but small solid sets are. The authors prove that there is an absolute constant $b>0$ such that every non-empty solid subset $C$ of a finite abelian group $G$ with $|C|\le b(|G|/\log|G|)^{1/4}$ is a maximal supplement in $G$, but it is unclear whether this bound is anywhere near optimal; they also show that in an infinite abelian group every finite non-empty solid subset is a maximal supplement. This is the dual of the analogous question for minimal complements ($W+C=G$ with $C$ minimal), where every non-empty subset of size $O(n^{1/3}/(\log n)^{2/3})$ of a group of order $n$ is a minimal complement. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

name: AX_minimal_complements_random_subset_threshold
title: Question 10
statement_text: How does the probability that a random subset of a finite group $G$ with parameter $p = p(|G|)$ is a minimal complement (or maximal supplement) vary with $p$? Is there a (sharp) threshold?
context_text: All groups are abelian. For subsets $W,C$ of a group $G$, $C$ is a complement for $W$ if $W+C=G$, and a minimal complement for $W$ if moreover no proper subset of $C$ is a complement for $W$; $C$ is a minimal complement in $G$ if it is a minimal complement for some $W\subseteq G$. $C$ is a supplement for $W$ if the translates $W+c$, $c\in C$, are pairwise disjoint, and a maximal supplement for $W$ if no proper superset of $C$ is a supplement for $W$; $C$ is a maximal supplement in $G$ if it is one for some $W$. A random subset with parameter $p$ contains each element of $G$ independently with probability $p$. Being a minimal complement is not a monotone property, but the authors' results and proofs show that for small $p$ a random set is with high probability a minimal complement (every non-empty set of size at most about $|G|^{1/3}/(\log|G|)^{2/3}$ is one), and that for any $p>|G|^{\varepsilon-1/4}$ bounded away from $1$ (e.g. $p=1/2$) a random set is with high probability not a minimal complement. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

name: AX_sparse_h_free_anticomplete_pairs_linear
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: For every graph $H$ there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that in every $H$-free $\varepsilon$-bounded graph $G$ with $|G| > 1$ vertices, there is an anticomplete $(\varepsilon|G|^{\varepsilon}, \varepsilon|G|)$-pair.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices, and $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph is isomorphic to $H$. $G$ is $\varepsilon$-bounded if $|N[v]|<\varepsilon|G|$ for every vertex $v$ (closed neighbourhood), i.e. maximum degree less than $\varepsilon|G|-1$. An $(x,y)$-pair is a pair $(A,B)$ of disjoint vertex sets with $|A|\ge x$ and $|B|\ge y$; it is anticomplete if there is no edge between $A$ and $B$, pure if it is complete or anticomplete, $c$-sparse if there are at most $c|A||B|$ edges between $A$ and $B$, and $c$-dense if there are at least $c|A||B|$. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov conjectured that for every $H$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that every $H$-free graph $G$ with $|G|>1$ contains a pure $(\varepsilon|G|^\varepsilon,\varepsilon|G|)$-pair (one side linear); in an $\varepsilon$-bounded graph no such pair can be complete, so this implies the sparse linear conjecture: for every $H$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that every $H$-free $\varepsilon$-bounded graph $G$ with $|G|>1$ has an anticomplete $(\varepsilon|G|^\varepsilon,\varepsilon|G|)$-pair. By a theorem of Rödl, $H$ satisfies the first conjecture if and only if both $H$ and $\overline{H}$ satisfy the second, so the two are equivalent over all $H$, though the second is much more tractable for particular $H$. A graph $H$ is almost-bipartite if it is triangle-free and its vertex set can be partitioned into a stable set and a set inducing a subgraph of maximum degree at most one (e.g. any graph in which every edge of another graph is subdivided at least once). The authors' main result is that every almost-bipartite $H$ satisfies the sparse linear conjecture; as a consequence the first conjecture also holds for $C_4$ and its complement. The case $H=K_3$ remains open.

name: AX_sparse_h_free_c_sparse_pairs
title: Conjecture 3.4
statement_text: For every graph $H$ there exist $\varepsilon, s > 0$ such that for every $H$-free $\varepsilon$-bounded graph $G$ with $|G| > 1$, and every $c$ with $0 \leq c \leq 1$, there is a $c$-sparse $(\varepsilon c^s |G|,\, \varepsilon|G|)$-pair in $G$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices, and $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph is isomorphic to $H$. $G$ is $\varepsilon$-bounded if $|N[v]|<\varepsilon|G|$ for every vertex $v$ (closed neighbourhood), i.e. maximum degree less than $\varepsilon|G|-1$. An $(x,y)$-pair is a pair $(A,B)$ of disjoint vertex sets with $|A|\ge x$ and $|B|\ge y$; it is anticomplete if there is no edge between $A$ and $B$, pure if it is complete or anticomplete, $c$-sparse if there are at most $c|A||B|$ edges between $A$ and $B$, and $c$-dense if there are at least $c|A||B|$. Erdős and Hajnal proved that for every $H$ there are $\varepsilon,s>0$ such that every $H$-free $G$ with $|G|>1$ contains, for every $0\le c\le1$, a $c$-sparse or a $(1-c)$-dense $(\varepsilon c^s|G|,\varepsilon c^s|G|)$-pair, a key step towards their bound $2^{\varepsilon\sqrt{\log|G|}}$ on cliques or stable sets. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov asked whether one side can be made linear, i.e. a $c$-sparse or $(1-c)$-dense $(\varepsilon c^s|G|,\varepsilon|G|)$-pair; in $\varepsilon$-bounded graphs the dense outcome is impossible, which gives this conjecture. The authors note the implications: the Conlon–Fox–Sudakov question implies this conjecture, which in turn implies the sparse linear conjecture (every $H$-free $\varepsilon$-bounded graph with $|G|>1$ has an anticomplete $(\varepsilon|G|^\varepsilon,\varepsilon|G|)$-pair). For almost-bipartite $H$ (triangle-free, with vertex set partitioned into a stable set and a set inducing maximum degree at most one) they prove a stronger statement: there are $\varepsilon,t>0$ such that every graph $G$ with $|G|>1$ and maximum degree less than $\varepsilon|G|$ contains, for every $0<c\le1$, either $\varepsilon c^t|G|^{|H|}$ induced copies of $H$ or a pair $A,B$ with $|A|\ge\varepsilon c^t|G|$, $|B|\ge\varepsilon|G|$ and at most $c|A||B|$ edges between them; in particular this conjecture holds for almost-bipartite $H$.

name: AX_bipartite_concatenation_phi_ceiling_formula
title: Informal Conjecture (Introduction) — analogue of Kneser's theorem
statement_text: Maybe something like the following is true (the authors' original 'wild conjecture' that the upper bound $\phi(x,y)\le \frac{\lceil kx\rceil+\lceil ky\rceil-1}{k}$, valid for every integer $k\ge 1$, is always attained turns out to be false, 'but perhaps not ridiculously false'): for all $x, y \in (0, 1]$, there is an integer $k > 0$ with $\phi(x, y) = \frac{\lceil kx \rceil + \lceil ky \rceil - 1}{k}$.
context_text: A tripartition of a graph $G$ is a partition $(A,B,C)$ of $V(G)$ into three nonempty stable sets. For $x,y\in(0,1]$, $G$ is $(x,y)$-constrained via $(A,B,C)$ if every vertex of $A$ has at least $x|B|$ neighbours in $B$, every vertex of $B$ has at least $y|C|$ neighbours in $C$, and there are no edges between $A$ and $C$. For a vertex $v$, $N^2_A(v)$ is the set of vertices of $A$ at distance exactly two from $v$. $\phi(x,y)$ is the maximum $z$ such that every $(x,y)$-constrained graph (via some $(A,B,C)$) has a vertex $v\in C$ with $|N^2_A(v)|\ge z|A|$ (the maximum exists). Trivially $\phi(x,y)\ge\max(x,y)$, and a circulant construction on three sets of size $k$ gives $\phi(x,y)\le\frac{\lceil kx\rceil+\lceil ky\rceil-1}{k}$ for every integer $k\ge1$. The authors were motivated by extending Kneser's theorem from additive group theory to a general graph-theoretic setting; the conjecture that this upper bound is always tight is false, but they suggest that something like it may still be true, leaving the correct characterisation of $\phi(x,y)$ open.

name: AX_bipartite_concatenation_psi_symmetry
title: Open Question — symmetry of $\psi$ (biconstrained case)
statement_text: Does $\psi(x, y) = \psi(y, x)$ hold for all $x, y \in (0, 1]$?
context_text: A tripartition of a graph $G$ is a partition $(A,B,C)$ of $V(G)$ into three nonempty stable sets. For $x,y\in(0,1]$, $G$ is $(x,y)$-constrained via $(A,B,C)$ if every vertex of $A$ has at least $x|B|$ neighbours in $B$, every vertex of $B$ has at least $y|C|$ neighbours in $C$, and there are no edges between $A$ and $C$; it is $(x,y)$-biconstrained if moreover every vertex of $B$ has at least $x|A|$ neighbours in $A$ and every vertex of $C$ has at least $y|B|$ neighbours in $B$. For a vertex $v$, $N^2_A(v)$ is the set of vertices of $A$ at distance exactly two from $v$. $\phi(x,y)$ is the maximum $z$ such that every $(x,y)$-constrained graph has a vertex $v\in C$ with $|N^2_A(v)|\ge z|A|$, and $\psi(x,y)$ is the same maximum taken over $(x,y)$-biconstrained graphs (both maxima exist, and $\phi\le\psi$). The authors prove, via a linear-programming argument, that $\phi(x,y)=\phi(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in(0,1]$, and remark that they have been unable to establish the analogous symmetry for $\psi$, although they have no counterexample.

name: AX_gnp_subgraph_count_anticoncentration_bound
title: Conjecture 1.12
statement_text: Fix $p \in (0,1)$ and fix a graph $H$ with $h$ non-isolated vertices. Let $G \in G(n,p)$. Then for any $x \in \mathbb{N}$, $$\Pr(X_H = x) = O\!\left(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_H)}\right) = O\!\left(1/n^{h-1}\right).$$
context_text: $G(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph on vertex set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ where each pair is an edge independently with probability $p$, and $X_H$ is the number of copies of the fixed graph $H$ in $G$ (subgraphs isomorphic to $H$); for fixed $p$ and $H$ with $h$ non-isolated vertices, $\mathrm{Var}(X_H)$ is of order $n^{2h-2}$, which gives the second equality. It is well known that $X_H$ satisfies a central limit theorem, but its anti-concentration (how likely it is to take one particular value) is less understood: a quantitative CLT of Barbour, Karoński and Ruciński gives $\Pr(X_H=x)=O(1/\sqrt n)$, and Meka, Nguyen and Vu proved $\Pr(X_H=x)\le n^{o(1)-1}$. The authors prove, via a Littlewood–Offord-type inequality for polynomials with nonnegative coefficients, that if a graph $G$ has $r$ edge-disjoint copies of $H$ then the number of copies of $H$ in the random subgraph $G_p$ (each edge kept with probability $p$) takes any given value with probability $O(1/\sqrt r)$, hence $O(1/n)$ in $G(n,p)$, and believe this is far from optimal. The conjectured bound would imply that the Lévy concentration function satisfies $\sup_x\Pr(x\le X_H\le x+t)=O((t+1)n^{1-h})$, which would be best possible by the CLT. The authors prove the coarse-scale bound $\Pr(|X_H-x|\le n^{h-2})=O(1/n)$ for any $H$ with an edge, and the almost-optimal $\Pr(X_{K_h}=x)\le n^{o(1)+1-h}$ for cliques; they note that a local limit theorem of Berkowitz implies a strengthening of the conjecture when $H$ is a clique, so the conjecture holds for cliques.

name: AX_surface_triangle_free_3_coloring_linear
title: Open Problem (linear-time 3-coloring output)
statement_text: Does there exist a linear-time algorithm to output a 3-coloring of a triangle-free graph embedded in a fixed surface (with a bounded number of precolored boundary vertices), using ideas similar to those of the authors' linear-time algorithm deciding 3-colorability of such graphs?
context_text: Here a surface is a compact connected 2-manifold, possibly with boundary (obtained from the sphere by adding handles and crosscaps and removing disjoint open discs); graphs are embedded in it, and vertices lying on the boundary are boundary vertices. For a fixed surface $\Sigma$ and integer $k$, the input is a triangle-free graph $G$ embedded in $\Sigma$ with at most $k$ boundary vertices together with a precoloring $\psi$ of the boundary vertices with colours $\{1,2,3\}$, and the task is to find a proper 3-coloring of $G$ extending $\psi$ (if one exists). 3-colorability of planar graphs is NP-complete, whereas Grötzsch's theorem says planar triangle-free graphs are 3-colorable. Building on their earlier result that in a 4-critical graph on a fixed surface almost all faces have length 4, and on their linear-time 3-coloring algorithm for quadrangulations, the authors give a linear-time algorithm deciding whether such a precoloring extends to a 3-coloring (it only decides whether there is a 4-critical subgraph, without producing a coloring), and a quadratic-time algorithm that also outputs a 3-coloring in the affirmative case, by reducing in quadratic time to graphs of girth at least 5. They believe a linear-time algorithm outputting a coloring exists, using ideas similar to those of the decision algorithm, but note significant technical challenges and leave it open; even for planar graphs, a linear-time algorithm finding the 3-coloring guaranteed by Grötzsch's theorem was found only recently (Dvořák, Kawarabayashi, Thomas).

name: AX_even_hole_k4_diamond_free_treewidth
title: Open Question: (even hole, K4, diamond)-free treewidth/cliquewidth
statement_text: Is it true that (even hole, $K_4$, diamond)-free graphs have bounded treewidth (or cliquewidth)?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; a graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and $(H_1,H_2,\dots)$-free if it is $H_i$-free for every $i$. A hole is a chordless cycle of length at least 4, even or odd according to its length; $K_t$ is the complete graph on $t$ vertices and the triangle is $K_3$. A theta is a graph formed by three internally vertex-disjoint chordless paths of length at least 2 between two vertices $a$ and $b$, with no edges between the paths other than those at $a$ and $b$ (a theta contains an even hole, so even-hole-free graphs are theta-free). A pyramid consists of three chordless paths $a\dots b_1$, $a\dots b_2$, $a\dots b_3$ of length at least 1, two of them of length at least 2, vertex-disjoint except at $a$, such that $b_1b_2b_3$ is a triangle and there are no other edges between the paths. For $0\le i\le j\le k$, $S_{i,j,k}$ is the tree obtained from a vertex $v$ by attaching three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges (so $S_{0,0,k}=P_{k+1}$, the path on $k+1$ vertices, and $S_{1,1,1}$ is the claw); these are exactly the subdivided claws and paths. The diamond is $K_4$ minus an edge. The authors prove that, for fixed $i,j,k,t$, (theta, triangle, $S_{i,j,k}$)-free graphs and (even hole, pyramid, $K_t$, $S_{i,j,k}$)-free graphs have bounded treewidth, while the first paper of the series shows that (theta, triangle)-free graphs and (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs (even (even hole, pyramid, $K_4$)-free graphs) have unbounded treewidth and cliquewidth. Known results: (even hole, diamond)-free graphs with no clique separator, and even (even hole, pyramid, diamond)-free graphs, have unbounded cliquewidth; even-hole-free graphs with no $K_t$-minor, and even-hole-free graphs of bounded maximum degree, have bounded treewidth. The question of excluding the diamond together with $K_4$ (instead of a subdivided claw) is listed by the authors as open.

statement_text: For every fixed integer $t \geq 4$, do (theta, triangle)-free graphs of maximum degree $t$ have bounded treewidth?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; a graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and $(H_1,H_2,\dots)$-free if it is $H_i$-free for every $i$. The authors prove that, for fixed $i,j,k,t$, (theta, triangle, $S_{i,j,k}$)-free graphs and (even hole, pyramid, $K_t$, $S_{i,j,k}$)-free graphs have bounded treewidth, while the first paper of the series shows that (theta, triangle)-free graphs and (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs (even (even hole, pyramid, $K_4$)-free graphs) have unbounded treewidth and cliquewidth. Known results (surveyed from Dabrowski and Paulusma): with $\mathcal{H}_U=\{P_7,S_{1,1,4},S_{2,2,2}\}$ and $\mathcal{H}_B=\{P_6,S_{1,1,3}\}$, the class of (triangle, $H$)-free graphs has unbounded cliquewidth if $H$ contains a graph of $\mathcal{H}_U$ as an induced subgraph, and bounded cliquewidth if $H$ is an induced subgraph of a graph of $\mathcal{H}_B$; (triangle, $S_{1,2,2}$)-free graphs also have bounded cliquewidth. The case $H=S_{1,2,3}$ is open; the authors refer to work of Dabrowski, Dross and Paulusma for other open problems of the same flavour.

name: AX_mis_complexity_even_hole_k4_free
title: Maximum Independent Set complexity for (even hole, K4)-free and (theta, triangle)-free graphs
statement_text: Determine the computational complexity of the Maximum Independent Set problem for (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs and for (theta, triangle)-free graphs.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; a graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and $(H_1,H_2,\dots)$-free if it is $H_i$-free for every $i$. A hole is a chordless cycle of length at least 4, even or odd according to its length; $K_t$ is the complete graph on $t$ vertices and the triangle is $K_3$. A theta is a graph formed by three internally vertex-disjoint chordless paths of length at least 2 between two vertices $a$ and $b$, with no edges between the paths other than those at $a$ and $b$ (a theta contains an even hole, so even-hole-free graphs are theta-free). A pyramid consists of three chordless paths $a\dots b_1$, $a\dots b_2$, $a\dots b_3$ of length at least 1, two of them of length at least 2, vertex-disjoint except at $a$, such that $b_1b_2b_3$ is a triangle and there are no other edges between the paths. For $0\le i\le j\le k$, $S_{i,j,k}$ is the tree obtained from a vertex $v$ by attaching three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges (so $S_{0,0,k}=P_{k+1}$, the path on $k+1$ vertices, and $S_{1,1,1}$ is the claw); these are exactly the subdivided claws and paths. An independent set is a set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices; the Maximum Independent Set problem asks for one of maximum cardinality. The authors prove that, for fixed $i,j,k,t$, (theta, triangle, $S_{i,j,k}$)-free graphs and (even hole, pyramid, $K_t$, $S_{i,j,k}$)-free graphs have bounded treewidth, while the first paper of the series shows that (theta, triangle)-free graphs and (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs (even (even hole, pyramid, $K_4$)-free graphs) have unbounded treewidth and cliquewidth. Bounded treewidth gives polynomial algorithms for Maximum Independent Set on the first class (the second was already known to be polynomial). Maximum Independent Set is known to be polynomial for (even hole, triangle)-free and (even hole, pyramid)-free graphs, the latter via a polynomial bound on the number of minimal separators; this method cannot work for (even hole, $K_4$)-free or (theta, triangle)-free graphs, which contain graphs (the $k$-ladders and $k$-turtles) with exponentially many minimal separators. The complexity for these two classes is stated as unknown.

name: AX_mis_complexity_subdivided_claw_free_p7
title: Maximum Independent Set complexity for H-free graphs when H contains P7, S1,1,3, or S1,2,2
statement_text: Determine the computational complexity of the Maximum Independent Set problem for $H$-free graphs whenever $H$ is some $S_{i,j,k}$ that contains either $P_7$, $S_{1,1,3}$, or $S_{1,2,2}$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; a graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and $(H_1,H_2,\dots)$-free if it is $H_i$-free for every $i$. A hole is a chordless cycle of length at least 4, even or odd according to its length; $K_t$ is the complete graph on $t$ vertices and the triangle is $K_3$. For $0\le i\le j\le k$, $S_{i,j,k}$ is the tree obtained from a vertex $v$ by attaching three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges (so $S_{0,0,k}=P_{k+1}$, the path on $k+1$ vertices, and $S_{1,1,1}$ is the claw); these are exactly the subdivided claws and paths. $H\subseteq H'$ means that $H$ is an induced subgraph of $H'$, and $(i,j,k)\le(1,1,2)$ is componentwise. The Maximum Independent Set problem asks for a set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices of maximum cardinality. Alekseev showed it is NP-hard on $H$-free graphs whenever $H$ is not an induced subgraph of some $S_{i,j,k}$. It is polynomial for $H$-free graphs when $H$ is an induced subgraph of $P_6$ (Lokshantov–Vatshelle–Villanger for $P_5$, Grzesik–Klimošová–Pilipczuk–Pilipczuk for $P_6$) or of $S_{i,j,k}$ with $(i,j,k)\le(1,1,2)$, and also for ($P_7$, triangle)-free and ($S_{1,2,4}$, triangle)-free graphs. name: AX_oriented_matroid_even_directed_circuit
title: Problem 1.4
statement_text: Given an oriented matroid $\vec{M}$, decide whether there exists a directed circuit of even size in $\vec{M}$.
context_text: An oriented matroid $\vec{M}$ on ground set $E$ is given by its signed circuits $(C^+,C^-)$ (pairs of disjoint subsets satisfying the oriented matroid axioms); their supports $C^+\cup C^-$ are the circuits of the underlying matroid. A signed circuit is directed if $C^+=\emptyset$ or $C^-=\emptyset$, and its size is $|C^+\cup C^-|$. Every digraph $D$ yields an oriented graphic matroid whose directed circuits are the edge sets of the directed cycles of $D$, so the problem generalizes the even dicycle problem (does a digraph have a directed cycle of even length?), solved in polynomial time by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas and independently McCuaig. A digraph is non-even if some edge set $J$ meets every directed cycle an odd number of times; Seymour and Thomassen showed that recognizing non-even digraphs is polynomially equivalent to the even dicycle problem. The authors define an oriented matroid to be non-even if its underlying matroid is regular and some $J\subseteq E$ meets every directed circuit an odd number of times, and prove that, for oriented regular matroids given by a totally unimodular matrix, detecting an even directed circuit is polynomially equivalent to recognizing non-even oriented matroids (odd directed circuits can be detected in polynomial time). For general oriented matroids accessed through a signed-circuit oracle, no algorithm with polynomially many oracle calls exists, even for graphic ones. The complexity remains open for regular oriented matroids in general; already the case of bond (cographic) matroids, i.e. deciding whether a digraph has a directed bond (minimal directed edge cut) of even size, is open.

name: AX_near_sunflower_exponential_bound
title: Near-sunflower analogue of the Erdős-Rado Sunflower Conjecture
statement_text: Let $r \geq 4$. If $\mathcal{F}$ is a $k$-uniform family of sets containing no near-sunflower of size $r$, then $|\mathcal{F}| \leq C^k$, where $C$ is a constant depending only on $r$.
context_text: A family of $r$ distinct sets is a sunflower if all pairwise intersections are equal, i.e. every element belongs to $0$, $1$ or $r$ of the sets; it is a near-sunflower of size $r$ if every element of the ground set belongs to $0$, $1$, $r-1$ or $r$ of the sets (this is interesting only for $r\ge4$, and is invariant under taking complements). A family is $k$-uniform if all its sets have $k$ elements; the ground set is arbitrary. The Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture asserts that a $k$-uniform family with no sunflower of size $r$ has at most $C_r^k$ members; the best known bound, of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang, is $(\log k)^{(1+o(1))k}$, and it applies a fortiori to near-sunflowers. This conjecture is a weaker version of Erdős–Rado. In the setting of subsets of $[n]$ (the Erdős–Szemerédi setting), the authors prove an exponential bound $c^n$ with $c<2$ for near-sunflower-free families, but they could not make progress on this conjecture, even for $r=4$. They prove $|\mathcal{F}|\le2.148^k$ for large $k$ under the stronger condition that $(A\triangle B)\cap(C\triangle D)\ne\emptyset$ for all distinct $A,B,C,D\in\mathcal{F}$. This is extremal set theory rather than graph theory.

name: AX_binary_focal_family_bound_not_tight
title: Informal conjecture on non-tightness of upper bound for binary focal families
statement_text: For $q = 2$ and large $n$, the upper bound $g^{q\text{-ff}}_r(n) \leq (r-1)\, q^{\lceil (r-2)n/(r-1) \rceil}$ (valid for all $q\ge2$ and $r\ge3$) is not tight.
context_text: A family $x^{(0)},x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(r-1)}$ of $r$ distinct vectors in $[q]^n$ is focal with focus $x^{(0)}$ if for every coordinate $i$, at least $r-2$ of the $r-1$ entries $x^{(1)}_i,\dots,x^{(r-1)}_i$ equal $x^{(0)}_i$. $g^{q\text{-ff}}_r(n)$ is the maximum size of a family in $[q]^n$ containing no focal family of size $r$ (for $q=2$, vectors are identified with subsets of $[n]$). The authors prove, for all $q\ge2$ and $r\ge3$, that $c\,\big(q/((q-1)(r-1)+1)^{1/(r-1)}\big)^n\le g^{q\text{-ff}}_r(n)\le(r-1)q^{\lceil(r-2)n/(r-1)\rceil}$ for some constant $c=c(q,r)>0$. When $q\ge n$ is a prime power, a Reed–Solomon-type construction gives $g^{q\text{-ff}}_r(n)\ge q^{\lceil(r-2)n/(r-1)\rceil}$, so the upper bound is tight up to a factor depending on $r$. For $q=2$ the authors believe it is not; as support, they show that for $r=4$ every linear subspace of $\{0,1\}^n$ of dimension at least $0.44n$ ($n$ large) contains a focal family of size $4$, whereas the general upper bound is $3\cdot2^{\lceil2n/3\rceil}$. Focal families are a special kind of near-sunflower (every element lies in $0$, $1$, $r-1$ or $r$ of the sets). This is extremal combinatorics of codes rather than graph theory.

name: AX_single_conflict_coloring_euler_genus_sqrt
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: There exist $C, C' > 0$ such that, for any simple graph $G$ that is embeddable on a surface of Euler genus $g$, if every edge is assigned at most $Ck$ conflicts from $[k]^2$, then $G$ is conflict $k$-colourable, provided $k \geq C'\sqrt{g}$.
context_text: In the conflict $k$-colouring problem (introduced by Dvořák and Postle, and by Fraigniaud, Heinrich and Kosowski), each edge $uv$ of a graph $G$ is assigned a list of ordered pairs, called conflicts, of colours from $[k]=\{1,\dots,k\}$, and one asks for a colouring $c:V\to[k]$ such that no edge is in a conflict, i.e. there is no edge $uv$ and conflict $(\kappa_u,\kappa_v)$ on it with $c(u)=\kappa_u$ and $c(v)=\kappa_v$. Having at most $\mu$ conflicts per edge is equivalent to having exactly one conflict per edge in a multigraph of maximum edge multiplicity $\mu$: a local $k$-partition of a multigraph is a family of maps $\kappa_v:E(v)\to[k]$ ($E(v)$ the edges at $v$), the edge $e=uv$ forbidding $c(u)=\kappa_u(e)$ together with $c(v)=\kappa_v(e)$; the single-conflict chromatic number $\chi_=(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $G$ is conflict-colourable for every local $k$-partition. It is at least the adaptable choosability and the separation choosability of $G$. The authors prove that for a multigraph of maximum multiplicity $\mu$ embeddable on a surface of Euler genus $g$, $\chi_=(G)\le\max\{C_1\sqrt{\mu}(g+1)^{1/4}\log(\mu^2(g+2)),8\mu\}$; in the regime $\mu=\Theta(\sqrt g)$ this gives $\chi_=(G)=O(\sqrt g\log g)$, evocative of Heawood's bound since both the number of colours and the multiplicity are around $\sqrt g$, and the conjecture asks to remove the logarithmic factor. The authors note that necessarily $C<1/2$, because of an example built from $K_{2,(2\mu)^2}$ with every edge of multiplicity $\mu$ (a planar multigraph with $\chi_=>2\mu$), and that a previous version of the manuscript incorrectly conjectured that $C$ could be taken arbitrarily close to $1$.
paper_title: Single-conflict colouring

name: AX_single_conflict_coloring_degenerate_log_n
title: Informal conjecture on single-conflict chromatic number of degenerate graphs
statement_text: There might yet be some constant $C' > 0$ such that the single-conflict chromatic number of any $d$-degenerate graph on $n$ vertices is at most $C'\sqrt{d}\log n$.
context_text: In the conflict $k$-colouring problem (introduced by Dvořák and Postle, and by Fraigniaud, Heinrich and Kosowski), each edge $uv$ of a graph $G$ is assigned a list of ordered pairs, called conflicts, of colours from $[k]=\{1,\dots,k\}$, and one asks for a colouring $c:V\to[k]$ such that no edge is in a conflict, i.e. there is no edge $uv$ and conflict $(\kappa_u,\kappa_v)$ on it with $c(u)=\kappa_u$ and $c(v)=\kappa_v$. Having at most $\mu$ conflicts per edge is equivalent to having exactly one conflict per edge in a multigraph of maximum edge multiplicity $\mu$: a local $k$-partition of a multigraph is a family of maps $\kappa_v:E(v)\to[k]$ ($E(v)$ the edges at $v$), the edge $e=uv$ forbidding $c(u)=\kappa_u(e)$ together with $c(v)=\kappa_v(e)$; the single-conflict chromatic number $\chi_=(G)$ is the least $k$ such that $G$ is conflict-colourable for every local $k$-partition. It is at least the adaptable choosability and the separation choosability of $G$. A graph is $d$-degenerate if each of its subgraphs has a vertex of degree at most $d$. The authors prove that a simple graph embeddable on a surface of Euler genus $g$ has $\chi_=(G)\le C(g+1)^{1/4}\log(g+2)$, and wonder whether degeneracy could give an alternative proof, as in Heawood's original approach for the chromatic number. A construction of Kostochka and Zhu shows that $d$-degenerate graphs can have single-conflict chromatic number greater than $d$, but the bound $C'\sqrt d\log n$ would still imply the surface result in the simple-graph case. The authors' general bound $\chi_=(G)\le C_2(\mu m)^{1/4}\log(\mu m)$ for multigraphs with $m\ge3$ edges and maximum multiplicity $\mu$ gives only $C_2(nd)^{1/4}\log(nd)$ here; they say they have not been able to prove the $\sqrt d\log n$ bound.

name: AX_heroic_sets_bounded_dichromatic_characterization
title: Problem 1.2
statement_text: What are the finite sets $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs for which the class $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ has bounded dichromatic number?
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs, but both arcs $xy$ and $yx$ (a digon) may be present; an oriented graph is a digraph with at most one arc between any two vertices. The dichromatic number $\vec\chi(D)$ is the minimum number of colours in a colouring of the vertices of $D$ in which no colour class contains a directed cycle (for a graph $G$ seen as the symmetric digraph $\overleftrightarrow{G}$ it equals $\chi(G)$). For a set $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs, $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ is the class of digraphs with no member of $\mathcal{F}$ as an induced subdigraph, and $\mathcal{F}$ is heroic if this class has bounded dichromatic number. $\overleftrightarrow{K_2}$ is the digon, $\overrightarrow{K_2}$ the single arc, $\overline{K}_k$ the digraph with $k$ vertices and no arc, and $TT_k$ the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices. A tournament $H$ is a hero if tournaments not containing $H$ have bounded dichromatic number, i.e. $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2,H\}$ is heroic (note that $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2)$ is the class of tournaments); Berger, Choromanski, Chudnovsky, Fox, Loebl, Scott, Seymour and Thomassé characterized heroes recursively. The problem is the digraph analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner question, asking which finite sets of forbidden induced subgraphs bound the chromatic number. A heroic set must contain a complete symmetric digraph $\overleftrightarrow{K_k}$, an oriented forest (an orientation of a forest), a tournament, and a symmetric forest, because of families of digraphs of growing dichromatic number; the unique heroic set of size two is $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overrightarrow{K_2}\}$. The paper focuses on heroic sets of size three: it shows that for a hero $H$ and $k,\alpha\ge2$, $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_k},\overline{K}_\alpha,H\}$ is heroic if and only if $H$ is transitive or $k=2$, and conjectures a characterization of the heroic sets $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},H,F\}$ with $H$ a hero and $F$ an oriented forest.
paper_title: Extension of Gyarfas-Sumner conjecture to digraphs

name: AX_heroic_sets_hero_oriented_forest
title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: Let $H$ be a hero and let $F$ be an oriented forest. The set $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2}, H, F\}$ is heroic if and only if: either $F$ is the disjoint union of oriented stars, or $H$ is a transitive tournament.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs, but both arcs $xy$ and $yx$ (a digon) may be present; an oriented graph is a digraph with at most one arc between any two vertices. The dichromatic number $\vec\chi(D)$ is the minimum number of colours in a colouring of the vertices of $D$ in which no colour class contains a directed cycle (for a graph $G$ seen as the symmetric digraph $\overleftrightarrow{G}$ it equals $\chi(G)$). For a set $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs, $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ is the class of digraphs with no member of $\mathcal{F}$ as an induced subdigraph, and $\mathcal{F}$ is heroic if this class has bounded dichromatic number. $\overleftrightarrow{K_2}$ is the digon, $\overrightarrow{K_2}$ the single arc, $\overline{K}_k$ the digraph with $k$ vertices and no arc, and $TT_k$ the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices. A tournament $H$ is a hero if tournaments not containing $H$ have bounded dichromatic number, i.e. $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2,H\}$ is heroic (note that $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2)$ is the class of tournaments); Berger, Choromanski, Chudnovsky, Fox, Loebl, Scott, Seymour and Thomassé characterized heroes recursively. An oriented forest is an orientation of a forest, an oriented star is an orientation of a star (a tree with at most one vertex of degree more than 1), and a disjoint union of oriented stars is an oriented forest whose components are oriented stars. Forbidding $\overleftrightarrow{K_2}$ restricts to oriented graphs, so this is a digraph analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture for oriented graphs. The authors prove the 'only if' direction. When both conditions hold ($H$ transitive and $F$ a disjoint union of oriented stars), Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour proved that even the chromatic number of the underlying graphs is bounded. As partial evidence the authors prove that $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\vec C_3,\overrightarrow{K_2}+K_1\}$ is heroic, where $\vec C_3$ is the directed triangle and $+$ denotes disjoint union, and that oriented graphs with no induced directed path on 3 arcs and no orientation of $K_4$ have bounded dichromatic number.

name: AX_heroic_sets_clique_oriented_forest
title: Conjecture 4.4
statement_text: Given an oriented forest $F$ and for every integer $k$, $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2}, K_k, F\}$ is heroic.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs, but both arcs $xy$ and $yx$ (a digon) may be present; an oriented graph is a digraph with at most one arc between any two vertices. The dichromatic number $\vec\chi(D)$ is the minimum number of colours in a colouring of the vertices of $D$ in which no colour class contains a directed cycle (for a graph $G$ seen as the symmetric digraph $\overleftrightarrow{G}$ it equals $\chi(G)$). For a set $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs, $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ is the class of digraphs with no member of $\mathcal{F}$ as an induced subdigraph, and $\mathcal{F}$ is heroic if this class has bounded dichromatic number. $\overleftrightarrow{K_2}$ is the digon, $\overrightarrow{K_2}$ the single arc, $\overline{K}_k$ the digraph with $k$ vertices and no arc, and $TT_k$ the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices. A tournament $H$ is a hero if tournaments not containing $H$ have bounded dichromatic number, i.e. $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2,H\}$ is heroic (note that $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2)$ is the class of tournaments); Berger, Choromanski, Chudnovsky, Fox, Loebl, Scott, Seymour and Thomassé characterized heroes recursively. Here $K_k$ is the (undirected) complete graph: when an undirected graph is put in the forbidden set, all of its orientations are forbidden, so $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\overleftrightarrow{K_2},K_k,F)$ is the class of oriented graphs whose underlying graph has clique number less than $k$ and with no induced copy of the oriented forest $F$ (an orientation of a forest). The authors conjecture that, for a hero $H$ and an oriented forest $F$, $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},H,F\}$ is heroic if and only if $F$ is a disjoint union of oriented stars or $H$ is a transitive tournament. Since every tournament on at least $2^k$ vertices contains $TT_k$, the special case of that conjecture where $H=TT_k$ for every $k$ is equivalent to this conjecture, which is thus a $\chi$-boundedness-type statement for the dichromatic number of oriented graphs. The authors prove the case $k=4$, $F=P^+(3)$, the directed path with 3 arcs.

name: AX_heroic_sets_minimal_tournament_families
title: Research direction: minimal heroic tournament families
statement_text: Characterize all finite and minimal families $\mathcal{H} = \{H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_k\}$ of tournaments such that $\{\overline{K_2}, \overleftrightarrow{K_2}, H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_k\}$ is a heroic set.
context_text: Digraphs have no loops or parallel arcs, but both arcs $xy$ and $yx$ (a digon) may be present; an oriented graph is a digraph with at most one arc between any two vertices. The dichromatic number $\vec\chi(D)$ is the minimum number of colours in a colouring of the vertices of $D$ in which no colour class contains a directed cycle (for a graph $G$ seen as the symmetric digraph $\overleftrightarrow{G}$ it equals $\chi(G)$). For a set $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs, $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ is the class of digraphs with no member of $\mathcal{F}$ as an induced subdigraph, and $\mathcal{F}$ is heroic if this class has bounded dichromatic number. $\overleftrightarrow{K_2}$ is the digon, $\overrightarrow{K_2}$ the single arc, $\overline{K}_k$ the digraph with $k$ vertices and no arc, and $TT_k$ the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices. A tournament $H$ is a hero if tournaments not containing $H$ have bounded dichromatic number, i.e. $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2,H\}$ is heroic (note that $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\overleftrightarrow{K_2},\overline{K}_2)$ is the class of tournaments); Berger, Choromanski, Chudnovsky, Fox, Loebl, Scott, Seymour and Thomassé characterized heroes recursively. Since $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\overline{K_2},\overleftrightarrow{K_2})$ is the class of tournaments, the question asks for the minimal finite sets of tournaments whose exclusion bounds the dichromatic number of tournaments. The characterization of heroes by Berger et al. settles the case of families of size 1, and implies that a minimal family of size 2 or more cannot contain a hero. Berger et al. also implicitly show that larger minimal heroic sets exist: they identify five tournaments $H_1,\dots,H_5$ (among them $C_3(\overrightarrow{K_2},\overrightarrow{K_2},\overrightarrow{K_2})$ and $C_3(\vec C_3,\vec C_3,K_1)$, where $C_3(D_1,D_2,D_3)$ has all arcs from $D_1$ to $D_2$, from $D_2$ to $D_3$ and from $D_3$ to $D_1$) such that the heroes are exactly the tournaments containing none of them; since every hero is 2-dicolourable, $\{\overline{K_2},\overleftrightarrow{K_2},H_1,\dots,H_5\}$ is heroic, and any minimal heroic subset of it has at least four elements. The authors call the characterization an interesting direction of research.
