name: AX_planar_fractional_vertex_arboricity_2
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: Every planar graph has fractional vertex-arboricity at most two.
context_text: A fractional arborization of a graph $G$ assigns to each vertex $v$ a measurable set $\phi(v)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ of Lebesgue measure one such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, the vertices $v$ with $\alpha\in\phi(v)$ induce a forest; it is a fractional $k$-arborization if all $\phi(v)\subseteq(0,k)$, and the fractional vertex-arboricity $\mathrm{va}_f(G)$ is the infimum of the reals $k$ for which a fractional $k$-arborization exists. Equivalently it is the fractional relaxation of the vertex-arboricity $\mathrm{va}(G)$, the minimum number of classes in a partition of $V(G)$ into sets inducing forests. With $a(G)$ the maximum size of a vertex set inducing a forest, $|V(G)|/a(G)\le\mathrm{va}_f(G)\le\mathrm{va}(G)$, and $\chi_f(G)\le 2\,\mathrm{va}_f(G)$. The conjecture generalizes the Albertson–Berman conjecture (1979) that $a(G)\ge|V(G)|/2$ for planar $G$ (tight for $K_4$); if true, it would also give $\chi_f(G)\le4$ for planar graphs, a consequence of the Four Color Theorem for which no other proof is known. Planar graphs can have vertex-arboricity three, and Borodin's acyclic 5-colouring theorem gives $\mathrm{va}_f(G)\le5/2$ (and $a(G)\ge2|V(G)|/5$); any improvement on $5/2$ would be significant. The authors make analogous conjectures for triangle-free planar graphs ($8/5$) and planar graphs of girth at least five ($10/7$), and prove that planar graphs of girth at least five have fractional vertex-arboricity at most $2-1/324$.
paper_title: Fractional vertex-arboricity of planar graphs

name: AX_shortest_even_hole_detection
title: Open Problem: Finding a Shortest Even Hole
statement_text: Find, in polynomial time, a shortest even hole in a graph (if one exists).
context_text: A hole in a graph is an induced cycle of length at least four; it is even or odd according to the parity of its length (number of edges), and $|G|$ denotes the number of vertices. For odd holes, polynomial algorithms are known to detect an odd hole ($O(|G|^9)$ by Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour and Spirkl, improved to $O(|G|^8)$ by Lai, Lu and Thorup), to detect an odd hole of length at least $\ell$ for fixed $\ell$, and to find a shortest odd hole in time $O(|G|^{14})$ (Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour). For even holes, detection is polynomial (Conforti, Cornuéjols, Kapoor and Vušković; Chudnovsky, Kawarabayashi and Seymour; Chang and Lu; $O(|G|^9)$ by Lai, Lu and Thorup), and this paper gives a polynomial algorithm to detect an even hole of length at least $\ell$ for every fixed $\ell$. The remaining analogue, finding a shortest even hole if there is one, the authors have not been able to solve.
notes: Stated informally in the introduction without a labelled environment.
paper_title: Detecting a long even hole

name: AX_holes_length_divisible_3_detection
title: Open Question: Detecting Holes of Length Divisible by Three
statement_text: Can holes whose length is a multiple of three be detected in polynomial time?
context_text: A hole in a graph is an induced cycle of length at least four; it is even or odd according to the parity of its length (number of edges), and $|G|$ denotes the number of vertices. Polynomial-time algorithms are known for detecting odd holes, even holes, long odd holes and (by this paper) even holes of length at least any fixed $\ell$. On the other hand, a result of Hajebi (private communication) shows that when $\ell$ is part of the input, detecting a hole of length at least $\ell$ in a prescribed residue class modulo a fixed $m\ge2$ is W[1]-hard. The authors remark that even versus odd has been almost the entire focus of previous research, and ask about holes whose length is a multiple of three: triangle-free graphs with no such hole have very interesting structural properties, but the authors currently have no idea how to recognize such graphs.
notes: Stated informally in the introduction as a rhetorical open question; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Detecting a long even hole

name: AX_crossing_number_kn_minus_matching
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: The crossing number of $M_{n,t}$ is equal to $$H(n) - \frac{1}{2}\,t(k-1)(k-2),$$ where $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.
context_text: For $n\ge5$ and $0\le t\le n/2$, $M_{n,t}$ is the graph obtained from the complete graph $K_n$ by removing a matching of size $t$, and $H(n)=\frac14\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-1}2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-2}2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-3}2\rfloor$ is the Hill number, conjectured (Harary–Hill) to be the crossing number of $K_n$. The authors work with antipodal point sets on the unit sphere: take a set $P$ of $k$ points in general position, add the antipodal point $\bar p$ of each $p\in P$ (so $n=2k$), and join every two non-antipodal points by a geodesic (shorter great-circle arc); this draws $K_n$ minus a perfect matching with $\frac14k(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)$ crossings, and each added half-circle joining an antipodal pair creates $\frac12(k-1)(k-2)$ more crossings. A point set has strength $s$ if half-circles joining each of its points to its antipode can be chosen so that they cross each other exactly $s$ times. If $P'\subseteq P$ has strength $0$ and $|P\setminus P'|=t$, adding the half-circles for $P'$ gives a geodesic drawing of $M_{n,t}$ with $H(n)-\frac12t(k-1)(k-2)$ crossings (and of $K_n$ with $H(n)$ crossings when $t=0$). Since sets of strength $0$ are abundant, the authors conjecture that this number is the crossing number of $M_{n,t}$ (for $t=0$ this is Hill's conjecture). The paper's construction is for even $n=2k$; reading $k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ for odd $n$ is the natural interpretation, as the paper does not define $k$ explicitly in the conjecture.
notes: PDF source; the algebraic expression is unambiguous.
paper_title: On a conjecture by Anthony Hill

name: AX_induced_detour_path_excess_3
title: Open Problem (induced st-path of excess length three)
statement_text: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm to test whether a graph contains an induced path between specified vertices $s, t$ of length at least three more than the shortest $st$-path?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, and the length of a path is its number of edges. Given two vertices $s,t$ of a graph $G$, the question is whether $G$ has an induced path from $s$ to $t$ whose length exceeds the distance between $s$ and $t$ by at least three. Berger, Spirkl and Seymour (Seymour being a co-author of this paper) have a polynomial-time algorithm to test whether there is an induced $st$-path longer than the shortest $st$-path (i.e. of excess at least one). The authors mention, as related work on detecting long induced subgraphs of specific type, that the corresponding problem for excess at least three is open. The paper itself gives, for every fixed $\ell\ge5$, a polynomial-time algorithm testing whether a graph has an odd hole (induced cycle of length at least four) of length at least $\ell$.
notes: Stated in passing as 'It is open whether...' with no formal label. Arises from related work by Berger, Spirkl, and Seymour; one of the present paper's authors (Seymour) is involved in the related work.
paper_title: Detecting a long odd hole

name: AX_long_odd_hole_heavy_path_lemma
title: Informal Conjecture (heavy path extension)
statement_text: If $C$ is a shortest long odd hole in a graph $G$ and $M$ is a set of $C$-major vertices such that one vertex of $M$ is nonadjacent to all the others, then there exists a path of $C$ of bounded length such that every vertex of $M$ has a neighbour in that path.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices of $G$, and the length of a path or cycle is its number of edges. A hole of $G$ is an induced subgraph that is a cycle of length at least four. Throughout, $\ell\ge5$ is a fixed integer, and a long path or hole is one of length at least $\ell$. If $C$ is a hole of $G$, a vertex $v\in V(G)\setminus V(C)$ is $C$-major if there is no three-vertex path of $C$ containing all the neighbours of $v$ in $V(C)$; $C$ is clean if no vertex is $C$-major. A shortest long odd hole is a long odd hole of minimum length. Bounded length means bounded by a constant depending only on $\ell$. The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm to test for a long odd hole, using the cleaning method: one generates polynomially many sets $X$ such that, if $G$ has a long odd hole, some $X$ contains all $C$-major vertices of a shortest long odd hole $C$ and no vertex of $C$. In the earlier odd hole detection algorithm (the case without the length constraint), the cleaning list relied on a theorem that if $C$ is a shortest odd hole and $M$ is a set of $C$-major vertices such that one vertex of $M$ is nonadjacent to all the others, then $C$ has a heavy edge $uv$, i.e. every vertex of $M$ is adjacent to $u$ or $v$. The authors tried to extend this to shortest long odd holes, where a heavy path of $C$ of bounded length would serve just as well; they say this extension might be true but they were unable to prove it, and instead prove that there is a bounded set of paths of $C$, each of bounded length, such that every vertex of $M$ has a neighbour in one of them, and only when the exceptional vertex of $M$ is carefully chosen.
notes: Stated as 'this extension might be true, but we were unable to prove it.' No formal labelled environment. PDF source — math notation may be partially garbled.
paper_title: Detecting a long odd hole

name: AX_long_odd_hole_detection_running_time
title: Open Question (running time improvement for long hole detection)
statement_text: Can the running times of $O(|G|^{\ell+1})$ for detecting a long hole and $O(|G|^{20\ell+40})$ for detecting a long odd hole — both $|G|^{O(\ell)}$ — be substantially improved for fixed $\ell$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices of $G$, and the length of a path or cycle is its number of edges. A hole of $G$ is an induced subgraph that is a cycle of length at least four. Throughout, $\ell\ge5$ is a fixed integer, and a long path or hole is one of length at least $\ell$. The authors give an algorithm deciding whether $G$ has a long odd hole (an odd hole of length at least $\ell$) in time $O(|G|^{20\ell+40})$, without trying hard to optimise the exponent. Testing for a long hole (of any parity) is easy: enumerate all induced paths of length $\ell-1$ and test whether each extends to a hole, in time $O(|G|^{\ell+1})$. Both problems are NP-hard when $\ell$ is part of the input (for long holes, subdivide each edge of an $n$-vertex graph once and take $\ell=2n$: there is a long hole if and only if the original graph is Hamiltonian; for long odd holes, take $n$ odd, subdivide every edge twice and take $\ell=3n$). The authors do not know whether either running time $|G|^{O(\ell)}$ can be substantially improved.
notes: Stated as 'We do not know if either can be substantially improved.' No formal labelled environment.
paper_title: Detecting a long odd hole

name: AX_even_hole_free_bounded_degree_treewidth
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: There is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every even-hole-free graph of degree at most $d$ has tree-width at most $f(d)$.
context_text: Graphs are simple and undirected; a hole is an induced cycle of length at least $4$, it is even or odd according to its number of edges, and a graph is even-hole-free if it has no even hole as an induced subgraph. Here 'degree at most $d$' means maximum degree at most $d$. The class of all even-hole-free graphs has unbounded tree-width (it contains all complete graphs and all chordal graphs), even-hole-free graphs with no triangle have bounded tree-width, but Sintiari and Trotignon constructed (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs of unbounded tree-width; that construction uses vertices of large degree and large clique minors, which motivates the conjecture. If true, it would imply that even-hole-freeness is testable with constant query complexity and polylogarithmic running time in the bounded-degree graph model of property testing, via CMSO testability on graphs of bounded degree and bounded tree-width. The authors prove that every even-hole-free graph excluding $K_\ell$ as a minor has tree-width bounded by a function of $\ell$, prove the conjecture for $d\le 3$ (every subcubic even-hole-free graph, and even every subcubic (theta, prism)-free graph, has tree-width at most $3$), and prove for $d=4$ the weaker statement that (even hole, pyramid)-free graphs of maximum degree at most $4$ have bounded tree-width. The conjecture is trivial for $d\le 2$.
paper_title: On the tree-width of even-hole-free graphs

name: AX_bounded_degree_treewidth_induced_wall
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f_d : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every graph with degree at most $d$ and tree-width at least $f_d(k)$ contains a $(k \times k)$-wall or the line graph of a $(k \times k)$-wall as an induced subgraph.
context_text: Graphs are simple and undirected; 'degree at most $d$' means maximum degree at most $d$. An elementary $(k\times k)$-wall is the usual wall of the excluded-grid theorem: a hexagonal grid (brick wall) of maximum degree $3$ with $k$ horizontal paths and $k$ vertical paths; a $(k\times k)$-wall is any subdivision of an elementary $(k\times k)$-wall. Robertson and Seymour proved that graphs of large tree-width contain a large wall as a subgraph; this cannot be strengthened to induced subgraphs in general, since $K_n$ has tree-width $n-1$. The authors prove an induced grid theorem for minor-free graphs: for every graph $H$ there is $f_H$ such that every $H$-minor-free graph of tree-width at least $f_H(k)$ contains a $(k\times k)$-wall or the line graph of a chordless $(k\times k)$-wall (a graph is chordless if no cycle of length at least $4$ has a chord) as an induced subgraph. Graphs with no induced subdivision of a $6\times 3$ wall and with arbitrarily large tree-width and girth exist, but their construction (like that of (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs of unbounded tree-width) needs vertices of large degree and large clique minors, which motivates this bounded-degree analogue. It is described as wide open, and it implies the authors' conjecture that even-hole-free graphs of bounded degree have bounded tree-width. Status note (November 2026): proved by Korhonen ('Grid induced minor theorem for graphs of small degree', arXiv 2203.13233, 2022; J. Combin. Theory Ser. B, 2023): graphs of maximum degree at most $d$ and treewidth at least $f(k,d)=O(k^{10}+2^{d^5})$ contain the $k\times k$ grid as an induced minor, which together with the routing arguments of Aboulker, Adler, Kim, Sintiari and Trotignon gives the wall statement.
paper_title: On the tree-width of even-hole-free graphs

name: AX_list_ramsey_k12_odd_k
title: Open question on $R_\ell(K_{1,2}, k)$ for odd $k$
statement_text: We do not know whether $R_\ell(K_{1,2}, k)$ is $k + 1$ or $k + 2$ when $k$ is odd.
context_text: The $k$-colour list Ramsey number $R_\ell(G,k)$ of a graph $G$ (the subscript $\ell$ stands for "list") is the minimum $n$ such that there is an assignment $L$ of lists of $k$ colours (subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ of size $k$) to the edges of $K_n$ such that every $L$-colouring of $E(K_n)$ (each edge receives a colour from its own list) contains a monochromatic copy of $G$; $R(G,k)$ is the ordinary $k$-colour Ramsey number, obtained when all lists are equal, so $R_\ell(G,k)\le R(G,k)$. An edge-colouring has no monochromatic $K_{1,2}$ if and only if it is proper, so $R(K_{1,2},k)$ (resp. $R_\ell(K_{1,2},k)$) is the smallest $n$ with $\chi'(K_n)>k$ (resp. $\chi'_\ell(K_n)>k$), where $\chi'_\ell$ is the list chromatic index (the list chromatic number of the line graph). Häggkvist and Janssen proved $\chi'_\ell(K_n)\le n$ for every $n$, so $\chi'_\ell(K_n)=\chi'(K_n)$ for odd $n$; this gives $R_\ell(K_{1,2},k)=k+1=R(K_{1,2},k)$ when $k$ is even. For odd $k$, $R(K_{1,2},k)=k+2$, and deciding whether $R_\ell(K_{1,2},k)$ equals $k+1$ or $k+2$ amounts to deciding whether $\chi'_\ell(K_{k+1})=k+1$ or $k$, i.e. the List Colouring Conjecture ($\chi'_\ell=\chi'$) for cliques of even order $k+1$, which is open. The authors conjecture more generally that $R_\ell(K_{1,r},k)=R(K_{1,r},k)$ for all $r,k$; they prove the two differ by at most one and are equal for two colours or for $r$ large compared to $k$.
notes: Stated in prose; directly tied to the open case of the List Colouring Conjecture for cliques of even order.
paper_title: List Ramsey numbers

name: AX_list_ramsey_clique_2_colors_equality
title: Open problem on equality $R_\ell(K_r, 2) = R(K_r, 2)$ for $r > 3$
statement_text: For $r > 3$ we cannot even decide the equality of the two Ramsey numbers $R_\ell(K_r,2)$ (list Ramsey number) and $R(K_r,2)$ (ordinary Ramsey number) of $K_r$ when $k = 2$.
context_text: The $k$-colour list Ramsey number $R_\ell(G,k)$ of a graph $G$ (the subscript $\ell$ stands for "list") is the minimum $n$ such that there is an assignment $L$ of lists of $k$ colours (subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ of size $k$) to the edges of $K_n$ such that every $L$-colouring of $E(K_n)$ (each edge receives a colour from its own list) contains a monochromatic copy of $G$; $R(G,k)$ is the ordinary $k$-colour Ramsey number, obtained when all lists are equal, so $R_\ell(G,k)\le R(G,k)$. The classic probabilistic lower bounds for $R(K_r,2)$ all go through in the list setting, hence $2^{r/2}<R_\ell(K_r,2)\le R(K_r,2)<2^{2r}$, and the authors cannot improve the lower bound. It is not difficult to see that $R_\ell(K_3,2)=6=R(K_3,2)$, but for larger cliques it is open whether the list and ordinary 2-colour Ramsey numbers coincide. In their concluding remarks the authors ask more generally whether $R_\ell(K_r,k)=R(K_r,k)$ for all $r,k$. A conjecture, posted on MathOverflow, that $R_\ell(G,k)=R(G,k)$ always holds is disproved in the paper (for instance for matchings, and for $\ell$-uniform hypergraph cliques with $\ell\ge3$ the list Ramsey number is at most single exponential while the ordinary one grows like a tower).
notes: Stated in prose. The extracted text does not include Section 3 (the paper's dedicated open problems section), so further explicit problems posed there are not captured here.
paper_title: List Ramsey numbers

name: AX_4_colorability_fixed_surface_complexity
title: 4-colorability on Fixed Surfaces (Open Step in Thomassen's Program)
statement_text: Whether 4-colorability of graphs embedded in a fixed surface can be tested in polynomial time remains open; the authors remark that prospects for its resolution in the near future are not very bright.
context_text: Thomassen initiated a research program asking whether, for fixed integers $k$ and $q$, the $k$-colorability of graphs of girth at least $q$ embedded in a fixed surface can be tested in polynomial time. A graph is $4$-critical if it is not 3-colorable but all its proper subgraphs are. Grötzsch's theorem says that triangle-free planar graphs are 3-colorable, but on every non-planar surface there are infinitely many $4$-critical graphs, and Gimbel and Thomassen characterized the 3-colorable triangle-free graphs in the projective plane (no subgraph that is a non-bipartite quadrangulation). The authors' main theorem states that there is a constant $\kappa$ such that every $4$-critical graph $G$ embedded in a surface of Euler genus $g$, with $t$ triangles and $c$ four-cycles not bounding a 2-cell face, satisfies $\sum_{f}(|f|-4)\le\kappa(g+t+c-1)$, the sum being over the faces $f$ of $G$. They announce that this yields a polynomial-time (even linear-time) algorithm testing whether a triangle-free graph embedded in a fixed surface is 3-colorable, which settles a problem of Gimbel and Thomassen and completes one of the two missing steps of Thomassen's program. The other missing step concerns 4-coloring graphs embedded in a fixed surface, and the authors remark that prospects for its resolution in the near future are not very bright.
notes: Stated informally in the introduction as the outstanding second step of Thomassen's research program; no formal problem number is assigned.
paper_title: Three-coloring triangle-free graphs on surfaces IV. Bounding face sizes of 4-critical graphs

name: AX_symmetric_intersecting_vector_families_size
title: Size of symmetric intersecting families in $[k]^n$
statement_text: How large can a symmetric, intersecting subfamily of $[k]^n$ really be (for fixed $k \geq 3$)?
context_text: Here $[k]^n$ is the set of vectors of length $n$ with entries in $[k]=\{1,\dots,k\}$, and $k\ge3$ is fixed while $n\to\infty$. A family $A\subseteq[k]^n$ is intersecting if any two of its vectors agree in at least one coordinate. The symmetric group $S_n$ acts on $[k]^n$ by permuting coordinates, and $A$ is symmetric if its automorphism group $\{\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(A)=A\}$ is transitive on $[n]$. Without symmetry the largest intersecting families have size $k^{n-1}$ (fix one coordinate). For $k=2$ and $n$ odd, the vectors with more $1$'s than $2$'s form an intersecting family of size $2^{n-1}$ invariant under all of $S_n$, but nothing similar happens for $k\ge3$: the authors prove that there is a universal $c>0$ such that every symmetric intersecting $A\subseteq[k]^n$ has $|A|=O(k^n/n^{c/k})$, in particular $|A|=o(k^n)$. A family $A$ is set-intersecting if there are a symmetric intersecting family $\mathcal{B}$ of subsets of $[n]$ (any two members meet, with transitive automorphism group) and $\ell\in[k]$ such that $x\in A$ if and only if $x_i=\ell$ for all $i\in B$, for some $B\in\mathcal{B}$; such $A$ is symmetric and intersecting. Taking $n=q^2+q+1$ with $q$ a prime power and $\mathcal{B}$ the lines of the projective plane $PG(2,q)$ gives size roughly $k^{n-\sqrt{n}}$, the best construction known to the authors. The authors describe determining the true maximum size as the most obvious question raised by their work. This is extremal set theory rather than graph theory.
notes: PDF source — math notation may be garbled. No labeled environment; described by the authors as 'the most obvious question raised by the present work' in Section 4.
paper_title: On symmetric intersecting families of vectors

name: AX_symmetric_intersecting_vector_families_set_intersecting
title: Largest symmetric intersecting families are set-intersecting
statement_text: It seems possible (but maybe impossible to prove) that the largest symmetric intersecting families in $[k]^n$ are set-intersecting.

name: AX_symmetric_intersecting_vector_families_polynomial_gain

statement_text: Show that there exist constants $c, \delta > 0$ (possibly depending on $k$) such that for any symmetric intersecting $A \subset [k]^n$, we have $\log_k |A| \leq n - cn^{\delta}$.
context_text: Here $[k]^n$ is the set of vectors of length $n$ with entries in $[k]=\{1,\dots,k\}$, and $k\ge3$ is fixed while $n\to\infty$. A family $A\subseteq[k]^n$ is intersecting if any two of its vectors agree in at least one coordinate. For $k=2$ and $n$ odd, the vectors with more $1$'s than $2$'s form an intersecting family of size $2^{n-1}$ invariant under all of $S_n$, but nothing similar happens for $k\ge3$: the authors prove that there is a universal $c>0$ such that every symmetric intersecting $A\subseteq[k]^n$ has $|A|=O(k^n/n^{c/k})$, in particular $|A|=o(k^n)$. name: AX_neighbor_sum_distinguishing_delta_plus_constant
title: Open Problem: $\Delta + O(1)$ bound for neighbour sum distinguishing colourings
statement_text: It is an intriguing open problem whether a $\Delta + O(1)$ bound holds on the number of colours required for a neighbour sum distinguishing edge colouring.
context_text: Graphs have no parallel edges, and colourings are edge colourings. For a proper edge colouring $c$ of $G$ and a vertex $u$, $S_c(u)$ is the set of colours on the edges incident to $u$; $c$ is adjacent vertex distinguishing (an AVD-colouring) if $S_c(u)\ne S_c(v)$ for every edge $uv$ (a constraint only when $u,v$ have the same degree). Zhang, Liu and Wang conjectured in 2002 that every graph with maximum degree $\Delta\ge3$ and no isolated edge has an AVD-colouring with $\Delta+2$ colours ($C_5$ needs five colours). Hatami proved, with the Local Lemma, that $\Delta+300$ colours suffice when $\Delta>10^{20}$, and the authors improve this to $\Delta+19$ for large enough $\Delta$ using entropy compression. A neighbour sum distinguishing colouring is a proper edge colouring with positive integer colours such that for every edge $uv$, the sum of the colours of the edges incident to $u$ differs from the sum of the colours of the edges incident to $v$; it is in particular an AVD-colouring. Flandrin et al. conjectured that every graph with no isolated edge and maximum degree $\Delta\ge3$ has such a colouring with colours in $\{1,\dots,\Delta+2\}$, a strengthening of the Zhang–Liu–Wang conjecture. The best known asymptotic bound on the number of colours, due to Przybyło, is $\Delta+O(\Delta^{1/2})$. The authors note that neither Hatami's proof for AVD-colourings nor their own entropy compression argument seems adaptable to this setting.
notes: Stated in running prose without a labelled environment; clearly posed as an open problem by the authors.
paper_title: Progress on the adjacent vertex distinguishing edge colouring conjecture

name: AX_avd_edge_coloring_probabilistic_barrier
title: Informal Conjecture: probabilistic methods insufficient for the $\Delta+2$ bound
statement_text: One could suspect, as we do, that probabilistic methods such as the Local Lemma or entropy compression will probably not be enough on their own to prove the $\Delta+2$ bound from the conjecture of Zhang, Liu and Wang (every graph with maximum degree $\Delta\geq 3$ and no isolated edge has an AVD-colouring with $\Delta+2$ colours), assuming the conjecture is true.
context_text: Graphs have no parallel edges, and colourings are edge colourings. For a proper edge colouring $c$ of $G$ and a vertex $u$, $S_c(u)$ is the set of colours on the edges incident to $u$; $c$ is adjacent vertex distinguishing (an AVD-colouring) if $S_c(u)\ne S_c(v)$ for every edge $uv$ (a constraint only when $u,v$ have the same degree). Zhang, Liu and Wang conjectured in 2002 that every graph with maximum degree $\Delta\ge3$ and no isolated edge has an AVD-colouring with $\Delta+2$ colours ($C_5$ needs five colours). Hatami proved, with the Local Lemma, that $\Delta+300$ colours suffice when $\Delta>10^{20}$, and the authors improve this to $\Delta+19$ for large enough $\Delta$ using entropy compression. The authors find it remarkable that probabilistic techniques come so close to the conjectured bound and see this as extra supporting evidence for the conjecture, but suspect that such methods alone cannot reach $\Delta+2$ since, intuitively, some extra colours are bound to be 'wasted' in any random process. This is a methodological belief rather than a precise mathematical statement.
notes: Conjectural belief expressed in prose using 'one could suspect, as we do'; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Progress on the adjacent vertex distinguishing edge colouring conjecture

name: AX_exterior_algebra_self_annihilating_extremal
title: Question on extremal self-annihilating subspaces (Theorem 2.3)
statement_text: For $r < n/2$, are all extremal self-annihilating subspaces $W \subseteq \bigwedge^r V$ (those with $\dim W = \binom{n-1}{r-1}$) of the form $\{v \wedge z : z \in \bigwedge^{r-1} V\}$ for some fixed $v \in V$?
context_text: Let $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ (the arguments work over any field of characteristic $0$) and let $\bigwedge^r V$ be its $r$-th exterior power, of dimension $\binom{n}{r}$, with wedge product $\wedge$. A subspace $W$ of the exterior algebra is self-annihilating if $u\wedge w=0$ for all $u,w\in W$, and two subspaces $U,W$ are mutually annihilating if $u\wedge w=0$ for all $u\in U$, $w\in W$. These are exterior analogues of intersecting and cross-intersecting families of sets: for a basis $f_1,\dots,f_n$, the monomial $f_A=f_{a_1}\wedge\dots\wedge f_{a_r}$ wedged with $f_B$ vanishes exactly when $A\cap B\ne\emptyset$. By the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem an intersecting $r$-uniform family on $[n]$ with $r\le n/2$ has at most $\binom{n-1}{r-1}$ sets, and for $r<n/2$ the extremal families are exactly the stars (all sets containing a fixed element). The authors prove an exterior Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem: a self-annihilating subspace $W$ of $\bigwedge V$ has $\dim W\le2^{n-1}$, and if $W\subseteq\bigwedge^r V$ with $r\le n/2$ then $\dim W\le\binom{n-1}{r-1}$ (the proof shows that the initial hypergraph of $W$ with respect to a basis is intersecting; Woodroofe gave another proof). Both bounds are attained by $\{v\wedge z\}$ for a fixed $v\in V$, the analogue of a star. The authors ask whether, as for sets, these are the only extremal examples; this holds trivially for $r=1$, and also for $r=2$ since then elements of self-annihilating spaces are decomposable.
notes: Stated in running prose after Theorem 2.3: 'It is an interesting question to describe the extremal examples for Theorem 2.3 ... Could all extremal examples be of this form?' PDF source.
paper_title: Combinatorics in the exterior algebra and the Bollobás Two Families Theorem

name: AX_exterior_algebra_mutually_annihilating_extremal
title: Question on extremal mutually annihilating pairs (Theorem 2.4)
statement_text: For $r, s < n/2$, characterize all pairs of subspaces $U \subseteq \bigwedge^r V$ and $W \subseteq \bigwedge^s V$ that are mutually annihilating and attain $\dim U \cdot \dim W = \binom{n-1}{r-1}\binom{n-1}{s-1}$.
context_text: Let $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ (the arguments work over any field of characteristic $0$) and let $\bigwedge^r V$ be its $r$-th exterior power, of dimension $\binom{n}{r}$, with wedge product $\wedge$. A subspace $W$ of the exterior algebra is self-annihilating if $u\wedge w=0$ for all $u,w\in W$, and two subspaces $U,W$ are mutually annihilating if $u\wedge w=0$ for all $u\in U$, $w\in W$. These are exterior analogues of intersecting and cross-intersecting families of sets: for a basis $f_1,\dots,f_n$, the monomial $f_A=f_{a_1}\wedge\dots\wedge f_{a_r}$ wedged with $f_B$ vanishes exactly when $A\cap B\ne\emptyset$. By the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem an intersecting $r$-uniform family on $[n]$ with $r\le n/2$ has at most $\binom{n-1}{r-1}$ sets, and for $r<n/2$ the extremal families are exactly the stars (all sets containing a fixed element). The authors prove that if $1\le r,s\le n/2$, $U\subseteq\bigwedge^r V$ and $W\subseteq\bigwedge^s V$ are mutually annihilating, then $\dim U\cdot\dim W\le\binom{n-1}{r-1}\binom{n-1}{s-1}$, by reduction to the Pyber and Matsumoto–Tokushige bound for cross-intersecting families; the case $U=W$ recovers the exterior Erdős–Ko–Rado bound. Equality is attained by fixing $v\in V$ and taking $U=\{v\wedge z : z\in\bigwedge^{r-1}V\}$ and $W=\{v\wedge z : z\in\bigwedge^{s-1}V\}$. As for single self-annihilating subspaces, the authors find it interesting to characterise all extremal pairs when $r,s<n/2$.
notes: Stated in running prose after Theorem 2.4: 'it would be interesting to characterize the extremal examples when $r, s < n/2$.' PDF source.
paper_title: Combinatorics in the exterior algebra and the Bollobás Two Families Theorem

name: AX_sublinear_separator_expansion_exponent_exact
title: Informal open question on the exact value of $b_\varepsilon$
statement_text: It is unclear whether the upper or the lower bound on $b_\varepsilon$ can be improved for $0<\varepsilon<\frac{1}{2}$. While the fact that $b_{1/2}=0$ matches the lower bound suggests that a better construction improving the upper bound in general could exist, it is also plausible that this is just a "dimension 2" artifact and in fact the lower bound might be possible to improve for $\varepsilon<1/2$ (possibly leading to discontinuity of $b_\varepsilon$ at $\varepsilon=1/2$).
context_text:
For an $n$-vertex graph, a balanced separator is a set $X$ of vertices such that each component of $G-X$ has at most $2n/3$ vertices; $s(G)$ is the minimum size of a balanced separator, and for a class $\mathcal{G}$, $s_\mathcal{G}(n)=\max\{s(G):G\in\mathcal{G},|V(G)|\le n\}$. An $r$-shallow minor of $G$ is a graph obtained from a subgraph of $G$ by contracting pairwise vertex-disjoint subgraphs of radius at most $r$; $
abla_r(G)$ is the maximum density $|E(H)|/|V(H)|$ of an $r$-shallow minor $H$ of $G$, and $
abla_\mathcal{G}(r)=\sup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}
abla_r(G)$ (the expansion of $\mathcal{G}$). For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $b_\varepsilon$ is the supremum of reals $b$ such that every hereditary class $\mathcal{G}$ with $s_\mathcal{G}(n)=\Theta(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ satisfies $
abla_\mathcal{G}(r)=\Omega(r^b)$, and $B_\varepsilon$ is the infimum of reals $B$ such that every such class satisfies $
abla_\mathcal{G}(r)=O(r^B)$. Results of Plotkin, Rao and Smith and of Esperet and Raymond give $\max( rac{1}{2\varepsilon}-1,0)\le b_\varepsilon\le B_\varepsilon\le rac1\varepsilon-1$, and Esperet and Raymond asked whether these bounds can be improved. The author shows that $B_\varepsilon= rac1\varepsilon-1$ for all $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $b_\varepsilon=0$ for $ rac12\le\varepsilon\le1$, and $ rac{1}{2\varepsilon}-1\le b_\varepsilon\le rac{1}{2\varepsilon}- rac12$ for $0<\varepsilon< rac12$, so the bounds on $b_\varepsilon$ differ by at most $ rac12$. The value $b_{1/2}=0$ is witnessed by planar graphs, which have separators of order $\Theta(n^{1/2})$ (Lipton and Tarjan) and all of whose minors have density at most $3$.
notes: Stated as an open remark in the concluding summary. PDF source.
paper_title: A note on sublinear separators and expansion

name: AX_sublinear_separator_expansion_exponent_one_sided
title: Informal conjecture $b'_\varepsilon = b_\varepsilon$ for $0<\varepsilon<\tfrac{1}{2}$
statement_text: It seems likely that $b'_\varepsilon = b_\varepsilon$ when $0 < \varepsilon < \frac{1}{2}$ as well.
context_text:
For an $n$-vertex graph, a balanced separator is a set $X$ of vertices such that each component of $G-X$ has at most $2n/3$ vertices; $s(G)$ is the minimum size of a balanced separator, and for a class $\mathcal{G}$, $s_\mathcal{G}(n)=\max\{s(G):G\in\mathcal{G},|V(G)|\le n\}$. An $r$-shallow minor of $G$ is a graph obtained from a subgraph of $G$ by contracting pairwise vertex-disjoint subgraphs of radius at most $r$; $
abla_r(G)$ is the maximum density $|E(H)|/|V(H)|$ of an $r$-shallow minor $H$ of $G$, and $
abla_\mathcal{G}(r)=\sup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}
abla_r(G)$ (the expansion of $\mathcal{G}$). For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $b_\varepsilon$ is the supremum of reals $b$ such that every hereditary class $\mathcal{G}$ with $s_\mathcal{G}(n)=\Theta(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ satisfies $
abla_\mathcal{G}(r)=\Omega(r^b)$, and $B_\varepsilon$ is the infimum of reals $B$ such that every such class satisfies $
abla_\mathcal{G}(r)=O(r^B)$. The variants $b'_\varepsilon$ and $B'_\varepsilon$ are defined in the same way, except that $b'_\varepsilon$ only requires $s_\mathcal{G}(n)=\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ and $B'_\varepsilon$ only requires $s_\mathcal{G}(n)=O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$. The author proves $\max( rac{1}{2\varepsilon}-1,0)\le b'_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon\le B_\varepsilon\le B'_\varepsilon\le rac1\varepsilon-1$, hence $b'_\varepsilon=b_\varepsilon=0$ for $ rac12\le\varepsilon\le1$, $B'_\varepsilon=B_\varepsilon= rac1\varepsilon-1$ for all $\varepsilon$, and $ rac{1}{2\varepsilon}-1\le b'_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon\le rac{1}{2\varepsilon}- rac12$ for $0<\varepsilon< rac12$. Equality $b'_\varepsilon=b_\varepsilon$ is not obvious: from a class $\mathcal{G}'$ with $s_{\mathcal{G}'}(n)=\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ (which may be assumed closed under subgraphs), the natural hereditary class $\mathcal{G}$ of its graphs all of whose induced subgraphs $H$ satisfy $s(H)=O(|V(H)|^{1-\varepsilon})$ need not satisfy $s_\mathcal{G}(n)=\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})$.
notes: Conjectural language 'It seems likely' appears in the final section. PDF source.
paper_title: A note on sublinear separators and expansion

name: AX_chi_bounded_not_polynomially_chi_bounded
title: Open problem: χ-bounded vs. polynomially χ-bounded
statement_text: Is there a hereditary graph class that is $\chi$-bounded but (provably) not polynomially $\chi$-bounded?
context_text: A graph class is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; it is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded if $f$ can be chosen to be a polynomial. The authors remark that no hereditary graph class is known to be $\chi$-bounded but provably not polynomially $\chi$-bounded (referring to Esperet's habilitation thesis), although for many classes, such as in the advances on variants of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture, the known proofs only give exponential bounds, and polynomial $\chi$-boundedness of circle graphs was established only recently by Davies and McCarty. Their main result is a step in this direction: for every $k$, graphs of cliquewidth at most $k$, known to be $\chi$-bounded by Dvořák and Král' with an exponential bound, are in fact polynomially $\chi$-bounded (with a bounding polynomial whose degree must grow at least like $\log k$).
notes: Stated as informal running prose in the introduction; citation [Esp17] (Esperet 2017, likely a survey) is appended, suggesting the observation may originate there. The paper text is truncated before Section 5, so any further explicitly labelled open problems or conjectures in later sections are not visible and could not be extracted.
paper_title: Graphs of bounded cliquewidth are polynomially $χ$-bounded

name: AX_small_classes_bounded_twin_width
title: The Small Conjecture
statement_text: Every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width.
context_text: Twin-width is defined through contraction sequences: starting from $G$, repeatedly merge two vertices into one, keeping black edges to common neighbours and turning into red edges the adjacencies that are inconsistent (to vertices adjacent to only one of them, or already red); $G$ has twin-width at most $d$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex while every intermediate trigraph has red degree at most $d$. A class has bounded twin-width if all its graphs have twin-width at most some $d$. A class is small if there is a constant $c$ such that it contains at most $n!\,c^n$ graphs on the vertex set $[n]$, for every $n$; it is hereditary if closed under induced subgraphs. The authors prove that every class of bounded twin-width is small, unifying the facts that bounded treewidth classes, proper subclasses of permutation graphs (Marcus–Tardos) and proper minor-closed classes (Norine et al.) are small, and provocatively conjecture the converse for hereditary classes. As evidence they show that seemingly complex small hereditary classes have bounded twin-width: the $s$-subdivisions of $K_n$ have bounded twin-width if and only if $s=\Omega(\log n)$, graphs of bounded stack or queue number, and some cubic expanders (from iterated random $2$-lifts), whereas non-small classes such as interval graphs, subcubic graphs or random cubic graphs do not. A prerequisite is bounded symmetric difference (every graph has two vertices whose neighbourhoods differ on at most $d$ vertices), and even showing that small hereditary classes have this property is unclear; a very particular case is that every small hereditary class with no $K_{2,2}$ subgraph has bounded minimum degree. They also note a possible connection with group theory via Cayley graphs. Status note (November 2026): refuted by Bonnet, Geniet, Tessera and Thomassé ('Twin-width VII: groups', arXiv 2204.12330, 2022), as also noted in the final version of Twin-width I (arXiv 2004.14789).
notes: Explicitly named 'the small conjecture' repeatedly in the abstract and introduction; no labelled theorem environment visible in the extracted text. The PDF extraction is truncated, so later numbered conjecture environments may exist.
paper_title: Twin-width II: small classes

name: AX_polynomial_expansion_bounded_twin_width
title: Question: polynomial expansion and twin-width
statement_text: Do classes with polynomial expansion have bounded twin-width?
context_text: Twin-width is defined through contraction sequences: starting from $G$, repeatedly merge two vertices into one, keeping black edges to common neighbours and turning into red edges the adjacencies that are inconsistent (to vertices adjacent to only one of them, or already red); $G$ has twin-width at most $d$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex while every intermediate trigraph has red degree at most $d$. A class has bounded twin-width if all its graphs have twin-width at most some $d$. A class is small if there is a constant $c$ such that it contains at most $n!\,c^n$ graphs on the vertex set $[n]$, for every $n$; it is hereditary if closed under induced subgraphs. For $r\ge0$, an $r$-shallow minor of $G$ is a minor whose branch sets induce subgraphs of radius at most $r$; $\nabla_r(G)$ is the maximum of $|E(H)|/|V(H)|$ over $r$-shallow minors $H$ of $G$, and a class has expansion $f$ if $\nabla_r(G)\le f(r)$ for all its graphs and all $r$; it has polynomial expansion if $f$ can be taken polynomial (proper minor-closed classes even have constant expansion). Dvořák and Norine showed that classes with expansion $r\mapsto c^{r^{1/3-\varepsilon}}$ are small, so classes with polynomial expansion are small, and the small conjecture of the authors (every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width) would imply that they have bounded twin-width. The authors propose, as a first but challenging step towards the small conjecture, to show that small sparse classes have bounded (sparse) twin-width, this question being a particular instance. The authors show that five natural ways of restricting twin-width to sparse classes coincide (bounded sparse twin-width), e.g. hereditary classes of bounded twin-width excluding some $K_{t,t}$ subgraph, or whose graphs have linearly many edges. The converse inclusion fails: the authors construct cubic expanders of bounded twin-width, so bounded sparse twin-width classes do not necessarily have polynomial expansion.
notes: Stated as an explicit open question in the introduction without a labelled environment. PDF extraction is truncated; additional numbered questions may appear in later sections.
paper_title: Twin-width II: small classes

name: AX_planar_recoloring_girth_5_six_colors
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: If $G$ is a planar graph of girth at least five on $n$ vertices, then $R_6(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$.
context_text: The reconfiguration graph $R_k(G)$ has as vertices all proper $k$-colourings of $G$, two colourings being adjacent if they differ in the colour of exactly one vertex (so paths in $R_k(G)$ correspond to recolouring vertices one at a time while keeping the colouring proper). Bousquet and Perarnau proved that for a $d$-degenerate graph on $n$ vertices and $c\ge2d+2$, $R_c(G)$ has diameter at most $(d+1)n$, while Bonamy et al. showed that $d+2$ colours may give quadratic diameter. A general lemma also shows that if a $d$-degenerate graph $G$ is colourable from every assignment of lists of size $c$, then for every independent set $I$, the diameter of $R_{c+d+1}(G)$ is at most $2(n+|I|)$ plus the diameter of $R_{c+d}(G-I)$. For planar graphs the authors obtain linear diameter with $10$ colours, and for triangle-free planar graphs with $7$ colours ($R_7(G)$ has diameter at most $7n$). Since planar graphs of girth at least five are colourable from lists of size three (Thomassen), the lemma together with the Bousquet–Perarnau theorem already gives linear diameter with $7$ colours, and the authors believe $6$ suffice; they suspect a variation of their method could prove it, but several complications arise. For girth at least six, the bound $6$ follows from 2-degeneracy and the Bousquet–Perarnau theorem.
paper_title: A Thomassen-type method for planar graph recoloring

name: AX_planar_expansions_edge_erdos_posa
title: Open Problem (edge-EP property characterization for planar graph expansions)
statement_text: Finding a characterization for the planar graphs $J$ such that $J$-expansions have the edge-Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa property remains an intriguing open problem.
context_text: A class $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs has the vertex-Erdős–Pósa property (resp. edge-Erdős–Pósa property, edge-EP property) if there is a bounding function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ such that for every $k$, every graph $G$ contains either $k$ vertex-disjoint (resp. edge-disjoint) subgraphs belonging to $\mathcal{H}$, or a set $F$ of at most $f(k)$ vertices (resp. edges) such that $G-F$ has no subgraph in $\mathcal{H}$. For a graph $J$, a $J$-expansion is a graph that contains $J$ as a minor. Robertson and Seymour showed that $J$-expansions have the vertex-EP property if and only if $J$ is planar (and an $O(k\log k)$ bounding function is now known). Planarity of $J$ is also necessary for the edge version. The edge-EP property is known for $\theta_r$-expansions ($\theta_r$ being two vertices joined by $r$ parallel edges), for $K_4$-expansions and for long cycles (cycles of length at least $\ell$), for which the authors give a bounding function $O(k\ell\log(k\ell))$ via a ball-packing technique. On the other hand, Bruhn, Heinlein and Joos showed that $J$-expansions do not have the edge-EP property when $J$ is a ladder with at least $71$ rungs or a subcubic tree of pathwidth at least $19$. The question was raised by Raymond, Sau and Thilikos and by Bruhn, Heinlein and Joos.
notes: Stated in prose in the introduction as 'an intriguing open problem'; no labelled theorem environment. Section 5, which the paper explicitly announces contains further open problems, appears to be missing from the PDF extraction — additional items likely exist there.
paper_title: Erdős-Pósa from ball packing

name: AX_layered_treewidth_bounded_queue_number
title: Open problem on queue-number of bounded layered treewidth graphs
statement_text: It is open whether graphs of bounded layered treewidth have bounded queue-number.
context_text: A layering of a graph $G$ is a partition $(V_0,V_1,\dots,V_t)$ of $V(G)$ such that for every edge $vw$ with $v\in V_i$ and $w\in V_j$ we have $|i-j|\le 1$ (e.g. the BFS layering from a vertex). The layered width of a tree decomposition $(B_x:x\in V(T))$ of $G$ is the minimum $\ell$ such that, for some layering of $G$, each bag $B_x$ contains at most $\ell$ vertices of each layer; the layered treewidth of $G$ is the minimum layered width of a tree decomposition of $G$ (layered pathwidth is defined in the same way with path decompositions). A class has bounded layered treewidth if some constant bounds the layered treewidth of all its members. The queue-number of $G$ is the minimum $k$ such that there is a linear ordering of $V(G)$ and a partition of $E(G)$ into $k$ queues, i.e. sets of edges no two of which are nested (no edges $ab$, $cd$ with $a<c<d<b$ in the ordering). Planar graphs have layered treewidth at most 3, graphs of Euler genus $g$ at most $2g+3$, and graphs drawable on a surface of Euler genus $g$ with at most $k$ crossings per edge at most $2(2g+3)(k+1)$, so bounded layered treewidth allows arbitrarily large clique minors. Dujmović, Morin and Wood proved that every $n$-vertex graph with layered treewidth $k$ has track- and queue-number $O(k\log n)$, while graphs of layered pathwidth $k$ have queue-number at most $3k$. In a footnote the authors remark that, subsequent to the submission of this paper, improved bounds on the queue-number have been obtained (by Dujmović, Joret, Micek, Morin, Ueckerdt and Wood, who showed that planar graphs have bounded queue-number), but that it is still open whether all graphs of bounded layered treewidth have bounded queue-number.
notes: Stated in a footnote without a formal labeled environment.
paper_title: Minor-closed graph classes with bounded layered pathwidth

name: AX_coherent_ideal_forest_filleting
title: Conjecture 2.4
statement_text: Let $H$ be a graph and let $P$ be a forest of $H$. Then every coherent ideal contains a $P$-filleting of $H$.
context_text: Graphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges. An ideal is a class of graphs closed under isomorphism and under taking induced subgraphs; to contain a graph means to contain a graph isomorphic to it. Two disjoint vertex sets $A,B$ are anticomplete if there is no edge between them. For $\epsilon>0$, a graph $G$ is $\epsilon$-coherent if $|G|\ge2$, every vertex has fewer than $\epsilon|G|$ neighbours, and $\min(|A|,|B|)<\epsilon|G|$ for every two anticomplete sets $A,B\subseteq V(G)$. An ideal is incoherent if for some $\epsilon>0$ none of its members is $\epsilon$-coherent, and coherent otherwise. For a graph $H$ and a subgraph $P$ of $H$, a $P$-filleting of $H$ is any graph obtained from $H$ by subdividing at least once every edge of $H$ not in $E(P)$, and not subdividing the edges of $P$. The authors' main theorem is the case where $P$ is a path of $H$: every coherent ideal contains a $P$-filleting of $H$. Consequences include that the ideal of graphs with no induced subdivision of $K_t$ is incoherent, and that every coherent ideal contains every caterpillar subdivision (a tree with a path containing all vertices of degree at least three), a theorem of Liebenau, Pilipczuk, Seymour and Spirkl. The conjectured strengthening to forests would be best possible, since the conclusion fails if $P$ contains a cycle of $H$ (there are coherent ideals in which every graph has arbitrarily large girth), and it would imply, in the same way, the main theorem of Pure pairs I (Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour, Spirkl) that every coherent ideal contains every forest.
paper_title: Pure pairs. II. Excluding all subdivisions of a graph

name: AX_induced_detour_path_fixed_k
title: Question 1.5
statement_text: For fixed $k > 1$, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a graph $G$ and $u, v \in V(G)$, decides whether there is an induced $uv$-path $P$ in $G$ of length at least $d(u, v) + k$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $d(u,v)=d_G(u,v)$ is the number of edges of a shortest $uv$-path, and the length of a path is its number of edges. An induced $uv$-path is a non-shortest $uv$-path ($uv$-NSP) if its length is more than $d(u,v)$; equivalently, $G$ has two induced $uv$-paths of different lengths. The authors' main result is an algorithm that decides whether there is a $uv$-NSP in time $O(|G|^{16})$, which is surprisingly non-trivial since the paths must be induced (for non-induced paths the question is much easier); this is the case $k=1$ of the question, and the algorithm can be adjusted to do the case $k=2$, but the question remains open even for $k=3$. If both paths are required to be shortest paths, or at most a fixed constant longer than a shortest path, the problem is polynomial by a dynamic programming argument. Fixing $k$ is necessary: the authors prove that deciding whether there is a $uv$-NSP of length at least $2d_G(u,v)$ is NP-hard.
paper_title: Finding an induced path that is not a shortest path

name: AX_cop_number_girth_exponent_quarter
title: Optimality of the exponent 1/4
statement_text: Is the coefficient $\frac{1}{4}$ of $g$ in the lower bound $\Omega\!\left((\delta-1)^{g/4}\right)$ for the cop number of graphs of girth $g$ and minimum degree $\delta$ best possible, i.e., can the exponent be improved to $\left(\frac{1}{4}+\varepsilon\right)g$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$?
context_text: In the game of cops and robbers on a finite connected graph $G$, the cops first occupy vertices, then the robber chooses a vertex; players alternate, each cop (resp. the robber) moving to a vertex of its closed neighbourhood, and the cops win if one of them reaches the robber's vertex. The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops guaranteeing capture. The authors prove that if $t\ge1$ and $G$ has girth $g\ge 4t+1$ and minimum degree $\delta$, then $c(G)>\frac{1}{et}(\delta-1)^t$, a bound of the form $\Omega(g^{-1}(\delta-1)^{g/4})$, improving Frankl's $\Omega((\delta-1)^{g/8})$. They show that $\frac14$ would be best possible assuming two conjectures: Meyniel's conjecture ($c(G)=O(\sqrt n)$ for every connected $n$-vertex graph) and the folklore conjecture that for all $g,d$ there is a $d$-regular graph of girth at least $g$ and order $\Theta((d-1)^{(\frac12+o(1))g})$; together these would give graphs with cop number $O((d-1)^{(\frac14+o(1))g})$. Unconditionally, using a family of Ramanujan graphs, they prove that the optimal constant $c$ in a lower bound $\Omega((\delta-1)^{cg})$ satisfies $\frac14\le c\le\frac38$. They suspect $\frac14$ is correct and ask to close this gap, possibly without using these conjectures.
notes: Stated as prose without a labelled environment; the abstract frames it as 'several reasons for conjecturing that the exponent $\frac{1}{4}g$ cannot be improved to $(\frac{1}{4}+\varepsilon)g$'.
paper_title: On the cop number of graphs of high girth

name: AX_group_connectivity_exponentially_many_flows
title: Conjecture 1.10
statement_text: There exists a fixed constant $c > 1$ so that the following holds. For every 3-edge-connected oriented graph $G = (V, E)$ of order $n$, every abelian group $\Gamma$ with $|\Gamma| \geq 6$, and every $f : E \to \Gamma$, there exist at least $c^n$ flows $\phi : E \to \Gamma$ with $\phi(e) \neq f(e)$ for every $e \in E$.
context_text: Graphs may have loops and parallel edges. For an oriented graph $G=(V,E)$ and an additive abelian group $\Gamma$, a flow (or $\Gamma$-flow) is a function $\phi:E\to\Gamma$ such that at every vertex $v$ the sum of $\phi$ over the edges leaving $v$ equals the sum over the edges entering $v$; it is nowhere-zero if $0\notin\phi(E)$. Following Jaeger, Linial, Payan and Tarsi, $G$ is $\Gamma$-connected if for every $f:E\to\Gamma$ there is a flow $\phi$ with $\phi(e)\neq f(e)$ for every $e\in E$ (taking $f=0$ forces $\phi$ to be nowhere-zero); this is the flow analogue (dual) of group coloring, a choosability-type version of nowhere-zero flows. Jaeger et al. proved that every 3-edge-connected oriented graph is $\Gamma$-connected whenever $|\Gamma|\ge 6$; the conjecture asks for exponentially many such flows. The authors prove that, with $\ell=|E|-|V|$ and $|\Gamma|=k\ge 6$, the number of such flows is at least $\frac12(\frac{k-6}{2})^{\ell}$ for odd $k$ and $\frac12(\frac{k-4}{2})^{\ell}$ for even $k$; this is exponential for $k\ge 8$ but for $k=6,7$ gives only the existence of one flow, which they attribute to a shortcoming of their techniques. Hence the conjecture holds for all abelian groups except $\mathbb{Z}_6$ and $\mathbb{Z}_7$. For $\mathbb{Z}_7$ they have no interesting lower bound; for $\mathbb{Z}_6$ they prove a superpolynomial bound: if $\ell\ge 11$ there are at least $2^{\sqrt{\ell}/\log\ell}$ such flows (log base 2).
paper_title: Many flows in the group connectivity setting

name: AX_short_rainbow_cycles_proper_incident_edges
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: Let $G$ be a simple $n$-vertex graph and $c$ be a colouring of $E(G)$ with $n$ colours, where each colour class has size at least $r$. Then $(G, c)$ contains a cycle $C$ of length at most $\lceil n/r \rceil$ such that no two incident edges of $C$ are the same colour.
context_text: A colouring $c$ of $E(G)$ is an arbitrary (not necessarily proper) assignment of colours to edges; a subgraph is rainbow if no two of its edges have the same colour. The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture states that every simple $n$-vertex digraph (at most one arc from $u$ to $v$ for all $u,v$) with minimum outdegree at least $r$ has a directed cycle of length at most $\lceil n/r\rceil$; it is known for $r\le5$ but open in general, e.g. for $r=n/3$. Aharoni proposed the strengthening: if $G$ is a simple $n$-vertex graph and $c$ colours $E(G)$ with $n$ colours, each colour class of size at least $r$, then $(G,c)$ contains a rainbow cycle of length at most $\lceil n/r\rceil$. The present conjecture weakens rainbow to the condition that consecutive (incident) edges of the cycle have distinct colours. The authors show it still implies the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture: forget the orientations of a digraph on $[n]$ and colour the edge $ij$ with colour $i$ when $(i,j)$ is an arc; a cycle with no two incident edges of the same colour is then a directed cycle. The paper proves Aharoni's conjecture (hence this one) for $r=2$, which is best possible, and asks to prove either conjecture for $r\in\{3,4,5\}$.

paper_title: Short rainbow cycles in graphs and matroids
paper_authors: Sebastián González Hermosillo de la Maza

name: AX_short_rainbow_circuits_matroids
title: Conjecture 12
statement_text: Let $M$ be a simple rank-$(n-1)$ matroid and $c$ be a colouring of $E(M)$ with $n$ colours, where each colour class has size at least $2$. Then $M$ contains a rainbow circuit of size at most $\lceil n/2 \rceil$.
context_text: A matroid $M$ on a finite ground set $E(M)$ is given by its circuits (nonempty, pairwise incomparable sets satisfying circuit elimination); a set is independent if it contains no circuit, the rank of $M$ is the size of a largest independent set, and $M$ is simple if it has no circuits of size 1 or 2. A colouring of $E(M)$ is arbitrary, and a circuit is rainbow if its elements have distinct colours. The graphic matroid $M(G)$ has the cycles of $G$ as circuits (rank $n-1$ for connected $n$-vertex $G$), and the cographic matroid has the minimal edge-cuts as circuits; a matroid is binary if representable over $GF(2)$ and regular if representable over every field. The conjecture is the matroid analogue of the authors' main theorem: if $G$ is a simple $n$-vertex graph and $E(G)$ is coloured with $n$ colours, each class of size at least $2$, then there is a rainbow cycle of length at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$. Thus it holds for graphic matroids, and the authors prove it for cographic matroids. However, the paper itself notes that the conjecture is false in general: the uniform matroid $U_{n-1,m}$ (rank $n-1$, every $n$-subset a circuit) has no circuit of size less than $n$; and it fails even for binary matroids: for each even $n\ge6$ there is a simple rank-$(n-1)$ binary matroid on $2n$ elements, coloured with classes of size 2, whose rainbow circuits all have size greater than $n/2$ (a forthcoming paper of Bai, Bowler and Huynh gives rank-$6n$ examples where the shortest rainbow circuit has size $4n$). The authors instead conjecture that it holds for regular matroids, via Seymour's decomposition theorem.

name: AX_mis_approximation_h_free_improved
title: Conjecture 5 (Improved Approximation Conjecture)
statement_text: Every graph $H$ satisfies the improved approximation property, i.e., there exists a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ such that MIS admits a (randomized) $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation polynomial algorithm on every $H$-free $n$-vertex graph $G$.
context_text: MIS (Maximum Independent Set) asks for a largest independent set; an $r$-approximation algorithm outputs an independent set of size at least $\mathrm{OPT}/r$. A graph $G$ is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. In general $n$-vertex graphs MIS is NP-hard to approximate within $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. $H$ satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal property if there is $\delta>0$ such that every $H$-free $n$-vertex graph has a clique or an independent set of size $n^\delta$, and the constructive Erdős–Hajnal property if moreover such a set can be found in polynomial time. The conjecture is an algorithmic analogue of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture: the inapproximability of MIS in general graphs could always be beaten in any class defined by one forbidden induced subgraph. The two are not known to be comparable. On one hand, MIS is polynomial-time solvable in $P_6$-free and fork-free graphs, so these graphs satisfy the improved approximation property while it is open whether $P_5$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property. On the other hand, the authors prove that every $H$ with the constructive Erdős–Hajnal property with constant $0<\delta\le 1/2$ satisfies the improved approximation property with any constant below $\delta-\delta^2$ (all graphs known to have the Erdős–Hajnal property have the constructive version). They also prove that the improved approximation property is preserved under substitution (replacing a vertex of $H_1$ by a copy of $H_2$), the operation known to preserve the Erdős–Hajnal property.
paper_title: An algorithmic weakening of the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture

name: AX_mis_approximation_h_free_optimal_exponent
title: Question: optimal approximation exponent for MIS in H-free graphs
statement_text: For a given $H$, what is the largest $\varepsilon > 0$ such that MIS admits an $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$-approximation algorithm in $H$-free graphs?
context_text: MIS (Maximum Independent Set) asks for a largest independent set; an $r$-approximation algorithm outputs an independent set of size at least $\mathrm{OPT}/r$. A graph $G$ is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. In general $n$-vertex graphs MIS is NP-hard to approximate within $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. $H$ satisfies the Erdős–Hajnal property if there is $\delta>0$ such that every $H$-free $n$-vertex graph has a clique or an independent set of size $n^\delta$, and the constructive Erdős–Hajnal property if moreover such a set can be found in polynomial time. $H$ satisfies the improved approximation property if for some $\varepsilon>0$ MIS has a (randomized) polynomial-time $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation on $H$-free graphs; the authors conjecture every $H$ has it and here ask for the best exponent. Partial results of the paper: a graph $H$ is locally easy if it has a universal vertex $v$ such that MIS is polynomial on $(H-v)$-free graphs (e.g. $H-v$ is $P_6$, the fork, or $tK_{1,3}$), and for locally easy $H$ MIS can be $\sqrt{\mathrm{OPT}}$-approximated on $H$-free graphs (in particular $\sqrt n$ for triangle-free graphs); MIS can be $\mathrm{OPT}^{1-1/t}$-approximated on $K_{t+1}$-free graphs, and local search gives $O(\mathrm{OPT}^{1-1/t})$ on $K_{t,t}$-free graphs. On the negative side, in triangle-free graphs the ratio cannot be improved to $n^{1/4-\varepsilon}$ unless $\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}$ (it is NP-hard to distinguish $\alpha(G)\le n^{5/6-\varepsilon}$ from $\alpha(G)\ge n^{1-\varepsilon}$), with generalizations to graphs of girth $\gamma+1$.
notes: Posed as an open research direction in running prose in the 'Results and organization' section; partially investigated within the paper but not fully resolved.
paper_title: An algorithmic weakening of the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture

name: AX_plane_triangle_free_distant_precoloring_extension
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: There exists an absolute constant $d \geq 2$ with the following property. Let $G$ be a plane triangle-free graph, let $S$ be a set of vertices of $G$ and let $\psi : S \to \{1, 2, 3\}$ be an arbitrary function. If the distance between every two vertices of $S$ is at least $d$, then $\psi$ extends to a 3-coloring of $G$.
context_text: A plane graph is a planar graph with a fixed embedding; a separating $4$-cycle is a $4$-cycle that does not bound a face; distances are graph distances in $G$. By Grötzsch's theorem every triangle-free planar graph is $3$-colorable. The authors prove that there is an absolute constant $d\ge2$ such that, in a plane graph without separating $4$-cycles, any prescribed colors on a set of vertices pairwise at distance at least $d$ extend to a $3$-coloring (this is a special case of a more general result that also allows distant $(\le 5)$-cycles, which must include all triangles, to be colored with a prescribed coloring up to permutation of colors, and distant vertices of degree at most $4$ to have monochromatic neighbourhoods of a prescribed color). Forbidding separating $4$-cycles is necessary for some of these anomalies (by constructions of Thomas and Walls), but there seems to be no principal reason to exclude them when only single vertices are precolored, which motivates this conjecture for all plane triangle-free graphs. The authors show it is implied by the seemingly simpler statement that there is an absolute constant $d\ge2$ such that, for every plane triangle-free graph $G$ with a $4$-cycle $C$ bounding a face and a vertex $v$ at distance at least $d$ from $C$, every $3$-coloring of $C+v$ extends to a $3$-coloring of $G$. The final version of the paper notes that this simpler statement was confirmed by Dvořák and Lidický while the paper was under review, so the conjecture holds.
notes: The paper states that Conjecture 1.5 was subsequently confirmed by Dvořák and Lidický [16], which implies Conjecture 1.4 is also true.
paper_title: Three-coloring triangle-free graphs on surfaces V. Coloring planar graphs with distant anomalies

name: AX_cubic_many_3_edge_colorings_reflexive
title: Informal Conjecture on reflexive graphs and coloring abundance
statement_text: Graphs with a large number of colorings tend to be reflexive.
context_text: Colorings are considered here for $k=3$. A 3-coloring of a graph $X$ is viewed as a partition of $V(X)$ into 3 independent sets, its color classes. The 3-coloring complex $B(X)$ is the graph whose vertices are all color classes occurring in some 3-coloring of $X$, two classes being adjacent if they appear together in a 3-coloring; under mild conditions (e.g. $X$ contains an edge) $B(X)$ is again 3-colorable, and each 3-coloring of $X$ gives a triangle of $B(X)$. Fisk showed that, when every edge of $X$ lies in a triangle and $X$ has no isolated vertices, the canonical map $\phi_X$ sending a vertex $v$ to the set of color classes containing $v$ is a homomorphism from $X$ to $B^2(X)=B(B(X))$; $X$ is reflexive if $\phi_X$ is an isomorphism. The paper studies 3-edge-colorings of cubic graphs in which half-edges (edges with only one end) are allowed: a cubic graph $G$ is edge-reflexive if its line graph $L(G)$ is reflexive. The main result is that a connected cubic outerplanar graph (with half-edges) is edge-reflexive if and only if it is triangle-free; $K_{3,3}$, even prisms and many theta graphs are also edge-reflexive. There is no obvious reason why any graph should be reflexive, and the authors state that the real open question is why there are so many reflexive graphs. The informal claim that graphs with many colorings tend to be reflexive is supported by their results and extensive computations, although it seems counterintuitive: many colorings make the complex $B(X)$ large, so it may have too many colorings for $X$ to be reflexive. It is not given a precise mathematical formulation.
notes: Stated in prose in the introduction without a labelled environment; backed by 'extensive computational evidence' but not given a precise mathematical formulation. The paper text is truncated mid-proof, so further conjectures in later sections may be missing.
paper_title: Reflexive coloring complexes for 3-edge-colorings of cubic graphs

name: AX_pentagon_contact_representation_algorithm_terminates
title: Algorithm Termination Conjecture
statement_text: The authors' iterative algorithm for computing regular pentagon contact representations (solve the linear system associated with the current five color forest; if the solution has negative variables, change the five color forest along the directed cycles separating negative from non-negative variables and restart) terminates with a non-negative solution for every graph $G$ which is an inner triangulation of a $5$-gon, and for every initial five color forest $F$ of $G$.
context_text: An inner triangulation of a $5$-gon is a simple plane graph whose outer face is a 5-cycle $a_1,\dots,a_5$ (clockwise), whose inner faces are triangles, and with no edges among $a_1,\dots,a_5$ other than the outer cycle. A regular pentagon contact representation of $G$ represents each inner vertex by a regular pentagon with a horizontal side at the bottom (so all pentagons are homothetic) and the outer vertices $a_1,\dots,a_5$ by the five sides $s_1,\dots,s_5$ of a large pentagon with all angles $3\pi/5$ ($s_1$ horizontal at the top), with pairwise interior-disjoint shapes such that two shapes touch exactly when the vertices are adjacent. Its existence for every such $G$ follows from Schramm's Convex Packing (Monster Packing) Theorem. A five color forest of $G$ is an orientation and colouring of the inner edges with colours $1,\dots,5$ (mod 5) such that (F1) every edge at $a_i$ is oriented towards $a_i$ and has colour $i$; (F2) at every inner vertex $v$ the incoming edges form five possibly empty blocks $B_1,\dots,B_5$ of colours $1,\dots,5$ in clockwise order, $v$ has at most one outgoing edge of each colour $i$, located between $B_{i+2}$ and $B_{i-2}$; (F3) for each $i$, $B_i$ is nonempty or $v$ has an outgoing edge of colour $i-2$ or $i+2$. Every regular pentagon contact representation induces a five color forest; five color forests are relatives of Schnyder woods, are in bijection with certain $\alpha_5$-orientations and form a distributive lattice. The algorithm starts from any five color forest $F$, builds a linear system $A_F\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{e}_1$ whose unknowns are side lengths of the skeleton of the would-be representation; a non-negative solution gives the representation, and otherwise the authors prove the negative and non-negative variables are separated by a nonempty disjoint union of directed cycles of the $\alpha_5$-orientation, which is used to change $F$. They cannot prove progress, but two implementations always succeeded in experiments; analogous algorithms for homothetic triangles and squares also lack termination proofs. A proof would give an existence proof independent of Schramm's theorem and exact coordinates; with a polynomial bound on the number of iterations, a strongly polynomial algorithm over $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt5]$.
notes: Stated in running prose in the introduction without a labelled theorem environment. PDF extraction quality is adequate for this prose statement.
paper_title: Pentagon contact representations

name: AX_blowup_ramsey_prefactor_depends_on_g
title: Conjecture on unavoidable G-dependence in Theorem 2
statement_text: For some graph $H$, the dependence on $G$ in the multiplicative factor $a = a(G, H, r)$ of the bound $B(G \xrightarrow{r} H; t) \leq a \cdot b^t$ (proved by the authors with $b=b(H,r)$ independent of $G$) is unavoidable. Precisely: there exist a graph $H$ and integers $r,t\ge2$, and graphs $G_1,G_2,\ldots$ such that $G_i\xrightarrow{r}H$ for all $i$ and $\sup_i B(G_i\xrightarrow{r}H;t)=\infty$.
context_text: $G\xrightarrow{r}H$ means that every $r$-edge-colouring of $G$ contains a monochromatic copy of $H$. The $t$-blowup $H[t]$ is obtained by replacing each vertex of $H$ by an independent set of size $t$ and each edge by a complete bipartite graph $K_{t,t}$; a copy of $H[t]$ in $G[n]$ is canonical if it is the $t$-blowup of a copy of $H$ in $G$. For $G\xrightarrow{r}H$, the blowup Ramsey number $B(G\xrightarrow{r}H;t)$, introduced by Souza, is the least $n$ such that every $r$-edge-colouring of $G[n]$ contains a monochromatic canonical copy of $H[t]$. Souza proved $B(G\xrightarrow{r}H;t)\le c^t$ with $c=c(G,H,r)$, and a lower bound exponential in $t$ with a constant independent of $G$, and conjectured that the dependence on $G$ is unnecessary. The authors prove $B(G\xrightarrow{r}H;t)\le a\cdot b^t$ with $a=a(G,H,r)$ and $b=b(H,r)$, so the exponential rate does not depend on $G$, but, unlike Souza, they believe the prefactor must depend on $G$ for some $H$, and even conjecture this for $H=K_3$, $r=t=2$: for every $s$ there is $G$ with $G\xrightarrow{2}K_3$ but $G[s]\not\xrightarrow{2}K_3[2]$. Such an $H$ cannot be $r$-Ramsey-finite (having finitely many minimal $G$ with $G\xrightarrow{r}H$), and $H=P_3$, the path with two edges, does not work for $r=2$ although it is Ramsey-infinite: then $B(G\xrightarrow{2}P_3;t)\le c^t$ with $c$ absolute.
notes: Stated in both the abstract and the introduction as a belief/conjecture without a labelled theorem environment; concluding remarks section was not fully captured in the PDF extraction.
paper_title: Extremal and Ramsey results on graph blowups

name: AX_3_graph_homeomorph_exponent_5_2
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: For each 3-graph $H$, there exists $C_H > 0$ such that any 3-graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least $C_H n^{5/2}$ edges contains a homeomorph of $H$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph, viewed as a two-dimensional simplicial complex whose facets (triangles) are its edges. Two $3$-graphs are homeomorphic if they are homeomorphic as topological spaces (as 2-complexes), and $G$ contains a homeomorph of $H$ if some subgraph of $G$ is homeomorphic to $H$; for instance, a homeomorph of the complete $3$-graph $K^3_4$ (the sphere $S^2$) is a set of triangles triangulating the sphere. This is the topological Turán problem for $3$-graphs, raised by Linial as a two-dimensional analogue of Mader's theorem that every $n$-vertex graph with at least $C_Hn$ edges contains a homeomorph (subdivision) of a graph $H$. The authors prove the universal exponent $3-1/5$: every $n$-vertex $3$-graph with at least $C_Hn^{3-1/5}$ edges contains a homeomorph of $H$ (a cheap argument via degenerate Turán problems only gives an $H$-dependent exponent $3-\varepsilon_H$). They do not believe $3-1/5$ is tight and conjecture $5/2=3-1/2$, motivated by the Brown–Erdős–Sós theorem that $\Theta(n^{5/2})$ edges is the threshold for a homeomorph of $S^2$, and by the analogy that homeomorphs in graphs appear roughly once cycles (homeomorphs of $S^1$) can be found. They note that the methods of the paper conjecturally cannot go beyond $3-1/4$, and that any proof must allow homeomorphs of unbounded size, since bounded-size homeomorphs of $S^2$ require an exponent strictly greater than $5/2$. Even the special case of the torus, reiterated by Linial, is open (exponent $3-1/3$ is known there).
paper_title: A universal exponent for homeomorphs

name: AX_mycielski_graphs_independence_ratio
title: Open problem on minimum independence ratio of Mycielski graphs
statement_text: The exact value of the minimum independence ratio $\mathrm{mir}(M_k)$ of the Mycielski graphs $M_k$ seems to be unknown.
context_text: The independence ratio of a graph $G$ is $\alpha(G)/|V(G)|$, and the minimum independence ratio $\mathrm{mir}(G)$ is the minimum independence ratio of an induced subgraph of $G$ with at least one vertex (its inverse is the Hall ratio). $M_k$ denotes the $k$-th Mycielski graph, obtained by iterating Mycielski's construction (from a graph $G$ on $v_1,\dots,v_n$, add copies $u_1,\dots,u_n$ with $u_i$ adjacent to the neighbours of $v_i$, and a new vertex adjacent to all $u_i$), normalized so that $M_2$ is the $5$-cycle; $M_k$ is triangle-free and $\chi(M_k)=k+1$. Every proper subgraph of $M_k$ is $k$-colourable, which gives $\mathrm{mir}(M_k)\ge\frac1k$ for $k\ge3$; so, unlike the case $k=2$ (minimum independence ratio at least $\frac12$ forces bipartiteness), a minimum independence ratio at least $\frac1k$ does not force chromatic number at most $k$. Cropper, Gyárfás and Lehel proved that every triangle-free graph is an induced subgraph of a Mycielski graph and deduced that there are $c_1,c_2>0$ with $c_1\frac{\sqrt{\log m}}{m}\le\mathrm{mir}(M_s)\le c_2\frac{\log m}{m}$ for every integer $m\ge3$, where $s$ is one less than the Ramsey number $R(3,m)=\Theta(m^2/\log m)$. The remark is made in passing, without a formal question.
notes: Stated informally in passing ('seems to be unknown'); no labelled environment. Question 1.2 is posed in the paper but immediately resolved negatively and so is not extracted as an open problem.
paper_title: Revisiting a theorem by Folkman on graph colouring

name: AX_epsilon_t_nets_size_computation
title: The $\varepsilon$-$t$-Net Problem
statement_text: How small are the smallest $\varepsilon$-$t$-nets for $H$? Can we compute them efficiently?
context_text: Given a finite hypergraph $H=(V,E)$, a positive integer $t$, and $\varepsilon\in(t/|V|,1)$, an $\varepsilon$-$t$-net for $H$ is a family $S\subseteq\binom{V}{t}$ of $t$-element subsets of $V$ such that every hyperedge $e\in E$ with $|e|\geq\varepsilon|V|$ contains some $s\in S$ as a subset. For $t=1$ this is the classical notion of an $\varepsilon$-net (a set of vertices hitting every hyperedge of size at least $\varepsilon|V|$), and for $t=\Theta(\varepsilon|V|)$ it corresponds to $\varepsilon$-Mnets; the minimum size of an $\varepsilon$-$t$-net is sandwiched between the minimum sizes of $\varepsilon$-nets and of Mnets. The question is posed for general hypergraphs, with motivations from secret sharing (distributing keys to $t$-subsets so that any sufficiently large coalition of a prescribed kind can open a lock), Turán numbers of hypergraphs (a smallest $(k/n)$-$t$-net of the complete $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices has size $\binom{n}{t}-T(n,k,t)$), $\chi$-boundedness and edge-colouring of hypergraphs. The authors prove that every hypergraph of VC-dimension $d$ (and dual shatter function $\pi^*_H(m)\le Cm^{d^*}$) on at least $C_1((t-1)/\varepsilon)^{d^*}$ vertices has an $\varepsilon$-$t$-net of size $O(\frac{d(1+\log t)}{\varepsilon}\log\frac1\varepsilon)$, which is tight for $t=O(1)$; that hypergraphs of VC-dimension 1 have $\varepsilon$-$t$-nets of size at most $t\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1$; give an explicit (efficient) construction of size $O_d(\varepsilon^{-(d+t-1)})$ for hypergraphs of $t$-VC-dimension $d$; and obtain $O(1/\varepsilon)$-size $\varepsilon$-2-nets for several geometric hypergraphs in the plane.
notes: Stated as an explicitly labelled Problem environment in Section 1.2. PDF source causes epsilon to render as (cid:15) throughout, but the statement itself is unambiguous.
paper_title: The $ε$-$t$-Net Problem

name: AX_corruption_detection_expansion_threshold
title: Open Problem: Expansion vs. Corruption Detection
statement_text: There is still a significant gap between the expansion properties that suffice for solving the corruption detection problem (strong spectral expansion, as in Ramanujan graphs) and the necessary condition that the graph cannot be split into components of size at most $\epsilon n$ by removing at most $\epsilon n$ vertices. It will be interesting to obtain tighter relations between expansion and corruption detection.
context_text: In the corruption detection problem, each vertex (agent) of a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is either truthful or corrupt; every truthful vertex reports the true type of each of its neighbours, while corrupt vertices may report arbitrarily (and collude). From the reports, one wants to identify with certainty the types of as many vertices as possible, assuming a majority $|T|>|B|$ of truthful vertices (otherwise nothing can be identified). An $(n,d,\lambda)$-graph is a $d$-regular $n$-vertex graph whose eigenvalues other than the largest have absolute value at most $\lambda$; it is Ramanujan if $\lambda\le2\sqrt{d-1}$. The authors prove that for a Ramanujan $(n,d,\lambda)$-graph with $d\ge100$ one can, from any report compatible with a truthful majority, identify all but at most $\frac{32}{d}|B|$ truthful and all but $\frac{32}{d}|B|$ corrupt vertices (in linear time if $|T|>(1+\frac{12}{d})\frac n2$, while the problem is NP-hard for a bare majority even on expanders).
