Conversely, if removing at most $\epsilon n$ vertices leaves only components of size at most $\epsilon n$, then even with $|T|\ge(1-2\epsilon)n$ no truthful vertex can be identified (e.g. planar or minor-free graphs with $\epsilon=\Theta(n^{-1/3})$). In the concluding discussion the authors ask for sharp criteria, in terms of expansion and the fraction $|T|/n$, enabling corruption detection, and give a weak result: if $G$ is $\epsilon$-connected (every two disjoint sets of sizes at least $\epsilon n$ and $(1-3\epsilon)n$ are joined by an edge) and $|T|=(1-\epsilon)n$, then a subset of $T$ of size at least $(1-2\epsilon)n$ can be identified, which is tight up to constants. A follow-up work relates the question to the Small Set Expansion hypothesis.
notes: No labelled theorem environment; stated as a research direction at the end of Section 1.1. Section 4, where this is said to be 'further discussed', is not present in the extracted text (PDF extraction appears truncated).
paper_title: Distributed Corruption Detection in Networks

name: AX_perfect_graphs_combinatorial_mwis_algorithm
title: Combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm for MWIS in perfect graphs
statement_text: Design a combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm for the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem in perfect graphs.
context_text: Given a graph with non-negative vertex weights, Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) asks for an independent set of maximum total weight; it is NP-hard in general. A graph is perfect if the chromatic number of every induced subgraph equals its clique number; by the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem, equivalently, it has no odd hole (induced odd cycle of length at least 5) and no odd antihole (complement of one). Grötschel, Lovász and Schrijver gave a polynomial-time algorithm for MWIS in perfect graphs, but it relies on the ellipsoid method; a combinatorial algorithm means one avoiding such general convex-optimization machinery. The authors call the design of a combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm an important open problem. A related question, the existence of a combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm for Maximum Weight Clique in perfect graphs without long antiholes (equivalently MWIS in graphs with no hole of length at least 5 and no odd antihole), also received much attention; the authors give a polynomial-time algorithm for MWIS in all graphs with no hole of length at least 5 (long-hole-free graphs), via potential maximal cliques and a container method.
notes: Stated in prose without a labelled environment: 'Designing a combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm for MWIS in perfect graphs remains an important open problem.' A classical community-wide open problem acknowledged by the authors as ongoing context.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of bounded treewidth and the container method

name: AX_mwis_p7_free_complexity
title: MWIS in P7-free graphs
statement_text: Determine the computational complexity of the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem in $P_7$-free graphs.
context_text: Given a graph with non-negative vertex weights, Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) asks for an independent set of maximum total weight; it is NP-hard in general. $P_t$ is the path on $t$ vertices and a graph is $P_t$-free if it has no induced $P_t$. No NP-hardness result for MWIS is known in $P_t$-free graphs for any $t$. $P_4$-free graphs have bounded cliquewidth, so MWIS is solvable there in linear time; polynomial-time algorithms were found for $P_5$-free graphs (Lokshtanov, Vatshelle, Villanger, 2014) and $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimošová, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2019), and the case of $P_7$-free graphs remains open. The authors show that, for graphs with no induced cycle of length at least 6 and no induced extended $C_5$ (a 5-cycle plus a vertex adjacent to one or two consecutive vertices of it), a maximum-weight induced subgraph of treewidth less than $k$ can be found in time $n^{O(k)}$; this class contains all $P_5$-free graphs, so it generalizes the $P_5$-free result and also gives Feedback Vertex Set in $P_5$-free graphs in polynomial time, but it does not cover $P_6$- or $P_7$-free graphs.
notes: Stated in passing prose: 'the case of P7-free graphs remains open.' No labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of bounded treewidth and the container method

name: AX_outerplanar_strongly_perfect_characterization
title: Informal Conjecture (outerplanar strongly perfect graphs)
statement_text: While obtaining a complete list of minimal non-strongly-perfect graphs appears to be out of reach, one might conjecture that the characterization of outerplanar strongly perfect graphs can be obtained through the minimal examples given in this paper.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A strong stable set of $G$ is a stable set meeting every nonempty maximal clique of $G$. $G$ is strongly perfect if every induced subgraph has a strong stable set (a subclass of perfect graphs), and minimal non-strongly-perfect if it is not strongly perfect but all its proper induced subgraphs are. Characterizing strongly perfect graphs by forbidden induced subgraphs is open in general; the claw-free case was conjectured by Ravindra and proved by Wang. Ravindra also conjectured in 1990 that a graph is strongly perfect iff it contains no odd hole, no antihole of length at least six, and none of five specific graphs. Maffray later gave another minimal non-strongly-perfect graph. The present paper extends this list with several new infinite families of minimal non-strongly-perfect graphs. They are built from a larva (an even hole plus a vertex adjacent to two consecutive hole vertices) and its relatives, pupas and butterflies, by joining two such pieces by odd or even paths, by 'evolution' (subdividing a side edge an even number of times and making a hole vertex complete to the new vertices) and by 'mutation'. The minimal examples referred to in the statement are these families and the earlier known graphs, given in the paper by figures. The informal conjecture is that, restricted to outerplanar graphs, these examples suffice to characterize strong perfection, even though a complete list of all minimal non-strongly-perfect graphs seems out of reach.
notes: PDF source; the complete final-page sentence was verified in the cached paper.
paper_title: New Examples of Minimal Non-Strongly-Perfect Graphs

name: AX_clique_factor_product_dimension_asymptotics
title: Open Problem: asymptotic behavior of $Q(s,r)$ when $s$ and $r$ grow together
statement_text: Determine the asymptotic behavior of $Q(s, r)$ when $s$ and $r$ grow together (i.e., when $s$ is not fixed as $r \to \infty$).
context_text: The product dimension of a graph $G$ is the minimum number $d$ of proper vertex colourings of $G$ such that every pair of nonadjacent vertices gets the same colour in at least one of them (and any two distinct vertices get different colours in some colouring); equivalently, the minimum $d$ such that vertices can be assigned distinct vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with two vertices adjacent if and only if their vectors differ in every coordinate, or the minimum number of complete graphs whose tensor product contains $G$ as an induced subgraph. For $s,r\ge2$, $K_s(r)$ is the disjoint union of $r$ copies of $K_s$, and $Q(s,r)$ is its product dimension. Lovász, Nešetřil and Pultr proved $Q(2,r)=\lceil\log_2(2r)\rceil$ and raised the problem of estimating $Q(s,r)$ for larger $s$; Kleinberg and Weinberg studied it in connection with prophet inequalities for intersections of matroids. The authors prove $Q(s,r)=(1+o(1))\log_2 r$ for every fixed $s$ as $r\to\infty$, using covering families of vectors in $\mathbb{Z}_s^q$ and the Gargano–Körner–Vaccaro method on Sperner capacities. Simple facts: $Q(s,r)\ge s$ for $r\ge2$, $Q(s,r)\ge\lceil\log_2(2r)\rceil$, $Q$ is non-decreasing in both arguments, $Q(s,r_1r_2)\le Q(s,r_1)+Q(s,r_2)$, and $Q(s,r)=s$ if and only if a resolvable transversal design $TD(r,s)$ exists (so $Q(s,r)=s$ for prime powers $s$ and $2\le r\le s$). The bounds are far apart when $r$ is much bigger than $s$ but much smaller than $2^{s^{3\log\log s}}$; for instance $s\le Q(s,2^s)\le(1+o(1))s^2/\log s$, and the authors say it would be interesting to close this gap.
notes: Section 4 (concluding remarks and open problems) is referenced in the introduction but its full content is not present in the extracted PDF text; additional open problems from that section may be missing.
paper_title: On the product dimension of clique factors

name: AX_planar_recoloring_linear_diameter_min_colors
title: Problem 3
statement_text: What is the minimum integer $\kappa$ such that for every planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, $R_{\kappa}(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$?
context_text: The reconfiguration graph $R_k(G)$ has as vertices all proper $k$-colorings of $G$, two colorings being adjacent if they differ in the color of exactly one vertex; so the distance between two colorings is the minimum number of single-vertex recolorings, keeping the coloring proper, needed to transform one into the other. Cereceda conjectured that $R_{k+2}(G)$ has diameter $O(n^2)$ for $k$-degenerate $n$-vertex graphs. Planar graphs are $5$-degenerate and have maximum average degree less than $6$, so known results (Feghali; Bousquet and Perarnau, who show that $R_c(G)$ has diameter at most $(k+1)n$ for $k$-degenerate $G$ and $c\ge2k+2$) give that $R_8(G)$ has diameter $O(n(\log n)^7)$ and $R_{12}(G)$ has diameter at most $6n$ for planar $G$. The authors prove that $R_{10}(G)$ has diameter at most $8n$ for every $n$-vertex planar graph, so $\kappa\le10$. Conversely, the $6$-coloring of the icosahedron giving opposite vertices the same color is an isolated vertex of $R_6$, so $\kappa\ge7$. A natural candidate planar graph with quadratic diameter of $R_7$, built from copies of a cylinder obtained by cutting the toroidal drawing of $K_7$, is $3$-degenerate and chordal and hence has linear diameter by a result of Bartier and Bousquet; so the authors cannot exclude $\kappa=7$.
paper_title: An update on reconfiguring $10$-colorings of planar graphs

name: AX_gnm_subgraph_moderate_deviations_sparse
title: Remark 1.2 (Open Problem on Sparse Densities)
statement_text: The problem of finding the asymptotic rate of moderate deviations of subgraph counts in $G(n,m)$ (i.e. the asymptotics of $\log\mathbb{P}(D_H(G_{n,t})>\alpha_n n^{v-3/2})$) across the whole range of sparse densities $t=t(n)\to 0$ remains open.
context_text: For graphs $H,G$, $N_H(G)$ is the number of embeddings of $H$ in $G$, i.e. injective maps $\phi:V(H)\to V(G)$ sending edges to edges. Let $H$ be a fixed graph with $v$ vertices and $e$ edges, $N=\binom{n}{2}$, and $L_H(m)=(n)_v(m)_e/(N)_e$ the expected number of embeddings of $H$ in $G(n,m)$ (falling factorials). For $t=t(n)\in(0,1)$, $G_{n,t}$ denotes $G(n,m)$ with $m=\lfloor tN\rfloor$, and $D_H(G_{n,t})=N_H(G_{n,t})-L_H(m)$ is the deviation of the $H$-count; moderate deviations are deviations $\alpha_n n^{v-3/2}$ with $\alpha_n\to\infty$ (the standard deviation in the dense case is of order $n^{v-3/2}$). Writing $\binom{H}{P_2}$ and $\binom{H}{K_3}$ for the numbers of paths of length two and of triangles in $H$, let $\gamma_H(t)=\big(4\binom{H}{P_2}^2t^{2e-2}(1-t)^2+12\binom{H}{K_3}^2t^{2e-3}(1-t)^3\big)^{-1}$. The authors prove that, for $t$ bounded away from $1$ and $\binom{H}{P_2}\ge1$, $\mathbb{P}(D_H(G_{n,t})>\alpha_n n^{v-3/2})=\exp(-\gamma_H(t)\alpha_n^2(1+o(1)))$ (and likewise for the lower tail) when either $t\in(0,1)$ is constant and $1\ll\alpha_n\ll n^{1/2}$, or $\max\{t^{1/2}n^{-1/2}\log n,\,t^{e-3/2}\}\ll\alpha_n\ll\min\{t^{2e-5/2}n^{1/2},\,t^{e+2}n^{1/2}\}$. They first proved the results in the dense case ($t$ constant) and have only partially extended them to sparser regimes; the remaining sparse ranges are left open. This is a problem on random graphs (probability) rather than structural graph theory.
notes: Stated in Remark 1.2 as an open problem in prose form, without a dedicated labeled theorem environment. PDF source — math notation in surrounding theorems may be partially garbled.
paper_title: Moderate deviations of subgraph counts in the Erdős-Rényi random graphs $G(n,m)$ and $G(n,p)$

name: AX_surface_excluded_minors_hoppers_exist
title: Informal Conjecture on Existence of Hoppers for Large Euler Genus
statement_text: Hoppers (graphs with two terminals in which deleting or contracting any edge reduces the Euler genus, or the Euler genus after adding the edge $xy$, by at least $2$) may show up when the Euler genus is large enough.
context_text: The paper studies obstructions (minimal excluded minors) for embeddability in surfaces that have a $2$-vertex-cut $\{x,y\}$, which decompose as $xy$-sums of graphs with two terminals $x,y$. For a graph $G$ with terminals $x,y$ and without the edge $xy$, the minor-operations are the deletions and contractions of single edges (contracting an edge at a terminal yields a terminal), $\widehat g(G)$ is the Euler genus of $G$, and $\widehat g^+(G)$ is the Euler genus of $G^+=G+xy$. For a parameter $P$ (here $\widehat g$ or $\widehat g^+$), $G$ is $P$-critical if every minor-operation decreases $P$, and $G$ is a $P$-hopper if every minor-operation decreases $P$ by at least $2$; weak hoppers are similar mixed versions (e.g. a weak $\widehat g$-hopper is not $\widehat g^+$-critical, and each minor-operation decreases $\widehat g^+$ by at least $1$ and $\widehat g$ by at least $2$). Critical graphs, cascades and hoppers are the building blocks of obstructions of connectivity two. The authors prove that hoppers and weak hoppers do not exist when the parameter equals $2$ (small genus), which, together with the classification of cascades, yields the complete list of Klein bottle obstructions of connectivity $2$. They could not construct any hopper for larger genus but believe they may appear. Their existence is closely related to an old open problem (Archdeacon, Richter, Širáň; Problem 1 in Archdeacon's 1995 list) asking whether some graph is simultaneously an obstruction for two different nonorientable surfaces, for which deleting or contracting any edge would decrease the nonorientable genus by at least $2$.
notes: Expressed as a belief in running prose: 'we believe that they may show up when the genus is large enough.'
paper_title: Excluded minors for the Klein Bottle I. Low connectivity case

name: AX_fractional_chromatic_hall_ratio_gap_function
title: Problem 4
statement_text: Determine the smallest function $g : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ such that for every graph $G$, $\chi_f(G) \leq \rho(G)\,g(|V(G)|)$.
context_text: The Hall ratio of $G$ is $\rho(G)=\max_H |V(H)|/\alpha(H)$ over all subgraphs $H$ of $G$. For a weight assignment $w:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$, $\alpha_w(G)$ is the maximum weight $w(Y)$ of an independent set $Y$; the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is the supremum of $w(V(G))/\alpha_w(G)$ over all weight assignments, and $\rho(G)$ is the same maximum restricted to $\{0,1\}$-valued weights, so $\rho(G)\le\chi_f(G)$. Harris conjectured that $\chi_f$ is bounded by a (linear) function of $\rho$; Blumenthal et al. showed it cannot be bounded by a polynomial. The authors answer the question negatively: for every $c$ there is a graph with $\chi_f(G)\ge c$ and $\rho(G)\le18$. This follows from two results on $1$-subdivisions (subdividing every edge once): every graph of average degree at least $256c^3$ ($c\ge10$) contains the $1$-subdivision of a graph of fractional chromatic number at least $c$, while for every $d$ there is a bipartite graph of average degree at least $d$ containing no $1$-subdivision of a graph with Hall ratio greater than $18$. For an $n$-vertex graph, repeatedly extracting a largest independent set gives $\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G)=O(\rho(G)\log n)$, so $g(n)=O(\log n)$ suffices. The graphs of fractional chromatic number at least $c$ and Hall ratio at most $18$ obtained by the authors have a number of vertices double exponential in their fractional chromatic number, which gives $g(n)=\Omega(\log\log n)$.
paper_title: 1-subdivisions, fractional chromatic number and Hall ratio

name: AX_fractional_chromatic_hall_ratio_degree_weighted
title: Problem 5
statement_text: Do there exist, for some constant $c > 0$, graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large fractional chromatic number such that $\rho(G) \leq c$ and $\alpha_{\deg_H}(H) \geq |E(H)|/c$ for every $H \subseteq G$?
context_text: The Hall ratio of $G$ is $\rho(G)=\max_H |V(H)|/\alpha(H)$ over all subgraphs $H$ of $G$. For a weight assignment $w:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$, $\alpha_w(G)$ is the maximum weight $w(Y)$ of an independent set $Y$; the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is the supremum of $w(V(G))/\alpha_w(G)$ over all weight assignments, and $\rho(G)$ is the same maximum restricted to $\{0,1\}$-valued weights, so $\rho(G)\le\chi_f(G)$. Harris conjectured that $\chi_f$ is bounded by a (linear) function of $\rho$; Blumenthal et al. showed it cannot be bounded by a polynomial. The authors answer the question negatively: for every $c$ there is a graph with $\chi_f(G)\ge c$ and $\rho(G)\le18$. This follows from two results on $1$-subdivisions (subdividing every edge once): every graph of average degree at least $256c^3$ ($c\ge10$) contains the $1$-subdivision of a graph of fractional chromatic number at least $c$, while for every $d$ there is a bipartite graph of average degree at least $d$ containing no $1$-subdivision of a graph with Hall ratio greater than $18$. Here $\alpha_{\deg_H}(H)$ denotes $\alpha_w(H)$ for the weight assignment $w(v)=\deg_H(v)$, i.e. the maximum, over independent sets $Y$ of $H$, of the sum of the degrees in $H$ of the vertices of $Y$; note $\sum_v\deg_H(v)=2|E(H)|$. The authors ask more generally whether some natural non-trivial family $\mathcal{F}$ of weight functions, between $\{0,1\}$-valued weights (Hall ratio) and all weights (fractional chromatic number), gives a parameter $\rho_{\mathcal{F}}(G)=\max_{w\in\mathcal{F}}w(V(G))/\alpha_w(G)$ bounding $\chi_f$; since their lower bound on $\chi_f$ for the random graphs used in the $1$-subdivision theorem uses weights asymptotically proportional to degrees, degree weights are the first natural case to consider.
notes: PDF source — the notation $\alpha_{\deg_H}$ for the degree-weighted maximum independent set weight may be slightly garbled.
paper_title: 1-subdivisions, fractional chromatic number and Hall ratio

name: AX_bounded_expansion_hall_ratio_shallow_minors
title: Problem 8
statement_text: Is it true that a class $\mathcal{C}$ has bounded expansion if and only if there exists a function $f_6 : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $G \in \mathcal{C} \mathbin{\triangledown} r$, $\rho(G) \leq f_6(r)$?
context_text: The Hall ratio of $G$ is $\rho(G)=\max_H|V(H)|/\alpha(H)$ over all subgraphs $H$ of $G$. A shallow minor at depth $r$ of $G$ is a graph obtained from $G$ by deleting vertices and edges and contracting pairwise vertex-disjoint subgraphs each of radius at most $r$; $\mathcal{C}\mathbin{\triangledown}r$ is the class of shallow minors at depth $r$ of graphs of $\mathcal{C}$. A class $\mathcal{C}$ has bounded expansion if there is $f_1$ such that every graph of $\mathcal{C}\mathbin{\triangledown}r$ has average degree at most $f_1(r)$; equivalently, the maximum average degree, the colouring number, or the chromatic number of graphs in $\mathcal{C}\mathbin{\triangledown}r$ is bounded by a function of $r$. A class is nowhere dense if the clique number of graphs in $\mathcal{C}\mathbin{\triangledown}r$ is bounded by a function of $r$. The authors show (from the fact that graphs of average degree at least $256c^3$ contain the $1$-subdivision of a graph of fractional chromatic number at least $c$) that bounded expansion is also characterised by bounded fractional chromatic number $\chi_f$ in $\mathcal{C}\mathbin{\triangledown}r$. Since $\chi_f(G)\ge\rho(G)\ge\omega(G)$, bounded expansion implies the Hall-ratio property, which implies nowhere density; but the same argument fails for the Hall ratio, because there are graphs of arbitrarily large average degree containing no $1$-subdivision of a graph with Hall ratio greater than $18$. The authors also show a nowhere dense class with unbounded Hall ratio (from regular graphs of large girth and small independence number), and know no class with unbounded expansion whose shallow minors have bounded Hall ratio.
paper_title: 1-subdivisions, fractional chromatic number and Hall ratio

name: AX_perfect_graphs_combinatorial_mis_algorithm
title: Combinatorial Polynomial-Time Algorithm for MIS/MWIS in Perfect Graphs
statement_text: No combinatorial polynomial-time algorithm is known for any of MIS, MWIS, MC, and MWC in perfect graphs; finding one is a major open problem in the field. At the moment we do not even have a polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm to solve MIS in perfect graphs with no hole of length four.
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least $4$, an antihole is the complement of one, and a hole or antihole is long if its length is at least $5$. MIS, MWIS, MC and MWC denote the Maximum (Weight) Independent Set and Maximum (Weight) Clique problems (weights are non-negative on vertices). All four problems are solvable in polynomial time on perfect graphs by the algorithm of Grötschel, Lovász and Schrijver, which however uses the ellipsoid method. The authors have no precise definition of a combinatorial algorithm (a good rule of thumb: an algorithm not using division), but roughly mean one described as a sequence of operations applied directly to the vertices and edges of the graph, without techniques such as the ellipsoid or simplex method. Besides MIS in $C_4$-free perfect graphs, another important special case is MC in perfect graphs with no long antihole, which by complementation is a special case of MIS in long-hole-free graphs; the latter was open when the paper was submitted and has since been solved in polynomial time by Abrishami, Chudnovsky and Pilipczuk, as the authors note. This is a long-standing community problem, not introduced by the authors.
notes: A long-standing community open problem cited as motivation in the introduction; not introduced by these authors. PDF source — math may be garbled.
paper_title: On the Maximum Weight Independent Set Problem in graphs without induced cycles of length at least five

name: AX_mwis_long_hole_prism_free_fpt
title: FPT Algorithm for MWIS in (Long-Hole, k-Prism)-Free Graphs
statement_text: We do not see how to turn the $n^{O(k)}$-time algorithm for MWIS in (long-hole, $k$-prism)-free $n$-vertex graphs into an FPT-algorithm (parameterized by $k$), without using the result of Abrishami, Chudnovsky and Pilipczuk (polynomial-time MWIS in long-hole-free graphs).
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least $4$, an antihole is the complement of one, and a hole or antihole is long if its length is at least $5$. MIS, MWIS, MC and MWC denote the Maximum (Weight) Independent Set and Maximum (Weight) Clique problems (weights are non-negative on vertices). For an integer $k>0$, the $k$-prism is the graph on $\{a_1,\dots,a_k,b_1,\dots,b_k\}$ in which $\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}$ and $\{b_1,\dots,b_k\}$ are cliques, $a_ib_i$ is an edge for every $i$, and there are no other edges; it is long-hole-free but has exponentially many minimal separators. The authors prove, using the potential maximal cliques framework of Bouchitté and Todinca, that for every integer $k>0$ MWIS can be solved in time $n^{O(k)}$ on $n$-vertex graphs containing neither a long hole nor the $k$-prism as an induced subgraph (and deduce a subexponential algorithm for MWIS on all long-hole-free graphs). An FPT algorithm would run in time $f(k)\,n^{O(1)}$. The authors note that, after submission, Abrishami, Chudnovsky and Pilipczuk solved MWIS in polynomial time on all long-hole-free graphs (with a conceptually much more complicated algorithm), which in particular gives such a running time; the question is therefore only whether the simpler approach of this paper can be made FPT, and is not a genuine open problem about complexity.
notes: Implicit open question stated in prose without a labelled environment. PDF source — math may be garbled.
paper_title: On the Maximum Weight Independent Set Problem in graphs without induced cycles of length at least five

name: AX_hat_guessing_number_degree_degeneracy_bounds
title: Problem 1.4
statement_text: Do there exist functions $f_i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $1 \leq i \leq 3$ such that (i) if the maximum degree of $G$ is $\Delta$, then $HG(G) \leq f_1(\Delta)$; (ii) if $G$ is $d$-degenerate, then $HG(G) \leq f_2(d)$; (iii) if the minimum degree of $G$ is $\delta$, then $HG(G) \geq f_3(\delta)$, and $f_3(\delta)$ tends to infinity when $\delta$ tends to infinity.
context_text: In the hat guessing game on a simple graph $G$, each vertex is a player who receives a hat colored arbitrarily with one of $q$ colors; each player sees exactly the hat colors of its neighbours (not its own), and all players simultaneously guess their own color according to a strategy agreed in advance, without communication. The players win if at least one guesses correctly for every hat assignment. The hat guessing number $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is the largest $q$ for which a winning strategy exists ($G$ is then called $q$-solvable). Complete graphs, which have large hat guessing number, show that large cliques force large $\mathrm{HG}$, but $K_{n,n}$ has clique number $2$ and $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})\to\infty$. Of the three functions, only $f_1$ is known to exist: by the Lovász Local Lemma $\mathrm{HG}(G)<e\Delta$ (folklore). Complete graphs and cycles suggest $f_1(\Delta)=\Delta+1$ might hold, and trees and complete bipartite graphs suggest $f_2(d)=d+1$, but it is not even clear whether $f_2$ exists. As partial progress on (ii), the authors show that if $G$ has a vertex of degree one and is $q$-solvable with $q\ge3$, then so is $G$ minus that vertex (so trees are not $3$-solvable, i.e. $f_2(1)\le2$), give a Local-Lemma bound $\mathrm{HG}(G)<ek^2q^k$ when the subgraph induced by the vertices of degree larger than $k$ is not $q$-solvable, and prove that the linear version (guessing functions affine over $\mathbb{F}_q$) satisfies $\mathrm{HG}_{lin}(G)\le d+1$ for $d$-degenerate $G$.
paper_title: The hat guessing number of graphs

name: AX_hat_guessing_number_complete_bipartite
title: Open question: exact value of $HG(K_{n,n})$
statement_text: What is the exact value of $HG(K_{n,n})$?
context_text: In the hat guessing game on a simple graph $G$, each vertex is a player who receives a hat colored arbitrarily with one of $q$ colors; each player sees exactly the hat colors of its neighbours (not its own), and all players simultaneously guess their own color according to a strategy agreed in advance, without communication. The players win if at least one guesses correctly for every hat assignment. The hat guessing number $\mathrm{HG}(G)$ is the largest $q$ for which a winning strategy exists ($G$ is then called $q$-solvable). Butler et al. showed $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})=\Omega(\log\log n)$ and asked whether $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})\ge n^{\alpha}$ for some constant $\alpha>0$; Gadouleau and Georgiou proved $\mathrm{HG}(K_{m,n})\le\min\{m+1,n+1\}$ and $\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})=\Omega(\log n)$. The authors answer the question of Butler et al. positively: more generally, the complete $r$-partite graph with $r-1$ parts of size $m=(2q\ln q)^{1/(r-1)}$ and one part of size $cr(q\ln q)^{r/(r-1)}$ is $q$-solvable, so the balanced complete $r$-partite graph satisfies $\mathrm{HG}\ge n^{(r-1)/r-o(1)}$. Hence $\Omega(n^{1/2-o(1)})=\mathrm{HG}(K_{n,n})\le n+1$, and determining the exact value is left open. They also ask whether $\mathrm{HG}(K_{g(q),q^c})\ge q$ for some $g(q)=o(q\ln q)$ and constant $c\ge1$, possibly $g(q)=\Theta(q)$.
notes: No labelled environment; stated as an open question in running prose immediately after Theorem 1.2.
paper_title: The hat guessing number of graphs

name: AX_grundy_coloring_half_graph_free_fpt
title: FPT on $H_{t,t}$-free graphs for Grundy Coloring and b-Chromatic Core
statement_text: Are \textsc{Grundy Coloring} and \textsc{b-Chromatic Core} fixed-parameter tractable on $H_{t,t}$-free graphs when parameterized by $k$?
context_text: Given an ordering of the vertices of $G$, the first-fit (greedy) coloring gives each vertex in turn the smallest color not used on its already colored neighbors; the Grundy number $\Gamma(G)$ is the largest number of colors used by first-fit over all orderings, and Grundy Coloring asks, given $G$ and $k$, whether $\Gamma(G)\ge k$. A $b$-chromatic core of order $k$ is a vertex set $C$ with a partition $V_1\uplus\cdots\uplus V_k$ such that each $V_i$ contains a vertex $v_i$ with a neighbor in every $V_j$, $j\neq i$; b-Chromatic Core asks, given $G$ and $k$, whether $G$ contains one. The half-graph of height $t$, $H_{t,t}$, is the bipartite graph with parts $\{a_1,\dots,a_t\}$ and $\{b_1,\dots,b_t\}$ where $a_ib_j$ is an edge if and only if $i<j$. $K_{t,t}$-free means having no $K_{t,t}$ as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph; excluding $K_{t,t}$ implies excluding a large half-graph but not vice versa, so $H_{t,t}$-free graphs (presumably excluding $H_{t,t}$ as an induced subgraph; the paper does not spell this out) form a larger class. All problems are parameterized by the number $k$ of colors. The authors prove that Grundy Coloring is W[1]-complete (and, under ETH, not solvable in time $f(k)n^{o(2^{k-\log k})}$) and that b-Chromatic Core is W[1]-complete, both hardness proofs using large half-graphs to propagate colors; all three problems are FPT on nowhere dense graphs, and Partial Grundy Coloring and b-Chromatic Core are FPT on $K_{t,t}$-free graphs, even parameterized by $k+t$. Since the hardness constructions rely heavily on large half-graphs, excluding them might restore tractability; however, the key combinatorial lemma behind the $K_{t,t}$-free algorithms (many high-degree vertices in a $K_{t,t}$-free graph yield $k$ disjoint pairwise non-adjacent $k$-vertex stars, a witness) collapses on $H_{t,t}$-free graphs, so the question is left open.
notes: Stated as an explicit open problem in the 'Limits and further questions' section; no formal numbered theorem environment.
paper_title: Grundy Coloring & friends, Half-Graphs, Bicliques

name: AX_grundy_coloring_biclique_free_fpt
title: FPT on $K_{t,t}$-free graphs for Grundy Coloring
statement_text: Does \textsc{Grundy Coloring} admit a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm on $K_{t,t}$-free graphs when parameterized by $k$?
context_text: Given an ordering of the vertices of $G$, the first-fit (greedy) coloring gives each vertex in turn the smallest color not used on its already colored neighbors; the Grundy number $\Gamma(G)$ is the largest number of colors used by first-fit over all orderings, and Grundy Coloring asks, given $G$ and $k$, whether $\Gamma(G)\ge k$. A proper coloring $V_1\uplus\cdots\uplus V_k$ is a partial Grundy coloring of order $k$ if for each $i$ some $v_i\in V_i$ has a neighbor in every $V_j$ with $j<i$; Partial Grundy Coloring asks, given $G$ and $k$, whether $G$ has one. A $b$-chromatic core of order $k$ is a vertex set $C$ with a partition $V_1\uplus\cdots\uplus V_k$ such that each $V_i$ contains a vertex $v_i$ with a neighbor in every $V_j$, $j\neq i$; b-Chromatic Core asks, given $G$ and $k$, whether $G$ contains one. $K_{t,t}$-free graphs are those with no $K_{t,t}$ as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph; this dense class contains nowhere dense graphs and graphs of bounded degeneracy. The authors prove that Grundy Coloring is W[1]-complete (and, under ETH, not solvable in time $f(k)n^{o(2^{k-\log k})}$) and that b-Chromatic Core is W[1]-complete, both hardness proofs using large half-graphs to propagate colors; all three problems are FPT on nowhere dense graphs, and Partial Grundy Coloring and b-Chromatic Core are FPT on $K_{t,t}$-free graphs, even parameterized by $k+t$. The question is whether the $K_{t,t}$-free tractability extends to Grundy Coloring, for which a minimal induced witness of $\Gamma(G)\ge k$ has at most $2^{k-1}$ vertices (against $k^2$ for the two other problems).
notes: Stated explicitly as unsettled in the 'Limits and further questions' section; no formal numbered theorem environment.
paper_title: Grundy Coloring & friends, Half-Graphs, Bicliques

name: AX_partial_grundy_coloring_parameterized_complexity
title: Parameterized complexity of Partial Grundy Coloring on general graphs
statement_text: What is the parameterized complexity of \textsc{Partial Grundy Coloring} on general graphs, parameterized by $k$?
context_text: A proper coloring $V_1\uplus\cdots\uplus V_k$ is a partial Grundy coloring of order $k$ if for each $i$ some $v_i\in V_i$ has a neighbor in every $V_j$ with $j<i$; Partial Grundy Coloring asks, given $G$ and $k$, whether $G$ has one. (Erdős et al. showed that the largest such $k$, the partial Grundy number, equals the upper ochromatic number.) The parameter is $k$. The authors prove that the related problems Grundy Coloring (is the largest number of colors used by first-fit over all vertex orderings at least $k$?) and b-Chromatic Core are W[1]-complete, using large half-graphs to propagate colors, and that Partial Grundy Coloring is FPT on nowhere dense graphs and on $K_{t,t}$-free graphs (even parameterized by $k+t$), but its complexity on general graphs resisted their efforts. Half-graphs cannot be used for it, since the partial Grundy number is already large on a large half-graph $H_{t,t}$ (the bipartite graph on $\{a_1,\dots,a_t\}\cup\{b_1,\dots,b_t\}$ with $a_ib_j$ an edge if and only if $i<j$); hence the authors suggest that $H_{t,t}$-free graphs are a promising class to study in order to settle the general case.
notes: Stated as an open problem in the 'Limits and further questions' section; no formal numbered theorem environment.
paper_title: Grundy Coloring & friends, Half-Graphs, Bicliques

name: AX_circular_digraph_homomorphism_complexity
title: Problem 2.15
statement_text: Let $F$ be a fixed (multi-)digraph. Instance: A (multi-)digraph $D$. Decide whether $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable.
context_text: Digraphs are loopless but may have parallel and anti-parallel arcs; a digon is a directed cycle of length two, and a vertex set is acyclic if it induces an acyclic subdigraph. A circular homomorphism from a digraph $D_1$ to a digraph $D_2$ is a map $\phi:V(D_1)\to V(D_2)$ such that the preimage of every acyclic set of $D_2$ is acyclic in $D_1$; equivalently, for every directed cycle $C$ of $D_1$, $D_2[\phi(V(C))]$ contains a directed cycle. For symmetric digraphs (each edge replaced by a digon) these are exactly graph homomorphisms, and acyclic homomorphisms are a special case. A digraph $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable if there is a circular homomorphism from $D$ to $F$. An acyclic $(k,d)$-colouring of $D$ is a map $c:V(D)\to\mathbb{Z}_k$ such that for every $i$ the preimage of the cyclic interval $\{i,\dots,i+d-1\}$ is acyclic, and the star dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}^{*}(D)$ is the infimum of $k/d$ over such colourings; $\vec{\chi}^{*}(D)\le k/d$ if and only if $D$ is circularly $\vec{C}(k,d)$-colourable, where $\vec{C}(k,d)$ has vertex set $\mathbb{Z}_k$ and an arc $(i,j)$ whenever $(j-i)\bmod k\ge d$. The problem, a directed analogue of the $H$-colouring problem for graphs, is to determine for which fixed $F$ this decision problem is polynomial and for which it is NP-complete. It generalises the question, posed by Hochstättler, of the complexity of deciding $\vec{\chi}^{*}(D)\le p$, which the authors prove NP-complete for every rational $p>1$. If $F$ is acyclic only acyclic digraphs map circularly to $F$, so the problem is polynomial; the authors conjecture that it is NP-complete whenever $F$ contains a directed cycle, and prove this when $F$ is digon-free, or the symmetric part of $F$ (the graph of its digons) contains an odd cycle, or $F$ is 2-colourable (dichromatic number at most $2$).
notes: The complete dichotomy (all F with a directed cycle) is conjectured but not fully proved within the paper.
paper_title: On the Complexity of Digraph Colourings and Vertex Arboricity

name: AX_circular_digraph_homomorphism_np_complete_cyclic
title: Conjecture 2.16
statement_text: Let $F$ be a digraph which contains a directed cycle. Then the circular $F$-colouring problem is NP-complete.
context_text: Digraphs are loopless but may have parallel and anti-parallel arcs; a digon is a directed cycle of length two, and a vertex set is acyclic if it induces an acyclic subdigraph. A circular homomorphism from a digraph $D_1$ to a digraph $D_2$ is a map $\phi:V(D_1)\to V(D_2)$ such that the preimage of every acyclic set of $D_2$ is acyclic in $D_1$; equivalently, for every directed cycle $C$ of $D_1$, $D_2[\phi(V(C))]$ contains a directed cycle. For symmetric digraphs (each edge replaced by a digon) these are exactly graph homomorphisms, and acyclic homomorphisms are a special case. A digraph $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable if there is a circular homomorphism from $D$ to $F$. The circular $F$-colouring problem asks, for a fixed digraph $F$, whether an input (multi-)digraph is circularly $F$-colourable; it is a directed analogue of the $H$-colouring problem, and for $F=\vec{C}(k,d)$ (vertex set $\mathbb{Z}_k$, arc $(i,j)$ whenever $(j-i)\bmod k\ge d$) it amounts to deciding whether the star dichromatic number is at most $k/d$. If $F$ is acyclic, only acyclic digraphs map circularly to $F$, so the problem is polynomial; the conjecture says that, assuming P$\ne$NP, these are the only polynomial cases. The authors prove it when $F$ is digon-free, or the symmetric part of $F$ (the graph on $V(F)$ whose edges are the digons) contains an odd cycle, or $F$ is 2-colourable (dichromatic number at most $2$); this parallels the classification of Feder et al. for acyclic homomorphisms.
paper_title: On the Complexity of Digraph Colourings and Vertex Arboricity

name: AX_fractional_dichromatic_number_complexity
title: Problem 3.21
statement_text: Let $p\geq 1$ be a fixed real number. Instance: A (multi-)digraph $D$. Decide whether $\vec{\chi}_{f}(D)\leq p$.
context_text: Digraphs are loopless but may have parallel and anti-parallel arcs; a digon is a directed cycle of length two, and a vertex set is acyclic if it induces an acyclic subdigraph. For a digraph $D$, let $\mathcal{A}(D)$ be the family of acyclic vertex sets and $\mathcal{A}(D,v)$ those containing $v$; the fractional dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}_f(D)$ is the minimum of $\sum_{A\in\mathcal{A}(D)}x_A$ subject to $\sum_{A\in\mathcal{A}(D,v)}x_A\ge1$ for every vertex $v$ and $x\ge0$ (equivalently, the minimum $k/b$ such that each vertex can be assigned $b$ colours out of $k$ with every colour class acyclic). For $p=1$ the problem is equivalent to acyclicity, hence polynomial, and it is in NP for every $p$. The paper proves that it is NP-complete for every real $p>1$ with $p\ne2$, mirroring results of Feder et al. for the circular dichromatic number; thus only the case $p=2$ remains open, and the authors strongly believe it is also NP-complete.
notes: The case $p=2$ remains unresolved after this paper.
paper_title: On the Complexity of Digraph Colourings and Vertex Arboricity

name: AX_directed_kneser_graphs_existence
title: Problem 5.40
statement_text: For given $k,b\in\mathbb{N}$ with $k\geq b$, is there a directed graph $\vec{K}(k,b)$ with vertex set $\binom{[k]}{b}$ such that the following holds? The subdigraph of $\vec{K}(k,b)$ induced by any $\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{l}\}\subseteq\binom{[k]}{b}$ is acylic if and only if $\bigcap_{i=1}^{l}{B_{i}}\neq\emptyset$.
context_text: Digraphs are loopless but may have parallel and anti-parallel arcs; a digon is a directed cycle of length two, and a vertex set is acyclic if it induces an acyclic subdigraph. A $b$-tuple $k$-colouring of a digraph $D$ assigns to each vertex a set of $b$ colours from $[k]=\{1,\dots,k\}$ so that, for each colour $i$, the vertices whose set contains $i$ induce an acyclic subdigraph; the fractional dichromatic number of $D$ is the minimum $k/b$ for which a $b$-tuple $k$-colouring exists. For graphs, a $(k,b)$-colouring (sets of $b$ colours, disjoint on adjacent vertices) exists if and only if there is a homomorphism to the Kneser graph $K(k,b)$. A circular homomorphism from $D_1$ to $D_2$ is a map whose preimages of acyclic sets are acyclic. If a digraph $\vec{K}(k,b)$ as in the problem exists, then $D$ is $b$-tuple $k$-colourable if and only if there is a circular homomorphism from $D$ to $\vec{K}(k,b)$, a directed analogue of the Kneser graph reformulation. For $k=b+1$ such a digraph exists: the directed cycle of length $b+1$ on the sets $[b+1]\setminus\{i\}$.
paper_title: On the Complexity of Digraph Colourings and Vertex Arboricity

name: AX_strong_coloring_numbers_tame_representation
title: Question 6
statement_text: Given a polynomial $p$, do there necessarily exist real numbers $c, s \geq 1$ and a positive integer $d$, such that the following holds: every graph $G$ satisfying $\mathrm{col}_r(G) \leq p(r)$ for every non-negative integer $r$ admits a $(c, \sqsubseteq_s)$-tame representation in $\mathbb{R}^d$?
context_text: An intersection representation of a graph $G$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ assigns to each vertex $v$ a non-empty set $\varphi(v)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ such that, for distinct $u,v$, the sets $\varphi(u)$ and $\varphi(v)$ intersect if and only if $uv\in E(G)$; it is $c$-thin if every point of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in at most $c$ of the sets $\varphi(v)$. A shape is a compact set not contained in any proper affine subspace. For sets $B_1,B_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ and real $s\ge 1$, write $B_1\sqsubseteq_s B_2$ if for every point $x\in B_2$ there is a translate $B_1'$ of $B_1$ with $x\in B_1'$ and $\mathrm{vol}(B_1'\cap B_2)\ge\frac{1}{s}\mathrm{vol}(B_1)$; $B_1$ and $B_2$ are $\sqsubseteq_s$-comparable if $B_1\sqsubseteq_s B_2$ or $B_2\sqsubseteq_s B_1$. A representation $\varphi$ is $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame if it is $c$-thin, every $\varphi(v)$ is a convex shape, and $\varphi(u),\varphi(v)$ are $\sqsubseteq_s$-comparable for all $u,v$. For a linear ordering $\prec$ of $V(G)$, a path from $v$ to $x$ respects $\prec$ if $v\prec z$ for all its internal vertices $z$; $L_{G,\prec,r}(v)$ is the set of vertices $x\preceq v$ joined to $v$ by a $\prec$-respecting path of length at most $r$; $\mathrm{col}_{\prec,r}(G)=\max_v|L_{G,\prec,r}(v)|$, and the strong coloring number $\mathrm{col}_r(G)$ is the minimum of $\mathrm{col}_{\prec,r}(G)$ over all linear orderings $\prec$. The authors prove that for all $c,s\ge1$ and $d$ there is $\delta$ such that if $G$ has a $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame representation $\varphi$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, then ordering the vertices by non-increasing volume of $\varphi(v)$ gives $\mathrm{col}_{\prec,r}(G)\le\delta r^d$ for every $r$ (hence such graphs have balanced separators of size $O(n^{1-1/(2d+4)})$). This parallels the theorem of Krauthgamer and Lee: for every polynomial $p$ there is $d$ such that every graph $G$ whose growth is bounded by $p$ (every ball of radius $r$ has at most $p(r)$ vertices) has an injection $\varphi:V(G)\to\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $\|\varphi(u)-\varphi(v)\|_\infty=1$ for every edge $uv$, which characterizes classes of polynomial growth. A positive answer to the question would give a similar rough geometric characterization of graphs with polynomially bounded strong coloring numbers. The authors suspect that the answer is negative.
notes: The notation $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame and $\sqsubseteq_s$ are rendered as '(cid:118)s' in the PDF extraction; interpreted as the paper's comparability relation defined via volume overlap.
paper_title: Sublinear separators in intersection graphs of convex shapes

name: AX_strong_coloring_numbers_tame_representation_negative
title: Informal conjecture: negative answer to Question 6
statement_text: There exists a polynomial $p$ such that for all real numbers $c,s\ge 1$ and every positive integer $d$, some graph $G$ satisfying $\mathrm{col}_r(G)\le p(r)$ for every non-negative integer $r$ does not admit a $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame representation in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
context_text: An intersection representation of a graph $G$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ assigns to each vertex $v$ a non-empty set $\varphi(v)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ such that, for distinct $u,v$, the sets $\varphi(u)$ and $\varphi(v)$ intersect if and only if $uv\in E(G)$; it is $c$-thin if every point of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in at most $c$ of the sets $\varphi(v)$. A shape is a compact set not contained in any proper affine subspace. For sets $B_1,B_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ and real $s\ge 1$, write $B_1\sqsubseteq_s B_2$ if for every point $x\in B_2$ there is a translate $B_1'$ of $B_1$ with $x\in B_1'$ and $\mathrm{vol}(B_1'\cap B_2)\ge\frac{1}{s}\mathrm{vol}(B_1)$; $B_1$ and $B_2$ are $\sqsubseteq_s$-comparable if $B_1\sqsubseteq_s B_2$ or $B_2\sqsubseteq_s B_1$. A representation $\varphi$ is $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame if it is $c$-thin, every $\varphi(v)$ is a convex shape, and $\varphi(u),\varphi(v)$ are $\sqsubseteq_s$-comparable for all $u,v$. For a linear ordering $\prec$ of $V(G)$, a path from $v$ to $x$ respects $\prec$ if $v\prec z$ for all its internal vertices $z$; $L_{G,\prec,r}(v)$ is the set of vertices $x\preceq v$ joined to $v$ by a $\prec$-respecting path of length at most $r$; $\mathrm{col}_{\prec,r}(G)=\max_v|L_{G,\prec,r}(v)|$, and the strong coloring number $\mathrm{col}_r(G)$ is the minimum of $\mathrm{col}_{\prec,r}(G)$ over all linear orderings $\prec$. The authors prove that $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame representability in $\mathbb{R}^d$ implies $\mathrm{col}_r(G)\le\delta r^d$ for all $r$, with $\delta$ depending on $c,s,d$, and asked whether, for every polynomial $p$, there exist $c,s\ge1$ and $d$ such that every graph with $\mathrm{col}_r(G)\le p(r)$ for all $r$ admits a $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame representation in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and write that they suspect the answer is negative. Their evidence: by analogy with the Krauthgamer–Lee embedding of graphs of polynomial growth into $\mathbb{Z}^d$ (a product of maps to a path) one could hope for a representation by boxes (products of $d$ closed intervals), but they prove that for all $c,s\ge1$, every $d$ and every non-decreasing unbounded $f:\mathbb{N}\to[3,+\infty)$, there is a graph $G$ with an ordering $\prec$ such that $\mathrm{col}_{\prec,r}(G)\le f(r)$ for every $r$ which has no $(c,\sqsubseteq_s)$-tame intersection representation in $\mathbb{R}^d$ by boxes.
notes: Stated as suspicion in prose ('we suspect'); Theorem 7 provides partial supporting evidence by ruling out box-shaped tame representations, but the full Question 6 remains open. PDF source — math notation may be garbled.
paper_title: Sublinear separators in intersection graphs of convex shapes

name: AX_lattice_cube_list_colorability_threshold
title: Optimal n for $L^d_n$-list-colorability
statement_text: Fixing $d$, what is the optimal value of $n$ such that $[n]^d$ is $L^d_n$-list-colorable?
context_text: Here $[n]^d=\{1,\dots,n\}^d$ is viewed as an induced subgraph of the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ (two points adjacent iff they differ by $1$ in exactly one coordinate). For a graph $G$ and $L:V(G)\to\mathbb{N}$, $G$ is $L$-list-colorable if for every choice of lists $S_v$ with $|S_v|\ge L(v)$ there is a proper coloring $f$ with $f(v)\in S_v$ for all $v$. The function $L_n^d:[n]^d\to\{2,\dots,d+2\}$ is $L_n^d(i_1,\dots,i_d)=2+|\{k: 1<i_k<n\}|$, i.e. two plus the number of coordinates that are not on the boundary of the box. The authors prove that $[n]^d$ is $L_n^d$-list-colorable whenever $n\ge d+2$; consequently, for $q\ge d+2$ colors any partial proper $q$-coloring of the boundary of a box of side $n\ge d+2$ extends to the whole box, which is used to classify the mixing properties of proper $q$-colorings of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. The property is monotone: if $[n]^d$ is $L_n^d$-list-colorable then so are $[n]^{d-1}$ (with $L_n^{d-1}$) and $[n+1]^d$ (with $L_{n+1}^d$), which justifies asking for the smallest such $n$. The threshold $d+2$ is not always optimal: $[2]^2$ is $L_2^2$-list-colorable although $2<4$, while $[2]^3$ is not $L_2^3$-list-colorable. The authors did not try to optimise $n$.
notes: Stated in running prose: 'Fixing d, the question of the optimal value of n such that [n]^d is L^d_n-list-colorable remains.' Section 5 (not fully reproduced in the extracted text) apparently contains additional formal open questions including a labeled Question 5.7 concerning whether $[n]^2$ is $\min\{L^2_n, 3\}$-list-colorable; its full statement could not be extracted.
paper_title: Mixing properties of colorings of the $\mathbb{Z}^d$ lattice

name: AX_prism_pyramid_theta_turtle_free_separators
title: Conjecture 2.2
statement_text: There is a polynomial $P$ such that every graph $G$ that contains no prism, pyramid, theta or turtle has at most $P(|V(G)|)$ minimal separators.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $G$ contains $H$ if some induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, and $G$ is $H$-free otherwise; paths are chordless. A hole is an induced cycle on at least $4$ vertices (a square is a hole of length $4$), and a graph is even-hole-free if it has no hole with an even number of vertices. A theta consists of three internally disjoint chordless paths of length at least $2$ between two vertices $a,b$, with no edges between the paths except at $a$ and $b$; a pyramid consists of three chordless paths $a\dots b_1$, $a\dots b_2$, $a\dots b_3$ of length at least $1$, two of length at least $2$, disjoint except at $a$, such that $b_1b_2b_3$ is a triangle and there are no other edges between the paths; a prism consists of three disjoint chordless paths $a_i\dots b_i$ ($i=1,2,3$) of length at least $1$ such that $a_1a_2a_3$ and $b_1b_2b_3$ are triangles and there are no other edges between the paths. A wheel is a hole (the rim) plus a vertex (the center) with at least three neighbours on it; it is an even wheel if the center has an even number of neighbours on the rim. A turtle consists of two internally disjoint chordless $u$–$v$ paths $P_1,P_2$ forming a hole, plus two adjacent vertices $x,y$ outside them such that $x$ has at least three neighbours in $P_1$ and none in $P_2$, and $y$ at least three neighbours in $P_2$ and none in $P_1$. A set $C\subseteq V(G)$ is a minimal separator if it is a minimal set separating some pair of vertices $a,b$ (equivalently, $G\setminus C$ has two components $L,R$ such that every vertex of $C$ has neighbours in both). By results of Bouchitté and Todinca, a polynomial bound on the number of minimal separators in a class gives a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum weight independent set on that class. The $k$-prisms (two $k$-cliques joined by a perfect matching), their variants the $k$-pyramids and $k$-thetas, and the $k$-turtles have exponentially many minimal separators and contain respectively a prism, pyramid, theta and turtle; since the authors could not imagine other examples with exponentially many minimal separators, they propose this conjecture as in some sense the best possible statement. The authors prove that every (square, prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graph on $n$ vertices has $O(n^8)$ minimal separators (enumerable in $O(n^{10})$ time); this class contains all (even hole, pyramid)-free graphs, so maximum weight independent set is polynomial-time solvable on (even hole, pyramid)-free graphs. Every prism, theta and turtle contains an even hole (turtles contain even wheels), so restricting the conjecture to (prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graphs gives a weakening, which the authors could only prove after also excluding squares.
paper_title: Maximum independent sets in (pyramid, even hole)-free graphs

name: AX_even_hole_free_independent_set_complexity
title: Open problem: MIS complexity in even-hole-free graphs
statement_text: The complexity of computing a maximum independent set in an even-hole-free graph is not known; that is, can a maximum independent set be computed in polynomial time in even-hole-free graphs (graphs with no induced cycle of even length at least $4$)?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $G$ contains $H$ if some induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, and $G$ is $H$-free otherwise; paths are chordless. A hole is an induced cycle on at least $4$ vertices (a square is a hole of length $4$), and a graph is even-hole-free if it has no hole with an even number of vertices. Even-hole-free graphs have been the object of much research (see Vušković's survey), but this question is open. The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum weight independent set on (even hole, pyramid)-free graphs, where a pyramid consists of three chordless paths $a\dots b_1$, $a\dots b_2$, $a\dots b_3$ of length at least $1$, two of length at least $2$, disjoint except at $a$, such that $b_1b_2b_3$ is a triangle and there are no other edges between the paths. The method is a decomposition theorem plus a polynomial bound ($O(n^8)$) on the number of minimal separators, which yields the algorithm via results of Bouchitté and Todinca; the bound holds more generally for (square, prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graphs. The authors hope that the pyramid-free case may help to understand the whole class, since the presence of a pyramid strongly restricts the structure of an even-hole-free graph.
notes: Stated as a known open problem in the field (referencing a survey [10]); no specific attribution to individual authors is given in the text.
paper_title: Maximum independent sets in (pyramid, even hole)-free graphs

name: AX_prism_pyramid_theta_wheel_free_separators
title: Open problem: polynomial separator property for (prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graphs
statement_text: Do (prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graphs have polynomially many minimal separators, i.e. is there $b$ such that every such graph $G$ has at most $|V(G)|^b$ minimal separators? The authors were not able to prove it.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple; $G$ contains $H$ if some induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, and $G$ is $H$-free otherwise; paths are chordless. A hole is an induced cycle on at least $4$ vertices (a square is a hole of length $4$), and a graph is even-hole-free if it has no hole with an even number of vertices. A theta consists of three internally disjoint chordless paths of length at least $2$ between two vertices $a,b$, with no edges between the paths except at $a$ and $b$; a pyramid consists of three chordless paths $a\dots b_1$, $a\dots b_2$, $a\dots b_3$ of length at least $1$, two of length at least $2$, disjoint except at $a$, such that $b_1b_2b_3$ is a triangle and there are no other edges between the paths; a prism consists of three disjoint chordless paths $a_i\dots b_i$ ($i=1,2,3$) of length at least $1$ such that $a_1a_2a_3$ and $b_1b_2b_3$ are triangles and there are no other edges between the paths. A wheel is a hole (the rim) plus a vertex (the center) with at least three neighbours on it; it is an even wheel if the center has an even number of neighbours on the rim. A turtle consists of two internally disjoint chordless $u$–$v$ paths $P_1,P_2$ forming a hole, plus two adjacent vertices $x,y$ outside them such that $x$ has at least three neighbours in $P_1$ and none in $P_2$, and $y$ at least three neighbours in $P_2$ and none in $P_1$. A set $C\subseteq V(G)$ is a minimal separator if it is a minimal set separating some pair of vertices $a,b$ (equivalently, $G\setminus C$ has two components $L,R$ such that every vertex of $C$ has neighbours in both). By results of Bouchitté and Todinca, a polynomial bound on the number of minimal separators in a class gives a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum weight independent set on that class. The authors conjecture that graphs containing no prism, pyramid, theta or turtle have polynomially many minimal separators. Since every turtle contains an even wheel, restricting to (prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graphs gives a weakening of that conjecture; (prism, theta, even wheel)-free graphs are known as odd-signable graphs and capture essential properties of even-hole-free graphs. The authors prove that every (square, prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graph on $n$ vertices has $O(n^8)$ minimal separators (enumerable in $O(n^{10})$ time); this class contains all (even hole, pyramid)-free graphs, so maximum weight independent set is polynomial-time solvable on (even hole, pyramid)-free graphs. The remaining open case is thus whether excluding squares is necessary.
notes: Implicit open problem arising from the gap between Conjecture 2.2 and Theorem 2.3; not labeled as a formal conjecture or problem in the paper.
paper_title: Maximum independent sets in (pyramid, even hole)-free graphs

name: AX_triangulation_4_coloring_complex_mixed_parity
title: Conjecture 8
statement_text: For every planar triangulation whose 4-coloring complex is disconnected, there is a component of even parity and a component of odd parity.
context_text: For a 4-colorable graph $G$, a color class is an independent set that is one of the color classes of some 4-coloring of $G$. The 4-coloring complex $B(G)$ (introduced by Tutte) is the graph whose vertices are the color classes of $G$, two being adjacent if they appear together in some 4-coloring; each 4-coloring is a 4-clique of $B(G)$, and two colorings lie in the same component exactly when they are linked by a sequence of colorings, consecutive ones sharing a color class. For a 4-coloring $f$ with classes $A,B,C,D$, let $p(X,Y)$ be the number of components of $G[X\cup Y]$ (the $XY$-Kempe chains); Tutte defined $J_A(f)=p(A,B)+p(A,C)+p(A,D)-p(B,C)-p(B,D)-p(C,D)$, and $f$ is even or odd according to the parity of $J_A(f)$ (which does not depend on the choice of the class $A$). For a triangulation of the plane, all colorings in a component of $B(T)$ have the same parity, so components are even or odd. Tutte asked whether some planar triangulation has two components of the same parity. The authors answer yes: they give 12-vertex examples (none exist on 11 or fewer vertices), infinitely many triangulations with more than $k$ even and more than $k$ odd components for any $k$, 4-connected triangulations whose complex has $2^k+1$ components, and 5-connected examples with two components of the same parity. Based on extensive computations they conjecture instead that whenever $B(T)$ is disconnected, both parities occur.
notes: The conjecture is described verbatim in both the abstract and the introduction with a forward reference to 'Conjecture 8', but the formal conjecture environment itself is not present in the extracted PDF text (the paper body appears truncated after Section 5). Statement reconstructed from the abstract and introduction prose.
paper_title: The Last Temptation of William T. Tutte

name: AX_bounded_vc_dimension_erdos_hajnal
title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: For $d \geq 2$, there exists a constant $\varepsilon(d)$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices with VC-dimension at most $d$ contains a clique or an independent set of size $n^{\varepsilon(d)}$.
context_text: The VC-dimension of a set system $\mathcal{F}$ on a ground set $V$ is the largest $d$ such that some $d$-element set $S\subseteq V$ is shattered, i.e. for every $B\subseteq S$ there is $A\in\mathcal{F}$ with $A\cap S=B$. The VC-dimension of a graph is the VC-dimension of the set system of its vertex neighbourhoods $N(v)$; for instance, every $K_{2,2}$-free graph has VC-dimension at most $2$, and graphs of bounded VC-dimension form a hereditary family. Erdős and Hajnal proved that for every hereditary graph property $P$ not satisfied by all graphs, every $n$-vertex graph with $P$ has a clique or independent set of size $e^{\varepsilon(P)\sqrt{\log n}}$, and conjectured (the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture) that this can be improved to $n^{\varepsilon(P)}$. For graphs of VC-dimension at most $d$, the authors had earlier improved the bound to $e^{(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}$; this conjecture is the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture restricted to bounded VC-dimension. The paper's main result proves the Schur–Erdős conjecture for colourings of bounded VC-dimension: for every $k\ge3$ and $d\ge2$, every $m$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ with $n\ge2^{cm}$, $c=c(k,d)$, whose colour-class neighbourhoods form a set system of dual VC-dimension at most $d$, has a monochromatic $K_k$; the authors suggest proving other conjectures, especially Erdős–Hajnal, under bounded VC-dimension. Status note (November 2026): proved by Nguyen, Scott and Seymour ('Induced subgraph density. VI. Bounded VC-dimension', arXiv 2312.15572, 2023; Adv. Math., 2025), in the stronger form that graphs of VC-dimension at most $d$ have the polynomial Rödl property.
paper_title: Bounded VC-dimension implies the Schur-Erdos conjecture

name: AX_planar_fvs_face_packing_ratio_2
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every planar graph $G$, we have $\mathrm{fvs}(G) \leq 2 \cdot \mathrm{fp}(G)$, where $\mathrm{fp}(G)$ is the maximum size of a face-packing of $G$, i.e., a cycle-packing where, for some embedding of $G$, every cycle bounds a face.
context_text: A cycle packing of a (multi)graph $G$ is a set of vertex-disjoint cycles of $G$, and $\mathrm{cp}(G)$ is the maximum size of a cycle packing; a feedback vertex set is a set $S$ of vertices such that $G-S$ is a forest, and $\mathrm{fvs}(G)$ is the minimum size of a feedback vertex set. A face-packing is a cycle packing whose cycles all bound faces in one common embedding of $G$ in the plane (the embedding may be chosen), so $\mathrm{fp}(G)\le\mathrm{cp}(G)$ and the conjecture is stronger than Jones' Conjecture (Kloks, Lee and Liu), which states $\mathrm{fvs}(G)\le2\,\mathrm{cp}(G)$ for every planar graph. The best known bound is $\mathrm{fvs}(G)\le3\,\mathrm{cp}(G)$ (Chappell et al., Chen et al., Ma et al.), obtainable by a simple discharging argument, while no factor $3-\epsilon$ is known; the authors prove Jones' Conjecture for subcubic planar multigraphs. They pose this stronger conjecture to highlight how little is understood around Jones' Conjecture. The example of many nested disjoint cycles shows that the embedding cannot be fixed in advance, and the discharging argument does not even give the face-packing version with factor $3$ instead of $2$.
paper_title: Jones' Conjecture in subcubic graphs

name: AX_f3n_subspace_free_sets_exponential_base
title: Informal Question (correct exponential constant in r(n,m))
statement_text: Is $3$, the lower bound on $r(n,m)$ given by considering a random set, the right exponential constant? That is, does $r(n,m) = N^{1-\varepsilon_m}$ hold with the same exponential base $3$ as in the random lower bound $r(n,m) \geq N^{1-(m+1)3^{-m}}$, rather than the base $C \approx 13.901$ appearing in the upper bound $r(n,m) \leq (1+o(1))N^{1-C^{-m}}$?
context_text: $r(n,m)$ is the maximum size of a subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ containing no affine $m$-dimensional subspace (the multidimensional cap set problem), and $N=3^n$. A random set gives $r(n,m)\ge N^{1-(m+1)3^{-m}}$. In the other direction, the arithmetic triangle removal lemma of Fox and Lovász implies that every subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ of density $\alpha$ has three-term arithmetic progression density at least $\alpha^C$ with $C\approx13.901$; choosing the most popular nonzero common difference $d$ and inducting on $m$ gives $r(n,m)\le(1+o(1))N^{1-C^{-m}}$. Both bounds have the form $N^{1-\varepsilon_m}$ with $\varepsilon_m\to0$ exponentially fast in $m$, but with exponential base $3$ versus $C$; the authors ask whether the right base is $3$, $C$, or something in between. For a prime $p$, $\alpha>0$ and $\beta<\alpha^3$, $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ is the least positive integer such that for every $n\ge n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ and every $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ of density at least $\alpha$, there is a nonzero $d\in\mathbb{F}_p^n$ such that the density of three-term arithmetic progressions $x,x+d,x+2d$ (over $x$) lying in $A$ is at least $\beta$; it exists by a theorem of Green (popular differences), and fails to exist for $\beta\ge\alpha^3$. If $n\ge n_3(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\beta=\alpha^{3+o(1)}$, the same induction would show that $3$ is the correct base; but the authors determine, for $p\ge19$, the tower height of $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ up to constant factors, and it grows for $\beta=\alpha^{3+o(1)}$, giving strong evidence that this popular-differences approach cannot settle the question. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
notes: Stated as an open question in running prose in the introduction without a formal labelled environment. PDF source — exponent notation in r(n,m) bounds may be garbled.
paper_title: Popular progression differences in vector spaces II

name: AX_popular_progression_tower_height_small_primes
title: Conjecture (Theorem 2 extends to primes p < 19)
statement_text: The following bounds on the tower height of $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$, proved for primes $p\ge19$, should also hold for all primes $p<19$: for $0<\alpha\le1/2$, $\alpha^3>\beta>\alpha^{3+e^{-133}}$ and $\epsilon=\alpha^3-\beta$, (i) if $\epsilon<\alpha^3/(\log(1/\alpha))^{\log p}$, then $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ grows as a tower of $p$'s of height $\Theta(\log(\alpha^3/\epsilon))\pm O_p(1)$; (ii) if $\alpha^3/(\log(1/\alpha))^{\log p}\le\epsilon<\alpha^3(1-2^{-8-8C_p})$, it grows as a tower of $p$'s of height $\Theta((\log p)\log\log(1/\alpha))\pm O_p(1)$; (iii) otherwise it grows as a tower of $p$'s of height $\Theta\big((\log p)\log\frac{\log(1/\alpha)}{\log(\alpha^3/\beta)}\big)\pm O_p(1)$ with a $1/\beta$ on top.
context_text: For a prime $p$, $\alpha>0$ and $\beta<\alpha^3$, $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ is the least positive integer such that for every $n\ge n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ and every $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ of density at least $\alpha$, there is a nonzero $d\in\mathbb{F}_p^n$ such that the density of three-term arithmetic progressions $x,x+d,x+2d$ (over $x$) lying in $A$ is at least $\beta$; it exists by a theorem of Green (popular differences), and fails to exist for $\beta\ge\alpha^3$. $C_p=\Theta(\log p)$ is the exponent in the arithmetic triangle removal lemma in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ (every set of density $\alpha$ has three-term progression density at least $\alpha^{C_p}$), and $\pm O_p(1)$ means up to an additive error depending only on $p$. For $\beta$ much smaller (below $\alpha^{3+e^{-133}}$) the growth of $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ is a tower of constant height with $\log(1/\alpha)$ on top, and for $\alpha$ close to $1$ the behaviour is different and determined separately. The authors prove the three-case result for $p\ge19$ (for instance, half the random bound, $\beta=\alpha^3/2$, requires a tower of height $\Theta((\log p)\log\log(1/\alpha))$) and conjecture it for $p<19$. The upper bounds hold for all primes, as does the lower bound when $\epsilon$ is small; only the case of large $\epsilon$ is missing, because the lower-bound construction uses bounds on the largest subset of $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ without a three-term progression, and the known bounds are not good enough for small $p$. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
notes: Stated in prose immediately before Theorem 2 with the words 'We conjecture these bounds should also hold for p < 19.' No formal labelled environment.
paper_title: Popular progression differences in vector spaces II

name: AX_binary_matroid_claw_triangle_chi_bounded
title: Conjecture 1.6
statement_text: For all $s \geq 1$ there exists an integer $k$ such that if $M$ is a simple binary matroid with no induced $I_s$-restriction or $PG(1, 2)$-restriction, then $\chi(M) \leq k$.
context_text: Here a simple binary matroid is a pair $M=(E,G)$ where $G$ is a finite-dimensional binary projective geometry $\mathrm{PG}(n-1,2)$ (the nonzero vectors of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, with $n$ the dimension of $M$) and $E\subseteq G$ is the ground set. $M$ contains $N=(F,G')$ as a restriction if there is a linear injection $\varphi:G'\to G$ with $\varphi(F)\subseteq E$, and as an induced restriction if moreover $\varphi(F)=E\cap\varphi(G')$; equivalently, an induced restriction is $M$ restricted to a flat. $\mathrm{PG}(t-1,2)$ also denotes the matroid whose ground set is the whole geometry; in particular $\mathrm{PG}(1,2)$ is a triangle (three points $x,y,x+y$), the analogue of a clique $K_3$. $I_s$ is the $s$-dimensional matroid whose ground set is a basis of $s$ elements, the analogue of a tree; $I_3$ is called a claw. The critical number $\chi(M)$ of an $n$-dimensional $M$ is the least $k$ such that $G\setminus E$ contains a projective geometry of dimension $n-k$; it is the matroid analogue of the chromatic number, and $\chi(M(G))=\lceil\log_2\chi(G)\rceil$ for cycle matroids of graphs. The natural matroid analogue of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture (excluding $I_s$ and $\mathrm{PG}(t-1,2)$ bounds $\chi$) fails: the authors construct matroids with no induced $I_3$ or Fano plane $F_7=\mathrm{PG}(2,2)$ restriction and arbitrarily large critical number. They conjecture that excluding a triangle ($t=2$) restores a bound. They show the conjecture is easy for $s\in\{1,2,3\}$, where $k=1$ suffices, but new ideas are needed for larger $s$. The graph analogue (excluding an induced tree $T$ and a triangle) is easy for stars but open in general. Matroid theory rather than graph theory.
paper_title: The structure of binary matroids with no induced claw or Fano plane restriction

name: AX_induced_arithmetic_removal_higher_complexity
title: Open Problem (Extending Induced Arithmetic Removal to Higher Complexity and General Groups)
statement_text: Extend the induced arithmetic removal lemma beyond complexity 1 patterns over finite fields to higher complexity patterns and to general abelian groups (even the case of $\mathbb{Z}$ is open).
context_text: Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and $V$ a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space. An $r$-colored pattern $H=(A,\psi)$ is an $\ell\times k$ matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ together with a coloring $\psi:[k]\to[r]$ of its columns; for a coloring $\phi:V\to[r]$, an $H$-instance is a tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in V^k$ with $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ and $\phi(x_i)=\psi(i)$ for all $i$, the $H$-density is the number of $H$-instances divided by $|V|^{k-\mathrm{rank}A}$, and $\phi$ is $H$-free if there is no $H$-instance in $(V\setminus\{0\})^k$ (zero is ignored, since e.g. the solution $x=y=z=0$ of $x+y+z=0$ cannot be removed by recoloring). For functions $f_1,\dots,f_k:V\to\mathbb{C}$ let $\Lambda_A(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ be the average of $f_1(x_1)\cdots f_k(x_k)$ over all $\mathbf{x}\in V^k$ with $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$, and let $\widehat f(\gamma)$ denote the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at a character $\gamma$ of $V$. The matrix $A$ has complexity 1 if for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that for every $V$ and all $f_1,\dots,f_k:V\to[-1,1]$, $|\Lambda_A(f_1,\dots,f_k)|\le\epsilon$ whenever $\min_i\|\widehat f_i\|_\infty\le\delta$; examples are any single equation with at least three nonzero coefficients, or 3-term progressions, whereas 4-term progressions have complexity 2 (complexity $s$ means control by the Gowers $U^{s+1}$ norm, after Green and Tao). The authors prove the induced arithmetic removal lemma for complexity 1 patterns over finite fields: for a finite set $\mathcal{H}$ of $r$-colored complexity 1 patterns over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that, for every $V$, if a coloring $\phi:V\to[r]$ has $H$-density at most $\delta$ for every $H\in\mathcal{H}$, then there is a recoloring $\phi':V\setminus\{0\}\to[r]$ that is $H$-free for all $H\in\mathcal{H}$ and differs from $\phi$ on at most $\epsilon|V|$ elements. This is an arithmetic analogue of the induced graph removal lemma of Alon, Fischer, Krivelevich and Szegedy (patterns of colors play the role of induced subgraphs), extending earlier work over $\mathbb{F}_2$ via a new recoloring technique. The authors state that extending this lemma to higher complexity patterns and to general abelian groups remains open (even over $\mathbb{Z}$). For affine-invariant patterns, a special case avoiding the difficulty of regularization near the origin, the problem for bounded complexity patterns over finite fields has been solved by Bhattacharyya, Fischer, Hatami, Hatami and Lovett. This is a problem of additive combinatorics.
paper_title: Induced arithmetic removal: complexity 1 patterns over finite fields

name: AX_induced_arithmetic_removal_abelian_groups
title: Informal Conjecture (Induced Arithmetic Removal for Arbitrary Abelian Groups)
statement_text: A statement analogous to the induced arithmetic removal lemma for complexity 1 patterns over finite fields (a coloring with small density of every pattern of a fixed finite family can be made free of all of them by recoloring few elements) holds for arbitrary patterns (with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$) in arbitrary abelian groups, subject to appropriate caveats concerning infinite complexity patterns and trivial solutions.
context_text: Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and $V$ a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space. An $r$-colored pattern $H=(A,\psi)$ is an $\ell\times k$ matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ together with a coloring $\psi:[k]\to[r]$ of its columns; for a coloring $\phi:V\to[r]$, an $H$-instance is a tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in V^k$ with $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ and $\phi(x_i)=\psi(i)$ for all $i$, the $H$-density is the number of $H$-instances divided by $|V|^{k-\mathrm{rank}A}$, and $\phi$ is $H$-free if there is no $H$-instance in $(V\setminus\{0\})^k$ (zero is ignored, since e.g. the solution $x=y=z=0$ of $x+y+z=0$ cannot be removed by recoloring). For functions $f_1,\dots,f_k:V\to\mathbb{C}$ let $\Lambda_A(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ be the average of $f_1(x_1)\cdots f_k(x_k)$ over all $\mathbf{x}\in V^k$ with $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$, and let $\widehat f(\gamma)$ denote the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at a character $\gamma$ of $V$. The matrix $A$ has complexity 1 if for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that for every $V$ and all $f_1,\dots,f_k:V\to[-1,1]$, $|\Lambda_A(f_1,\dots,f_k)|\le\epsilon$ whenever $\min_i\|\widehat f_i\|_\infty\le\delta$; examples are any single equation with at least three nonzero coefficients, or 3-term progressions, whereas 4-term progressions have complexity 2 (complexity $s$ means control by the Gowers $U^{s+1}$ norm, after Green and Tao). The authors prove the induced arithmetic removal lemma for complexity 1 patterns over finite fields: for a finite set $\mathcal{H}$ of $r$-colored complexity 1 patterns over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that, for every $V$, if a coloring $\phi:V\to[r]$ has $H$-density at most $\delta$ for every $H\in\mathcal{H}$, then there is a recoloring $\phi':V\setminus\{0\}\to[r]$ that is $H$-free for all $H\in\mathcal{H}$ and differs from $\phi$ on at most $\epsilon|V|$ elements. This is an arithmetic analogue of the induced graph removal lemma of Alon, Fischer, Krivelevich and Szegedy (patterns of colors play the role of induced subgraphs), extending earlier work over $\mathbb{F}_2$ via a new recoloring technique. The authors conjecture that a similar statement holds for arbitrary patterns with integer coefficients in arbitrary abelian groups, but do not state a precise conjecture, because caveats are needed: in $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ colored red on $1,\dots,\lfloor N/2\rfloor$ and blue elsewhere, the pattern $x=y+1$ with $x$ blue and $y$ red has a single instance but cannot be removed by recoloring fewer than $\lfloor N/2\rfloor$ elements (this pattern has infinite complexity), and some trivial solutions, such as zero, must be ignored. This is a problem of additive combinatorics.
notes: Authors explicitly decline to state a precise conjecture: 'we do not state a precise conjecture here'. Classified as Informal accordingly.
paper_title: Induced arithmetic removal: complexity 1 patterns over finite fields

name: AX_induced_arithmetic_removal_complexity_1_polynomial
title: Informal Conjecture (Polynomial Quantitative Bound for Complexity 1 Systems)
statement_text: For complexity 1 systems, the dependence of $\delta$ on $\epsilon$ in the definition of complexity 1 satisfies $\delta = \epsilon^{O_A(1)}$, i.e., polynomial dependence.
context_text: Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field and $A$ an $\ell\times k$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$. For a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space $V$ and functions $f_1,\dots,f_k:V\to\mathbb{C}$, let $\Lambda_A(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ be the average of $f_1(x_1)\cdots f_k(x_k)$ over all $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in V^k$ with $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$, and let $\widehat f(\gamma)=\mathbb{E}_{x\in V}f(x)\overline{\gamma(x)}$ be the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at a character $\gamma$ of $V$. The matrix $A$ has complexity 1 if for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that for every $V$ and all $f_1,\dots,f_k:V\to[-1,1]$, $|\Lambda_A(f_1,\dots,f_k)|\le\epsilon$ whenever $\min_i\|\widehat f_i\|_\infty\le\delta$. Examples: any single equation $\sum a_ix_i=0$ with at least three nonzero coefficients, or the cycle relations of a directed graph; a system given by linear forms $L_1,\dots,L_k$ has complexity 1 if and only if $L_1^2,\dots,L_k^2$ are linearly independent (with a technical modification for even $q$), by work of Gowers–Wolf and Hatami–Hatami–Lovett. The authors remark that the general dependence of $\delta$ on $\epsilon$ is a wide open problem, and that conjecturally $\delta=\epsilon^{O_A(1)}$ works (they point to work of Manners for discussion). The paper uses complexity 1 to prove an induced arithmetic removal lemma over finite fields. This is a problem of additive combinatorics.
notes: Stated as 'conjecturally' in running prose without a labelled environment and without explicit attribution to named individuals; reference [20] is cited for discussion but no author names are given in the extracted text.
paper_title: Induced arithmetic removal: complexity 1 patterns over finite fields

name: AX_edge_statistics_induced_density_1_over_e
title: Conjecture 1.1 (The Edge-statistics Conjecture)
statement_text: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $k_0 = k_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for all integers $k > k_0$ and $0 < \ell < \binom{k}{2}$ we have $\mathrm{ind}(k, \ell) \leq 1/e + \varepsilon$.
context_text: For a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and $0\le\ell\le\binom k2$, let $I(n,k,\ell)$ be the maximum, over graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices, of the probability that a uniformly random $k$-subset of $V(G)$ spans exactly $\ell$ edges; this is non-increasing in $n$, and the edge-inducibility is $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\lim_{n\to\infty}I(n,k,\ell)$. It equals $1$ for $\ell\in\{0,\binom k2\}$ (empty or complete graphs) and satisfies $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\mathrm{ind}(k,\binom k2-\ell)$. For a graph $H$, the inducibility $\mathrm{ind}(H)$ (Pippenger and Golumbic) is the limit as $n\to\infty$ of the maximum, over $n$-vertex graphs $G$, of the number of induced copies of $H$ in $G$ divided by $\binom{n}{|H|}$; clearly $\mathrm{ind}(H)\le\mathrm{ind}(|H|,e(H))$. The random graph $G(n,p)$ with $p=\binom k2^{-1}$ gives $\mathrm{ind}(k,1)\ge1/e+o_k(1)$, and the complete bipartite graph with smaller part of size $n/k$ gives $\mathrm{ind}(k,k-1)\ge\mathrm{ind}(K_{1,k-1})\ge1/e+o_k(1)$; these constructions and additional data motivate the conjecture that $1/e$ is asymptotically tight. The $o_k(1)$ is necessary, as $\mathrm{ind}(3,1)=\mathrm{ind}(3,2)=3/4$.
