The authors prove that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)<1-\varepsilon$ for an absolute $\varepsilon>0$ and all $0<\ell<\binom k2$, that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)\le1/2+\varepsilon$ when $Ck\le\ell\le\binom k2-Ck$, that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=O(k^{-0.1})$ when $\min\{\ell,\binom k2-\ell\}=\Omega(k^2)$ (so the conjecture holds 'almost everywhere'), and that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)\le3/4+o_k(1)$ for fixed $\ell$, with $1/2$ for $\ell=1$.
paper_title: Edge-statistics on large graphs

name: AX_edge_statistics_large_inducibility_1_over_e
title: Conjecture 1.2 (The Large Inducibility Conjecture)
statement_text: $\limsup\{\mathrm{ind}(H) : H \notin \{K_{|H|}, \overline{K}_{|H|}\}\} = 1/e$.
context_text: For a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and $0\le\ell\le\binom k2$, let $I(n,k,\ell)$ be the maximum, over graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices, of the probability that a uniformly random $k$-subset of $V(G)$ spans exactly $\ell$ edges; this is non-increasing in $n$, and the edge-inducibility is $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\lim_{n\to\infty}I(n,k,\ell)$. It equals $1$ for $\ell\in\{0,\binom k2\}$ (empty or complete graphs) and satisfies $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\mathrm{ind}(k,\binom k2-\ell)$. For a graph $H$, the inducibility $\mathrm{ind}(H)$ (Pippenger and Golumbic) is the limit as $n\to\infty$ of the maximum, over $n$-vertex graphs $G$, of the number of induced copies of $H$ in $G$ divided by $\binom{n}{|H|}$; clearly $\mathrm{ind}(H)\le\mathrm{ind}(|H|,e(H))$. Here the $\limsup$ is that of the set of inducibilities of all graphs $H$ that are neither complete nor empty (its largest limit point). This is the analogue for graph inducibilities of the authors' Edge-statistics Conjecture (that for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)\le1/e+\varepsilon$ for all large $k$ and $0<\ell<\binom k2$), which would imply it since $\mathrm{ind}(H)\le\mathrm{ind}(|H|,e(H))$. The value $1/e$ is attained asymptotically, e.g. $\mathrm{ind}(K_{1,k-1})=1/e+o_k(1)$, and $\mathrm{ind}(H)=\mathrm{ind}(k,1)\ge1/e+o_k(1)$ for the $k$-vertex graph with one edge. The authors prove that the inducibility of every graph that is neither complete nor empty is bounded away from $1$ by an absolute constant.
paper_title: Edge-statistics on large graphs

name: AX_erdos_posa_planar_minor_constant_polynomial
title: Open Problem (constant c vs. |H|)
statement_text: For a planar graph $H$, find good bounds on $c=c(H)$ as a function of $|H|$ in the Erdős–Pósa bounding function $f(k)=ck\log(k+1)$ for $H$-models (that is, such that $\tau_H(G)\le f(\nu_H(G))$ for every graph $G$); in particular, determine whether $c$ could depend polynomially on $|H|$.
context_text: An $H$-model in a graph $G$ is a collection $\{M_x:x\in V(H)\}$ of vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of $G$ such that $M_x$ and $M_y$ are joined by an edge of $G$ for every edge $xy\in E(H)$ (so $G$ has an $H$-model if and only if $H$ is a minor of $G$); two models are disjoint if their vertex sets are. $\nu_H(G)$ is the maximum number of pairwise disjoint $H$-models in $G$, and $\tau_H(G)$ is the minimum size of a set $X\subseteq V(G)$ such that $G-X$ has no $H$-model. The Erdős–Pósa property holds for $H$-models with bounding function $f$ if $\tau_H(G)\le f(\nu_H(G))$ for every graph $G$; by Robertson and Seymour this holds for some $f$ if and only if $H$ is planar. Chekuri and Chuzhoy obtained $f(k)=ck\log^d(k+1)$ for a universal constant $d$, with $c$ depending polynomially on $|H|$ (using the Polynomial Grid Minor Theorem). The authors prove that for each planar $H$ there is $c=c(H)$ such that $f(k)=ck\log(k+1)$ works, which is best possible up to $c$ when $H$ contains a cycle (for forests an $O(k)$ bound is known). However, their constant $c$ is enormous and not even known to be computable, since the proof uses a non-constructive result of Fomin, Lokshtanov, Misra and Saurabh on minor-minimal graphs with $\tau_H(G)=t$.

name: AX_book_number_triangle_count_extremal_density
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: If $n/6 \leq b < n/4$, then every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges and book number at most $b$ which is not the balanced complete bipartite graph has at least $b^2(n - 4b)$ triangles, with equality if and only if the graph is $S_{b,n}$.
context_text: A book of size $s$ in a graph is a set of $s$ triangles sharing a common edge, and the book number $b(G)$ is the size of the largest book, i.e. the maximum number of triangles containing a single edge. The $3$-prism graph consists of two disjoint triangles joined by a perfect matching. For $b\le n/4$, $S_{b,n}$ is the blow-up of the $3$-prism with six parts $U_1,U_2,U_3,V_1,V_2,V_3$, where $|U_1|=|U_2|=|V_1|=|V_2|=b$, $|U_3|=\lfloor(n-4b)/2\rfloor$, $|V_3|=\lceil(n-4b)/2\rceil$, $U_i$ is complete to $U_j$ and $V_i$ to $V_j$ for $i\ne j$, $U_i$ is complete to $V_i$ for each $i$, and there are no other edges; it has $n$ vertices, $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ edges, $b^2(n-4b)$ triangles, and book number $b$ when $b\ge n/6$. By Mantel and Rademacher, graphs with $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$ edges have at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ triangles, and by Edwards and Khadžiivanov–Nikiforov they have book number at least $n/6$. Mubayi asked for the minimum number $t(n,b)$ of triangles in a graph on $n$ vertices with $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$ edges and book number at most $b$; he showed that for each $\beta\in(1/6,1/4)$ there is $\gamma>0$ with $t(n,\beta n)\ge\gamma n^3$, and asked for the optimal $\gamma(\beta)$. This conjecture (which allows $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ edges instead) would imply an asymptotically tight bound on $t(n,b)$ for $n/6\le b\le n/4-\omega(1)$, answering Mubayi's question; an almost identical construction appeared in the original arXiv version of Mubayi's paper. The authors prove the conjecture, for graphs with at least $n^2/4$ edges, when $0.2495n\le b<n/4$ and when $b=n/6$.
paper_title: Books versus triangles at the extremal density

name: AX_perfect_graphs_combinatorial_independent_set_algorithm
title: Open problem: Combinatorial algorithm for MIS on perfect graphs
statement_text: It remains an open question to find a combinatorial algorithm for the maximum independent set problem on perfect graphs. In fact, we do not even have a combinatorial FPT algorithm for the maximum independent set problem on perfect graphs.
context_text: A combinatorial algorithm here means one that does not rely on the ellipsoid method. A graph is perfect if every induced subgraph $H$ satisfies $\chi(H)=\omega(H)$; by the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem these are exactly the Berge graphs (no induced odd cycle of length at least $5$ and no induced complement of one). An FPT algorithm for maximum independent set parameterized by the solution size $k$ decides whether the input $n$-vertex graph has an independent set of size $k$ in time $f(k)n^{O(1)}$ for some computable $f$. Maximum independent set is polynomial-time solvable on perfect graphs by the ellipsoid method (Grötschel, Lovász and Schrijver), and combinatorially on subclasses such as bipartite, chordal and claw-free graphs. This open problem is mentioned as motivation: the paper studies the structurally similar class of even-hole-free graphs (no induced cycle of even length at least $4$), where the complexity of maximum independent set is a long-standing open question, and shows that maximum independent set is FPT parameterized by the solution size there, whereas it is W[1]-hard on graphs with no induced $C_4$.
notes: Stated as a known open problem in the community without a specific attribution cite; no labeled theorem environment.
paper_title: The independent set problem is FPT for even-hole-free graphs

name: AX_p_entropic_matroids_prime_representable
title: Open problem: p-entropic matroids linear for prime p
statement_text: Our results leave open the possibility for $p$-entropic matroids to be linear whenever $p$ is prime.
context_text: For a positive integer $q$, a matroid $M$ on ground set $[m]$ with rank function $r$ is $q$-entropic if there is a probability distribution $\mu$ on $[q]^m$ (equivalently, random variables $X_1,\dots,X_m$ each with support of size at most $q$) such that $r(S)=H(\mu_S)$ for every $S\subseteq[m]$, where $\mu_S$ is the marginal of $\mu$ on the coordinates in $S$ and $H$ is the Shannon entropy in base $q$; so the joint entropies of the variables must all be integers and equal to the ranks. Here linear means representable over the field $\mathbb{F}_p$. Every $\mathbb{F}$-representable matroid is $|\mathbb{F}|$-entropic (take $X=AY$ for a representing matrix $A$ and a uniform random vector $Y$), and the question is whether the converse holds. The authors prove that, for every $p$, being $p$-entropic is equivalent to being a secret-sharing matroid with ground set of size $p$ (equivalently, an almost affine matroid with alphabet size $p$) and is closed under taking minors; that $p$-entropic matroids are exactly the $\mathbb{F}_p$-representable ones for $p=2$ and $p=3$; and, by a known example, that this fails for $p=9$ (there is a 9-entropic matroid representable over no field). For prime $p$ they make partial progress: every $p$-entropic matroid of rank at most two is $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear, the uniform matroid $U_{2,p+2}$ is not $p$-entropic, and the Fano plane is not $p$-entropic for $p>2$. This is a matroid-theory question.

paper_title: Entropic matroids and their representation

name: AX_independent_set_h_free_polynomial_dichotomy
title: Classical MIS Dichotomy Conjecture
statement_text: For every connected graph $H$, Maximum Independent Set in $H$-free graphs is in $\mathsf{P}$ if and only if $H \in \{P_\ell\}_{\ell} \cup \{S_{i,j,k}\}_{i \leq j \leq k}$.
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. Alekseev observed that subdividing each edge $2t$ times increases the independence number by exactly $t|E(G)|$, so MIS stays NP-hard on graphs that locally look like paths or subdivided claws; hence if a connected $H$ is neither a path nor a subdivided claw, MIS is NP-complete on $H$-free graphs. The conjecture asserts the converse. Known polynomial cases include $P_4$-free graphs (cographs), $P_5$-free (Lokshtanov, Vatshelle, Villanger) and $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik et al.), claw-free and fork-free ($S_{1,1,2}$-free) graphs. The complexity is open for $P_7$-, $S_{1,1,3}$- and $S_{1,2,2}$-free graphs, and there is no triple $i\le j\le k$ for which MIS is known to be NP-hard on $S_{i,j,k}$-free graphs. A stronger conjecture was proposed by Lozin.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled. $\{P_\ell\}_\ell$ denotes the family of paths and $\{S_{i,j,k}\}_{i \leq j \leq k}$ denotes the family of subdivided claws. Presented as a conjecture formalising a well-known open problem; no explicit citation in the header.
paper_title: When Maximum Stable Set can be solved in FPT time

name: AX_independent_set_h_free_fpt_dichotomy
title: Parameterized MIS Dichotomy
statement_text: For each connected graph $H$, is MIS (randomized) FPT or $W[1]$-hard in $H$-free graphs, parameterized by the size $k$ of the solution?
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. FPT means solvable in time $f(k)n^{O(1)}$, and $W[1]$-hardness is the standard evidence against FPT; MIS is $W[1]$-hard in general graphs. This is the parameterized counterpart of the classical P versus NP-complete dichotomy for MIS in $H$-free graphs, and may be even harder. No FPT algorithm is known for the classical open cases ($P_7$-, $S_{1,1,3}$- and $S_{1,2,2}$-free graphs), and Alekseev's NP-hardness reduction does not show $W[1]$-hardness, so a priori more graphs $H$ are candidates; for instance MIS is FPT on $K_t$-free graphs by Ramsey's theorem. Dabrowski et al. initiated the systematic study and showed FPT for all four-vertex $H$ except $C_4$. Bonnet et al. gave parameterized analogues of Alekseev's reduction, leaving as connected candidates for FPT roughly the paths and subdivided claws whose vertices are blown up into cliques. This paper settles all five-vertex graphs $H$: the four remaining five-vertex cases (including the dart and the cricket) are randomized FPT.

paper_title: When Maximum Stable Set can be solved in FPT time

name: AX_independent_set_fpt_blownup_p4_free

statement_text: For any integer $t$, MIS can be solved in FPT time in $P(t,t,t,t)$-free graphs.

name: AX_independent_set_fpt_h_free_candidates
title: Informal belief on FPT candidates
statement_text: There will be very few connected candidates $H$ (connected graphs $H$ for which known reductions do not show MIS to be $W[1]$-hard on $H$-free graphs) for which MIS in $H$-free graphs will not end up in (randomized) FPT.
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. FPT means solvable in time $f(k)n^{O(1)}$, and $W[1]$-hardness is the standard evidence against FPT; MIS is $W[1]$-hard in general graphs. Bonnet et al. gave parameterized analogues of Alekseev's NP-hardness reduction, which show $W[1]$-hardness unless $H$ has a restricted form. According to the paper, the connected FPT candidates must be chordal, have no induced $K_{1,4}$ and no induced tree with two vertices of degree at least three. They must also fit either a path whose vertices are blown up into cliques (consecutive cliques joined by complete bipartite graphs minus at most one edge, with at most one junction instead a $2K_2$-free bipartite graph), or both a subdivided claw and the line graph of a subdivided claw with blown-up vertices, plus further technical restrictions. Some graphs outside these forms (for instance $T(1,2,2)$) are $W[1]$-hard, showing how delicate the dichotomy is. As first evidence for their belief, the authors show that the four remaining five-vertex candidates among the 34 graphs on five vertices all give (randomized) FPT algorithms.

name: AX_disproportionate_division_2n_minus_2_cuts
title: Informal Conjecture (f(n) = 2n−2)
statement_text: We suspect that Segal-Halevi's construction showing $f(n)\ge 2n-2$ reflects the truth and that $f(n) = 2n - 2$ for all $n \geq 2$.
context_text: In this cake-cutting setting the cake is $[0,1]$ and $n\ge2$ agents have non-atomic Borel probability measures $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ on it. Given non-negative demands $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ summing to $1$, a disproportionate division is a partition $X_1\cup\dots\cup X_n$ of $[0,1]$ with $\mu_i(X_i)\ge\alpha_i$ for all $i$, and $f(n)$ is the maximum, over all measures and demands, of the minimum number of cuts (points splitting $[0,1]$ into intervals that are then distributed) needed for a disproportionate division with $n$ agents. For equal demands $1/n$, $n-1$ cuts suffice and are necessary. Folklore arguments based on the Stromquist–Woodall theorem give $O(n^2)$ cuts, and Segal-Halevi gave $O(n\log n)$; the authors prove $f(n)\le3n-4$ for all $n\ge2$ by a constructive combinatorial argument. Segal-Halevi's lower-bound construction takes $\mu_1$ uniform on $[0,1]$ and, for $1\le i\le n-1$, $\mu_{i+1}$ uniform on a tiny interval around $i/n$, with demand nearly $1$ for agent 1 and tiny equal demands for the others: any disproportionate division needs two cuts in the support of each of $\mu_2,\dots,\mu_n$, hence $f(n)\ge2n-2$. The authors believe deeper topological considerations drive the conjecture: they propose a measure-partitioning conjecture on the circle (for $n$ non-atomic probability measures on $S^1$ and demands summing to $1$, there are a partition $[n]=P\cup Q$ into nonempty sets and a partition of $S^1$ into two intervals $X,X^c$ with $\min_{i\in P}\mu_i(X)=\sum_{j\in P}\alpha_j$ and $\min_{i\in Q}\mu_i(X^c)=\sum_{j\in Q}\alpha_j$) which would imply $f(n)=2n-2$ by a simple induction. This is a measure-partitioning problem rather than a graph problem.
paper_title: Disproportionate division

name: AX_disproportionate_division_circle_measure_bipartition
title: Conjecture 3.1
statement_text: For any $n \geq 2$ non-atomic probability measures $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_n$ on the unit circle $S^1$ and non-negative reals $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ summing to $1$, there exists a partition of the set $[n] = P \cup Q$ into two nonempty sets and a partition of the circle $S^1 = X \cup X^c$ into two intervals such that $$\min_{i \in P} \mu_i(X) = \sum_{j \in P} \alpha_j \quad \text{and} \quad \min_{i \in Q} \mu_i(X^c) = \sum_{j \in Q} \alpha_j.$$
context_text: In this cake-cutting setting the cake is $[0,1]$ and $n\ge2$ agents have non-atomic Borel probability measures $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ on it. Given non-negative demands $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ summing to $1$, a disproportionate division is a partition $X_1\cup\dots\cup X_n$ of $[0,1]$ with $\mu_i(X_i)\ge\alpha_i$ for all $i$, and $f(n)$ is the maximum, over all measures and demands, of the minimum number of cuts (points splitting $[0,1]$ into intervals that are then distributed) needed for a disproportionate division with $n$ agents. For equal demands $1/n$, $n-1$ cuts suffice and are necessary. Folklore arguments based on the Stromquist–Woodall theorem give $O(n^2)$ cuts, and Segal-Halevi gave $O(n\log n)$; the authors prove $f(n)\le3n-4$ for all $n\ge2$ by a constructive combinatorial argument. Segal-Halevi's construction shows $f(n)\ge2n-2$, and the authors suspect $f(n)=2n-2$. They propose this measure-partitioning conjecture as the topological statement behind it: if true, a simple inductive argument would give $f(n)=2n-2$ for all $n\ge2$, which would be optimal. Here an interval of the circle is a connected arc, and $X^c$ is the complementary arc. The case of two measures is known and is essentially the Stromquist–Woodall theorem, but the authors were unable to decide the conjecture even for three measures. This is a measure-partitioning problem rather than a graph problem.

name: AX_graph_isomorphism_h1_h2_free_dichotomy
title: Research Question (Introduction)
statement_text: Is it possible to determine the computational complexity of Graph Isomorphism for $(H_1, H_2)$-free graphs for all pairs $H_1, H_2$?
context_text: A graph is $(H_1,H_2)$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H_1$ or $H_2$. $P_r$, $K_t$ are the path and complete graph on $r$, $t$ vertices, $G+H$ is the disjoint union and $sG$ the disjoint union of $s$ copies of $G$; the diamond is $\overline{2P_1+P_2}$ ($K_4$ minus an edge), the gem is $\overline{P_1+P_4}$ (a $P_4$ plus a dominating vertex), and the subdivided claw $S_{h,i,j}$ is the tree with one vertex $x$ of degree 3 and exactly three leaves, at distances $h,i,j$ from $x$. Since the class of $(\overline{H_1},\overline{H_2})$-free graphs is equivalent to that of $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs (by complementation), pairs are considered up to complementing both graphs. Graph Isomorphism is GI-complete if it is polynomially equivalent to Graph Isomorphism on general graphs. On $H$-free graphs it is polynomial-time solvable if $H$ is an induced subgraph of $P_4$ and GI-complete otherwise (Booth–Colbourn, Kratsch–Schweitzer). For pairs, Kratsch and Schweitzer initiated the classification and Schweitzer proved that only finitely many cases remain open, without specifying them. Using that Graph Isomorphism is polynomial on classes of bounded clique-width (Grohe–Schweitzer), the authors narrow the open cases to 14, then prove three polynomial and five GI-complete, leaving exactly six open pairs: $H_1=K_3$ and $H_2\in\{P_7,S_{1,2,3}\}$; $H_1=K_4$ and $H_2=S_{1,1,3}$; $H_1=\text{diamond}$ and $H_2\in\{P_1+P_2+P_3,P_1+P_5\}$; $H_1=\text{gem}$ and $H_2=P_2+P_3$.
notes: Explicitly posed as a research question in the introduction; the paper resolves all but six pairs $(H_1,H_2)$, leaving those six as the residual open cases.

name: AX_graph_isomorphism_fpt_clique_width
title: Open Question: FPT Algorithm for Graph Isomorphism Parameterized by Clique-Width
statement_text: Whether an FPT algorithm exists for Graph Isomorphism when parameterized by clique-width is still open.
context_text: The clique-width of $G$ is the minimum number of labels needed to construct $G$ using the operations: create a single vertex with some label; take the disjoint union of two labelled graphs; join every vertex with label $i$ to every vertex with label $j$ ($i\ne j$); rename label $i$ to $j$. A class has bounded clique-width if some constant bounds the clique-width of all its members. A problem is FPT (fixed-parameter tractable) with respect to a parameter $k$ if it is solvable in time $f(k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$ for some computable function $f$, and in XP if it is solvable in time $n^{f(k)}$, i.e. polynomial for each fixed $k$. Lokshtanov, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk and Saurabh gave an FPT algorithm for Graph Isomorphism parameterized by treewidth (later improved by Grohe, Neuen, Schweitzer and Wiebking). Grohe and Schweitzer proved that Graph Isomorphism parameterized by clique-width is in XP: for every constant $c$ it is polynomial-time solvable on graphs of clique-width at most $c$; Grohe and Neuen extended this to the more general Canonisation problem. Whether an FPT algorithm exists for the clique-width parameter is open.

name: AX_widespread_multigraph_all
title: Conjecture 1.8
statement_text: Every multigraph is widespread.
context_text: A subdivision of a multigraph $H$ is a graph obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path of length at least one between $u$ and $v$, these paths being internally disjoint; a graph $G$ is $H$-subdivision-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $H$. For an integer $\rho\ge0$, $\chi^{\rho}(G)$ is the maximum over all vertices $v$ of the chromatic number of the subgraph induced on the set $N^{\rho}[v]$ of vertices at distance at most $\rho$ from $v$. An ideal is a class of graphs closed under taking induced subgraphs; it is colourable if its members have bounded chromatic number, and $\rho$-bounded if $\chi^{\rho}(G)\le\tau$ for some $\tau$ and all its members. A multigraph $H$ is widespread if for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ there is $\rho\ge0$ such that every $\rho$-bounded ideal of $J$-subdivision-free graphs is colourable, i.e. for all $\tau$ there is $c$ such that every $J$-subdivision-free graph $G$ with $\chi^{\rho}(G)\le\tau$ has $\chi(G)\le c$. $H$ is pervasive in a class $\mathcal{C}$ if for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ and every $\kappa$ there is $c$ such that every $J$-subdivision-free $G\in\mathcal{C}$ with clique number at most $\kappa$ has $\chi(G)\le c$. Scott conjectured that every multigraph is pervasive in the class of all graphs, which was disproved by Pawlik, Kozik, Krawczyk, Lasoń, Micek, Trotter and Walczak; only forests of chandeliers can be pervasive there (a chandelier is a tree plus a new vertex, the pivot, adjacent to its leaves; a forest of chandeliers is built by repeatedly gluing chandeliers at their pivots, component by component), and forests of chandeliers are pervasive in every controlled ideal (one in which, for some $\rho$, every $\rho$-bounded subideal is colourable). The authors originally expected the widespread multigraphs to be exactly the forests of chandeliers, but in this paper they prove that every multigraph obtained from a tree by replacing edges with bundles of parallel edges (a banana tree) is widespread, and give widespread graphs that are not forests of chandeliers; this conjecture is their resuscitated version of Scott's conjecture. They are very far from proving it: they do not know whether every chandelier is widespread, and all multigraphs proved widespread so far are subdivisions of outerplanar graphs.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. VI. Banana trees

name: AX_widespread_multigraph_chi_2_subdivision_free
title: Conjecture 1.10
statement_text: For all graphs $J$ and for all integers $\tau \geq 0$, there exists $c$ such that if $G$ is a graph with chromatic number more than $c$, then either some induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $J$ or $\chi^2(G) > \tau$.
context_text: A subdivision of a multigraph $H$ is a graph obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path of length at least one between $u$ and $v$, these paths being internally disjoint; a graph $G$ is $H$-subdivision-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $H$. $\chi^{2}(G)$ is the maximum, over all vertices $v$ of $G$, of the chromatic number of the subgraph induced on the set of vertices at distance at most $2$ from $v$ (more generally $\chi^{\rho}(G)$ uses distance at most $\rho$). So the conjecture says that graphs of huge chromatic number either contain an induced subdivision of $J$ or contain a ball of radius $2$ with large chromatic number. A multigraph $H$ is widespread if for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ there is $\rho$ such that for all $\tau$ there is $c$ with $\chi(G)\le c$ for every $J$-subdivision-free graph $G$ with $\chi^{\rho}(G)\le\tau$; the authors conjecture that every multigraph is widespread (a resuscitated version of Scott's disproved conjecture). Using their result with Chudnovsky that, for all $\rho\ge2$ and every multigraph $J$, every $\rho$-controlled class of $J$-subdivision-free graphs is $2$-controlled (an ideal is $\rho$-controlled if each of its subideals with bounded $\chi^{\rho}$ has bounded chromatic number), they show that this conjecture is equivalent to the statement that every multigraph is widespread, and present it as a nicer reformulation (not used in the paper). In this paper they prove that every tree with edges replaced by bundles of parallel edges is widespread.
notes: PDF source — subscript in $\chi_2(G)$ rendered as 'χ2(G)' in the extraction; reconstructed as $\chi_2(G)$.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. VI. Banana trees

name: AX_subdivision_free_chi_bounded_multigraph_characterization
title: Open Question: first pervasiveness characterisation
statement_text: Which multigraphs $H$ have the property that for all $\kappa$ there exists $c$ such that every $H$-subdivision-free graph with clique number at most $\kappa$ has chromatic number at most $c$?
context_text: A subdivision of a multigraph $H$ is a graph obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path of length at least one between $u$ and $v$, these paths being internally disjoint; a graph $G$ is $H$-subdivision-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a subdivision of $H$. The question asks for which multigraphs $H$ the class of $H$-subdivision-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded in the weak sense that bounded clique number implies bounded chromatic number. The authors contrast it with a second question: for which $H$ does this hold for every subdivision $J$ of $H$ in place of $H$ (i.e. graphs of bounded clique number and huge chromatic number contain an induced subdivision of $H$ in which every edge is subdivided at least a prescribed number of times); $H$ is then called pervasive. They find the second question perhaps better: when restricted to controlled classes (ideals in which large chromatic number forces a ball of bounded radius with large chromatic number) its answer is known (forests of chandeliers, i.e. trees of chandeliers glued at pivots, are pervasive in every controlled ideal, and only they can be pervasive in all graphs, by work of Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour), whereas the first question remains open. Scott conjectured that every multigraph is pervasive in the class of all graphs, which was disproved; the authors prove that multigraphs obtained from a tree by adding parallel edges are pervasive in the class of all graphs.
notes: No numbered label in the paper; appears as a bullet-point question with the subsequent remark 'the first remains open'.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. VI. Banana trees

name: AX_bounded_subdeterminant_integer_programs_polynomial
title: Conjecture on polynomial-time solvability of bounded sub-determinant integer programs
statement_text: Integer programs with bounded sub-determinants can be solved in polynomial time. In particular, the stable set problem on graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G) \leq k$ is polynomial for every fixed $k$.
context_text: An integer program has bounded sub-determinants if its (integer) constraint matrix $A$ has all square submatrices with determinant bounded in absolute value by a fixed constant $\Delta$; the belief is that for every fixed $\Delta$ such programs $\max\{w^\top x: Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}$ can be solved in polynomial time (for $\Delta=1$, totally unimodular matrices, this is linear programming). The odd cycle packing number $\mathrm{ocp}(G)$ is the maximum number of vertex-disjoint odd cycles in $G$. The stable set problem asks for a maximum-weight stable (independent) set for given vertex weights $w$; it can be written as the integer program $\max\{w^\top x: Mx\le\mathbf{1},\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V(G)}\}$, where $M$ is the edge-vertex incidence matrix of $G$, and the largest absolute value of a determinant of a square submatrix of $M$ is $2^{\mathrm{ocp}(G)}$. Exact polynomial-time algorithms were known only for $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=0$ (bipartite graphs) and $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=1$ (Artmann, Weismantel and Zenklusen, who solve integer programs whose constraint matrix has all sub-determinants bounded by 2 in absolute value, in strongly polynomial time); for bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ a PTAS is known. The authors note that recent work links the complexity of integer programs to the magnitude of their sub-determinants, making the belief tempting; it would imply that stable set is polynomial for every fixed bound $k$ on $\mathrm{ocp}(G)$, which remains open for $k\ge2$. The paper proves this consequence for graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G)\le k$ embedded in a surface of Euler genus at most $g$, for fixed $k$ and $g$.
notes: Stated as 'it is tempting to believe'; the paper explicitly confirms the problem is open for $k \geq 2$. No labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: The stable set problem in graphs with bounded genus and bounded odd cycle packing number

name: AX_stable_set_bounded_ocp_arbitrary_genus
title: Open question on stable set for bounded ocp and arbitrary Euler genus
statement_text: Is the stable set problem polynomial-time solvable for graphs $G$ with $\mathrm{ocp}(G) \leq k$ (for fixed $k$) embedded in a surface of arbitrary Euler genus?
context_text: The odd cycle packing number $\mathrm{ocp}(G)$ is the maximum number of vertex-disjoint odd cycles in $G$. The stable set problem asks for a maximum-weight stable (independent) set for given vertex weights $w$; it can be written as the integer program $\max\{w^\top x: Mx\le\mathbf{1},\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V(G)}\}$, where $M$ is the edge-vertex incidence matrix of $G$, and the largest absolute value of a determinant of a square submatrix of $M$ is $2^{\mathrm{ocp}(G)}$. Exact polynomial-time algorithms were known only for $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=0$ (bipartite graphs) and $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=1$ (Artmann, Weismantel and Zenklusen, who solve integer programs whose constraint matrix has all sub-determinants bounded by 2 in absolute value, in strongly polynomial time); for bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ a PTAS is known. The Euler genus of a surface obtained from the sphere by adding $h$ handles and $c$ crosscaps is $2h+c$; surfaces may be non-orientable. The paper's main result is a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum-weight stable set in graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G)\le k$ embedded in a (possibly non-orientable) surface of Euler genus at most $g$, for fixed $k$ and $g$, together with a polynomial-size extended formulation of the stable set polytope. Without a bound on $\mathrm{ocp}$ the problem is NP-hard already for planar graphs. The natural examples of graphs with bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ come from embeddings in non-orientable surfaces of Euler genus $k$ in which every odd cycle is one-sided (Lovász's characterization of graphs with no two disjoint odd cycles). The authors do not know whether the genus bound can be dropped, i.e. whether only the bound on $\mathrm{ocp}$ suffices; a positive answer for all graphs would follow from polynomial solvability of bounded sub-determinant integer programs.
notes: Stated as 'we do not know whether'; no labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: The stable set problem in graphs with bounded genus and bounded odd cycle packing number

name: AX_quantum_ergodicity_small_spectral_window
title: Open problem on quantum ergodicity over small spectral windows (Remark 1.2)
statement_text: It would be interesting to see whether the authors' examples (sequences of $(d+1)$-regular expanders on $m$ vertices with high girth having $\alpha\log_d(m)$ eigenvalues in $(-2\sqrt{d},2\sqrt{d})$ of multiplicity $\Omega(m^{1-4\alpha})$, each eigenspace having an orthogonal basis of eigenvectors supported on sets of size $O(m^{\alpha})$) can prove a lower bound on the length of the smallest spectral window $I\subset(-2\sqrt{d},2\sqrt{d})$ for which quantum ergodicity over $I$ holds; the problem of controlling the other eigenvectors in such a window well enough to say that the quantum-ergodicity average in a small window of width roughly $1/\log(m)$ is not equidistributed is not pursued and remains open.
context_text: Let $G_m$ be a sequence of $(d+1)$-regular graphs on $m$ vertices with adjacency matrices $A_m$ and an orthonormal eigenbasis $\psi^{(m)}_1,\dots,\psi^{(m)}_m$. Anantharaman and Le Masson (see also Brooks, Le Masson and Lindenstrauss) proved quantum ergodicity on graphs: if $G_m$ converges to the tree in the Benjamini–Schramm sense (e.g. girth tending to infinity) and has a uniform spectral gap ($|\lambda_i(A_m)|<(d+1)(1-\beta)$ for all nontrivial eigenvalues), then for every sequence of test functions $a_m:V_m\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\sum_x a_m(x)=0$ and $\|a_m\|_\infty\le1$, the average $\frac1m\sum_{i\le m}|\langle\psi^{(m)}_i,a_m\psi^{(m)}_i\rangle|^2$ tends to $0$, i.e. eigenvectors are equidistributed on average; a refined version takes this average only over the eigenvectors whose eigenvalues lie in a spectral window $I\subset(-2\sqrt d,2\sqrt d)$, and holds for windows of width roughly $1/\log(m)$. For every prime $p$ with $d=p+1$ and $\alpha\in(0,1/6)$, the authors construct explicit $(d+1)$-regular graphs with all nontrivial eigenvalues at most $(3/\sqrt2)\sqrt d$ in absolute value, girth at least about $2\alpha\log_d(m)$, and many eigenvectors with eigenvalues in $(-2\sqrt d,2\sqrt d)$ supported entirely on a set of size $O(m^\alpha)$ (a discrete analogue of scarring), showing that these hypotheses do not imply quantum unique ergodicity; a variant yields many localized eigenvectors of very high multiplicity in a very small spectral window.
notes: Stated in prose inside Remark 1.2, not a labelled theorem environment. PDF source — surrounding math may be partially garbled.
paper_title: High-girth near-Ramanujan graphs with localized eigenvectors

name: AX_avoidable_paths_two_disjoint_pk
title: Question 1.12
statement_text: For every positive integer $k$, does every graph $G$ either not contain two disjoint $P_k$, or contain two disjoint avoidable $P_k$?
context_text: Cycles are induced unless stated otherwise, and $P_k$ means an induced path on $k$ vertices ($G$ is $P_k$-free if it has none). An extension of an induced path $P$ is an induced path $xPy$ for some vertices $x,y$; an induced path is failing if no induced cycle of $G$ contains it; and a path is avoidable if it is induced and has no failing extension. Thus an avoidable vertex is one such that every induced $P_3$ with middle vertex $v$ lies in an induced cycle (in chordal graphs, avoidable vertices are simplicial). The authors prove the conjecture of Beisegel et al. that for every $k$ every graph either is $P_k$-free or contains an avoidable $P_k$, and more generally that if $G[X]$ is connected then $G-N[X]$ is $P_k$-free or contains a $P_k$ that is avoidable in $G$. As a consequence, every graph either has no two non-adjacent $P_k$ or has two non-adjacent avoidable $P_k$. This question asks the analogue for (vertex-)disjoint copies. The answer is positive for $k\in\{1,2\}$ by results of Beisegel et al., but the paper itself answers it negatively for every $k\ge3$: take a cycle on $2k-1$ vertices plus a vertex adjacent to two consecutive cycle vertices; it has two disjoint $P_k$, which must be complementary and both meet the triangle, so one of them contains a single triangle vertex and has a failing extension. So the question is resolved, not open.
notes: The question is posed and then fully answered (negatively for $k \geq 3$) within the same paper; it is not open.
paper_title: Avoidable paths in graphs

name: AX_avoidable_non_path_family_existence
title: Question 4.1
statement_text: Does there exist a family $\mathcal{H}$ of connected graphs, not containing any path, such that any graph is either $\mathcal{H}$-free or contains an avoidable element of $\mathcal{H}$?
context_text: Cycles are induced unless stated otherwise, and $P_k$ means an induced path on $k$ vertices ($G$ is $P_k$-free if it has none). An extension of an induced path $P$ is an induced path $xPy$ for some vertices $x,y$; an induced path is failing if no induced cycle of $G$ contains it; and a path is avoidable if it is induced and has no failing extension. Thus an avoidable vertex is one such that every induced $P_3$ with middle vertex $v$ lies in an induced cycle (in chordal graphs, avoidable vertices are simplicial). The authors prove the conjecture of Beisegel et al. that for every $k$ every graph either is $P_k$-free or contains an avoidable $P_k$, and more generally that if $G[X]$ is connected then $G-N[X]$ is $P_k$-free or contains a $P_k$ that is avoidable in $G$. A graph is $\mathcal{H}$-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of $\mathcal{H}$. The authors ask whether avoidability extends beyond paths. They note that for some structures the very notion of extension becomes unclear (what should an extension of a clique be?), and that no other structure seems to survive the test of chordal graphs or simple ad hoc constructions, even when a family of graphs is allowed instead of a single pattern. The notion of avoidability in this question is deliberately left up to interpretation by the authors. They also ask, more vaguely, when a graph admits three or more disjoint (or pairwise non-adjacent) avoidable paths, noting that the picture is murky already for chordal graphs.
notes: PDF source — mathematical content is clear; the family $\mathcal{H}$ notation is inferred from context.
paper_title: Avoidable paths in graphs

name: AX_kt_minor_free_independence_n_over_t
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: For every positive integer $t$, if an $n$-vertex graph $G$ does not contain $K_{t+1}$ as a minor then $\alpha(G) \geq n/t$.
context_text: $\alpha(G)$ denotes the independence number. Since every $n$-vertex graph has chromatic number at least $\lceil n/\alpha(G)\rceil$, Hadwiger's conjecture (every graph with no $K_{t+1}$ minor is $t$-colourable) would imply this statement, which is therefore a natural weakening of it that has received a lot of attention (see Seymour's survey on Hadwiger's conjecture). Duchet and Meyniel proved in 1982 that the bound holds within a factor of $2$: every $n$-vertex graph with no $K_{t+1}$ minor has $\alpha(G)\ge\frac{n}{2t}+\frac{1}{2}$; Fox gave the first constant-factor improvement, $\alpha(G)\ge n/((2-c)t)$ with $c>0.017$, improved by Balogh and Kostochka to $c>1/19.2$. The present paper studies the conjecture for triangle-free graphs, proving that for every $0<\varepsilon<1/26$ and $t$ large enough every triangle-free $n$-vertex graph with no $K_t$ minor has $\alpha(G)\ge n/t^{1-\varepsilon}$, much more than the $\Omega(n\sqrt{\log t}/t)$ given by combining the Kostochka–Thomason average-degree bound with Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi.
notes: No explicit attribution appears in the conjecture header; the paper describes it as having 'received quite a lot of attention' and directs the reader to Seymour's survey [31], indicating it is a community/folklore conjecture rather than one originated by the paper authors. Classified as 'states' per the no-attribution-in-header rule.
paper_title: Independence number in triangle-free graphs avoiding a minor

name: AX_minor_ramsey_ks_free_sublinear_bound
title: Conjecture on $MR_t(s,k)$ for $s \geq 4$
statement_text: Fix an integer $s\geq 4$. Is it true that for every $0<\varepsilon<1/s$ there exists a positive integer $t_0$ such that for all $t\geq t_0$, if $G$ is a $K_s$-free graph without a $K_{t}$-minor, then $\alpha(G)\geq \frac{|G|}{t^{1-\varepsilon}}$? (In terms of $t$-minor Ramsey numbers: $MR_t(s,k)\le t^{1-\varepsilon}k$ for sufficiently large $t$; here $\varepsilon$ cannot be larger than $1/s$.)
context_text: $K_s$-free means having no $K_s$ subgraph (clique number less than $s$), and $\alpha(G)$ is the independence number. The $t$-minor Ramsey number $MR_t(s,k)$ is the smallest $n$ such that every $K_t$-minor-free graph on $n$ vertices contains a copy of $K_s$ or an independent set of size $k$; it generalises the planar Ramsey numbers of Walker and of Steinberg and Tovey, which grow linearly. The authors' main theorem is the case $s=3$: for every $0<\varepsilon<1/26$ there is $t_0$ such that for all $t\ge t_0$ every triangle-free $n$-vertex graph with no $K_t$ minor has $\alpha(G)\ge n/t^{1-\varepsilon}$, i.e. $MR_t(3,k)\le t^{1-\varepsilon}k$; by a random construction of Erdős this cannot hold beyond $\varepsilon=1/3$ (up to a logarithmic factor). For fixed $s\ge4$, the lower bounds on $R(s,k)$ of Bohman ($s=4$) and Bohman–Keevash ($s\ge5$) give graphs with no $K_s$ subgraph and no independent set of order $n^{2/(s+1)}$ up to polylogarithmic factors, which are $K_t$-minor-free for $t=n^{1-\frac{s-2}{s(s-1)-2}}$ and have no independent set of size $n/t^{1-\frac{1}{s}}$, so $\varepsilon<1/s$ is necessary; the authors nevertheless expect a result similar to the triangle-free case. A less ambitious goal is to answer the question for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, for some $\varepsilon_0>0$.
notes: Section 4 is not included in the provided text; this conjecture is described only by a forward reference in the introduction. The exact formal statement may differ from what is reconstructed here.
paper_title: Independence number in triangle-free graphs avoiding a minor

name: AX_cycle_count_m_edges_exponential_base
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: Every simple graph with $m$ edges has at most $O(\kappa_1^m)$ cycles, where $\kappa_1 = (2+2\sqrt{2})^{1/5} \approx 1.3701$.
context_text: Graphs are simple here (the paper proves a separate bound for multigraphs). Trivially a graph with $m$ edges has at most $2^m$ cycles; Király conjectured an $O(1.4^m)$ bound, which the authors prove in the stronger form $O(\gamma^m)$ with $\gamma=442368^{1/10}\approx1.384$. The best known lower bound is the construction of Arman and Tsaturian: take two cycles $u_1\dots u_\ell$ and $v_1\dots v_\ell$ and add the edges $u_iv_i$, $u_{i+1}v_i$ and $u_iv_{i+1}$ (indices modulo $\ell$), so that every four consecutive vertices $u_i,v_i,u_{i+1},v_{i+1}$ induce a $K_4$; it has $5\ell$ edges and $\Omega(\kappa_1^m)$ cycles. The authors verified by computer a number of similar constructions without finding a better one, and conjecture that this construction is optimal. They also show that a simple graph with $m$ edges, minimum degree $2$ and average degree $d$ has at most $m\gamma_d^m$ cycles for an explicit function $\gamma_d$, and since $\gamma_d>\kappa_1$ only when $4.24<d<7.18$, any counterexample to the conjecture must have average degree in this range. For $4$-regular graphs (average degree $4$) they prove $O(1.365^m)$, while Patkós constructed $4$-regular graphs with at least $1.356^m$ cycles.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled; value of $\kappa_1$ reconstructed from surrounding prose.
paper_title: Bounding the number of cycles in a graph in terms of its degree sequence

name: AX_tree_decomposition_edge_connectivity_leaf_count
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: There is a function $f$ such that, for any fixed tree $T$ with $m$ leaves, every $f(m)$-edge-connected graph with minimum degree at least $f(|E(T)|)$ and number of edges divisible by $|E(T)|$ has a $T$-decomposition.
context_text: For graphs $G$ and $H$, an $H$-decomposition of $G$ is a partition of $E(G)$ into sets each of which forms an isomorphic copy of $H$; this requires $|E(H)|$ to divide $|E(G)|$. The Barát–Thomassen conjecture, proved by Bensmail, Harutyunyan, Le, Merker and Thomassé, states that for every tree $T$ there is $k_T$ such that every $k_T$-edge-connected graph with number of edges divisible by $|E(T)|$ has a $T$-decomposition; its case where $T$ is the claw $K_{1,3}$ is equivalent to the weak $3$-flow conjecture (every sufficiently edge-connected graph has a nowhere-zero $3$-flow), proved by Thomassen and improved by Lovász, Thomassen, Wu and Zhang. A strengthening posed earlier asked for a function $f$ such that every $f(\Delta_T)$-edge-connected graph with minimum degree at least $f(|E(T)|)$ and number of edges divisible by $|E(T)|$ has a $T$-decomposition, where $\Delta_T$ is the maximum degree of $T$; it holds for paths but the authors showed it fails already for some trees of maximum degree three. The present conjecture is the authors' alternative, bounding the edge-connectivity in terms of the number of leaves of $T$ instead. The paper's main result is that for every $\ell$ there is $d(\ell)$ such that every $3$-edge-connected graph with minimum degree at least $d(\ell)$ and number of edges divisible by $\ell$ decomposes into paths of length $\ell$ (edges), which is optimal in the connectivity and shows one can take $f(2)=3$; the existence of $f(3)$ would already contain the claw case. The authors would find it very interesting to have a proof not using the claw case as a starting point.
paper_title: Edge-partitioning 3-edge-connected graphs into paths

name: AX_bipartite_digraph_caccetta_haggkvist_girth
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 1$, if $G$ is a bipartite digraph, with $n > 0$ vertices in each part, and every vertex has out-degree more than $n/(k+1)$, then $G$ has girth at most $2k$.
context_text: Digraphs are finite without loops or parallel edges, but may have both $uv$ and $vu$ (directed 2-cycles). A digraph has girth at most $k$ if it has a directed cycle of length at most $k$; it is bipartite if its underlying graph is, and a bipartition of it is one of the underlying graph. The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture states that every $n$-vertex digraph with all out-degrees at least $n/k$ has girth at most $k$; it is open for every $k\ge3$. This bipartite analogue is motivated by the following example: take disjoint sets $V_1,\dots,V_{2k+2}$ of size $t$ and make every vertex of $V_i$ adjacent from every vertex of $V_{i-1}$ (indices mod $2k+2$); this gives a bipartite digraph with parts of size $n=(k+1)t$, all out-degrees exactly $n/(k+1)$, and no directed cycle of length at most $2k$. The authors show the conjecture is implied by the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture, and, using good approximate versions of Caccetta–Häggkvist, prove it for $k=1,2,3,4,6$ and all $k\ge224{,}539$. They also prove it when every vertex has in-degree and out-degree exactly $\alpha n$ with $\alpha>1/(k+1)$.
paper_title: Short directed cycles in bipartite digraphs

name: AX_bipartite_digraph_caccetta_haggkvist_asymmetric
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 1$, and every pair of reals $\alpha, \beta > 0$ with $k\alpha + \beta > 1$, if $G$ is a non-null bipartite digraph with bipartition $(A, B)$, where every vertex in $A$ has out-degree at least $\beta|B|$, and every vertex in $B$ has out-degree at least $\alpha|A|$, then $G$ has girth at most $2k$.
context_text: Digraphs are finite without loops or parallel edges, but may have both $uv$ and $vu$ (directed 2-cycles). A digraph has girth at most $k$ if it has a directed cycle of length at most $k$; it is bipartite if its underlying graph is, and a bipartition of it is one of the underlying graph. The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture states that every $n$-vertex digraph with all out-degrees at least $n/k$ has girth at most $k$; it is open for every $k\ge3$. For $\alpha=\beta$ this conjecture is equivalent to the authors' bipartite analogue of Caccetta–Häggkvist (a bipartite digraph with $n>0$ vertices in each part and all out-degrees more than $n/(k+1)$ has girth at most $2k$), which they prove for $k=1,2,3,4,6$ and $k\ge224{,}539$; letting $\beta\to0$ it implies the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture, so it would be optimistic to hope to prove it for $k=3$. For each $k$, if true it is best possible for infinitely many pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$, via circulant-type constructions. It is easy for $k=1$, and the authors prove it for $k=2$ (if $2\alpha+\beta>1$ the girth is at most four), which is their fundamental tool; for $k=3,4$ they prove the weakening where $k\alpha+\beta>1$ is replaced by $\alpha+\beta\ge2/(k+1)$.
paper_title: Short directed cycles in bipartite digraphs

name: AX_hypercube_coloring_1_ball_reconstruction_threshold
title: Gap problem for 1-ball reconstruction threshold
statement_text: Determine the correct threshold $q^*(n)$ such that almost every $q$-colouring of the hypercube $Q_n$ is reconstructible from the multiset of its coloured 1-balls, narrowing the gap between the lower bound $q = \Omega(n)$ and the upper bound $q \geq n^{2+\varepsilon}$.
context_text: $Q_n$ is the $n$-dimensional hypercube on $\{0,1\}^n$, and the $r$-ball $B_r(v)$ is the subgraph induced by the vertices at distance at most $r$ from $v$; a $q$-colouring here is an arbitrary (not necessarily proper) assignment of $q$ colours to the vertices, and a random $q$-colouring colours each vertex independently and uniformly. Two colourings are equivalent if they differ by an automorphism of $Q_n$; they are $r$-locally equivalent if there is a bijection $f$ of $V(Q_n)$ such that the coloured $r$-ball around each $v$ in the first is isomorphic (as a coloured graph) to the coloured $r$-ball around $f(v)$ in the second. A colouring is $r$-distinguishable (reconstructible from the multiset of its coloured $r$-balls) if every $r$-locally equivalent colouring is equivalent to it. The authors prove that almost every $2$-colouring (indeed every random $(p,1-p)$-colouring with $p\ge n^{-1/4+\varepsilon}$) is $2$-distinguishable, and that a random $q$-colouring is $1$-distinguishable with high probability when $q\ge n^{2+K\log^{-1/2}n}$, in particular when $q\ge n^{2+\varepsilon}$. A counting argument shows that $\Omega(n)$ colours are necessary for reconstruction from $1$-balls. They expect $n^{1+o(1)}$ colours should suffice (neighbourhoods are already unique in that range), and believe but cannot prove that $1$-distinguishability with high probability is monotone in $q$.

name: AX_planar_c4_c5_fractional_chromatic_infimum
title: Problem 1.3
statement_text: What is the infimum of fractional chromatic numbers of planar graphs without cycles of length 4 or 5?
context_text: For positive integers $b\le a$, an $(a:b)$-coloring of $G$ assigns to each vertex a $b$-element subset of $\{1,\dots,a\}$ so that adjacent vertices receive disjoint subsets (an $(a:1)$-coloring is a proper $a$-coloring); the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is the infimum of $a/b$ over all $(a:b)$-colorings of $G$, and $\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G)$. Steinberg's conjecture, that every planar graph without cycles of length 4 or 5 is 3-colorable, was disproved by Cohen-Addad et al.; it is natural to ask for a constant $c<4$ with $\chi_f(G)\le c$ for all such graphs. The authors prove that every planar graph without cycles of length 4 or 5 is $(11:3)$-colorable, hence has $\chi_f\le\frac{11}{3}$ and independence ratio at least $\frac{3}{11}$. The question asks for the optimal such constant; the paper writes "infimum", but given the discussion it means the best possible upper bound $c$, i.e. the supremum of $\chi_f(G)$ over planar graphs without cycles of length 4 or 5. The authors suspect $\frac{11}{3}$ is not optimal, and remark that the counterexample to Steinberg's conjecture is $(6:2)$-colorable, so they cannot even exclude that the answer is $3$.
paper_title: Planar graphs without cycles of length 4 or 5 are (11:3)-colorable

name: AX_planar_c4_c5_fractional_chromatic_11_3
title: Informal conjecture on optimality of 11/3
statement_text: It is not clear whether the constant $\frac{11}{3}$ in the bound $\chi_f(G)\le\frac{11}{3}$ for every planar graph $G$ without cycles of length 4 or 5 is the best possible, and we suspect this is not the case.
context_text: For positive integers $b\le a$, an $(a:b)$-coloring of $G$ assigns to each vertex a $b$-element subset of $\{1,\dots,a\}$ so that adjacent vertices receive disjoint subsets (an $(a:1)$-coloring is a proper $a$-coloring); the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is the infimum of $a/b$ over all $(a:b)$-colorings of $G$, and $\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G)$. Steinberg's conjecture, that every planar graph without cycles of length 4 or 5 is 3-colorable, was disproved by Cohen-Addad et al.; it is natural to ask for a constant $c<4$ with $\chi_f(G)\le c$ for all such graphs. name: AX_behrend_sets_avoiding_mixed_sign_patterns
title: Informal question on Behrend-style sets avoiding affine patterns with mixed-sign coefficients
statement_text: We do not know if there are subsets of $[N]$, in the style of Behrend's construction, with $N^{1-o(1)}$ elements avoiding such patterns, i.e. avoiding (non-trivial) solutions of a linear equation $a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3+a_4x_4=0$ with $a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4=0$ and two positive and two negative coefficients (e.g., $2x + 2y = 3w + z$).
context_text: $[N]=\{1,\dots,N\}$. Behrend's construction gives subsets of $[N]$ of size $N^{1-o(1)}$ (density $e^{-O(\sqrt{\log N})}$) with no 3-term arithmetic progression, i.e. no non-trivial solution of $x+z=2y$. A popular difference for a pattern in a set $A$ is a common difference $d\ne0$ shared by many copies of the pattern in $A$ (about as many as in a random set of the same density). Bergelson, Host, Kra and Ruzsa constructed sets without popular differences for $k$-term progressions, $k\ge5$, from Behrend-type sets, while Green and Tao's positive result for 4-term progressions relies on the identity $P(0)-3P(1)+3P(2)-P(3)=0$ for quadratic $P$, which has a symmetric form $P(0)-3P(1)=P(3)-3P(2)$. The authors construct sets $A\subseteq[N]^3$ of density $\delta$ in which every $d\ne0$ is the common difference of at most $\delta^{c\log(1/\delta)}N^3$ three-dimensional corners $(x,y,z),(x+d,y,z),(x,y+d,z),(x,y,z+d)$. They explain that a 3-dimensional corner projects to other 4-term patterns such as $x,x+y,x+2y,x+4y$, and that the Bergelson–Host–Kra–Ruzsa approach would need an identity expressing one value $P(b_i)$ as a convex combination of the others for all quadratic $P$; but any identity $a_1P(b_1)+\dots+a_4P(b_4)=0$ valid for all quadratic $P$, with $a_1+\dots+a_4=0$, distinct $b_i$ and not all $a_i$ zero, must have two positive and two negative $a_i$ (by Lagrange interpolation). The paper does not spell out what 'avoiding' means for such a pattern; presumably no non-trivial solution of the corresponding linear equation. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

name: AX_corners_popular_difference_abelian_groups
title: Informal conjecture on extending Mandache's Theorem 1.1 to all abelian groups
statement_text: It seems likely that Mandache's lower bound $M(\delta) \geq m_{\mathrm{convex}}(\delta)$, proved for $G_n=\mathbb{F}_p^n$ with fixed prime $p$, can be extended to all sequences of finite abelian groups via Bohr sets, though as far as we know this has not yet been worked out.
context_text: A corner in $G\times G$, for an abelian group $G$, is a triple $(x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d)$ with $d\ne0$; for $A\subseteq G\times G$, $S_d(A)=\{(x,y):(x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d)\in A\}$, so $|S_d(A)|$ counts corners of common difference $d$. For a sequence of finite abelian groups $G=G_n$ with $|G_n|\to\infty$, $M(\delta)$ is the largest number such that for every $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ large, every $A\subseteq G\times G$ with $|A|\ge\delta|G|^2$ has some $d\ne0$ with $|S_d(A)|\ge(M(\delta)-\epsilon)|G|^2$ (a popular difference). The triforce is the 3-uniform hypergraph on 6 vertices with edges $\{1,2,3'\},\{1,2',3\},\{1',2,3\}$; for measurable $W:[0,1]^3\to[0,1]$ its density is $\int W(x',y,z)W(x,y',z)W(x,y,z')\,dx\,dy\,dz\,dx'\,dy'\,dz'$, and $m(\delta)$ is the minimum triforce density over all $W$ with $\int W=\delta$. Mandache proved $M(\delta)\le m(\delta)$ for all $G_n$ (by a random construction), and that for $G_n=\mathbb{F}_p^n$ with $p$ a fixed prime, $M(\delta)\ge m_{\mathrm{convex}}(\delta)$ for every convex function $m_{\mathrm{convex}}\le m$ pointwise, via an arithmetic regularity argument combined with Fourier-analytic ideas. The authors prove $m(\delta)=\delta^{4-o(1)}$ and $m(\delta)=\omega(\delta^4)$, hence $M(\delta)\le\delta^{4-o(1)}$ for all $G_n$ and $M(\delta)=\omega(\delta^4)$ for $\mathbb{F}_p^n$; the expected extension would give the lower bound for all abelian groups. They also show that popular differences fail for 3-dimensional corners. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

paper_title: Triforce and Corners

name: AX_minor_closed_class_dichromatic_number_2
title: Question 1
statement_text: What is the largest minor-closed class $\mathcal{G}_2$ of undirected graphs with dichromatic number at most 2?
context_text: Digraphs are loopless, without parallel or anti-parallel arcs (no 2-cycles). An acyclic colouring of a digraph $D$ with $k$ colours is a map $V(D)\to[k]$ whose colour classes induce acyclic subdigraphs; the dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the minimum such $k$, and for an undirected graph $G$, $\vec{\chi}(G)$ is the maximum dichromatic number of an orientation of $G$. Since the union of minor-closed classes with $\vec{\chi}\le 2$ is again such a class, $\mathcal{G}_2$ is the class of graphs all of whose minors have dichromatic number at most 2. Neumann-Lara and Škrekovski conjectured that every planar graph has $\vec{\chi}\le2$ (Li and Mohar proved it for planar digraphs without directed triangles), and the authors show that this conjecture is equivalent to the statement that every $K_5$-minor-free graph has $\vec{\chi}\le2$ (moreover with an acyclic 2-colouring of any orientation having no monochromatic triangle); so conjecturally $\mathcal{G}_2$ contains all $K_5$-minor-free graphs. Since $\vec{\chi}(K_6)=2$ and $\vec{\chi}(K_7)=3$, $\mathcal{G}_2$ is a subclass of the $K_7$-minor-free graphs, but it seems much smaller: the authors exhibit an oriented $K_{3,3}$-minor-free graph with no acyclic 2-colouring.
paper_title: A Note on Graphs of Dichromatic Number 2

name: AX_hypergraph_max_cut_excess_sqrt_m
title: Θ(√m) excess conjecture for hypergraph cuts
statement_text: For any fixed $2 \leq r \leq k$, the smallest maximum $r$-cut over all $m$-edge $k$-graphs has excess $\Theta(\sqrt{m})$.
context_text: A $k$-graph is a $k$-uniform hypergraph; for $2\le r\le k$, an $r$-cut of a $k$-graph $H$ with $m$ edges is a partition of $V(H)$ into $r$ parts, and its size is the number of edges meeting every part. A uniformly random $r$-cut has expected size $\frac{S(k,r)\,r!}{r^k}m$, where $S(k,r)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind, and the excess of an $r$-cut is its size minus this quantity; the statement concerns the minimum, over all $m$-edge $k$-graphs, of the maximum excess of an $r$-cut. The authors call this a second plausible conjecture: chromatic-number methods give an $\Omega(\sqrt m)$ lower bound on the maximum excess, the standard deviation of a random cut is $\Theta(\sqrt m)$ for linear $k$-graphs (no two edges sharing two vertices), and $\Theta(\sqrt m)$ is correct for $r=k=2$ (Edwards) and for $r=2$, $k=3$ (Steiner triple systems are extremal). However, the paper's main theorem disproves it in all other cases: for fixed $2\le r\le k$ with $r\ge3$ or $k\ge4$, every $m$-edge $k$-graph has an $r$-cut with excess $\Omega(m^{5/9})$. So the conjecture holds exactly for $r=2$ and $k\in\{2,3\}$. The authors also show that for $k>3$ random $k$-graphs have all $r$-cuts of excess $O(m^{2/3})$, disproving Scott's conjecture that complete $k$-graphs minimize the max-cut.
notes: Stated in the introduction as a 'natural guess' without a labelled environment; largely disproved by Theorem 1.2 of this same paper — the conjecture holds only for $r=2$, $k \in \{2,3\}$.
paper_title: Hypergraph cuts above the average

name: AX_perfect_matching_flip_switchable_recognition
title: Open Question: Recognition of Switchable Graphs
statement_text: It is not clear whether graphs in the Switchable class (the hereditary class of graphs for which the reconfiguration graph of perfect matchings under flips is connected) can be recognized in polynomial time.
context_text: A flip transforms a perfect matching $M$ into another one by exchanging the edges of an alternating cycle of length four: if $uv,xy\in M$ and $ux,vy\in E(G)$, replace $uv,xy$ by $ux,vy$. The reconfiguration graph of perfect matchings under flips has the perfect matchings of $G$ as vertices, two being adjacent when one is obtained from the other by a flip (flips are the switches of the switch Markov chain used to sample perfect matchings). Dyer, Jerrum and Müller proved that the largest hereditary class of bipartite graphs for which this reconfiguration graph is connected is the class of chordal bipartite graphs; Dyer and Müller generalized this by characterizing the hereditary class of general (non-bipartite) graphs for which it is connected, called Switchable. The authors remark that it is not clear whether this class can be recognized in polynomial time. Their own results concern the decision problem (Perfect Matching Reconfiguration: can one given perfect matching be transformed into another by flips?), which they prove PSPACE-complete for split graphs and for bipartite graphs of bounded bandwidth and maximum degree five, and polynomial for strongly orderable graphs (including interval and strongly chordal graphs), outerplanar graphs and cographs, with linear-length sequences. They also leave open on which classes a shortest reconfiguration sequence can be found in polynomial time.
notes: Stated as a passing remark rather than a labelled problem; paper text is truncated before any concluding open-problems section, so additional conjectures may be present in the full paper.
paper_title: The Perfect Matching Reconfiguration Problem

name: AX_direct_product_multipartite_independence_equals_irredundance
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: If $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ are complete multipartite graphs and $G = \prod_{i=1}^{n} H_i$, then $\alpha(G) = IR(G)$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. The direct (tensor) product $\prod_{i=1}^n H_i$ has vertex set $V(H_1)\times\dots\times V(H_n)$, two vertices $(g_1,\dots,g_n)$ and $(g'_1,\dots,g'_n)$ being adjacent if and only if $g_i g'_i\in E(H_i)$ for every $i$. A complete multipartite graph is balanced if all its parts have the same size. For $S\subseteq V(G)$, $N[S]$ is the closed neighbourhood of $S$; $S$ is irredundant if $N[S\setminus\{v\}]\ne N[S]$ for every $v\in S$, and the upper irredundance number $IR(G)$ is the maximum size of an irredundant set. Since every maximal independent set is an irredundant dominating set, $\alpha(G)\le\Gamma(G)\le IR(G)$, where $\Gamma(G)$ is the upper domination number. Motivated by unitary Cayley graphs of finite rings (which are direct products of balanced complete multipartite graphs), Defant and Iyer conjectured $\alpha(G)=\Gamma(G)$ for such products, and Burcroff conjectured the stronger $\alpha(G)=IR(G)$ for direct products of balanced complete multipartite graphs. The authors prove Burcroff's conjecture except for at most $37$ specific products, and show that for any direct product of $n$ (not necessarily balanced) complete multipartite graphs, $IR(G)\le\alpha(G)+2^n$. This conjecture removes the balancedness assumption.
paper_title: Isoperimetry, Stability, and Irredundance in Direct Products

name: AX_pt_free_3_coloring_polynomial_large_t
title: Open Problem: Complexity of 3-colourability of $P_t$-free graphs
statement_text: Determine the complexity of $3$-colourability of $P_t$-free graphs for $t \geq 8$.
context_text: $P_t$ is the path on $t$ vertices, and $P_t$-free means having no induced subgraph isomorphic to $P_t$. For fixed $k\ge3$, $k$-colourability is NP-complete on $F$-free graphs whenever $F$ contains a cycle or a claw, so the interesting case is when $F$ is a disjoint union of paths. Polynomial-time algorithms for $k$-colourability of $P_t$-free graphs exist for $t\le5$ (all $k$), for $(k,t)=(4,6)$ and for $(k,t)=(3,7)$, while Huang showed $4$-colourability is NP-complete for $P_7$-free graphs and $5$-colourability is NP-complete for $P_6$-free graphs. So $3$-colourability is polynomial for $P_7$-free graphs and open for $t\ge8$. The authors show that, for multigraphs $H$ in which any two distinct vertices have at most one common neighbour, the generating function of (list) homomorphisms from a $P_t$-free graph $G$ to $H$ can be computed in time $2^{O(\sqrt{tn\log n})}$, $n=|V(G)|$; this covers deciding and counting $3$-colourings (homomorphisms to $K_3$) and computing the independent set polynomial, so both problems are solvable in subexponential time on $P_t$-free graphs. The key property is that $P_t$-free graphs have pathwidth $O(t\Delta)$, linear in the maximum degree $\Delta$. In contrast, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis no subexponential algorithm exists for $4$-colourability of $P_t$-free graphs. The authors remark that this suggests an NP-hardness proof for $3$-colourability of $P_t$-free graphs ($t$ large) via bounded-size gadgets from 3-SAT is unlikely under ETH.

name: AX_pt_free_independent_set_polynomial_t_7
title: Open Problem: Polynomial-time maximum independent set on $P_t$-free graphs
statement_text: Determine whether maximum independent set is decidable in polynomial time for $P_t$-free graphs for $t \geq 7$.
context_text: $P_t$ is the path on $t$ vertices, and $P_t$-free means having no induced subgraph isomorphic to $P_t$. Brause and, independently, Bacsó, Marx and Tuza showed that a greedy exhaustive approach gives a subexponential-time algorithm for maximum independent set on $P_t$-free graphs. The authors show that, for multigraphs $H$ in which any two distinct vertices have at most one common neighbour, the generating function of (list) homomorphisms from a $P_t$-free graph $G$ to $H$ can be computed in time $2^{O(\sqrt{tn\log n})}$, $n=|V(G)|$; this covers deciding and counting $3$-colourings (homomorphisms to $K_3$) and computing the independent set polynomial, so both problems are solvable in subexponential time on $P_t$-free graphs. The key property is that $P_t$-free graphs have pathwidth $O(t\Delta)$, linear in the maximum degree $\Delta$. The authors also ask whether, for fixed $t$, $3$-colourability and maximum independent set are polynomial-time solvable on graphs with no induced cycle of length greater than $t$, since their algorithm extends to that class using Seymour's tree decompositions.

name: AX_generalized_coloring_number_cc_characterization
title: Open Problem: Characterization of parameters satisfying (CC)
statement_text: Characterize the (hereditary, connected) graph parameters $f$ satisfying property (CC): for all integers $p$ and $s$, there exist two integers $p'$ and $s'$ such that $\mathrm{col}_{f,p'}(G) \leq s'$ for every graph $G$ satisfying $\chi^\ell_{f,p}(G) \leq s$.
context_text: A graph parameter $f$ assigns to every graph a value in $\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$, equal on isomorphic graphs; it is hereditary if $f(H)\le f(G)$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$, and connected if $f(G)=\max(f(G_1),f(G_2))$ whenever $G$ is the disjoint union of $G_1$ and $G_2$. Following Dvořák and Norin, a colouring $\varphi$ of $G$ is $(f,p)$-proper if $f(G[\varphi^{-1}(c)])\le p$ for every colour $c$, and $\chi^\ell_{f,p}(G)$ is the least $s$ such that $G$ has an $(f,p)$-proper $L$-colouring for every list assignment $L$ with all lists of size at least $s$ (for $f=\Delta$ this is defective choosability, for $f$ the maximum component order it is clustered choosability). Following Esperet and Ochem, an $s$-island of $G$ is a non-empty set $I$ of vertices each having fewer than $s$ neighbours outside $I$, and $\mathrm{col}_{f,p}(G)$ is the least $s$ such that every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$ contains an $s$-island $I$ with $f(H[I])\le p$; for connected hereditary $f$ one has $\chi^\ell_{f,p}(G)\le\mathrm{col}_{f,p}(G)$, generalising $\chi^\ell(G)\le\mathrm{col}(G)$ for the ordinary colouring number. Alon proved that the colouring number is bounded by an exponential function of the choosability, and property (CC) asks for a weak converse of this kind for $f$. The authors show that $\mathrm{fan}$ (the maximum order of a fan, i.e. a path plus a vertex adjacent to all its vertices, contained as a subgraph) is monotone and connected but does not satisfy (CC). They give two sufficient conditions: a hereditary parameter satisfies the stronger property that $\chi^\ell_{f,p}(G)\le s$ bounds the ordinary colouring number if and only if $f$ bounds the average degree (which covers maximum degree, component size and treewidth); and (CC) holds when $f(G)$ is bounded by a function of $f(G[X])$ and $f(G-X)$ for all $X$, which covers the chromatic number. They were unable to fully describe the parameters satisfying (CC).

name: AX_cluster_vertex_deletion_2_approximation
title: 2-Approximation Conjecture for Cluster-VD
statement_text: Cluster-VD can be 2-approximated in polynomial time.
context_text: Given a graph $G$ and a cost function $c:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}_+$, the cluster vertex deletion problem (Cluster-VD) asks for a minimum-cost set $X$ of vertices such that every component of $G-X$ is a complete graph, equivalently such that $G-X$ has no induced $P_3$ (path on three vertices); the conjecture concerns arbitrary nonnegative weights. Being a special case of vertex cover in a 3-uniform hypergraph, it has a straightforward 3-approximation, and You, Wang and Cao gave a $5/2$-approximation for the unweighted version. Adding a pendant edge at every vertex reduces Vertex Cover to Cluster-VD, so it is UGC-hard (hard assuming Khot's Unique Games Conjecture) to approximate Cluster-VD within any ratio better than 2, which makes 2 the natural target. The authors give a $9/4$-approximation algorithm based on the local ratio technique, and observe that it is in fact a 2-approximation on $K_5$-free graphs, and can be adapted to a 2-approximation on diamond-free graphs (the diamond is $K_4$ minus an edge), which supports the conjecture. By contrast, deleting vertices to destroy all triangles is UGC-hard to approximate within a ratio better than 3 (Guruswami and Lee).
notes: Stated in prose in both the abstract and the introduction without a labelled conjecture environment; language is unambiguously conjectural ('We further conjecture that …').

name: AX_quantum_sorting_poset_lower_bounds_equivalent
title: Conjecture on LB and QLB equivalence
statement_text: The two lower bounds $\mathrm{LB}(P)$ and $\mathrm{QLB}(P)$ are within a constant factor of each other for all posets $P$.
context_text: Let $P=([n],\le_P)$ be a poset and $\Delta(P)$ its set of linear extensions. Sorting under partial information means determining the unknown linear extension by comparisons; the information-theoretic lower bound is $\ln|\Delta(P)|$ (natural logarithms). The chain polytope $C(P)$ is the set of $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $y\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in K}y_i\le1$ for every chain $K$ of $P$. With $h(z)=-\frac1n\sum_{i\in[n]}\ln z_i$, the entropy of $P$ is $H(P)=\min_{z\in C(P)}h(z)$, a special case of graph entropy for the comparability graph. Its averaged variant is $QH(P)=\mathbb{E}_{z\in C(P)}[h(z)]$, the expectation for $z$ uniform in $C(P)$, which lies in $[1,H_n]$. Here $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number. Kahn and Kim showed that $\mathrm{LB}(P)=n(\ln n-H(P))$ approximates $\ln|\Delta(P)|$ within a constant factor (in fact $\ln|\Delta(P)|\le\mathrm{LB}(P)\le2\ln|\Delta(P)|$). The authors show that the quantum adversary lower bound for this sorting problem is, up to a constant, $\mathrm{QLB}(P)=n(H_n-QH(P))$. By analysing this bound they prove Yao's conjecture, that quantum query complexity is $\Omega(\log|\Delta(P)|)$, for series-parallel posets and an extended class. Their findings support the conjecture that $\mathrm{LB}$ and $\mathrm{QLB}$ are always within a constant factor, which would give Yao's conjecture for all posets. Proving it requires understanding how $H(P)$ and $QH(P)$ compare, but tools are lacking: unlike the entropy, $\mathbb{E}_{z\in C}[h(z)]$ is not monotone under inclusion of the convex corner $C$. This is order theory / quantum complexity rather than graph theory.

paper_title: Information-theoretic lower bounds for quantum sorting

name: AX_local_search_ptas_monotone_fo_optimization
title: Open Problem (Section 1.1)
statement_text: It is an open problem whether some variation on the local search approach can give PTAS for all monotone FO optimization problems.
context_text: First-order (FO) formulas on graphs use the adjacency relation, finitely many unary predicates (vertex colours), equality, Boolean connectives and quantification over vertices. For a unary predicate $X$, a sentence $\varphi$ is $X$-positive (resp. $X$-negative) if every occurrence of $X$ lies under an even (resp. odd) number of negations, so the solutions are upward (resp. downward) closed. A monotone FO optimization problem is either a positive FO minimization problem (find a minimum set $A$ with $X:=A$ satisfying an $X$-positive $\varphi$; e.g. minimum dominating set, minimum vertex cover, hitting all triangles) or a negative FO maximization problem (maximum set satisfying an $X$-negative $\varphi$; e.g. maximum independent set, maximum $r$-independent set, largest induced subgraph of maximum degree $d$). A PTAS returns, for each fixed $k$, a solution within a factor $1\pm1/k$ of the optimum in polynomial time. Dawar et al. gave PTASes for all monotone FO optimization problems on proper minor-closed classes via Baker's technique and the graph minor structure theorem; the authors prove the same, without the structure theorem, for all classes in which their 'Baker game' (repeated Baker layering interspersed with vertex removal) is won in a bounded number of rounds, which includes all proper minor-closed classes. Cabello and Gajser (proper minor-closed classes) and Har-Peled and Quanrud (classes with polynomial expansion, equivalently strongly sublinear separators) showed that the trivial local search algorithm (repeatedly improving a solution by bounded-size changes) is a PTAS for maximum independent set, minimum dominating set and many related problems. The open problem asks whether a variation of local search gives a PTAS for all monotone FO optimization problems; the paper does not specify the graph classes, presumably those where local search is known to work (proper minor-closed classes or classes with strongly sublinear separators).

paper_title: Baker game and polynomial-time approximation schemes

name: AX_disjoint_paths_stability_two_np_complete
title: Informal Conjecture (vertex-disjoint paths, stability number two)
statement_text: We suspect the $k$ vertex-disjoint paths problem might be NP-complete for digraphs with stability number two.
context_text: Digraphs are finite, without loops or parallel edges, but may have both edges $uv$ and $vu$; paths are directed. Given distinct vertices $s_1,t_1,\dots,s_k,t_k$ of a digraph $G$, the $k$ vertex-disjoint paths problem asks whether there are pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths $P_1,\dots,P_k$ with $P_i$ from $s_i$ to $t_i$. A set of vertices is stable if no edge has both ends in it, and the stability number is the size of a largest stable set; a digraph is semicomplete if for all distinct $u,v$ at least one of $uv,vu$ is an edge (so semicomplete digraphs are exactly those of stability number one). The problem is NP-complete in general digraphs even for $k=2$ (Fortune, Hopcroft and Wyllie), and NP-complete for tournaments when $k$ is not fixed (Bang-Jensen and Thomassen); the authors had earlier shown it is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed $k$ on semicomplete digraphs, and here extend this to digraphs whose vertex set is given partitioned into a bounded number of sets each inducing a semicomplete digraph. A natural further extension would be to digraphs of bounded stability number: the edge-disjoint version is polynomial-time solvable there, but the vertex-disjoint version remains out of reach, and the authors suspect that it might already be NP-complete for stability number two (the paper does not say explicitly whether $k$ is meant to be fixed, but the discussion concerns extending the fixed-$k$ result).
