name: AX_distributed_coloring_sparse_sublinear_rounds
title: Open problem on sublinear round complexity
statement_text: For a deterministic distributed algorithm that, given an $n$-vertex graph $G$ and an integer $d\ge\max(3,\mathrm{mad}(G))$, either finds a $(d+1)$-clique in $G$ or a $d$-list-coloring of $G$, it remains interesting to obtain a bound on the round complexity that is sublinear in $n$ regardless of the value of $d$.
context_text: In the LOCAL model of distributed computing, each node of an $n$-vertex graph has a unique identifier in $\{1,\dots,n\}$, knows $n$ (and here its own list of colors, or the integer $d$), and exchanges messages of unbounded size with its neighbors in synchronous rounds, with unbounded local computation; each vertex must output its own color in a proper coloring, and the round complexity is the number of rounds needed (so the output of $v$ depends only on its ball of radius equal to the round complexity, and any problem can be solved in a number of rounds linear in the diameter). A $d$-list-coloring is a proper coloring in which each vertex gets a color from its own list of $d$ colors. The maximum average degree $\mathrm{mad}(G)$ is the maximum of $2|E(H)|/|V(H)|$ over subgraphs $H$ of $G$. The authors' main result is a deterministic distributed algorithm that, given an $n$-vertex graph $G$ and an integer $d\ge\max(3,\mathrm{mad}(G))$, either finds a $(d+1)$-clique or a $d$-list-coloring of $G$ in $O(d^4\log^3 n)$ rounds, and in $O(d^2\log^3 n)$ rounds if every vertex has degree at most $d$. This is optimal in the number of colors, and the $\log n$ dependence cannot be replaced by $o(\log n)$ even for fixed $d$ (Linial: trees cannot be colored with a constant number of colors in $o(\log n)$ rounds); the assumption $d\ge3$ is needed since $n$-vertex paths cannot be 2-colored in $o(n)$ rounds. Using network decompositions, the round complexity can be replaced by $d^3 2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ (and $d\,2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ for maximum degree at most $d$), but the authors find these bounds not very satisfying (in most applications they have in mind $d$ is a constant).
notes: Stated as an open direction in prose, no labelled environment; PDF source.
paper_title: Distributed coloring in sparse graphs with fewer colors

name: AX_distributed_delta_list_coloring_randomized_rounds
title: Question on randomized list-coloring round complexity
statement_text: There is a deterministic distributed algorithm of round complexity $O(\Delta^2\log^3 n)$ that, given any $n$-vertex graph $G$ of maximum degree $\Delta\ge3$ and any assignment $L$ of lists of size $\Delta$ to its vertices, either finds an $L$-list-coloring of $G$ or finds that no such coloring exists. Is it possible to avoid the multiplicative factor polynomial in $\Delta$ in a randomized version of this algorithm?
context_text: In the LOCAL model of distributed computing, each node of an $n$-vertex graph has a unique identifier in $\{1,\dots,n\}$, knows $n$ (and here its own list of colors, or the integer $d$), and exchanges messages of unbounded size with its neighbors in synchronous rounds, with unbounded local computation; each vertex must output its own color in a proper coloring, and the round complexity is the number of rounds needed (so the output of $v$ depends only on its ball of radius equal to the round complexity, and any problem can be solved in a number of rounds linear in the diameter). A $d$-list-coloring is a proper coloring in which each vertex gets a color from its own list of $d$ colors. The maximum average degree $\mathrm{mad}(G)$ is the maximum of $2|E(H)|/|V(H)|$ over subgraphs $H$ of $G$. The authors' main result is a deterministic distributed algorithm that, given an $n$-vertex graph $G$ and an integer $d\ge\max(3,\mathrm{mad}(G))$, either finds a $(d+1)$-clique or a $d$-list-coloring of $G$ in $O(d^4\log^3 n)$ rounds, and in $O(d^2\log^3 n)$ rounds if every vertex has degree at most $d$. As a corollary, the authors obtain a distributed list version of Brooks' theorem: the deterministic $O(\Delta^2\log^3 n)$-round algorithm for $\Delta$-list-coloring graphs of maximum degree $\Delta\ge3$ (or certifying that no coloring exists). Panconesi and Srinivasan gave a deterministic $O(\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\log^3 n)$-round algorithm that $\Delta$-colors every $n$-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge3$ other than $K_{\Delta+1}$, and a randomized variant in $O(\log^3 n/\log\Delta)$ rounds, i.e. with no polynomial factor in $\Delta$; it is not clear whether the same can be achieved for the list version. In a section on recent developments, the authors mention that Ghaffari, Hirvonen, Kuhn and Maus later gave, for $d$-coloring non-complete graphs of maximum degree at most $d$, a deterministic algorithm in $O(d^{1/2}\log^2 n)$ rounds and a randomized one in $d^{1/2+o(1)}(\log\log n)^2$ rounds.
notes: Implicit question in prose: "it is not clear whether we can similarly avoid the multiplicative factor polynomial in $\Delta$ in a randomized version of our algorithm"; PDF source.
paper_title: Distributed coloring in sparse graphs with fewer colors

name: AX_bounded_clique_large_chi_consecutive_holes
title: Conjecture 1.8
statement_text: For all integers $\kappa, \ell \geq 0$, there exists $c \geq 0$ such that every graph with chromatic number greater than $c$ contains either a complete subgraph on $\kappa$ vertices or holes of $\ell$ consecutive lengths.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and holes of $\ell$ consecutive lengths means holes of lengths $k,k+1,\dots,k+\ell-1$ for some $k$. The authors previously proved that for every $\ell$ there is $c$ such that every triangle-free graph with chromatic number greater than $c$ contains holes of $\ell$ consecutive lengths, and conjectured in that earlier paper that the same holds when only $K_\kappa$ is excluded; this conjecture remains open. In this paper they prove that for all $\kappa,\ell$ there is $c$ such that every graph with $\chi(G)>c$ and $\omega(G)\le\kappa$ contains holes of every length modulo $\ell$ (implying Gyárfás's three conjectures on odd holes, long holes and long odd holes, and the Kalai–Meshulam conjecture proved by Bonamy, Charbit and Thomassé on holes of length divisible by three), and, as a small step towards this conjecture, that such graphs contain holes of two consecutive lengths, both of length more than $\ell$. They say they could get three consecutive long holes with a great deal of omitted work, but no more. Note that holes of a specific length cannot be forced, since there are graphs of arbitrarily large girth and chromatic number.
notes: Explicitly labelled 'Conjecture' in the paper. The authors state it was conjectured in their earlier paper [14]; the theorem header carries no parenthetical attribution, so classified as 'states' per schema rules. Theorem 1.9 of this paper (holes of two consecutive long lengths) is proved as a step towards this conjecture.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. X. Holes of specific residue

name: AX_separation_choosability_grows_min_degree
title: Conjecture 1.3
statement_text: There is a function $x_1(d)$ that satisfies $x_1(d) \to \infty$ as $d \to \infty$ such that $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G) \geq x_1(d)$ for any graph $G$ with minimum degree $d$.
context_text: A $k$-list-assignment of $G$ assigns to each vertex a set $L(v)$ of $k$ positive integers; it has maximum separation if $|L(u)\cap L(v)|\le1$ for every edge $uv$. $G$ is separation $k$-choosable if it has a proper colouring $c$ with $c(v)\in L(v)$ for every $k$-list-assignment $L$ with maximum separation, and the separation choosability $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G)$ is the least such $k$ (so $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G)\le\mathrm{ch}(G)$, the choosability). Alon proved $\mathrm{ch}(G)\ge C\log d$ for every graph of minimum degree $d$, and Füredi, Kostochka and Kumbhat showed $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(K_{d,d})=(1+o(1))\log_2 d$. The authors prove that there is $C>0$ with $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G)\ge C\log d$ for every bipartite $G$ of minimum degree $d$, and conjecture that the bipartiteness assumption can be dropped in some form. The usual reduction (every graph of average degree $d$ has a bipartite subgraph of minimum degree $d/2$) fails, since a list assignment with maximum separation need not keep it when edges are added. Kratochvíl, Tuza and Voigt showed $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(K_{d+1})\sim\sqrt{d}$, so it would suffice to find in every graph of large minimum degree a large clique or a bipartite induced subgraph of large minimum degree. In a note added to the final version, the authors report that Kwan, Letzter, Sudakov and Tran proved that any graph of minimum degree at least $d$ contains a clique on $x_2(d)$ vertices or a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $x_3(d)$ with $x_2,x_3\to\infty$, which confirms this conjecture.

paper_title: Separation choosability and dense bipartite induced subgraphs

name: AX_dense_bipartite_induced_or_large_clique
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: There are functions $x_2(d)$ and $x_3(d)$ satisfying $x_2(d) \to \infty$ and $x_3(d) \to \infty$ as $d \to \infty$ such that any graph with minimum degree at least $d$ contains a complete subgraph on $x_2(d)$ vertices or a bipartite induced subgraph with minimum degree at least $x_3(d)$.
context_text: A $k$-list-assignment of $G$ assigns to each vertex a set $L(v)$ of $k$ positive integers; it has maximum separation if $|L(u)\cap L(v)|\le1$ for every edge $uv$. $G$ is separation $k$-choosable if it has a proper colouring $c$ with $c(v)\in L(v)$ for every $k$-list-assignment $L$ with maximum separation, and the separation choosability $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G)$ is the least such $k$ (so $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G)\le\mathrm{ch}(G)$, the choosability). This Ramsey-type conjecture would imply the conjecture that $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G)\ge x_1(d)$ for some $x_1(d)\to\infty$ and every graph $G$ of minimum degree $d$: Kratochvíl, Tuza and Voigt showed $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(K_{d+1})\sim\sqrt{d}$, and the authors prove that $\mathrm{ch}_{\mathrm{sep}}(G)\ge C\log d$ for every bipartite graph of minimum degree $d$, which applies to a bipartite induced subgraph (an induced subgraph inherits maximum separation of a list assignment). The authors find this problem intriguing irrespective of separation choosability, and show that any graph with chromatic number at most $k$ and minimum degree $d$ has a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $d/2k$. In a note added to the final version, they report that Kwan, Letzter, Sudakov and Tran proved this conjecture (and thus the separation choosability conjecture).

name: AX_dense_bipartite_induced_triangle_free_log
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: There is a constant $C > 0$ such that any triangle-free graph with minimum degree at least $d$ contains a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $C \log d$.
context_text: This is a quantitative variation, for triangle-free graphs, of the conjecture that any graph of minimum degree at least $d$ contains a clique on $x_2(d)$ vertices or a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $x_3(d)$, for some functions $x_2,x_3\to\infty$. If true, the bound $C\log d$ would be sharp up to the choice of $C$: the authors show there are triangle-free graphs of minimum degree $d$ with no bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree more than $O(\log d)$. They also show that any graph with chromatic number at most $k$ and minimum degree $d$ has a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $d/2k$, and obtain partial results. In a note added to the final version, the authors report that Kwan, Letzter, Sudakov and Tran nearly settled it, establishing bipartite induced subgraphs of minimum degree $\Omega(\log d/\log\log d)$ in $K_r$-free graphs of minimum degree $d$ for every fixed $r\ge3$.

paper_title: Separation choosability and dense bipartite induced subgraphs

name: AX_dense_bipartite_induced_large_girth
title: Conjecture 1.6
statement_text: There exist $d_0$ and $g_0$ such that any graph of girth at least $g_0$ with minimum degree at least $d_0$ contains a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $3$.
context_text: This is a variation, with large girth instead of triangle-freeness, of the conjecture that any graph of minimum degree at least $d$ contains a clique on $x_2(d)$ vertices or a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $x_3(d)$, for some functions $x_2,x_3\to\infty$. If $3$ is replaced by $2$, the conclusion is equivalent to containing an even hole (an induced cycle of even length at least four), and this weaker statement holds with $g_0=4$ and $d_0=3$ by Radovanović and Vušković; even holes can be detected in polynomial time, whereas detecting a bipartite induced subgraph of minimum degree at least $3$ is NP-complete. In a note added to the final version, the authors report that this conjecture is confirmed by work of Kwan, Letzter, Sudakov and Tran, who established bipartite induced subgraphs of minimum degree $\Omega(\log d/\log\log d)$ in $K_r$-free graphs of minimum degree $d$ for every fixed $r\ge3$.

name: AX_frozen_coloring_glauber_delta_o_n
title: Informal: Δ = o(n) condition not necessary for Corollary 2
statement_text: In the statement 'for every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with maximum degree $\Delta=o(n)$, Glauber dynamics for $(\Delta+1)$-colourings of $G$ started at a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring gives an almost uniform sampler for random $(\Delta+1)$-colourings', the condition $\Delta=o(n)$ is probably not necessary.
context_text: Let $G$ have $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$. A $(\Delta+1)$-colouring is a proper colouring with colours in $[\Delta+1]$; it is frozen if every colour appears in the closed neighbourhood of every vertex, so that no single vertex can be recoloured. Glauber dynamics for $k$-colourings is the Markov chain on proper $k$-colourings that at each step picks a vertex $v$ and a colour $c\in[k]$ uniformly at random and recolours $v$ with $c$ if no neighbour of $v$ has colour $c$. For $k=\Delta+1$ frozen colourings are fixed points, and Feghali, Johnson and Paulusma showed that for $\Delta\ge3$ they are the only obstruction: the recolouring graph consists of one component containing all non-frozen colourings plus isolated frozen colourings. The authors' main theorem: if $3\le\Delta\le n-2$ and $G$ is connected, a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring $\alpha$ satisfies $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\le(6/7)^{n/(\Delta+1)}$ (the conditions are needed, e.g. every $(\Delta+1)$-colouring of $K_{\Delta+1}$ is frozen). The authors deduce the sampling statement: when $\Delta=o(n)$, the probability of starting at a frozen colouring is $o(1)$ and frozen colourings contribute $o(1)$ to the stationary distribution, so the chain converges to the uniform distribution on the non-frozen component, which is close in total variation to the uniform distribution on all $(\Delta+1)$-colourings. They remark right after that the condition $\Delta=o(n)$ is probably not necessary. The remark is informal: the paper does not say which weaker condition is intended (some condition is needed, since all colourings of $K_{\Delta+1}$ are frozen).
notes: Stated in running prose immediately after Corollary 2: 'The condition Δ = o(n) is probably not necessary.' PDF source.
paper_title: Frozen $(Δ+1)$-colourings of bounded degree graphs

name: AX_frozen_coloring_probability_exponent
title: Informal: Exponent in Theorem 1 not optimal
statement_text: The dependence on $\Delta$ in the exponent of the bound $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\le(6/7)^{n/(\Delta+1)}$, valid for every connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with maximum degree $\Delta$, $3\le\Delta\le n-2$, and a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring $\alpha$ of $G$, is not best possible.
context_text: Let $G$ have $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$. A $(\Delta+1)$-colouring is a proper colouring with colours in $[\Delta+1]$; it is frozen if every colour appears in the closed neighbourhood of every vertex, so that no single vertex can be recoloured. Glauber dynamics for $k$-colourings is the Markov chain on proper $k$-colourings that at each step picks a vertex $v$ and a colour $c\in[k]$ uniformly at random and recolours $v$ with $c$ if no neighbour of $v$ has colour $c$. For $k=\Delta+1$ frozen colourings are fixed points, and Feghali, Johnson and Paulusma showed that for $\Delta\ge3$ they are the only obstruction: the recolouring graph consists of one component containing all non-frozen colourings plus isolated frozen colourings. The authors' main theorem: if $3\le\Delta\le n-2$ and $G$ is connected, a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring $\alpha$ satisfies $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\le(6/7)^{n/(\Delta+1)}$ (the conditions are needed, e.g. every $(\Delta+1)$-colouring of $K_{\Delta+1}$ is frozen). On the other hand, for every $n_0$ and every $\Delta\ge3$ there are $n\ge n_0$ and a connected $\Delta$-regular graph on $n$ vertices with $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\ge e^{-\frac{3\log\Delta}{\Delta}n}$; this is only a factor $\log\Delta$ off in the exponent from the upper bound, and the authors believe the upper bound's dependence on $\Delta$ can be improved. These examples contain many cliques of size $\Delta$; the authors also show that $\Delta$-regular graphs of arbitrarily large girth can have frozen colourings, while a uniformly random $\Delta$-regular graph has a frozen colouring with probability at most $e^{-cn}$.

name: AX_generalized_turan_additive_approximation_np_hard
title: Conjecture 1.8
statement_text: For every graph $T$, family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ such that no $F \in \mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, and $\epsilon > 0$, it is NP-hard to approximate $\mathrm{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ up to additive error of $n^{v(T)-\epsilon}$ for a given input graph $G$ on $n$ vertices.
context_text: For graphs $G$ and $T$ and a family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$, $\mathrm{ex}(G,T,\mathcal{F})$ denotes the maximum number of copies of $T$ in a subgraph of $G$ that contains no copy of any $F\in\mathcal{F}$ ($\mathcal{F}$-free); $v(T)$ is the number of vertices of $T$, and for $G=K_n$, $T=K_2$ this is the classical Turán number. For a graph $T$, an $m$ blow-up of $T$ is obtained by replacing each vertex of $T$ by an independent set of size $m$ and each edge by a complete bipartite graph between the corresponding sets. The authors prove that for every fixed $T$, finite $\mathcal{F}$ and $\epsilon>0$ there is a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximating $\mathrm{ex}(G,T,\mathcal{F})$ within additive error $\epsilon n^{v(T)}$, generalising a result of Alon, Shapira and Sudakov for $T=K_2$. If some $F\in\mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, then $\mathrm{ex}(K_n,T,F)\le n^{v(T)-\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon=\epsilon(T,\mathcal{F})>0$, so $0$ is already an approximation within additive error $n^{v(T)-\epsilon}$; the conjecture asserts that outside this easy case no significantly better approximation than $\epsilon n^{v(T)}$ is possible in polynomial time. For $T=K_2$ this is the theorem of Alon, Shapira and Sudakov (NP-hardness of additive error $n^{2-\delta}$ when $\mathcal{F}$ contains no bipartite graph). The authors prove the case $T=K_m$, $\mathcal{F}=\{K_k\}$ with $k\ge m+2$, and show that for a 3-connected $T$ on $t$ vertices and a family of 3-connected graphs none of which is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, approximating within additive error $n^{t-2-\epsilon}$ is NP-hard. They also ask, as special cases, whether approximating $\mathrm{ex}(G,K_m,K_{m+1})$ within $n^{m-\epsilon}$ is NP-hard for every $m\ge2$ (known for $m=2,3$), and whether the same holds for $\mathrm{ex}(G,K_m,\mathcal{F})$ when every $F\in\mathcal{F}$ has chromatic number at least $m+2$.
paper_title: Additive Approximation of Generalized Turán Questions

name: AX_degenerate_graphs_flexibility_d_plus_1_lists
title: Problem 1
statement_text: Does there for every integer $d \geq 0$ exist $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every $d$-degenerate graph with an assignment of lists of size $d + 1$ is weighted $\varepsilon$-flexible? Or at least $\varepsilon$-flexible?
context_text: A list assignment $L$ for $G$ gives each vertex $v$ a set $L(v)$ of colors, and an $L$-coloring is a proper coloring $\phi$ with $\phi(v)\in L(v)$ for all $v$. A request is a function $r$ with domain $\mathrm{dom}(r)\subseteq V(G)$ and $r(v)\in L(v)$; for $\varepsilon>0$ it is $\varepsilon$-satisfiable if some $L$-coloring $\phi$ has $\phi(v)=r(v)$ for at least $\varepsilon|\mathrm{dom}(r)|$ vertices $v\in\mathrm{dom}(r)$, and $G$ with $L$ is $\varepsilon$-flexible if every request is $\varepsilon$-satisfiable. A weighted request is a function $w$ assigning a nonnegative real $w(v,c)$ to each pair with $c\in L(v)$; it is $\varepsilon$-satisfiable if some $L$-coloring $\phi$ satisfies $\sum_{v}w(v,\phi(v))\ge\varepsilon\sum_{v,\,c\in L(v)}w(v,c)$, and $G$ with $L$ is weighted $\varepsilon$-flexible if every weighted request is $\varepsilon$-satisfiable (this implies $\varepsilon$-flexibility). A $d$-degenerate graph is $(d+1)$-choosable by a greedy argument; the authors prove that with lists of size $d+2$ every $d$-degenerate graph is weighted $\varepsilon$-flexible for some $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(d)>0$, and ask whether lists of size $d+1$ suffice. Even satisfying requests with a single vertex in their domain is non-trivial here: they prove it only when $d+1$ is prime. For $d=0$ the problem is trivial and for $d=1$ (forests with lists of size 2) weighted $1/2$-flexibility is easy, so the first open case is $d=2$.

paper_title: List coloring with requests

name: AX_online_ramsey_random_painter_growth_rate
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: (a) The diagonal online random Ramsey numbers satisfy $$\tilde{r}_{rand}(n, n) = 2^{(1+o(1)) \frac{2}{3} n}.$$ (b) The off-diagonal online random Ramsey numbers ($m \geq 3$ fixed and $n \to \infty$) satisfy $$\tilde{r}_{rand}(m, n) = n^{(1+o(1)) \frac{2}{3} m}.$$
context_text: In the $(m,n)$-online Ramsey game, played on an infinite set of initially isolated vertices, Builder adds one edge per turn and Painter immediately colours it red or blue; the online Ramsey number $\tilde r(m,n)$ is the minimum number of turns Builder needs to guarantee a red $K_m$ or a blue $K_n$. One has $\frac12r(m,n)\le\tilde r(m,n)\le\binom{r(m,n)}{2}$. $\tilde r(m,n;p)$ is the number of turns Builder needs to win with probability at least $1/2$ against a Painter who colours each edge red independently with probability $p$, and the online random Ramsey number is $\tilde r_{rand}(m,n)=\max_{p\in(0,1)}\tilde r(m,n;p)$. In the Subgraph Query Game on the random graph $G(\mathbb{Z},p)$, Builder queries one pair of vertices per step and learns whether it is an edge (each edge present independently with probability $p$, each pair queried at most once), and $f(H,p)$ is the minimum number of queries needed to find a copy of $H$ with probability at least $1/2$. The two games are related: $\tilde r(m,n;p)\le\min\{f(K_m,p),f(K_n,1-p)\}\le3\tilde r(m,n;p)$. The authors conjecture $f(K_m,p)=2^{o(m)}p^{-\frac23m+c_m}$ for $m\ge4$ with an explicit $c_m$, prove the upper bound and the cases $m=4,5$, and show that this conjecture implies both parts of the present one. Using a random Painter they prove $\tilde r(n,n)\ge2^{(2-\sqrt2)n-O(1)}$ and, for fixed $m\ge3$, $\tilde r(m,n)\ge n^{(2-\sqrt2)m-O(1)}$.
paper_title: Online Ramsey Numbers and the Subgraph Query Problem

name: AX_subgraph_query_complexity_km_random
title: Conjecture 9
statement_text: For any $m\ge4$, $f(K_m,p)=2^{o(m)}p^{-\frac{2}{3}m+c_m}$, where $c_m=\frac{m}{2m-3}$ if $m\equiv0\pmod 3$, $c_m=\frac{2}{3}$ if $m\equiv1\pmod 3$, and $c_m=\frac{2m+8}{6m-3}$ if $m\equiv2\pmod 3$.
context_text: In the Subgraph Query Game on the random graph $G(\mathbb{Z},p)$, Builder queries one pair of vertices per step and learns whether it is an edge (each edge present independently with probability $p$, each pair queried at most once), and $f(H,p)$ is the minimum number of queries needed to find a copy of $H$ with probability at least $1/2$. (The variant counting expected copies is avoided because some strategies have tiny success probability but huge expectation.) The authors prove the upper bound of the conjecture by an explicit strategy. They also show that if $H$ contains $k$ vertex-disjoint edges then $f(H,p)=\Omega_H(p^{-(e(H)-k(k-1))/(v(H)-k)})$, which gives $f(K_3,p)=\Theta(p^{-3/2})$, $f(K_4,p)=\Theta(p^{-2})$ and $f(K_5,p)=\Theta(p^{-8/3})$, proving the conjecture for $m=4,5$. For $m=6$ they only know $\Omega(p^{-13/4})\le f(K_6,p)\le O(p^{-10/3})$ and believe the upper bound is correct. The conjecture is motivated by, and would imply, the conjectured growth rates $2^{(1+o(1))\frac23n}$ and $n^{(1+o(1))\frac23m}$ of online random Ramsey numbers, through the inequality $\tilde r(m,n;p)\le\min\{f(K_m,p),f(K_n,1-p)\}\le3\tilde r(m,n;p)$, where $\tilde r(m,n;p)$ is the number of turns Builder needs to force a red $K_m$ or a blue $K_n$ with probability $1/2$ in the online Ramsey game against a Painter colouring each edge red with probability $p$.

paper_title: Online Ramsey Numbers and the Subgraph Query Problem

name: AX_online_ramsey_off_diagonal_alteration_bound
title: Informal conjecture on generalization of Theorem 4 to all $\tilde{r}(m,n)$
statement_text: The authors prove $\tilde r(3,n)=\Omega(n^3/\log^2n)$ by a Painter strategy close in spirit to Erdős's alteration proof of the lower bound on the Ramsey number $r(3,n)$. This alteration method for lower bounding $r(3,n)$ was later generalized to all $r(m,n)$ by Krivelevich, and we suspect that the bound $\tilde r(3,n)=\Omega(n^3/\log^2n)$ can be generalized to $\tilde r(m,n)$ in the same way.
context_text: In the $(m,n)$-online Ramsey game, played on an infinite set of initially isolated vertices, Builder adds one edge per turn and Painter immediately colours it red or blue; the online Ramsey number $\tilde r(m,n)$ is the minimum number of turns Builder needs to guarantee a red $K_m$ or a blue $K_n$. One has $\frac12r(m,n)\le\tilde r(m,n)\le\binom{r(m,n)}{2}$. The Painter strategy paints every edge blue while one of its endpoints has low degree (less than $(n-1)/4$), paints an edge blue whenever red would complete a red triangle, and otherwise paints randomly. The resulting bound is $n$ times the bound on $r(3,n)$ given by the Lovász Local Lemma. With the upper bound $\tilde r(m,n)=O_m(n^m/(\log n)^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor-1})$ proved in the paper, this determines $\tilde r(3,n)$ up to a polylogarithmic factor. For general fixed $m$ the best known lower bound is $\tilde r(m,n)\ge n^{(2-\sqrt2)m-O(1)}$, from a purely random Painter. No explicit target bound for general $m$ is stated in the paper. The authors also conjecture that the triangle-free process would improve the $m=3$ lower bound to $cn^3/\log n$.
notes: No explicit quantitative bound for general $m$ is stated; only the suspicion of generalizability is expressed.
paper_title: Online Ramsey Numbers and the Subgraph Query Problem

name: AX_correlation_polytope_extension_complexity_treewidth
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every $n$-vertex graph $G$, the extension complexity of $\mathrm{COR}(G)$ is $2^{\Omega(\mathrm{tw}(G)+\log n)}$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. The correlation polytope $\mathrm{COR}(G)$ of $G=(V,E)$ is the convex hull in $\mathbb{R}^{V\cup E}$ of the vectors $(\chi(X),\chi(E(X)))$ for $X\subseteq V$, where $E(X)$ is the set of edges with both ends in $X$ and $\chi$ denotes characteristic vectors (in machine learning it is the marginal polytope). A polytope $Q$ is an extension of $P$ if $P$ is an affine image of $Q$, and the extension complexity of $P$ is the minimum number of facets of an extension of $P$. The authors prove the upper bound $2^{O(\mathrm{tw}(G)+\log n)}$ for every $n$-vertex graph (via Kolman and Koutecký), that extension complexity of $\mathrm{COR}$ is minor-monotone, and that the conjectured lower bound holds for every graph in a proper minor-closed class; for every graph their proof gives $2^{\Omega(h+\log n)}$ with $h$ the largest height of a grid minor, hence $2^{\Omega(\mathrm{tw}(G)^{\delta}+\log n)}$ for some universal $\delta>1/20$ by the polynomial grid-minor theorem. If true, the conjecture would improve the bound $2^{\Omega(n/\log n)}$ of Göös, Jain and Watson for stable set polytopes (convex hulls of stable sets) to $2^{\Omega(n)}$, and would yield explicit $0/1$-polytopes with extension complexity exponential in their dimension, as predicted by a counting argument of Rothvoß.
notes: The paper proves this conjecture for the special case of proper minor-closed graph classes (Theorem 3), but the general statement remains open.
paper_title: Extension Complexity of the Correlation Polytope

name: AX_sparse_neighborhoods_critical_bounded_clique
title: Question 1.3
statement_text: Let $G$ be a $\lfloor (1-\varepsilon)(\Delta(G)+1) \rfloor + 1$-critical graph with $\omega(G) \leq (1-\alpha)(\Delta(G)+1)$. What is the largest $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon,\alpha)$, such that $G$ is $\delta$-sparse?
context_text: A graph $G$ is $\delta$-sparse if every vertex neighbourhood induces at most $(1-\delta)\binom{\Delta(G)}{2}$ edges, and $(k+1)$-critical if it is not $k$-colourable but every proper subgraph is. Reed's conjecture states $\chi\le\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)+\varepsilon\omega\rceil$ for all $\varepsilon\le1/2$; King and Reed proved it for large $\Delta$ and some small $\varepsilon>0$ in two steps: reduce to graphs with $\omega\le\frac23(\Delta+1)$ and show that such critical graphs are $\delta$-sparse, then show that $\delta$-sparse graphs are $(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)$-colourable for some $\varepsilon(\delta)>0$ (they obtain roughly $\delta=1/160$ and $\varepsilon<1/(320e^6)$); improving either step improves the $\varepsilon$ in Reed's conjecture. This question isolates the first step. The authors prove (even for list colourings) that if $\varepsilon<\alpha/2$, $\omega(G)\le(1-\alpha)(\Delta(G)+1)$ and $G$ is critical with respect to some list assignment with lists of size $\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta(G)+1)\rceil$, then $G$ is $\frac{(\alpha-2\varepsilon)^2}{2}$-sparse; for $\alpha=1/3$ this is an eightfold improvement over King and Reed's $\frac14(\frac16-\varepsilon)^2$. Combined with their answer to the second step, this gives Reed's conjecture for $\varepsilon\le1/26$ when $\Delta$ is large.
notes: PDF source; statement is clearly readable.
paper_title: Colouring Graphs with Sparse Neighbourhoods: Bounds and Applications

name: AX_sparse_neighborhoods_chromatic_below_delta
title: Question 1.4
statement_text: Let $G$ be a $\delta$-sparse graph. What is the largest $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\delta)$ such that $\chi(G) \leq (1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)$?
context_text: A graph $G$ is $\delta$-sparse if every vertex neighbourhood induces at most $(1-\delta)\binom{\Delta(G)}{2}$ edges, and $(k+1)$-critical if it is not $k$-colourable but every proper subgraph is. Reed's conjecture states $\chi\le\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)+\varepsilon\omega\rceil$ for all $\varepsilon\le1/2$; King and Reed proved it for large $\Delta$ and some small $\varepsilon>0$ in two steps: reduce to graphs with $\omega\le\frac23(\Delta+1)$ and show that such critical graphs are $\delta$-sparse, then show that $\delta$-sparse graphs are $(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)$-colourable for some $\varepsilon(\delta)>0$ (they obtain roughly $\delta=1/160$ and $\varepsilon<1/(320e^6)$); improving either step improves the $\varepsilon$ in Reed's conjecture. This question isolates the second step (bounds are meant for $\Delta$ large enough in terms of $\delta$). For $\delta\in[0,0.9]$, Molloy and Reed obtained $\varepsilon(\delta)\approx0.0238\delta$ and Bruhn and Joos $\varepsilon(\delta)\approx0.1827\delta-0.0778\delta^{3/2}$, both with one application of the naive colouring procedure; using an iterated version, the authors improve this by a factor $\sqrt e$ to $\varepsilon=0.3012\delta-0.1283\delta^{3/2}$, even for the list chromatic number. This yields Reed's conjecture for $\varepsilon\le1/26$ when $\Delta$ is large, and the bound $\chi'_s(G)\le1.835\Delta(G)^2$ on the strong chromatic index for large $\Delta$.
notes: PDF source; statement is clearly readable.
paper_title: Colouring Graphs with Sparse Neighbourhoods: Bounds and Applications

name: AX_sparse_strong_erdos_hajnal_forests
title: Conjecture 1.5 (sparse strong EH-property)
statement_text: A graph $H$ has the sparse strong EH-property if and only if $H$ is a forest.
context_text: A graph $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$; two disjoint vertex sets are anticomplete if there is no edge between them. A graph $H$ has the sparse strong EH-property if there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that every $H$-free graph $G$ with $|V(G)|\ge2$ either has a vertex with at least $\varepsilon|V(G)|$ neighbours, or contains two anticomplete sets of vertices, each of cardinality at least $\varepsilon|V(G)|$. Erdős's construction of graphs with large girth and large chromatic number shows that every graph with this property is a forest; the conjecture is the converse. The authors also conjecture that $H$ has the symmetric strong EH-property (every $G$ that is both $H$-free and $\overline{H}$-free with $|V(G)|\ge2$ has two disjoint sets of size at least $\varepsilon|V(G)|$ that are complete or anticomplete to each other) if and only if $H$ or $\overline{H}$ is a forest; by a theorem of Rödl the first conjecture implies the second. These properties are strengthenings related to the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture. The paper proves the sparse strong EH-property for every caterpillar subdivision (a tree with a path containing all vertices of degree at least three). The final version notes that since submission both conjectures have been proved, by Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour and Spirkl ('Trees and linear anticomplete pairs').
notes: The paper explicitly notes that since submission both conjectures in 1.5 have been proved in reference [4].
paper_title: Caterpillars in Erdős-Hajnal

name: AX_ternary_graphs_3_colorable
title: Open Problem: 3-colourability of ternary graphs
statement_text: It may be that all ternary graphs are 3-colourable.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A graph is ternary if no induced cycle has length a multiple of three; in particular ternary graphs are triangle-free. Kalai and Meshulam conjectured that ternary graphs have bounded chromatic number, which was proved by Bonamy, Charbit and Thomassé (every ternary graph is $c$-colourable for some absolute constant $c$); a much stronger result of Scott and Seymour says that for all $p,q\ge0$, graphs with bounded clique number and no induced cycle of length $p$ modulo $q$ have bounded chromatic number. The authors remark that it may be that all ternary graphs are 3-colourable, and that this remains open. If all cycles (not only induced ones) have length not divisible by three, Chen and Saito proved there is a vertex of degree at most two, so such graphs are 3-colourable. Král' asked whether every ternary graph with an edge has an edge whose deletion leaves a ternary graph, which would have implied 3-colourability, but Wrochna found a counterexample (a 5-cycle and a 10-cycle with each vertex of the 5-cycle joined to two opposite vertices of the 10-cycle, in order). The paper itself proves the other Kalai–Meshulam conjecture: in every ternary graph the numbers of stable sets of even and of odd cardinality differ by at most one.
notes: Stated as a parenthetical remark in the introduction ('it may be that all ternary graphs are 3-colourable, and this remains open'); no formal conjecture environment.
paper_title: Proof of the Kalai-Meshulam conjecture

name: AX_girth_5_planar_fractional_hub_colors
title: Informal conjecture on improved color ratio in Theorem 5
statement_text: The authors prove that for every triangle-free planar graph $G$ and every vertex $x\in V(G)$, $G$ has a set coloring by subsets of $\{1,\ldots,6\}$ in which every vertex gets at least two colors and $x$ gets three. It might be possible to improve the ratio of extra colors assigned to the vertex $x$ a bit; e.g., it could be true that for every triangle-free planar graph $G$ and every vertex $x$ there exists a set coloring by subsets of $\{1,\ldots,9\}$ such that all vertices get at least three colors and $x$ gets five.
context_text: A set coloring of a graph $G$ assigns to each vertex $v$ a set $\varphi(v)$ of colors so that adjacent vertices receive disjoint sets; $G$ is $(a:b)$-colorable if it has a set coloring by $b$-element subsets of $\{1,\ldots,a\}$, and the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is the infimum of $a/b$ over all $(a:b)$-colorings. By Grötzsch's theorem triangle-free planar graphs are $3$-colorable, and there are triangle-free planar graphs with fractional chromatic number arbitrarily close to $3$. The authors' result with one boosted vertex $x$ (subsets of $\{1,\ldots,6\}$, at least two colors everywhere, three on $x$) implies, by taking the union over all choices of $x$ of colorings with disjoint palettes, that every triangle-free planar graph on $n$ vertices is $(6n:2n+1)$-colorable, so $\chi_f(G)\le3-\frac{3}{2n+1}$; it is also the key step in showing that planar graphs of girth at least five and bounded maximum degree have fractional chromatic number bounded away from $3$. The ratio cannot be improved arbitrarily: if $G$ is the wheel with five spokes with each spoke subdivided once, $x$ is the centre of the wheel, and $\varphi$ is a set coloring by subsets of $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ in which every vertex has at least $k/3$ colors, then $|\varphi(x)|\le\frac{k}{3}+\frac{2k}{9}$.
notes: PDF source — doubly hedged language ('might be possible', 'could be true'); included because it specifies a concrete mathematical claim. The bound formula in the surrounding text may be garbled.
paper_title: Fractional coloring of planar graphs of girth five

name: AX_arithmetic_k_cycle_removal_optimal_exponent
title: Question 1.4
statement_text: What is the smallest possible exponent $C_{p,k}$ for which the following theorem is true: let $k\geq 3$, $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $\delta=\varepsilon^{C_{p,k}}$; then for any $X_1,\dots,X_k\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p^n$, at least one of the following holds: the number of $k$-cycles $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in X_1\times \dots\times X_k$ is at least $\delta N^{k-1}$, or we can delete less than $\varepsilon N$ elements from each of the sets $X_1,\dots,X_k$ so that afterwards no $k$-cycles remain?
context_text: Throughout, $p\geq 2$ is a fixed prime, $n$ is arbitrary and $N=|\mathbb{F}_p^n|=p^n$. Given sets $X_1,\dots,X_k\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$, a $k$-cycle is a $k$-tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in X_1\times\dots\times X_k$ with $x_1+\dots+x_k=0$. This is the arithmetic $k$-cycle removal lemma of Green (proved for all finite abelian groups with tower-type bounds); the question is about the best polynomial dependence of $\delta$ on $\varepsilon$ when the group is $\mathbb{F}_p^n$. For $k\geq 3$ let $0<c_{p,k}<1$ be defined by $\inf_{0<t<1}\frac{t^0+t^1+\dots+t^{p-1}}{t^{(p-1)/k}}=p^{1-c_{p,k}}$. For $k=3$, Fox and Lovász proved the statement with exponent $C_{p,3}=1+\frac{1}{c_{p,3}}=\Theta(\log p)$, and this exponent is optimal for $k=3$. The paper proves the statement for every $k\geq 3$ with exponent $C_{p,k}=(k-2)(C_{p,3}-1)+1=\frac{k-2}{c_{p,3}}+1$, and shows via constructions of $k$-colored sum-free sets that the smallest possible exponent must be at least $\frac{k-2}{c_{p,k}}+1$. The achieved exponent is within a factor of $O(\log p)$ from this lower bound (independently of $k$), but the exact optimum remains open.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled; the exponent expressions involve infimum definitions of constants $c_{p,k}$ and $c_{p,3}$ that appear clean in context.
paper_title: A polynomial bound for the arithmetic $k$-cycle removal lemma in vector spaces

name: AX_kt_immersion_free_clique_count
title: Conjecture on maximum cliques with no $K_t$-immersion
statement_text: The maximum number of cliques in a graph on $n \geq t-2$ vertices with no $K_t$-immersion is $2^{t-2}(n-t+3)$.
context_text: A weak $H$-immersion in $G$ is an injective map $\phi:V(H)\to V(G)$ together with pairwise edge-disjoint paths, one for each edge $uv$ of $H$, joining $\phi(u)$ and $\phi(v)$; it is strong if no internal vertex of these paths lies in $\phi(V(H))$, and if moreover the paths are internally vertex-disjoint it is an $H$-subdivision (topological minor). The number of cliques counts all complete subgraphs, including the empty one (as in the count below). The authors prove that for $t$ sufficiently large every $n$-vertex graph with no strong (hence no weak) $K_t$-immersion has at most $2^{t+\log_2^2t}n$ cliques, which is sharp up to a factor $2^{O(\log^2t)}$. The conjectured value comes from the following graph with no weak $K_t$-immersion: a clique $K$ on $t-2$ vertices plus $n-t+2$ further vertices each adjacent exactly to $K$; the outside vertices have degree less than $t-1$, while the $t$ branch vertices of a $K_t$-immersion need degree at least $t-1$, and the cliques are a subset of $K$ together with at most one outside vertex, giving $2^{t-2}(n-t+3)$ cliques. The conjecture is stated in prose for '$K_t$-immersion' without specifying weak or strong. For comparison, the maximum number of cliques is $3^{2t/3+o(t)}n$ for $K_t$-minor-free graphs.
notes: PDF source — stated in running prose in the introduction without a labeled conjecture environment; math notation garbled in extraction and reconstructed.
paper_title: On the number of cliques in graphs with a forbidden subdivision or immersion

name: AX_kt_subdivision_free_clique_count_exponent
title: Conjecture on optimal exponential constant for $K_t$-subdivision clique count
statement_text: The maximum number of cliques in an $n$-vertex graph with no $K_t$-subdivision is $3^{2t/3+o(t)}n$, i.e., the optimal exponential constant in the exponent is $\frac{2}{3}\log_2 3 \approx 1.06$.
context_text: A weak $H$-immersion in $G$ is an injective map $\phi:V(H)\to V(G)$ together with pairwise edge-disjoint paths, one for each edge $uv$ of $H$, joining $\phi(u)$ and $\phi(v)$; it is strong if no internal vertex of these paths lies in $\phi(V(H))$, and if moreover the paths are internally vertex-disjoint it is an $H$-subdivision (topological minor). The number of cliques counts all complete subgraphs, including the empty one (as in the count below). Norine, Seymour, Thomas and Wollan, and independently Reed and Wood, showed that $n$-vertex $K_t$-minor-free graphs have at most $c(t)n$ cliques; Lee and Oum proved $c(t)<c^t$ for an absolute constant $c$ (also for subdivisions), and the authors proved earlier that $c(t)=3^{2t/3+o(t)}$ for minors. Here they prove that every $n$-vertex graph with no $K_t$-subdivision has at most $2^{1.817t+o(t)}n$ cliques. Wood's lower-bound construction for minors also has no $K_t$-subdivision, so the constant $1.817$ cannot be improved below $\frac23\log_23\approx1.06$; the conjecture is that this constant is best possible, as for minors. Note that $n$-vertex graphs with no $K_t$-subdivision have $O(t^2n)$ edges (Komlós–Szemerédi, Bollobás–Thomason).
notes: PDF source — stated in both the abstract and the introduction in running prose without a labeled conjecture environment; math notation garbled in extraction and reconstructed. The conjecture is presented consistently in two places.
paper_title: On the number of cliques in graphs with a forbidden subdivision or immersion

name: AX_large_fractional_chromatic_high_girth_subgraph
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: For every real number $x \geq 1$ and any integer $g \geq 3$, there exists a positive number $k(x,g)$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi_f(G) \geq k(x,g)$ contains a subgraph $H$ of girth at least $g$ and with $\chi_f(H) \geq x$.
context_text: The fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is the minimum of $\sum_I y_I$ over nonnegative weights $y_I$ on the independent sets $I$ of $G$ such that, for every vertex $v$, the independent sets containing $v$ have total weight at least $1$. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (1969) states that for all $k,g$ every graph of sufficiently large chromatic number contains a subgraph of chromatic number at least $k$ and girth at least $g$; Rödl proved the case $g=4$ (triangle-free subgraphs), the only nontrivial case known. Erdős showed that graphs of large girth and large fractional chromatic number exist. The authors prove the fractional analogue of Rödl's theorem: for every real $x\ge1$ there is $k(x)$ such that every graph with $\chi_f(G)\ge k(x)$ contains a triangle-free subgraph $H$ with $\chi_f(H)\ge x$. The conjecture is the fractional version of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for every girth (the case $g=4$ being their theorem). They also show that the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture holds for Kneser graphs, natural examples of graphs with large chromatic number but bounded fractional chromatic number.
notes: PDF source — math appears readable.
paper_title: Triangle-free subgraphs with large fractional chromatic number

name: AX_large_chromatic_high_girth_dense_subgraph
title: Conjecture 6
statement_text: For every positive integers $k$ and $g \geq 3$, there exists a positive number $c(k,g)$ such that every graph with chromatic number at least $c(k,g)$ contains a subgraph of girth at least $g$ and with average degree at least $k$.
context_text: Two conjectures are weakened here. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (1969): for all positive integers $k,g$ there is $h(k,g)$ such that every graph with $\chi(G)\ge h(k,g)$ contains a subgraph with chromatic number at least $k$ and girth at least $g$ (proved by Rödl for $g=4$). Thomassen's conjecture (1983): for all positive integers $k$ and $g\ge3$ there is $d(k,g)$ such that every graph with average degree at least $d(k,g)$ contains a subgraph of girth at least $g$ and average degree at least $k$; Kühn and Osthus proved it for $g\le6$, and it is known under the additional assumption that the maximum degree is not too large compared with the average degree. The proposed conjecture is implied by each of them, since every graph of chromatic number at least $d+1$ has a subgraph of minimum degree at least $d$: its hypothesis is chromatic number (stronger than average degree, as in Thomassen's) and its conclusion is only large average degree (weaker than large chromatic number, as in Erdős–Hajnal's) for the high-girth subgraph.
notes: PDF source — math appears readable.
paper_title: Triangle-free subgraphs with large fractional chromatic number

name: AX_clustered_chromatic_minor_closed_treedepth_bound
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: For every graph $H$, $\chi_\star(\mathcal{M}_H) \leq 2\,\mathrm{ctd}(H) - 2$.
context_text: Graphs are simple and finite. A graph is $k$-colourable with clustering $c$ if its vertices can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every monochromatic component (connected component of the subgraph induced by one colour class) has at most $c$ vertices; the clustered chromatic number $\chi_\star(\mathcal{G})$ of a class $\mathcal{G}$ is the minimum $k$ such that, for some integer $c$, every graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is $k$-colourable with clustering $c$. $\mathcal{M}_H$ is the class of $H$-minor-free graphs. For a rooted tree $T$, its depth is the maximum number of vertices on a root-to-leaf path and its closure is obtained by adding an edge between every ancestor and descendant; the connected tree-depth $\mathrm{ctd}(H)$ is the minimum depth of a rooted tree whose closure contains $H$ as a subgraph. The usual tree-depth $\mathrm{td}(H)$ is the maximum of $\mathrm{ctd}$ over the components of $H$; $\mathrm{ctd}(H)=\mathrm{td}(H)$ unless $H$ has two components of tree-depth $\mathrm{td}(H)$, in which case $\mathrm{ctd}(H)=\mathrm{td}(H)+1$. The authors prove $\mathrm{ctd}(H)-1\le\chi_\star(\mathcal{M}_H)\le 2^{\mathrm{ctd}(H)+1}-4$ for every graph $H$, and construct for each $k\ge2$ a graph $H_k$ with $\mathrm{ctd}(H_k)=\mathrm{td}(H_k)=k$ and $\chi_\star(\mathcal{M}_{H_k})\ge 2k-2$. This contrasts with defective colouring (each colour class inducing bounded maximum degree), for which Ossona de Mendez, Oum and Wood conjectured that the defective chromatic number of $\mathcal{M}_H$ equals $\mathrm{ctd}(H)-1$. The authors conjecture that the lower bound $2k-2$ is tight, and prove the conjecture when $\mathrm{ctd}(H)=3$ (four colours suffice, which is best possible). They also propose a more general conjecture for the clustered chromatic number of an arbitrary minor-closed class, which generalises this one.

paper_title: Clustered Colouring in Minor-Closed Classes

name: AX_erdos_posa_planar_minor_k_log_k
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: For every planar graph $H$, the Erdős-Pósa property holds for $H$-models with a $O(k \log k)$ bounding function.
context_text: An $H$-model in $G$ is a collection $\{S_x: x\in V(H)\}$ of vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of $G$ such that $S_x$ and $S_y$ are joined by an edge of $G$ whenever $xy\in E(H)$ (so $G$ has an $H$-model iff $H$ is a minor of $G$). Let $\nu_H(G)$ be the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint $H$-models in $G$ and $\tau_H(G)$ the minimum size of a set $X$ with $G-X$ having no $H$-model. The Erdős–Pósa property holds for $H$-models with bounding function $f$ if $\tau_H(G)\le f(\nu_H(G))$ for every graph $G$; Robertson and Seymour proved it holds for some $f$ if and only if $H$ is planar. Chekuri and Chuzhoy showed there are integers $a,b,c$ such that for every planar $H$ on $h$ vertices one can take $f(k)=ah^b\,k\log^c(k+1)$ ($c$ apparently a double-digit integer), derived from their result that there are $a',b',c'$ such that every graph of treewidth at least $a'r^{b'}k\log^{c'}(k+1)$ has $k$ vertex-disjoint subgraphs of treewidth at least $r$; this approach loses a $\log k$ factor ($c=c'+1$), and $c'\ge1$ is necessary, so it always gives $c\ge2$. For planar $H$ containing a cycle there is an $\Omega(k\log k)$ lower bound (from Erdős and Pósa's triangle case, or from graphs of linear treewidth and logarithmic girth), and for forests $H$ the right order is $O(k)$, so the conjecture would settle the growth rate for all planar $H$. It was known for cycles (Fiorini and Herinckx; Erdős–Pósa for triangles) and for multigraphs consisting of two vertices joined by parallel edges. The paper proves it for all wheels $W_t$ ($t\ge3$, a cycle of length $t$ plus a vertex adjacent to all its vertices), which also covers all minors of wheels, since an $O(k\log k)$ bounding function is preserved under taking minors of $H$.
paper_title: A tight Erdős-Pósa function for wheel minors

name: AX_erdos_posa_treewidth_packing_k_log_k
title: Conjecture 1.4
statement_text: There is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for all integers $r, k \geq 1$, every graph $G$ of treewidth at least $f(r) \cdot k \log(k + 1)$ has $k$ vertex-disjoint subgraphs $G_1, \ldots, G_k$, each of treewidth at least $r$.

u_H(G)<k$, deleting $O(k\log k)$ vertices leaves a graph of treewidth bounded by a function of $r$ (Grid Theorem), so $G$ has treewidth $O(k\log k)$.

name: AX_pt_free_3_coloring_polynomial_all_t
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Is it true that for every (fixed) integer $t > 0$, the 3-coloring problem can be solved in polynomial time when restricted to the class of $P_t$-free graphs?
context_text: $P_t$ denotes the path on $t$ vertices, and a graph $G$ is $H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to $H$; polynomial time means polynomial in $|V(G)|$ for the input graph $G$. The $k$-coloring problem asks whether the input graph admits a proper coloring with $k$ colors. A known result from the literature states that if, for some fixed $k>2$, the $k$-coloring problem is polynomial-time solvable on $H$-free graphs, then every connected component of $H$ is a path. For $k=3$ the converse may hold (it is known to fail for $k>4$), and this question asks exactly that for $H=P_t$, since every graph whose components are paths is an induced subgraph of a long path. Known positive results include polynomial-time list-3-coloring of $P_7$-free graphs, of $(P_5+P_2)$-free and $(P_4+P_3)$-free graphs, and a subexponential algorithm for $P_t$-free graphs. The present paper shows that list-3-coloring (hence 3-coloring) is polynomial for $(P_6+rP_3)$-free graphs, where $P_6+rP_3$ is the disjoint union of a $P_6$ and $r$ copies of $P_3$, and that $k$-coloring of $(P_5+P_2)$-free graphs is NP-hard for $k\ge5$.
notes: The question has no explicit attribution citation in the header; it is recorded as a standing open problem in the field by the paper's authors. Full paper text was truncated in the supplied PDF extraction, so later sections could not be checked for additional conjectural statements.
paper_title: List-three-coloring graphs with no induced $P_6+rP_3$

name: AX_algebraic_connectivity_graph_complement_supremum
title: Closing Question
statement_text: What is the supremum of all real numbers $c$ such that for any graph $G$ of order at least $2$, $$\max\{\lambda_2(G), \lambda_2(\bar{G})\} \geq c\,?$$
context_text: For a graph $G$ of order $n$, the Laplacian is $L(G)=D(G)-A(G)$, with $D(G)$ the diagonal matrix of degrees and $A(G)$ the adjacency matrix; its eigenvalues are $0=\lambda_1(G)\le\lambda_2(G)\le\dots\le\lambda_n(G)$, and $\lambda_2(G)$ is the algebraic connectivity of $G$ (positive if and only if $G$ is connected). $\bar G$ denotes the complement of $G$; since the Laplacian eigenvalues of $\bar G$ are $0$ and $n-\lambda_i(G)$ for $i\ge2$, one has $\lambda_2(\bar G)=n-\lambda_n(G)$. The Laplacian spread conjecture states that $\lambda_n(G)-\lambda_2(G)\le n-1$, equivalently $\lambda_2(G)+\lambda_2(\bar G)\ge1$ for every graph of order $n\ge2$; it was known for trees, unicyclic, bicyclic, tricyclic, cactus and quasi-tree graphs, graphs of diameter other than 3, and bipartite and triangle-free graphs. The authors give the first positive constant lower bound, proving $\max\{\lambda_2(G),\lambda_2(\bar G)\}\ge\frac25$ by a routing (weighted congestion) argument, and ask for the best constant. The self-complementary path $P_4$ has $\lambda_2(P_4)=2-\sqrt2<0.5858$, so the supremum lies between $\frac25$ and $2-\sqrt2$.
paper_title: The Algebraic Connectivity of a Graph and its Complement

name: AX_list_decodable_zero_rate_codes_asymptotics
title: Informal Conjecture on exact asymptotics of maxcode_L for even L
statement_text: We believe that in fact $\mathrm{maxcode}_L(\varepsilon) = c_L \varepsilon^{-1} + O(1)$ for even $L$.
context_text: A binary code $C\subset\{0,1\}^n$ is $<L$-list-decodable with radius $\tau$ if for every word $w\in\{0,1\}^n$ there are fewer than $L$ codewords within Hamming distance $\tau n$ from $w$ (equivalently, no point of the hypercube is covered by $L$ or more of the Hamming balls of relative radius $\tau$ centred at the codewords). Let $\tau_L=\frac{1}{2}-\binom{2k}{k}/2^{2k+1}$ if $L=2k$ or $L=2k+1$. By Blinovsky, for radius below $\tau_L$ the largest such code is exponentially large in $n$, while for radius above $\tau_L$ its size is bounded independently of $n$. For $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathrm{maxcode}_L(\varepsilon)$ is the maximum size $|C|$ of a $<L$-list-decodable code $C\subset\{0,1\}^n$ of radius $\tau_L+\varepsilon$, the maximum being over all block lengths $n$. For $L=2$ (unique decoding) Levenshtein's construction shows $\mathrm{maxcode}_2(\varepsilon)=\frac{1}{4\varepsilon}+O(1)$. The authors prove, for every $L\ge 2$, that $\mathrm{maxcode}_L(\varepsilon)\ge c_L\varepsilon^{-1}+O(1)$ where $c_L=2^{-L}\lfloor L/2\rfloor\binom{L-1}{\lfloor L/2\rfloor}$, and that $\mathrm{maxcode}_L(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ when $L$ is even; the conjecture says the lower bound is tight up to an additive constant for even $L$. For odd $L$ the behaviour differs: they prove $\mathrm{maxcode}_3(\varepsilon)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-3/2})$, refuting a claimed $O(1/\varepsilon)$ bound of Blinovsky.

name: AX_triangle_free_digraph_domination_polynomial_alpha
title: Conjecture 3.5
statement_text: There is an integer $\ell$ such that if $G$ is a directed-triangle-free digraph with $\alpha(G) = \alpha$, then $\gamma(G) \leq \alpha^{\ell}$.
context_text: All digraphs here are finite, loopless and simple in the sense that between any two vertices there is at most one arc (so no 2-cycles). The independence number $\alpha(G)$ of a digraph $G$ is the independence number of its underlying undirected graph. A vertex dominates itself and all its out-neighbours; a set $S$ of vertices is dominating if every vertex is in $S$ or is an out-neighbour of some vertex of $S$, and the domination number $\gamma(G)$ is the minimum size of a dominating set. A digraph is directed-triangle-free if it contains no directed (cyclically oriented) triangle. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(G)$ is the minimum number of colours in a colouring of the vertices in which every colour class induces an acyclic digraph. The authors prove that every digraph on $n$ vertices has $\gamma(G)\le\alpha(G)\log n$ (and fractional domination number at most $2\alpha(G)$), but $\gamma$ cannot in general be bounded by a function of $\alpha$ alone (random tournaments have domination number of order $\log n$). For directed-triangle-free digraphs it can: the domination number is at most $\alpha(G)\cdot\alpha(G)!$, and at most $3$ when $\alpha(G)=2$. The same authors previously conjectured that the dichromatic number of a directed-triangle-free digraph is bounded by a polynomial in $\alpha(G)$; since every acyclic digraph has a kernel (an independent dominating set), $\gamma(G)\le\alpha(G)\cdot\vec{\chi}(G)$ for every digraph, so that conjecture would imply this one. A disjoint union of cyclically oriented pentagons shows that one cannot do better than $\gamma(G)\le\frac{3}{2}\alpha(G)$ in general.
notes: The hypothesis uses $\alpha(D) = \alpha$ in the PDF source, but the digraph is consistently called $G$ throughout the paper; this appears to be a typo for $\alpha(G) = \alpha$.
paper_title: Domination and fractional domination in digraphs

name: AX_cop_number_planar_classification
title: Classification of planar graphs by cop number
statement_text: Classify which planar graphs have cop number $i$, for $1 \leq i \leq 3$.
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. Aigner and Fromme proved that every planar graph has cop number at most 3 (using the fact that one cop can guard an isometric path), so every connected planar graph has cop number 1, 2 or 3; the Petersen graph is 3-cop-win and it is conjectured (Baird et al.) that the smallest 3-cop-win planar graph is the dodecahedron, on 20 vertices. Cop-win graphs are precisely the dismantlable graphs (Nowakowski–Winkler, Quilliot), i.e. those whose vertices can be deleted one at a time so that each deleted vertex $u$ has a neighbour $v$ in the remaining graph with $N[u]\subseteq N[v]$; this characterization may eventually help to classify planar cop-win graphs, but the classification of planar graphs with cop number $i$, for $1\le i\le3$, remains open.
notes: PDF source; stated as open in survey prose
paper_title: Topological directions in Cops and Robbers

name: AX_cop_number_outerplanar_classification
title: Classification of outerplanar graphs by cop number
statement_text: Classify which outerplanar graphs are $1$-cop-win and which are $2$-cop-win.
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. A graph is outerplanar if it can be embedded in the plane with all vertices on the outer face, equivalently if it has no $K_4$ or $K_{2,3}$ minor. Clarke proved that every outerplanar graph has cop number at most 2 (in the 2-connected case the outer face is a Hamilton cycle along which two cops successively enlarge their territory). Cop-win graphs are exactly the dismantlable graphs (vertices can be deleted one at a time, each deleted vertex $u$ having a remaining neighbour $v$ with $N[u]\subseteq N[v]$), but no specific classification of the outerplanar graphs with cop number 1 versus 2 is known; the smallest outerplanar graph with cop number 2 is the 4-cycle.

name: AX_capture_time_planar_linear_tightness
title: Tightness of linear capture time bound for planar graphs
statement_text: Is the bound $\mathrm{capt}_3(G) \leq 2n$ tight for planar graphs of order $n$? Does there exist a planar graph $G$ of order $n$ with $\mathrm{capt}(G) > n$?
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. For $k\ge c(G)$, the $k$-capture time $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)$ is the number of rounds (not counting the initial placement) of an optimal play with $k$ cops, i.e. the minimum over cop strategies of the maximum over robber strategies of the length of the game, and $\mathrm{capt}(G)=\mathrm{capt}_{c(G)}(G)$ is the capture time. Every planar graph has cop number at most 3 (Aigner and Fromme). For planar graphs of order $n$, it was first shown that $\mathrm{capt}_3(G)\le(\mathrm{diam}(G)+1)n=O(n^2)$, improving the general bound $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)\le n^{c(G)+1}$ for $k\ge c(G)$, and then the linear bound $\mathrm{capt}_3(G)\le2n$. For cop-win graphs of order $n\ge7$, $\mathrm{capt}(G)\le n-4$, which is attained by planar examples, while in general there are graphs with cop number $k$ and $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)=\Theta(n^{c(G)+1})$ (Kinnersley; Brandt et al.). It is unknown whether the linear bound is tight, and even an example of a planar graph with $\mathrm{capt}(G)>n$ is open at the time of the survey; the survey also asks for tight bounds on the capture time of planar graphs with cop number 2 and 3.
notes: PDF source
paper_title: Topological directions in Cops and Robbers

name: AX_capture_time_higher_genus_bounds
title: Capture time bounds for higher genus graphs
statement_text: What are good bounds on the capture time of graphs of higher genus? (If Schroeder's conjecture holds and $\gamma(G) = g$, then one would have $\mathrm{capt}_k(G) = O(n^{g+4})$ for every $k \geq g+3$.)
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers on a (connected) graph $G$, a set of cops and then a robber choose initial vertices; in each round every cop moves to a neighbouring vertex or stays, and then the robber does the same, with perfect information; the cops win if one of them eventually occupies the robber's vertex (capture). The cop number $c(G)$ is the minimum number of cops that guarantees capture; $G$ is $k$-cop-win if $c(G)=k$, and cop-win if $c(G)=1$. For $k\ge c(G)$, the $k$-capture time $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)$ is the number of rounds (not counting the initial placement) of an optimal play with $k$ cops, i.e. the minimum over cop strategies of the maximum over robber strategies of the length of the game, and $\mathrm{capt}(G)=\mathrm{capt}_{c(G)}(G)$ is the capture time. The genus $\gamma(G)$ of $G$ is the minimum genus of an orientable surface on which $G$ embeds, and $n$ is the number of vertices. Schroeder's conjecture states that a graph of genus $g$ has cop number at most $g+3$; it holds for planar and toroidal graphs, and known general bounds are $c(G)\le\lfloor3g/2\rfloor+3$ (Schroeder) and $c(G)\le\lfloor4g/3\rfloor+D$ (Bowler, Erde, Lehner, Pitz). Since $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)\le n^{c(G)+1}$ whenever $k\ge c(G)$ (Berarducci and Intrigila), Schroeder's conjecture would immediately give $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)=O(n^{g+4})$ for every $k\ge g+3$. For planar graphs it is known that $\mathrm{capt}_3(G)\le2n$, and for many cops ($k\ge(19+66\sqrt g)\sqrt n$) one has $\mathrm{capt}_k(G)\le6r(G)\log n$, where $r(G)$ is the radius. The survey raises the examination of capture-time bounds for higher genus graphs as an interesting open question.

paper_title: Topological directions in Cops and Robbers

name: AX_c_closed_graphs_maximal_cliques_exponent
title: Open Problem (exact exponent for maximal cliques in c-closed graphs)
statement_text: For a fixed positive integer $c$, determine the exact exponent of $n$ (between $3/2$ and $2 - 2^{1-c}$) in the expression for the maximum number of maximal cliques in a $c$-closed graph on $n$ vertices.
context_text: For a positive integer $c$, a graph is $c$-closed if any two distinct vertices with at least $c$ common neighbours are adjacent. This models triadic closure in social networks: $1$-closed graphs are disjoint unions of cliques, $c=n-1$ allows all graphs, and $2$-closed graphs are exactly the graphs with no induced $C_4$ or diamond ($K_4$ minus an edge), e.g. graphs of girth at least $5$. A maximal clique is a clique not contained in a larger one. The authors prove that every $c$-closed $n$-vertex graph has at most $\min\{3^{(c-1)/3}n^2,\,4^{(c+4)(c-1)/2}n^{2-2^{1-c}}\}$ maximal cliques, so for constant $c$ the number is $O(n^{2-2^{1-c}})$ (e.g. $O(n^{3/2})$, $O(n^{7/4})$, $O(n^{15/8})$ for $c=2,3,4$), and conversely construct, for every $c$, $c$-closed graphs with $\Omega(c^{-3/2}2^{c/2}n^{3/2})$ maximal cliques (from girth-$5$ graphs). For $c=2$ the answer $\Theta(n^{3/2})$ was known (Eschen, Hoàng, Spinrad and Sritharan, via projective planes), so the question concerns $c\ge3$. The authors also show that $c$-closed $K_k$-free graphs attaining the upper bound would need a specific distribution of clique sizes: such graphs have $O(n^{3/2})$ edges and $n_{j+1}(G)=O(n_j(G)^{1/2}n)$, where $n_j(G)$ is the number of $K_j$'s.

paper_title: Finding Cliques in Social Networks: A New Distribution-Free Model

name: AX_erdos_ginzburg_ziv_constant_fixed_k
title: Open Question on s((Z/kZ)^n) for fixed k
statement_text: It remains an interesting question to estimate $s((\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})^n)$ when $k$ is fixed and $n$ is large.
context_text: For a finite abelian group $G$ with exponent $\exp(G)$, the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant $s(G)$ is the smallest integer $s$ such that every sequence of $s$ (not necessarily distinct) elements of $G$ has a subsequence of length $\exp(G)$ summing to zero; Erdős, Ginzburg and Ziv proved $s(\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})=2k-1$. Geometrically, $s((\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})^n)$ is the least $s$ such that among any $s$ points of the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^n$ one can choose $k$ whose centroid is a lattice point. Harborth proved $(k-1)2^n+1\le s((\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})^n)\le(k-1)k^n+1$, with equality on the left for $k$ a power of 2; Reiher proved $s((\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})^2)=4k-3$; Alon and Dubiner proved $s((\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})^n)\le(cn\log n)^nk$ for an absolute constant $c$, so for fixed $n$ it grows linearly in $k$. Elsholtz obtained $s((\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})^n)\ge1.125^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}(k-1)2^n+1$ for odd $k\ge3$, in particular $\ge2.08^n$ for large $n$. Writing $r_3(\mathbb{F}_p^n)$ for the largest size of a subset of $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ with no three-term arithmetic progression, the authors prove $s((\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z})^n)<3k(r_3(\mathbb{F}_{p_1}^n)+\dots+r_3(\mathbb{F}_{p_m}^n))$ where $p_1,\dots,p_m$ are the prime factors of $k$ (and $s(\mathbb{F}_p^n)\le2p\,r_3(\mathbb{F}_p^n)$); with the Ellenberg–Gijswijt bound $r_3(\mathbb{F}_p^n)\le(J(p)p)^n$, $0.8414\le J(p)\le0.9184$, this gives exponential upper bounds, but since $r_3(\mathbb{F}_p^n)\ge(p/2)^{(1-o(1))n}$ a large gap remains for odd $k\ge3$ and large $n$. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
notes: Stated as a general open problem in the field with no labeled environment; no specific attribution to prior work given.
paper_title: Erdős-Ginzburg-Ziv constants by avoiding three-term arithmetic progressions

name: AX_ramsey_nice_forest_families_eventually
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Is it true that for any finite family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ that contains at least one forest, there exists a constant $k_0 = k_0(\mathcal{F})$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ is $k$-nice for all $k \geq k_0$?
context_text: For a finite family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs and an integer $k\ge1$, $R_k(\mathcal{F})$ is the smallest $n$ such that every $k$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy (as a subgraph, not necessarily induced) of some member of $\mathcal{F}$; $\mathcal{F}$ is $k$-nice (Ramsey-nice) if, for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G)=R_k(\mathcal{F})$ and every $k$-colouring of $E(G)$, there is a monochromatic copy of some $F\in\mathcal{F}$. This extends the question of Bialostocki and Gyárfás for tuples $(H_1,\dots,H_k)$; note that colours are not associated with specific members of $\mathcal{F}$ and $k$ is independent of $|\mathcal{F}|$. If no member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a forest, then by Erdős' graphs of large chromatic number and large girth, $\mathcal{F}$ is not $k$-nice for any $k$. The question asks whether containing a forest is also sufficient, for all large $k$. The answer is easily yes for families containing a graph with at most $2$ edges. With $K_3$, $P_4$ (path on four vertices) and $S_3$ (star with three edges) the connected graphs with three edges, the authors show that $\{K_3,P_4\}$ is $k$-nice for every $k$, $\{K_3,S_3\}$ for every $k\ge2$ but not $k=1$, $\{P_4,S_3\}$ for all $k$ in an explicit set containing all large $k$ not congruent to $0$ modulo $3$ and all $k\equiv0\pmod 3$ except $3,6,18,21,24,30,33,39,42,51,66$; Garrison showed $\{P_4\}$ is $k$-nice for all $k\ne3$ and every star is $k$-nice for all $k$.
paper_title: Ramsey-nice families of graphs

name: AX_ramsey_nice_forest_families_infinitely_often
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: Any finite family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ that contains at least one forest is $k$-nice for infinitely many integers $k$.
context_text: For a finite family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs and an integer $k\ge1$, $R_k(\mathcal{F})$ is the smallest $n$ such that every $k$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy (as a subgraph, not necessarily induced) of some member of $\mathcal{F}$; $\mathcal{F}$ is $k$-nice (Ramsey-nice) if, for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G)=R_k(\mathcal{F})$ and every $k$-colouring of $E(G)$, there is a monochromatic copy of some $F\in\mathcal{F}$. This extends the question of Bialostocki and Gyárfás for tuples $(H_1,\dots,H_k)$; note that colours are not associated with specific members of $\mathcal{F}$ and $k$ is independent of $|\mathcal{F}|$. If no member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a forest, then by Erdős' graphs of large chromatic number and large girth, $\mathcal{F}$ is not $k$-nice for any $k$. The authors ask whether every finite family containing a forest is $k$-nice for all sufficiently large $k$, and propose this weaker conjecture. With $K_3$ the triangle, $P_4$ the path on four vertices and $S_3=K_{1,3}$ the star with three edges, they prove that $\{K_3,P_4,S_3\}$ is $k$-nice for infinitely many $k$, and that for every $r\ge1$, every family consisting of $K_{1,r+1}$ together with graphs that each contain a cycle (with no bound on the number or size of the members) is $k$-nice for infinitely many $k$.

name: AX_permutation_property_testing_query_bounds
title: Open Problem (better query complexity bounds for property testing)
statement_text: It remains a major open problem if better bounds on the query complexity hold for the various general property testing results (which show that natural properties of combinatorial objects can be tested with query complexity depending only on $\epsilon$ and the property, but with enormous or no explicit bounds).
context_text: In property testing one wants to distinguish quickly (with few queries to the object) objects satisfying a property $P$ from objects that are $\epsilon$-far from satisfying it. $P$ is one-sided testable if there are $q(\epsilon)$ and a randomized algorithm making $q(\epsilon)$ queries that always accepts inputs with $P$ and rejects with probability at least $2/3$ inputs that are $\epsilon$-far from $P$; it is two-sided testable if it answers correctly in both cases with probability at least $2/3$. General results give constant (size-independent) query complexity, but with huge bounds: for instance, Alon and Shapira's theorem that every hereditary graph property is one-sided testable gives a bound at least of wowzer type in $1/\epsilon$ (one level above the tower function in the Ackermann hierarchy), because it uses the strong regularity lemma; other results use compactness and give no bound at all, and testing $\sigma$-freeness of permutations with respect to Kendall's tau distance (Klimošová and Kráľ) gives an Ackermann-type bound. For permutations, the rectangular (cut) distance between $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of length $n$ is $\frac1n\max_{S,T}\big||\pi_1(S)\cap T|-|\pi_2(S)\cap T|\big|$ over intervals $S,T\subseteq[n]$, and a permutation property is hereditary if closed under taking subpermutations (patterns). The paper makes progress on this problem for permutations: there is a universal polynomial-in-$1/\epsilon$ query complexity bound (not depending on the property) for two-sided testing of hereditary properties of sufficiently large permutations with respect to the rectangular distance, and a nearly linear bound for a related metric depending on the smallest forbidden subpermutation. This is a general community-level problem rather than a precise conjecture.

name: AX_euclidean_ramsey_l3_vs_lm
title: Open problem: $E^n \not\to (\ell_3, \ell_m)$ for large $m$
statement_text: For every natural number $m$, does there exist a natural number $n$ such that $\mathbb{E}^n \to (\ell_3, \ell_m)$?
context_text:
$\mathbb{E}^n$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean distance, $\ell_m$ is a sequence of $m$ points on a line with consecutive points at distance one (so $\ell_2$ is a pair of points at distance one), and a copy of a set always means an isometric copy. For sets $X,K$, $\mathbb{E}^n	o(X,K)$ means that every red/blue-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ contains a red copy of $X$ or a blue copy of $K$, and $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(X,K)$ means that some red/blue-coloring contains neither. A set is $t$-separated if any two of its points are at distance at least $t$; logarithms are base 2. A finite set $X$ is Ramsey if for every $r$ there is $n$ such that every $r$-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $X$. The authors show that for every Ramsey set $X$ and finite $K$ there is $n$ with $\mathbb{E}^n	o(X,K)$, and conversely (assuming the axiom of choice) if a finite $X$ is not Ramsey then there is a finite set $K$ with $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(X,K)$ for all $n$. Being more particular about the choice of $K$, they were unable to decide this question for $X=\ell_3$ and $K=\ell_m$. They think it unlikely to hold for large $m$ (i.e. they suspect that for large $m$ one has $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(\ell_3,\ell_m)$ for all $n$) but could not exhibit a coloring confirming this. A first step was made by Erdős et al., who showed that $\mathbb{E}^n
ot	o(\ell_6,\ell_6)$ for all $n$.

name: AX_euclidean_ramsey_diameter_free_bound
title: Open problem: removing diameter dependence from Theorem 1.1
statement_text: The authors prove that if $R>2$ and $K\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ is a $1$-separated set of diameter at most $R-1$ with $|K|>10^{4n}\log R$, then $\mathbb{E}^n\not\to(\ell_2,K)$. Can the dependence on the diameter $R$ be removed from this result? That is, does there exist a function $f(n)$, independent of the diameter of $K$, such that $\mathbb{E}^n \not\to (\ell_2, K)$ for every $1$-separated set $K \subset \mathbb{E}^n$ with $|K| > f(n)$?
context_text: $\mathbb{E}^n$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean distance, $\ell_m$ is a sequence of $m$ points on a line with consecutive points at distance one (so $\ell_2$ is a pair of points at distance one), and a copy of a set always means an isometric copy. For sets $X,K$, $\mathbb{E}^n\to(X,K)$ means that every red/blue-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ contains a red copy of $X$ or a blue copy of $K$, and $\mathbb{E}^n\not\to(X,K)$ means that some red/blue-coloring contains neither. A set is $t$-separated if any two of its points are at distance at least $t$; logarithms are base 2. Erdős et al. asked whether for every $n$ there is $m=m(n)$ such that for every set $K\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ of size $m$ there is a two-coloring of $\mathbb{E}^n$ with no monochromatic copy of $K$. Rescaling so that the smallest distance in $K$ is one, $K$ contains a copy of $\ell_2$ and is $1$-separated, so the authors' theorem (with its dependence on the diameter) gives a partial answer, and removing the dependence on $R$ would answer that question completely; the authors also find the problem interesting in its own right. The exponential dependence on $n$ is necessary, since $\mathbb{E}^n\to(\ell_2,K)$ for every $K$ of size at most $2^{c'n}$.
