name: AX_rodl_theorem_polynomial_delta_dependence
title: Polynomial dependence of $\delta$ on $d$ in Rödl's theorem
statement_text: A polynomial dependence of $\delta$ on $d$ holds in Rödl's theorem (for every graph $H$ and all $d>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that for every $H$-free graph $G$ there exists $X\subseteq V(G)$ with $|X|\ge\delta|V(G)|$ such that in one of $G[X]$, $\overline{G}[X]$ every vertex of $X$ has degree at most $d|X|$), i.e., the $\delta$ satisfying Rödl's theorem can be taken to be polynomial in $d$; and this would imply the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture itself.
context_text: Here $H$-free means with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, $\alpha(G)$ and $\omega(G)$ are the stability and clique numbers, $\overline{G}$ is the complement of $G$, and logarithms are base $2$. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asserts that for every graph $H$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that every $H$-free graph $G$ satisfies $\max(\alpha(G),\omega(G))\ge|V(G)|^\varepsilon$; the best general bound, due to Erdős and Hajnal, is $2^{c\sqrt{\log n}}$. From $d,\delta$ satisfying Rödl's theorem one gets, by Turán's theorem, a stable set or clique of size about $\min(\frac{1}{2d},\frac{\delta n}{2})$, so better bounds in Rödl's theorem give better Erdős–Hajnal-type bounds. Rödl's original proof uses the regularity lemma and gives a tower-type bound on $1/\delta$; Fox and Sudakov proved $\delta=2^{-15|V(H)|(\log(1/d))^2}$, which implies the Erdős–Hajnal bound $2^{c\sqrt{\log n}}$. The statement that a polynomial dependence holds (presumably $\delta=d^{C}$ for some constant $C$ depending on $H$) is presented as a known conjecture without attribution. For $H=C_5$ the authors indicate that one can take $\delta=2^{-O((\log(1/d))^2/\log\log(1/d))}$, giving another route to their main result $\max(\alpha(G),\omega(G))\ge2^{c\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}}$ for $C_5$-free graphs.
notes: Stated in passive voice ('It is conjectured that…') without a specific citation; appears to be a community/folklore conjecture presented without explicit attribution. For $H = C_5$ the authors note one can achieve the intermediate bound $\delta = 2^{-O((\log(1/d))^2 / \log\log(1/d))}$.
paper_title: Towards Erdos-Hajnal for graphs with no 5-hole

name: AX_list_chromatic_fraction_delta_small_clique
title: Question 1.5
statement_text: Does there exist a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, for every $c > 1$ and every graph $G$ of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ with no clique of size greater than $\Delta^{1/f(c)}$, we have $\chi_\ell(G) \leq \Delta/c$?
context_text: A list-assignment $L$ gives each vertex $v$ a set $L(v)$ of available colours; $G$ is $k$-choosable if it has a proper colouring with $\phi(v)\in L(v)$ for every $v$ whenever all $|L(v)|\ge k$, and the list-chromatic number $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least such $k$ (so $\chi\le\chi_\ell$). Molloy proved $\chi_\ell(G)\le(1+o(1))\Delta/\ln\Delta$ for triangle-free graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$, and $\chi_\ell(G)\le200\,\omega\frac{\Delta\ln\ln\Delta}{\ln\Delta}$ when there is no clique of size greater than $\omega$, which implies Reed's bound $\chi\le\lceil\frac12(\Delta+1+\omega)\rceil$ when $\omega=o(\ln\Delta/\ln\ln\Delta)$. The question asks whether a bound much stronger than Reed's holds already when $\omega$ is a small power of $\Delta$; Spencer's Ramsey construction (graphs on $n$ vertices with independence number $2$ and cliques of size at most $n^{1/2+o(1)}$) shows that nothing better than about $\Delta/2$ can hold when $\omega=\Omega(\Delta^{1/2})$. The paper answers the question affirmatively: the authors prove $\chi_\ell(G)=O\left(\Delta\sqrt{\ln\omega/\ln\Delta}\right)$, so that $f(c)=(72c)^2$ suffices for $\Delta$ large enough (in fact a local version for correspondence colouring). Determining the best possible $f$ is left open; Spencer's lower bounds on Ramsey numbers give $f(c)\ge c/2+1$ for integer $c$, and in particular $f(2)\ge2$.
notes: The paper answers Question 1.5 in the affirmative via Theorem 1.6, with $f(c) = (72c)^2$ sufficing for large enough $\Delta$.
paper_title: Bounding $χ$ by a fraction of $Δ$ for graphs without large cliques

name: AX_list_chromatic_reed_bound
title: List-chromatic analogue of Reed's Conjecture
statement_text: Reed's conjecture may also be true for the list-chromatic number, i.e., $\chi_\ell(G)\leq\left\lceil\frac{1}{2}(\Delta+1+\omega)\right\rceil$ for every graph $G$ of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ with no clique of size greater than $\omega$.
context_text: A list-assignment $L$ gives each vertex $v$ a set $L(v)$ of available colours; $G$ is $k$-choosable if it has a proper colouring with $\phi(v)\in L(v)$ for every $v$ whenever all $|L(v)|\ge k$, and the list-chromatic number $\chi_\ell(G)$ is the least such $k$ (so $\chi\le\chi_\ell$). Reed's $\omega,\Delta,\chi$ conjecture asserts that every graph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ with no clique of size greater than $\omega$ satisfies $\chi(G)\le\lceil\frac12(\Delta+1+\omega)\rceil$. Reed proved that there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $\chi(G)\le\lceil(1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)+\varepsilon\omega\rceil$ (the conjecture is the case $\varepsilon=\frac12$); Bonamy, Perrett and Postle obtained $\varepsilon=\frac1{26}$ for large $\Delta$, and Delcourt and Postle proved the list-colouring version of Reed's theorem with $\varepsilon=\frac1{13}$ for large $\Delta$. No value $\varepsilon>\frac12$ works (Spencer's Ramsey graphs, or blowups of $C_5$, which also show that the rounding is necessary). Molloy's bound $\chi_\ell(G)\le200\,\omega\frac{\Delta\ln\ln\Delta}{\ln\Delta}$ implies the list version when $\omega=o(\ln\Delta/\ln\ln\Delta)$. The authors only remark that the list version is possible.
notes: Stated informally in the introduction: 'It is possible that Conjecture 1.3 is also true for the list-chromatic number.'
paper_title: Bounding $χ$ by a fraction of $Δ$ for graphs without large cliques

name: AX_triangle_free_planar_2_degenerate_7_8
title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: Every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac{7}{8}$ of its vertices.
context_text: A graph is $k$-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $k$ (2-degenerate graphs are those whose every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most 2); planar graphs are 5-degenerate and triangle-free planar graphs are 3-degenerate, so the question is how large an induced subgraph of smaller degeneracy one can find. The conjecture would be tight for the cube (the unique 3-regular triangle-free planar graph on 8 vertices), and more generally for every triangle-free planar graph whose vertex set can be partitioned into parts inducing cubes. The authors prove two weaker results: every triangle-free planar graph on $n$ vertices and $m$ edges contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $(6n-m-\lambda)/5$ vertices, where $\lambda$ is the number of 'difficult' components, which gives $\frac45 n$ by Euler's formula; and if $G$ has $n_3$ vertices of degree at most three, it contains one on at least $\frac78 n-18n_3$ vertices. This shows that graphs with almost all vertices of degree at least four (which are close to 4-regular grids) are not counterexamples. Analogous problems are the Albertson–Berman conjecture (an induced forest, i.e. an induced 1-degenerate subgraph, on half the vertices of any planar graph) and bounds on induced 3-degenerate subgraphs of planar graphs.
paper_title: Induced 2-degenerate Subgraphs of Triangle-free Planar Graphs

name: AX_triangle_free_planar_2_degenerate_5_6
title: Informal belief: 5/6 bound attainable
statement_text: We believe the argument we use can be strengthened to give a bound $\frac{5}{6}$ (every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac{5}{6}$ of its vertices), however the technical issues are substantial and since we do not see this as a viable way to prove in full the conjecture that every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac{7}{8}$ of its vertices, we prefer to present the easier argument giving the bound $\frac{4}{5}$.
context_text: A graph is $k$-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $k$ (2-degenerate graphs are those whose every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most 2); planar graphs are 5-degenerate and triangle-free planar graphs are 3-degenerate, so the question is how large an induced subgraph of smaller degeneracy one can find. The authors prove that every triangle-free planar graph contains an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac45$ of its vertices, via a discharging-type argument giving the bound $(6n-m-\lambda)/5$ for graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and $\lambda$ components of a special 'difficult' kind (every block a vertex, an edge or a cube, cube blocks vertex-disjoint). The remark is that this method could probably be pushed to $\frac56$, which they do not pursue because it would not reach the conjectured optimal $\frac78$ (tight for the cube). This is an authors' belief about their method rather than a conjecture proper; its mathematical content is that every triangle-free planar graph has an induced 2-degenerate subgraph on at least $\frac56$ of its vertices.
notes: Stated as an authorial belief in running prose, not a labelled environment.
paper_title: Induced 2-degenerate Subgraphs of Triangle-free Planar Graphs

name: AX_bounded_clique_large_chi_consecutive_holes_extension
title: Informal Conjecture (generalization of 1.3 to bounded clique number)
statement_text:
The result that triangle-free graphs of large chromatic number have holes of $
u$ consecutive lengths is also true for graphs with bounded clique number rather than just triangle-free graphs: for all integers $
u > 0$ and $k \geq 3$ there exists $n$ such that if $G$ has no clique of cardinality $k$ and has chromatic number at least $n$, then for some $t$, $G$ has a hole of length $t+i$ for $1 \leq i \leq 
u$.
context_text:
A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). The main result of the paper is that for every integer $
u>0$ there exists $n$ such that every triangle-free graph with chromatic number at least $n$ has, for some $t$, holes of all lengths $t+1,\dots,t+
u$ ($
u$ consecutive lengths, the smallest possibly arbitrarily large). This contains the triangle-free cases of earlier results on Gyárfás's conjectures (long holes, long odd holes, holes of length a multiple of three). The authors conjecture the same for graphs with bounded clique number, but have made no progress in proving it. They mention that since submission they (with Chudnovsky and Spirkl) proved Gyárfás's long odd holes conjecture, and that, for all $k,s,t$, graphs with no $k$-clique and large enough chromatic number have a hole of length $s$ modulo $t$; these do not give consecutive lengths.
notes: PDF source — exact statement inferred from prose; the phrase 'the corresponding result' refers to Theorem 1.3 in context
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IV. Consecutive holes

name: AX_constricting_hole_lengths_bounded_gaps
title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: Let $F$ be an infinite set of positive integers with bounded gaps. Then $F$ is constricting.
context_text:
A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). A set $F$ of integers is $k$-constricting if there exists $n$ such that every graph with chromatic number at least $n$ contains either a clique with $k$ vertices or a hole with length in $F$, and constricting if it is $k$-constricting for every $k$. Every constricting set is infinite, since there are graphs of arbitrarily large chromatic number and girth. The main result of the paper is that for every integer $
u>0$ there exists $n$ such that every triangle-free graph with chromatic number at least $n$ has, for some $t$, holes of all lengths $t+1,\dots,t+
u$ ($
u$ consecutive lengths, the smallest possibly arbitrarily large). As a consequence, the authors prove that every infinite set of positive integers with bounded gaps is $3$-constricting, and they conjecture this extension to all $k$, presenting it as the counterpart of their conjecture that graphs with bounded clique number and large chromatic number have holes of $
u$ consecutive lengths.
notes: PDF source — math appears cleanly readable
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IV. Consecutive holes

name: AX_constricting_hole_lengths_density_zero
title: Problem 1.6
statement_text: Is there an infinite set $F$ of positive integers such that $F$ is constricting and has density $0$?
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). A set $F$ of integers is $k$-constricting if there exists $n$ such that every graph with chromatic number at least $n$ contains either a clique with $k$ vertices or a hole with length in $F$, and constricting if it is $k$-constricting for every $k$. Every constricting set is infinite (graphs of large girth and chromatic number exist), and the authors conjecture that every infinite set with bounded gaps is constricting (they prove it is $3$-constricting). Not every infinite set is constricting, not even one of upper density one: take $G_1$ null and, for $i>1$, $G_i$ triangle-free with girth at least $2^{|V(G_{i-1})|}$ and chromatic number at least $i$; the set of cycle lengths occurring in no $G_i$ is not constricting. Lower density seems closer to the truth; the authors cannot rule out that a set is constricting if and only if it has positive lower density, although this does not seem likely. They conjecture the answer to this question is positive, and ask the even stronger question whether some constricting $F=\{f_1,f_2,\dots\}$ has $f_{i+1}-f_i\to\infty$; both questions would be very interesting even for $3$-constricting sets.
notes: PDF source — math appears cleanly readable; authors conjecture the answer is positive
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IV. Consecutive holes

name: AX_controlled_triangle_free_chromatic_4_hole
title: Informal Question (on 2.1 for ℓ = 4)
statement_text: The following might be true when $\ell = 4$ (it is proved for all $\ell\ge5$): let $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a non-decreasing function; does there exist $n$ such that every $(2,\varphi)$-controlled triangle-free graph with chromatic number more than $n$ has a $4$-hole?
context_text: A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and an $\ell$-hole is a hole of length $\ell$ (number of edges). For a vertex $v$ and integer $\rho\ge0$, $N^\rho[v]$ is the set of vertices at distance at most $\rho$ from $v$, and $\chi^\rho(G)$ is the maximum over $v$ of $\chi(G[N^\rho[v]])$. For $\rho\ge1$ and a non-decreasing $\varphi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, a graph $G$ is $(\rho,\varphi)$-controlled if $\chi(H)\le\varphi(\chi^\rho(H))$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of $G$; roughly, every induced subgraph of large chromatic number has a vertex whose radius-$\rho$ ball has large chromatic number. In a triangle-free graph $\chi^1\le2$, so the radius-$2$ case is the first nontrivial one. The authors prove that for every non-decreasing $\varphi$ and every $\ell\ge5$ there exists $n$ such that every $(2,\varphi)$-controlled triangle-free graph with chromatic number more than $n$ has an $\ell$-hole (this is one of three steps of their proof that triangle-free graphs of large chromatic number have holes of $\nu$ consecutive lengths). They remark that it might be true for $\ell=4$ as well, but they have not been able to decide this.
notes: PDF source — phrased by authors as 'might be true … but we have not been able to decide this'; no formal conjecture label
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IV. Consecutive holes

name: AX_polynomial_expansion_balanced_separator_constant_m
title: Informal Conjecture (constant-size M)
statement_text: I conjecture that for every class of graphs with polynomial $\omega$-expansion and every integer $\ell\ge1$, there is a constant $m$ (dependent on the class and $\ell$, but not on $|V(G)|$) such that for every graph $G$ in the class and every cost function $q:V(G)\to\mathbb{Q}_{\ge0}$, there actually always exists a balanced separator $C \cup M$ of $G$ with $q(C) \leq q(V(G))/\ell$ for some set $M$ of size at most $m$.
context_text: A balanced separator of $G$ is a set $C\subseteq V(G)$ such that every component of $G-C$ has at most $\frac23|V(G)|$ vertices. For a cost function $q:V(G)\to\mathbb{Q}_{\ge0}$ and $X\subseteq V(G)$, $q(X)=\sum_{x\in X}q(x)$. A model of $K_m$ of depth $d$ is a family of $m$ disjoint vertex sets, each inducing a connected subgraph of radius at most $d$, with an edge between any two of them; $\omega_d(G)$ is the largest $m$ for which $G$ has such a model. A class has polynomial $\omega$-expansion if $\omega_r(G)\le f(r)$ for all $G$ in the class and all $r\ge1$, for some polynomial $f$; by results of Dvořák and Norin and of Plotkin, Rao and Smith, this is equivalent to polynomial expansion and to having strongly sublinear separators (every subgraph $H$ has a balanced separator of order $O(|V(H)|^{1-\varepsilon})$). The author proves a weighted version of the Plotkin–Rao–Smith algorithm: given $G$ with $n$ vertices, $\ell$ and $q$, it finds either a large shallow clique model or disjoint sets $C,M$ with $C\cup M$ a balanced separator, $q(C)\le q(V(G))/\ell$, and $M$ the support of a model of a clique of depth $d=O(\ell\log n)$, so that $|M|\le\omega_d(G)^2d$, which for classes with polynomial $\omega$-expansion is polylogarithmic in $n$. The cost of $M$ cannot be bounded in general: in a star with cost $1/4$ on the centre and $3/4$ spread over the leaves, every balanced separator has cost at least $1/4$. The conjecture is that the dependence of $|M|$ on $n$ can be removed.
notes: Stated as inline prose in the bullet-point remarks following Theorem 5; no labelled theorem environment.
paper_title: On classes of graphs with strongly sublinear separators

name: AX_jaeger_antisymmetric_z5_flow_edge_connected_digraphs
title: Antisymmetric variant of Jaeger's weak 3-flow conjecture
statement_text: There is a constant $k$ such that every directed $k$-edge-connected graph has a $\mathbb{Z}_5$-antisymmetric flow.
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops, and a directed graph is $k$-edge-connected if its underlying undirected graph is. For an abelian group $B$, a $B$-flow in a directed graph is a map $f$ from the arcs to $B$ such that at every vertex the sum of the values on outgoing arcs equals the sum on incoming arcs; it is nowhere-zero if no arc gets $0$, and antisymmetric if moreover no two arcs receive mutually inverse elements of $B$ (an antisymmetric flow is nowhere-zero since $0=-0$). Antisymmetric flows were introduced by Nešetřil and Raspaud; a directed 2-edge-cut is an obstruction, and every directed graph without one has a $\mathbb{Z}_2^3\times\mathbb{Z}_3^9$-antisymmetric flow (Dvořák, Kaiser, Král', Sereni). Jaeger's weak 3-flow conjecture (some constant $k$ such that every $k$-edge-connected graph has a nowhere-zero $\mathbb{Z}_3$-flow) was proved by Thomassen for $k=8$ and by Lovász, Thomassen, Wu and Zhang for $k=6$; this is its natural antisymmetric variant. $\mathbb{Z}_5$ would be best possible: in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ every element is its own inverse, and a $\mathbb{Z}_3$- or $\mathbb{Z}_4$-antisymmetric flow must give the same value to all arcs, impossible for two vertices joined by $k\equiv1\pmod{12}$ parallel arcs in the same direction. The paper itself proves this statement: for every $k\ge2$, every directed $\lceil 6k/(k-1)\rceil$-edge-connected graph has a $\mathbb{Z}_{2k+1}$-antisymmetric flow, so in particular every directed 12-edge-connected graph has a $\mathbb{Z}_5$-antisymmetric flow. Since there are directed 7-edge-connected graphs with no $\mathbb{Z}_5$-antisymmetric flow, the authors conjecture that 8-edge-connectivity suffices.
notes: Stated in prose as 'The natural antisymmetric variant … would be the following' without a labelled environment.
paper_title: Additive bases and flows in graphs

name: AX_spaghetti_tree_path_decomposition_chi_bounded
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: There exists a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $\chi(G) \leq f(k)$ for every $k \geq 1$ and every graph $G$ admitting a spaghetti tree-decomposition $(T, \{B_t\}_{t \in V(T)})$ and a path-decomposition $(P, \{B_p\}_{p \in V(P)})$ such that $|B_t \cap B_p| \leq k$ for every $t \in V(T)$ and $p \in V(P)$.
context_text: A tree-decomposition $(T,\{B_t\}_{t\in V(T)})$ of $G$ (with bags $B_t\subseteq V(G)$) is a spaghetti tree-decomposition if $T$ is rooted at some vertex $r$ and, orienting all edges of $T$ away from $r$, the subtree $T_v$ of $T$ induced by $\{t\in V(T): v\in B_t\}$ is a directed path for each vertex $v$ of $G$; a path-decomposition is a tree-decomposition whose tree is a path. Motivation: a classic result of Asplund and Grünbaum states that intersection graphs of axis-aligned rectangles in the plane are $\chi$-bounded (here $\chi(G)\in O(\omega(G)^2)$); equivalently, there is a function $f$ such that every graph having two path-decompositions in which each bag of the first meets each bag of the second in at most $k$ vertices has chromatic number at most $f(k)$. Dujmović, Joret, Morin, Norin and Wood asked whether this remains true for two tree-decompositions. The authors answer this negatively: the Burling graphs (triangle-free with unbounded chromatic number) admit a tree-decomposition and a path-decomposition such that every bag of the first meets every bag of the second in at most two vertices. The conjecture, posed as an open problem in the spirit of extending the Asplund–Grünbaum result, asks whether restricting the tree-decomposition to be a spaghetti one restores a bound. The authors remark that, for all they know, it could even hold with two spaghetti tree-decompositions; graphs having a spaghetti tree-decomposition where $uv\in E(G)$ if and only if $T_u$ and $T_v$ intersect (a subclass of chordal graphs) were studied by Galvin.
paper_title: Burling graphs, chromatic number, and orthogonal tree-decompositions

name: AX_gnp_h_free_clique_count_threshold
title: Motivating Question (Introduction)
statement_text: Let $m\ge2$ and let $H$ be a fixed graph with $\chi(H)=k>m$. For which values of $p$ is it true that $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p), K_m, H) = (1+o(1))\binom{k-1}{m}\left(\frac{n}{k-1}\right)^m p^{\binom{m}{2}}$ w.h.p.?
context_text: For graphs $T$ and $H$, $\mathrm{ex}(n,T,H)$ is the maximum number of copies of $T$ in an $H$-free subgraph of $K_n$, and $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),T,H)$ is the random variable equal to the maximum number of copies of $T$ in an $H$-free subgraph of the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$; w.h.p. means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$, and $f\gg g$ means $f/g\to\infty$. The 2-density of $H$ is $m_2(H)=\max\{\frac{e(H')-1}{v(H')-2}: H'\subseteq H, v(H')\ge3\}$; note $m_2(K_m)=\frac{m+1}{2}$. Alon and Shikhelman showed $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_m,H)=(1+o(1))\binom{k-1}{m}(\frac{n}{k-1})^m$ when $\chi(H)=k>m$ (attained by the balanced $(k-1)$-partite graph), so the question asks when the random analogue matches the deterministic count times $p^{\binom m2}$. For $T=K_2$ the answer (Conlon–Gowers, Schacht) is that $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),H)=(1-\frac{1}{\chi(H)-1}+o(1))\binom n2p$ for $p\gg n^{-1/m_2(H)}$, while for $p\ll n^{-1/m_2(H)}$ almost all edges can be kept. The authors prove that if $m_2(H)\ge m_2(K_m)$ the formula holds w.h.p. for $p\gg n^{-1/m_2(H)}$, and if $m_2(H)>m_2(K_m)$ then $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),K_m,H)=(1+o(1))\binom nm p^{\binom m2}$ for $p\ll n^{-1/m_2(H)}$; this covers every $H$ with $\chi(H)\ge m+2$. When $\chi(H)=m+1$ there are infinitely many $H$ with $m_2(H)<m_2(K_m)$, and for some of them almost all copies of $K_m$ can still be kept for $p\le n^{-1/m_2(H)+\delta}$, so the critical value of $p$ is bounded away from $n^{-1/m_2(H)}$ and its exact location is left open. In their concluding remarks the authors suggest that the transition should occur when $n^{m-2}p^{\binom m2}$ crosses $n^{-1/m_2(H)}$, based on the random graph formed by the edges lying in copies of $K_m$.

name: AX_cop_number_genus_sqrt_g_growth
title: Conjecture 8
statement_text: $c(g) = g^{\frac{1}{2}+o(1)}$ and $\widetilde c(g) = g^{\frac{1}{2}+o(1)}$. In other words, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $g_0$ such that for every $g \geq g_0$, $$g^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon} < c(g) < g^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}$$ and $$g^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon} < \widetilde c(g) < g^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}.$$
context_text: In the Cops and Robber game on a graph, $k$ cops and then a robber choose vertices, and then alternately the cops (each moving along an edge or staying) and the robber move, with full information; the cop number $c(G)$ is the least $k$ for which the cops can always catch the robber. Here $c(g)=\max\{c(G) : g(G)\le g\}$ and $\widetilde c(g)=\max\{c(G) : \widetilde g(G)\le g\}$, where $g(G)$ is the (orientable) genus of $G$ and $\widetilde g(G)$ its nonorientable genus (crosscap number). Planar graphs have cop number at most $3$; guarding a shortest homologically non-trivial cycle with two cops gives $c(G)\le 2g+3$, and Schröder proved $c(G)\le\frac{3}{2}g+3$ for graphs of genus $g$ and conjectured $c(G)\le g+3$; most people believe Schröder's bound is tight up to a constant, but the author notes there is no evidence for this. Incidence graphs of projective planes give $c(g)=\Omega(g^{1/3})$, and random graphs $G(n,p)$ with $p=\frac{5}{2}\log(n)/n$ (using the Bollobás–Kun–Leader bounds on their cop number) give, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and large $g$, graphs of genus $g$ with $g^{1/2-\varepsilon}\le c(G)\le g^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, so $c(g)\ge g^{\frac{1}{2}(1-o(1))}$. The author (Mohar, 2009) conjectures that this is the true order, i.e. a much stronger upper bound than Schröder's; the conjecture was unchallenged when the note was written.

name: AX_cop_number_riemannian_surfaces_genus_bounded
title: Question (Riemannian surfaces): cop number bounded by genus
statement_text: Is the cop number of Riemannian surfaces bounded in terms of the genus?
context_text: The author proposes a Cops and Robber game on a Riemannian surface $S$: $k$ cops and a robber are placed on $S$, all move with velocity at most $1$ (during time $t$ each player moves along a path of length at most $t$), the players know each other's positions at all times, and the robber is caught when some cop gets at distance less than $\frac{1}{2}$ from him; the cop number of $S$ is the least $k$ for which the cops can always catch the robber. The question asks whether there is a bound on the cop number of a Riemannian surface depending only on its topological genus.

name: AX_gnp_chromatic_concentration_lower_bound
title: Open problem on lower bound for concentration interval
statement_text: For $p$ fixed, nothing is known from below concerning concentration: it has not even been shown that the chromatic number cannot be concentrated in an interval of constant length.
context_text: $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the Erdős–Rényi random graph on $n$ vertices in which each pair is an edge independently with probability $p$; here $0<p<1$ is a fixed constant. Saying that $\chi(G)$ is concentrated in an interval of length $\ell(n)$ means that there is a function $h(n)$ such that, for $G\in\mathcal{G}(n,p)$, $|\chi(G)-h(n)|<\ell(n)$ with probability $1-o(1)$; $\omega(n)$ denotes any function tending to infinity. Shamir and Spencer proved concentration in an interval of length $\omega(n)\sqrt{n}$, and the paper gives a proof (of a result due to Alon) of concentration in an interval of length $\omega(n)\sqrt{n}/\log n$. For sparse random graphs much stronger results hold: Łuczak and Alon–Krivelevich obtained two-point concentration for $p<n^{-1/2-\epsilon}$. All these are upper bounds on the concentration width; for fixed $p$, the author notes that no lower bound is known, i.e. it has not been ruled out that $\chi(G(n,p))$ is concentrated on a bounded number of values. Bollobás is cited for further discussion of this question.

name: AX_minor_closed_col_star_characterization
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: A minor-closed class of graphs $\mathcal{G}$ satisfies $\mathrm{col}^\star(\mathcal{G}) \leq t$ if and only if there exists $m \geq 1$ such that $K_{t,m} \notin \mathcal{G}$ and $I_{t-1}+P_m \notin \mathcal{G}$.
context_text: A $t$-island in a graph $G$ is a non-empty set $S$ of vertices such that each vertex of $S$ has fewer than $t$ neighbours in $V(G)\setminus S$, and $\mathrm{col}_C(G)$ is the smallest $t$ such that every non-empty subgraph of $G$ contains a $t$-island of size at most $C$ (so $\mathrm{col}_1$ is the usual coloring number). For a class $\mathcal{G}$, the clustered coloring number $\mathrm{col}^\star(\mathcal{G})$ is the smallest $t$ such that for some $C$, $\mathrm{col}_C(G)\le t$ for all $G\in\mathcal{G}$ (written $\mathrm{col}_\star$ in the paper). A colouring has clustering $C$ if every monochromatic connected subgraph has at most $C$ vertices, and the clustered (list) chromatic number $\chi_\star(\mathcal{G})$ (resp. $\chi^\ell_\star(\mathcal{G})$) is the least $t$ such that for some $C$ every graph of $\mathcal{G}$ has a $t$-colouring (resp. an $L$-colouring for every assignment $L$ of lists of size $t$) with clustering $C$; one has $\mathrm{col}^\star\ge\chi^\ell_\star\ge\chi_\star$. $K_{t,m}$ is the complete bipartite graph and $I_{t-1}+P_m$ is a path on $m$ vertices together with $t-1$ further vertices adjacent to all vertices of the path. For every $C$ there is $m$ such that all $t$-islands of $K_{t,m}$ and of $I_{t-1}+P_m$ have more than $C$ vertices, so the condition is necessary, and even necessary for $\chi^\ell_\star(\mathcal{G})\le t$. The authors prove the conjecture for minor-closed classes of bounded treewidth (equivalently, those not containing all planar graphs). The conjecture would imply $\chi^\ell_\star(\mathcal{G})=\mathrm{col}^\star(\mathcal{G})$ for every minor-closed class, and $\mathrm{col}^\star=\chi_\star=t$ for $K_{t+1}$-minor-free graphs, since $K_{t+1}$ is a minor of $K_{t,m}$ and of $I_{t-1}+P_m$ for $m\ge t$.

name: AX_ryser_near_extremal_hypergraphs_projective_planes
title: Informal Problem (projective plane structure in near-extremal constructions)
statement_text: It would be interesting either to find a different type of construction of near-extremal intersecting $r$-partite hypergraphs $H$ with $\tau(H)$ close to $r$, or to show that near-extremal constructions must contain large pieces from a projective plane.
context_text: A hypergraph is $r$-partite if its vertex set has a partition $V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_r$ such that each edge contains at most one vertex of each $V_i$; it is $r$-uniform if all edges have size $r$, and intersecting if any two edges meet. $\tau(H)$ is the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge) and $\nu(H)$ the maximum number of pairwise disjoint edges. Ryser's conjecture states that every $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraph satisfies $\tau(H)\le(r-1)\nu(H)$; in particular every intersecting one could be covered by $r-1$ vertices. It is known for $r=2$ (Kőnig) and $r=3$, and for intersecting hypergraphs for $r\le5$. The projective plane of order $p$ gives tight intersecting examples for $r=p+1$ ($p$ a prime power), and tight examples are also known for $r=p+2$ and $r=7,11,12$. Answering a question of Abu-Khazneh, Barát, Pokrovskiy and Szabó, the authors construct, for all sufficiently large $r$, intersecting $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraphs with $\tau(H)\ge r-4$, again built from finite projective planes. They remark that, except for a few sporadic small examples, all constructions of intersecting $r$-partite hypergraphs with $\tau(H)$ close to $r$ seem to be based in some way on finite projective planes and hence depend on the existence of these special structures. The problem is informal: 'near-extremal' is not defined precisely.

name: AX_planar_cover_graph_poset_dimension_height
title: Open problem: dimension of posets with planar cover graphs vs. height
statement_text: It is not known whether the dimension of posets with planar cover graphs is bounded by a linear function of their height (or any polynomial function for that matter).
context_text: Posets are finite. The dimension $\dim(P)$ of a poset $P$ is the least integer $d$ such that $P$ is the intersection of $d$ linear orders (linear extensions of $P$). A chain is a set of pairwise comparable elements, and the height of $P$ is the maximum size of a chain. A relation $a<b$ is a cover relation if there is no $c$ with $a<c<b$; the cover graph of $P$ is the undirected graph on the elements of $P$ whose edges are the cover relations, i.e. the (Hasse) diagram seen as an undirected graph. $P$ is a planar poset if its diagram can be drawn in the plane without crossings with every cover relation $a<b$ drawn as a curve going upwards from $a$ to $b$; planar posets have planar cover graphs, but for every $h\ge3$ there are non-planar posets of height $h$ with planar cover graphs. The paper's main result is that every planar poset of height $h$ has dimension at most $192h+96$, while Kelly's construction shows that planar posets of height $h$ can have dimension about $h$, so a linear bound is optimal up to a constant factor. By a theorem of Streib and Trotter, the dimension of posets with planar cover graphs is bounded by some function of the height, but the known bound is exponential. The authors also construct posets of height $h$ with planar cover graphs and dimension at least $2h-2$, and show that planarity is essential: there are posets whose cover graphs exclude $K_5$ as a minor with dimension at least $2^{h/2}$ for height $h$.

name: AX_independent_fvs_linear_forest_free_complexity
title: Complexity of Independent Feedback Vertex Set for H-free graphs (linear forest cases)
statement_text: Only the cases where $H$ is a linear forest, that is, a disjoint union of paths, remain open for the complexity classification of \textsc{Independent Feedback Vertex Set} on $H$-free graphs. In particular, the case where $H$ is a single path $P_h$ with $h \geq 6$ has not yet been resolved.
context_text: A feedback vertex set of $G$ is a set $S$ of vertices such that $G-S$ is a forest; Independent Feedback Vertex Set asks, given $G$ and $k$, whether $G$ has a feedback vertex set of size at most $k$ that is an independent set. Equivalently, it asks for a proper 3-colouring in which one colour class has at most $k$ vertices and the other two classes induce a forest; graphs having an independent feedback vertex set are called near-bipartite, and recognising them is NP-complete. $G$ is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and $P_h$ is the path on $h$ vertices. The authors prove that the problem (even Near-Bipartiteness) is NP-complete on line graphs, hence on $H$-free graphs whenever $H$ contains a claw, and NP-complete on graphs of arbitrarily large girth, hence whenever $H$ contains a cycle. Tamura et al. solved it in polynomial time for $P_4$-free graphs (cographs), and the main result of the paper is a polynomial-time algorithm for $P_5$-free graphs (also for Independent Odd Cycle Transversal). For comparison, 3-Colouring is polynomial on $P_r$-free graphs for $r\le7$ and open for $r\ge8$; no NP-hardness is known for these problems on $P_r$-free graphs, and the authors ask whether Near-Bipartiteness on $P_r$-free graphs is polynomially equivalent to 3-Colouring on $P_{f(r)}$-free graphs for some function $f$.

name: AX_additive_chi_approx_minor_closed_triangle_free
title: Open question: additive approximation for triangle-free graphs
statement_text: Does there exist $\alpha \geq 0$ such that for every proper minor-closed class $\mathcal{G}$, the chromatic number of triangle-free graphs in $\mathcal{G}$ can be approximated in polynomial time within additive error $\alpha$?
context_text: Approximating the chromatic number within additive error $\alpha$ on a class means a polynomial-time algorithm that, given $G$ in the class, returns an integer $c$ with $\chi(G)\le c\le\chi(G)+\alpha$. A graph $H$ is $t$-apex if deleting at most $t$ vertices makes it planar. Thomas conjectured, and Kawarabayashi et al. conjectured even for list coloring, that a single constant $\alpha$ works for every proper minor-closed class; the paper disproves this: for a $K_{4k_0+1}$-minor-free input, returning $c$ with $\chi(G)\le c\le\chi(G)+k_0-1$ is NP-hard. Its construction has clique number of order $k_0$. Forbidding triangles makes coloring more tractable for embedded graphs (all planar triangle-free graphs are 3-colorable by Grötzsch's theorem, and 3-colorability of triangle-free graphs on any fixed surface is decidable in linear time), and the authors explicitly state that the triangle-free version of the question is still open. On the negative side they show that forbidding $K_4$ is not sufficient: for $K_{4k_0+8}$-minor-free graphs with $\omega(G)\le 3$, additive error $d=\Omega(k_0^{1/4}/\log^{1/2}k_0)$ is NP-hard. On the positive side, for triangle-free $H$-minor-free graphs with $H$ $t$-apex they achieve additive error $\lceil(13t+172)/14\rceil$, and the answer is positive (with $\alpha=6$) for graphs of girth at least 5 in any proper minor-closed class.
notes: PDF source; stated in prose as 'this question is still open'.
paper_title: Additive non-approximability of chromatic number in proper minor-closed classes

name: AX_additive_chi_approx_kk_minor_free
title: Open question: better additive approximation for $K_{4k_0+1}$-minor-free graphs
statement_text: Is a better additive approximation of the chromatic number of $K_k$-minor-free graphs than the additive error $k-2$ of Kawarabayashi et al. possible in polynomial time (necessarily with additive error above roughly $k/4$, since for $k=4k_0+1$ additive error $k_0-1$ is NP-hard)?
context_text: Approximating the chromatic number of $K_k$-minor-free graphs within additive error $\alpha$ means a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a $K_k$-minor-free graph $G$, returns an integer $c$ with $\chi(G)\le c\le\chi(G)+\alpha$. Kawarabayashi et al. showed this is possible with $\alpha=k-2$. The paper shows that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm takes a $K_{4k_0+1}$-minor-free graph $G$ and returns $c$ with $\chi(G)\le c\le\chi(G)+k_0-1$, so additive error about $k/4$ is impossible; this disproves conjectures of Thomas and of Kawarabayashi et al. that a constant additive error suffices for every proper minor-closed class. The authors leave open whether a better additive approximation than $k-2$ is possible, leaving a gap of roughly a factor of 4 between the algorithmic and hardness bounds. They also give, for $H$-minor-free graphs with $H$ $t$-apex (i.e. $H$ becomes planar after deleting at most $t$ vertices), an algorithm with additive error $t+3$.

name: AX_perfect_graphs_tight_skew_partitions_count
title: Open Question on Number of Tight Skew Partitions
statement_text: We do not know how many tight skew partitions an $n$-vertex graph can really have; the authors do not know of a graph with more than linearly many tight skew partitions.
context_text: A skew partition of a graph $G$ is a partition $(A,B)$ of $V(G)$ such that $G[A]$ is not connected and the complement $\overline{G}[B]$ is not connected. An anticomponent of $G[B]$ is a component of its complement. A skew partition $(A,B)$ is loose if some vertex of $A$ is adjacent to every vertex of some anticomponent of $G[B]$, or some vertex of $B$ has no neighbour in some component of $G[A]$; it is tight otherwise. Skew partitions are central in the structure theory of Berge (perfect) graphs, and the paper uses them to obtain a combinatorial algorithm that optimally colours perfect graphs with clique number $k$ in time polynomial for fixed $k$. Modifying the Kennedy–Reed algorithm, the authors list all tight skew partitions of any $n$-vertex graph in time $O(n^6)$, which shows there are at most $n^4$ of them; they improve this to at most $n^3\log n$, because for every tight skew partition $(A,B)$ the set $B$ appears at least $k_2$ times in the Kennedy–Reed list, where $k_2$ is the size of the second largest anticomponent of $G[B]$. In contrast, loose skew partitions can be exponentially many (e.g. in the star $K_{1,n}$). The true maximum number of tight skew partitions is unknown.
notes: Stated as prose without a labelled theorem environment. PDF source.
paper_title: Colouring perfect graphs with bounded clique number

name: AX_girth_5_planar_list_critical_bounded
title: Conjecture 1.7
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 5$, there exists an integer $K$ with the following property. Let $G$ be a planar graph of girth at least five, let $C_1, C_2$ be two cycles in $G$ of lengths at most $k$, and for every $v \in V(G)$ let $L(v)$ be a set such that $|L(v)| = 1$ if $v \in V(C_1 \cup C_2)$ and $|L(v)| \geq 3$ otherwise. If there exists no proper coloring $\phi$ of $G$ such that $\phi(v) \in L(v)$ for every $v \in V(G)$, then $G$ has a subgraph $H$ on at most $K$ vertices such that $C_1$ and $C_2$ are subgraphs of $H$ and there exists no proper coloring $\psi$ of $H$ such that $\psi(v) \in L(v)$ for every $v \in V(H)$.
context_text: Here a proper coloring $\phi$ with $\phi(v)\in L(v)$ for all $v$ is a list coloring from the lists $L$; vertices of the two cycles $C_1,C_2$ have a single allowed colour, i.e. they are precolored, and the conjecture asks that whenever this precoloring of two short cycles does not extend to an $L$-coloring of $G$, there is a bounded-size obstruction containing both cycles. The paper is part of a series on 3-colorability of graphs on surfaces with restricted triangles; its main result is the single-cycle, non-list version: if $G$ is a planar graph of girth at least five, $C$ a cycle of $G$ and $\phi$ a 3-coloring of $C$ that does not extend to a 3-coloring of $G$, then some subgraph $H$ of $G$ containing $C$ with $|V(H)|\le 1715|V(C)|$ already has no 3-coloring extending $\phi$ (Dvořák and Kawarabayashi generalized this to list coloring with a better constant). The authors' broader result states that there is an absolute constant $K$ such that every 4-critical graph (not 3-colorable but every proper subgraph is) drawn in a surface of Euler genus $\gamma$ with no separating cycles of length at most four and with $t$ triangles satisfies $\sum|f|\le K(t+\gamma)$, the sum being over faces of length at least five. They ask whether the analogue of this bound for graphs of girth at least five holds in the list-coloring setting, and note that an affirmative answer would follow from the conjecture. Luke Postle (private communication) believes he has a proof, not yet written down at the time of the paper. In the paper's displayed conjecture the final condition reads $\phi(v)\in L(v)$, an evident typo for $\psi(v)\in L(v)$.
notes: The PDF extraction renders the final clause with $\phi$ instead of $\psi$; from context the intended quantifier variable in the conclusion is $\psi$, corrected here.
paper_title: Three-coloring triangle-free graphs on surfaces II. 4-critical graphs in a disk

name: AX_large_chromatic_rainbow_hole_consecutive_vertices
title: Question (rainbow hole with $s$ consecutive rainbow vertices)
statement_text: Is it true that for all fixed $s$, $\kappa$, if $G$ is a graph with $\omega(G)\leq\kappa$ and $\chi(G)$ sufficiently large, then in every colouring of $G$ there is a hole in which some set of $s$ consecutive vertices is rainbow?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A colouring of $G$ is any proper colouring (not necessarily optimal), and a subgraph is rainbow if its vertices receive pairwise distinct colours. The authors prove that for all $\kappa,s\ge1$ there is $c$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\omega(G)\le\kappa$ and $\chi(G)>c$ and every colouring of $G$, some $s$-vertex induced path is rainbow (extending Gyárfás and Sárközy, who assumed girth at least five). A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four. Asking for a fully rainbow hole fails: in the shift graph of triples (vertex set the $3$-subsets of $[n]$, two triples adjacent if the two smallest elements of one are the two largest of the other), which is triangle-free with large chromatic number, colouring each triple by its middle element gives a colouring with no hole in which every three consecutive vertices are rainbow, since every rainbow three-vertex path is monotone and cannot close up into a cycle. The question is whether some set of $s$ consecutive vertices of a hole can always be made rainbow. The authors note that every graph with bounded clique number and large enough chromatic number does at least contain a long hole (resolving an old conjecture of Gyárfás).
notes: Stated as prose in the Conclusion with 'we do not know the following'.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IX. Rainbow paths

name: AX_large_chromatic_induced_path_uniquely_covered
title: Question (uniquely-covered vertices in an induced path)
statement_text: Let $G$ be a triangle-free graph with very large chromatic number, and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a set of stable subsets (not necessarily pairwise disjoint) of $V(G)$ with union $V(G)$. Does there necessarily exist an $s$-vertex induced path $P$ of $G$ such that for each $v\in V(P)$, some $X\in\mathcal{A}$ satisfies $X\cap V(P)=\{v\}$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A colouring of $G$ is any proper colouring (not necessarily optimal), and a subgraph is rainbow if its vertices receive pairwise distinct colours. The authors prove that for all $\kappa,s\ge1$ there is $c$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\omega(G)\le\kappa$ and $\chi(G)>c$ and every colouring of $G$, some $s$-vertex induced path is rainbow (extending Gyárfás and Sárközy, who assumed girth at least five). In this question $s$ is fixed and the chromatic number of $G$ is very large in terms of $s$. A stable set is a set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices. If $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of colour classes of a proper colouring, the required property says exactly that $P$ is rainbow, so a positive answer would extend the authors' theorem (for triangle-free graphs) from partitions into stable sets to arbitrary covers by stable sets.
notes: Stated as prose in the Conclusion with 'another question to which we do not know the answer'.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IX. Rainbow paths

name: AX_h_free_clique_maximizers_polynomial_error
title: Informal Conjecture (error term in Proposition 1.4)
statement_text: Let $m<k$ and $t$ be integers with $t=1$ or $k=m+1$, let $H$ be a graph with $\chi(H)=k$, and let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $\delta(G)>(1-\epsilon)n$ for a suitable $\epsilon=\epsilon(m,t,k)>0$ and $n$ large. The authors prove that every $H$-free subgraph of $G$ with the maximum possible number of copies of $K_m(t)$ can be made $(k-1)$-colorable by deleting $o(n^2)$ edges, and believe that the error term $o(n^2)$ can be improved to $O(n^{2-\delta})$ for some $\delta := \delta(H)>0$.
context_text: $K_m(t)$ is the $t$-blow-up of $K_m$, obtained by replacing each vertex of $K_m$ by an independent set of size $t$ and each edge by a complete bipartite graph ($K_m(1)=K_m$). For a host graph $G$, $\mathcal{G}_{ex}(T,H)$ is the family of $H$-free subgraphs of $G$ with the maximum possible number of copies of $T$. A graph $H$ is edge critical if deleting some edge reduces its chromatic number. Generalizing results on Turán's theorem in host graphs of high minimum degree (Bondy–Shen–Thomassé–Thomassen, Balogh–Keevash–Sudakov, Alon–Shapira–Sudakov), the authors prove that if $H$ is edge critical with $\chi(H)=k>m$ and $\delta(G)\ge(1-\epsilon)n$, then every member of $\mathcal{G}_{ex}(K_m,H)$ is $(k-1)$-colorable, and similarly every member of $\mathcal{G}_{ex}(K_m(t),H)$ is $m$-colorable when $\chi(H)=m+1$. These cannot be directly generalized to non-edge-critical $H$, since one can add an edge to any $(k-1)$-partite graph without creating such an $H$, which is why only an approximate statement (deleting few edges) holds in general. The belief is supported by a theorem of Alon and Sudakov: if $\chi(H)=k\ge3$, $|V(H)|=h$, and $G$ is an $H$-free graph with $\delta(G)\ge(1-\frac{3}{3k-4}+o(1))n$, then deleting $O(n^{2-1/(4(k-1)^{2/3}h)})$ edges makes $G$ $(k-1)$-colorable.
notes: Stated in the introduction as 'we believe'; Section 6 (concluding remarks and open problems) is not present in the extracted text and may contain additional items.
paper_title: $H$-free subgraphs of dense graphs maximizing the number of cliques and their blow-ups

name: AX_kk_free_bounded_treewidth_max_chromatic
title: Problem 3
statement_text: For integers $k \geq 4$ and $t \geq k - 1$, what is the maximum chromatic number of $K_k$-free graphs of tree-width at most $t$?
context_text: Every graph of tree-width $t$ is $t$-degenerate, hence $(t+1)$-colourable, and $K_{t+1}$ shows this is tight. The authors prove that triangle-free graphs of tree-width at most $t$ have chromatic number at most $\lceil(t+3)/2\rceil$, and that this is tight. More generally, define $g(t,2)=g(0,k)=1$ for all $t\ge0$, $k\ge2$, and $g(t,k)=\lceil(t+1)/2\rceil+g(\lfloor(t-1)/2\rfloor,k-1)$ for $t\ge1$, $k\ge3$; they prove that for all $t\ge0$ and $k\ge2$ there is a $K_k$-free graph of tree-width at most $t$ with chromatic number at least $g(t,k)$. Here $g(t,3)=\lceil(t+3)/2\rceil$ for $t\ge1$ (so the case $k=3$ is completely resolved) and $g(t,k)>(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-2}})t$. This lower bound motivates the question for $k\ge4$, which the authors were not able to resolve. In the list colouring setting the analogous question is easy: $K_{t,t^t}$ has tree-width $t$ but is not colourable from some assignment of lists of size $t$.

paper_title: Triangle-free graphs of tree-width t are ceil((t + 3)/2)-colorable

name: AX_multitasking_interference_increases_with_depth
title: Open Problem (interference worsens with depth)
statement_text: We believe that it is also the case that interference gets worst with $r$ (namely that interference worsens as $r$ increases to $r+1$ for $r > 2$), although whether this is indeed the case is an open problem.
context_text: A network of depth 2 is a bipartite graph $G=(A\cup B,E)$ with $|A|=|B|=n$ (inputs and outputs, edges being tasks); a task set to be performed in parallel is a matching, and it can be performed without interference if it is an induced matching (no edge of $G$ joins two of its edges). $G$ is a $(k,\alpha(k))$-multitasker if every matching $M$ of size $k$ contains an induced matching $M'\subseteq M$ with $|M'|\ge\alpha(k)|M|$, and an $\alpha$-multitasker if this holds with $\alpha$ for all $k=1,\dots,n$; $\alpha(k)\in(0,1]$ is the multitasking capacity. A network with $r$ layers (depth $r$) of width $n$ and degree $d$ has vertex set partitioned into independent sets $V_1,\dots,V_r$ of size $n$, consecutive layers inducing $d$-regular bipartite graphs and no other edges; task sets are families of vertex-disjoint top-bottom paths $v_1\dots v_r$ ($v_i\in V_i$), and such a family is induced if no edge of $G$ joins edges of two different paths; the multitasking capacity is defined as before with induced path families in place of induced matchings. For $d$-regular bipartite (depth 2) graphs the authors prove $\alpha(n)=O(1/\sqrt d)$; for depth $r$ they prove that the capacity for task sets of size $n$ is $O(r/d^{1-1/r})$, so depth-$r$ networks with $2<r\ll d$ suffer strictly more interference than depth-2 networks ($r$ is thought of as a constant and $d\to\infty$). The open problem is whether the capacity keeps getting worse at each step from $r$ to $r+1$ for $r>2$.
notes: Statement appears in running prose without a labelled environment; PDF source.
paper_title: A Graph-Theoretic Approach to Multitasking

name: AX_multitasking_capacity_average_degree_log_n
title: Open Problem (multitasker at average degree $\Theta(\log n)$)
statement_text: It is an interesting question whether there exists a multitasker with $\alpha > 0$ independent of $n$, for average degree $\Theta(\log n)$, which, if true is the largest average degree possible. This is left as an open problem.
context_text: A network of depth 2 is a bipartite graph $G=(A\cup B,E)$ with $|A|=|B|=n$ (inputs and outputs, edges being tasks); a task set to be performed in parallel is a matching, and it can be performed without interference if it is an induced matching (no edge of $G$ joins two of its edges). $G$ is a $(k,\alpha(k))$-multitasker if every matching $M$ of size $k$ contains an induced matching $M'\subseteq M$ with $|M'|\ge\alpha(k)|M|$, and an $\alpha$-multitasker if this holds with $\alpha$ for all $k=1,\dots,n$; $\alpha(k)\in(0,1]$ is the multitasking capacity. Here $n$ is the number of vertices on each side, $\alpha>0$ independent of $n$ means a fixed constant capacity, and the graphs need not be regular. The authors prove that every $\alpha$-multitasker of average degree $d$ satisfies $\alpha\le O((\log n/d)^{1/3})$, so average degree $\Theta(\log n)$ is the largest possible for constant $\alpha$; for $d$-regular graphs the capacity even satisfies $\alpha(n)=O(1/\sqrt d)$. On the other hand there are multitaskers of average degree $\Omega(\log\log n)$ with $\alpha>1/3-\varepsilon$, so for the capacity to decay with the average degree one must assume $d$ grows faster than $\log\log n$. The question is whether constant-capacity multitaskers exist with average degree $\Theta(\log n)$.
notes: Statement appears in running prose without a labelled environment; PDF source.
paper_title: A Graph-Theoretic Approach to Multitasking

name: AX_quartic_eulerian_digraphs_diplanar_obstructions
title: Problem 1.2
statement_text: Determine the complete set of obstructions for diplanar quartic Eulerian digraphs.
context_text: An Eulerian digraph has in-degree equal to out-degree at every vertex; loops, parallel arcs and digons ($uv,vu$) are allowed, and digraphs need not be connected. An embedding of an Eulerian digraph in a surface is an embedding of the underlying graph in which in- and out-arcs alternate in the rotation at each vertex; a digraph with such an embedding in the plane is diplanar. Quartic Eulerian digraphs are those with in- and out-degree $2$ at every vertex; they are ordered by $H\preceq G$ if $H$ is obtained from $G$ by removing directed cycles, deleting isolated vertices and suppressing vertices of degree $2$ (replacing arcs $uv,vw$ by $uw$). For containment of general Eulerian digraphs embeddability is not hereditary, but the authors show it is hereditary under $\preceq$ for quartic ones, so diplanarity is characterised by its obstructions, the $\preceq$-minimal non-diplanar quartic Eulerian digraphs. Equivalently, the problem is to characterise the directed medial graphs of planar graphs. The authors present all known obstructions (doubled cycles, circulants and Möbius ladders, sporadic examples), reduce obstructions with digons to those without (by splitting vertices and inserting paths of digons), and classify all obstructions containing parallel arcs (anti-digons); it is not known whether their list is complete. They suggest treating next the case of simple underlying graphs, planar or not (using Möbius ladders in the non-planar case), and hope the simple, planar, $3$-connected case is more straightforward.
paper_title: Embedding Quartic Eulerian Digraphs on the Plane

name: AX_identifying_codes_hereditary_vc_dimension_dichotomy
title: VC-Dimension Dichotomy for Identifying Codes (Approximation)
statement_text: For any hereditary class of graphs $\mathcal{C}$, either (1) the minimum identifying code size has a logarithmic lower bound and Min Id Code is log-APX-hard in $\mathcal{C}$, or (2) the minimum identifying code size has a polynomial lower bound and Min Id Code admits a constant factor approximation algorithm in $\mathcal{C}$.
context_text: An identifying code of a graph $G$ is a set $C$ of vertices such that $N[v]\cap C\neq\emptyset$ for every vertex $v$ and $N[u]\cap C\neq N[v]\cap C$ for all distinct $u,v$, where $N[v]$ is the closed neighbourhood; it exists if and only if $G$ is twin-free (no two vertices with the same closed neighbourhood), and Min Id Code asks for one of minimum size $\mathrm{id}(G)$. Always $\mathrm{id}(G)\ge\log(n+1)$; Min Id Code is NP-complete and log-APX-hard in general (no $(1-\varepsilon)\log n$-approximation). A hereditary class is closed under induced subgraphs; 'logarithmic lower bound' means that the best lower bound on $\mathrm{id}$ in the class is $\Theta(\log n)$, while 'polynomial lower bound' means $\mathrm{id}(G)\ge n^{\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ and all twin-free $G$ in the class. The VC-dimension of a graph is that of the hypergraph of its closed neighbourhoods (the largest vertex set $X$ such that every subset of $X$ is $N[v]\cap X$ for some $v$), and that of a class is the supremum over its members. The dichotomy is an informal pattern observed by the authors in the known results (split, bipartite, co-bipartite, chordal graphs on one side; line, planar, unit interval graphs on the other), not a conjecture they make. The paper settles it: the lower-bound half holds (classes of infinite VC-dimension contain arbitrarily large graphs with identifying codes of logarithmic size, while classes of VC-dimension $d$ have $\mathrm{id}(G)\ge(n-1)^{1/d}$), and Min Id Code is log-APX-hard in every hereditary class of infinite VC-dimension; but the approximation half is false: $C_4$-free bipartite graphs have VC-dimension $2$ and $\mathrm{id}(G)=\Theta(n^{1/2})$, yet Min Id Code cannot be approximated within $c\log n$ for some $c>0$ in this class unless $NP\subseteq ZTIME(n^{O(\log\log n)})$. The authors give a $6$-approximation for interval graphs; constant-factor approximability remains open for graphs of girth at least $5$, chordal bipartite graphs, unit disk graphs and undirected path graphs.
notes: The lower-bound half of the dichotomy is fully proved as Theorem 2.2. The approximation half is shown to fail in general: C4-free bipartite graphs have finite VC-dimension but Min Id Code cannot be approximated within a factor of c log|V| for some c > 0 (Thm 4.3). The question of which finite VC-dimension classes admit constant-factor approximations remains open (Table 2 lists Girth ≥ 5, Chordal bipartite, Unit disk, and Undirected path graphs as open). paper_title: Identifying codes in hereditary classes of graphs and VC-dimension

name: AX_ordered_removal_lemma_regularity_free_proof
title: Open Problem: Regularity-free proof for the ordered removal lemma
statement_text: It will be interesting to try to obtain a proof for the ordered graph removal lemma that does not go through the strong regularity lemma needed in the current proof.
context_text: An ordered graph over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ ($|\Sigma|\ge2$) is an edge-coloured complete graph $G:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\Sigma$ on a totally ordered vertex set (ordinary graphs correspond to $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$); the ordered (induced) subgraph on $u_1<\dots<u_k$ is $H(ij)=G(u_iu_j)$, and $G$ is $\mathcal{F}$-free if none of its ordered subgraphs lies in $\mathcal{F}$. $G$ is $\epsilon$-far from $\mathcal{F}$-freeness if one must change at least $\epsilon\binom{n}{2}$ edge values to make it $\mathcal{F}$-free. The authors' ordered removal lemma states: for every (finite or infinite) family $\mathcal{F}$ of ordered graphs and every $\epsilon>0$ there are $q_0$ and $\delta>0$ such that every ordered graph $G$ on $n$ vertices that is $\epsilon$-far from $\mathcal{F}$-freeness contains at least $\delta n^q$ induced ordered copies of some $F\in\mathcal{F}$ on $q\le q_0$ vertices; consequently every hereditary property of ordered graphs is strongly testable (testable with a number of queries independent of $n$). An analogous lemma holds for ordered matrices $M:[m]\times[n]\to\Sigma$, with copies being submatrices on increasing rows and columns. The proof relies on strong variants of the regularity lemma: Szemerédi's regularity lemma already imposes a tower-type dependence of $\delta^{-1}$ on $\epsilon^{-1}$, and the variant used is at least as strong as the strong regularity lemma of Alon, Fischer, Krivelevich and Szegedy, which has a wowzer-type (tower of towers) dependence; for infinite families the dependence may be arbitrarily bad. Fox gave the first proof of the (unordered) graph removal lemma that avoids the regularity lemma, though still with tower-type dependence. The open problem is to find a proof of the ordered removal lemma that does not go through strong regularity.
notes: Stated as a research direction in Section 1.3 without a formal labelled environment.
paper_title: Testing hereditary properties of ordered graphs and matrices

name: AX_ordered_removal_lemma_binary_matrices_polynomial
title: Open Problem: Better parameter dependence for ordered binary matrix removal
statement_text: It will be interesting to combine the ideas from the current proof with the binary matrix regularity lemma of Alon, Fischer and Newman to obtain a removal lemma for finite families of ordered binary matrices with better dependence between the parameters $\delta^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}$; ideally polynomial dependence, but even exponential dependence would be interesting.
context_text: An ordered graph over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ ($|\Sigma|\ge2$) is an edge-coloured complete graph $G:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\Sigma$ on a totally ordered vertex set (ordinary graphs correspond to $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$); the ordered (induced) subgraph on $u_1<\dots<u_k$ is $H(ij)=G(u_iu_j)$, and $G$ is $\mathcal{F}$-free if none of its ordered subgraphs lies in $\mathcal{F}$. $G$ is $\epsilon$-far from $\mathcal{F}$-freeness if one must change at least $\epsilon\binom{n}{2}$ edge values to make it $\mathcal{F}$-free. The authors' ordered removal lemma states: for every (finite or infinite) family $\mathcal{F}$ of ordered graphs and every $\epsilon>0$ there are $q_0$ and $\delta>0$ such that every ordered graph $G$ on $n$ vertices that is $\epsilon$-far from $\mathcal{F}$-freeness contains at least $\delta n^q$ induced ordered copies of some $F\in\mathcal{F}$ on $q\le q_0$ vertices; consequently every hereditary property of ordered graphs is strongly testable (testable with a number of queries independent of $n$). An analogous lemma holds for ordered matrices $M:[m]\times[n]\to\Sigma$, with copies being submatrices on increasing rows and columns. For binary matrices, $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. Alon, Fischer and Newman obtained an efficient conditional regularity lemma for ordered binary matrices, in which $\delta^{-1}$ is polynomial in $\epsilon^{-1}$, and conjectured that it could yield a removal lemma for finite families of ordered binary matrices; the present paper proves such a removal lemma (in a generalized form, for any finite alphabet and infinite families), but its proof uses a variant of the strong regularity lemma and so inherits a wowzer-type (tower of towers) dependence of $\delta^{-1}$ on $\epsilon^{-1}$. The problem is to obtain, for finite families of ordered binary matrices, a removal lemma with polynomial, or even exponential, dependence of $\delta^{-1}$ on $\epsilon^{-1}$. More generally, the authors ask for large families of hereditary ordered graph or matrix properties with more efficient testers.
notes: Stated as a research direction in Section 1.3 without a formal labelled environment.
paper_title: Testing hereditary properties of ordered graphs and matrices

name: AX_bipartite_johnson_lindenstrauss_bounded_norms
title: Conjecture 2.4
statement_text: There exists an absolute positive constant $C$ such that for all vectors $a_1,\ldots,a_n,b_1,\ldots,b_n\in\mathbb{R}^n$, each of Euclidean norm at most $1$, and for every $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $t=\lfloor C\log(2+\varepsilon^2 n)/\varepsilon^2\rfloor$, there are vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb{R}^t$ such that $|\langle x_i,y_j\rangle-\langle a_i,b_j\rangle|\le\varepsilon$ for all $i,j$, together with the further requirement that $\|x_i\| \leq O(1)$ and $\|y_i\| \leq O(1)$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$.
context_text: This is a problem of high-dimensional geometry (dimension reduction and compression of inner products). The authors prove the statement without the norm requirement (a bipartite Johnson–Lindenstrauss-type reduction, with a randomized polynomial-time algorithm), motivated by the suggestion of Larsen and Nelson that for small $\varepsilon$ the Johnson–Lindenstrauss dimension $\frac{\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$ might be improvable to $\frac{\log(2+\varepsilon^2n)}{\varepsilon^2}$. The conjecture asks that the output vectors can moreover be taken of bounded norm. It is trivial for $\varepsilon<\sqrt{C/(2n)}$ (then $t\ge n$), and for $\varepsilon>1/n^{0.49}$ it follows from the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma. If true, together with the paper's methods it would determine up to a constant factor $f(n,n,\varepsilon)$, the minimum number of bits needed to store all inner products between $n$ vectors of norm at most $1$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ up to additive error $\varepsilon$, for all $\varepsilon\ge2/\sqrt n$: the authors currently have $\Omega(nt)\le f(n,k,\varepsilon)\le O(n\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ for $t\le k\le n$, where $t=\log(2+\varepsilon^2n)/\varepsilon^2$. The authors support the conjecture by proving it when $t=\Omega(n)$, i.e. $\varepsilon=\Theta(1/\sqrt n)$, via a Gaussian random construction.
notes: PDF source — norm notation $\|\cdot\|$ appears as bare vertical bars in the raw extract; reconstructed from context. The paper proves two partial results supporting the conjecture: the case $t = \Omega(n)$ (i.e., $\varepsilon = \Theta(1/\sqrt{n})$) is established as Theorem 2.5, and a matching bit-count estimate is proved for the column-query variant.
paper_title: Optimal compression of approximate inner products and dimension reduction

name: AX_thin_overlays_sublinear_separators_unbounded_degree
title: Informal Conjecture (Section 1.2): dropping bounded-degree assumption
statement_text: The authors prove that subgraph-closed graph classes with strongly sublinear separators and bounded maximum degree admit thin systems of overlays. It seems plausible that the additional assumption of bounded maximum degree could be dropped, i.e. that every subgraph-closed class with strongly sublinear separators admits thin systems of overlays, leading to a much more general result strengthening the majority of the known approximation algorithms (Baker-type, bidimensionality-based, local search) that the authors survey.
context_text: An overlay of a graph $G$ is a triple $(H,f,\ell)$ where $H$ is a graph, $f:V(H)\to V(G)$ is a homomorphism and $\ell:V(H)\to\{0,1,2,\dots\}$; it is an $r$-neighborhood overlay if $\ell\le r$, every $v\in V(G)$ has a preimage $x$ with $\ell(x)=r$, and it is walk-preserving: for every $x$ with $\ell(x)\ge1$ and every neighbour $w$ of $f(x)$ in $G$, $x$ has a neighbour $y$ with $f(y)=w$ and $\ell(y)\ge\ell(x)-1$ (so the radius-$r$ neighbourhood of each vertex is faithfully represented). A system of overlays is a multiset $\mathcal{L}$ of them; its thickness is $\max_v\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{(H,f,\ell)\in\mathcal{L}}|f^{-1}(v)|$ and its treewidth the maximum treewidth of the graphs $H$. Roughly, a class admits thin systems of overlays if for all positive integers $r,k$ every $n$-vertex member has a system of $r$-neighborhood overlays of thickness at most $1+1/k$, treewidth bounded by a function $t(r,k)$, and size polynomial in some function $q(n)$ (for the classes considered $q(n)$ is constant or $e^{(\log\log n)^2}$), computable efficiently. Such systems generalize Baker's bounded-treewidth layerings and yield simple polynomial-time approximation schemes for maximum independent set, minimum dominating set and their distance-$r$ versions, $H$-matching, vertex cover, and some monotone MSO-expressible problems. A balanced separation of $G$ is a pair $(A,B)$ of edge-disjoint subgraphs with $A\cup B=G$ and $|V(A)\setminus V(B)|,|V(B)\setminus V(A)|\le 2|V(G)|/3$, of size $|V(A)\cap V(B)|$; a class has sublinear separators if every $n$-vertex member has one of size $o(n)$, and strongly sublinear separators if of size at most $cn^{\delta}$ for constants $c\ge1$, $\delta<1$ (for subgraph-closed classes this is equivalent to polynomial expansion, by Dvořák and Norin). The authors prove that all proper minor-closed classes, and all subgraph-closed classes with bounded maximum degree and strongly sublinear separators, admit thin systems of overlays (in the latter case with $q(n)=e^{(\log\log n)^2}$). Every class admitting thin systems of overlays is fractionally treewidth-fragile, and the authors note that even the simpler question (raised earlier by Dvořák) whether subgraph-closed classes with strongly sublinear separators are fractionally treewidth-fragile is open.

name: AX_independent_set_apx_hard_nonsublinear_separators
title: Open Problem (Section 1.2): APX-hardness on classes without sublinear separators
statement_text: It would be interesting to see whether this intuition can be made precise and for example show that the maximum independent set problem is APX-hard on any subgraph-closed class of graphs that does not have sublinear separators (or at least has exponential expansion).
context_text: A balanced separation of $G$ is a pair $(A,B)$ of edge-disjoint subgraphs with $A\cup B=G$ and $|V(A)\setminus V(B)|,|V(B)\setminus V(A)|\le 2|V(G)|/3$, of size $|V(A)\cap V(B)|$; a class has sublinear separators if every $n$-vertex member has one of size $o(n)$, and strongly sublinear separators if of size at most $cn^{\delta}$ for constants $c\ge1$, $\delta<1$ (for subgraph-closed classes this is equivalent to polynomial expansion, by Dvořák and Norin). The expansion of a class measures the maximum average degree of its bounded-depth minors as a function of the depth (polynomial, subexponential or exponential expansion); the class of 3-regular graphs has exponential expansion, and subexponential expansion implies sublinear separators. Maximum independent set (and minimum dominating set) is APX-hard already on graphs of bounded maximum degree, in particular on 3-regular graphs, so approximation schemes cannot extend to classes containing all 3-regular graphs. The authors give approximation schemes (via so-called thin systems of overlays, a generalization of Baker's bounded-treewidth layerings) for proper minor-closed classes and for bounded-degree subgraph-closed classes with strongly sublinear separators, and observe that every class admitting their decompositions has sublinear separators. They suggest that this intuition might be made precise, e.g. by showing APX-hardness of maximum independent set on every subgraph-closed class without sublinear separators, or at least on every such class with exponential expansion.

name: AX_tournament_large_domination_forces_si
title: Problem 3
statement_text: For every integer $i \geq 1$, there exists $f(i)$ such that every tournament $T$ with dominating number at least $f(i)$ contains an isomorphic copy of $S_i$.
context_text: The chromatic number $\vec{\chi}(T)$ of a tournament $T$ (its dichromatic number) is the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices so that each color class induces an acyclic, i.e. transitive, subtournament. A set $S$ of vertices is dominating if every vertex outside $S$ has an in-neighbor in $S$, and the dominating number $\gamma(T)$ is the minimum size of a dominating set. A tournament is $t$-local if the out-neighborhood of every vertex induces a subtournament of chromatic number at most $t$; the paper's main result, answering a conjecture of Berger et al., is that $t$-local tournaments have chromatic number bounded by a function of $t$. A key step is that for every $k$ there are $K$ and $\ell$ such that every tournament with dominating number at least $K$ contains a subtournament on $\ell$ vertices with chromatic number at least $k$. The problem asks whether large dominating number forces a specific high-chromatic subtournament. $S_1$ is the one-vertex tournament and, for $i>1$, $S_i$ is the tournament on $2^i-1$ vertices obtained from a cyclically oriented triangle by blowing up two of its vertices into copies of $S_{i-1}$ (replacing a vertex by a copy of $S_{i-1}$, all arcs to and from it being kept for every vertex of the copy); one can check that $\vec{\chi}(S_i)\ge i$. The problem is trivial for $i\le2$, verified for $i=3$ by Chudnovsky, Kim, Liu, Seymour and Thomassé, and open for all $i\ge4$.

name: AX_tournament_large_domination_small_subtournament
title: Problem 4
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 1$, there exist integers $K$ and $\ell$ such that every tournament $T$ with dominating number at least $K$ contains a subtournament with $\ell$ vertices and dominating number at least $k$.
context_text: The chromatic number $\vec{\chi}(T)$ of a tournament $T$ (its dichromatic number) is the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices so that each color class induces an acyclic, i.e. transitive, subtournament. A set $S$ of vertices is dominating if every vertex outside $S$ has an in-neighbor in $S$, and the dominating number $\gamma(T)$ is the minimum size of a dominating set. A key step is that for every $k$ there are $K$ and $\ell$ such that every tournament with dominating number at least $K$ contains a subtournament on $\ell$ vertices with chromatic number at least $k$. This problem asks for the analogue of that step with dominating number also in the conclusion. The analogous question with chromatic number in the hypothesis fails for every $k\ge3$: orienting a graph of huge chromatic number and girth larger than $\ell$ along a vertex enumeration (forward along edges, backward along non-edges) gives tournaments of arbitrarily large chromatic number in which every subtournament on $\ell$ vertices has chromatic number at most $2$.

name: AX_planar_independence_number_n_over_4
title: Open Problem (independence number of planar graphs)
statement_text: It is an intriguing open problem to describe planar graphs on $n$ vertices whose independence number is exactly $n/4$, and we do not even know any polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether an $n$-vertex planar graph has an independent set larger than $n/4$.
context_text: By the Four Colour Theorem every planar graph is 4-colourable, giving an independent set of size at least $n/4$, and there are infinitely many planar graphs for which this bound is tight. The paper studies the easier related problem for triangle-free planar graphs (where Grötzsch's theorem raises the bound to $n/3$) as a tractable surrogate for this harder general question.

name: AX_planar_graphs_bounded_queue_number
title: Queue Number of Planar Graphs
statement_text: A challenging open problem in the area of queue layouts is to decide whether planar graphs have constant queue number.
context_text: A queue layout of a graph is an ordering of its vertices (the spine) together with a colouring of its edges such that no two edges of the same colour are nested, where two edges are nested if their four endpoints are distinct and the endpoints of one edge induce an interval of the spine containing the endpoints of the other edge. The queue number of a graph is the minimum number of colours in a queue layout; the question is whether there is a constant $c$ such that every planar graph has queue number at most $c$. This is a known open problem from the queue-layout literature, mentioned by the authors as background. Every graph has a subdivision with queue number $2$, and Dujmović and Wood showed that graphs of bounded queue number form a class of bounded expansion (a notion of sparsity of Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez). The paper's main theorem says that posets of bounded height whose cover graphs belong to a fixed class of bounded expansion have bounded dimension; hence posets whose cover graph has bounded queue number have dimension bounded by a function of the queue number and the height. Status note (November 2026): solved; Dujmović, Joret, Micek, Morin, Ueckerdt and Wood proved that planar graphs have bounded queue number ('Planar graphs have bounded queue-number', arXiv 2019, J. ACM 2020).
notes: This is an existing open problem from the queue-layout literature, referenced via citation [3]; it is not introduced by the paper's authors but is presented in running prose as background motivation. No labelled theorem environment. PDF source — math notation appears clean for this item.
