name: AX_spanning_tree_polytope_xc_bounded_genus
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: If $G = (V, E)$ is a connected graph embedded in a fixed surface, then $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G)) = O(|V|)$.
context_text: For a connected (simple, finite) graph $G=(V,E)$, the spanning tree polytope $P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^E$ is the convex hull of the characteristic vectors of the spanning trees of $G$. An extended formulation of a polytope $P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ is a linear system $Ax+By\le b$, $Cx+Dy=c$ in variables $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $y\in\mathbb{R}^k$ such that $P=\{x:\exists y,\ Ax+By\le b,\ Cx+Dy=c\}$; its size is its number of inequalities (equalities are not counted), and the extension complexity $\mathrm{xc}(P)$ is the minimum size of an extended formulation of $P$, equivalently the minimum number of facets of a polytope that affinely projects onto $P$. Known bounds: $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G))=O(|V||E|)$ for every connected graph (Wong, Martin), and $O(|V|)$ for connected planar graphs (Williams). Here the genus $g$ of a surface is its number of handles or crosscaps (orientable and non-orientable surfaces are both allowed), and the constant in the $O(\cdot)$ may depend on the surface. The authors prove that $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G))=O(g^{1/2}|V|^{3/2}+g^{3/2}|V|^{1/2})$ for connected graphs embedded in a surface of genus $g$, hence $O(|V|^{3/2})$ for fixed $g$ (previously known formulations had size $O(|V|^2+g|V|)$), and conjecture that the linear planar bound extends to every fixed surface.
paper_title: Smaller Extended Formulations for the Spanning Tree Polytope of Bounded-genus Graphs

name: AX_spanning_tree_polytope_xc_minor_closed
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: If $\mathcal{C}$ is a proper minor-closed family of graphs and $G = (V, E)$ is a connected graph in $\mathcal{C}$, then $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G)) = O(|V|)$.
context_text: For a connected (simple, finite) graph $G=(V,E)$, the spanning tree polytope $P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^E$ is the convex hull of the characteristic vectors of the spanning trees of $G$. An extended formulation of a polytope $P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ is a linear system $Ax+By\le b$, $Cx+Dy=c$ in variables $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $y\in\mathbb{R}^k$ such that $P=\{x:\exists y,\ Ax+By\le b,\ Cx+Dy=c\}$; its size is its number of inequalities (equalities are not counted), and the extension complexity $\mathrm{xc}(P)$ is the minimum size of an extended formulation of $P$, equivalently the minimum number of facets of a polytope that affinely projects onto $P$. Known bounds: $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G))=O(|V||E|)$ for every connected graph (Wong, Martin), and $O(|V|)$ for connected planar graphs (Williams). A minor-closed family is proper if it does not contain all graphs; the constant in the $O(\cdot)$ may depend on $\mathcal{C}$. This generalizes the authors' conjecture that the bound is linear for graphs embedded in any fixed surface (they prove $O(|V|^{3/2})$ there). The conjecture is known to hold when the graphs in $\mathcal{C}$ have bounded treewidth (Kolman, Koutecký, Tiwary), and the authors prove it for $k$-apex graphs (graphs $G$ with a set $X$ of at most $k$ vertices such that $G-X$ is planar), showing $\mathrm{xc}(P_{\mathrm{sp.trees}}(G))=O(k|E|)=O(k^2|V|)$.
paper_title: Smaller Extended Formulations for the Spanning Tree Polytope of Bounded-genus Graphs

name: AX_fair_representation_path_partition_independent_set
title: Conjecture 1.6
statement_text: Given a partition of the vertex set of a path into sets $V_1, \ldots, V_m$ there exists an independent set $S$ and integers $b_i$, $i \leq m$, such that $|S \cap V_i| \geq \frac{|V_i|}{2} - b_i$ for all $i$, and 1. $\sum_{i \leq m} b_i \leq \frac{m}{2}$ and 2. $b_i \leq 1$ for all $i \leq m$.
context_text: The paper studies fair representation. For a simplicial complex $\mathcal{C}$ (a down-closed hypergraph, e.g. the independent sets of a graph, or the matchings of a graph, called its matching complex), $\beta(\mathcal{C})$ is the minimum number of members of $\mathcal{C}$ covering $V(\mathcal{C})$. A member $S$ represents a vertex set $A$ fairly if $|S\cap A|\ge\lfloor|A|/\beta(\mathcal{C})\rfloor$, and almost fairly if $|S\cap A|\ge\lfloor|A|/\beta(\mathcal{C})\rfloor-1$; the goal is to represent all parts of a partition of $V(\mathcal{C})$ (almost) fairly at once, like a parliament representing parties. This always works in matroids but not in general independence complexes. Matching complexes (independence complexes of line graphs) behave better: for every graph $H$ and partition $E_1,\dots,E_m$ of $E(H)$ there is a matching $M$ with $|M\cap E_i|\ge\lfloor|E_i|/(\Delta(L(H))+2)\rfloor$, where $L(H)$ is the line graph, a consequence of a topological connectivity bound for independence complexes of line graphs. For a path on $n$ vertices the independent sets have $\beta=2$, so fair representation means $|S\cap V_i|\ge|V_i|/2$ roughly; the matching complex of a path is the independence complex of a path one vertex shorter. The conjecture is a slightly stronger form of almost fair representation for paths: the total deficit $\sum b_i$ is at most $m/2$ and each individual deficit is at most 1. The authors prove each condition separately. Using the Borsuk–Ulam theorem, they get an independent set and integers $b_i$ with $\sum_i b_i\le m/2$ and $|S\cap V_i|\ge|V_i|/2-b_i$. Using Schrijver's strengthening of Lovász's Kneser theorem, they show that for every partition of the vertex set of a cycle into $V_1,\dots,V_m$ there is an independent set with $|S\cap V_i|\ge|V_i|/2-1$ for all $i$. Having both conditions at once is open. The conjecture is related to Ryser's conjecture on transversals of Latin squares.

name: AX_fair_representation_knn_perfect_matching
title: Conjecture 1.9
statement_text: For any partition $E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_m$ of $E(K_{n,n})$ and any $j \leq m$ there exists a perfect matching $F$ in $K_{n,n}$ satisfying $|F \cap E_i| \geq \left\lfloor \frac{|E_i|}{n} \right\rfloor$ for all $i \neq j$, and $|F \cap E_j| \geq \left\lfloor \frac{|E_j|}{n} \right\rfloor - 1$.
context_text: The paper studies fair representation. For a simplicial complex $\mathcal{C}$ (a down-closed hypergraph, e.g. the independent sets of a graph, or the matchings of a graph, called its matching complex), $\beta(\mathcal{C})$ is the minimum number of members of $\mathcal{C}$ covering $V(\mathcal{C})$. A member $S$ represents a vertex set $A$ fairly if $|S\cap A|\ge\lfloor|A|/\beta(\mathcal{C})\rfloor$, and almost fairly if $|S\cap A|\ge\lfloor|A|/\beta(\mathcal{C})\rfloor-1$; the goal is to represent all parts of a partition of $V(\mathcal{C})$ (almost) fairly at once, like a parliament representing parties. This always works in matroids but not in general independence complexes. Matching complexes (independence complexes of line graphs) behave better: for every graph $H$ and partition $E_1,\dots,E_m$ of $E(H)$ there is a matching $M$ with $|M\cap E_i|\ge\lfloor|E_i|/(\Delta(L(H))+2)\rfloor$, where $L(H)$ is the line graph, a consequence of a topological connectivity bound for independence complexes of line graphs. For the matching complex of $K_{n,n}$, $\beta=n$ (the edges split into $n$ perfect matchings), so the conjecture says that any partition of $E(K_{n,n})$ is represented almost fairly by a perfect matching, with a deficit of at most one in a single prescribed class $E_j$ only. The authors prove it for $m=2$, where the main work is characterizing when a deficit is needed, and for $m=3$, by a topological argument using Sperner's lemma. A special case is the Stein-type conjecture that if $E(K_{n,n})$ is partitioned into $n$ sets of size $n$, some matching contains one edge from all but at most one set, related to the Brualdi–Stein conjecture on partial transversals of Latin squares. The paper's display has $\lfloor|E_i|/n\rfloor-1$ in the last inequality, an evident typo for $\lfloor|E_j|/n\rfloor-1$.

name: AX_fair_representation_matching_delta_plus_2
title: Conjecture 1.14
statement_text: If the edge set of a graph $H$ is partitioned into sets $E_1, \ldots, E_m$ then there exists a matching $M$ satisfying $|M \cap E_i| \geq \left\lfloor \frac{|E_i|}{\Delta(H)+2} \right\rfloor$ for all $i \leq m$.
context_text: The paper studies fair representation. For a simplicial complex $\mathcal{C}$ (a down-closed hypergraph, e.g. the independent sets of a graph, or the matchings of a graph, called its matching complex), $\beta(\mathcal{C})$ is the minimum number of members of $\mathcal{C}$ covering $V(\mathcal{C})$. This always works in matroids but not in general independence complexes. Matching complexes (independence complexes of line graphs) behave better: for every graph $H$ and partition $E_1,\dots,E_m$ of $E(H)$ there is a matching $M$ with $|M\cap E_i|\ge\lfloor|E_i|/(\Delta(L(H))+2)\rfloor$, where $L(H)$ is the line graph, a consequence of a topological connectivity bound for independence complexes of line graphs. $\Delta(H)$ is the maximum degree of $H$. The conjecture is a stronger version of a conjecture of Aharoni, Barát and Wanless on rainbow matchings: if $E_1,\dots,E_m$ are sets of edges of a bipartite graph with $|E_i|>\Delta(\bigcup_i E_i)+1$ for all $i$, then there is a rainbow matching (one edge from each $E_i$, pairwise disjoint). There is an example where $|E_i|\ge\Delta+1$ does not suffice, and that conjecture fails for multisets. The bound $\Delta(H)+2$ mirrors the connectivity bound for independence complexes of line graphs, which gives the weaker known result above with $\Delta(L(H))+2$ in place of $\Delta(H)+2$.

name: AX_fair_representation_bipartite_matching_under_representation
title: Conjecture 1.15
statement_text: For every $m$ there exists a number $c(m)$ for which the following is true: if $G$ is a bipartite graph and $E_1, \ldots, E_m$ are any sets of edges, then there exists a matching $S$ in $G$ of size at least $\frac{|E(G)|}{\Delta(G)} - c(m)$ such that $|S \cap E_i| \leq \left\lceil \frac{|E_i|}{\Delta(G)} \right\rceil$ for all $i \leq m$.
context_text: The paper studies fair representation. For a simplicial complex $\mathcal{C}$ (a down-closed hypergraph, e.g. the independent sets of a graph, or the matchings of a graph, called its matching complex), $\beta(\mathcal{C})$ is the minimum number of members of $\mathcal{C}$ covering $V(\mathcal{C})$. A member $S$ represents a vertex set $A$ fairly if $|S\cap A|\ge\lfloor|A|/\beta(\mathcal{C})\rfloor$, and almost fairly if $|S\cap A|\ge\lfloor|A|/\beta(\mathcal{C})\rfloor-1$; the goal is to represent all parts of a partition of $V(\mathcal{C})$ (almost) fairly at once, like a parliament representing parties. This always works in matroids but not in general independence complexes. Matching complexes (independence complexes of line graphs) behave better: for every graph $H$ and partition $E_1,\dots,E_m$ of $E(H)$ there is a matching $M$ with $|M\cap E_i|\ge\lfloor|E_i|/(\Delta(L(H))+2)\rfloor$, where $L(H)$ is the line graph, a consequence of a topological connectivity bound for independence complexes of line graphs. $\Delta(G)$ is the maximum degree of $G$; by König's theorem the edges of a bipartite graph $G$ split into $\Delta(G)$ matchings, so a matching of size about $|E(G)|/\Delta(G)$ is a natural target. Over-representation statements like the conjectures above easily fail when the sets $E_i$ are not a partition, which suggests stating them as under-representation by a large matching. When the $E_i$ form a partition, the under-representation condition implies that all but $c(m)$ sets are fairly represented, and it defines a generalized partition matroid, so the conjecture concerns representation by a set in the intersection of three matroids. The authors suggest that $c(m)=m/2$ may suffice.

name: AX_k_coloring_maximal_local_connectivity_k
title: Question 1.7
statement_text: For fixed $k \geq 4$, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a $k$-connected graph $G$ with maximal local connectivity $k$, finds a $k$-colouring of $G$, or determines that none exists?
context_text: The local connectivity $\kappa(x,y)$ of distinct vertices $x,y$ is the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint $x$–$y$ paths, and the local edge-connectivity $\lambda(x,y)$ the maximum number of edge-disjoint $x$–$y$ paths. A graph has maximal local connectivity $k$ if $\kappa(x,y)\le k$ for all distinct $x,y$, and maximal local edge-connectivity $k$ if $\lambda(x,y)\le k$ for all distinct $x,y$; the first class contains the second, which contains all graphs of maximum degree $k$. By a theorem of Mader, all these graphs are $(k+1)$-colourable. For a $k$-connected graph with maximal local connectivity $k$, $\kappa(x,y)=k$ for all pairs. The authors prove a Brooks-type theorem: for $k\ge3$, a $k$-connected graph with maximal local edge-connectivity $k$ is $k$-colourable unless it is a complete graph or an odd wheel, which gives a polynomial-time $k$-colouring algorithm for that class. For $k=3$ the two $3$-connected classes coincide, and a $3$-connected graph with maximal local connectivity $3$ is $3$-colourable iff it is not an odd wheel, but for $k=4$ they differ, so the case of $k$-connected graphs with maximal local connectivity $k$, $k\ge4$, remains open. In contrast, $k$-colourability is NP-complete for minimally $k$-connected graphs ($k\ge3$), and $3$-colourability is NP-complete for $(k-1)$-connected graphs with maximal local connectivity $k$.
paper_title: Colouring graphs with constraints on connectivity

name: AX_planar_c4_c7_free_3_choosable
title: Open Question on 3-Choosability for Forbidden Cycles 4–7 and 4–6
statement_text: It is not known whether excluding cycles of lengths 4 to 7, or even 4 to 6, forces a planar graph to be 3-choosable. The latter question is wide open even for ordinary coloring.
context_text: After establishing 3-choosability for planar graphs without cycles of lengths 4 to 8, the authors remark that the analogous questions for shorter forbidden cycle ranges remain open. They note that the case of forbidden lengths 4 to 7 might be approachable with the methods of the paper, whereas the case 4 to 6 is wide open even for ordinary 3-colorability.
paper_title: Correspondence coloring and its application to list-coloring planar graphs without cycles of lengths 4 to 8

name: AX_planar_c4_c8_free_correspondence_coloring
title: Informal Conjecture on Correspondence Chromatic Number of Planar Graphs Without Cycles 4–8
statement_text: Every planar graph $G$ without cycles of lengths 4 to 8 has correspondence chromatic number at most 3, i.e., $G$ is $C$-colorable for every 3-correspondence assignment $C$ (without the additional assumption of consistency on closed walks of length 3).
context_text: Graphs are simple. A $k$-correspondence assignment $C$ for a graph $G$ assigns to each edge $uv$ a partial matching $C_{uv}$ between $\{u\}\times[k]$ and $\{v\}\times[k]$; a $C$-coloring is a map $\varphi:V(G)\to[k]$ such that for every edge $uv$ the pairs $(u,\varphi(u))$ and $(v,\varphi(v))$ are not matched in $C_{uv}$, and the correspondence chromatic number of $G$ is the least $k$ such that $G$ is $C$-colorable for every $k$-correspondence assignment $C$ (a notion introduced in this paper). It generalizes list coloring: for a closed walk $v_1v_2\dots v_m$ with $v_m=v_1$, $C$ is inconsistent on it if there are colors $c_1,\dots,c_m$ with $(v_i,c_i)(v_{i+1},c_{i+1})\in C_{v_iv_{i+1}}$ for all $i$ and $c_1\ne c_m$, and a graph is $k$-choosable if and only if it is $C$-colorable for every $k$-correspondence assignment consistent on all closed walks. Correspondence coloring allows reductions by identifying vertices, which is what the authors use to prove, answering a question of Borodin, that every planar graph without cycles of lengths $4$ to $8$ is $3$-choosable; in fact they prove that such a graph is $C$-colorable for every $3$-correspondence assignment $C$ consistent on every closed walk of length $3$. This consistency restriction is needed for their main reduction, and they remark that they know no counterexample to the stronger claim stated here.
paper_title: Correspondence coloring and its application to list-coloring planar graphs without cycles of lengths 4 to 8

name: AX_outdegree_transitive_tournament_subdivision_semidegree
title: Conjecture 3
statement_text: There exists a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^0}(TT_k)$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\delta^0(D) \geq \mathrm{mader}_{\delta^0}(TT_k)$ contains a subdivision of $TT_k$.
context_text: A subdivision of a digraph $F$ is obtained by replacing arcs of $F$ by directed paths (internally disjoint, with new internal vertices). For a digraph parameter $\gamma$, a digraph $F$ is $\gamma$-maderian if there is a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\gamma(D)\ge\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ contains a subdivision of $F$. Here $\delta^+(D)$ and $\delta^-(D)$ are the minimum out- and in-degree and $\delta^0(D)=\min\{\delta^+(D),\delta^-(D)\}$; every $\delta^+$-maderian digraph is $\delta^0$-maderian. This is motivated by Mader's theorem that graphs of large minimum degree contain a subdivision of $K_k$, whose naive directed analogue fails. $TT_k$ denotes the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices. Mader conjectured that every acyclic digraph is $\delta^+$-maderian, equivalently (as every acyclic digraph is a subdigraph of a transitive tournament of the same order) that there is a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^+}(TT_k)$ such that every digraph with $\delta^+(D)\ge\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^+}(TT_k)$ contains a subdivision of $TT_k$; he proved $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^+}(TT_4)=3$, but even the existence of $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^+}(TT_5)$ is open. This $\delta^0$ version is implied by Mader's conjecture and is in fact equivalent to it: if transitive tournaments are $\delta^0$-maderian then $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^+}(TT_k)\le\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^0}(TT_{2k})$, by applying the $\delta^0$ statement to the digraph made of $D$ and a reversed copy of $D$ with all arcs from the reversed copy to $D$.

name: AX_digraph_subdivision_oriented_trees_min_outdegree
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: Every oriented tree is $\delta^+$-maderian.
context_text: A subdivision of a digraph $F$ is obtained by replacing arcs of $F$ by directed paths (internally disjoint, with new internal vertices). For a digraph parameter $\gamma$, a digraph $F$ is $\gamma$-maderian if there is a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\gamma(D)\ge\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ contains a subdivision of $F$. Here $\delta^+(D)$ and $\delta^-(D)$ are the minimum out- and in-degree and $\delta^0(D)=\min\{\delta^+(D),\delta^-(D)\}$; every $\delta^+$-maderian digraph is $\delta^0$-maderian. This is motivated by Mader's theorem that graphs of large minimum degree contain a subdivision of $K_k$, whose naive directed analogue fails. An oriented tree is an orientation of an undirected tree. A greedy procedure shows that every oriented tree $T$ is $\delta^0$-maderian with $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^0}(T)=|T|-1$, but whether oriented trees are $\delta^+$-maderian is open; this is posed as a natural important step towards Mader's conjecture that every acyclic digraph is $\delta^+$-maderian. As evidence, the authors prove that every oriented path $P$ is $\delta^+$-maderian with $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^+}(P)=|V(P)|-1$, and that in-arborescences (oriented trees with all arcs directed towards a root) are $\delta^+$-maderian, which is not obvious since minimum out-degree gives no control on in-degrees; out-arborescences trivially satisfy $\mathrm{mader}_{\delta^+}(T)=|T|-1$.

name: AX_digraph_subdivision_maderian_disjoint_union
title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: If $F_1$ and $F_2$ are $\delta^+$-maderian, then the disjoint union of $F_1$ and $F_2$ is also $\delta^+$-maderian.
context_text: A subdivision of a digraph $F$ is obtained by replacing arcs of $F$ by directed paths (internally disjoint, with new internal vertices). For a digraph parameter $\gamma$, a digraph $F$ is $\gamma$-maderian if there is a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\gamma(D)\ge\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ contains a subdivision of $F$. Here $\delta^+(D)$ and $\delta^-(D)$ are the minimum out- and in-degree and $\delta^0(D)=\min\{\delta^+(D),\delta^-(D)\}$; every $\delta^+$-maderian digraph is $\delta^0$-maderian. This is motivated by Mader's theorem that graphs of large minimum degree contain a subdivision of $K_k$, whose naive directed analogue fails. This would follow from a conjecture of Alon that there is a function $h$ such that every digraph with minimum out-degree at least $h(k)$ has a vertex partition $(V_1,V_2)$ with both induced subdigraphs of minimum out-degree at least $k$ (even the existence of $h(2)$ is open). A digraph $F$ has the Erdős–Pósa property if for every $k$ there is $\phi(k)$ such that every digraph either contains a subdivision of $k\times F$ (the disjoint union of $k$ copies of $F$) or has a set of at most $\phi(k)$ vertices whose deletion leaves no subdivision of $F$. The authors observe that if $F$ is $\delta^+$-maderian and has the Erdős–Pósa property then $k\times F$ is $\delta^+$-maderian for all $k$; with results of Reed et al. and Akhoondian et al., this shows that disjoint unions of directed cycles are $\delta^+$-maderian.

name: AX_digraph_subdivision_oriented_trees_chromatic_2k
title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: If $T$ is an oriented tree of order $k$, then $\mathrm{mader}_{\chi}(T) \leq 2k-2$.
context_text: A subdivision of a digraph $F$ is obtained by replacing arcs of $F$ by directed paths (internally disjoint, with new internal vertices). For a digraph parameter $\gamma$, a digraph $F$ is $\gamma$-maderian if there is a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\gamma(D)\ge\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ contains a subdivision of $F$. Here $\delta^+(D)$ and $\delta^-(D)$ are the minimum out- and in-degree and $\delta^0(D)=\min\{\delta^+(D),\delta^-(D)\}$; every $\delta^+$-maderian digraph is $\delta^0$-maderian. This is motivated by Mader's theorem that graphs of large minimum degree contain a subdivision of $K_k$, whose naive directed analogue fails. Here $\chi(D)$ is the chromatic number of the underlying graph of $D$, and an oriented tree (forest) is an orientation of a tree (forest); the order of $T$ is its number of vertices. Burr proved that every digraph with chromatic number at least $(k-1)^2$ contains every oriented forest of order $k$ (improved to $k^2/2-k/2+1$ by Addario-Berry et al.), so oriented forests are $\chi$-maderian, and conversely only oriented forests are $\chi$-maderian (Cohen et al.). Determining $\mathrm{mader}_\chi(T)$ is open. Burr conjectured that every digraph with chromatic number $2k-2$ contains every oriented tree of order $k$ as a subdigraph; this statement, which only asks for a subdivision, is a consequence of Burr's conjecture and is proposed as an interesting step towards it.

name: AX_digraph_subdivision_dichromatic_complete_digraph
title: Problem 12
statement_text: What is $\mathrm{mader}_{\vec{\chi}}(\vec{K}_n)$?
context_text: A subdivision of a digraph $F$ is obtained by replacing arcs of $F$ by directed paths (internally disjoint, with new internal vertices). For a digraph parameter $\gamma$, a digraph $F$ is $\gamma$-maderian if there is a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\gamma(D)\ge\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ contains a subdivision of $F$. Here $\delta^+(D)$ and $\delta^-(D)$ are the minimum out- and in-degree and $\delta^0(D)=\min\{\delta^+(D),\delta^-(D)\}$; every $\delta^+$-maderian digraph is $\delta^0$-maderian. This is motivated by Mader's theorem that graphs of large minimum degree contain a subdivision of $K_k$, whose naive directed analogue fails. The dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}(D)$ is the least $k$ such that $V(D)$ can be partitioned into $k$ sets each inducing an acyclic subdigraph, and $\vec{K}_n$ is the complete digraph on $n$ vertices (all $n(n-1)$ arcs). The authors prove that every digraph is $\vec{\chi}$-maderian; more precisely, if $F$ has $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs and $c$ connected components then $\mathrm{mader}_{\vec{\chi}}(F)\le4^{m-n+c}(n-1)+1$, which gives $\mathrm{mader}_{\vec{\chi}}(\vec{K}_n)\le4^{n^2-2n+1}(n-1)+1$. Since every digraph of order $n$ is a subdigraph of $\vec{K}_n$, $\mathrm{mader}_{\vec{\chi}}(\vec{K}_n)$ bounds $\mathrm{mader}_{\vec{\chi}}(F)$ for all such $F$, which makes its exact value the natural question.
notes: PDF source — dichromatic number denoted $\vec{\chi}$; upper bound exponent reconstructed from context as $n^2-2n+1 = n(n-1)-n+1$ for $\vec{K}_n$ with $n(n-1)$ arcs and 1 component.

name: AX_digraph_subdivision_strong_connectivity_maderian
title: Problem 16
statement_text: Are all digraphs $\kappa$-maderian? $\kappa'$-maderian?
context_text: A subdivision of a digraph $F$ is obtained by replacing arcs of $F$ by directed paths (internally disjoint, with new internal vertices). For a digraph parameter $\gamma$, a digraph $F$ is $\gamma$-maderian if there is a least integer $\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ such that every digraph $D$ with $\gamma(D)\ge\mathrm{mader}_\gamma(F)$ contains a subdivision of $F$. Here $\delta^+(D)$ and $\delta^-(D)$ are the minimum out- and in-degree and $\delta^0(D)=\min\{\delta^+(D),\delta^-(D)\}$; every $\delta^+$-maderian digraph is $\delta^0$-maderian. This is motivated by Mader's theorem that graphs of large minimum degree contain a subdivision of $K_k$, whose naive directed analogue fails. Here $\kappa(D)$ is the strong connectivity of $D$ (the least number of vertices whose removal leaves a digraph that is not strongly connected) and $\kappa'(D)$ its strong arc-connectivity (the analogue for arcs). Since $k$-connected and $k$-edge-connected graphs have minimum degree at least $k$, Mader's theorem implies that graphs with large connectivity or edge-connectivity contain a subdivision of $K_k$; the question asks for the directed analogue. A conjecture of Thomassen would imply that all digraphs are $\kappa$-maderian: there is $f_1(k)$ such that if $\kappa(D)\ge f_1(k)$ then for any distinct vertices $x_1,\dots,x_k,y_1,\dots,y_k$ there are disjoint directed paths $P_1,\dots,P_k$ with $P_i$ from $x_i$ to $y_i$ (it would also imply Lovász's conjecture that highly strongly connected digraphs contain an even directed cycle).

name: AX_tree_pathwidth_path_partition_height_2k
title: Optimality of factor 2 in Lemma 4
statement_text: Every tree of pathwidth $k$ has a path-partition of height at most $2k$. We do not know whether the factor $2$ is unavoidable in this bound.
context_text: A path-partition of a tree $T$ is a pair $(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{P})$ where $\mathcal{T}$ is a rooted tree and $\mathcal{P}=\{P_x:x\in V(\mathcal{T})\}$ is a collection of vertex-disjoint paths of $T$ partitioning $V(T)$, such that $xy\in E(\mathcal{T})$ if and only if $T$ has an edge between a vertex of $P_x$ and a vertex of $P_y$ (so $\mathcal{T}$ is a minor of $T$). Its height is the height of $\mathcal{T}$, i.e. the maximum number of edges on a path from the root to a leaf. The authors prove the $2k$ bound by induction on the pathwidth, made no effort to optimise it, and leave open whether the factor $2$ can be reduced. The lemma is the key structural tool in their proof that the Thue choice number of a tree is bounded by a function of its pathwidth; the Thue choice number is the least $\ell$ such that for every assignment of lists of size $\ell$ there is a nonrepetitive colouring from the lists, where nonrepetitive means that no path has a colour sequence of the form $x_1\dots x_nx_1\dots x_n$. By contrast, they show it is unbounded for graphs of pathwidth $2$.
notes: Stated as 'we do not know whether the factor 2 is unavoidable' in prose immediately following the proof of Lemma 4; no labelled environment.
paper_title: Pathwidth and nonrepetitive list coloring

name: AX_triangular_lattice_5_colorings_kempe_class
title: Open case: WSK algorithm on the triangular lattice for q=5
statement_text: Determine whether the Wang-Swendsen-Koteck\'{y} algorithm for $q = 5$ colourings of the triangular lattice (with periodic boundary conditions) is valid (i.e., whether the set of $5$-colourings of the triangular lattice is a Kempe class).
context_text: For a proper colouring $\alpha$ and colours $a,b$, a Kempe chain is a connected component of the subgraph induced by the vertices coloured $a$ or $b$; a Kempe change swaps $a$ and $b$ on one Kempe chain. Two colourings are Kempe equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a sequence of Kempe changes, and a set of mutually Kempe equivalent colourings is a Kempe class. A triangular lattice with periodic boundary conditions is obtained from a toroidal grid (Cartesian product of two cycles) by adding one diagonal edge in each face, all diagonals parallel; it is a 6-regular triangulation of the torus. The Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký (WSK) algorithm is a Markov chain Monte Carlo cluster dynamics for the antiferromagnetic $q$-state Potts model; at zero temperature the configurations are the proper $q$-colourings, and the algorithm is valid (ergodic) exactly when the set of all $q$-colourings is a Kempe class. The paper proves Mohar's conjecture for $k\ge4$: every connected non-complete $k$-regular graph has all its $k$-colourings in one Kempe class (for $k=3$ the triangular prism is the only exception). Hence WSK is valid on the triangular lattice for $q=6$, and for $q\ge7$ because all $k$-colourings of a $d$-degenerate graph form a Kempe class when $k\ge d+1$; Mohar and Salas showed it is not valid for $q\le4$. Similarly WSK is valid on the Kagomé lattice iff $q\ge4$. This leaves $q=5$ on the triangular lattice, where neither argument applies (5 colours are fewer than the degree 6).
notes: Stated as an observation ('We observe that this leaves the single open case of a triangular lattice with q = 5') rather than in a formal labelled environment.
paper_title: On a conjecture of Mohar concerning Kempe equivalence of regular graphs

name: AX_gallai_path_decomposition_odd_semi_cliques
title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Does every connected graph $G$ that is not an odd semi-clique admit a path decomposition into $\lfloor \frac{|V(G)|}{2} \rfloor$ paths?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A path decomposition of $G$ is a collection of paths of $G$ such that each edge belongs to exactly one of them. Gallai's conjecture states that every connected graph on $n$ vertices can be decomposed into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ paths; it is sharp when all degrees are odd, holds (by Lovász's path-and-cycle decomposition theorem) for graphs with at most one vertex of even degree, and the authors confirm it for graphs of maximum degree at most five. Because the ceiling causes technical complications, the authors propose a stronger, ceiling-free version with explicit exceptions. An odd semi-clique is a graph obtained from a clique on $2k+1$ vertices by deleting at most $k-1$ edges; such a graph has at least $\binom{2k+1}{2}-(k-1)=2k^2+1$ edges while $k$ paths on $2k+1$ vertices have at most $2k^2$ edges, so it cannot be decomposed into $k=\lfloor|V(G)|/2\rfloor$ paths. The question asks whether these are the only obstructions.
paper_title: Gallai's path decomposition conjecture for graphs of small maximum degree

name: AX_subcubic_tsp_walk_5_4_n
title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: Every 2-connected subcubic $n$-vertex graph with $n_2$ vertices of degree two has a TSP walk of length at most $\frac{5}{4}n + \frac{1}{4}n_2 - 1$.
context_text: Graphs are simple (no parallel edges). A graph is subcubic if all its vertices have degree at most three. A TSP walk of a graph is a closed walk visiting every vertex at least once (graphic TSP: all edges have unit weight), and its length is its number of edges, counted with multiplicity; $n$ is the number of vertices and $n_2$ the number of vertices of degree two. The authors prove (with a polynomial-time algorithm) that every 2-connected subcubic $n$-vertex graph with $n_2$ vertices of degree two has a TSP walk of length at most $\frac{9}{7}n+\frac{2}{7}n_2-1$. They construct a 2-connected cubic $n$-vertex graph with no TSP walk shorter than $\frac{5}{4}n-2$ (found independently by Mazák and Lukot'ka) and a 2-connected subcubic $n$-vertex graph with $n_2=\Theta(n)$ degree-two vertices and no TSP walk shorter than $\frac{5}{4}n+\frac{1}{4}n_2-1$, and believe these constructions are tight, whence the conjecture. They stress that simplicity matters: allowing parallel edges, there are cubic multigraphs on $n=6\ell+2$ vertices with no TSP walk shorter than $8\ell+2\approx\frac{4}{3}n$.
notes: PDF source — 'n2' in the extracted text consistently denotes $n_2$, the number of degree-two vertices, as defined throughout the paper. The phrase 'with n2 vertices of degree' in the raw extraction is a truncation of 'degree two'. The conjecture is explicitly marked as a labelled environment.
paper_title: Graphic TSP in cubic graphs

name: AX_cone_crossing_number_minimum_function
title: Problem 1
statement_text: For each $k \geq 0$, find the smallest integer $f(k)$ for which there is a graph $G$ with crossing number at least $k$ and its cone has $\operatorname{cr}(CG) = f(k)$.
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops (simple graphs have no multiple edges); $\operatorname{cr}(G)$ is the crossing number. The cone $CG$ of a graph $G$ is obtained from $G$ by adding a new vertex (the apex) adjacent to every vertex of $G$. Richter asked whether $\operatorname{cr}(G)\ge\operatorname{cr}(K_n)$ implies $\operatorname{cr}(CG)\ge\operatorname{cr}(K_{n+1})$ for $n\ge5$; this holds for $n=5$ but fails for $n=6$: the authors exhibit a graph with crossing number 3 whose cone has crossing number at most 6, less than $\operatorname{cr}(K_7)=9$. This motivates asking for the minimum possible crossing number of a cone over all graphs of a given crossing number; equivalently, $f(k)$ is the largest integer such that every graph with $\operatorname{cr}(G)\ge k$ satisfies $\operatorname{cr}(CG)\ge f(k)$. The paper proves $f(k)=k+\Theta(\sqrt{k})$ when multiple edges are allowed. For simple graphs the analogous function $f_s(k)$ satisfies $f_s(1)=3$, $f_s(2)=5$, $f_s(3)=6$, $f_s(4)=8$, $f_s(5)=10$ and $f_s(k)=k+o(k)$.
paper_title: The crossing number of the cone of a graph

name: AX_cone_crossing_number_2_page_redrawing
title: Problem 4
statement_text: Given a 1-page drawing of a graph $G$ with $k$ crossings, find an upper bound on the number of crossings of an optimal 2-page drawing of $G$ while having the order of vertices of $G$ on the spine unchanged.
context_text: For $k\ge1$, a $k$-page book consists of $k$ half-planes sharing their boundary line (the spine); a $k$-page drawing places the vertices on the spine and draws each edge inside one page. A 1-page drawing is equivalent to a drawing in which all vertices lie on the outer face. An optimal 2-page drawing here means one minimizing the number of crossings among 2-page drawings with the same cyclic order of the vertices on the spine. Equivalently: if $G$ is drawn in the plane with all vertices on the outer face and $k$ crossings, what is the most efficient way to redraw some edges in the outer face to reduce crossings? The circle graph $C_D$ of a 1-page drawing $D$ has the edges of $G$ as vertices, two being adjacent if they cross in $D$; choosing a 2-page drawing amounts to a bipartition of $V(C_D)$, so minimizing crossings is a max-cut problem on $C_D$. Using Edwards' max-cut bound, the authors show that some edges can be moved to a second page to obtain at most $\frac{1}{2}k-\sqrt{\frac{1}{8}k+\frac{1}{64}}+\frac{1}{8}$ crossings, which is a partial answer. The question is closely related to the crossing number of the cone of $G$ (the graph obtained by adding a vertex adjacent to all vertices), since the face containing the apex in a drawing of the cone yields 1-page drawings. A related notion is Kainen's outerplanar crossing number.
paper_title: The crossing number of the cone of a graph

name: AX_cone_crossing_number_simple_graphs_asymptotics
title: Conjecture on $f_s(k)$ asymptotics
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops (simple graphs have no multiple edges); $\operatorname{cr}(G)$ is the crossing number. The cone $CG$ of a graph $G$ is obtained from $G$ by adding a new vertex (the apex) adjacent to every vertex of $G$. $f_s(k)$ is the smallest integer for which there is a simple graph $G$ with $\operatorname{cr}(G)\ge k$ and $\operatorname{cr}(CG)=f_s(k)$; the authors write $\phi_s(k)=f_s(k)-k$, so the conjecture states $\phi_s(k)=\sqrt{2}\,k^{3/4}(1+o(1))$. The small values $f_s(1)=3$, $f_s(2)=5$, $f_s(3)=6$, $f_s(4)=8$, $f_s(5)=10$ might suggest $f_s(k)\ge 2k$, but the authors show $f_s(k)=k+o(k)$. In contrast, for multigraphs the corresponding function satisfies $f(k)=k+\Theta(\sqrt{k})$. As justification, they prove that if the Harary–Hill conjecture holds ($\operatorname{cr}(K_n)=\frac{1}{64}n(n-2)^2(n-4)$ for even $n$ and $\frac{1}{64}(n-1)^2(n-3)^2$ for odd $n$), then $\phi_s(k)\le\sqrt{2}\,k^{3/4}(1+o(1))$, using $G=K_{n-1}\cup K_{n_1}$ for suitable $n,n_1$; they conjecture this gives the precise asymptotics.
notes: Stated as an informal conjecture in running prose without a labelled theorem environment; PDF source — math notation ($\sqrt{2}\,k^{3/4}$) may be partially garbled.
paper_title: The crossing number of the cone of a graph

name: AX_properly_colored_kn_longest_rainbow_cycle
title: Open Problem: error term for longest rainbow cycle
statement_text: Determine the correct order of the error term in the maximum length of a rainbow cycle guaranteed in every properly edge-coloured $K_n$; currently the deficit is known to lie between $-1$ and $-O(n^{3/4})$.
context_text: An edge-colouring is proper if edges sharing a vertex get distinct colours, a subgraph is rainbow if all its edges have distinct colours, and the length of a path or cycle is its number of edges. Hahn conjectured that every $1$-factorization of $K_{2n}$ has a rainbow Hamilton path; this is false, as Maamoun and Meyniel found $1$-factorizations of $K_n$, $n=2^k$, without a rainbow Hamilton path, but slight weakenings are widely believed: Hahn and Thomassen suggested a rainbow Hamilton path when each colour has fewer than $n/2$ edges, Akbari, Etesami, Mahini and Mahmoody asked whether every $1$-factorization of $K_n$ has a rainbow cycle of length at least $n-2$, and Andersen conjectured that every properly edge-coloured $K_n$ has a rainbow path of length $n-2$. Previous bounds were rainbow paths of length $n/2-1$ (greedy), $(2n+1)/3$ for $1$-factorizations (Gyárfás–Mhalla) and $(3/4-o(1))n$ (Gebauer–Mousset, Chen–Li), and rainbow cycles of length $n/2-1$ and $(4/7-o(1))n$. The authors prove that for $n$ large every properly edge-coloured $K_n$ has a rainbow cycle of length at least $n-24n^{3/4}$ (the constant $24$ is not optimised), via a result on random subgraphs of properly coloured complete graphs. The open problem is to find the correct order of the deficit $n-L$, where $L$ is the guaranteed length, which they state is currently between $1$ and $O(n^{3/4})$.
notes: Stated in prose immediately after Theorem 1.2: 'leaving as an open problem to pin down the correct order of the error term (currently between −1 and −O(n^{3/4}))'.
paper_title: Random subgraphs of properly edge-coloured complete graphs and long rainbow cycles

name: AX_majority_coloring_digraphs_3_colors
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: Every digraph has a majority 3-colouring.
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). They conjecture that $3$ colours suffice, which would be best possible: in an odd directed cycle every out-degree is $1$, so a majority colouring is a proper colouring and needs $3$ colours, and circulant digraphs with $N^+(v_i)=\{v_{i+1},\dots,v_{i+k}\}$ for odd $k$ and prime $n\gg k$ show that large out-degree does not help. They prove the conjecture for digraphs of minimum out-degree greater than $72\log(3n)$, and for digraphs of minimum out-degree at least $1200$ and maximum in-degree at most $\exp(\delta/72)/12\delta$ ($\delta$ the minimum out-degree).
paper_title: Majority Colourings of Digraphs

name: AX_majority_coloring_digraphs_1_over_k
title: Conjecture 9
statement_text: For $k \geq 2$, every digraph has a vertex $(k+1)$-colouring such that for each vertex $v$, at most $\frac{1}{k}\deg^+(v)$ out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$.
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). The same proof generalises to give $k^2$ colours with at most $\frac1k\deg^+(v)$ same-coloured out-neighbours, and it is open whether $O(k)$ colours suffice. The case $k=2$ of the conjecture is the conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring. It would be best possible: the $k$-th power of a directed $n$-cycle (each vertex pointing to the next $k$ vertices) with $n\ge2k+3$ and $n\not\equiv0\pmod{k+1}$ has no $(k+1)$-colouring in which every vertex has fewer than one out-neighbour of its colour. For undirected graphs, Lovász proved that every graph has a $k$-colouring in which every vertex $v$ has at most $\frac1k\deg(v)$ neighbours of its colour.
notes: PDF source — '$k > 2$' in extracted text likely renders '$k \geq 2$'; LaTeX corrected to $k \geq 2$ for mathematical consistency with the stated generalisation of Conjecture 2.
paper_title: Majority Colourings of Digraphs

name: AX_majority_coloring_digraphs_beta_3_colors
title: Open Problem 1
statement_text: Is there a constant $\beta < 1$ for which every digraph has a 3-colouring such that for every vertex $v$, at most $\beta \deg^+(v)$ out-neighbours receive the same colour as $v$?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). The case $\beta=\frac12$ is the authors' conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring, which they prove under extra degree assumptions: minimum out-degree greater than $72\log(3n)$, or minimum out-degree $\delta\ge1200$ and maximum in-degree at most $\exp(\delta/72)/12\delta$. For Eulerian digraphs (in-degree equal to out-degree at every vertex), an argument of Lovász gives a 3-colouring in which each vertex $v$ has at most $\frac23\deg(v)$ in- or out-neighbours of its colour, proving a special case of this question.

title: Open Problem 2
statement_text: Does every tournament have a majority 3-colouring?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). Bogdanov's bound for tournaments (orientations of complete graphs) uses a bounded number of colours, but it is open whether $3$ colours always suffice; this is a special case of the authors' conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring.
paper_title: Majority Colourings of Digraphs

name: AX_majority_coloring_eulerian_digraphs_3_colors
title: Open Problem 3
statement_text: Does every Eulerian digraph have a majority 3-colouring?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). An Eulerian digraph is one in which every vertex $v$ has in-degree equal to its out-degree, say $\deg(v)$. By Lovász's result that every undirected graph has a $k$-colouring in which each vertex $v$ has at most $\frac1k\deg(v)$ neighbours of its colour, applied to the underlying graph with $k=4$, every Eulerian digraph has a majority 4-colouring, and an analogous argument gives a 3-colouring in which each vertex has at most $\frac23\deg(v)$ in- or out-neighbours of its colour. Whether a majority 3-colouring always exists is open.
paper_title: Majority Colourings of Digraphs

name: AX_majority_coloring_digraphs_2_colorable_recognition
title: Open Problem 5
statement_text: Is there a characterisation of digraphs that have a majority 2-colouring, or a polynomial-time algorithm to recognise such digraphs?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Not every digraph has a majority 2-colouring (an odd directed cycle does not), and majority 2-colourability is not closed under taking induced subdigraphs: the digraph with vertices $a,b,c,d$ and arcs $ab,bc,ca,cd$ has the majority 2-colouring giving colour $1$ to $a,c$ and colour $2$ to $b,d$, but its induced subdigraph on $\{a,b,c\}$ is a directed triangle, which has none. Every acyclic digraph has a majority 2-colouring (colour greedily in reverse topological order).

name: AX_majority_coloring_digraphs_choosability_constant
title: Open Problem 7
statement_text: A digraph $G$ is majority $c$-choosable if for every assignment of a set $L(v)$ of integers to each vertex $v\in V(G)$ with $|L(v)| \geq c$ for each vertex $v$, there is a majority colouring of $G$ with each vertex $v$ coloured from $L(v)$. Is every digraph majority $c$-choosable for some constant $c$?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. name: AX_majority_coloring_digraphs_fractional_weight
title: Open Problem 8
statement_text: Call a set $T$ of vertices of a digraph $G$ stable if for each vertex $v\in T$, at most half the out-neighbours of $v$ are also in $T$. Let $S(G)$ be the set of all stable sets of $G$ and $S(G,v)$ the stable sets containing $v$. A fractional majority colouring assigns each $T \in S(G)$ a weight $x_T \geq 0$ such that $\sum_{T \in S(G,v)} x_T \geq 1$ for each vertex $v$. What is the minimum $k$ such that every digraph $G$ has a fractional majority colouring with $\sum_{T \in S(G)} x_T \leq k$? Perhaps $k < 3$.
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). A majority colouring is exactly a partition of the vertex set into stable sets in the above sense (not the usual independent sets), so a fractional majority colouring is the natural LP relaxation, and the answer is at most $4$ by the authors' theorem. They also show that every digraph with minimum out-degree at least $22$ has a stable set with at least a third of the vertices, and that large minimum out-degree forces stable sets of nearly half the vertices. The guess $k<3$ would be a fractional analogue of the conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring.

name: AX_barat_thomassen_refined_max_degree_connectivity
title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: There is a function $f$ such that, for any fixed tree $T$ with maximum degree $\Delta_T$, every $f(\Delta_T)$-edge-connected graph with its number of edges divisible by $|E(T)|$ and minimum degree at least $f(|E(T)|)$ can be $T$-decomposed.
context_text: For graphs $G$ and $H$ with $|E(H)|$ dividing $|E(G)|$, $G$ is $H$-decomposable ($H$-decomposed) if $E(G)$ can be partitioned into sets $E_1,\dots,E_k$ each inducing an isomorphic copy of $H$. The Barát–Thomassen conjecture states that for every fixed tree $T$ there is $c_T$ such that every $c_T$-edge-connected graph with number of edges divisible by $|E(T)|$ has a $T$-decomposition; it was proved by the authors with Merker, but the essentially probabilistic proof gives a huge, far from optimal, edge-connectivity bound. The present conjecture is the authors' refinement, asserting that the edge-connectivity can be lowered to a constant depending only on the maximum degree $\Delta_T$ of $T$, provided this is offset by a large minimum degree. The authors prove it when $\Delta_T\le2$, i.e. for paths: for every $\ell\ge2$ there is $d_\ell$ such that every $24$-edge-connected graph with minimum degree at least $d_\ell$ decomposes into paths of length $\ell$ (edges) plus one additional path of length at most $\ell$, so $f(2)\le24$; they also show $f(2)\ge3$, since there are $2$-edge-connected graphs of arbitrarily large minimum degree with no decomposition into paths of length $9$. Status note (November 2026): Klimošová and Thomassé give a counterexample to this conjecture when the maximum degree of $T$ is $3$ ('Edge-decomposing graphs into coprime forests', arXiv 1803.03704, 2018).
notes: PDF source — math symbols rendered as unicode in extraction; LaTeX reconstructed from context.
paper_title: Edge-partitioning a graph into paths: beyond the Barát-Thomassen conjecture

name: AX_triangle_free_planar_fractional_chromatic_bound
title: Fractional Chromatic Number Bound for Planar Triangle-Free Graphs
statement_text: The fractional chromatic number of $n$-vertex planar triangle-free graphs might be bounded by $3 - 3/(n+1)$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. The fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$ is the minimum of $a/b$ over all positive integers $a\ge b$ such that each vertex can be assigned a $b$-element subset of $\{1,\dots,a\}$ with adjacent vertices receiving disjoint subsets; $\chi_f(G)\le\chi(G)$ and $\alpha(G)\ge|V(G)|/\chi_f(G)$. By Grötzsch's theorem planar triangle-free graphs are 3-colorable, so $\alpha(G)\ge n/3$; Steinberg and Tovey proved $\alpha(G)\ge(n+1)/3$ for every $n$-vertex planar triangle-free graph and described an infinite class of graphs attaining it, and the authors prove that every other $n$-vertex planar triangle-free graph has $\alpha(G)\ge(n+2)/3$. Since a graph with $\alpha=(n+1)/3$ has $\chi_f\ge n/\alpha=3-3/(n+1)$, these results indicate that $\chi_f(G)\le 3-3/(n+1)$ might hold for every $n$-vertex planar triangle-free graph $G$. Dvořák, Sereni and Volec proved this for planar triangle-free graphs of maximum degree at most 4; in general only the weaker bound $3-3/(3n+1)$ is known.
notes: Stated with hedged language ('might be bounded'); the paper presents it as a consequence suggested by its main results together with the known partial result for maximum degree at most 4.
paper_title: Triangle-free planar graphs with the smallest independence number

name: AX_chen_chvatal_lines_bridges_finite_exceptions
title: Conjecture 2.2
statement_text: There is a finite set of graphs $F_0$ such that every connected graph $G \notin F_0$ either has a pendant edge or satisfies $\ell(G) + \mathrm{br}(G) \geq |G|$.
context_text: Let $G$ be a connected graph. For vertices $a,b,c$ of $G$, write $[abc]$ when $d(a,b)+d(b,c)=d(a,c)$ (shortest-path distance), i.e. $b$ lies between $a$ and $c$. The line induced by two distinct vertices $a,b$ is $\overline{ab}=\{a,b\}\cup\{x: [abx]\text{ or }[axb]\text{ or }[xab]\}$; $\ell(G)$ is the number of distinct lines of $G$, a line is universal if it contains all vertices, $\mathrm{br}(G)$ is the number of bridges (edges whose deletion disconnects $G$), $|G|$ the number of vertices, and a pendant edge is an edge incident to a vertex of degree one. The Chen–Chvátal conjecture (a metric version of the De Bruijn–Erdős theorem) asserts that every metric space on $n\ge2$ points has at least $n$ distinct lines or a universal line; for graph metrics, every bridge $ab$ satisfies $\overline{ab}=V(G)$, so counting each bridge as a separate line, $\ell(G)+\mathrm{br}(G)\ge|G|$ is a strengthening of the conjecture. The authors prove $\ell(G)+\mathrm{br}(G)\ge|G|$ for every connected graph $G$ outside the six graphs $C_4$, $K_{2,3}$, $W_4$ and three other small graphs, in the class of graphs all of whose induced subgraphs are chordal, have a cut-vertex, or have a non-trivial module (this class contains chordal and distance-hereditary graphs). As observed by Yori Zwols, the inequality is false for infinitely many graphs: replacing a bridge of a counter-example by a path of arbitrary length gives another counter-example. In the three known minimal counter-examples containing a bridge, the bridge is a pendant edge, which motivates excluding graphs with a pendant edge; any such family $F_0$ must contain the known exceptions. The authors also propose the variant that $\ell(G)+\mathrm{ul}(G)\ge|G|$ for every connected graph $G$, where $\mathrm{ul}(G)$ is the number of pairs of vertices inducing a universal line.
notes: Source is PDF; statement is cleanly readable.
paper_title: A new class of graphs that satisfies the Chen-Chvátal Conjecture

name: AX_chen_chvatal_lines_bridges_path_elongation
title: Open question on counter-examples to ℓ(G)+br(G)≥|G|
statement_text: It remains unknown whether all counter-examples to $\ell(G) + \mathrm{br}(G) \geq |G|$ can be obtained from a finite set of graphs by replacing a bridge by a path of arbitrary length.
context_text: Let $G$ be a connected graph. For vertices $a,b,c$ of $G$, write $[abc]$ when $d(a,b)+d(b,c)=d(a,c)$ (shortest-path distance), i.e. $b$ lies between $a$ and $c$. The line induced by two distinct vertices $a,b$ is $\overline{ab}=\{a,b\}\cup\{x: [abx]\text{ or }[axb]\text{ or }[xab]\}$; $\ell(G)$ is the number of distinct lines of $G$, a line is universal if it contains all vertices, $\mathrm{br}(G)$ is the number of bridges (edges whose deletion disconnects $G$), $|G|$ the number of vertices, and a pendant edge is an edge incident to a vertex of degree one. The Chen–Chvátal conjecture (a metric version of the De Bruijn–Erdős theorem) asserts that every metric space on $n\ge2$ points has at least $n$ distinct lines or a universal line; for graph metrics, every bridge $ab$ satisfies $\overline{ab}=V(G)$, so counting each bridge as a separate line, $\ell(G)+\mathrm{br}(G)\ge|G|$ is a strengthening of the conjecture. name: AX_gyarfas_sumner_oriented_iff_forest
title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: $\mathrm{Forb}(H)$ is $\chi$-bounded if and only if $H$ is a forest.
context_text: Here graphs are undirected. For a graph $H$, $\mathrm{Forb}(H)$ is the class of graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$, and a class of graphs is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ such that $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture states that for every integer $k$ and tree $T$ there is $f(k,T)$ such that every graph with chromatic number at least $f(k,T)$ contains a clique of size $k$ or an induced copy of $T$, i.e. $\mathrm{Forb}(T)$ is $\chi$-bounded for every tree $T$. The authors note that an easy argument shows it is equivalent to the present statement. The 'only if' direction is known: by Erdős' theorem there are graphs of arbitrarily large girth and chromatic number, so $\mathrm{Forb}(H)$ is not $\chi$-bounded when $H$ contains a cycle. The conjecture is known for stars (Ramsey's theorem), paths (Gyárfás) and trees of radius two (Kierstead and Penrice), among others. The paper studies extensions to oriented graphs, where one forbids only some orientations of a tree.

paper_title: $χ$-bounded families of oriented graphs

name: AX_oriented_chi_bounded_forbidden_oriented_star
title: Conjecture 4
statement_text: For any oriented star $S$, $\mathrm{Forb}(S)$ is $\chi$-bounded.
context_text: Oriented graphs are digraphs with no loops and no digons (orientations of simple graphs); their chromatic number and clique number are those of the underlying graph. For a set $\mathcal{H}$ of oriented graphs, $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathcal{H})$ is the class of oriented graphs containing no member of $\mathcal{H}$ as an induced subdigraph, and a class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every member $G$. $\mathrm{Or}(H)$ denotes the set of orientations of $H$, so $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathrm{Or}(T))$ is just the class of (orientations of) $T$-free graphs. An oriented star is an orientation of $K_{1,n}$; $S_{k,\ell}$ denotes the oriented star on $k+\ell+1$ vertices whose centre has in-degree $k$ and out-degree $\ell$. This conjecture extends to oriented graphs the (known) undirected fact that $\mathrm{Forb}(K_{1,t})$ is $\chi$-bounded. By directional duality and monotonicity it suffices to prove it for $S_{k,k}$ for all $k$; the cases $k=0$ and $k=\ell=1$ were known. Equivalently, for every $p$, $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathrm{Or}(K_p)\cup\{S\})$ (no tournament on $p$ vertices and no induced $S$) has bounded chromatic number. The authors determine $\chi(\mathrm{Forb}(\vec{C}_3,TT_3,S))$ exactly, where $\vec{C}_3$ is the directed triangle and $TT_3$ the transitive tournament on three vertices; Kierstead and Rödl proved that $\mathrm{Forb}(\vec{C}_3,S)$ is $\chi$-bounded, and the authors prove that $\mathrm{Forb}(TT_3,S)$ has bounded chromatic number for every oriented star $S$. The next step would be $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathrm{Or}(K_4)\cup\{S\})$.

paper_title: $χ$-bounded families of oriented graphs

name: AX_oriented_chi_bounded_forbidden_p4_orientations
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a non-empty subset of $\mathrm{Or}(P_4)$. If $\mathcal{P} \neq \{P^+(3)\}$ and $\mathcal{P} \neq \{P^+(1,1,1)\}$, then $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathcal{P})$ is $\chi$-bounded.
context_text: Oriented graphs are digraphs with no loops and no digons (orientations of simple graphs); their chromatic number and clique number are those of the underlying graph. For a set $\mathcal{H}$ of oriented graphs, $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathcal{H})$ is the class of oriented graphs containing no member of $\mathcal{H}$ as an induced subdigraph, and a class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every member $G$. $\mathrm{Or}(H)$ denotes the set of orientations of $H$, so $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathrm{Or}(T))$ is just the class of (orientations of) $T$-free graphs. $P_4$ is the path on four vertices; it has four orientations up to isomorphism: $P^+(3)$ is the directed path $a\to b\to c\to d$, $P^+(2,1)$ is $a\to b\to c\leftarrow d$, $P^-(2,1)$ is $a\leftarrow b\leftarrow c\to d$, and $P^+(1,1,1)$ is $a\to b\leftarrow c\to d$. Since $P_4$-free graphs (cographs) are perfect, $\mathrm{Forb}(\mathrm{Or}(P_4))$ is $\chi$-bounded. Kierstead and Trotter showed that $\mathrm{Forb}(P^+(3))$ is not $\chi$-bounded, and orientations of shift graphs show that $\mathrm{Forb}(P^+(1,1,1))$ is not $\chi$-bounded. The conjecture asserts these are the only obstructions among non-empty sets of orientations of $P_4$. The authors prove it when $P^+(3)\in\mathcal{P}$: $\mathrm{Forb}(P^+(3),P^+(2,1))$, $\mathrm{Forb}(P^+(3),P^-(2,1))$ and $\mathrm{Forb}(P^+(3),P^+(1,1,1))$ are $\chi$-bounded. Known partial results for the remaining cases include that $\mathrm{Forb}(\vec{C}_3,P^+(2,1))$ is $\chi$-bounded (Kierstead and Rödl), and the authors show $\chi(\mathrm{Forb}(\vec{C}_3,TT_3,P^+(2,1)))=3$ and $\chi(\mathrm{Forb}(TT_3,P^+(2,1)))=4$.

name: AX_block_stable_random_graph_diameter_bound
title: Informal Conjecture (diameter bound improvement)
statement_text: The extra factor $\sqrt{\log n}$ (compared with the random tree $T_n$) in the diameter bound $5\sqrt{n \log n}$ for the block tree $BT(R_n)$ could be replaced by any function tending to $\infty$.
context_text: A block of a graph is a maximal 2-connected subgraph, or a bridge, or an isolated vertex. A class of graphs (closed under isomorphism) is block-stable if a graph belongs to it if and only if each of its blocks does (e.g. forests, any minor-closed class with 2-connected excluded minors, graphs whose blocks are triangles); more generally it is weakly block-stable if it is closed under replacing a graph by any graph with the same vertex set whose components have the same numbers of blocks of each isomorphism type. The block tree $BT(G)$ of a connected graph $G$ is the bipartite graph with a node $x_v$ for each vertex $v$ and a node $y_B$ for each block $B$, $x_v$ and $y_B$ being adjacent if and only if $v\in B$; the block forest $BF(G)$ is the disjoint union of the block trees of the components. $R_n$ is a uniformly random graph on vertex set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ from the class, and whp means with probability tending to $1$. The authors prove that for every weakly block-stable class, whp $BF(R_n)$ has diameter at most $5\sqrt{n\log n}$ (and in particular this holds for the block tree of a random connected graph from a block-stable class). A uniformly random labelled tree $T_n$ has diameter of order $\sqrt n$ with probability close to $1$, so the bound is off by a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$; the conjecture is presumably that, for any function $\omega(n)\to\infty$, the diameter should be whp at most $\omega(n)\sqrt n$.
notes: Stated in prose immediately before Theorem 1.2: 'We conjecture that the extra factor √log n (compared with the random tree Tn) could be replaced by any function tending to ∞.' No labelled conjecture environment.
paper_title: Random graphs from a block-stable class

name: AX_token_sliding_chordal_clique_tree_degree
title: Question 1
statement_text: For any integers $k$, $D$, for any chordal graph $G$ of clique-tree degree at most $D$, can the connectivity of $TS_k(G)$ be decided in polynomial time?
context_text: For a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, the $k$-token-sliding reconfiguration graph $TS_k(G)$ has the independent sets of size $k$ of $G$ as vertices, two independent sets $I,J$ being adjacent if $J\setminus I=\{u\}$, $I\setminus J=\{v\}$ and $uv$ is an edge of $G$ (a token is slid along an edge while the token set stays independent). A clique tree of a chordal graph $G$ is a tree whose nodes are the maximal cliques of $G$ such that, for every vertex $v$, the cliques containing $v$ induce a subtree (every chordal graph has one; interval graphs are exactly the chordal graphs admitting a clique tree that is a path). The clique-tree degree of a chordal graph $G$ is the smallest maximum degree of a clique tree of $G$. Deciding whether two independent sets are in the same component of $TS_k(G)$ is PSPACE-complete even for planar graphs (Hearn and Demaine), and Demaine et al. asked about interval and chordal graphs. The authors prove that the connectivity of $TS_k(G)$ (and whether two given independent sets are in the same component) can be decided in polynomial time for interval graphs, while deciding whether $TS_k(G)$ is connected is co-NP-hard, and co-W[2]-hard parameterized by $k$, for split graphs. In light of these two results they ask whether bounding the clique-tree degree restores tractability.
paper_title: Token Sliding on Chordal Graphs

name: AX_ordered_ramsey_matching_vs_triangle_order
title: Open problem: ordered Ramsey number of matchings vs triangles
statement_text: What is the correct order of magnitude of $r_<(M, K_3)$ for an ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices? In particular, does there exist an $\varepsilon>0$ such that any ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices satisfies $r_<(M,K_3)=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$? (The authors can only prove the trivial upper bound $r_<(M, K_3) \leq r_<(K_n, K_3) = O\!\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n}\right)$, while some ordered matchings $M$ on $n$ vertices have $r_<(M, K_3) \geq c\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{4/3}$.)
context_text: An ordered graph on $n$ vertices is a graph with vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; an ordered graph on $[N]$ contains an ordered graph $H$ on $[n]$ if there is an increasing map $\phi:[n]\to[N]$ sending edges of $H$ to edges. The ordered Ramsey number $r_<(H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on $[N]$ contains a monochromatic ordered copy of $H$, and $r_<(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every such colouring contains a red ordered copy of $G$ or a blue ordered copy of $H$; for complete graphs the order is irrelevant, so $r_<(K_n,K_3)=r(K_n,K_3)$. An ordered matching is a perfect matching on $[n]$ with this vertex order. Logs are base $2$. The trivial upper bound comes from $r(K_n,K_3)=\Theta(n^2/\log n)$ (Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi and Kim). The authors prove that there is $c>0$ such that for all even $n$ some ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices has $r_<(M,K_3)\ge c(n/\log n)^{4/3}$, a considerable improvement on the trivial linear lower bound. They are not sure where the truth lies, but expect the upper bound to be far from optimal, and pose as a problem whether $r_<(M,K_3)=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ and all ordered matchings $M$.

paper_title: Ordered Ramsey numbers

name: AX_ordered_ramsey_matching_exponent_gap
title: Open problem: true ordered Ramsey number of matchings
statement_text: Close the gap between the upper and lower bounds for ordered Ramsey numbers of matchings: there is $c>0$ such that for every even $n$ some ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices has $r_<(M) \geq n^{c\log n/\log\log n}$, while every ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices has $r_<(M) \leq n^{\lceil \log n \rceil}$.
context_text: An ordered graph on $n$ vertices is a graph with vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; an ordered graph on $[N]$ contains an ordered graph $H$ on $[n]$ if there is an increasing map $\phi:[n]\to[N]$ sending edges of $H$ to edges. The ordered Ramsey number $r_<(H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on $[N]$ contains a monochromatic ordered copy of $H$, and $r_<(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every such colouring contains a red ordered copy of $G$ or a blue ordered copy of $H$; for complete graphs the order is irrelevant, so $r_<(K_n,K_3)=r(K_n,K_3)$. An ordered matching is a perfect matching on $[n]$ with this vertex order. Logs are base $2$. The usual Ramsey number of a matching is linear, but the authors show that the ordered Ramsey number of a matching can be superpolynomial: the lower bound $n^{c\log n/\log\log n}$ holds for almost every ordering of a matching, and the simple upper bound $n^{\lceil\log n\rceil}$ (which in slightly weaker form also follows from work of Cibulka, Gao, Krčál, Valla and Valtr) almost matches it. More generally they prove $r_<(H)\le n^{cd\log n}$ for ordered graphs $H$ of degeneracy $d$. Related problems in the paper: for matchings of interval chromatic number $2$ (the vertex set splits into two intervals with all edges between them) one has $r_<(M)\le n^2$ and some have $r_<(M)=\Omega(n^2/(\log^2n\log\log n))$; for $q\ge3$ colours only $r_<(M;q)\le n^{(2\log n)^{q-1}}$ is known, and the authors ask for $n^{c_q\log n}$.

name: AX_social_graphs_contraction_clique_count_characterization
title: Characterization of Social Graphs
statement_text: Characterize social graphs, i.e., graphs $G$ such that contracting any edge of $G$ does not increase the number of cliques of $G$.
context_text: Here a clique is any set of pairwise adjacent vertices, of any size, and the number of cliques of $G$ counts all of them (with this count the complement of a matching with $x$ edges on $n$ vertices has $3^x2^{n-2x}$ cliques, so the empty set is counted). A social graph is a graph such that contracting any edge of it does not increase the number of cliques. The paper determines the maximum number of cliques in an $n$-vertex graph with no $K_t$-minor, namely $3^{2t/3+o(t)}n$, and more generally with no $H$-minor for a connected graph $H$. Social graphs arise in the proof: after a peeling process one is left with a very dense $H$-minor-free induced subgraph, and passing to a minor of it with the most cliques yields a social graph. The authors show that any very dense social graph is, apart from a small number of vertices, the complement of a (not necessarily perfect) matching: a social graph with maximum missing degree $\Delta$ (maximum degree of the complement) has at most $300\Delta^2$ bad vertices (vertices contained in less than a fraction $\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2}-0.001\approx0.29$ of the cliques), and all but at most $600\Delta^3$ vertices have degree at most one in the complement. They remark that a full characterization of social graphs appears to be a challenging problem.

name: AX_4_colorability_fixed_surface_polynomial_time
title: Open Problem: polynomial-time 4-colorability on fixed surfaces
statement_text: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for testing 4-colorability of graphs drawn in $\Sigma$ when $\Sigma$ is a fixed surface other than the sphere?
context_text: Here $\Sigma$ is a fixed surface (compact 2-manifold, orientable or not) and the input is a graph drawn (embedded) in $\Sigma$. A graph is $k$-critical if it is not $(k-1)$-colorable but every proper subgraph is. On the sphere every graph is 4-colorable by the Four-Color Theorem. By Euler's formula, large graphs on $\Sigma$ have a vertex of degree at most six, so only finitely many $k$-critical graphs embed in $\Sigma$ for $k\ge8$; Thomassen extended this to $k=6$, which gives a linear-time algorithm to test $5$-colorability of graphs drawn in $\Sigma$. This finiteness fails for $5$-critical graphs (a construction of Fisk), and testing $3$-colorability is NP-hard already for planar graphs. The authors note that whether $4$-colorability can be tested in polynomial time on a fixed surface other than the sphere is open, and that the techniques currently available do not give much hope for a positive resolution in the near future. The paper itself is the first in a series on testing $3$-colorability of triangle-free graphs on a fixed surface (for triangle-free graphs, $k$-colorability for $k\ge4$ is decidable in linear time by the same finiteness argument).

name: AX_szeged_wiener_difference_2_connected_2n
title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: Let $G$ be a 2-connected graph of order $n \geq 10$ not isomorphic to $K_n$, $K^2_n$, or $K^{n-2}_n$. Then $\eta(G) \geq 2n$.
context_text: Graphs are simple. The Wiener index is $W(G)=\sum_{\{a,b\}\subseteq V}d(a,b)$, the sum of distances over all pairs of vertices, and the Szeged index is $\mathrm{Sz}(G)=\sum_{ab\in E}n_{ab}(a)\,n_{ab}(b)$, where $n_{ab}(a)$ is the number of vertices strictly closer to $a$ than to $b$. Let $\eta(G)=\mathrm{Sz}(G)-W(G)$; it is non-negative for connected graphs, with equality exactly for block graphs. For $2\le t\le n-2$, $K_n^t$ is the graph obtained from $K_{n-1}$ by adding a new vertex adjacent to $t$ of the old vertices (it is $2$-connected and non-complete). The authors prove that every $2$-connected non-complete graph on $n$ vertices has $\eta(G)\ge2n-6$ (which implies the conjecture of Nadjafi-Arani, Khodashenas and Ashrafi that $\eta(G)\ge\sum_i(2n_i-6)$ over the non-complete blocks of orders $n_i$), and $\eta(G)\ge2n-5$ unless $G$ is $K_n^2$ or $K_n^{n-2}$. Since $\eta(K_n)=0$ and $\eta(K_n^2)=\eta(K_n^{n-2})=2n-6$, and a computer search found $2$-connected graphs with $\eta(G)<2n$ only on at most $9$ vertices (none on $10$ vertices), they conjecture this stronger bound.
paper_title: On the difference between the Szeged and Wiener index

name: AX_set_mapping_theorem_l_equals_1
title: Open Problem: Reducing l to 1 in the Set Mapping Theorem
statement_text: Determine whether $l$ can be decreased from $(k-1)!$ to $1$ for all $k$; that is, whether $p(m,k,1)=\Theta(m^{1/k})$.
context_text: Let $M$ be a set with $|M|=m$ and consider all set mappings $f:\binom{M}{k}\to\binom{M}{l}$ such that $X$ is disjoint from $f(X)$ for every $k$-subset $X$ of $M$. Let $p(m,k,l)$ be the maximum $p$ such that for every such mapping $f$ there is a subset $P\subset M$ with $|P|=p$ such that $f(X)$ and $P$ are disjoint for all $X\in\binom{P}{k}$ (i.e. $P$ is an independent set of the $(k+1)$-uniform hypergraph with edges $X\cup\{y\}$, $y\in f(X)$). Erdős and Hajnal (1958) proved $cm^{1/(k+1)}\le p(m,k,l)\le c'(m\log m)^{1/k}$ with $c,c'$ depending only on $k$ and $l$, and asked for a more exact dependence on $m$; Spencer's hypergraph Turán bound gives $p(m,k,l)\ge cm^{1/k}$. The authors solve the Erdős–Hajnal problem when $l$ is large in terms of $k$, proving $p(m,k,(k-1)!)=\Theta(m^{1/k})$, where the implied constants depend only on $k$. Since $(k-1)!=1$ when $k=2$, this is best possible for $k=2$ (a case solved independently earlier by Füredi). The authors remark that it would be very interesting to determine whether $l$ can be decreased to $1$ for all $k$; as $p$ is non-increasing in $l$, what is missing is the upper bound $p(m,k,1)=O(m^{1/k})$.

name: AX_normal_graphs_cover_sizes_max_order
title: Problem 1
statement_text: How large can a $(c, s)$-normal graph be?
context_text: A graph $G$ is normal if it admits a set $\mathcal{C}$ of cliques covering $V(G)$ and a set $\mathcal{S}$ of stable sets covering $V(G)$ such that every clique of $\mathcal{C}$ and every stable set of $\mathcal{S}$ have a vertex in common; $(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{S})$ is a normal cover. A graph is normal iff its complement is. Every perfect graph is normal, as is every odd cycle of length at least 9, and De Simone and Körner's conjecture that graphs with no induced $C_5$, $C_7$ or $\overline{C_7}$ are normal has been disproved. Normal graphs are closely related to graph entropy in information theory. A normal cover is $(c,s)$-normal if all its cliques have size at most $c$ and all its stable sets size at most $s$, and a graph is $(c,s)$-normal if it admits such a cover; $N(c,s)$ is the maximum number of vertices of a $(c,s)$-normal graph. The authors prove $N(c,s)\le2^{c+s}$ by a linear-algebra argument, and $N(c,c)\ge\sqrt5^{\,c}$ for $c\ge6$ (also $N(4,4)\ge25$, $N(5,5)\ge55$) by an explicit construction, so the truth is exponential, unlike the bound near $c\cdot s$ one might expect by analogy with perfect graphs. They determine $N(1,m)=m$ and the extremal graphs when $c\le2$ or $s\le2$, and prove $N(3,s)=\Theta(s^3)$. As with Ramsey numbers, the bases of the exponential upper and lower bounds differ and the exact values seem out of reach even for small $c,s$; the authors describe their results as far from conclusive. They also ask whether $N(c,s)$ is bounded by a polynomial in $s$ for every fixed $c$.
paper_title: Minimal normal graph covers

name: AX_normal_graphs_random_gnp_whp
title: Open Question (normality of random graphs)
statement_text: Are random graphs $G(n,p)$ normal with high probability?
context_text: A graph $G$ is normal if it admits a set $\mathcal{C}$ of cliques covering $V(G)$ and a set $\mathcal{S}$ of stable sets covering $V(G)$ such that every clique of $\mathcal{C}$ and every stable set of $\mathcal{S}$ have a vertex in common; $(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{S})$ is a normal cover. A graph is normal iff its complement is. Every perfect graph is normal, as is every odd cycle of length at least 9, and De Simone and Körner's conjecture that graphs with no induced $C_5$, $C_7$ or $\overline{C_7}$ are normal has been disproved. Normal graphs are closely related to graph entropy in information theory. $G(n,p)$ is the Erdős–Rényi random graph, and the question asks whether $\Pr(G(n,p)\text{ is normal})\to1$ as $n\to\infty$. Partial motivation for the paper came from this question, which the authors state is still unresolved. Every normal cover of an $n$-vertex graph contains a clique or a stable set of size at least $\frac12\log_2 n$; random graphs have clique and independence number $\Theta(\log n)$. Using a random completion of their construction, the authors show that for all $n$ there are normal graphs on $n$ vertices with clique number and independence number of order $\Theta(\log n)$, comparable to random graphs.
